paragraphs.text:
THE AMPHILOCHIA OF PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE: SACRED DISCOURSES ON SACRED SAYINGS AND QUESTIONS. TO AMPHILOCHIUS, THE MOST HOLY METROPOLITAN, WHO IN THE TIME OF TRIALS ASKED FOR THE SOLUTION OF VARIOUS QUESTIONS AMOUNTING TO THREE HUNDRED IN NUMBER.

Your sincere zeal put me to shame, and so I have let your request come to completion, as I hoped it would. Yet there were many reasons, and strong ones, that held my mind back from it. The first is that very many of your difficulties have already been properly resolved by a good number of holy men before us. The second is that we ourselves have resolved not a few of them elsewhere. Besides this, working through so great a crowd of questions takes a long time, and the time is short, as the divine voice of the Herald says, and it is already late. For us the time is drawing in, as you see, not only by the common reckoning of human life but now also by our own particular circumstances. How could a multitude of questions totalling three hundred (for your

eagerness in these matters saw fit to stretch our present straits that far) fail to take up a great deal of time and [?] our leisure? And why were the questions put forward in a scattered way? When you could have heard them answered in person, with our own tongue clearing away the difficulty of some of them (for what [?] to keep in memory the things heard), you instead demand of us a second labour, and that the writing [be swelled] into bulk

[?] less than what has been said to hinder me, though it would have been enough for others as grounds for refusal. I will not, then, find fault with these things, except that so many and such weighty considerations pulled the other way. Nevertheless you have, as we said at the outset, what you asked for. The treatise is not adorned with polished diction; it clears up the meaning of the difficulties in whatever words come to hand, and in terms that are not [?] to the ears of the many. And may you prove not only good at seeking and receiving, but may I also see you all the more zealous in enjoying the gift.

QUESTION 1. The Amphilochia of Photius to Amphilochius the metropolitan [?] the questions of divine Scripture [?]. Of these, the first to be examined is that saying of the Lord: "[?] but now let whoever has a purse take it, and likewise a bag," and what follows.

1. Many difficulties need some groundwork laid beforehand, and their solution slips away if one comes at them without a preliminary statement. In the opinion and judgment of some, your shrewd question also calls for a discussion arranged in this way. So this must be said first and take first place in the instruction: not everything that presents an apparent conflict is in truth found to be in conflict. Many things often seem to contradict one another, yet do not. Conflict does not arise simply or at random, whether in words or in deeds; it is a concurrence of many circumstances that produces and constitutes it. Nor is this hard to see. For not only those who have chosen to study ancient philosophy and practise the art of the orators [?] "but these things," he says, "twenty less one" [?]

in these alone was a difference, suspected to be great and boundless, later freed of all difference once precise judgment was applied. Even in the ordinary usage of the many, many things, when simply heard, seem to conflict, yet once examined the conflict turns into agreement. Suppose, then, that someone distinguishes with impartial judgment between the apparent discord found in everyday speech and real conflict, and among those who lead the life of philosopher or orator also separates what truly conflicts from what merely seems to. If he does not keep the same rule when it comes to our sacred philosophy, but forces even a superficial contradiction into an irreconcilable one, such a man shows himself a slanderer and a bad judge, even with no one to accuse him.

2. To begin straight away with common custom: for most people killing is both a guardian of the state and a cause of defilement, and trade is both an ornament to a city and no less a disgrace. How are these not contrary? Because it is not lawful to kill a benefactor, or a citizen loyal to the city, or anyone who is innocent; but an enemy, a criminal or a traitor, or anyone else who deserves it, may justly be put to death. Again, when a man who violates another's marriage is caught in the act, the wronged party has the right to exact the penalty himself and stays free of defilement; [?] otherwise he must seek another judge for the charge. Again, those who belong to the humble ranks of the citizenry make the city grow by their trade, but those appointed as generals or popular leaders or the like, if they stoop to that occupation, disgrace the dignity of their office. There is no end of examples for anyone who wants to go through them. You see how many things give an appearance of opposition, yet on examination embrace agreement. So too we must look at our sacred Scripture, from which your problem is also a saying, and toward which, clearly, this whole discussion has been shaped.

3. Moses the lawgiver said, or rather the common Creator and Lawgiver said through him, "You shall not kill"; and again, "Each of you put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate through the camp, and each of you kill his brother, and each his neighbour, and each the one nearest him." How then do these utterances not decree each other's abolition? Clearly the meaning is this: you shall not kill the innocent; but the one who deserves death, who has outraged the laws of his fathers and attached the worship due to the Creator to idols, you shall punish with death. I think I will pass over "You shall not commit adultery" and "Take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry," for that has something deeper in it than the present question. All the same, here too circumstance makes the apparent conflict no conflict.

[It is no]t lawful to insult a prophet of God, whether by hand or by tongue or in any other way. As witness, there are the children who were playing and made a prophet their laughingstock, and paid for their jests with the destruction of their bodies. Yet you will find a man who paid the ultimate penalty because he did not strike a prophet in the face. And what makes the difficulty still greater, a wild beast mauled those who were carried away into insult, and another beast tore apart the man who shrank from following that example. What then? Are these not contrary? Not at all; far from it. It is not lawful at all to do so when stirred by one's own judgment and impulse; but when God commands and the sentence comes from above, not only does "It is not lawful" have no place, but justice pursues bitterly the one who neglected the command. Each of these examples from the sacred writings, then, clears away the seeming contradiction: the one from the circumstance of guilt and innocence, the other from the difference between the divine sentence and human impulse.

4. Many other things too that seem to conflict with others come into agreement once the circumstances are rightly distinguished. One thing comes about sometimes through place, another through time, and sometimes through person. Time involves no small number of differences, but person far more: ruler and ruled; the one introducing and the one being introduced; the one perfecting and the one being perfected; disciple and teacher; the guilty and the innocent. There is also a general division of person: its change and alteration. One kind results when the character changes while the person remains the same, and another when one person is substituted for another. For example, God made Saul king and then removed him from the kingship; and "Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown," yet the city remains beyond the appointed time, free of the calamity and untouched by it. Countless other cases, where the person is divided by a change of character, call the discord of our reasonings to resolution. That Aaron was not punished for making the calf, when the sword passed judgment on those who shared the same guilt, can also be put down to other causes, and the contradiction can be brought into consistency from that quarter. But the difference of persons also goes a long way toward dissolving the contradiction, especially since everything else in the case proceeds from it and turns on it. The variety of circumstances concerning person is great and frequent throughout divine Scripture, and many things that involve no conflict are put forward, through ignorance or malice in interpretation, as though they could find no way at all toward agreement.

5. It is from such ignorance or malice, then, that "Have neither belt nor sandals nor bag," and "But now let whoever has a purse take it, and likewise a bag," and "Whoever has none shall sell

[?] his garments and buy a sword," are put forward as contrary and in conflict. I will not yet speak of the other points, but only this: how did the arrangement of the sayings, one after another in a continuous sequence, not shame them into abandoning the assumption of conflict, and instead send them to inquire and track down the depth of the command? For at one and the same moment, with no forgetfulness intervening, no wavering of judgment, no compulsion at work, and no difference of hearers to account for it, how could the same person, knowingly stating contraries, legislate that they should choose what he had ordered them to flee? A well-disposed reader might perhaps take this as an occasion for contemplation. But the fact that he explicitly changes the time will also stand against those who twist things. For he says, "I sent you," and then, "But now I say to you." To fit one commandment to one time and another to another is not only nothing absurd; sometimes it is more fitting than if someone gave the same commands when the difference of the times necessarily demands otherwise.

6. With these points set out in this way, some who resolve the problem before us say that the common Master, in training his disciples at first and introducing them into the arena of poverty, did not let them drag along with them anything material that could drag them down to earth, not even the things that sustain this fleeting life as it hastens toward corruption. For care for necessities is often apt, especially in the less perfect, to draw in little by little an eagerness for superfluous things beyond need, and to do the soul great harm. For this reason, they say, the Saviour forbade his disciples, when they were only just being initiated, to drag along anything earthly or bodily. But later, when they had come through the contest unharmed and given all the proof that was needed of their contempt for the flesh, and when moreover the saving passion was now at hand, after which blizzards of many trials were let loose to surround the contestants and an unbearable storm of persecutions and afflictions awaited them, for these reasons he allows them to possess modest things, which hold life together so that it does not waste away. Since the passion of avarice had been overthrown from its very foundation in the character and ways of the apostles, and persecution was blowing fiercely and unbearably, they needed to carry some comfort as provision for a life assailed on every side. Neither commandment in any way damages the other. It is just as when someone leads a soldier home from the contests of war after his victories and trophies and gives him drink and all that peace has to offer; or when someone trains a boy who goes to school in one set of exercises, but drills the young man who is further advanced in deeper laws and loftier contemplations; or as a flock thrives under one set of customs and rules while the shepherd is not guided by the same path of life.

7. In this way, then, some bring into agreement the meanings in [these]

sayings. Others are no less fond of the rest of what has been proposed, but they say that when the disciples were first being introduced and still held the rank of those being perfected, it was necessary not to let their thoughts be divided over anything else, but to have their whole mind turned to learning and practising the things of salvation. This was all the more so because their Teacher was present and supplied on the spot not only what nature cannot provide, having no means to do so, but also hands that served uncultivated food to great multitudes. But when they had outgrown the schooling of the imperfect and come nearer to perfection, and he himself was now about to deprive them of his bodily presence through his voluntary and saving death, and to entrust them with the preaching and raise them to the privilege of teachers and shepherds, he then declares them free to carry the necessary provisions for life. This, having sprung from that beginning, bore fruit also in provision for those they taught, as one can see in the events themselves as they unfolded: for people brought the price of their houses and fields and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as anyone had need.

8. They also suggest that the following be considered carefully. The Creator and Sustainer of the universe himself, at the very time he was leading his disciples away from all attachment to material things and possessions, had a money-box and accepted those who put money into it. So it is not simply possessing, but clinging and being nailed to these things, that he forbids by this commandment. For he himself, as we said, had without having: it was for the sake of the needy, as a comfort to the destitute, and as a sort of averting and relief of necessity. Just as it is not contradictory that he carried a money-box while forbidding them altogether to carry anything, so it is not contradictory either that at first they ran up the rough and hard path of poverty, and later were relieved of many toils by a modest possession of necessities and had comfort in their extreme straits. Besides this, or rather before all that has been said, when you see, they say, that wealth is the prize of poverty, and pay closer attention, you will understand that the two do not cancel each other out, and that the commandment not to possess does not fight against the one permitting possession, provided that you clearly attach the former to possession held with passion, while your own possession is free of passion. For how could a mind free of avarice and an unsurpassed poverty have sprouted into something manifold and more wonderful, and borne the fruit of abundant plenty, if just possession and the principle of poverty were [?] at war with each other? And who is the witness? Who supports this argument? The common Saviour and Master of our race himself, who promised that those who left all they had for his sake would receive a hundredfold. Nor did he limit the prize to these things, but raised it to something still greater, and
greater beyond all telling, he exalts and sets it higher still: for [he promised] them the kingdom of heaven as their inheritance

9. Such, then, is what those who came after the first group say in showing that the sacred oracles agree with each other. Clearly each party was able to arrive at the solution of the difficulty by means of the circumstance of person. Other opinions, as far as we have gone through them, took their impulse from much the same starting points, close to those, but they keep to the same conclusions neither with the preceding ones nor with each other; for they too resolve the difficulty from the difference of persons. They say that the first commandment, which introduced the law of poverty, was truly spoken to the disciples and applies only to them and to those who keep the intensity of philosophy and the like unbroken throughout their lives. The second, they say, disturbs nothing of the law of poverty given to these athletes; it presents the person of the disciples, but refers to others. Up to this point the two opinions agree, but from here on they part ways. One takes as its subject all who are engaged in civic life and the mixed multitude, who cannot bear any higher philosophy, being hard to lead upward and hard to rein in. To these, it says, the commandment prescribes the management and possession of modest goods, and releases them from the legislation that sets the contest for the disciples. The other substitutes the Jews for the disciples and explains the words of the second commandment as a prophecy against the whole nation. This prophecy was fulfilled when Vespasian and Titus came to besiege the city of Jerusalem and, having subdued it by the law of war, made the Jewish nation the work of the sword. For then, precisely then, those whose possessions were furniture and whatever else was easy to carry took these with them and fled from their own metropolis to cities beyond Judea. But those who were otherwise weighed down by wealth, or tied down in some other way, were compelled to stay in the city and were driven to buy swords and knives and other armour of war, since the war forced them into action even against their will. And this, precisely this, is what the Master's mouth foretold: "But now let whoever has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has none shall sell his garments and buy a sword." And this, they say, was also foreshown by oracles from above, when God proclaimed beforehand: "Beat your plowshares into swords, and your sickles into spears." In this way, then, they say, having neither belt nor sandals nor bag in no way conflicts with "But now let whoever has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has none

[?]

10. Against those who resolve the difficulty in this way, however, the Master's own words may perhaps stand. "When I sent you," he says; and, "But now

[I say] to you": not to others, but to you yourselves, whom I also sent to preach. So here the change of persons finds no room to be accepted. Moreover, what sense, what coherence will "But now let whoever has a purse take it, and a bag" have with the commandment of poverty? How could someone without possessions have a purse? And what prophecy of the Jews' overthrow is described by taking a bag in addition to a purse? Yet such scrutiny, applied with impartial judgment, might also stand in the way of some of the interpretations given earlier and keep the solution from going undisputed. For granted that he first forbade the disciples to possess anything and later allowed it, how could "But now let whoever has a purse take it, and a bag" and "Whoever has none shall sell his garment and buy a sword" be brought into harmony with these commandments? Even if this is granted, those who received the first commandment are in no way found to have kept it, for then a purse would have had no place. And the second commandment brings in not so much permission to possess as a rebuke for not having kept the earlier one. Still, those holy men must be revered and honoured as divine for their first attempt and their devout intention. Those who came after them received from them the beginning of their resourcefulness, taking from them the seeds and firstfruits of more precise solutions. This makes them rather our fathers and shows us to be in their debt for our upbringing, because through their intense efforts and labours one can see that most of the sacred writings have been worked out to the highest degree, leaving no one any excuse for ignorance or dispute.

11. But someone with the Spirit as guide might perhaps say, so as to escape the objections just mentioned, that it has been rightly and justly said that many things in divine Scripture seem to conflict because of the ignorance or malice of those who approach the sayings. Some fail to see the circumstances by which the conflicts are resolved, while others reinforce the difficulty by evil scheming. Here, however, the circumstance of person contributes nothing much to the present inquiry; rather, a careful comparison of the sacred writings themselves, drawn from themselves, scatters the ignorance that clouds the purity of the meaning. Consider it with me, then, and follow the undertaking. First, the Master does not command the disciples to carry a purse; he allows those who have one to bring a bag as well. Where, then, is the discord here, and how could these conflict? He makes the disciples guardians of the law of poverty, makes allowance for those who had broken it, and [?] does not dissolve the command for those like them; for a rule of strictness does not suit a weak will. And he who gave those who had gone before the reproof of their negligence himself reins in [?] the lawgiver's provision for those to come. It is granted, then, as we said, to those who had acquired them, the purse and the

[?] Question [?] 62 … a bag. Or, if you prefer, he is foretelling the kind of life that lies ahead for those who had not kept the earlier commands. This could in no way be seen as contrary to the commandment through which those who were made perfect achieved complete poverty. You see how the solution comes cleanly out of the wording itself, with nothing laborious or contrived about it. "But now," he says, "whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag." 12. Two groups are now in view, as one can find with every other commandment as well: some fulfill it, while others transgress the precept. To those who have fulfilled it, the labor of greater things is entrusted. On those who have been negligent no further burden is laid; their past failure is even pardoned, so that they do not lose everything through despair. He granted the disciples to possess nothing, yet he left them lacking none of the necessities, small or great. They found no occasion or pretext for inventing a transgression, and they themselves bear witness that, while they kept the law, they were in want of nothing. "Did you lack anything?" he says, and they answer, "Nothing." The commandment had been given to all alike, and all alike had plenty for their needs. Yet some, who ought not to have carried one, had a purse, while others were faithful to the commandment. As for those who had disregarded the precept, he at once rebuked them, let them follow their own judgment without constraining them by force, and at the same time, if you like, foretold to them what their way of life would be: "Whoever has a purse," he says, "let him take it, and likewise a bag." For to the transgressor, by what he had already done in disregarding the commandment, he proclaimed beforehand what kind of disposition [?] he would show in the future concerning things of the same order. But to those who had embraced the precept with a pure heart, he approved the firmness of their resolve, granted them the crown of their achievements as the prize of a contest, and through what he now introduces raised them to the summit of philosophy. 13. Therefore he speaks to each group, his words dividing between them, as if to say: "But now, when my passion has come in earnest, and the war against you grows strong, and thoughts will be put to the proof in many, those by whom the word of the commandment was not kept, though it was not so hard, will be followed by the getting of a bag along with the purse. But those who have toiled to rise above disregarding it will also crown what they have already contended for with a fitting end." Those who have fallen short of the highest philosophy, and therefore of poverty too, will be taken up by the worries and cares of the many; for them, with the purse comes the bag as well, and everything that the encumbered life requires will not cease to be a burden. But to those who kept the contest with zeal and toil [?]: "Since," he says, "you have accomplished this rightly and carefully, and have laid the contest of poverty like an unbreakable foundation for the contests to come, it remains for you to be even more prepared and ready now than before for death on my behalf; for I too am already undergoing death on behalf of the world. You did well to lay aside beforehand everything belonging to this life. Nothing clings to you that could hold you back from

coming joyfully to the crown of all things, to being slaughtered for my sake. It will surely follow that you are eager to give up even your last garment, and to exchange life for death on my behalf." This is what not having a purse, the selling of the cloak, and the sword would signify, more aptly than anything else that has been said. It is as though the one who has completed the course of poverty will not spare even his last garment, but will give that up too as he goes cheerfully to the sword. That is why he does not say "let him sell" or "let him buy," but "he will sell" and "he will buy." He is not making his words into a law or a command, and at the same time he is foretelling the future, as if to say: "I do not command that this happen. Knowing what will happen, I foretell that keeping the commandment marks out for you in advance the last and great achievement. For being free of every worldly care, so as to turn toward nothing bodily and to devote everything to my service, will persuade you to choose death on my behalf gladly." What follows plainly shows that the word, in speaking of the swords that were the problem from the beginning, speaks in riddles for no other reason than that it has made them a symbol of his own passion and that of the disciples. For when the disciples replied that there were two swords, he did not ask anything further of them, such as selling a cloak, or ask those who had a purse whether they had taken a bag too, nor did he shift to some other meaning. He said, "It is enough," meaning: "What the symbols indicate has been sketched out, and they are sufficient to show the purpose." For the two swords sketch out the whole need and announce the intent of the symbol. One of them represented the Master's passion, and the other that of the genuine and true disciples of the Word, who exchanged everything for their love of the Master and gave up even their last garment besides. Stripped of earthly things, and even of nature itself, they ran rejoicing, when the time summoned the athletes, to be slaughtered for the one they longed for. 14. Such, then, is the present interpretation, which shows the harmony of the passages. It does not use the distinction of persons, since the wording of sacred Scripture did not allow it. Instead, it unfolds the symbolic meaning of the words from the events themselves and from the orderly progress of the narrative. It is possible, then, truly possible, to remove the appearance of conflict not only in the ways described but in many more besides. Setting these out systematically and summarizing them belongs to a separate subject, however, and not to the present one. Still, nothing prevents us from going through some of them, since they also give those who examine them with us a way through some of your other difficulties. For many things that do not conflict produce the illusion of contradiction when one statement speaks of the economy and another of what follows from nature, and you fail to distinguish them. Economy (10) might be said

properly to mean the awe-inspiring incarnation of the Word, which surpasses understanding. In another sense, it means the temporary withholding or suspension of stricter laws, or the introduction of more lenient ones in view of the weakness of those who receive them, when the lawgiver manages his precept by economy. From the first kind of economy other, different modes branch out, since the second kind is not indivisible either. For instance, the Savior was in agony and begged to be spared death, yet he also had authority to lay down his life and to take it up again. See how, if one does not assign the one to the economy and the other to the divine authority, he will entangle himself in contradictions. The term "economy" here derives, as has been said, from the sense that denotes the incarnation, which would properly and primarily be called economy because of its dignity and because it is the cause of what comes from it. Yet the term is not wholly bound up with that sense. For this too divides, for the moment, into two, and one part of it fits the meaning more closely and the other less closely. If someone wishes to take the agony and the plea against death as occurring because he became man, he will have here the sense of economy more closely bound to the term set first. But someone may suppose that he was in agony and begged to be spared death not simply because he became a man (for many martyrs and ascetics went to death willingly and with joy), but that the agony and the plea against death were arranged by economy to confirm the incarnation, and to refute in advance those who held that the awesome and wondrous incarnation was a mere appearance. Such a person has found the sense of economy that is less closely connected to be his helper in resolving the conflict. Either way, however, the appearance of conflict is driven off no less. 15. Among these there are also different meanings of economy, though they share the same origin. But for now, countless other things that are brought into difficulty are led to clarity by a solution that comes from discerning and distinguishing the term that properly signifies economy. And through this approach, no less than through any other, a resolution may be found for "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth?" and "I and the Father are one." To the unintelligent, or to those who handle them mischievously, the passages seem somehow to clash with one another. But the wise word of truth refers one of the sayings to the pure and blessed nature of the Godhead, and the other to the nature through which the Word took on our substance, and so thrusts away all dispute. Nor would anyone stray from what is reasonable if he resolved "My Father is greater than I" by the same inquiry. For even on its own this sacred passage requires intelligent hearers. It would need them even more when the saying already mentioned, which showed equality with the Father, is examined and compared with it. For even if by other

[?] considerations the apparent conflict in these sayings has been shown to be harmony (for example, that "greater" refers to the cause, while "one" indicates equality of nature), still the account of the economy, by taking "greater" upon itself, helps to establish, through "one," an equality of the Father with the Son that is free from attack. Nothing prevents those who uphold words on which strife has been imposed from clearing it away by different approaches. Indeed, the saying just mentioned, "My Father is greater than I," has been cleared of difficulty by other examinations of ours, which surpassed what the hearers expected, and it carried off a solution that is not, I think, open to fault. 16. Apart from what has been said, words maliciously forced into difficulty also convict those who attack them of slander when necessity and permission are taken into account. That is why the common Master, Fashioner and Savior of our race acquits David, who ate the loaves of the presentation, of breaking the laws. As the one who laid down the law, he knew the nature and force of the law and of those whose way of life it was laid down to regulate. He judges that the insolent, and those whose transgression comes from contempt, rightly undergo punishment, as he often does in other cases. But those who have affection and reverence for the laws, yet whose affection and reverence are loosened by necessity through weakness, he pardons for their feebleness and judges with a merciful heart. Just so he releases David from the charge of transgressing the laws. He does not accuse those who took the loaves of daring against the laws out of contempt; rather, the strength of their nature did not stretch as far as their resolve. Setting this down as their reason, the lover of mankind writes out their freedom. And many other difficulties are made easy by the same approach. 17. But why go through the other circumstances? The manner of reading by itself, when the sound of the voice is fitted properly to the meaning, walls off every approach of difficulty. When the voice suited to the meaning is taken away, however, what was clear sinks into what cannot be understood. "I chose you," says the Savior to the disciples, and "Did I not choose you?" If someone gives each of these sentences the same tone of voice, or conversely reads the first as a question and delivers the second as a statement, as the first was, he will make clear things obscure and make things that rise above all criticism open to blame. For he who chose them knew that he had chosen them, and he reminded the disciples of their election so that their long-standing debt of goodwill toward him

might not be swept away by the stream of forgetfulness, and so that they might be more obedient to his commands. Clearly, then, he is not denying or disowning what he did, but rather confirming it through the question itself: "Did I not choose you?" For Scripture is accustomed in many places to put as questions those benefits whose evidence is most conspicuous and which none of those who received the favor can deny. Under the same rule might come "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true," and "If I bear witness about myself, is my testimony not true?" For even if the apparent conflict here finds a solution through another examination, still no one would find fault, seeing [?] the justice of it, if one said that he is not declaring that his testimony is not true. Rather, through the question he is stripping bare and uncovering the purpose of apostasy and wickedness that lay deep-seated and coiled within the Jews. If someone reads the negations in the same form as the affirmations, however, he will truly fill himself with conflict and confusion, even though the marvel of the divine utterance is seen to be established above all plotting and contradiction. The Master's testimony would belong to the same kind of examination: "Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist," followed by "But the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he." For when "But the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he?" is read as a question [?], no room at all is found for quibbling, and indeed the clarity of the words at hand will need no further ingenuity. But this has received separate treatment elsewhere (15). Such too would be "Are you still sleeping (16) and taking your rest?" For he does not speak the words as a statement, but delivers his rebuke of their negligence as a question, and it is followed, consistently and fittingly, by "Rise, let us go from here." In no other way could the sequence of the words more readily allow a verdict that frees them from all conflict, unless "Sleep on now and take your rest" [receives] the interrogative [tone] through the

18. One of those accustomed to such audacity might act mischievously and weave his mischief out of a confusion of causes. Against "If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well," he might put forward the Master's reply to the one who struck him, "Why do you strike me?" as if it contradicted it (17). But to what is most evident [?] … epistle [?] 180 [?].

Photius [?] … once it is established that the cause is different, the refutation is quickly called for [?]. When someone suffers loss in money or other possessions, or even in his own body, the God of peace commands him not to strike back, but to leave vengeance to the judge of all. But when someone stretches out unjust hands, not to inflict harm on any of these things, but to outrage, by insulting the person, the piety that person professes (18), then we are commanded not to bear the insult indolently, nor by our silence to help the enemy heap abuse on what we worship. The divine Paul, as a genuine disciple of the Word, also fulfilled this commandment with wisdom. On one occasion he deprived Elymas the sorcerer (19), who was plotting against the preaching, of his sight, checking his audacity and exacting a penalty. On another he held the fear of Rome over the tribune, so that he would not, when it was easier to save himself, be found a betrayer of salvation who had yielded to the enemy of piety. On yet another he silenced with long refutations those who were contriving slander against the faith. For the same reason the divine choir of gloriously victorious martyrs spoke boldly to the tyrants with undaunted tongues and unabashed eyes, setting out the case for piety and refuting the blasphemy of impiety. When the tyrant maliciously conceals within himself the real reason for the martyrdom and tests the athlete with other abuses, as if with preliminary bouts, it is better to keep silent and bear the [?] gently. But when he drops the pretense and launches openly into his mockery of piety, then, yes then, it is noble and dear to God, and an imitation of the Master's own work, to answer back with words, and not to betray what is worshiped to mockery through silence. It is better to show oneself above every attempt to seize and entrap, partly by true words and partly by courage of soul. Does someone plot against your money or your fields, or raise an insulting hand against your body? It is fitting to bear it patiently, to soothe his inflamed anger with long-suffering, and to check his insatiable greed by making light of the loss. But when the enemy of piety drives out the workers of virtue and the heralds of piety as accursed and impious, and hands them over to evils, we will not bear the outrage in silence. Since we ourselves suffer unjustly for being pious, and the holy message of the preaching suffers unjustly, we will speak boldly with both mind and tongue. In the first case, silence is a picture of wonderful virtue; in the second, keeping silent rather encourages impiety to grow bold against the word.

19. Under the same pattern of distinction would come Ananias and Sapphira, who were punished by the chief of the apostles, and the commandment of seventy times seven, which sets the measure of forgiveness for those who sin. Through that commandment Peter himself, and we too, are taught to forgive many times the sins committed against ourselves. But we have no commandment to overlook an insult to God, and Peter did not overlook it: he exacted the ultimate penalty from those who had acted impiously, embezzled what had been offered, and lied to the Holy Spirit. Yes, and the companion of the chief apostle, who holds a privilege of rank no less than the other disciples (I mean Paul again, the teacher of the world): this divine man, when he says "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse," and again "Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm," would be cleared of the apparent contradiction. For calling down a penalty on the wrongdoer is prompted by the outrage and the war against the preaching, of which Alexander too was guilty. What has been commanded is to repay with blessings those who insult us for the persecution they devise against ourselves. 20. I am not unaware that some say the divine Paul's words about the coppersmith do not amount to a curse. They say these words are rather a prediction of the evils that would finally overtake him for his impiety and for breathing war against piety. In their view, the herald proclaims and sketches these things beforehand in words, both to draw the apostate away from such great madness and to offer consolation to his fellow contestants: the abuser will surely pay the penalty, and nothing he has done will escape the notice of Providence, from which nothing escapes. Through these words one can see Paul restoring those of the many who were faltering and bringing them back to courage. If I had never seen the saints show any indignation or rebuke against those who plot against doctrine, I myself would seek no other way out of the supposed conflict than the prediction. But there is the sorcerer Elymas, full of all deceit and full of villainy, denounced as a son of the devil and an enemy of all righteousness, who was bitterly deprived of his very sight. There is the whitewashed wall, whether or not he bore the mark of the high priesthood when the athlete was struck. And there are all the other things said a little earlier, and more besides, found everywhere in sacred Scripture. These very things clearly show me that taking refuge in prediction is neither generally applicable nor safe. 21. However, our concern now is not precise interpretation, but only examples of questions whose solution exercises the mind. For I also know another explanation of the passage before us, which sets aside both the curse and the prediction, [and has] nothing difficult or

[?] PHOTIUS, PATR[IARCH] [?] attributes [?] to Alexander. For he says that the Lord, who is the fount of love for humankind and of salvation, repays evildoers, not by taking vengeance on his own creature or punishing it, but by turning it away from wicked works and reshaping it toward the practice of better ones. What sort of curse would that be? What sort of prophecy crying out for penalties? Yet just as with the other interpretation, so with this one too the words that follow seem to me to conflict, for he adds: “Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our words.” But while these words perhaps stand in the way of the other readings, they agree better with those who take the passage as a curse.

22. Nor will Stephen, the first of the martyrs, oppose us at all, though he answered his murderers with blessings and not with curses; nor will the common Master before him, who sought to reconcile the Father to those who were crucifying him. The Saviour’s word holds something deeper and more mystical than the present inquiry. As for the gloriously victorious martyr, how could he fail to come over to our side without a struggle? Consider: he saw the Jews inflamed with rage against him, drunk with madness, and wholly plunged in murder. He himself was already standing at the gates of the martyr’s [?]. Their lust for blood walled off every opportunity for exhortation and left no room for rebuke, partly because he stood on a razor’s edge, and partly because neither rebuke nor exhortation is of any use to people so [?]. So the athlete seized the one thing that remained, the last remedy for his murderers: he asked the common Master not to hold this sin against them. And who is this man? The one who earlier had spent long admonition and teaching on them. But when he saw that they grew ever more disobedient to words of exhortation and were only provoked further toward impiety, then indeed, and with full justice, he subjected them to words that refuted and pilloried them, showing them to be, and calling them, uncircumcised in heart and stiff-necked (17), murderers and betrayers, bearing an inherited defilement as children of the prophet-killers. So not only is the man full of grace and wisdom and the Holy Spirit and power in no way our opponent; he is [?] rather our foremost ally and champion. And if the true disciple of the Master and first of the martyrs showed by his deeds that he followed the same view as ours, then clearly his teacher did too. Not to mention here: “You are of your father the devil” (18), or “An evil and adulterous generation,” and countless other charges to which the nation of the Jews is liable. That the giver of the crown both did and taught the same things, the crowned one showed brilliantly and beyond doubt by the genuineness of his preaching and by his [witness] through blood [?], even if, with prayer and pardon, after [?]

NOTES. (17) The codex reads “hard-hearted.” [?] (18) [?] “of the devil” [?] “of the father” [?]

every other method of providence and love for humankind had first been laid down, the Saviour of our race brought before the Father those who had inflicted death on him by the cross.

23. But these matters perhaps go beyond the present subject. Apart from what has already been set out, however, one could also confuse the intention of Scripture in many places because of the double meaning of a word. For instance: “Evils, and there are none that the Lord does not create”; and again: “He is the cause of no evil.” How could these be reconciled unless one recognizes [?] the double meaning of the word? Sins are properly called evils, and of these the Divine is not the cause. But things that grieve us and that we do not want are also called evils: disease and poverty and wounds, locust and grasshopper, blight and caterpillar, and hail, and all the other things that Providence is often said and believed to send upon the guilty, to check the impulses of offenders and cleanse them of their stains. It does not make human nature evil, nor reshape its handiwork for the worse—God forbid!—but rather leads it away from what makes it evil, and by treatment suited to the sick restores the ailing will to a better state. Of the same kind would be: “He handed them over to worship the host of heaven”; “And he handed them over to dishonourable passions”; and “He gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that should not see.” Here too, if the double meaning of the word is not distinguished, it twists the sense into absurdity. For how and when does God blind the eye of the soul? How does the one who destroys passions, impiety and error hand people over to them? But once the word is distinguished according to its meanings, the statement is freed of every sophistry. “Handed over” means “entrusted” and “sent on,” or “thrust” and “drove.” But it means no less, and above all in the intention of Scripture, “permitted,” “gave way,” “yielded,” “allowed to be carried along by their impulses,” “left the free will to its own mastery.” When “handed over” is taken in this sense, nothing absurd at all follows. For by a law of love for humankind and providence the Divine draws humanity away from passions and sins. But when, through an excess of wickedness, the one being restrained will not tolerate the benefaction and grace, and refuses to obey the one drawing it away, then indeed he gives way and lets the disobedient be carried along by its own momentum, and allows it to follow its own will. Otherwise, by restraining it further and reining it back from its inclination, he might seem to destroy its free will, and the ungrateful and thankless might turn his benefaction and providence into a charge against him.

24. It is in this sense that our holy Scriptures customarily use “gave,” “handed over” and the like, and, as is plain to all, this attaches no blame and gives no handle whatever against God’s love for humankind and his justice. Thus again he is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart: not that he found it yielding and obedient to his commands and then reshaped it to be hard and unbending

[?] 1:26. Rom. 11:8. Exod. 7:[?]

PHOTIUS [?]

and disobedient. Rather, he kept drawing him away and lifting him out of his disobedience and resistant frame of mind. But since he found the Egyptian in no way yielding or moving toward persuasion, but giving himself wholly to the opposing and hostile will, the one who never destroys free will let the man who refused to be persuaded by the better course be carried along by his own judgment. Nor would it be out of tune if someone took “hardened” here to mean that, through the signs he brought upon Pharaoh, God exposed a heart that was already hard and harsh, made a public show of its disobedience, and conspicuously pilloried the implacable and incurable character of his will, which was not yet so known and notorious to everyone. For the overwhelming greatness of the wonders, which surpasses all the laws of exhortation and persuasion and yet was defeated by Pharaoh’s will—how does it not demonstrate that his hardness of heart was unsurpassable and incurable? Thus “God gave,” “He handed them over to dishonourable passions,” and “He hardened Pharaoh’s heart” escape every assault and harshness of slander.

25. But why must I go through the other words with several meanings? Even the single syllable tis (“who,” “someone”), when it escapes the rules of distinction, brings no small confusion and disturbance to those who have no knowledge of these matters. It signifies the very thing now in hand, a question; and it is also spoken together with the negative that most opposes it, “no one” (19). At other times it signifies the indefinite. Nor does it refuse to express wonder and amazement; it also leans toward rarity, and sometimes again toward rebuke, or helplessness and perplexity. And since tis is familiar to philosophers as a specifier, it does not leave aside lowliness or other such senses either. The holy Scriptures are full of examples. If someone fails to distinguish them carefully and does not assign to each its proper sense of the word, there is no need to say how much error he will fill his reasoning with. This is quite plain from simply setting the passages side by side. For instance, “Who is this king of glory?” and “Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us?” and all such sayings signify a question (20) and raise no difficulty. But if someone, because the word is the same, should force into the same meaning “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” and “Who has given to him first, so that he will be repaid?” and “Who is the man who will live and not see death?”—if anyone forces these too into the same sense because of the same form of the word, he will stray far from the truth. For these carry the force of a negation and do not admit the role of a question. No one has known the mind of the Lord or become his counsellor; nor is there any man who will live and not see

death. Nor, again, does “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem [the codex reads Israel] to Jericho” agree with any of the senses mentioned, even though the form of the word does not differ. For here the word signifies the indefinite, set apart from the other senses, just as “There are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God” fulfils the function of specification. The mention of a single example is enough to show this use of the word and that it does not coincide with any of those listed before.

26. And what would the following have in common with the preceding, even if the sound of the word is identical: “Who told you that you were naked?” and “Who made you a ruler and judge over us?” and “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” and “Who struck down Abimelech son of Jerubbaal?” and “Who is this who hides counsel from me?” These look toward indignation and rebuke and present nothing like the senses shown before. If anyone should drag these too under the rule of the question—not to mention other consequences—he would accuse the Divine of ignorance, as though God were not finding fault with the deeds through these words, but out of ignorance seeking to learn who had given license to do them. Then again, “Who am I, my Lord, O Lord? And what is my father’s house?” displays a difference as evident as the word it uses is identical. It reveals an acknowledgment of one’s own lowliness and a disposition of thanksgiving toward God. It does not lead the mind to a question, still less to rebuke or indignation, or to any of the other senses mentioned.

27. Rarity, however, if anything at all, is signified by “Who is wise, and will keep these things?” and “Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” For even if not all, at least some have believed, and have been counted worthy to perceive God’s guarding, governing and all-ruling power from his benefaction and providence toward themselves and toward the universe, and to have their minds lit by the beams of the radiance that comes from there. And how does the one who says “Who is this who comes from Edom?” and “Who is this, that even the sea and the winds obey him?” not at once convey wonder and amazement—something none of the senses listed earlier could signify? To these one might add “Who will give water to my head?” and “Who would set me back to the months of former days?” and “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?”

[?] Job 29:2.

PHOTIUS, PA[TRIARCH]

These sayings will show a resort to prayer out of helplessness, and would fit none of the senses distinguished before. They depict a plea for release from what oppresses, not a question, nor specification, nor the indefinite, nor rebuke, nor rarity, nor thanksgiving or lowliness, nor wonder and amazement.

28. Look further, if you will, into this as well: “Who will deceive Ahab?” and “Whom shall I send?” and “Who will go to the people?” These give some impression that they could be referred to one of the senses already distinguished, but in truth they find no way in. They belong rather to a sense of challenge, or preserve the pattern of something else. And “What is my strength, that I endure? Or what is my time, that I bear up?”—how will it not call for yet another meaning, without which you will not discover its intent? The man worn down by misery wished to set forth the shortness, feebleness and brevity of life and strength, and by these words he unfolds both those things and the mind that laments over them and has given up. Again, “Who would know that I might find him?” and “Who knows whether he will turn?” are spoken in perplexity. Taken this way, they will not obscure the meaning or lead the hearer into any ambiguity. But if they are wrenched from this sense, they will fill him with as much perplexity as the correct sense was meant to give clarity. And whoever wishes to read through holy Scripture will find not only these but many other uses of this word that have been passed over here; it is no labour for him either to grasp them himself or to disclose them to others.

29. It is not only a single word, and a short one at that, used of many subjects but applied inappropriately, that clouds and disturbs the minds of those who think rightly. The change of a letter, or its addition or removal, even if not hard to correct, still commonly produces some absurdity. To leave other cases aside for now: in “The Lord possessed me as the beginning of his ways [the codex reads way] for his works,” suppose someone should write and understand ektēsen (“possessed”), which has the long vowel, with the short one (21), and then lean toward the opinion of Arius and sharpen his tongue against the divinity of the Son. This blasphemy is easy to strike down and refute in many ways. But no less, whoever points out and reveals [?] that the word is pronounced not with the letter iota but with eta will drive the babbling audacity of the heretical mind into the silence of shame. For the word written with the long vowel does not diminish the nature, nor contract it into something lesser, nor bring the uncreated essence down to a creature

—God forbid! Rather, it describes the appropriation, assumption and communion of the Father and the Son, who share one nature. For the Begetter is everywhere inseparably joined with his Offspring and does nothing cut off or divided from the Son’s counsel and will, whether in creation or in providence. Clearly, then, he would bring all things forth and deem them worthy of providence by appropriating and adopting the Son’s counsels. For where dignity, nature and authority are identical and shared, clearly creating and bringing forth are also undivided and inseparable and admit no difference of will. The present saying bears witness to this as well. Both for the coming into being of the universe and for the renewal and salvation of our race, which slipped and fell into ruin, it teaches that creation and providence are common to the Father and the Son. For the procession of all things from nothing, and the recovery and return to the better of our nature after it had declined to the worse, clearly belong to the creating and providential work of the Father and the Son and the Spirit. So, to take this as an example, the spelling with the short or the long vowel dispels the difficulty in this way. Likewise egennēsen (“begot”), if it suffers the loss of one nu, through malice or ignorance, introduces the existence of creatures; but when it receives back what was removed, it leads straight to what is of the same nature and consubstantial. And one could detect many other cases, both in secular writings and in our own holy oracles, that bear on the same consideration.

30. Not only does the addition or removal of a single letter bring about such overturning and alteration of many matters; an ill-timed use of accent (22), even when the spelling stays unchanged, has presented one word in place of another, and by displacing the mind into an utterly foreign meaning has produced either impious opinion or laughable nonsense. But why do I speak of letters? Even the shortest thing of all, the point of punctuation, when tampered with maliciously or overlooked and moved from its proper place, has given birth to great heresies of every kind. It has long held sway over the minds of the foolish, and has given the pious long contests before they could triumph over the doctrines of impiety. For instance—to pass over the rest—the man lifted on high, the teacher of the world, the great Apostle, says this in one of his letters (it is the Corinthians who receive the epistle): “In whom the God of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ should not shine on them.” He who said this initiates the perfected into a wonderful meaning, worthy of heavenly echoes, and into

PHOTIUS, AMPHILOCHIA [?]

his wisdom. But the impious followers of Mani and Marcion seized on the words and took them captive to their own purpose. Then, refusing to let the point stand between “God” and “of this age,” they reached such an extreme of impiety that they not only committed the worst blasphemies but even made the sacred words the cause of their war against God. They held that there is one God who is the source of the creation of invisible and intelligible things, and they proclaimed another, the God of the present age and of all that is of the same rank and order as it, to be the Creator. This deranged scheme regarding the text is shown elsewhere, from many sides, to be unsound. But it would be refuted no less by the fact that it did not let the point rest in its proper place. Besides, “the present age” sometimes means simply the extent of time, and sometimes the wicked deeds that tend to spring up in this present life. So even if one should grant them their tampering with the point, the text no less refutes their opinion and overthrows it. For since the author of evil is the sower and instigator of wicked works and deeds, if he should be called their lord, maker and god—the words being fitted especially to the opinion of those who serve his wickedness—the apostate scheme will gain nothing. After all, the idols of the nations were not what they were called, yet they were nonetheless called gods. He could never be said or thought to be god of any creation, or of things that have a stable and recognizable existence. But of lawless passions and of sin, in which he delights and revels, and to which he strives without ceasing to drag others by deceit, no one will strip him either of this destructive and wretched lordship or of his rule, so long as these things are at work.

31. I know that by this interpretation the holy text of Paul not only escapes the opinion of the apostates, but that even if one sets aside the argument about the point, it puts their rashness to shame no less. For just as our true God, the Creator of the universe and God of heaven and earth, may also be called the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of consolation and the God of peace, and is not for that reason anywhere not the God of things of the same rank and order—rather, from the things of which he is said to be God, the others are included too—so also when he is called the God of this age, the whole is understood and proclaimed together with the part: both what belongs to the intelligible realm and what belongs to the realm of sense. Moreover, if the text is read as a transposition of words, it easily escapes every handle the slanderers might seize. For God blinds the minds of the unbelievers of this age; that is, he judges them unworthy of the contemplation granted to the purified, through which they could have been lit by the illumination of the gospel. The unbelievers of the present age are allowed to rebel and contend against their own Master and Creator; but in the age to come, every knee will bow to him, of those in heaven

[?] of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess him, no darkness or mist of apostasy, contentiousness or ignorance will stand in the way of any of them and keep them from seeing his lordship and power over all things. 32. But, as was being said, the question of punctuation not only in the inspired words of Paul gives evil-doers occasions for error, while, when examined precisely, it overthrows the devices of deception; it also carries no small weight, one way or the other, in the very words of the Master and Lord. For the same lovers of apostasy do not wish to acknowledge that this beautiful and most marvellous masterpiece of the Master's creation, I mean this visible and lovely world, is the work of the Creator, and contentiously strive to trace it back to some other, absurd principle. So in the verse "All things were made through him, and without him was not anything made that was made" they do not care to end at a full stop; instead, joining "in him" to the preceding words, they let the phrase run on in this way to the stop. Why? So that, by saying only that the things "in him" came into being through him (whatever the vanity of their reasonings may fancy those to be), they may take away from him the bringing into being and creation of all the other things that have come to be. Do you see how a thing than which nothing smaller can be found, when it is not subjected to fitting judgment, becomes for the impious [?] a refuge for absurd and utterly ungodly notions? 33. I am not unaware that this very saying of the Master, word for word, has suffered other assaults for the same reason. For the common and unaffected reading of the truth places the stop after "All things were made through him, and without him was not one thing made that was made," as has been said already. Others, however, put the stop after "not one thing," and, beginning afresh, bring forward "What was made in him was life." They show no necessary sense, but they open a broad road for those who wish to dance in mockery over the mystical and awesome beauties of our sacred Oracles. For when one may be content with what is well known and has the finest interpretation, why overlook it and seek to pride oneself on readings that have nothing comparable to offer and only gratify a taste for novelty? I do not pass sentence on everyone, but on those whose opinion shows my words to be true. The leader on this road, as far as my memory has not failed me, is Origen, a man of great learning but no less of great error; and the imitation was taken up by the Spirit-fighter Macedonius [?], if not of his impiety (for Origen did not, at the same time as he moved the stop, teach impiety through the text), at least of his

[?] has the following: "It should be known that Apollinarius, Origen and Cyril [punctuated] according to the disputed [reading] [?]; but, passing over what was said by Apollinarius as being unintelligible, [we take] those of Cyril first [?]"

91 PHOTIUS [?] innovation regarding the stop and the reading. Having become a zealous follower of it, the Spirit-fighter makes this reading the instrument of his own impiety. For he combines the words "what was made in him," cutting the phrase off from its connection with what precedes and removing the stop that separates it from what follows, and boldly and fearlessly drags it against the Spirit (24). Because of the word "was made" he numbers the uncreated nature among the things that were made and that belong to the order of creatures, though neither does the sequence of the words tolerate such abuse, nor does any other reason lend support to his impiety. Apollinarius too took up the imitation of Origen in turn, but did not likewise imitate his thought. For Origen's view, even if it has something overly ingenious about it, at least drags no other absurdity along with it and is not wholly lacking in a certain elegance; whereas Apollinarius, besides saying nothing praiseworthy, turns their effort into long drivel and incoherent opinions, and by what he says very nearly illustrates the proverb about the bean and the salt (25). And if this placing of the stop also pleased the divine Cyril, still, as far as he stands apart from the opinion of the impious, so far does his unfolding of the text show itself [removed] from their purpose [?]

34. But that, instead of seeking, as one should not, to set the divine Oracles in collision with one another, it is better to raise difficulties in order to learn, and still more to train oneself in the inquiry and study of the so-called circumstances and of any other method similar to these—this, I well know, you yourself will need no words to grasp; but since I deem you worthy to become a teacher of others too, I would not despair of it. And the appearance of contradiction that seems to arise through the sacred Oracles is divided not only into these many modes, but of many others too I have not yet made mention [?] Some, then, have read it thus: "What was made in him," taking it to mean "through him." But how would it not have been foolish if the evangelist had meant to say this, as though teaching us something new and unknown to men, which any ordinary person could have said about any ordinary thing: "Without him not one of the things made through him was made"? For anyone at all would say this about anything whatever; since it is clear that about anything at all that is done, one could not say otherwise than that "of the things made through him, nothing was made without him." Others have read it differently: "And without him was not anything made." Then: "What was made in him was life"; for many things have no share in life, such as earth and mountains. There is thus a linking and confirmation of what precedes, and then also clarity. For having said, "All things were made through him," he added, "and without him was not one thing made that was made"; that is, to put it briefly, "None of the things that have come to be has come to be without him," only the Father being excepted from his making, together with the Holy Spirit; since, being always with them, he fittingly shared with them in the creation of all things [?]

[?] So, then, the training in the matters discussed does not confine its usefulness to them alone, but provides great strength and power for pursuing the truth methodically and discerning it, and so on. For whatever is contrived into an ambiguous and conflicting sense through the addition of sentences, words or names, or through their omission and curtailment, or through figurative turns and metaphor, these too the one who has trained himself in the approaches described above will, by applying the touchstone of precision here as well, sort out without difficulty, distinguishing what is confused and what is turned this way and that, toward the [?] discernment of the truth. For example, how did he not, starting from there, easily drive off the tribe of the Anthropomorphites to their refutation? For the one who took occasion to examine the differences in such matters, and saw that confusing them produces much error, at once recognized and distinguished that metaphorical expressions have one use and the proper sense of a word another. The heretical minds took none of this to heart. In whatever is said of God figuratively and by metaphor, they refused to see the difference between figurative and literal speech, and because they heard of hands and feet and eyes, of smelling, of a mouth and words, they impiously and senselessly fashioned the simple, incomprehensible and shapeless essence of God, the Divine, into a shape like our own. 35. In the same way, then, if a heretical or contentious mind should seize on anything else in the sacred Scriptures and strive to drag it toward impiety or perplexity: if it devises its mischief along one of the lines already sorted out, it will at once find an inescapable refutation bearing down on it; and if along one of those passed over, it is not difficult to extend the like judgment from the earlier cases to these as well, and to subject the imitators to the same refutations by which their predecessors were beaten down. And this, among other things, is what has [led] us not to go through all the causes in detail [?]; for we neither promised to compile an elementary treatise on them, nor is the study and discernment of those passed over hard to track down from what has been said. Moreover, the others do not, like these, float on the surface and spread among the many; and whatever difficulties you yourself have already raised, at least in the present and the previous request, have sufficiently received clarification and solution. 36. Unless, that is, someone should count this too among the prevalent ones (for it is a great refuge both for the other heretics and for the iconoclasts: the sacred word often casts a statement in universal form without requiring that a universal meaning be taken from it, but, confining the account to certain defined and previously understood things, indicates a particular statement). Such is the saying, "All who came before me are thieves and robbers." For the followers of Marcion and the neighbouring brotherhood bring Moses and the other prophets of God under the universal character of the expression, blaspheming the Old Testament as a contrivance [?] John 10:8.

37. Similar is the saying, "All things were made through him"; and it is likewise put forward as an instrument of error by the Spirit-fighters. For because of the universality of the expression they do not except the all-holy Spirit from "all things" that were made, and so they have blasphemed it too. And countless other things the sacred Oracles cast in universal form while making the meaning more particular; for example, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity"; for neither virtue, nor wisdom, nor piety is among vain things. And, "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless"; for this does not include those whom God displays in each and every generation as crowned victors over passions, demons and tyrants. And one could consider many other such things at leisure; but I think what has been set out is enough. For the madness of the iconoclasts, its folly shown in this mischief along with their other mind-destroying mischief, has been [?] specially exposed and led in triumph by us (26). But that many of the difficulties require prior [?], that your questions have been sorted out both by the holy men before us and by ourselves, led by the hand from that source, and that we have gone through most of the causes from which perplexity usually arises, the discourse has shown. We would not claim to have grasped everything with precision; but that we have contributed no less than was asked, no one, with truth as judge, would [accuse] us of boastful words [?]

QUESTION 2. If on the seventh day God rested from all his works, how does the saving Word of God [?] say, "My Father is working until now, and I am working"? We see four works of the Creator. The first of these is the original bringing- NOTES.

forth and creation of the things that exist; in this sense it is said, "And on the seventh day God rested"; for having completed the natures of all things and given them being in seven days, the Creator displayed no further production. The second is the continuance and preservation of things once established, at work from then until now, never allowing an entire species to perish and pass into non-being; such working and preservation is called the providence and care of God; and the true account knows no rest ever from this activity and work, so long as this earthly compound has its existence. We see further a third work of the Creator, by which each nature, doing what is proper to it, brings forth nothing unlike itself, but each, forming and shaping its offspring after what is proper and similar to it, displays an unadulterated succession; and this work too would be referred to the principle of providence and care. Of the three works mentioned, then, one has its aim in bringing into being, another in continuance, and another in likeness. To the same principle would also belong the unaltered and unmoving succession of the order of things that exist. The sun and the moon would never be caught changing their risings and settings, their conjunctions and separations, and the other activities which the creative Word implanted in them, nor destroying the orderly revolution of their course fixed for them from the beginning; nor would the rest of the chorus of stars be caught altering and breaking up the sequence of revolution and order, of appearing and hiding, given them from the beginning. Nights yielding to days, and days in turn giving way to nights, have preserved their orderly proportion unadulterated and unfalsified; likewise the natures of the seasons, handing on their successions to one another, have admitted no innovation, but have kept this ancient and wonderful change unchanged and immovable. And it is clear that this good order and proportion among things is held together and maintained by the principle of providence; and this too would be a work of God, who made all things in wisdom. Besides these there is yet another work, the Master's love for humankind, seen above all in the human race. It is twofold. One part concerns the body: through it maimings and countless other sufferings are driven away from his creature; these the Savior of our race did and worked when he came, freeing humanity in every way from sufferings and diseases. The other concerns the soul: for when it was buried under many sins and had become branded all over by the countless outrages of the evil one, our very Maker and Creator cleansed it and scraped it clean through his coming, which is beyond mind and reason, led it back to its ancient dignity, and, restoring once more what is according to the image, granted it strength and joy. This work, then, concerning the creature of his hands, gives sight [PATROL. GR. CI.]

to the blind, makes the paralytic firm, raises the four-days-dead from the tomb, and has displayed supernatural works beyond counting. When the Master was performing these according to the rule and law of his love for humankind, the ungrateful people of the Jews reproached the benefaction, putting forward the honour of the Sabbath as a pretext and cloak for their envy and wickedness; and they hear from the Master, speaking partly as Master and partly as teacher and Savior: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." In this way the Master silenced the ungrateful Jews, who disparaged and slandered the bodily healing because it took place on the Sabbath, and clearly taught us that neither has the Father ceased from these and similar works, nor does he himself leave off the work. From this declaration of the Master it is easy for you to grasp the meanings of "work" which the discourse distinguished a little earlier: from which works the Father and the Son rested, and which they do not cease working until now. For he rested long ago from creating natures; but in preserving created things from corruption, likewise in holding together by his providence the totalities of the things brought into being, unaltered and unadulterated, and in keeping unaltered the good order and sequence implanted in them, neither the Father nor the Son appears ever to have ceased—nor indeed the Holy Spirit; for the superessential, almighty and creative essence of all things has one and the same will, power and activity. And it is clear that at the time when our Savior was performing the divine signs, the Son was working, and the Father and the Holy Spirit were working together with him.

QUESTION 3. Why did the Master use clay, and not some other means, to heal the eyes? The Master [?] used clay and fashioned new eyes for the blind man in order to bring the minds of those who are perplexed about how the first man was formed from earth—since no one stood by as spectator or witness of that creation—to unambiguous faith. For the creation of the most precious of the members of the human body, set before the eyes of all, provides great strength and confirmation regarding the rest of the body too, whose forming no eye beheld, so that no one may doubt or be split into perplexed opinions. For when someone sees the best and most precious of our parts brought forth from clay in its forming and substance, how will he not, with incontrovertible reasoning, acknowledge that the rest of the instrument also came to be from the same matter and the same power? And besides, so that you may learn this clearly, that in all those respects in which the Father is known to be God—I mean in power, glory, essence and lordship—the Son too is understood to be equal and in no way different, he takes clay and no other matter and refashions the eyes of the blind man, just as the

Father long ago, together with him, created man from clay. And this too is shown along with it: that he who now went by the name of God in human form and changed clay into the nature of an eye was the very one who long ago joined in fashioning man from clay. QUESTION 4. What is meant by "Hating even the garment stained by the flesh"? We are taught by the divine Scripture that the wedding garment is the life of virtue and a way of living that is free from sins and pure. Those clothed in it are judged worthy of the mystical bridal chamber by Christ the Bridegroom himself, and recline at that blessed banquet of the Master; but those who soil such garments are driven away from this wonderful enjoyment and suffer bitter disgrace. If we have learned this, it will also be clear what is the garment called "stained" by the divine apostle, which he rightly and justly urges us to hate: the one spotted all over with sins and wholly filthy, this would be the stained garment. Revealing this more clearly, he speaks not simply of a stained garment, but of one stained and soiled by the flesh, and of all the things by which the flesh, desiring against the spirit, renders our life sullied and spotted; this he urges us to turn away from by every means, because it shuts the doors of the mystical bridal chamber against us, because it makes us unworthy of the fair Bridegroom, because it [keeps us] far from the awesome and saving banquet [?]

QUESTION 5. If everything subject to necessity does what force dictates even against its will, and it is necessary that offences come into the world, then it is not just to lay curses on the one who is forced, nor indeed to exact penalties for the sin. The construction of the argument has some plausibility, but impiety too is at the door; for it calls God to account for punishing what is forced and passing a bitter sentence on his own creature.
