For if it is necessary, it says, that offences come, our race too will of necessity be caught by the offences; and if I serve unwillingly, why does the judge pass over what forces me and lay curses on me, the one forced? "For woe to that man," it says, "through whom the offence comes." For he ought not to curse and trample on the one who has been wronged and become the prey of tyranny, but rather to count him worthy of kindness and compassion—not to mention that, before all this, he ought to have freed his own creature from the force. In this way someone might frame your difficulty even more sharply. But the beginning of the solution of the difficulty, they say, would be its strongest point. For to say, "He ought not to curse his own creature, but to subject the cause of the force to punishment," is nothing other than [?]
[?] but, "He ought to place the man under a curse" [?] and noble [?] of the [?]

[?] he leaves [?] to those who have made themselves unworthy of all pity, as he says somewhere else too, that for such people it would be better to have a millstone hung around their neck and to be thrown into the sea. The difficulty, then, is resolved by the very things by which it seemed to be strengthened: it is not the one forced who bears the curse, but the one who brings forth the offences, through whom the offences came; for once he has brought them forth, the offences then of necessity come into the world and parade themselves boldly in it.

Why Moses does not mention the kingdom of heaven [?], although the Saviour in the Gospels [?] said that it had been prepared for the righteous [?].

1. The divine Moses passed over many intelligible things. The kingdom of heaven, too, is superior to the senses both in its existence and in its enjoyment, for "eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man." So it is no wonder that Moses, who saw God, did not go into the creation of the incorporeal powers, because of the dullness and weakness of his hearers, and did not set out an account of the kingdom of heaven, which is beyond [?], for a people who lived by the senses rather than by contemplation. Some think that the kingdom of heaven, which is the same as the kingdom of Christ, is also included in the account of paradise, but careful reasoning would not accept this, for it would make it far lower than the kingdom of heaven. Paradise was made so that the eye could take it in, and it had the first-formed humans as its citizens. It is the most beautiful of all things in the world, yet it is still part of the earth. It is thick with lovely plants and watered by the clearest streams, but none of these things is higher than sight, and none has withdrawn beyond human reasoning, as the kingdom of heaven has. And no one can say how great the distance is between earth and heaven.

2. The noble thief said, "Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom," and the Saviour promised him paradise. Someone may therefore take the kingdom of heaven to be the lot of paradise, since it would not seem consistent for the thief to ask for one thing and receive another from God, who gives so generously. Let such a person consider instead that the thief had no idea at all what the kingdom of heaven, that is, the kingdom of Christ, was. How could he have been led to ask for things that defeat the power of reasoning and go beyond human understanding? The thief, then, had no idea at all what the kingdom of heaven was. When he made his request, his mind was not directed toward anything definite and known. Through such a request he was asking to share in certain good things and in blessed enjoyment. Paradise was better known to him than all other good things, because the Jewish nation knew of it from the teaching of Moses, and so it had not escaped his knowledge. For this reason the Master pledges paradise to him. He does not give one thing in place of another. He gives what the petitioner wanted to obtain. And what he wanted was to be remembered in the kingdom of Christ, that is, to be among good and blessed things.

And so he then receives the [?] in paradise. [?] conflicts with the argument. Rather, we shall know more precisely in the common resurrection and recompense of all; for now, full knowledge of this would belong to the Judge himself.

3. Moses, however, had neither the need nor the aim to unfold the kingdom of heaven. As we have said, when he wrote the account of the world's creation, he passed over many of the things that lie beyond the senses. Someone may wish to say that he hints at the kingdom of heaven itself, figuratively and in a riddle, when he says, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." If so, we will not quarrel with him. We do not claim anywhere that Moses, who was counted worthy of so great and so high a vision of God, was ignorant of these things and others like them. We say only that he kept them unspoken before the many and was very sparing of the ears of the motley crowd. He sowed seeds for those who were loftier and more perfect, and perhaps he himself went on [?] with loftier and more wonderful contemplations. Indeed, they say this is why, after speaking of the creation of the sensible world, he goes into fine detail and also describes the things that make it complete. When he records the origin of heaven, he likewise goes through those parts of it that concern the earthly world, treating the sun and the moon and the dominion and nature of the stars. But he did not treat in the same way the things that turn away from the earthly order and belong to the higher region [?]. If he did not treat these, much less did he treat the things that rise above them. He leaves the wise and precise account of these things to Christ our God, the Maker and Master of all. Christ came to dwell among us on earth and handed down heavenly and divine teachings and mysteries, and he also explained the kingdom of heaven. For the other things, laws and good tidings, curses and blessings, which are of a more bodily kind, are taken up everywhere by Moses. But the common Saviour of our race, intending to free the whole human being from error, promised us who obey the heavenly and divine good things. In the same way he also showed the disobedient that they will be received, not by temporary things that pass with time

But the truth would not readily accept this view. It is too forced. Moreover, by speaking of the making of the heavens, he would have helped the Jews toward the kingdom of heaven no more than if he had kept completely silent. Much else, too, stands against this supposition.

4. If paradise was also an arena, since the training ground was set before the first-formed man in it, how could the same place be both the prize and the racecourse? Paradise, then, is a prelude to the kingdom of heaven, but it is not the kingdom. It was blessed and greatly desirable to live in that place, but it is more blessed and more desirable to be escorted from there into the heavenly dwellings. The primordial light, too, which poured forth before the sun was created and made the day, leads us to think of the kingdom of heaven as a higher and more divine lot than paradise, a truly heavenly one, and that light [?] will serve its purpose for those who will be counted worthy to dwell there. It would be reasonable for the heavenly body to stand in the same relation to the kingdom of heaven as the earth stands to it. The earth plainly holds the place of a floor in relation to the [?] heavenly vault, and the heavenly body in turn will serve as a floor for those in the kingdom of heaven who are counted worthy to make their home there. So from now on there is no difficulty at all. We need not wonder why, although Christ the Master taught and promised us a heavenly kingdom at his saving coming, his servant Moses either did not mention it at all or mentioned it only in a riddle. Nor need we wonder whether paradise and the kingdom of heaven are the same or different.

Question 7. If the ends of the ages have come upon us, in what ages will the riches of Christ be shown to us?

There is no difficulty in saying both that the ends of the ages have come upon us and that the common Saviour and Redeemer of our race will show his riches toward us in the ages to come. For we are at the end of the ages, all of us who have been appointed to live out the span of the present world as it withers and wastes away toward its end. The ages to come, on the other hand, must be understood as those whose nature extends alongside the [?] of the things to come. Look at it this way as well. In the ages whose ends have come upon us, the mystery ordained before the ages for the common salvation of the human race reached its goal and was accomplished, namely God's union with human beings and his dwelling among them. In the ages to come, the ascent of human beings to God and a loftier union with him would be accomplished, and we would become gods by grace and no longer be subject to change for the worse. Further, in the ages whose ends we have reached, we are required to carry out the commandments, and we strip for the training ground. In the ages to come, we receive the reward for what we have done and are counted worthy of the prizes. Then indeed the riches of the

Master's goodness and generosity will be lavished on us in a way that cannot be told and by reckonings beyond our grasp. Or, if you like: in the ages that are coming to an end we live our life in a corruptible body, but in the ages to come we exchange corruption for incorruption and so continue through the endless age. And again, in the present ages we endure sin rising up against us and troubling us. In the ages to come we shall find it no longer making war on us or at work in us. Indeed, we shall find that it does not exist at all and cannot exist. One could add countless other points through which the difference is easily grasped between the ages hurrying toward their end and those that endure without limit. One can also see that the sayings in question neither contradict nor conflict with one another.

Question 8. How can the children of God be said not to commit sin, when the same Scripture says that they are those born of water and the Spirit, and yet we see many who were made sons through baptism committing sin?

Those born of water and the Spirit are called children of God, and the children of God, as the inspired John proclaims, do not commit sin. You ask, then, and are puzzled how it is that, after being counted worthy of the washing of regeneration, so great a gift, we are still carried down into sin. But before resolving these sayings that seem to contradict each other, we should examine the apostle's saying in itself: how can a person who has become a child of God be wholly unable to sin? Some point to the explanation John himself adds: "because his seed is in him." This is the Master's seed, that is, the word of teaching, for "the sower went out to sow," as Scripture says. As long as this seed has taken root and remains in the soul, the one who through that seed has acquired likeness to God who begot him cannot sin. But when such seed has been taken out of our mind, the enemy's seed is at once sown in its place, and the tares begin to sprout. Some have understood the apostle's saying in this way, and in my opinion they come close to the truth. Others explain it more simply. They say that the just man while he does justice, the temperate man while he practices temperance, and anyone else named after a virtue while he performs and practices it, could never be the author of sin. Some have said this, but it does not seem to me to reach the height of the apostle's thought. It is not wise to hold, much less to teach, that the just man does no injustice while he acts justly, or that the temperate man is not licentious while he is temperate. Perhaps it would be better to see the matter this way. The one born of God has received his seed into himself, that is, virtue, for every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. He has been perfected in it so far that it has become purely a settled habit in him, and he has no seed of evil mixed in with it. Such a person cannot sin. That is, his will does not lean toward the passions, and

his mind does not turn toward them. Untaught nature [?] strongly turns away from what is contrary to nature. In the same way, the habit that comes from teaching through practice in good deeds gains great strength, so that it does not lean toward anything base or take delight in it. Such, then, might be the examination of the saying in itself. The difficulty raised by putting the sayings together would be resolved no less by each of the explanations given. There is nothing puzzling in this: someone in whom the seminal principles are sprouting, whether of the virtues or the foundations of piety, does not at that time accept the evil one's sowing at all, but when we become bare of the [?] growth, we are then seen to be ready to receive the tares. Nor would anyone dispute that the one who practices virtue sincerely is inactive toward vice while he does so, but that if he neglects good works he is carried down to what is worse. In this way, as has been said, the apparent contradiction between the sayings with which we began would be resolved. A more fitting and particular solution, however, would be the following. The adoption from above comes about in two ways. One is displayed by the generosity of the one who adopts alone. The other comes with the contribution of our own effort, through which the practice of the virtues is brought in as well. When the grace of adoption given from above is joined with the practice of virtue that comes from our will, it reshapes, as it were, the adopted person into the likeness and character of God who begot him, as far as a human being can imitate him. So the one who has been called a child of God in this way, and has acquired an adoption so firm and immovable, receives an unchanging habit of the good. He hates sin, turns away from it and does not wish to commit it in any way. But there is another who has enjoyed the Master's generosity yet has contributed nothing great enough to show that his adoption is firm or to prove himself worthy of it by his works. Even if he has obtained the adoption that the Master's generosity grants, he does not support it with his own will and effort, and so he is easily carried toward [?] sinful acts. He leaves the seed given by grace without fruit, as it were, while through his own sloth the seed sown by the evil one is cultivated and brought to fruit. Since he carries this seed within himself, he is rightly called a child of the devil instead of a child of God.

How is it that David, the ancestor of God, said, "As for man, his days are like grass," and so on, while his son Solomon declares, "Man is a great thing, and a merciful man is precious"?

The divine David generally belittles human nature, and the wise Solomon magnifies it, but they do not put forward opinions contrary to each other. These two are not the only ones who make such statements about the human race. In many places of divine Scripture you will find passages that sometimes exalt human

[?] nature, and at other times belittle it and set it low. And that is not all. Those of our holy Fathers who were initiated into true wisdom from Scripture also set forth differing opinions about the human condition. Yet the difference in their judgments does not show them bringing in strife or conflict with themselves or with one another. On the contrary, they are seen to have achieved concord and harmony. How it is that no conflict or contradiction with the truth follows from their different statements can easily be grasped from what follows. Human beings have a twofold constitution, and they have lived a twofold life: one before the transgression, the other after the commandment was set aside. As for the constitution, one part of the human being is clay and dust, while the other is an image of the almighty nature that is master of all things. So whatever exalts the human being and raises him up shows either the greatness of the dignity given to him or the blessed and happy life before the transgression. Whatever belittles him and sets him low either describes the pains that came after the transgression or shows plainly that he is dust and returns to the earth. We say these things as setting out, so to speak, the first and most fundamental principles. Many other things grow from them. The human being has been made a kind of borderland. He is able to be deified if he wishes, yet no necessity holds back his impulse if he wishes to lean toward what is worse. When he is deified, he deserves countless praises. But when he turns into a beast and becomes brutish, not to say a rival of the wicked demons in evil, he falls under countless reproaches. Moreover, when his mind is busy with the delights and pleasures of life, he is flooded with countless evils every day, and he can scarcely ever see that it is "vanity of vanities, all is vanity." But when he separates himself by reason from the world and from the troubles and idle chatter of the world, he enjoys the greatest happiness. Even before he attains the things of the world to come, he delights in the present as in an image and a prelude of great blessedness. So the father does not fight with the son, I mean David the ancestor of God with the wise Solomon, though one praises the human being and the other brings him down. Divine Scripture does not contend with itself. Nor does the divine choir of our Fathers, though they sometimes extol human nature and at other times belittle it and shut it up in the utmost lowliness. And apart from what has been said, how do the sufferings of our poor body and the injuries we suffer every day not belittle our condition? And how do the mind's turning to contemplation and the pure pleasure that comes from it not show that our way of life is [?] and happy?

recording the [?] of the affliction, nor that the moon gives a person occasions for being caught by evil. Rather, he was eager to tell of the Master's wonders using names that were customary and familiar to the multitude. His aim was not to speak in polished Attic but to teach the truth clearly. This happens when someone reports events in the common use of words and in the way local custom prevails. Besides, the use of this word was no hindrance to the preaching of true religion. Many who had worshipped the sun and the moon were going to hear of the Master's miracles. Starting from their own belief and the words they used, he frees them from their ancient, impious error. It is almost as if he were calling out to them and crying: "People, how can you offer reverence to the moon and the sun and regard them as gods and benefactors, when, as you yourselves would say by this very word, you suffer such afflictions from them and such ruin spreads through the human race? You ought to be rid of the moon and the rest, since, as you suppose, they have left you so grievously and wretchedly afflicted. Instead you should offer reverence and pure worship to him who grants freedom from these and countless other afflictions [?] and lavishes eternal good things." In this way nothing stands in the way of pious reasoning.

I have heard some people say that the evangelist knows being moonstruck to be something different from being possessed by a demon. Otherwise, they say, he would not have said "moonstruck" and added "demon-possessed" in the same passage. According to them, the moonstruck person is driven not by a demon but by another kind of illness, which has its origin in putrefied humors in the body. These humors grow and attack more violently when the moon is full. Many other moist things and creatures that live in moisture, such as oysters and the like, are also seen to grow more [?]. It is not that the moon does this by its own independent power, far from it. It comes from the ineffable craftsmanship of him who made all things in wisdom and implanted such workings in the moon. For, the argument goes, the heat in the moon is lukewarm by nature. When it touches our bodies with its rays, it makes the moisture in us spread, but because its heat is not intense like the sun's, it does not disperse and expel what has spread. When these humors have spread and been stirred up in the body in this way, the illness grows stronger. It attacks the brain and the head more severely, distorts and alters the living creature, and by obstructing its natural functions causes it to be thrown down and convulsed. That is why the multitude calls those who suffer from such an illness moonstruck, and nothing prevents us from calling them so. There is also another explanation besides these. It holds that the people the multitude calls moonstruck are in fact possessed by demons. The demons, eager to slander the Creator's creatures to human beings, watch for the moon's waxing and then make their attack and the affliction more evident, so that wickedly

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. [?] …so that they may persuade people to suspect the good creatures of God, and from there go on to blaspheme the Creator. But this argument does not offer a view on why the divine apostle used such a word. It asks instead why on earth the demons watch for the phases of the moon and then attack us more violently and tighten their tyranny. However, since much has been said and none of it conflicts with pious reasoning, let each person hold to whichever view seems right to him.

[Wh]y, when Adam had sinned and had received the [sentence] of death [?], did his son, who had not sinned, die before him? The weightier and loftier account of this matter perhaps wants to dwell in the abyss of the divine judgments and leave human reasoning behind, except for whatever has come down to our knowledge as well. Adam receives the penalty, but his son dies first. In this way the guilty man sees with his own eyes how heavy and painful death is, and so comes to a fuller awareness of his sin. Cast into fear and anguish, he might then soften his punishment through repentance and mourning for what he had dared to do. For every threat, and every penalty held over someone, becomes fearsome only when the guilty somehow come to know the terrors by experience. If Adam had not seen his son dead, he would not have understood all the horrors that death brings with it: not that great and helpless struggle, not the turmoil of the soul, not its separation from the body, nor anything else that follows, such as dissolution and rot and stench, dust, oozing fluids and worms. So Adam sees in another person how fearsome and unbearable his own penalty is. Seeing it, he grasps more fully how great his fall was, and so he is led by the hand to repentance. In the end, though he is deprived of his son, he gains the salvation of his own soul. And if anyone should reckon that the loss of his son was no easier for Adam to bear than death, he will find many fathers to bear witness to that thought, men who would often trade many deaths of their own for the safety of their child. By this reasoning, then, the penalty decreed for Adam overtakes him through his son even before his own death, as he is seized by unbearable grief, a blow heavier than death. Consider a third point with me as well. At that time the whole world had three men for its citizens, and one woman lived among them. Some of them were parents, and the others were the children of those parents. Adam is not subjected to the penalty, for the reason already given. Eve is not subjected to death either, partly for the same reason and partly because she was the only woman, so her disappearance would have ended procreation and driven the whole race to destruction. Nor was it fitting that death by treachery should fall upon Cain, for he was the worse and Abel the better. And how could one who was free of guile and envy and every other wickedness lay murderous [?] hands on his brother? It remains, then, that it was that

one who rushed to the treacherous killing of his brother. Even before this lawless deed he had grieved God with the fruits he offered. He had been stirred to envy against someone who had done him no wrong, and with an evil mind and a deceitful plan he readied his own hands for fratricide. And see here, too, how wise and unsearchable Providence is. The wicked man thought he was prevailing when he raised his hands against the better man, but those very means brought him the first beginnings of his overthrow. For the plan of the divine dispensation, which passes all understanding, allows Abel to become the work of unjust and bloodstained hands, and the son dies before his father. But the power of Hades and its first foundation turn out to be weak. If Hades had received Adam first, its foundation would have been firmly laid, since the first one it received would have been condemned by divine sentence. But because it took in an innocent man through malice, its power is found to be overturned from the very start, since it laid a rotten foundation from the beginning. And so the death of the righteous man through malice becomes the beginning of the complete destruction of Hades.

Question 12. That, although some think otherwise, there is no conflict between "For judgment I have come into this world" and "I did not come to judge the world but to save the world." The sayings "For judgment I have come into this world" and "I did not come to judge the world but to save the world" are not in any way opposed to each other. On the contrary, they show a close connection and agreement. "For judgment," he says, "I have come into this world." This is because those who ought to see willingly make themselves blind, while those who were thought to be blind were shown to see the light of truth. The first group did not accept salvation, but the second ran to it when it came. "So," he says, "even though my coming took place for the salvation of the world, those who stubbornly and willfully turn away from their own good have made my presence a judgment on themselves." Why, then, do you not bring down fire on them, or shake the earth beneath them, or open the floodgates of heaven and drown their madness? Because, he says, "I did not come to judge the world but to save it," to call it back. "That is why I am patient, and why I hold judgment in reserve. The time of my first coming is not a time of judgment. It is a time of love for humankind, of compassion, of kindness, of calling back." So the divine oracles before us do not conflict with each other at all; as you see, they keep the fullest harmony. Besides, the words krima ("judgment") and krisis ("judging") agree in many respects but also differ. Krima means rather a condemnation, whereas krisis leans toward assigning to each what is fitting. So the Savior came into the world "for judgment" (krima), that is, for

condemnation. He became a condemnation to all who refused to look toward their own good and would not apply their understanding to recognize their own redemption. To these our common Savior became a judgment. He did not cause them to owe punishment; they themselves turned the medicine of salvation into a deadly poison. The words "so that those who see," and what follows, do not point to a cause. They describe those who willfully and wickedly preferred the worse to the better. That they made themselves liable to judgment and did not receive the common Savior proves their own wickedness, but it does not conflict in any way with the one who said that he came not to judge the world but to save it. On the contrary, it bears witness to a boundless sea of love for humankind. He drew many out of error, and he does not call to account, punish or condemn those who disobeyed and put themselves under judgment, but is kind to the disobedient. As he says, "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." So the Savior who came becomes a condemnation through the wickedness of those who [did not?] receive him. But he does not judge or punish them, because of his supreme love for humankind and because he wants to show that his first coming was a time not of judgment but of dispensation and compassion. Someone might want to force the matter more boldly and take krima to mean distinction and separation. I do not think he would find the word consistently used in this sense in the sacred writings, though perhaps he will find passages not at odds [?] with such a meaning. For example: "Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth; I did not come to bring peace but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law." Or: "His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather the wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire." And there are other such passages. Yet even so, the one who tries to set up a conflict between the sacred words will never succeed. I mean between "For judgment I have come into this world" and "I did not come to judge the world but to save it." For the Savior came to bring peace to the world and to reconcile to the Father those who had long been at war with him. He tore down the dividing wall that separated them, joined the things above to the things below, and made peace. But if some turned the peace into enmity for themselves and made the reconciliation into division, the blame does not lie with the one who gave peace and brought reconciliation. It lies with those who tore themselves away and broke off from those who had been reconciled to the Father and had enjoyed the blessings of peace.

Question 13. If it is far harder to be in unending punishment, racked [?] with pains and agonies, and far better to suffer nothing of the kind, then why, they ask, did God bring into being people who would spend their lives in sin? Did he not choose the worse over the better? 1. Our Savior himself taught in the Gospels that it would have been better for those who have gone on to grievous sins never to have come into being at all, when he said, "It would have been good for that man if he had not been born." For Judas and those like him, then, not being born was better than being born. But this is not true absolutely, and it was not better for God. Coming into being leads to the enjoyment of existence and proclaims God's providence and creation. But what has fallen away from being once and for all reveals nothing of God's surpassing wisdom and can share in nothing good either. Since coming into being is better than not coming into being, and being is better than not being, the Divine, as it set about [?] creating, had to produce not the worse but the better. So it is in no way fitting for God to leave in non-being those who were to exist, instead of bringing them into being. This holds even though the merciful [voice?] said of the traitor, as one lamented [?], "It would have been good for him if he had not been born." Besides, it would be most pleasing to sinners to be ranked equally with the sinless, but in God's judgment that is in no way tolerable or fitting. Not having to pay the penalty they owe would be a lesser good for them, but this too is far from God's righteous judgment. And countless other things could be said. 2. In the same way, by the same unchanging logic, bringing into being those who were to exist is both better for them and most fitting for God. This is so even if some of them later, by their own free choice, exchanged the better for the worse and made God's wonderful and saving creation perilous for themselves, striving to drag the best down to the worst. Further, the Divine always exists and is fixed within the unchanging and unalterable bounds of its own nature, while everything that has come into being through generation is subject to countless changes and alterations. So anyone who demands that God should not have brought into being those who would sin is ruling either that human nature should not exist at all, or that it should have been made unchangeable and unalterable. That amounts either to cutting the whole human race out of creation or to demanding that man should have been created with God's nature. One can see at once how much folly and impiety each of these involves; it stands exposed as if on a public pillar [?]. Besides, what has never come into being and does not exist cannot be good, but one who lives in sin can become good. And the good, being counted blessed, shows its superiority plainly [?]. 3. Apart from what has been said, whoever claims that because

some people were going to slip into sin they ought never to have come into being at all is saying nothing other than that sin, before it even existed, ought to prevail over God's creation. For if God's work of creating some people had to stop because they were going to sin, then clearly the power would belong to sin rather than to God's activity. Further, sinning belongs to human will and choice, but creation belongs to the one who formed us. Why, then, does anyone pass over the real cause of sin and try to shift it onto one who is not its cause? Equally foolish is the one who puts forward the verdict that those who were going to sin ought never to have received existence from the Creator at all, or been brought out into the light of the sun. Such a person seems to be annoyed when someone who has sinned pays the penalty, yet eager to exact punishment from people who have not yet sinned at all. For that is what it means to deprive those who will sin of birth and existence and to cut them out of God's creation. He seems to want to condemn sinners on the basis of divine foreknowledge, yet to have those who are actually doing the deeds let off from punishment. This kind of justice is known neither to humans nor to God. That no one should be made to pay a penalty before sinning is the common judgment of all humanity and fits the divine laws. But exacting the penalty for unrepented sin proves God's hatred of evil and his justice. How, then, could anyone who has thought it over hold the opposite of what everyone agrees on, and refuse to honor what shows God to be just and a hater of evil? Does such a person not make himself guilty of the utmost madness and impiety? What are you saying? That man should have been created unable to turn toward sin, so that he would escape punishment? Then how are you not plainly saying, even if you do not say it outright, that man should have been created unable to turn to sin, so that people would not be counted worthy of the crowns they win by struggling against sin and overcoming it? Suppose someone with any intelligence were given the power to choose between two things, even if he were at once an ardent lover of sin and someone who runs from torment. Either the crowns must be taken from the heads of those who have fought nobly, so that certain sinners will not pay the penalty; or else sin must not go unpunished, for the sake of those who will justly be counted worthy of prizes for their contests. Would he not much rather see the athletes adorned with the crowns of their valor, and the debtors paying off their debts? 4. In addition to what has been said, is it only the creation of human beings that troubles you? Or are you thrown into the same confusion over the bodiless and immaterial natures that have been raised to immortality? Of these heavenly ranks and that blessed realm, the devil willingly fell from there and became the author of evil, and so did all who turned their inclination toward his way of thinking and exchanged the better for the worse. But the rest of those immortal and divine choirs, through attentiveness and earnest watchfulness, changed nothing of their own beauty or order. Toward the common Master

and Creator they lift themselves up [?], and they never have their fill of the essence that gives all good things. They not only remain good themselves by participation, but also serve the divine will toward the human race and become fellow workers and helpers in doing good. Those who fell shudder when they see [?] the sign of the cross traced even as a mere figure, the sign by which the saving passion was accomplished; they tremble and flee as far away as they can. But those who stand around the divine throne receive the radiance of that blessed and awesome vision as far as their nature allows. For the first group, because of what they do and have done, the outer fire has been prepared. The second group preserve and have preserved the sovereign freedom of their inclination in ever better progress and ascent, and they already hold the verdict that they will remain in indescribable delight [?] and enjoyment. 5. You will surely ask, then: Why did that evil one come into being, along with all the ranks that rebelled with him? Since God is good, he ought to have removed such creatures from existence and done away with them beforehand, because that would have been better for them than being sent off to inescapable torment. But then the same meddlesome reasoning will carry you on to the rest of creation as well. The earth, once brought into being [?], ought to have stayed as it was first made, unmoving and walled about with unchangeability. Or, to pass over its other afflictions and alterations, it ought not to be flooded by waters [?], if not entirely then at least in many of its parts, and not to be hidden by the flood almost as completely as when it was invisible and unformed. And the air, which is pure and free from any spurious admixture and was set up to preserve the life of humans and the other animals, ought never to fall into a pestilential [?] condition that destroys what it preserves. And if it was their fixed lot [?], once brought into being, to change their nature, and not theirs alone but that of things of the same order, then it would have been better for none of them to be brought into being at all. Then, you who overturn the whole creation in this way, both the intelligible and the sensible, sparing not even inanimate things, but weighing everything so harshly in the scales of your own reasoning and approving none of it, what do you do about the creation of man? [?] Such a person is perplexed by every [?] kind of thing that exists and looks for another God and Creator (may God be merciful to us!). With a shameless face and an unbridled mouth he mocks the one who brought all these things into being as ignorant of what is better. But why do I say that he seeks another God and Creator? He has seated himself on the heights of madness and folly as the corrector of all that exists, and he strives to do away entirely with the very idea of God, which he had already removed from his own [?] human [?]. But these points, as a summary account, are enough, I think, to call to mind what has been left out as well, and to persuade those who have long been bold enough to argue against us to learn better. Let them fall suddenly silent, as though, in the words of the proverb, an ox had stepped [on their tongue]; for the silver ox [?]
Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Question 14. What is meant by "Their eyes were opened," and how did the transgression have the power to open

[?] The words "The eyes of both were opened" do not mean that the transgression opened their eyes. Perish the thought! Scripture does not say that their eyes were opened in the act of transgression itself, but after it. For it says: "And the woman took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband, and they ate, and the eyes of both were opened." This means that recognition of a sin usually comes after the sin, and that is when the full extent of what was dared is better recognized. Passion clouds our sight and the goad drives us toward sin, but after the lawless deed they cease and grow quiet. Then, and only then, reason peers out as if from that thick mist, sobers up and looks at what has been done. It grasps more clearly what state it has been brought into and from what state it has fallen. With its conscience wounding and rousing it, it now sees plainly what it could not see in the same way while passion was clouding its sight. Besides, as each of us moves toward sin, the evil one tickles and beguiles us, weakens us and fills us with darkness. He carries off our reasoning as if it were drugged, and blinds the eye of discernment. But after the deed he brings what we have dared before our eyes and bitterly uncovers what he had earlier hidden by many devices. Then, by making the whole weight of the deed plain, he tries to drive the sinner to despair. So the words "Their eyes were opened" must not be taken to refer to the earlier time, before they fell away from the commandment. At that time their eyes were open even wider, since they had not yet been led astray by the serpent's whisperings, and they kept their minds alert to discern what they should do. So it was not that they lacked sight before and gained it through the sin. On the contrary, they were blind while they were committing the sin, and when it was over they recovered their sight. The evil one, the author of evil and enemy of our nature, knew from his own experience that awareness of the offense comes after the evil deed is done, though he himself did not turn back and come to his senses. He had learned by experience that the sting of conscience follows sinners after their sin. So when he urged Adam and Eve to sin by transgressing, he said, "On the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened." Then, since he has been a contriver of evil from the beginning and is the father of lies, he mixes the whole darkness of falsehood into the lamp-wick of truth and says, "You will be like gods, knowing good and evil." But as blind while sinning, through their love of the transgression; but after the [?] … of the Athenians: that is, those who had taken bribes kept silent.

…sin, coming to an awareness of what they had dared and sobering up from it. But why, after their eyes were opened, do they first perceive the nakedness of the procreative parts and feel ashamed? Because the passion that works through these parts assails more fiercely than the other sins when it is not reined in by the laws of self-control. Because once the disposition toward sexual pleasure is stirred in a living creature, the other passions usually spring up along with it. And because from that time on all the other sins too are brought under judgment. Sins committed before that are, for the most part, put down to weakness of mind and to infancy, both by the spiritual law and by the law of civil life.

QUESTION 15. Why did Moses make no mention of the kingdom of heaven in his account of the world's creation, even though the Saviour says that it was prepared for the righteous from the foundation of the world? 1. Some say that the Jews were immature and bound to matter. They leaned toward the more elementary lessons, and they were less able to grasp things beyond the senses than things seen with bodily [?] eyes. For this reason, these people say, Moses kept silent toward them about the teaching on the kingdom of heaven. He did not want them, while they were only beginning to learn how the world came to be, to be confronted as well with teaching about the things in it that are more divine and beyond them, and so to become more listless in hearing the rest. A teacher must make the strength of his hearers the measure of his teaching. But others ask what stood in the way of [teaching them] about the kingdom of heaven [?]. The Hebrew race, they say, stood equally far from knowing how the world was created and from grasping the kingdom of heaven, even if the one falls under the senses and the other is beyond them. Since the Hebrews were bound to matter and busied with earthly things, it was necessary instead to make them lofty and raise them up by the promise and teaching of things immaterial and beyond the senses. A teacher of superior skill mixes things beyond the senses with familiar ones, and little by little accustoms his pupils to strive for the ascent to more divine things. That is why such people have even dared to say that Moses too introduced the kingdom of heaven, figuratively and in a riddle. Where? In the very opening, they say, when he says: “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” For after this he

unfolds the creation beneath the heavens and within the world. By placing heaven first, however, he hinted through its making at the state of things before the firmament and above the world. But the truth would hardly welcome this view. It is very forced, and by speaking of the making of heaven Moses benefited the Jews no more regarding the kingdom of heaven than if he had kept entirely silent. There are many other objections to this supposition as well. 2. Others say that the kingdom of heaven is also brought in with the account of paradise. Paradise, they argue, is a part of the eternal goods and an enjoyment of blessedness, which is why the thief who asked to be remembered in the kingdom of God is granted a dwelling in paradise. But perhaps paradise is far lowlier than the kingdom of heaven. Consider the flowers and beauties of its plants; the rivers and streams flowing round the place; the variety of ripe fruits and the kinds of herbs breathing sweet and pleasant scents; the face of the earth adorned and beautified by all of these; and a temperate air spread out in purity and clearness, receiving the first rays of the sun. How could these fail to make the whole place carry off the very height of delight and pleasure, as far as anything can charm the senses? Yet the goods of the kingdom surpass all this by an infinite measure. “For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.” Besides, paradise was not made known to Adam as the honour of prizes and rewards. The place was set before him rather as a training ground and a stadium of virtue. The prizes and crowns obviously bring a greater and more perfect enjoyment, and no one has ever found a stadium turning into the nature of prizes and rewards, nor even been taught so by hearsay. The thief is brought into paradise as one counted worthy of a kind of pledge and prelude of the good things to come. For the time of the common recompense of eternal goods had not yet arrived. Nor was he to be the only righteous man, out of all who have pleased God since the beginning of the ages, to reach the goal of final blessedness and be made perfect apart from those countless choirs of the saints, as the divine Paul testifies somewhere. 3. Of the points just mentioned, not a few of those before us [have put forward] some as reasons why the [kingdom] of [heaven] received no mention…

…and to teach [?] the way of life through which one can enter into the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. Having fittingly led us up to such a way of life, he also graciously gave us the clearest and most certain teaching and promise about the kingdom of heaven itself. But if anyone rises to a better understanding of the question before us and teaches it, he will be doing what I pray for and what would please me most. Why did Moses call the earth invisible? Moses said the earth was invisible because it had not yet received its right to be seen, since the flood of waters was poured over it. The strength and might of the abyss prevailed, both drenching the earth's natural dryness and not letting it receive its proper adornment, that is, the kinds of plants and herbs and all the other beauty of flowers and fruits. The earth was also invisible because the human being who would receive sight and see it was not yet there. It could also fittingly be called invisible because light, through which the visible is grasped by sight, had not yet come into being, so the earth did not have the brightness by which it could serve the eye. Suppose the water had been divided and drawn back into its own hollows, the earth had been adorned with plants and its other ornaments, and the human being who was to see it had arrived. If the nature of light was not yet shining, even then the earth would not have been called visible. In the same way, clearly, the air [would not have been visible] either. The air receives the ray of light and, becoming the medium, joins the activity of the one who sees to the thing seen. So without light having come into existence, neither the air nor the water would have been visible, even though the air was not screened by anything else, as the abyss was, nor deprived of any adornment of its own. That is why Moses, knowing that the air was poured over the water, named it darkness over the abyss. The illuminating radiance did not pass through its [airy?] nature, since not even light yet had this existence. So the air itself could not be visible, much less the abyss over which the airy spirit was poured, and for this reason it is fittingly called darkness. To say that it is the divine Spirit that was borne over the abyss might introduce a circumscription of the uncircumscribable. It might also restrict divine providence and [?] from the other creatures over which the Spirit was not borne. Perhaps it would not be worthy of theology, at the foundation of creation, to assign a place to the uncreated and blessed nature, that is, to the all-holy Spirit. But if the Syriac language also holds that the all-holy Spirit was borne upon the waters, brooding over them, as it were, and giving them life, I would not condemn it. For the time being it is enough to know, from whatever source one can, that the all-holy Spirit is of a life-giving and creative essence and power. The earth, then, and the rest of the elements were invisible for the reason just given and for those given earlier, except one: neither the water nor the air had anything screening it. As for the darkness, if anyone takes it not as the absence of light

but supposes it to be the devil, the author of evil, and the abyss to be the wicked powers under him, he would be straying far from the truth and be full of an impious opinion. He would also be unable to see the sequence of the narrative, or the order and enumeration of the created things perceived by the senses whose history Moses wrote. Nor could he see the creation and contemplation of the incorporeal and intellectual nature, or the proper occasion, which knows how to set apart the teaching about these things in due order. The air is called the spirit of God in the same way as the other things are called his, as his creature and work. “For he will send out his word and melt it; he will blow with his spirit, and waters will flow,” says David, speaking of snow melted by the south winds. And “spirit of God” would be said in the same sense as “God made the heaven and the earth.” Those things belong to God as his works, and this likewise is God's creature and his own work. So it is rightly called the spirit of God.

By the present command he lays down that the way of beasts and the life of human beings are to be distinct. When people are forbidden to share one and the same table, the law implies that their habits, diet, impulses and actions in every other respect also differ greatly. The beast seizes and grabs more than its share, it is utterly headlong in its impulses, and it knows no laws of kindness, fellowship or gentleness. A human being ought to be clean and free of all these things. Likewise with the other passions: the beast is without self-control and unbridled. Human life, then, proceeding by self-control and discipline, will display these marks of difference. Whoever does not bear these marks and cannot be recognised by them will be shunned as a beast, as something torn by beasts, falsely laying claim to a gentle and rational nature. Someone might say that by abstaining from what is torn by beasts the law trains and leads toward purity the masterpiece fashioned in the image of God. It keeps that masterpiece free of every abomination, both what defiles the taste and what comes in through the other senses, since watching over and guarding one sense ensures that the others too stay clean of impurity and abomination. If someone says this, that too would not be foreign to the providence of the commonwealth or to a holy way of life.

QUESTION 18. How should we understand “You shall not appear empty before me”? Some say that whoever goes to worship God must also bring gifts, as far as his means allow. This is not because God is in need of them, for what would God need? It is because here too the one who brings them is the one who benefits. For when someone is counted worthy to bear fruit for God, to reveal his inward piety through outward things, and when the creature is joined to its Creator through the medium of propitiatory offerings,

with God receiving graciously and the worshipper bringing faithfully and eagerly, how could this not be the enjoyment of a wonderful providence and kindness? What else could be more excellent or precious than this for the rational creature, by way of kindness and providence? What could be more gracious or sweeter? But it would be still more pleasing to understand the virtues and piety here, for one must never be seen before God empty of them. Whoever is emptied of virtue and piety, even if he seems to approach God, will neither see God nor be seen by him. For “the impious will not see the glory of God,” nor will “the sinner declare his ordinances.” Indeed, the Lord does not even know the workers of lawlessness, nor look on them with an eye of favour and friendship. So we must approach God carrying virtues and piety in the soul as gifts, and in this way fulfil the Master's command: “You shall not appear empty before me.” It would also be fitting that inquiry into God and divine things not be empty of reverence and spiritual discernment. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, and whoever throws himself rashly into questions that concern God will never track down the truth. “For you seek,” it says, “and do not receive, because you seek wrongly.” But the spiritual person, who examines and seeks the things of the Spirit with reverence, will arrive at finding the truth and will not be disappointed in his effort. The one who made the promise does not lie: “Ask, and it will be given to you; knock, and it will be opened to you.”

QUESTION 19. How is it not a contradiction to say “Behold, all things were very good,” and then afterwards to make distinctions, calling some animals clean and others unclean? Much could be said about this question, and not a few of those before us have solved it. Without straying far from precision, one might say that clean and good are not opposed to each other. Bad is at war with good, and clean with unclean, but unclean and good would not, strictly speaking, be in conflict. If, then, after saying earlier “All things very good,” he had added later that some of them were good and others bad, this would present the contradiction. But since, having said “very good,” he called some of them clean and others unclean, he avoided the conflict. That is how one might put it in a more general and logical way. But one must also see that “all things very good” is said of the nature of created things, whereas “clean and unclean” is said of their use by human beings. Use and nature differ enormously. Many things are very useful by nature but become very harmful to those who use them. This happens not because of their own nature but because of the wickedness of the users. To make what has been said credible from another direction as well, take heaven itself. That wonderful

[?] Photius, Patriarch [?] and wise masterpiece is among the things that are very good. But some supposed it to be a living, rational being and a god, and kindled reverence for the creation instead of the Creator, although they were free to use their fellow servant as a creature. For these very people the thing most beautiful by nature proves ruinous and most evil. It has lost nothing of its own innate beauty, but through the senseless audacity and misuse of its fellow servants it has become the worst of evils for them. So natural beauty is one thing and unfitting use is another. All things, then, are very good by the principle of their nature. But their use is neither good for everyone nor the same for all, not only when compared with human nature, but also when the other creatures are compared with one another. Perhaps, however, this solution has not reached the clarity proper to the question, and we must come closer still. So we say that “all things very good” refers to the principle of creation and nature. But the statement that some of them are clean and others unclean refers neither to the principle of creation nor to that of nature. It refers instead to sacrifice and human opinion. Creation and nature are walled off from opinion and sacrifice by a measure beyond telling, especially since sacrifices and opinions do not always stand under the same judgement. Moreover, things were not distinguished as clean and unclean from the beginning of creation; they received this difference from particular circumstances. The Egyptians, among whom the Israelite nation was serving, gave worship to many animals and misused them, though they were very good. So that the Israelite race would not also be carried away into that base use and attach divine worship to irrational creatures, Moses, as lawgiver, rightly named these animals unclean. They did not share in uncleanness from their creation—far from it—nor did their nature hold anything unclean. It was because the Egyptian nation used them not purely but in a thoroughly profane and unholy way. Moses did place some of the animals deified by the Egyptians, such as the ox and the goat, in the class of clean animals. But in doing so he acted neither against the explanation just given nor against his own aim. Among the animals they deified, he called some abominable, and he handed others over to slaughter, blood and killing. In both ways he equally kept the Israelites from worshipping them and from the harm that would spring up from that worship. Those who treat animals in these ways would never think a god either what is abominable or what is slaughtered and served up at a feast. God's act of creation, then, brought forth all created things very good, and the nature of all of them is excellent. But the irrational and lawless uses of human beings profaned many created things. Some of these they caused to be thought and called unclean. Others escaped the name of uncleanness, but still gave the man who saw God cause to find another method of cutting these too away from profanation. By each of these two ways [he sought]

to remove polytheism from the minds of the Israelites and to bring about blamelessness [?]. Both the name “unclean” and the use that sends the sacrificed animal to the belly leave no room to think anything divine or venerable about them, or even to entertain some bare fancy of it. But someone will ask: How then was Noah commanded to distinguish clean and unclean animals and bring them into the ark, when the Mosaic legislation had not yet been given? The figure here is prolepsis. If the animals were named not by what they were known as then but by what they were recognised as later, this is not contrary to the idiom of the passage. Genesis was written not by Noah, who lived before the legislation, but by Moses, who set out the law about clean and unclean animals. And if the law that was to be given later was proclaimed in advance to Noah, there is nothing surprising in that. Even before the common shipwreck came, he had received a certain knowledge of it. How, then, did he understand the difference between clean and unclean when he was ordered to make this distinction? This too is covered by what was just said. He discerned the worldwide shipwreck before it came, and he received from God the grace to preserve a seed for the human race. Such a man would by no means fall short of receiving from above the knowledge of clean and unclean as well, even though the use of sacrificial victims was not yet customary. QUESTION 16. Why can a man who turns away from heresy, if his life is not blameworthy, be [eligible?] for the priesthood, whereas one who [?] from unlawful deeds [?] … the rank of the priesthood not [?]

The problem that leads to perplexity is this. Why is it that a man who has left heresy, the gravest of all offences, can stand as a candidate for the priesthood, as long as his other deeds do not count against him? By contrast, consider a man of orthodox belief who has defiled his hand with the blood of kin, or dug up tombs, or been carried away bodily into a troubling [?] pleasure, or become guilty of some other unholy deed. Even if he turns to repentance and gives those who judge impartially an assurance that leaves no doubt [?] that he has been cleansed of his [defilements?], no such person is ever considered worthy of the priesthood, even with his other virtues testifying for him. The question is old, then, and belongs to this matter of advancement [?]. If any have solved it correctly, I would gladly become their disciple. Perhaps I might offer an answer, if not to others, then at least to you. Those who held impious opinions set out from a mind that did not choose what is bad but sought what is better. But they slipped from their holy love of better things and were carried off to the worse, which they had not intended. In them the impulse from the beginning blossomed toward the good, while their failure could take refuge in the frailty and weakness of nature. And these people, of worse things

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople.

…having changed over, they find pardon looking kindly upon them. But those who knew from the beginning that what they were doing was [wicked?], and yet fixed their minds on it, give those who change over to true religion a great advantage over themselves. The first group held to a good impulse and were swept into its opposite without intending it. The second group chose what was base from the start, and their ruin came about just as they had aimed. To the first, what they believed seemed so excellent that they gloried in their belief and sometimes even chose death rather than forswear their convictions. To the second, the evil was so plainly recognized that, even though no one outside knew of it, they blushed privately at what they had done, and thought it something to pray for that it should escape everyone's notice. So those whose aim was good from the beginning looked toward what is best. Their change went forward through knowledge and was laid on a firm foundation, with true discernment fixing it in place. For the most part, these keep the strength of their turn to true religion unshaken. With the others, the impulse was wicked from its very first stirring, for they knew well that they were taking hold of something wrong. Their change has indeed happened, but it cannot be anchored in what does not change. They have gained nothing beyond what they knew before, nothing in which they might be more firmly settled. Their will leaps freely this way and that, by its own authority, and leaves it uncertain which way it will lean. Naturally, then, it is not easy to trust them not to go back to their former wickedness. Add to this, if you like, that the first group openly professes both its earlier and its later belief to the same degree, not to say that the later one is often more prominent. In any case, the second belief is not second to the first in how widely it is known. But with the second group, the sin is paraded in triumph, for people love to ring out others' faults. Their repentance, however, is carried out quietly and in private. Not only does it escape the notice of the many by being hidden, but it also has envy as a bitter examiner, [?] public and manifest [?] of the cleansing. And one must not cause even one of the little ones to stumble. So their repentance does not give everyone the kind of knowledge that their failing did.

Question [?].

In what sense is the word "he answered" (apekrithē), and the other forms built from the same word, used in our sacred Scriptures?

1. Many words have several meanings, so many that a good number of people have undertaken to write whole treatises on them. It would be nothing strange, then, and should cause no perplexity, to see such words in our sacred Scriptures too. Even among those who cultivate the Attic tongue, one can find words that carry several meanings in display speeches and in histories. One can even find the same word splitting into opposite senses. For instance, Plato calls a virgin alochos, and seems to be saying something clever, since she has not yet gone to the marriage bed (lechos);

but he himself elsewhere, and many others who hold no second rank in letters, use the name for the woman who shares a man's bed. Again, sophist may be taken to mean one who teaches the arts of reasoning. Second, it means one who has trained himself in the art of speaking. Third, it means one who has corrupted his students' training in argument into abusive wrangling. Stathēros, too, is found to mean not only stationary but also strong, hot and sharp. Phaulos likewise covers not only bad, wicked and unseemly, but also great and small. In the same way it covers easy, simple and guileless, ordinary, and plain. Even pynthanesthai, which seems to refer to one thing only, is the root of various offshoots. It puts forward the senses "to learn", "to [?]", "to ask", and others of the kind. The word pelanos denotes a cake of meal fit for sacrifices. It also denotes the foam that congeals around the mouth, and a sap-like exudation that has thickened and dried, such as gum and the like. Fourth, it denotes the obol usually given to seers as their fee. The adverb homose means "face to face". But the usage of the ancients shows that it was also taken to mean "nearly" and "near". Nun dē, moreover, suggests not only what is present now, but also what happened a little before. Kompsos is divided into many meanings as well, both "very clear" and "skilful". Then there is the much-celebrated ē d' hos and ēn d' egō, Plato's favourite flourish. Ē d' hos generally means "and he said". But it also means simply "he said", with the conjunction and the article here serving as fillers. Or rather, they do not indicate a conjunction or an article at all, but are parts of a single expression, since the phrase can indicate neither gender nor number. Hence ē d' hos is seen to apply not only to a woman, meaning "she said", but also to pass from singular to plural, for it also means "they said". Whether it also means "O friend", it is not yet possible to [?] Critobulus [?]. For the present, this is how much ē d' hos indicates. Ēn d' egō has a similar form, but it divides into these three: "and I said", and [?] "I said", which they use alike of men and women. Brattein means to disturb and to trouble. It also means to prick and to stir, and even to be abashed and to be wary. You will also find teutazein applied to various subjects. It is used to mean to busy oneself, to contrive, to serve as a soldier, to spend time, and sometimes to take thought. It also means to do something attentively and to work at it, and even to be eager and to serve a meal.

[Consider?] also these common words that refuse to embrace a single meaning, such as epieikōs and epi korrēs. The first divides into "sufficiently", "moderately" and "nicely". Epi korrēs means being struck on the head, and also on the jaw. Nor is episkēptomenos confined to one meaning. It denotes one who presses upon something, one who lays information against someone, and one who gives instructions at the point of death. Besides these, it denotes what opposes. Dysōpeisthai, likewise, has many meanings. It conveys "to be wary", "to fear with suspicion" and "to look sullen". Some who write Greek with precision, even if they lack Attic elegance, use the word for "to feel shame before". Common usage, however, uses it for "to beseech" and "to entreat". Deuro means "come on!" and "here", but it does not refuse "come!" either. Consider also how gennaios denotes a kinsman and a good man, but no less a well-born and a brave man. You will also see atopos used not only of what is bad and wicked but also of what has no place, for they call that atopos too. It is likewise used of the unsuspected, meaning what one cannot guess (topasai). It further covers the strange, the paradoxical, the marvellous, and even the unreasonable. Besides these, arnymenos is rendered as "getting in exchange" and as "acquiring", and the same word may also include one who guards. Aei does not embrace a single undivided sense either, but splits into opposite meanings. It means "always", as everyone knows, but it also means the opposite, namely "for a time" and "up to a point". Heōs itself sometimes marks off a fixed time. At other times it refuses any limit and lets the time stretch out indefinitely. Antikrys, again, yields "right through", "straight", "in a straight line", "strongly", "wisely" and "directly", and also "simply" and "precisely". If it drops its last consonant and the accent moves from the beginning to the end, it also produces "opposite" and "facing". Do you not see ara as well? I do not mean the one whose accent is split and turned into two parts, but the one pitched with the same accent, which [?] is distinguished from the one that expresses doubt. It denotes the inferential conjunction. It also stands for the filler particle dē, and is used to mean "as it seems" and "apparently". Consider also how many senses atechnōs with the circumflex is divided into. It comes forward in the [sense?] of "truly", of "simply", "completely" and "wholly [?]", and indeed of "strongly" and "once and for all", as its meanings multiply. You may also find atta used in various ways. Now it means hatina ("which things"), now tina ("some"), at other times ha an ("whatever"), and at other times it may mean pote ("at some time"),

and so be divided into this many senses. In addition to those mentioned, there is the common word sophos. It means one who has some share of wisdom. More particularly, it means one devoted to the arts of reasoning. Then it means one who surpasses others in understanding, and also one whom the virtues adorn. It also means one who is fit and visibly ready for whatever he sets out to do. That is why people say, "He was wise at doing evil," and "wise at pursuing virtue." Thespesios may fittingly be ranked with these, for it too means "divine". It also means "gentle", and even "marvellous" and "abundant". Komidēi divides into "very" and "altogether", and also "purely" and "completely". Teōs also contains various senses. It is used in its own sense of "for the time being", but also for "before" and for "until a certain point". It also indicates "to such an extent". Alastōr simply means a criminal, but it also means one who has committed murder with his own hand. It also means the one who pursues such people, as one who watches over deeds not to be forgotten (alasta) and exacts punishment from those who did them. Hence among them Zeus too is called Alastor. You will also find pyon divided into five meanings. It means the drops squeezed from the teats before the milk comes, and the milk itself. It also means blood that has turned, and the milky fluid they also call whey. Some also call pyon new milk boiled together with yesterday's. Eien, too, can signify different things. It is used to begin a speech, and also to express assent and agreement. Some combine the two and take it to signify both agreement with what was said before and the beginning of what is about to be said. It has also been used for "come now!", and others take it in the sense of "I hear" and "I understand". One could fill a [book?] of many lines. One could not do it if one wanted to gather every word with several meanings from every source, for that would be laborious and next to impossible. One could, however, if one chose to collect in one place those that are more common than the rest and more frequent in literature. That is what I myself did when I was passing out of boyhood, as you yourself know. For now, the words mentioned are enough for the purpose. I would not have carried the discussion of them even this far, for I always like to guard against tastelessness. But I know that many people often inquire about some of the words explained here and bring zeal to learning them.

2. Such an abundance of words with several meanings is found in the writings of the ancients, whose life and wisdom, if anything, [consisted in?] choice words [?]. What, then, prevents our sacred writings too, whose aim is to teach and urge saving works, from using signs for different subjects [?]…

[?] For in reply to the Lord's question just before, "But who do you say that I am?", the leader of the apostles gives his own view and that of his fellow disciples. The same sense is seen in "He answered and said to them, Whoever has two tunics, let him share with the one who has none." To the crowds who had asked, he shows where they will reap salvation. So too with "John answered them, saying, I baptize with water; but among you stands one whom you do not know." This also serves the same purpose, and so do countless other passages. But in "At that time Jesus answered and said, I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth," the word clearly departs from the sense described above. Here it holds the place of a beginning. No question came before it, and it did not follow anyone's words. Jesus himself began the speech and offered thanksgiving to the Father. The same holds for "The ruler of the synagogue answered, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath," and also for "The high priest answered and said to him, I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God." The following may also hold the place of a beginning: "Jesus answered and said, Whoever receives you in my name receives me; and whoever receives me receives not me but the one who sent me."

3. In "Jesus answered and said to her, O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish," however, the word belongs to neither of the senses described. Instead, it introduces the continuation of a conversation. The Canaanite woman had lamented her daughter's suffering and begged for healing. When she met the rebuff meant to turn her zeal aside, she took it with good grace and said, "Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from their masters' table." Then, continuing the exchange, comes the reply, "Then Jesus answered and said to her, Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish." Clearly Jesus accepted her words of good grace and entreaty, praised her faith, and granted the healing. The passage "Jesus answered and said to him, Blessed are you, Simon

son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you" points to the same sense. He takes up in his reply the confession that had proclaimed him the Christ and the Son of the living God, and adds the blessing. To the same class belongs "John answered him, saying, Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, who does not follow us," and many others like it. Then there is the account of the divine manifestation at the Transfiguration. It presents Moses and Elijah conversing with the Lord, and in it Peter asked that three tents be made for them. There the words "Peter answered" signify supplication and entreaty. The same is true of "Peter answered and said, Lord, if it is you, bid me come to you on the waters." Jesus was leading the disciples out of their fearful state of mind, saying, "Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid." Peter seized on this as an occasion that moved him to entreaty, and said, "Lord, if it is you, bid me come to you on the waters." Clearly "answered" here signifies supplication and entreaty. So it does where the Scriptures say, "Peter answered and said, Explain this parable to us," for this too shows a need for supplication and entreaty. And who would fail to see that "he answered" is sometimes used for "he accepted" and "he agreed"? Our Saviour had declared the two first commandments of the Law, and the scribe concurred and agreed with the Lord's judgment. The evangelist then adds, "And when Jesus saw that he had answered wisely, he said to him, You are not far from the kingdom of God." It is quite plain that the Scriptures indicated the scribe's acknowledgment and agreement by the word "answered".

4. Elsewhere the word would signify something superfluous. The ruler of the synagogue had left his daughter sick and at the point of death, and had begged Jesus to come and become the child's saviour. Meanwhile the report came telling him of her death. Then the evangelist adds, "But Jesus, hearing it, answered him, Do not be afraid; only believe." It is evident that even if "answered" were not inserted at all, the rest of the sentence would convey the same meaning no less. The same holds for "Peter answered and said to him, Even if all fall away because of you, I never will." The evangelist Mark shows most clearly that "answered" is superfluous here. He covers the very same passage that Matthew narrated with "answered", yet has no need of the word at all: "But Peter said to him, Even if all fall away, yet I will not." It is shown just as clearly to be superfluous in the account of Pilate, when he tried to release Jesus from the murderous intent of the Jews. Each of the

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople.

…other evangelists framed the sentence with "answered". But the divinely wise Luke, recording the same event, did not use "answered" at all, and so showed that the others had used the word as a superfluous addition. He said, "Pilate therefore addressed them again, wishing to release Jesus." There would be many such cases. But our aim is not to collect a mass of testimonies. It is only to show by example what the word means, even if the example is limited to a single one. Take also what was said after the healing of the bent-over woman, "The ruler of the synagogue answered, indignant." If one removed "answered", the rest of the phrase would unfold the same meaning unimpaired. So, I think, it has been clearly shown that "answered" often marks the beginning of a speech. It also marks the continuation of words already spoken. It can stand as a superfluous addition, and it can serve the purpose of supplication.

5. The words of Peter, leader of the apostles, show plainly that it also takes on the sense of asking. The account reports what happened to Ananias and Sapphira, and the death exacted for their lying. It continues, "And his wife came in, not knowing what had happened." Then it adds, "And Peter answered her, Tell me whether you sold the land for so much?" What else could be found that fits better what "answered" means here than "he asked"? So too with "The Jews answered and said to him, What sign do you show us for doing these things?" And so with "Jesus answered them, Did I not choose you, the twelve?" In these cases it is clear that each word has the force of "he asked".

But "answered" does not mean only these things. Sometimes it is not directed at any spoken words at all, but at people's inward thoughts. Take the passage "Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, that she is a sinner."
