Notice that no question had come before. The word does not refer to the beginning of the speech that follows, and the phrase brings in none of the other senses mentioned above. Yet the evangelist adds, "And Jesus answered and said to him, Simon, I have something to say to you." Then, proceeding by way of a question, Jesus rebuked the blasphemy in Simon's thoughts and, as far as his own love for humanity could, reshaped them toward reverence and freedom from doubt. It is clear that "Jesus answered and said to him", placed before the explanation mentioned above, was given in response to the movement of thoughts in the depths of the heart. Of the same kind is "Jesus answered the lawyers". This is added in response to the turmoil and agitation in their minds when the man with dropsy [?] before

…they saw standing [before] them; and though their suffering should have moved them to pity, they would not let go of their madness. The same meaning would also be conveyed by: "Jesus answered and said to them, Truly, truly I tell you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be removed into the sea,' it will be removed." Going only by the obvious sense of the sequence, "answered" here might have stood for a meditation in the depth of the heart. But the divine Mark, who reports the passage more clearly, moves the meaning over to the taking up of the conversation. For after saying, "And Peter remembered and said to him, 'Rabbi, look, the fig tree that you cursed has withered,'" he brings in Jesus taking up the conversation and saying, "Have faith in God. For truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart but believes that what he says is happening, it will be done for him." 6. Now suppose the same passage of the Oracles were to be regarded as an example not of just one of the senses mentioned, but could be drawn to both the opening and the taking up of a conversation, and perhaps also to the redundant use. Even so, the number of meanings will not shrink to fewer, but [will keep] its [full] count [?]. It is enough not to confuse [?] the multiplicity, even if some of the examples are found that can be referred not to one meaning only but to different ones, so long as any one of them is found to take on fully the meaning of a single sense. For the fact that different meanings somehow coincide with one another in certain sayings is no reason to abolish their multiplicity, since they are characterized not by what they share but by how they differ. So one must consider each according to its difference and keep its form unconfused, and not use what draws them into common ground to destroy the otherness among them. 7. Not only do different meanings spring from "answered," as the discussion has shown, but "asked" also conveys at least two senses in our sacred Oracles. One of these lies on the surface even in outside writers, and usually expects an answer. The other stands far from this sense and means "entreated" and "requested," and it appears no less abundantly in the God-wise oracles than the former. For "he asked for alms"; and "they asked him, 'Rabbi, eat'"; and "I ask you, have me excused"; and "one of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him"; and countless other passages plainly take the place of supplicating and begging, as no one fails to see. "Asked" is also used in place of "commanded," "ordered," and "said." "For Jesus," it says, "getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, asked him to put out a little from the land." Here the expression is not a demand for an answer, nor does

["asked"] mean "entreated" here. Rather, it puts forward the force of an order and a command. This is shown above all by what comes before and after in the passage. It is not only that the Saviour was speaking as a teacher, with the crowd listening gladly and giving him the honour due to a teacher, and so spoke with authority. It is also that a little later, when Jesus orders Simon to do something similar close by, the evangelist puts "said" in place of "asked" for the same purpose: "For he said," it says, "to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.'" Both words have imperative force. But this summary account will, I think, be enough to meet your need. Since you remember what has been said, you will not fail to see which passages of the sacred oracles each of the meanings of "answered" fits. As for the other words that the sacred writings used for different matters, some have already been covered in our discussion, and others may perhaps be supplied if the divine love for humankind looks on us more kindly.

QUESTION 22. Why did the angel not appear before Joseph thought of sending Mary away, so as to forestall his deliberation, but appeared to stop him only when he had moved from deliberation to action? And why does he call the Virgin Joseph's wife? Not a few of our blessed Fathers have discussed the present question. I know that some of them said the angel appeared at that moment and held the righteous man back from his purpose so that, in announcing that the Virgin was pregnant, he would not need to be believed on other grounds, but would have the pregnancy itself as a witness to the conception. Others may perhaps have given similar reasons, insofar as they drew on the wisdom from above. It seems to me, however, that each thing said or done exerts its proper force when it waits for its proper time, for what comes out of season usually breaks the power of its effect. So when Joseph had fallen into perplexity in his thoughts, then the angel appeared to resolve the strife of those thoughts. That he was perplexed and tossed by the contrary winds of his deliberations is clear from his deliberating about the deed;

[?] her descent from an illustrious family (for she came from a royal and priestly tribe), and her consecration in the temple in her earliest years. These things, and more besides, kept the old man far from suspicion: not only from the suspicion that seeks to call someone to account, but even from the kind that is merely wary of impropriety. Nor, on the other hand, did he know that the conception was the work of God, for this deed of God's care for us lay beyond all human thought and reason. So, troubled in his thoughts, he could not see what he might do so as neither to outrage the name of "righteous" nor to fail to be seen doing what pleases God. When, then, he was being shaken by such things, and the leaning of human judgment to one side or the other had failed him, the angel came most fittingly and at the right time to steady his agitated mind on the point where it needed to stand unshaken. He says: "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife, for what is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus." No longer, he says, be at a loss, and do not let conflicting opinions persuade you to waver over what to do. What is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. The begetting [?] of the Holy Spirit and the will of the flesh cannot, as you well know, come together into one or claim the same act as their own. The word is astonishing, but it is the good news of a still more astonishing birth: "It is from the Holy Spirit," and "She will bear a son." See the son even before the birth. And when he is born, let the prediction be your proof of what has come to pass and of the rest of the truth of the Gospels. For he who knows what is still hidden in the chambers of nature, and announces beforehand that it is a son, also became the craftsman of the flesh fashioned without seed and beyond reason. He is the guardian of her virginity, leaving its seals unbroken before the birth just as after it. "And you shall call his name Jesus": the name too has its decision from above. For he is Jesus "because he will save his people." "Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife." These words not only remove all fear but also bestow a wealth of great joy and of hopes beyond hope. "Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife." When you hear the Virgin called your wife, you have from that word itself her purity from all intercourse with a man. For if she kept her virginity untouched and pure even with the one to whom she was joined by law, how could she accept the love of anyone else? Even if some shadow of suspicion remains: she who became a wife by law and yet kept herself higher and more exalted than betrothal and its lawful rights, how could she have allowed anyone else room to break the law? How could she exchange his favour for outrage, she who would not even endure leaving her virginity where no outrage was involved [?]? You therefore have within yourself an incontestable testimony to her purity. So "do not be afraid to take Mary your wife." For by the very means through which she kept her [virginity] undefiled toward you, [she can also silence] the gainsayers [?]. "A wife," he says, "you see, and

she is called mine [?], and you have had no experience of her." If the Virgin showed that she was clear of intercourse with the very man to whom the name "wife" was applied, how is it not plain that she was clear of every other man as well, in relation to whom no word, human or divine, was ever seen calling her wife? In this way, then, the angel teaches Joseph through the title "wife" that she is clear of every impure suspicion. He may perhaps also call her wife because the righteous man denied her none of the care a husband gives his wife. He did not neglect to provide for her in other respects; he looked after her as she lived with him at home; and as a decent husband of a chaste wife, he took pains that she should be seen to be above all blame and every slander. And if he called her wife because Joseph held the position of betrothed, I need not disagree. Just as custom does not forbid calling betrothed men husbands even though they have not yet come together in bed, so it allows betrothed women who still keep their virginity to be called their wives. Jacob the patriarch, too, plainly calls Rachel his wife, though he had not yet come to know her in intercourse. Having already completed the term of his servitude, he says to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her." So it is an old custom to call even betrothed women wives. From this, too, one may gather that the title "wife" is in no way meant to impair virginity. That the name "woman" does not conflict with virginity is also made clear by the usual division of the human race, which splits nature into man and woman. For the word "woman" includes not only those who have known a man, nor only those who have passed beyond girlhood with their virginity unchanged, but also the female before maturity, right down to the newborn. In just the same way, the designation "man" covers both those who have fathered children and those still in the ranks of unmarried youths, and also those below that age down to infancy. So from customary usage, too, one may gather that the word "wife" does not take away the claim to virginity. For [Scripture] names Eve the wife of Adam not once but many times, while she was still adorned with virginal beauty and blooming among the pure flowers of paradise. She stood far from the transgression of the Master's commandment, from nakedness, and from the serpent's counsel, and she led a loftier way of life. At that time, as you can reckon from the very course of events [?], she kept her thoughts untroubled by bodily pleasure. Though often named Adam's wife, she was deemed worthy of a higher calling than toiling in carnal habits.

…they say that the words before us were spoken [in mockery], and that they reproach Adam because, having imagined extravagant things, he lost through his own folly what the love of his Maker had held out to him in its hands. Others put forward a closely related explanation and think they are saying something different. They say that Adam's downfall is ridiculed and mocked by these words. Still others held that the deed itself was being mocked: the deed by which man ran up in his thoughts higher than his own [nature?] and was brought down from the rank over which his Maker had judged him worthy to preside. These views are similar and start from the same [root?], even if they seem to branch off into different shoots. I would not think it wise to reject them. Yet, following [them?], I would say that I perceive that sacred passage to point to another sense. Which one? Adam, instead of receiving laws, seized the rank of lawgiver. Instead of enjoying care and guidance from above, he steered the actions of his life by his own judgment and foresight. He thought he had the strength, without divine guidance and the assent of the higher power, to be sufficient by himself to tell good from worse. (For had he not settled and confirmed these things within himself, he would not have rushed to exalt himself in his own opinion to the greatness of the first principle, to whom belongs, from eternity, an innate and incomprehensible wisdom for judging and distinguishing good from evil. Yet he dared to put his own impulse ahead of that which rules over all things and is the source of every gift of discernment and distinction. Nor, had it been otherwise, would he have set the divine command at nothing and entrusted the management of what he should do to his own judgment.) Since, then, God says, he has given proof by his deeds: he has entrusted the providence of his life to himself, he no longer wishes to bow to our commands, he has misused the free will given him to insult the giver, and he has thought himself to be like one of us, a lawgiver who receives no law, a provider who needs no providence, a master who is not mastered. So it is better that he be cast out of paradise, chiefly for these two reasons. First, so that he may not come to an untimely and undisciplined enjoyment of delight and slip into worse things. Second, so that, suffering the hardships [?] of exile, he may learn from experience itself the measure of his own power. He would learn how much more profitable it was for him to fasten the movements of his mind and life to our providence, and how far he falls short of knowing good and evil by himself. I think Symmachus too rendered the content of the saying close to this sense: "Behold, Adam has become as one of us, by knowing good and evil of himself." The explanations of the saying given earlier would have taught us to look to nothing else, if we were used to seeing in our sacred oracles the opposite of what is

put forward being indicated and hinted at in a mocking, ironic and derisive manner, and … [?] has force through the letter [?]. Of course, nothing prevents such things from turning up across a wide range of texts, if rarely and unusually. But how could an expression framed as a comparison and likeness fail to slacken the tension of ridicule, irony and derision? On the contrary, if what was said hung together, every word that softens the harshness and bitterness of the reproaches would have had to be avoided. Yet "as one of us" cuts off the sting of irony and smooths the roughness of the insult. For it is not the same, far from it, to say in rebuke, "Behold, Adam has become one of us," and "as one of us." The first delivers mockery that is undiluted, vehement and well aimed. The second, by means of comparison and likeness, makes the rebuke somewhat tempered and moderate. It would then have to explain why it mocks and at the same time withdraws the mockery, when it could have avoided the mode of mockery altogether from the start. Consider this as well. If the speaker who said, "Behold, Adam has become as one of us," were ridiculing, deriding and speaking ironically, he would hardly let us see what connection or coherence the sequel has with it. It would be as if he said: "Since Adam has fallen from the hopes on which he rode with raised brows, he has let go of his irrational impulse, even if unwillingly; dejection has taken the place of his arrogance, and shame at his nakedness has walled him in." Then comes the sequel: "Therefore it was fitting that he be cast out of paradise, lest the boldness that had come over him and the haughtiness of his mind should make his hand bolder and drive it to seize the things that he had not before dared even to touch." Do these statements hang together at all, or do they preserve a sense free of contradiction? And indeed the sequel shows nothing other than what was said, for it says: "And now, lest he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life and eat, and live forever." For if he were being mocked for falling short of his expectation, as these words would show, how is it not evident that he would have turned all his power into weakness and lost the boldness he had swaggered in? It would not be fitting for one held back from within to be walled off from what he was formerly walled off from, since the very failure of his purpose and the shattering of his proud spirit would be enough to lead him away from a second act of boldness. It is also clear that our mockery would openly brand the collapse and weakness of his youthful reasonings. But keeping him from partaking of the tree of life testifies to his [boldness?] after the transgression, and to his daring to do what he could not do before. For no one bars a man who is already barred from within. But these are a few points out of many. Some of the more refined interpreters have said that "Behold, Adam has become as one of us" refers not to the

supremacy of the Trinity, but looks to the multitude of the ministering and incorporeal powers. This explanation is open to the objections already mentioned, and beyond that I do not see what room it has to be brought in here at all. For the passage does not mock the serpent's counsel, nor was Adam ever caught having somehow conceived a desire to enter into the nature of angels. Nor was he far removed from angelic glory, since he spent his days in paradise and enjoyed immortality through his Maker's providence. For these reasons I am not readily inclined to accept such an interpretation of the saying, especially because the part of speech used in place of a noun takes such a form. Perhaps others have contemplated things more divine and more perfect than what has been said here. As for me, the blow of many successive trials comes upon me, so that I neither remember these things nor have any leisure to set myself to research, for to this the envy of men has shut us in. Yet none of this has kept me from saying, at your most learning-loving request, what I could say from what I have understood, even though … [?] a pretext for silence. As a concise summary, and given the circumstances, what has been said should suffice. If you add something to it yourself, you will repay the favour no less to yourself than to us, your teachers. Perhaps, if you supply some starting point, we too may come to think something wiser about the matters before us, as our zeal presses on not far from the Mosaic vision of God, especially if the afflictions that beset us are eased by the goodwill of the One above.

QUESTION 24. How could the death of Christ be said to be both willed and unwilled by the Father? And again, how could the same death be both willed and unwilled by the evil one? 1. The difficulty calls for a more subtle contemplation and a reasoned distinction. It is not unacceptable to show that each side of the difficulty has considerable support. But we must first bring out the weight each side carries, and then try to offer the solution in proper order. That the cross of Christ was the Father's will, the Saviour himself teaches us when he asked to be spared death, saying, "Yet not my will, but yours be done." At that point, showing the reality of his human nature, he prayed to be spared the passion and called it unwilled. And not only then, but also when he rebuked Peter. He called his voluntary death the mind of God, and [the opposing view] the mind of the devil. Peter was carried along by that mind at the time, and for this he was condemned to bear that one's name. [They were together?], though not from the same disposition. The one acted from an affection that was out of season; the other [acted against] our salvation, by the evil and the snares he worked against it. Yet they flowed together into one, though from opposing purposes

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. [?] …having set out [?], by not wishing to suffer [?] he healed the passions of human nature. For the author of evil saw that all-immaculate and God-befitting body subject to the natural and blameless passions, and so he plotted his scheme and was eager to put it into action. But when he saw, in turn, the radiance of the divine dignity flashing out beyond all through the divine signs, he shrank back and withdrew. Swept toward both willing and at the same time not willing the Lord's death, he found his contrivance turning into helplessness. Nevertheless his madness overcame his cowardice: for that craftsman of bloodshed, habit counted for more than the fear that was springing up in him could frighten him. So then, our sacred Scriptures plainly proclaim that the death of the Son was willed by the Father, but unwilled by the evil one. And yet that the death by the cross was what he strove for more than anything can be gathered from many other things, and from sources where it is not obscure: for it was when he stirred them up to do evil that the nation of the Jews contrived the death of the Savior. In the same way it is evident that the passion of the Son was not willed by the Father either, and as the discussion proceeds this will be shown more fully.

2. Now that these points have been set out in order, it is fitting to reason and consider that, even if contrary things are said about the same matter (the Lord's death, I mean), they are not said in the same way. One is said with reference to the very suffering he underwent, the other with reference to its outcome. The outcome achieved through the death was the salvation of the human race and the overthrow of the devil's tyranny. This, clearly, was both willed by the Father and his good pleasure, and the culmination of all his providence for the human race. And how is it not plain that this same outcome was both unwilled by the enemy and his final blow? The slaughter of the Son, however, which was the act carried out through the passion, was in itself neither sweet to the Father nor acceptable, but even fully deserving of anger and wrath, just as to the evil one it was pleasing and the most delightful of all delights. That is why our loving Savior, too, in the form of a prayer, sought forgiveness for those who had outraged him: "Father," he says, "forgive them this sin, for they do not know what they are doing." So the slaughter of the Child was unwilled by the Father, and it stirred up such indignation that it needed the very intercession of the one wronged, so that the wrongdoers, cleansed through repentance, might not pay the penalty. Nor is it contradictory that the Father both wills and does not will the death of the Son. The one is said with reference to the achievement that resulted, the other with reference to the act itself that came first.

3. Consider a general who sees his champion receiving wounds, and by those wounds emptying the ranks of the enemy, and even striking down the enemy's commander. He rejoices at the

trophy the champion sets up over the adversaries, and when he looks at how astonishing the achievement is, he is not pained by the wounds. But when he considers the blows in themselves and turns his attention to them, he is not glad to see the man who has won the victory wounded. So too with the Father. Insofar as he saw the Son striking down the enemy of the human race through the blows on his body, it was a cause of the joy befitting God, and he took pride in the Child's valor. But insofar as his Beloved was wounded with blows and bruises, this in itself he did not count as something to be chosen. Indeed, the element of willing is greater here than in the example. There, when the wounds begin, the victory is still uncertain, and the sight is bitter to the general, since the rout of the enemy has not yet appeared. Here, however, from the wounds themselves, or rather even before the murderers outraged the Savior with wounds, the trophy was seen in all its splendor, no less than when the most accursed men dared what should never be dared. For to God even future things are present, and his knowledge of both proceeds equally. In this respect nothing still to come, and nothing that happened long ago, falls short of what is already present. So there is no longer any difficulty in the death of the Son being both willed and unwilled by the Father. Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that it was eagerly sought by the enemy of our nature, the author of evil, while the outcome [?] that came of his eagerness dealt him a blow harsher than any other. For the evil one rejoiced in the blood and gloated over the Savior, but before the joy [?] had sunk deep into his entrails, the incurable blow was already overtaking him, along with inescapable destruction. The Father, on the other hand, was not pleased by the shedding of the blood in itself, yet he was supremely pleased when he saw the end that came with it, and he received it with great joy. He did not love the slaughter of the Child for its own sake. Rather, as has been said, he made it his own because of its end and turned it into a matter of good pleasure.

4. And from this, if you wish, you also have a starting point that leads toward the solution of an old problem. Even if the problem is not unknown to those who study divine things, it is still more useful to state it for the common knowledge of all. If the saving blood was given as a ransom to bring about our race's deliverance from captivity, who received it? The slaughter of the Child was not sweet to the Father. And as for the robber and murderer, would it not be outrageous to let him become master of the Lord's blood? Many other things will provide the resolution of the question, and it may not be out of place to mention them shortly. But from what has been said it is clear [?] that the Father receives the blood of the Son out of longing for the outcome, while the evil one dared, in his boldness, to take it, but received in return the overthrow of his

tyranny and the unexpected and incurable blow. He even suspected it, so that at one and the same time he leapt upon the cross and shrank back and withdrew from his God-fighting impulse. I think the difficulty will no longer have the power to trouble the ears of the devout. Still, nothing prevents us from coming to what was promised. A ransom generally has reference to two things: it is the means of releasing those held captive, and it is also seen as a gift to the one who holds them. As the release of those held captive, the saving blood would be a ransom; as a gift to the captor, by no means. Indeed, many other features that belong to what is properly called a ransom do not belong to this ineffable dispensation, which is beyond reason. The one who gives a ransom can no longer be master of what he has handed over, so the loss inescapably follows; while the one who receives it gains, and becomes master of what he previously had no authority over. Here everything is the opposite. The one who laid down the ransom has plainly suffered no loss, for all things are in his hand, and neither the blood of Abel nor that of the martyrs stands outside his providence and his hand. Who could ever think to say that he takes account of his servants and of the blood they shed, and hears them crying out even after death as immortals, but does not keep the saving and life-giving blood of the world in the immortal treasuries of his providence, preserved for himself indestructible and untouched by bodily corruption? So the lover of mankind not only lost nothing in laying down the ransom, but gained besides the salvation of our whole race. And the one who thought he had received it, since he only thought he had received it, lost besides the very tyranny he prided himself on and thought he was strengthening. So the saving blood of the Lord would hold the place of a ransom, for it brought us back from captivity. But it differs from a ransom in that it was not offered to the one who enslaved our nature by deceit; and in that with this ransom the gain is seen to be great, with no loss at all to be reckoned against it, while for the one who held the captives the loss is double, or rather total. And, if you like, add this: other ransoms are preceded by negotiations for an agreement, but here, while the ransom was being prepared, the just judgment which long ago had decreed implacable hostility against the enemy then imposed on him an even heavier condemnation because of what he was doing. And in other cases truces are always made, whether for a long or a short time; but in the present ransom one cannot conceive, even in bare thought, of anything of the kind having been put forward beforehand. And how many other such points there are! So there is no need to press the argument in the way it can be pressed in the case of a ransom in the proper sense. For here, if anywhere, the word has been taken by metaphor.

5. And it is clear that we must not forcibly fit onto metaphorical expressions everything that usually accompanies the thing named by the word in its original sense. We must bring what has now been worked out on the problem before us into a common pattern. Then, for the many cases that can give rise to the same difficulty, we can apply the solution by a ready and more general method, and clear away what causes confusion. I do not say (far from it!) that we must not use figurative terms. Their use is familiar to us, hardly less than that of proper terms. If one removed them from everyday conversation, and from the very language of written works, especially those figures that are very similar and close to words used without any figure, one would confine the use of language to a narrow space, not much less [?] than if one banished the proper sense of words from our usage, so that many things could not even be expressed by name. So we must not condemn as useless the words that originate in a figure of speech. But this I would say: one must know the distinctive character of a word used in its proper sense and of one applied to things by some transference. One should use the words as custom allows, but not of necessity gather what they signify into the same nature and weave them together. That would be the cause of great errors, and difficulties will seem to emerge which do not in truth have the character of a difficulty, but arise from an unreasonable use of meanings, so that those who use words this way contrive a difficulty not so much against others as against themselves.

6. For instance, we call those who contended for Christ "martyrs," that is, witnesses, and we say that they offered their blood to God, and rightly and justly so. But each of these is said by a transfer of terms. Civic life is accustomed to call "witnesses" those who are present to confirm the truth in the affairs of life, and who lend credibility to what is put forward by what they know. From these we name the champions of true religion "martyrs," witnesses. For truly these men, proclaiming the divinity of the Truth who exists in his own person, bore witness before tyrants and kings. And we say that they offered their blood to Christ, transferring the term "offering" from those offerings in which Abel the righteous offered the fat of the lambs, Abraham the divided pieces, and Melchizedek bread and wine to Abraham, and, if you like, the tithe which the one who was blessed offered to Melchizedek. Clearly each of those who made an offering offered something other than himself, without suffering anything painful or having any of his limbs cut off. But the martyrs of Christ did not offer anything separate from themselves, nor did they remain unharmed in body as they made their offering. Nor did they come forward to bear witness because someone called them; they bore that wondrous, God-proclaiming witness of their own free resolve. If, then, someone does not distinguish the meanings of "martyr" and "witness," and applies to the one the accidents

[?]? That is why the word "answered" (apekrithē) as well, which you said often throws you into ambiguity—to pass over for now "was separated," and the senses that physicians in particular know: "was dispersed," "was excreted," "was poured out," and "ended in this." But where it is used in the familiar way of the divinely wise Scriptures, "answered" has the sense no one is ignorant of, the reply given to a question. Often, however, it serves merely as a filler. At other times it marks the beginning of a speech. Yes, and it can also imply taking up a word spoken earlier. And you will find it meaning "entreated" and "begged," and also "asked." Examples of the meaning everyone knows are many and easy to find, such as: "Simon Peter answered and said, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.'" For in reply to the Lord's preceding question, "But who do you say that I am?", the chief of the apostles gives his own view and that of his fellow disciples. And in "He answered and said to them, 'Whoever has two tunics should share with the one who has none,'" the same sense is seen, for to those who asked what they should do, he shows how they will gain salvation. So too: "John answered them, saying, 'I baptize with water; but among you stands one whom you do not know.'" For this too belongs to the same use, as do countless others. But "At that time Jesus answered and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,'" clearly differs from the sense just mentioned and marks a beginning, for no question came before it,

and insists on doing so [?], will he not fill the ears of less experienced listeners with perplexities? And he himself will be no less mistaken, thinking that he is putting forward a difficulty which arises not from the hardness of the subject, but from his own ignorant handling of the terms. For here too he will readily say: "When the martyrs offered their blood, who received it? If Christ, how can the lover of mankind delight in human blood? If the evil one, how could they bear to pour out their own blood as a libation to the enemy? And where is the judge who gave both parties under judgment an equal hearing? And who are the parties under judgment, to one of whom the witness has come forward to give the advantage that brings victory?"

7. And how many such things might someone take from civic witnesses and transfer to the witnesses who proclaim God, if he has a squalid passion for difficulties and sees no outrage in telling tales and playing games even in serious matters! It takes no effort to answer the first kind of difficulty: Christ was pleased not with the blood of the contestants but with their resolve, and so accepted both the slaughter and the blood that was shed. Nor is it hard to add that the martyrs were slain for Christ and shed their blood (this is said properly and not figuratively), but "they offered" and "they were offering" and the like are words that have taken on a figurative sense. So there is no need to ask to whom they offered it, just as there is no need to ask how those whose bodies were put to death by the shedding of their blood could be said to offer anything, or how they could offer without presenting something other than themselves, which is what those who offer in the proper sense do. Such things are so far from being a real difficulty that it is better to ignore them, lest by engaging with those who play games we should seem to you, not unreasonably, to share in their discredit. For just as playing in serious matters is senseless, so being serious about rather laughable things is ridiculous. But matters that are manifestly absurd and carry their own refutation with them [?] still cause confusion and uproar when they are put before the ears of the many, and of those who lack the judgment to distinguish words used without a figure from those that the law of figurative speech has shaped. For those who have examined the difference between them, by contrast, it is easier to fend off the idle curiosity of the apparent difficulty and dissolve it. So we should use the words and apply them to the things we are accustomed to apply them to, but we should know what accompanies each, and keep both the meaning and the distinctive character of each unconfused. This can be seen from the following. The civic witness supports one of the litigants and exposes the other as a false accuser, while the judge gives the parties an equal hearing. But in the case of the witness who proclaims God, where is there any such relationship? Or where does the [?] get its boldness? Again, the athlete strikes his opponent with hands and fists, overpowers him in the end, and wins the victor's crown. Here, by contrast, the martyr binds on the diadems of victory while being pelted and wounded and put to death by fire or sword, or by whatever other means public cruelty has devised against human nature to take people out of life. And in countless other cases the

difference is the same. How, then, is it not unreasonable to look for the same features in each of the two meanings, and to force onto the one what belonged to the other?

8. Many of the names assigned to different things show the difference most plainly, so that not even someone who has reached the extreme of shamelessness or feebleness would, without shame or scruple, transfer to the one what is acknowledged of the other. But many conceal their difference: for example, "martyr" or "witness," "athlete," "ransom," "trophy," "the palaces of Hades," and countless others. In such cases it is easier for the person trying to raise a difficulty often to be deceived himself, or to lead others into deception without noticing it. So one must take the rule from those words where the divergence is most obvious and the solution of what is proposed is entirely on the surface. Then, by the same common method, one can set straight those words which are very close to one another and so present a more plausible appearance of deception, and thus preserve in their case too the unerring judgment taken from the obvious cases. Take, for example, "the pinnacle of the temple," in Greek its pterygion, "little wing." Among those who care about the Attic tongue, some call the pterygion the aetos, others the aetōma. They say it is the roof of sacred buildings, whose shape imitates the creature in flight, and some also call it the pteron, "wing." Others distinguish the pteron and pterygion from the aetos and aetōma, saying that what these denote is the structure, built of stone, that rises up high in front of temples. But suppose someone brought up the pterygion and asked whether it was spread out in the air and, moving, served the bird in its flight, or was drawn in and folded, bringing the winged creature into the posture of one at rest. I think that instead of getting a solution to his difficulty, he would provoke laughter. He might even add a novel twist: whichever answer one gives, one will be caught saying something impossible. An outstretched wing cannot support the bulk of a body and a weight standing on it, and neither can a wing that is folded in; still less could it bear anything standing on it at all. Do not those who bring forward such things, instead of driving others into perplexity, lead themselves into ridicule long before? For anyone who happens to be there, I think, will readily say: "My good men, these clever puzzles might perhaps raise a difficulty in the other meaning, but here nothing of the kind can be said, and no pretext for a difficulty appears to arise." So from words that show their difference so clearly, it is easier, and no labor at all, to apply the common rule also to those that keep it hidden, and so to turn difficulties into easy solutions.

9. The cross of Christ is a trophy set up over the devil, and the most splendid of trophies, since even its mere sign traced in the air puts all his power to flight along with him. And surely no deeper reflection is needed if someone into a

[?] should choose to twist the saying into a difficulty [?]. From what has already been said, the matter is very easy to settle. For example: if the cross is a trophy, who set up the trophy? If it was the victor, why is the Jewish nation accused for nothing of killing Christ? But if they themselves fixed it in the ground, and that is not in dispute, how can Christ be said to have set up a trophy against the devil? In the same way, if someone speaks of the kingdom of Hades, he clearly brings in a king as well. And Paul, the herald of the truth, says somewhere that death reigned from Adam to Moses, not only over those whose sin was in the likeness of Adam's, but also over those who sinned by imitating that transgression. But if death is a king, then a king is entrusted with law, with rank, and with the consent of his subjects. If death has these things, how would it be reasonable for him to suffer loss instead of receiving the reward and honour due to one who reigned justly? Each of these points, perhaps even on its own, shows the solution no less than the difficulty to those who look more closely. Above all, though, what has already been said makes the answer easy. It is plain that the cross is called a trophy by a transfer of the word from the trophies set up in wars, since through it Christ brilliantly overthrew the enemy. It is not called a trophy because he set up the cross. He did not set it up himself. The God-fighting nation fixed it in the ground, not as a trophy against the enemy, but as an instrument for punishing the common Saviour. He, however, turned their wickedness into victory over the enemy, and so used the cross as a trophy. So the defilement of the Jews did not set up the trophy, and neither did the Saviour of our race fix the cross in place for himself. They fixed it to punish the Master, and he changed it into a trophy for the salvation of our nature. Likewise, Hades is said to have a kingdom and Death is called a king. This is not because he held lordship over his subjects by laws and with their consent, since these things belong to what the word "king" means in its proper sense. Rather, whoever reigns on earth holds unaccountable power over those under his hand, and death seized this power through the transgression. In this sense he can be called a king and his realm a kingdom, if the name is used in a transferred sense. Before the cross his rule over us could not be resisted: it cut off every hope of resurrection and made us dead. But since the Lord's passion stripped him of his strength entirely, it is fitting and reasonable for us to say that his kingdom was despoiled. 10. So it is possible, I think, to say with a glad mind and an outspoken tongue how the Son's death was both willed and not willed by the Father, and how each of these things is said with reference to the enemy. It is also possible to say that he endured the cross for us, and that in his love for humankind he poured out his own blood, but did not offer it to anyone. His aim was not to offer it, but to rescue through his passion what had been lost. So he did not offer it, unless someone likes to call his suffering for us an "offering" by meta-

phor. Because of the likeness, nothing prevents a word from being used in the figure called a trope. But in that case it is not proper to demand of the word the exact meaning of the term used in its proper sense. It is clear, then, that the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world neither offered nor presented the blood that saves and cleanses our race, even though the Father, because of what resulted from the passion, is said to have received his Child's blood with a delighted and glad mind. Your request perhaps called for a fuller treatment of these matters. Still, they have been set out here in summary form. I have not forgotten how often, in our leisurely studies of our most sacred doctrines, I heard your virtue sifting such questions. So if forgetfulness has taken anything from your reasonings, these remarks should make it easier for you to recall what has been left out.

QUESTION 25. Whose voice says, "All this took place": the evangelist's or the archangel's? That it belongs to someone astonished and marvelling at the extraordinary nature of the deeds and words is clearly shown both by this section of the passage and by the way the words are put together. "For all this took place," he says, meaning: how did all this come about? How, O wonder, did this astonishing thing appear, so full of amazement? How did the sun look on such a thing? How did human beings come to know such a thing? He had proclaimed the birth without seed, the conception from the Holy Spirit, and the name of Saviour, which Jesus received because he saves his people. He saves them not from bodily diseases, which the hands of physicians have often been able to treat, but from the very sicknesses and defilements of the soul, for which no cleansing or cure can be found without God's favour and assent. Because he had said these things, and had given the name of Saviour taken from that benefit to all, he immediately added: "All this took place to fulfil what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.'" It is clear, then, that these words belong to someone astonished and marvelling at the boundless ocean of providence toward the human race. But whether the angel said them or the evangelist himself, the sayings lose nothing either way. Things of great rank often gain added weight from the standing of those who speak them as well. But these things

[?] carry, beyond all measure, a superiority over everything. QUESTION 26 [or 25]. Why, when Christ was born, did he allow the slaughter of the infants to take place because of him? Your question is a fine one and shows compassion. Its solutions are perhaps not inferior to it; indeed, I think they lead to a sweeter judgement. Herod's bloodthirstiness had to be made plain and evident to all. If he had shown it by killing people who had reached full age, nothing would have prevented his crowd of flatterers and hangers-on from inventing reasons to make his guilt for the murder seem less. They could have declared the victims guilty of many crimes and said that a king should not leave wrongs unpunished. In the case of infants, however, not even the most shameless teller of tales will find room to imagine or invent anything of the kind. Instead his hatred of humankind is exposed naked through and through, without excuse, along with the unsurpassable [?] of his murderous mind, tongue and hand.

Besides, the new and sinless victim was to cleanse the sin of the race, and so the sacrifices that came before him had to be free of all sin, at least of the sin committed through deeds. They had to be pure, so that they would not dishonour the great victim by being sacrificed themselves. That is why a chorus of infants was more fitting than people caught in some lapses to [?] the divine Lamb who takes away the sin of the world.

And if you like, a consolation that has been tested in the greatest calamities can be seen springing up from this as well. The babies whose lives were incapable of sin are slaughtered. So when people suffer, they need not think they suffer because of the weight of their offences, and so take a heavier and more bitter blow from their sufferings and look toward despair. Instead, they have the sinlessness of the babies and the outrage committed against them by those accursed men as an example to comfort them, one that is enough to urge them to patience. And so they rise up to give thanks to the One who wisely orders all our affairs. There is more. Envy had no room to be kindled against the infants, for what pretext for envy could newborn babies give? Yet he rushed to slaughter them so shamelessly and without precedent. This makes it easy to solve another question and to make it simple. How did the Christ-hating race of the Jews condemn the Saviour to the cross and a shameful death, when he had done them good and healed incurable diseases, instead of glorifying him and repaying him with crowns of thanks? If the ruler of the Jews pursued with slaughter the blameless, against whom envy had no way in, what would those not dare who had been schooled and trained by him in murder, especially with so great an envy leading them as their general? When people can be seen doing great and wonderful works that turn the eyes and the goodwill of the many toward them, the more those works stir the grateful to praise, sweet wonder and reverence, the more this abominable passion takes hold of the ungrateful and malicious and arms itself with invincible power. And if you would like to consider still more reasons: first, the righteous Abel owed nothing, as far as any debt from his own deeds was concerned. When he was handed over and subjected to death, he showed that the foundation on which death's [kingdom] was being laid was rotten. After him, many who were guilty walled it round and roofed it over into a fortress. But the Saviour, who had come to benefit our race, was about to despoil its kingdom. So the infants, like bodyguards and forerunners of the great King, sinless and drenched in martyrs' blood, are arranged and sent ahead to reach those held in Hades. By their coming they announce the Lord's arrival and the redemption of all. They show the wounds of the slaughter they suffered for the Liberator of all, and through these they confirm that the Saviour of the race proclaimed by the prophets has come. What is more, they strike terror into Hades as it sees so great a phalanx of countless people, guilty of no sin, coming upon it, and by this prelude they show it the complete destruction about to fall upon it any moment. For when so many sinless ones were slaughtered at that time, [death's power?] is [?] entirely, and death's legal claim is taken away.

In addition to what has been said, the usual way of God's wisdom is displayed here with special clarity. What is this way? The incomprehensible and inexpressible wisdom of God is generally accustomed to bring things that give joy and gladness out of things that cause grief, and to make opposites spring from their contraries. For example, out of his brothers' envy it made Joseph, the one they envied, lord of Egypt. If those who were born of the same mother's womb had not cast an envious eye on him, he would not have been sold. If he had not been sold and become a slave, and had not refused to shame the freedom of his chastity, he would not have lived in prison. If he had not become a prisoner, he would not have interpreted the dreams of those who were in chains. He would not have come to the king's notice from there, and he would not have been entrusted with ruling Egypt as second to the king. Do you see how great a good grew out of envy and hatred of a brother, and with what glories God crowned Joseph? Later Pharaoh raged against the tribe of Israel, and in his lawlessness he made the river the executioner of the male infants. But because of his bloodthirstiness Moses was brought up in the palace of the Egyptians, instead of in his own home, which was one of many and no different from those of his kinsmen. Divine providence was showing from the outset that the one who was plotted against would himself become master of the power of the plotters. Later he avenged the murder, the wrongs the Egyptian had done to his kinsman, and when he was found out, [he fled] from there. Then, armed with signs and wonders, he appeared again against all expectation, scourged Egypt, and finally freed his kinsmen from their harsh slavery. As for those who had enslaved them, he drowned them with their whole army in the waters of the sea, in requital for the murder in the river. So the very means by which Pharaoh condemned the Hebrew babies to death in the river became the means by which the whole race was rescued from captivity. And the arrogance of the Egyptians, with their army, chariots and captains, went down beneath the water. A person could show many more such examples, gathering them like flowers from the sacred meadows of the Church. In just the same way, through the accursed and murderous slaughter of the infants, crowns of martyrdom, pure and undefiled, blossomed and were woven for those blessed ones. They received the right to stand boldly before God, to join the bodiless ranks in that unending dance with inexpressible joy and gladness, and to enjoy the most blessed and highest of all the sights anyone could desire. How many slaughters, what severe torments, could be counted an equal price for these things? So it was not better in any respect to prevent the lawless and untimely death of the babies. It was far better to let it go ahead and permit it, since so many eternal and inexpressible goods sprang up for them from it. But let these words be a kind of sacred offering to your sacred love of learning. If anyone who has been initiated into Paul's ineffable words wishes to initiate
us more fully, we would gladly become his disciples together, and we would acknowledge that we owe the man our gratitude all our lives.

QUESTION 27. We say there is one God and three hypostases, and we call the Father God, the Son likewise God, and the Spirit in the same way. Why, then, when we say there is one Godhead and three hypostases, can we no longer call the Father Godhead, or the Son, or the Spirit, or all of them together? We do not call the thearchic hypostases together Godhead, even though they are said to be contemplated in one Godhead, and, if you like, to be known and contained in it. A reasonable cause for this can be found in the fact that we cannot call each of those blessed and creative hypostases by itself Godhead. But why do we call each of the transcendent hypostases God, yet not also Godhead? One might perhaps consider it as follows. Or rather, before this we must ask whether God and Godhead are the same or different, since the present question grew from that starting point. If they are different, what is the Godhead, and what is there besides God? If they are the same, how is it that each of the life-originating hypostases is called God but is not called Godhead? Some have blamed the grammatical form of the words: one is masculine, while the other takes the feminine gender, and that is why both are not [equally] said of the Father, the Son and the Spirit. These people are refuted at once. The Spirit is spoken of with a word in the neuter, yet is called God no less than the Father and the Son. The difference in the gender of the names did nothing to prevent the same title from being applied, even though the title did not share the same grammatical gender. Clearer still, "essence", whose word happens to be of another gender, is predicated equally of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, for we call them essence and of one essence. Nor did the difference in grammatical gender prevent man from being called an animal or an essence. What, then, must we say? Is it that, just as man and

humanity do not have different definitions, and yet the one is predicated of Socrates without hindrance and the other is not, so also the words "God" and "Godhead", which do not unfold into different concepts, cannot be said of the thearchic hypostases in the same way? But perhaps someone more refined might say that this sharpens the difficulty rather than solving it, and does not escape the suspicion of begging the question. You may learn from what follows that this objection has missed the point of precision. The argument does not pass from a similar case to the question set for inquiry, nor does it strengthen the difficulty, nor does it incur the charge of begging the question. Rather, the objectors would be shown by this to have reached an incorrect judgement. In the study of nature we see names assigned in such a way that their sameness is not harmed, yet they cannot be used in the same way in predication. Is this not a clear and irrefutable proof that we should not think it baffling or unreasonable to find words used in a similar way in theology? Theology far transcends matter. In the deeper questions it walls the human mind in on every side with great perplexity, and no other names make it any easier to show precisely what is being sought. So we should not think it strange to find there words used in this way, since even in material things they are seen to fit by ancient and customary judgement, not departing from their sameness, yet differing in predication. Where, then, is the sharpening of the difficulty, or the suspicion of the other charge? I know of some who thought they could solve the question by taking man, nature and species, which seem somehow to coincide with one another, yet in predication of Socrates are treated as different rather than as agreeing. Socrates is a man, but he could not be called a species or a nature, nor, if you like, the form joined with these. These people seem to overlook the distinction between kinds of names. Names of natural things are applied clearly and purely to the things that underlie them. But names that came from dialectical conception and carry some dialectical sense have no power to pass over to the things that underlie them, the works of nature. Man and humanity, and indeed Godhead and God, are not products of logical devices, but names of an underlying reality. Still, even from this one can find certain clues that lead toward solving the difficulty. These two sorts of words, the names of things and those that belong to logical skill with regard to expressions, come together and share no small communion with one another even in their distinction. Both contain the particulars, are set above them, and are said in relation to them, even if

not in the same way. For we say that Socrates has a nature, a species and a form [?], even if, unlike what is seen with natural terms, not each part of the statement is put in the nominative case in agreement with him. Again, we say that man and rational mortal animal are the same, and indeed that "capable of laughter" is the same as each of them. Yet not everything that is said of one of these can be said of the others. The one is a property of man, the other a definition, and man could not be called either of these of man, even though they share sameness in the strictest sense. However, the account given of man, nature and species can be applied here as well, and admits the same judgement. For when the words of logic are removed, each of the three is the same as the others. But in the cases already mentioned, someone might blame the difference in grammatical gender and so turn the difficulty into something easily solved. What would he say about the case I am about to mention? Man is an essence and an animal. But "capable of laughter", although it is the same as man and is a word for a natural thing, could be called neither an essence nor an animal; otherwise man would be many essences and many animals. So whatever goes with one of two things joined in sameness does not necessarily go with the other. Or else this statement needs a qualification. If someone who says "capable of laughter" means the notion of a property, it would be neither an animal nor an essence. But if these words point to the underlying subject itself, they do not bring in anything further that did not belong to it from the beginning. Otherwise it would be more fitting to call man neither a rational animal nor a body, nor even an essence, so that Socrates would not be left with such a heap of nonsense. Still, even if on each side of the division we see that what was known to go with the one does not follow the other, the argument has nonetheless found what it was looking for. It did not need to show that all the things set out here have this difference. It was enough for the argument to establish whether any terms of this kind, said in communion with one another, also preserve their difference. But someone might say that none of these examples is like the cases we were puzzling over at the start. In those cases neither term is the property or the definition of the other. Instead, one might say, they are two names that revolve around one subject, like "cloak" and "garment". How then, they ask, is the one not recognized by the same prerogatives as the other? I know that an argument of this kind has been put forward in our exercises: that man and humanity have the same subject

[?] …they signify, but they are not understood in the same way, as you yourself may perhaps remember. When we say “man,” we have in mind the nature as it exists within the hypostasis. When we say “humanity,” we mean the same nature of man, but not as it exists within the hypostasis: we mean the nature that the mind separates from matter and examines by itself. So man and humanity are the same, and yet they differ in another way. It therefore does not follow that wherever the one is seen, the other must be seen in the same things. Insofar as they differ from each other, they will surely also serve different uses. That is why we rightly call Socrates a man, but not a humanity. Because the predication differs, we will say instead that Socrates has humanity, and that the individual is contained by it, as it is by man. It was in such cases that their identity also appeared. So humanity, too, can apply to the things of which man is said, even if not in the same way. One might say plainly that humanity contains the individuals, [?] that Socrates has it, and that it is seen in the individuals. The account of nature is then ready to settle the dispute about the things above nature as well. But what has just been said must be counted as the work of people who are perhaps still frisking about after their exercises in the dialectical wrestling-schools, and who have not yet reached the prize that the grasp of truth bestows. For how is humanity both separated from the individuals and present in them? And how does it contain them while not being predicated of them at all? “To have” and “to be” may differ by a slight change of letters, but they point to a great difference in things. The attack based on identity would be easier to repel. Even if someone grants that humanity is the same as man, it does not follow that when the one is predicated, the other is predicated as well. Socrates is the same as man, since one is not predicated as something other than the other. Yet man is clearly predicated of Socrates, while Socrates is not predicated of man in return: Socrates is called a man, but man is not called Socrates. So it is not absurd to say that with some names, difference goes along with identity. [?] But what has been said, though it has the plausibility of an example, does not have the same power to solve the difficulties raised at the start. For here one term is common and the other belongs to the individuals, whereas in those cases each term shares equally in what is common. What, then, is the [solution] that on every side and [editor’s note: for “puts forward” read “to put forward”]

has escaped every grip? It has been shown in some measure that not all things that come together in identity need to share everything with one another, and that the usage drawn from the words “man” and “humanity” settles the dispute in theology. Yet the question may still remain in part and inflame the curiosity of those who choose to philosophize, because they do not also see guidance for the rest.

What, then, can be said? What wiser answer is there to the original difficulty than this? The word “God” usually indicates the nature, and is no less suited to signifying each of the individuals. “Godhead,” by contrast, signifies and indicates the nature alone. Therefore Godhead, like nature, may rightly be said to contain the hypostases, but Godhead cannot be predicated of any of the things it contains (nor can nature). The word “God,” however, both includes and indicates the hypostases that are above nature. That is why Scripture consistently knows how to call each of the three God. Suppose someone, in a show of youthful bravado, asks the reason why “humanity” indicates the nature, while “man” indicates both the nature and the individual. He has failed to notice that, while hunting for a reputation for wisdom, he is being carried off into ignorance. He is looking for first principles behind first principles and is being dragged into demanding causes for things that have no cause. But this is the argument in summary outline.

QUESTION [?]. If the Son and the Spirit come forth from the same cause, why does the Spirit not receive the name of brother and take on the title of Son?

My good friend, theology teaches that both the Son and the Spirit come forth from the Father at the same moment and without interval. But no argument will force the Spirit to pass over into the name of Son or take on the relation of a brother, just as no one may think or say the reverse: that the Son shares in being the Spirit who proceeds, or has taken over the Spirit’s relation. Everyone who has been granted the mind of Christ and has learned to think as He does is ready to give others the grace of being taught these things. For it is not the case that, because they are said in theology to come forth from the same source, the Spirit will be moved into sonship and depart from

its own property, or that the Son will leave the generation that characterizes Him and be merged into the property of the Spirit. Both are from the same source, but not in the same way, and the coming forth of each does not follow the same property. The Son came forth from the Father by generation. The Spirit came forth by procession, which is its own (53) property, and procession does not match the character of generation. That is how it is, and no other way. Things that the sacred texts say come forth from the Father according to different relations have both different names and different properties in their hypostases, according to the way their relations have been defined. This is how the real solution to the apparent difficulty can be made beyond dispute. But perhaps you also want proof by example, drawing from material things to speak about immaterial ones. Everyone knows that the burning power and the illuminating power of fire come forth from the same cause, since both are works and emissions of fire. Yet no one in his right mind can say that the burning power works together with sight by making the air bright so that visible things can be perceived. That belongs to the illuminating power. Nor would anyone attribute to light, insofar as it illuminates, the power to destroy the matter it falls on. Neither power will give the other the name by which it makes its existence known. So things that come forth from the same cause, usually at the same time and with equal honor, but not in the same manner, keep their difference of properties toward each other unconfused and unchanged while they share in existence. If you want to expand on examples, consider Adam, Eve and Abel. Both of them came forth from Adam: the rib, from which Eve’s forming began, and the seed, the source from which the first-formed man’s offspring were born. Yet Eve will not be brought under the notion of sonship, nor will Abel cease to be a son and be moved into some other relation. That the sun both lights and burns is a fact about bodies and something everyone who sees it agrees on. Yet the flames have not exchanged burning for brightness, nor will the illuminating power be brought under the name or the hypostasis of [?] in place of illuminating. Each of them keeps the law that the Creator placed in nature from the beginning. In their undivided coming forth and their unchanged essence, each is seen to pre-

[?] puts forth flower and leaves. (Against those whose faith is entirely different, one should perhaps bring forward not one counterexample but several, and refute their idle curiosity until it collapses into futility.) Who could force the leaves to take on the property of the fruit? Who would call the flower fruit, when its falling is usually recognized as the fruit’s putting forth? Anyone who understands the nature of a species, the works of nature, and the difference within them together with what they share by nature would not change either of the others into one of those just mentioned or alter its hypostasis. So even in the coarseness of bodily works and emissions, things are seen to come forth from the same source and keep their own hypostasis without changing into one another. They offer a plain refutation of the objection raised against true religion and publicly expose how rotten this mischief is by means of things that are visible and close at hand, and countless others.

Moving from nature to art will furnish you with many other examples. (Notice how far it stays consistent with nature while still opposing the original claim.) The potter, too, will show you that he shapes both chamber pots and dishes fit for sacred rites from the same clay and the same lump. I think you will not find even irreligious people shamelessly turning either vessel to the use or name of the other, or confusing [?] of each hypostasis, unless some demonic blow has struck them with an incurable madness. If you want to return to man, you will bring a sharper refutation against them. Word and voice both pour forth from the same human mouth and are formed and produced through nearly the same organs. Most of the organs are shared, but the word is produced more at the tip of the tongue, and the voice at the glottis. What is greater and more wonderful still, a word cannot come forth without voice. In the very act of formation the voice supports and upholds the form of the word, subsisting with it and carrying it forward. Yet despite this close connection and blending, no dispute will ever trouble anyone of modest discernment about the fact that voice is not word. With these examples, free yourself firmly from the supposed difficulty and silence the meddling curiosity (54) of those who wish to do mischief.

If the baptism of John provided forgiveness of sins, as the divine Luke records, how does it differ from the Lord’s? It is not unclear that the divinely wise Luke records such a statement in the words of the Gospel he composed. It is not equally clear that the baptism administered by John, the minister of the rite, [granted] forgiveness. But let this be examined more carefully below. The divine Matthew does not add the phrase “for the forgiveness of sins.” Yet by saying “confessing their sins,” he too lets us understand that the baptism was for the forgiveness of sins. When we confess what we have done, provided we do not confess in vain, we condemn it and triumph over it, and for those things we gain forgiveness. So says the theologian who came from among the tax collectors. Blessed Mark is so far from disagreeing with Luke, who speaks the words of God, that he could reasonably be thought the source of Luke’s words. He says: “John came baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” So the argument advances from many sides with testimonies through which the faith boldly declares that John’s baptism brought about forgiveness of sins for those who were baptized. This is especially so because John did not undertake the act on his own. He obeyed the divine command and became the minister of this rite. “For the word of God came to him,” says Luke, and the herald of truth himself says, “He who sent me to baptize.” All of this clearly shows that the Forerunner’s baptism was a gift of divine favor and higher than the Jewish sprinklings, sacrifices and rites through which the Jews were granted cleansing from their sins in a figure. And if it was better than those, it clearly also granted forgiveness of sins. For what belonged

Yet even though each baptism, John’s and the Lord’s, granted forgiveness of sins, we must on no account ignore the difference between them. The sacrifices, rites and baptisms of the Law served to cleanse sins, but that will not require John’s baptism to be no different from them. Just as the Forerunner is “greater among those born of women,” so his baptism is greater than those of the Law. And just as the voice falls short of the Word, the herald of the one he announces, the forerunner of the royal coming, and the slave of the master, so John’s baptism, even though it provided cleansing of sins, is reckoned inferior to the Savior’s. John is the forerunner of the King of all and the herald of the salvation shared by all, an honored man and “greater among those born of women.” His baptism, too, is the forerunner of the Savior’s baptism, which is for the whole world. It is more perfect than those that came before it, but falls far short of the one that was to come. It cleanses sins more than the Law did (56), but not with fire and the Spirit, which is perfection. That is the gift and grace of the Lord’s rite alone, of His love for mankind and of His power, which befits God. Since none of these higher things belongs to John’s baptismal rite, some of our holy Fathers dared to say that it did not provide forgiveness of sins. It falls far short of the grace of the Savior’s baptism, as the comparison itself shows, since it was excluded from the equal gift and in no way supplied a similar cleansing. It is understandable, then, that they did not attribute forgiveness of sins to it either. But blessed Mark says, and Luke, the sacred herald, agrees, that John’s baptism provides forgiveness of sins. So how could it not be arrogance to insist that it provides no cleansing of sins and even to argue that it is far poorer than the rites of the Law in this very respect? (The only exception would be if this were meant in some other sense, the one the comparison allows, which softens the harshness of the contradiction.) Perhaps these Fathers might take refuge in interpreting the text of the divinely wise Luke favorably by way of blessed Mark, and so avoid the apparent disagreement with them. They might say that “proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” does not mean the baptism the Forerunner performed himself, but points to that baptism of which John was sent as herald. For they say

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE

that Mark is speaking of John’s baptism when he says, “John came baptizing in the wilderness,” but announcing the Savior’s baptism when he says, “proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” On this reading, they would say, blessed Mark distinguished the two baptisms. He testifies that John’s baptism did not provide forgiveness of sins and that the one who administered it did not himself claim that it did. That is why John said, with a truth-loving and most devout mind: “I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” If Mark clearly taught us the distinction between the baptisms, assigning forgiveness of sins and completion by the Holy Spirit to the Lord’s baptism, and saying that John’s is a baptism of water and is called one, then it is clear that Luke too keeps in agreement with his fellow evangelist and companion and so upholds the inviolable dignity of the truth. His words, “And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,” would then refer not to the baptism that the Forerunner’s hands performed, but to the saving baptism of the Lord, which cleansed all who were baptized from the defilements of the soul. A little later Luke himself introduces John saying: “I baptize you with water, but one more powerful than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.” He then adds the dignity of the Lord’s baptism: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” Mark, too, after the Pharisees and Sadducees flee from the wrath to come (and there could be no flight except by running to baptism), adds: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance.” This implies that the baptism already given did not have the power to provide complete redemption from sins. Or one might suppose this was said not to those whom the consecrated streams had received and washed of their defilements, but to those who had set out for baptism and had not yet been granted cleansing. But even if one applies the saying to those already baptized, it would not necessarily deprive the Forerunner’s baptism of forgiveness of sins. The fruit of the virtues is closer to a soul that has been cleansed than to one that many thorns of the passions and shoots of tares have defiled and soiled. But this explanation may soon receive a more complete judgment. They say that the Savior, too, indicated that the Forerunner’s baptism did not provide forgiveness of sins when He spoke with Nicodemus about rebirth and declared: “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of

heaven.” But John did not baptize in the Spirit, so he did not send people on to the kingdom of heaven. And if he did not send them on, neither did he grant forgiveness of the things that bar the way in. Now the points in dispute have been set out, and the argument has hurried toward a verdict. From all this we must consider what we shall count as gain, where we shall take our stand on the question, and how the mind will be fixed on what cannot be shaken. But before the end, let a brief argument that still remains come before the verdict. Some force the saying of the divine Mark to mean two baptisms (57), when by a natural (58) reading and in apostolic phrasing only John’s is meant. They also take what is ambiguous and use it to build a meaning that suits a different position. This is illogical. The opposite is true: Luke’s sacred words have a single sense. Through them only one baptism, John’s, is clearly announced, and forgiveness of sins is attributed to it. If the words of blessed Mark allowed any ambiguity about dividing the baptism, they should rather be read in line with Luke and fitted to the meaning of a single baptism. Moreover, we know that John baptized with water and Jesus in the Spirit. This tells us how great the difference is and that the two cannot be compared, but it does not take away forgiveness of sins from John’s rite. And asking the baptized, after their baptism, for fruits worthy of the repentance that came before, urging them to display these fruits and not to shame what came earlier by what they did later, would rather confirm and show (59) that those washed in the waters of the Jordan through John’s rite had been cleansed. It does not cancel the cleansing of those who had been washed. Now that these points have been set out, and the apparent objections have been either cleared away or brought into agreement, one may think and say with truth-loving and God-loving frankness that the Forerunner’s baptism did provide forgiveness of sins, but not of all sins, just as the rites and sacrifices of the Law did not.
