Neither the Law nor John’s baptism brought cleansing for premeditated murder, for breaking into another man’s marriage, for the sins on which that dreadful heavenly fire brought punishment upon the guilty, or for many other abominable deeds of the same kind. For all these, the Law appointed the sword as judge, except where the first lawgiver had already exacted the penalty. John’s baptism, however, sent them on to the com-

mon and saving baptism, since that baptism was far greater than its own strength. That is why our Savior reproached the Pharisees for their hardness of heart and disobedience. He showed that their minds were worse and harder to correct than those of people who lived in fornication and tax-collecting. At the same time, He taught who it was that turned back from sin and which sins they were freed from, when He said, “John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him.” So through his baptism John brought about cleansing from tax-collecting, fornication and similar sins for those who sincerely repented. But he did not free robbers, grave-robbers or others who committed unspeakable crimes from their defilements. These did not dare to come forward and confess what they had done, because their conscience confronted them, held over them the penalty prescribed by the laws, and did not allow them to be counted among the others. So, as has been said, the Forerunner’s baptism provided forgiveness of sins, but not of all sins, for that is the special prerogative of the Lord’s most divine baptism. John’s baptism provided forgiveness while preparing the way for the perfection of the Savior’s baptism. It was a bath before the bath, a partial forgiveness before complete forgiveness, an imperfect cleansing that served as a prelude to the one that makes perfect. But it granted nothing secure or guaranteed for the future. The saving baptism of the Lord delivers from all earlier sins and also gives strength not to be dragged back into the passions, as in former falls. It lifts us up to the kingdom of heaven and, greatest of all, grants adoption as sons. John’s baptism provided forgiveness of the sins mentioned, but it did not grant a share in the kingdom of heaven, still less raise anyone to the dignity of adoption.

How is it that, when our Savior says, "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall [to the ground apart from the will] of my Father in heaven," Paul, who had Christ speaking in him, says, "Is it for oxen that God cares?" For the disciple's words give the impression of contradicting the teacher. That God's providence reaches even to the sparrows, and does not stop its care at them but extends also to plants and herbs, and, in short, that for whatever he is known to have created he bears an unchanging and unceasing concern for its preservation and ordering — this the other sacred Scriptures clearly teach us, and so does our innate reason, which requires that he who brought things forth and gave them being out of nothing should also hold together what he brought forth and provide for it according to the principle of providence that befits each thing. Indeed, our Savior himself, lovingly drawing us away from our great zeal and wearing toil over human affairs, and urging on us freedom and release from preoccupation with things that flow away and dissolve, draws this most excellent lesson not only from the sparrows and the other birds but even from the very herbs. "Consider," he says, "the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin." Then he speaks of the beauty and dignity of their clothing: "I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of these" — and this of things that are shortly thrown into the furnace. If God has such providence for things that serve so small a human need (for how much fire does the stalk of a lily kindle? Or for how long does the bloom of its color delight the eye?), how much more, and by an incomparable difference, does he have it for human beings? So, then, not only do the birth, growth and preservation of sparrows depend on God, and again their dissolution at their proper times, but so too do those of the herbs of the field; for from the one [?] the same line of reasoning passes over to the others of the same kind. Thus the care of the divine [providence] is attached not only to oxen but even to those creatures that received a less perfect nature from the beginning.

What, then, is it that Paul says — that man raised on high, the tongue of the Spirit? There is nothing difficult in it, nor anything that requires much contention [?]. For, calling to mind ancient ordinances, many of which [the Law] lays down by means of irrational animals, using them to educate the rational creature:

[?] that one must not, when taking the young of birds from the nest, also take the parents; nor boil a lamb in its mother's milk; and, if you like, not sow the vineyard with different kinds of seed; nor put on a garment woven of different threads; and many such things, among which is also: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing." That man learned in the Law, then, having need of the ordinance at hand, and weaving his exhortation from it — that one who urges others toward virtue should first enjoy it himself, and only then summon his hearers to imitate it; or, if you like, that those who labor should not be deprived of relief from their toils — reinforced these points from the Mosaic legislation too, and added: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing." Then, lest anyone say, "What has the race of oxen to do with human nature?", he says, "It is not for oxen that God cares here." For the law about them was laid down for our sake: it does not have its primary foundation in them, nor does the Mosaic legislation aim at regulating the life of irrational animals; but even if it was applied to other subjects, these things were said for our sake. For God does care for oxen, as for his other creatures, but not so as to set out laws about them and patterns of conduct by which they are to live. Rather, even where an ordinance about them was issued, he directed its introduction to the need and instruction of human beings. And this is made no less clear from the other animals, for which no laws are shown to have been introduced at all. For what law has been introduced about lions? What about elephants, or unicorns, or dragons, or countless other kinds, some of which are seen to become tame, while others utterly shun contact with human beings and sharing their roof? This, then, that blessed and divine man knew better than anyone, being especially learned in the Law — the trumpet of the Church, the mind raised on high. In many places and many times he proclaims that the providence of all things depends on God, and yet he declares that the laws concerning irrational animals which the Mosaic letter employed were not enacted primarily for the sake of their life, nor does God care for them so much as to have statutes concerning their conduct written down. Rather, he teaches that these laws were both spoken and written down, by a most wise and concise judgment, for the instruction and governance of the stubborn Jewish nation. It is clear, then, that the herald in no way contradicts the teachings of the teacher, but actually becomes their confirmation, especially by suitably adjusting the difference of usage to the difference of subject matter, keeping the distinctions of interpretation unconfused for each need, and setting himself forth as a rule for the pious of how one ought to [Editor's note (62): Supply τὸ παρέχον, "the present," with τῷ πάρετος, or write [?]]

track down the sense of our sacred Oracles, and, when the meaning contradicts the surface of the words, above all not to be swept along the easier path. It is possible, then, taking as one's teacher the common teacher of the Church — for those whose love is piety, for whom discernment is the work of wisdom, and on whom the grace of words from above shines — and proceeding methodically in imitation of our guide, to show still more clearly that such a use of words neither damages any of our sacred doctrines nor incurs any reproach, but on the contrary works toward complete harmony and blamelessness. So it is when someone draws a person away from pitilessness and lack of sympathy, or reins in a mind running toward greed, or straightens and supports one who, as the saying goes, is "limping on both legs" and directs him to the single saving path. Each of these, if someone tried to recover him from his irrational inclination by many other exhortations, [Paul] ties together very aptly and timely: For did you not learn, O man, from the Mosaic laws and precepts, not to boil a lamb in its mother's milk, nor to sow the vineyard [with mixed seed], nor to make yourself a cloak woven of heterogeneous threads of wool and linen? Or is it not plain to all that these decrees have their primary reference neither to lambs and mother's milk, nor indeed to a vineyard, nor yet to fabrics made of different threads? For when does God care about threads, or vineyards, or lambs and milk, so as to subject them to laws, as though human nature, for whose sake all things were brought into being, were no different from them? No, it is clear that such things were both provided for from the beginning and set down in writing for our sake. The law about lambs — and, if you like, about sparrows — so that, having been trained in sympathy and compassion toward irrational creatures, we might show far more kindness and mercy toward those of our own kind who share the same nature. The law [about the vineyard], so that we might not be carried along, gaping after greed, into misfortune in other things as well; for greed is the cause of many evils, and with it there usually flows away even what would rightly have remained to us from being content with enough. The law about woven fabrics, so that we might not be motley and shifty in our judgments, made up of different doctrines, or nations, or counsels, or words, or deeds, and wretchedly and ridiculously at war with ourselves. So not only does the method of the divine Paul, and the radiance of doctrine poured out from him, in no way bring pious minds into any division and confusion, but it is also a teaching able to [?] [Editor's note (63): "As the saying goes" is governed by an implied κατὰ, according to Greek usage [?]]

QUESTION 31. How is one to understand "God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham"? The plain sense of the saying, without any deeper interpretation, would teach this: just as God compacted the body of the living creature out of loose, crumbling, earthy matter, and shaped the dust into the nature and form of a human being, in the same way it is easy and no labor at all for human beings to be composed out of the more solid nature of stones, with God as the craftsman undertaking the shaping, and for those produced from such a substance to be called children of Abraham. For it is no less a wonder — not to say a greater one — to compact and fit together dust into human flesh than to remold the solid nature of stone into the body of a living creature.

Besides, it was not only the first man who had his origin, an extraordinary one, from dust. Lot's wife too, turned to stone as a pillar of salt, proclaims the indescribable and incomprehensible power of God. In the enduring wonder she displays the laying aside of [her nature?] without any visible decay, and the coming into being of another form and substance: what she had been, she was no longer, and what by human reckoning could not have come to be came into existence without the dissolution of what had been before. God, then, who works such marvels, and who at that time exacted punishment from a mere woman for transgressing a command — he "who wills that man be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth" — what would he not do out of his love for humankind, if he sees the nature of stones offering a more suitable means for producing children of Abraham? For it is not so easy for the Jews, a not inconsiderable part of whose race was cast out, to be called children of Abraham, as it is for God to make many such children for him out of stones. And if someone wishes to declare the saying a prophetic act as well: the stones mentioned then by the Forerunner, from which he foretold that children would rise up to Abraham, these, at the Savior's voluntary passion [and the universal salvation and resurrection], split apart and were rent asunder at the Lord's passion, and, as though made pregnant by the miracle, travailed and gave birth to many people into piety. As though with a splendid voice and a heavenly proclamation,

by what they suffered they called people back from their audacity against the Savior and from their error, led them by the hand to the knowledge of the truth, and gave them occasions to look toward the gift of regeneration. These the fellowship of faith knows to regard and to name as sons of Abraham, rather than those descended by blood. And if your love of God longs to rise through the letter to some higher contemplation, the stones might be understood as the hardened and hard-hearted among the Gentiles. From them Abraham's inheritance has been filled up, as they were changed from hardness to perceiving salvation, and from Hellenic error to initiation into the mysteries of the Spirit. Even so, I think, you would not be seen driving far from the turning-post which the grasp of truth through contemplation has fixed and set up in the stadium of the Church.

When the Forerunner was proclaiming the Savior, he set out various things about him in the language of theology, including that "he will baptize those who come to him in the Holy Spirit and fire." (The word "will baptize" shows and presents the richness of the gift and the abundance of his kindness; for in bestowing redemption and adoption he drenches us on every side with the ever-flowing streams of grace.) Having said these saving words, full of great generosity toward us, he did not want some to think that our Savior had the will and the power to give such great gifts and to establish such beneficence, but had no concern to punish and chastise the guilty and disobedient. For this reason he went on, correcting their unbelief: "His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clear his threshing floor." That is: he is not only beneficent and lavish with good things toward those fit for them, but he also chastises lawless deeds and punishes transgressions. For "the winnowing fork is in his hand" stands for: the punishment that repays wicked deeds is ready to his hand, just as is the reward of good ones. Therefore the power and authority that discerns and separates those liable to punishment from those worthy of kindness [is ready to his hand, or within his hand]. Hence the wheat, which is the name now given to the choir of the righteous,

he stores up in the mansions above, storehouses in which neither moth nor rust destroys, nor do thieves break in and steal; but those who drag along with their sins an unchangeableness [in evil], an addition to their wickedness [?], he will send away to unquenchable fire, whose punishment has no end. Fittingly, "the winnowing fork in his hand" hints at readiness and preparedness; for he does not separate the worse from the better by study and searching of reasons, but at once and on the spot he divides the part to be punished from the part to be saved. He willed it; the separation followed; the judgment went forth, and punishing justice went forth with it; for all things are present together before God. For the punishing power, justice, is the assessor and servant of God's judgments, just as is the generous and loving recompense that exceeds all deserving, through which better things are bestowed on us. Now the sacred oracles call "wheat" those who have kept their original nobility and preserved something unadulterated and pure of the primal and saving seed sown in our nature by God, right up to the bearing of fruit. They call "chaff" and fuel for the fire those in whom the admixture of tares, springing up alongside, has choked the cultivation of the Spirit, made it fruitless, and cast the hoped-for ripeness of the fruit away into the uselessness of refuse. As for "He will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire," this does not mean that two things of differing nature together accomplish the single need and perfection of baptism. For what further thing could be needed where the all-holy Spirit is at work? And what could be taken alongside to fill the place of something lacking? Rather, "in fire" is included here to announce the purifying power and operation of the Spirit. For the gifts of the all-holy Spirit are various, and one of his [manifold?] operations is that which purifies, destroys baser matter, and, in those upon whom it comes, recasts the whole nature through and through, so that nothing that defiles it can any longer lurk within and escape notice. Therefore, having said "in the Holy Spirit," he added "and fire," so that you might understand: in the Holy Spirit who purifies and consumes the passions of vice within us. Cleansed of these through his fiery, [?] and recasting operation, we are made worthy of holiness. "For our God
is a consuming fire" — consuming both all other corrupting wickedness and whatever has crept in and become stamped upon our nature through our inattention.

QUESTION [32?]. Why is it that, when the divine wrath had fallen upon Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and the rest of the multitude ought to have cowered in fear of danger to their lives, to have checked the swollen [?] arrogance and desperation of their minds, and to have come to acknowledge their sins, they showed nothing of the kind but murmured against Moses? Is it because, being a multitude carried away by irrational impulses and held fast by rather reckless reasonings, they thought that the Deity was charmed by Moses' incantations or rituals [?] and persuaded to do what pleased him, and that this was why punishments were being let loose against their kinsmen who offended him? Wandering in these deliberations and emboldened by their rashness, they thought that by rising up they could frighten Moses and turn him from his undertaking, so that he would no longer provoke God by the means with which he summoned him to punish wrongdoers, and that they could also deliver their kinsfolk from the divine wrath. For they themselves did not ground their minds on incorruptible judgment, dispassion and rectitude, but let their passions govern their judgment; and they imagined that not only Moses but even the common Master and Creator was subject to the same things. Besides, a moderate punishment, tempered for a human mind that has not been too greatly terrified, often brings about conversion and change: the chastisement frightens, yet by its mildness it softens the harshness and leads one by the hand to understanding. But when punishment comes in overwhelming measure because of the overwhelming measure of the sins, human nature generally, instead of looking toward pardon, turns to despair and desperation, though it ought not to, and rises up to ingratitude and blasphemy when it cannot show its anger in deeds. Yet the more it was afraid, the more it ought to have been drawn away from what is unlawful, directed toward what admonishes it, and kept from setting itself in battle against its own salvation. For Scripture says: "When he slew them" (this was another disease of Israel, as with lesser ailments [?]), "then they sought him, and turned back, and rose early to seek God." How is it not utterly senseless, and a way of calling down heavier penalties, not to be moved even by the severity of worse [afflictions] [?] to exchange [sin] for repentance? And

[PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE] One who is not brought to his senses by a moderate punishment might perhaps give good hope of being driven to correction by a greater one. But one who is not taught even by this, and does not count sound sense preferable to madness, confesses his offense to be incurable. And one who not only fails to change for the better but grows even worse is convicted — if not by his tongue, then by his deeds — of casting his vote that the rest of the punishment be added, not as an excessive penalty, but as what the nature of justice requires. "You have sinned," Scripture says; "be still." But they, sinning in other ways and also in grieving excessively for those who had justly paid the penalty, not only did not keep silent (for the [?] of their sins did not allow it), but even rose up to murmur against their guide, and through him dashed themselves against the common Master and Benefactor, striving to cover a lesser evil with a greater. Therefore they met a destruction like that of those who had gone before, and would have perished with their whole race had not Moses' propitiation and entreaty stopped the plague. Suppose, however, that those under the Law supposed that the lawgiver of virtue and of the knowledge of God relied on sorcerous tricks and spells that compel the gods, and believed that by these he was exacting punishment from those who vexed him, [rather than] that the God and Creator over all was watching what was done and was being called upon to check transgressions. Then the original difficulty is easily solved; but the solution gives birth to another absurdity no smaller. If the multitude was caught in such opinions, they deserved to perish not once but many times over. This is especially so because the sorcerers in Egypt had been put to shame not once but ten times, and their mischief had been most brilliantly exposed by Moses' wonder-working, and the people had their own eyes as witnesses and could raise no objection. Moreover, by what jugglery and trickery could anyone divide the sea, make a road for his followers that bore not even a trace of moisture, and at the same time turn it into an improvised tomb for his enemies? And how could anyone provide food from heaven and prepare a table, and do the other things that Moses accomplished by divine power for the salvation of Israel, propitiating and appeasing the Deity? Those men, then, paid a penalty for their uprising that cannot be faulted. As for those before us, none of the points discussed here has been raised as a difficulty, nor has any solution been devised for them. It is for you to judge whether this solution is the work of real contemplation or of chatter that is ashamed to keep silent.

QUESTION 34. In the Gospel saying, which children are we to understand as those who piped to the Jews, and they did not dance, who mourned, and they did not lament? For if one takes them to mean the Forerunner and our common Master, does not the charge against the Jews fall away along with the absurdity? After all, failing to obey children is not something one can be held to account for.

One might say that parables and similitudes keep to the pattern of their own particular character. But one would surely not say that they must accept, in every detail, a one-to-one distribution of names. Nor must they force the persons in the comparison, and those to whom they are compared, to fit like a shoe to the foot, keeping the likeness unvarying. Nor must the rest of the order of words and things be required to be identical in both senses. Nothing [?] permits either the things likened in the parable, or any whole part of the parable, to be added; it binds these to one another, and each is matched to each down to the smallest detail [?]. The account of history and narrative, whatever the matter its description refers to, takes great pains to fit the placement of its words to each name of its subjects; and it does not tolerate anything being supplied, whether understood or inserted, as [?] one might best put it. But the account of parable and similitude does not wish to be bound of necessity by the same rules, or to be subject to the same precepts. Why? Because history, and things like it, and narrative teach what was not known, and give hearers the beginning of knowledge. They are therefore required to attach words to things with the utmost precision, and they admit no word that is not fully in harmony, no matter that does not hang together, nothing that forces the sense; for such things destroy the subject and teaching put forward and do not build up understanding. With parable and similitude, on the other hand, it is clear first of all that they are drawn from things already known, and that those who construct them choose to set known things side by side in one way or another because they are more persuasive. Those who use this method have no other leading aim than to bring persuasion to souls and to lead the hearer to agree to welcome the exhortation as something that brings salvation, whether it is put forward simply as beneficial or [?] to accept it. When parables and similitudes have been put to use in a discourse for this purpose, then minute precision, the detailed distribution of each sense, and the fine connections and correspondences are relegated to a secondary concern, or to none at all.

This can often be seen not only in our sacred Scriptures but also in all those writings where the divine and pure enclosure of piety is [?] kept, even though their authors set great store by the wisdom of words. So no law requires the children either to be particular persons or to have a correspondence distinct from the others sought for them. Even when they are presented as indefinite, they are enough to fulfil the intention of the parable's arrangement. The aim of the Lord's parable and similitude is very clear and plain. It means to show that the nation of the Jews would not choose to embrace what was profitable through things that charm and delight, that is, through the customary and prevailing way of life (though they ought to have been drawn and attracted by what was like themselves). Nor would they [?] work the marvel through a life withdrawn from the many and restrained, though such a life knows how to put even the more devout to shame. Rather, since they were turned by none of these, they were to lay aside, and pay the penalty for, their licentiousness and their intractability toward piety. The parable also weaves in a persuasion that carries conviction: by not repenting, the people of the Jews cut off for themselves every defence and every pardon. This, then, is what the parable accomplishes. As for the rest of the names and things, which contribute nothing necessary and nothing that calls to salvation, it does not even deign to busy itself with them. For who are those [who bore] the heat of the day and the frost of the

and again, who? If the human race, divided into righteous and sinners, is indicated by the two sons in the parable, how is it that this one asks to be counted as one of his father's hired servants? And the elder son, who does his father's will, then watches his brother's return and salvation with envious eyes and is provoked into arguing his case with his father: how could he be assigned to any definite person? So it is clear that it is not fitting to pry into and demand an account of every part of the parable, but only to look to what is signified by it as a whole. Again, the rich man who put the steward of his house in charge, and who then had that steward accused: to what person would one assign him? And whom would one say the accusers were? And the requital of good things to Lazarus and of incurable evils to the rich man: how could it have happened when the common judgment has not yet taken place? And the conversations that the parable gives to Abraham and to the man condemned to punishment: how could they take place, when the torments impose silence on the one (and, apart from his own groans and wailings, put a bridle on everything else), and the other no longer turns, after the judgment, toward the one condemned once for all? By the same pattern and rule, then, the children in the parable would not need to express the characteristics of particular persons. One might instead approach the present parable through the peculiarities of a less usual way of speaking. These would be the features of similitude, since its riddling form, in which the parable now under examination was also set forth, [?] by other subtleties keeps it shut away from the many hearers who do not receive it. This, then, is what the Saviour's word also hinted at: 'To you,' he said to the disciples, 'it has been given to know the mysteries, but to them in parables.' He was setting understanding through parables over against the most exact and detailed knowledge and unveiling of the mystery. That is why the apostles too said, 'Explain this parable to us.' And that is why the synagogue of the disobedient Jews 'seeing did not see, and hearing did not hear,' since such parables and similitudes offer only this: to look and to hear. For even though the multitude of the Jews, through hardness of heart and through willingly shutting their eyes to the light of piety, 'did not see though they saw, nor hear though they heard,' still the parable (overshadowed as it was by obscurity) offers no pretext for their resisting disposition, nor any ground for ingratitude [?]. Rather, it exposes their insensibility all the more, because, though they ought to have sought

The Proverb-writer, too, hinted at how hard parable and similitude are to discern by setting parallel expressions side by side. Describing someone whose mind has been perfected by proverbs as wise and understanding, he says: 'He will understand a parable and a dark saying, the words of the wise and riddles.' This line of argument, which is not at all removed from the particular features of parable and similitude, can make many other questions easy in the way just described. But what is about to be said examines things and words more precisely than the theory set out above, and to that extent it marks out a solution peculiar to this one question. In our sacred oracles, 'children' has two senses: 'Let the children be, and do not hinder them from coming to me'; and, not far from the same sense, 'Unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven'; and then, 'Brothers, do not be children in your thinking, but be infants in evil.' So 'child' would have two senses, or rather three. For Paul, wise as anyone in things divine and human, and knowing how to fit appropriate words to the most closely related ideas, cried out: 'Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death.' It is clear that 'child' here signifies neither what is simple, guileless [?] and free of villainy, nor what is senseless and easily seen through in mind, but simply denotes human nature. So the Forerunner and the Saviour might not unfittingly be called children: first because they share the nature of children, and more closely and properly because their great gentleness and meekness in sufferings that took much endurance gave them a likeness of character to children. They showed these traits formed in themselves: they did not call fire down from heaven, or punish wrongdoers with the sword, or take vengeance by opening chasms, or drown the disobedient in water. Instead, putting themselves into the likeness [?] of children by meekness and freedom from anger, they trained those who would learn with childlike words, as in 'I gave you milk to drink, not solid food,' and again, 'I have many other things to say, but you cannot bear them now.' So, in a sense neither out of tune nor drifting toward insult, they could be considered and called children: both the one

who baptized in water and the one who baptizes in fire, according to the principle of nature and the more honourable and dignified of the meanings. But the children who are infants in folly are the crowds of the Jews. Whether piped to or mourned to, they were moved from their heedlessness by neither, and did not choose to seek release from their own wickedness. You often hear the Saviour called a lion, and our enemy, who roars, called by the same name. You hear the Creator of visible and invisible creation called a worm: 'For I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people.' Yet you also hear, 'Their worm (this is a form of the heaviest punishment) will not die.' In those cases you have become skilled at discerning. You draw the one lion into the image of the Master and fit the other to the beast who is the author of evil. You do not blush to take 'worm' at one time of the Saviour's flesh, which was unsown, undefiled and untilled, and at another to signify the bitterness and inexorability of punishment. In the same way, if you use your accustomed divine wisdom with the children of the Gospel, assigning and distributing to each its own, you will find nothing obscure or hard to follow. Many other uses of such names are scattered through our sacred Oracles. There is the lion's whelp: one roaring and seeking its food from God; the other lying down and rising up again, and raising up with himself the human race from the ancient fall and from the grip of death. There is the Morning Star: one 'rising early' and making 'the hearts of the faithful' shine still more with the light of the knowledge of God; the other fitted to darkness, led away by his own chosen wickedness from the spiritual and blessed brightness. There is the serpent who deceived Eve, and also the one whose imitators the Saviour's word commands us to be: 'Be wise,' he says, 'as serpents.' And there is a king: one the King of all, whose fingers' work is the whole creation; and also the king of the hardships and grimmest things in life, the one most to be fled yet impossible to flee [?], the most grievous of all, which is death. Again there is lightning: the one that fell from heaven because of his exaltation, and the one to which the dread and venerable second coming of Christ is likened. See, too, that there is a holy darkness, which [sets] the divine curtain of his hiding place [?]… [?] the remnant of Jacob, like a lion among the beasts in the forest… [?] and now the manner, when you divide and distinguish [?]

(247) PHOTIUS. [?] sets; and there is another darkness, on the one hand the outer darkness, on the other the one [?] through whom that darkness was prepared and made ready. So there are many words, both in our sacred treatises and in the writings that the Attic tongue prides itself on, that divide toward opposite things. This, I think, follows a rule that knows how to distinguish things whose distinction is not obvious. Each of the names mentioned is by nature able to express opposed powers and activities, and so allows those who wish to assign it, without hindrance or force, to either of the things that naturally fall under the same meaning. It is clear that this kind of doubling of names is exempt from the theory of homonyms. For with homonyms, so to speak, the account knows no cause why things that differ have come under the same name (while others arise through some likeness), and it admits neither of these. Rather, through opposites and contraries that nevertheless attain to the same name, [?] the nature and the ineffable differ. But let this be put in by way of seasoning and relief from the labour of sacred study, which crowds and sharpens the mind. How is the exhortation of the chief of the apostles, which says, 'Always be ready to make a defence to anyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you,' not in conflict with the Lord's command [?] not to prepare beforehand how to make one's defence when brought before the tribunals of rulers and kings to give an account of our faith? Because, best of lovers of sacred learning, each requirement, though it is expressed in different words, is directed to the same aim. They cannot be in conflict, far from it, since they lead to the same exhortation and command us to order our minds by the same rules. 'Being ready' means not putting off a question; it implies not hesitating in one's reasonings to answer those who ask. And not preparing beforehand means not making the time for bold speech a time for deliberation, and not being thrown into confusion by preliminary rehearsals when the contest is at hand. These run together into the same [?]

and complete the same meaning. The one who is ready is free of rehearsal, anxiety and doubt. Since he carries a conscience freed from this troubled state, he has no need to prepare beforehand, nor [?]. He is ready both to supply the benefit of teaching to those who wish to learn, and to answer, with a firm and unshaken mind, those who try to find fault with and mock the precision of doctrine, setting against them the refutation of the erroneous opinion and the blamelessness of piety. Firmness and steadiness of mind make those who are looking to learn more attentive, and know how to strike down the villainy of those who abuse, and [?]. So far are these sayings from conflicting with one another (as you can now see for yourself) that, if any sayings are in harmony and agreement, these yield to no others in it. Nor would the present consideration and examination of the texts take second place for agreement and concord. And suppose, as some say, the one was spoken to those who have leisure before the contests, so that they may not be careless or take little account of the truth, and the other to those already engaged in the contests, so that they may not, out of cowardice when brought to sudden trial and examination, shake the firmness of the faith within them. In that case such a distribution and arbitration of the words according to the difference of their subjects, together with their not contradicting one another, becomes a great and incontestable testimony to the Lord's providence and help. When persecutions are quiet, give your leisure to the study of the sacred Oracles. When they are fanned up against piety and rage, do not be afraid or troubled. Do not look ahead to what comes next, if your preparation should turn out that way, and show the tyrants a cowardly bearing of soul. For you have the Master for whom you bear the contest, who does not merely make up what is lacking but grants his help and power far more abundantly.

QUESTION 35 [?]. In what sense is it said, 'Let us make man according to our image'? And what is the image here? And what is the archetype? For every image must be considered together with its prototype

that man has come into being according to the image of God. Some have understood this to mean his being rational and having free will; others, his being a ruler, raised to lordship. In either of these the creature can image the Creator, and man can be called an image, or, if you like, can be said to have been made according to the image of God. From this one can immediately know both the image and the prototype: according to the nature of the archetype, or rather of the One who is rich in nature and is the reasonable cause of gifts, who grants likeness by grace to the one he lovingly brought into being. Now one writer, making Gregory the Theologian his own on the strength of what he especially thought and taught, in a manner worthy of God, about the Spirit, disregards the difference of a single syllable in the expression and brings the term 'image' and 'according to the image' together into one. Why? Because he saw in this no perversion of any sacred doctrine, and saw that the same meaning was conveyed by each to the ears of those who received it, men whose salvation was the man's glad concern.

However, since the greedy ear, thinking curiosity to be wisdom, looks for the difference between 'image' and 'according to the image', it would not be beyond pardon and sympathy to speak of this too. It will be discussed later, so that the sequence of the argument is not broken off now. For some hold a view opposed to what has been said. Finding that the rational and intellectual also belong to angels, it forcibly obscures the truth of those who said that man came to be according to the image of God in respect of being rational and intellectual. They think they can conclude that, since this is not proper to human nature, the 'according to the image' cannot be applied to it either, as if some necessity required that whatever does not image according to its own proper character (even if it displays an image clearly imprinted) should not

[?] [he made] man according to his own image and likeness, forming the body from earth and giving him a rational and intellectual soul through his own inbreathing, which we call the divine image. For 'according to the image' signifies the intellectual and free will, and 'according to the likeness' signifies likeness in virtue, so far as possible [?] … image of the archetype, God. (84) A better reading than παραδεχομένους … ἡδέως.

confess at all that what is imaged images [?]. Likewise they think they should reject the aspect of rule for the same reason, even though the sacred Oracles clearly show, by the continuity of the context, that 'according to the image' is meant to signify the dignity of rule. For the passage runs: 'Let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness, and let them rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and the cattle, and all the earth.' Not even put to shame by this, they say that rule is not indicated by 'according to the image', since the nature of angels too has attained to rule and authority. For the prophet Daniel plainly proclaims a ruler of the Assyrians and a ruler of the Jewish nation. And somewhere the one who saw God says: 'He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.' So, they argue, just as being rational and having free will are common to angels and men, so also is lordship and [?]… [?] 'angels of God' (85) [?]… But what of this? If the statement had added that man alone came to be according to the image of God, the nature of the angels might perhaps have been in conflict with it, because [?] it is defined [?] by the very things through which it joyfully takes the impress of the Divine. But since nothing of the kind is found written, not only is the dignity of being formed according to the image not taken away from the angels [?], but it also provides an exemplary and sufficient proof of the truth. So, just as the angel is not deprived of a rational and intellectual nature, neither would man be deprived of this power. But what eagerness possesses them to oppose what has been rightly decided? In my judgment, at least, they seem to attack those others only so far as they turn the accusation back on themselves. For where a contemplation proceeding from an upright mind and in keeping with the Scriptures has been worked out with great labour, above all by our blessed fathers, the task of fair-minded people who do not lack understanding is to support it, supplying anything that may have been left out and strengthening it as far as possible. But those whose intent is to shake what is well established with quibbles, and whose ambition is to seek novelty, have failed to notice that, in hunting a reputation for cleverness, they are being swept away from the sacred and innate

[?]…of mind. It is an insult to God, and the mark of a soul held by irrational fancies, to let such a notion creep in. They are seen to have supplied an unanswerable refutation against themselves. But let us leave them aside. A further point of the same kind, as far as it bears on the objection [?], is that man was fashioned after the image of God because his soul is incorporeal. This is not only because the superessential and supernatural quality of the superessential essence and of incorporeal beauty is mirrored in the soul, as it is in the angels by participation. It is also because otherness is seen within the identity of the Trinity, and that otherness keeps the persons unconfused. Or, if you like, it is because a word proceeds from the soul, the nature that brings it forth. The word keeps its proper relation and correspondence [?], and so shows that the hypostasis of the breath, which is of the same rank, is sent forth along with it. These points too would bear out that man was shaped from the beginning after the image of his Maker. And since many arguments start from here [?], you have an abundance of other examples as well. For wisdom, creative power, immortality and many such qualities are imprinted from that first wisdom, creation and eternity, which lie beyond the mind, and they bear the likeness of that nature. Someone might wish to paint a most godlike scheme, as if from various colours, and to show that the most beautiful and lovely form of man is shaped and moulded through all of these. If he also lets the image be seen more elegantly by including what is peculiar to our nature, he does not seem to me to miss the [?] according to the cause…

So nothing in what has been said prevents us from grasping the image, conceiving the archetype, and understanding what has been fashioned after the image of God [?]. Indeed, each of the fine and honourable things mentioned could be thought of as an image of God, such as the rational faculty in man and all the others named before. For these portray the kingship, wisdom and creative power that are contemplated in God beyond reason and thought. They also portray the Word, who is without flux, impassible and consubstantial. And man is fashioned after the creative, royal and rational image, and shares in wisdom. He is not himself that image, if one thinks it worthwhile to split hairs over these matters and to track down the exact force of the terms. Rather, he has been fashioned after it. In this way both the image and the 'after the image' may be seen more clearly, and ignorance of the prototype will not envelop us. But if someone wishes to fold these into the image and the prototype, he too is not wrong. For the things seen in God alone would belong to God,

and the one formed toward them could reasonably be said to be formed toward God. Likewise, the things in man received the power to portray their source, as the immaterial is portrayed in matter and the producer in what he produced. These things came about by divine grace and as a gift to man. If so, then by fitting reasoning man too might be said to have become an image of God. That is why the divine Gregory said: 'Having placed in him breath from himself, which reason knows as an intelligent soul and an image of God.' That holy man delighted in a concise style. He liked to convey a whole range of thoughts in a short weaving of words, and he tries to adorn almost all his discourses in this manner. So here too he says 'having placed breath', which held [?] the creative power of the soul. Instead of unfolding this distinction in an explanation, he stated it very concisely: 'which reason knows as an intelligent soul and an image of God.' Had he spelled out the thought itself, he would have said: 'which created and brought forth the intelligent soul, which reason saw as the image of God.' Thus one can gather the interpretation of this teaching into two terms, or again unfold it into three. Or rather, if one wishes to split hairs over each point and probe the teaching before us, there would be four to see, and through them the relation between what is imaged and what stamps the image is preserved. First there is the Divine, in which the God-befitting perfection of powers beyond cause and beyond all comprehension flashes forth. Then there are the radiances of these powers. Out of love for mankind they take the impress of grace from there, and for this reason they are called by the name of image. Below them man holds the fourth place, being fashioned after the image just mentioned. So those who look for the image and the 'after the image' in different things do not stop their search at three. They also bring in a fourth, which they were not even looking for. This, I think, is why the far-famed Gregory set aside such great precision and was content with the image and the pattern. For he had no intention of dissecting the saying and multiplying it into as many parts as he could. In a festal public oration, he took up the teaching to meet a need, adapting it to the crowd. Some have taken 'after the image' to mean

'by the image' [?]. For the all-holy Spirit, they say, is, like the Son, 'the radiance, the express stamp and the exact image of the Father'. And the soul of man was created directly through the Spirit, that is, through the breathing-in. So man might fittingly be said to have been brought to completion as a whole through the Image, and to have come into being 'after the image' of God. That is, he is called the work and masterpiece of the divine Image, and nothing prevents the terms from being interchanged. This is also why some who undertook the exposition of our sacred Scripture said not 'after the image' but that man was made 'in the image of God'. Even if this account is thought acceptable, it would do no harm to the truth. If it takes second place among the views mentioned, it would not, in my judgement, resent this or seek to be raised above it [?]. Others again can be found who have said that the phrase was spoken by the Word and extends to the incarnation and sojourn of the Word. (On their view, 'after the image' is referred from the outset to something proper [?] before it is grasped.) For if, they say, 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us', and became man 'in all respects except sin', then nothing would prevent us from thinking and saying rightly that the first-formed Adam was created after that holy and sinless statue, which also destroys all sin. This gives you another way, which follows as a corollary of this view, to understand the image, the prototype, and the image after which Adam was shaped into human nature. For the Son is the exact and connatural Image. He became man [?] like us and came together into one hypostasis with what he assumed, and so he showed man to be of equal honour with himself. The wisdom of God was already seeing and arranging what was to come. In an excess of love for mankind, it formed the founder of our race with undefiled and creative [?] hands after the form and pattern of this saving incarnation.

These matters, I think, have now been examined very clearly and distinctly. As for the nonsense of the Anthropomorphites, let it fall back on their own heads. In their madness they drag down God, who is without shape, without limit and beyond comprehension, to the form and figure of man. They did not even care to consider something easy and ready to hand: if the Divine from eternity, and not by reason of [?]…

…condescension and love for mankind, had been shaped in the form of man, then the assumption of our clay through the Son at the end of the ages would have taken place in vain. Nor, what derangement, would the Divine be free from the final absurdity of being divided into male and female [?]. For when the sacred oracle had declared, 'After the image of God he made them,' it immediately added, 'Male and female he made them.' The image, then, befits not Adam alone but applies with equal honour to Eve, and through them to the whole human race. If man was fashioned after God's bodily appearance and form, two things follow. Those who say this share the impiety of the error that was impious from the beginning. And they outrage the Godhead, which cannot be outraged, by making it subject to human passions. For what has human shape has nowhere been granted release from human passions. The objects of worship of the pagan error are of this kind. These people have done nothing other than [?] mix our God-befitting and venerable theology with idolatrous superstition, and they are forced to reduce it to that. Many other blasphemies follow, but these stand out most and plainly expose the madness of those who have wretchedly thrown themselves into this opinion. The fable of the much-erring Jews is refuted as a madness of the same kind. It does not accept that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and it will not confess that the Spirit has the dignity of Godhead by nature. Yet it does not notice that it is forced to raise an incorporeal power to the divine nature. For it felt no shame in saying that God spoke the words 'after our image' to the incorporeal ranks. By assigning one and the same image to God and to the incorporeal powers, it makes the nature of each identical and removes all difference between Creator and creature. For when beings have the same, exactly identical image, how can their nature admit any otherness? But enough of this as well. My discourse would not even have touched these things. It undertook to go through them only so that the beauty of the truth might shine out more brightly when set beside absurd opinions. It would have been far better if not even those who first fell into these errors had ever entertained them in their minds.

[?] Question [?] (in the Coislin and Turin manuscripts). How can 'An eye for an eye' not contradict 'I say to you, do not resist the evildoer', that is, do not retaliate in kind or take vengeance on your enemy? One may say what those before us have taught on this question. These sayings are not at war with each other, and laying down one does not abolish the other. Rather, the first is a road and a preparation that leads through a less perfect way of life to the perfect one. For whoever has trained himself to leave his affairs to the law is ready to choose the better course, and toward [?]…

[?]…being done? It is not inconsistent to demand equal requital from the one who started the unjust violence, and also [?] to enjoin the utmost gentleness and the rule of forbearance, and to calm the troubled part of the soul. The one is human, the other more divine. The first is beyond reproach, the second deserves praise. One may say this and so resolve the difficulty. But it is perhaps no worse to add the following. The one command concerns the judge. He must put nothing ahead of justice, set the balance of equality before the parties to the case, and be known as the incorruptible eye of justice. The other is given to the person who is judged. It reshapes and soothes, with the wealth of love for mankind, the inflamed desire for retaliation. He must not seek to increase his passion. He must not multiply wickedness by doing the very thing he hates and thinks deserves punishment. Nor must he help build up the [?] of contention.

Question 38. Some raise the difficulty: if the Godhead in the Son is uncircumscribed, is the flesh he assumed everywhere? For where the Godhead is, the flesh too must be present. [Or, being circumscribed by place, is it separated from the one who assumed it?] [?] There ought to be no perplexity for those who seek to be pious and

who know the Christian mysteries. The question is: if the Godhead is uncircumscribed and everywhere, is the flesh that the Son assumed present everywhere with the one who assumed it, so that it may not be thought separated from him? Or, being circumscribed by place, will it deny the assumption? Many trifles, or rather countless ones, could be set up as rivals to this supposed difficulty. But lest we seem to treat awesome things without awe, let the discussion rather take the soul and the body as its exercise. What prevents anyone who wishes from asking: how is the soul united to the body when it is not circumscribed in place? For in so far as it is not circumscribed along with the body, it stands convicted of denying the union, as the wisdom of these babblers would have it. To put it in terms closer to the senses: the human body is coloured, yet the soul united with it [?] cannot receive colours. The body is compounded of four humours, yet the soul is free from the conditions that come from the humours. Filling and emptying, following one another in a cycle, make up the body's life, yet the soul is seen to be above such states. And so on in countless ways. One could also turn the argument the other way round. Someone who likes not to be serious about serious things, but to pride himself on the sophistical subtleties of conjurers, will say: if the compound of the body is united to the rational soul, how is it not invisible [?], since the soul united to it is recognized in it? How is it not intangible? Indeed, how is it subject to colours? How is it not free of weight and downward pull, of emptyings and fillings? And countless other nonsense. Let me state briefly the mother-city of this nonsense, from which these youthful bravados found their way into arguments to settle there: if the soul is united to the body, how is the body not soul, or the soul not body? It is laughable to say such things about soul and body, and the sophistic chatter about the magnitude of the difficulty [?] becomes plain even to the untrained. How much more, then, is it utterly ridiculous to say similar things about the divine Word and what he assumed from us, and to fail, before those who know, to distinguish between mere babbling and a real difficulty? Let me speak of our own mysteries, or rather of the works and sufferings that came from our Maker's love for mankind. When the body was pierced with nails, how was the Godhead not wounded with it? How was it not pierced by the spear? How was it not crucified?

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. The compound that was truly united to the Godhead suffered all these things. How then did the Godhead, though it was with the one who suffered, remain untouched by them? And how did it escape death, according to the holy [?] account? Yet Christ our God is said to have truly died for us, since he gave his own flesh to death for our sake. He is said to have dwelt in a tomb, and by his resurrection on the third day to have inaugurated and laid the foundation of the common resurrection of all. Those who insult the Divine by calling it passible will certainly be silenced by what has already been said. That argument puts forward the refutation drawn from the union of soul and body, along with many others like it. Others are not corrupted by that error, but they lie in one no more tolerable [?]: they mean to use circumscription in place as an argument against the divine union. Both those points and what has just been said can be drawn from their own premises, and the refutation can be brought straight home. My good man, you grant that the Divine is everywhere. How will you not grant that it is present everywhere as a whole? This is no less a part of the dignity that befits God. But if he is wholly [?] everywhere, and the Son exists whole in the flesh united to him, then even though he is present everywhere while the human nature is bounded by place and time, by beginning and end, and in countless other ways, this would allow no room at all to conceive of a separation. Rather, someone would be imagining the Divine as at some point existing in a place apart from the assumed flesh [?] if he fancies that it is present everywhere by parts, and not as a whole in whatever places the Divine is present. Whoever claims that what was assumed is not united to the divine hypostasis of the Word unless it is extended along with it is saying 'by parts', even if he does not say so. Extension, co-extension and the like, and not being present as a whole in things or in those on which it shines, belong to things that admit division and are cut up by these, losing their unity and indivisibility. If the Divine is divided as it pervades everywhere and holds all things, then it requires extension in itself, and co-extension, and indeed circumscription and being circumscribed along with things. But if you shun imagining what is blasphemous and unworthy of God (and shun it you would [?]… circumscribed place [?]

[?]… even if you do not shun it, so long as your mind has not been driven away from the activities of the intellect, or, if you like, from common notions), you would earn shame for great absurdities. You would come to your senses more easily, even as you set yourself up as the champion of such difficulties. So the man who thinks highly of himself attaches his own failing and ignorance to the argument when he says: 'If the flesh is united to the [Godhead] [?], it is everywhere and has been changed into the uncircumscribed; or else it is separated from the Godhead, being unable to be extended along with it.' And yet it is more consistent to think that, if the properties of the soul belonged to the body, or the soul were marked by those of the body, the union would never come about for them. And even if it did come about [?], how would the coming-together of the things united be preserved? For a change of one into the other stands as far from union properly so called as the proverbial borders of the Mysians and the Phrygians. The man who meddles with the union, raises bugbears and casts aside the conceptions that follow from it, condemns himself [?] for a transition into the flesh. He suspects the Lord's [?] of being subject to material extension, to every passion and addition, and to diffusion [?]. And I have not yet said that the Godhead's presence to the flesh by union and its presence everywhere refer to different meanings and ideas [?]. The account that recognizes and defines the 'everywhere' does not exclude the united nature from God's common visitation. For it does not wall off anything that God deigned to create from enjoying his providential presence. But the account that proclaims his presence by union restricts that presence to what is united alone. Even if it distinguishes the two kinds of presence by different ideas, whoever rashly meddles with and attacks the one would be shown not to spare the other either. For by the same reasoning he might ask: how will the Divine be present everywhere, when none of the things to which it is present is naturally able to be extended along with it? It is present to each being, yet each is not present along with it. Each remains within its own circumscription and nature, cut off from any such connection with it. Being present everywhere does not belong by nature to all things, and the creature cannot be extended along with its Creator. The Divine visits living things, and lifeless things are not present with them. Has it therefore withdrawn from visiting these? On the contrary, it is present to lifeless things, and again living things

[?] cannot be present with them. Have these, then, met the same fate and been left outside such presence? For this youthful nonsense insists that, because they are not extended along with him who is present everywhere, they do not enjoy his illumination at all. The pursuits of sophists are certainly not wisdom. This, then, is the outline in summary. If you wish, you can add what remains from what has been said.

Question 39. How does Scripture say that [?] were born to Jacob from Rachel [?], when it gives the genealogy of [?]: 'The sons of Bela [?] were Gera and Naaman [?]… These are the sons of Rachel, whom she bore to Jacob' [?]? Since Rachel bore [only two sons] [?], how are these said to have been born to Jacob from Rachel? Resolve the difficulty. The Scripture of our sacred oracles interprets itself. It gave the genealogy of Jacob's sons, but did not end its account with the sons. It went on to the third generation as well. Yet it does not ascribe the cause of the multitude to those who directly begot them. It ascribes it to the first cause, from whom they too came forth under his guidance, and to whom the promises foretold that his race would be glorified by becoming a multitude. So Moses listed Jacob's descendants in the fourth generation, who had Benjamin as their forefather, and showed how many they were. Then he went back to the promise and to the one who received the promises. In place of the second and third causes, which are causes only by participation, he took and named the first cause of the race's great number, and said: 'These are the sons of Rachel, whom she bore to Jacob.' Going back through Benjamin's line, and from there to Rachel and Jacob, he refers the cause of the others listed earlier to Jacob as well. This also gives you a further point: the sacred oracles commonly call descendants 'sons'. In the same way they call the children of brothers 'brothers'. They do this not only for those related to each other, but also when the children of one brother are compared with the other brother. For one can plainly find that, just as those born of the same parents are called brothers, so too those born of them

[?] …but brought forth from kindred springs and watered into existence, have drawn on themselves the name of brothers in their relation to one another. And not only in relation to one another: the name is also used when some of them are compared with those placed in a more distant degree. An example is the one now called a cousin, in relation to an uncle, whether near or more distant. For these too, according to the idiom of the Oracles, take on the [name] of brotherhood [?]…

Of this kind too is what Moses said after the death of Nadab and Abihu to the sons of Uzziel the Levite, Elzaphan and Mishael (or Misadael, for there are two readings): "Come near and carry your brothers away from before [the sanctuary, out of the camp] [?]." For he called them brothers, though they had not opened the same mother's womb. Yet their seed went back not to foreign loins but to [the same stock] [?]. Nadab and his brother were sons of Aaron; Elzaphan and his brother were sons of Uzziel; and Uzziel was the brother of Aaron's father. Common usage, when it wants to name their relations to one another, will call Uzziel the uncle of Aaron and the great-uncle of Nadab and Abihu. It will call Mishael and Elzaphan cousins of Aaron and uncles of Nadab and Abihu. But Moses' writing chooses to call them brothers. Many other kinships and relations in our sacred Oracles, both the Old [and the New] [?], whose grace is proclaimed, are also found to have taken on the name of brothers. An example is what the beloved disciple and theologian says: "There stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas." For it is plain that the Virgin's birth shared nothing with any other offspring going back to Joachim and Anna, through which the relationship could take on the name of sisters.

QUESTION 40 [?].
The Lord's command in Exodus urges Moses: "Stretch out [your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers and their canals,] and over their marshes, and over every gathering of water, and it will become blood." When the miracle [?] … had reached its end, where was other water found that [served] the enchantments of the magicians [?] for their illusion of blood?

Some of our blessed Fathers say that, since [Egypt] borders on that same sea…

(for the seven mouths of the Nile also pour out into it), those whose task it was to serve the sorcery collected water from there. They supplied the waters of the sea to the enchanters' sorcery, so that it could be stained with the colour of blood.

But perhaps someone who attends to the passage that gives rise to the question, and carefully examines what comes before it and what follows, will find that the river was changed into blood, but not the remaining bodies of water. Nor were those changed that stand at springs or are held in some other way within their own bounds. For when Scripture recounts, after the miracle had taken place, the step-by-step progress of the wondrous work, it says, "He changed all the water into blood." It does not say this without qualification, but at once adds, "in the river." Then: "And the fish stank." This does not mean all the fish without qualification. It does not mean those in the sea, but those in the river. "And the Egyptians could not drink water" (from where?) "from the river." In the same way, the beginning of the account of the miracle, before the deed had been displayed, suggests the same understanding. For Moses writes, "You shall stand on the bank of the river." A little later Moses, announcing the Lord's command, says: "Thus says the Lord: By this you shall know that I am the Lord. Behold, with the rod in my hand I strike the water that is in the river" (not the water in all the land of Egypt, but "that in the river"), "and it shall be changed into blood; and the fish" (which ones?) "that are in the river shall die." Then: "And the river shall stink." And besides these: "The Egyptians shall not be able to drink water" (what water?) "from the river." So the passage that lies between these two texts, which announces the Lord's command in a second account, should be understood in the same sense, if indeed it is fitting to the Oracle and pleasing to God not to destroy its agreement with each of them. That passage reads: "Stretch out over the waters of Egypt" [?] … "over the waters of Egypt" — not simply all waters, but those over [their rivers] [?] … "their canals." Yet a single river flows through Egypt; there are not many rivers dividing it with their streams. So by both words, "waters" and "rivers" [?], it names the Nile.

[?] …since [the rod] did not drip upon them. But of everything that was in the river, nothing escaped the affliction shared by the river's waters. I am aware that some have taken "wood and stones" to mean vessels of wood and of stone. Two things refute them well enough. First, nothing is said of earthenware, glass, or the other materials from which such vessels are made. Second, naming wood and stones is very different from speaking of vessels, which are made by art and skill to hold liquids.

If, then, the water of the river and of all the streams in the river was changed into blood, but the waters of the rest of the land of Egypt were not changed, it is no puzzle that the Egyptian sorcerers took water from elsewhere and gave it the look and appearance of blood. To imitate the miracle, it would have been more suitable to take drinkable, fresh water for the display of the portent than a salty or tasteless [?] substance. For a change of material spoils the resemblance of the act.

But suppose all the waters of Egypt were turned into streams of blood by the rod of Moses and Aaron. First, it would not have been reasonable to subject the wronged to the same affliction as the wrongdoers, and to punish with thirst the very people for whose sake such wonders were being worked. Second, Pharaoh does not seem greatly troubled by the affliction, since it was possible to drink from elsewhere. Nor does he press Moses to free the Egyptians from the plague, as he did in the case of the frogs and similar plagues, though the scourge of thirst was harsher than the punishment by frogs. Third, if the Egyptians had known that all [?] the water in Egypt had been changed into blood (for the miracle was done to astound their madness and soften their hardness of heart), they would not even have tried "to dig around the river, so as to drink water; for they could not drink water from the river." Others who took pains to translate the Hebrew tongue into Greek have rendered this in agreement. Symmachus says: "And all Egypt dug round about the stream for water to drink, because they could not drink from the [water] [?]…"

…of the river." Aquila and Theodotion have also rendered it so [?]: "The change into blood made by Moses and Aaron affected the waters of the river."

This leads to a reasonable conclusion. The river became abominable, polluted and useless — the very river that the Egyptian nation called a god and worshipped as the giver of fruit and the giver of life, and into which they threw the infants of the Israelites to be killed. For the infants' blood also cried out from the waters, as Abel's did from the earth. The Egyptians had to pay the penalty for two things. One was their impious making of gods, by which they assigned to water, which is subject to countless changes and corruptions, the dignity of the eternal, impassible and unchanging nature. The other was the bloodshed they carried out on those guiltless infants. Because the infants had come forth into the light, the Egyptians, against the law of nature, exacted from them as a penalty the loss of the light itself. But the loving nature [of God] postpones for a time the punishment of human beings. It chastises and instructs in another way, by defiling and scourging the lifeless thing through which they dared both the pollution of bloodshed and the unholy deed of impiety toward God.

But even if one grants that the waters throughout all the land of Egypt were transformed into the substance of blood, it is still not shown to be impossible that the Egyptian sorcerers appeared to imitate the divine work through their wickedness. The miracle had been foretold to Moses, and Pharaoh perceived this. From the rod's change into a serpent, the Egyptian enchanters knew that the threat would certainly be carried out, for what had already happened bore witness to what would happen. They too were eager not to seem inferior in their contrivances. So they had good reason to know that he would change all the open-air waters of the land into blood. While the miracle had been announced but the divine work had not yet taken place, they drew as much water as they needed to display the illusion of their trick, prepared it beforehand and stored it away. In this way, at the moment of need, they would be seen to have plenty of water. By giving it the colour of blood, they would lessen the wonder of the divine work with the illusion of their falsehood.

Some have said that while Moses was miraculously turning the river water into blood, the sophists of falsehood were present at that same moment using their own evil arts. The greater part of the water served Moses' miracle, but no small part of it was set aside for the magicians' needs. But this claim is contrary to the narrative. It is also unworthy of the mighty and all-wise providence at work in Moses. It makes the bitterest enemy a partner and mediator of his power, and presents the implacable foe as an ally…

…by sharing with him and dividing with him the material set apart for the miracle. Besides, the Egyptian would not willingly have fallen into such madness as to make the river he reveres a conspicuous monument to his own bloodshed, to defile it with gore, and to turn the thing he honoured into something more loathsome — even if the colour was not [?] the work of deceived sight.

Another claim is that all the Egyptian water became blood through Moses' miracle, and that the magicians, lacking unchanged water, took the water that had been changed into blood and deceived the eyes of the onlookers into imagining a watery colour instead of the red stain. Apart from the fact that the narrative shows nothing of the kind, this claim also gives the magicians grounds for a time to boast. The blood made to look like water really had the nature of blood, so they could boast of their art [?]. The claim also makes the portent double instead of single: a change of blood into water, and of the water back into gore.

It has occurred to some to say that the enchanters worked their sorcery on the water after Moses had restored it from blood to its own nature. Others say, more reasonably than the rest, that all the other waters of Egypt were changed into blood by the mighty power of Moses, but those set aside for the Israelites' use were kept free of the change. For it would not have been consistent to harm the people for whose sake the plagues struck those who had set out to harm them, nor at once to avenge a people and to punish them through that same vengeance. There is also an abundance of proof from similar cases: of the remaining nine plagues brought on the Egyptians in succession, Israel was shown to be marked by none. On this view, since the water among the Israelites remained unchanged, the enchanters took it from there and used it as material for the wonder-working of their own trick.

So it can be seen from many angles that there is no difficulty either in Moses miraculously changing the nature of water into blood or in the Egyptian enchanters not lacking water. Through that water the sight of their illusion would steal for them the name of a miracle.

[?] …["I will harden"] the heart of Pharaoh"): God was long-suffering toward him during the time of his disobedience. He did not hand him over to utter destruction, nor the nation that disobeyed along with him, but more lovingly [?] held back his punishments. In this way he gave him freedom to be contemptuous and to disregard what was commanded. Pharaoh made God's long-suffering an occasion for greater disobedience and madness, and so he is said to be hardened by God. It is as though the divine love for humankind gave way to his disobedience and hatred of humankind and, in a sense, cooperated with them.

Many receive this interpretation without offence and embrace this explanation of the words as pious. Yet perhaps it gives an objector an opening that is not easily answered. For God did not bring the punishments in order to display his long-suffering. He brought them to break the madness of Pharaoh and his servants, and their unrestrained and bitter [?] mistreatment of the Israelites. Nor was it God's chief aim to wipe out the Egyptian race. Through fear of punishment and chastisement he meant to make them more compassionate and humane toward Israel, and readier and kinder in accepting its release from captivity and misery. So the account given at the beginning of the explanation takes its proper place, and its success in grasping the sense of the passages keeps it unshaken and secure.

It would not show any lack of sound judgment to say that "I will harden the heart of Pharaoh" means: "Though it is already hard and unyielding, I will show it all the more to be so, softened neither by the presence of death nor by punishments." For the hardness of Pharaoh's heart became plainer, and so did the hardness of all who, vying with his attitude, turned their humanity into savagery. It was shown and proclaimed to all, since so many and such great plagues neither softened their hardness and stubbornness nor washed away the full force of their callousness. Even before, the Pharaonic soul had been callused by cruelty and hatred of humankind and would not allow itself to be changed to gentleness. Yet it was not then so well known to be hard, self-willed and implacable. Nor was it so noised abroad among all others, or set up as an indelible monument of triumph, as when it was scourged by extraordinary works and still persisted in the same savagery and beastly impulse.

And if someone wishes to take the oracle more simply, and understands "I will harden" as "I will allow and permit it to become hard," this interpretation too does not depart from pious doctrine. But this change of wording has no treatment peculiar to itself,

but falls back on the common solution, the general method by which many other passages are also resolved.
