Examples are: "He gave them up to dishonourable passions"; and "God gave them up in the desires of their hearts"; and "Since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind"; and "He blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel should not shine on them"; and "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that should not see and ears that should not hear"; and "God has hardened their heart"; and "You turned our paths aside from your way"; and countless others.

Each of these sacred oracles may be brought to its clearest and [?] sense by other approaches. Even so, this common change of wording, applied to all similar cases, does no less to clear away what clouds our reasoning, and it shows the change without lengthy argument. Take "gave up" and "gave" and each of the other expressions as meaning "permitted," "gave way," "allowed." Taken so, God did not force anyone against the direction of his own impulse, nor compel what is not chosen to rule over choice, nor deprive our reasoning of its free will. He did not define what is in our power and what is not by shutting them within the same bounds. He did not drag the unwilling toward the good, nor rein back from their purpose those who did not wish it. Many found these expressions perplexing because their different meanings are bound together, undivided, by sharing one word. To change them in this way into expressions of equivalent force and double meaning would be a safe understanding, and a single interpretation that resolves several questions.

How, then, will "permitted," "did not prevent," "did not restrain," "did not forcibly change" and the like be taken in place of "gave up," "hardened" and the like? Because in human affairs, someone who has the power to cut off lawlessness or some other offence, but does not prevent his neighbour from sinning, does not escape the charge of having helped the sinner in his wrongdoing. And may he not be said to have handed over to the passions the one who has fallen? For it was in your power to keep your neighbour safe; but by not holding him back you pushed him toward the passions. He has stretched out his hand to take what belongs to others: you are there and able, so draw him back. He casts his eyes on the doorways of licentiousness

; you can stop it, so restrain him. But if you neither restrain him, nor draw him back, nor check him as he is swept along, the deed is no less yours than his who has fallen into the transgressions. So the one who is able to check wrongdoing but does not check it may be said himself to cooperate with the wrongdoer. Given how we customarily speak, it would be neither difficult nor inconsistent to use the expression in a similar way of God. Much of Greek usage employs the words in this way, and so does much of the custom of our sacred Oracles. And [?] in countless cases, the incomparable and transcendent difference from human things (the divine will, power, good pleasure and the like) not only offers no objection to reinterpreting these words, but actually helps to support the argument. For where will, power and good pleasure exercise their own activity entirely without hindrance, they show that this transposition of terms comes close to sacred language [?]. But these points are enough to give you an elementary grasp of the question.

QUESTION 42.
How should we understand the words "You were angry, and we sinned," spoken by the God-inspired Isaiah?

One could take "we sinned" to mean not that we chose actions that ruin the virtues, but simply that we failed to gain the things we chose and strove for. For a man may also be said to miss the mark when he set out to accomplish one thing and bent his effort toward what he desired, but fell into the opposite and is held fast by what he never hoped for instead of what he preferred. Of this kind (to leave aside for now any further examination of what will be said) are also "A man's way is not in himself" and "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain"; "You were angry, and we sinned" [?]…

and "Unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman stays awake in vain"; and "He will not delight in the strength of the horse, nor take pleasure in the legs of a man"; and "[Woe to] those who make deep counsel in their reasonings, and not through the Lord." These too, instead of not falling short of their endeavour, not only missed it but also brought the "woe" on themselves. Similar is what was said to those who trusted in Egypt: "You made a plan not through me, and covenants not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sin, you who go down to Egypt." For them the refuge and the hope of help are turned to shame and reproach. Each of these actions, and of many others like them, if deprived of the influence from above, would not reach its intended end. Nor will effort come to fulfilment unless the rich mercy of the favour from above has first been laid down. And if [God] is even angry with those who rely on their own counsels, how can they fail entirely to miss the goal and gain none of the things their mind strove for?

This line of interpretation shows a fitting and suitable sense for the passages cited and for any like them. But it does not serve equally well to make the original subject easy [?]. For what comes before in the passage, and the rest of the arrangement of its words, urge us rather to be guided toward another sense. What then must we say? Surely "You were angry, and we sinned" does not mean this: "Because your anger came first, our sin gained the mastery"? Such a reading would not preserve God's just judgment. It would not make man the cause even of the wickedness he does by choice. Instead it would blasphemously drag down the one who is the cause of no evil to the position of the guilty party. It would also refashion free will, given as a gift at the original creation, into slavery and subjection. For if "we sinned because he was angry," then anger gave birth to sin; and if an irresistible anger drives us into transgression, who will withstand it? So there is no room for steering the sacred words toward such reasoning. This is all the more so because many other teachings everywhere in holy Scripture, and indeed in the prophet himself, bear witness to the contrary and confirm it. ("For," he says, "the Lord has not made his ear too dull to hear"…

[?] "But your sins stand between you and God, and because of your sins he has turned his face away so as not to show mercy." So our sinning does not come from God turning away, and sin does not draw its strength from his overlooking us and not hearing. It is the other way round: the turning away, the wrath and God's abandonment come from the sins and offences we commit. And again: "We waited for judgment, and there is no salvation; it has stood far off from us. Why? Because our lawlessness is great before you, and our sins have stood against us. Our lawless deeds are within us, and we know our iniquities. We have acted impiously and lied, and we have turned away from following our God." Both the Old Teachings and the writings in which grace is renewed are full of passages like these. Where, then, is the wisdom and understanding of the same Scripture, if it teaches in one place that wrath is the cause of sin and of God turning away, and in another that sin brings about the turning away and the wrath? Comparing and studying these passages has shown clearly [?] [that sin brings on] the wrath. But what exactly the saying itself means, it has not yet shown with the same clarity. So the need calls for another examination [?], and perhaps the saying means something like this [?]: "Often, when sins were stirred up from elsewhere [?], your love for humankind and your compassion came to light. So when we set out to sin, and to take vengeance into our own hands [?], and [?] those who rose up against us were being carried along, your grace came first, and your kindness scattered their scheme and snatched us away from both impulse and sin. But now nothing of the kind is seen being arranged by your providence. Instead, wrath [takes the place of?] your goodness and love for humankind, and our sinning follows unhindered, since no one holds it back. Back then there were many occasions for our salvation, because your compassion and providence held our slippery nature in check. But now the wrath has been fanned into flame by our burning for the passions, and since no one checks the momentum, we have slipped, thoughts and all, into the very pit of sin."[?]

[?] Besides, he foreknows all things before they come to be, and knows them better than if they had already happened. So when he weighs the wickedness of our will and our intent with impartial justice, [?] the wrath in judgment, and fixes the [penalty?] for the sin, then, even though [his love toward] infants [?] and his goodness are disposed toward us, he will not be able [?] to hold back the sentence [?] or soften the verdict [?]. This is what usually happens in cases where

the wrath comes before the time of judgment. So the progress of our wicked thoughts, at leisure and while we deliberate them, provokes the stirring of wrath, and the deed that we then dare to commit calls forth the punishing sentences of that wrath. [?] It is clear that the hierophant wanted to show that the wrath cannot be appeased, turned aside or hindered, and so in his words he presented it as concurrent with the sin and as coming before it. For the judgment and wrath behind the punishments and penalties that have already fallen on us for our sins is completed and carried through without hindrance, change or appeasement. Or, if you prefer, he says "You were angry, and we sinned" because wrath in judgment is at one point determined and at another, once the sentences have been issued, carried into action: the first while the sin is being set in motion, the second once it has been committed. For wrath is divided and takes two forms. One is seen while the sin is being set in motion, the other when it is dared. The first plainly comes before the lawless deed, while the second follows it and accompanies it. So the wrath at the stage of deliberation precedes the wrongdoing, while the wrath kindled by the daring goes along with the deed and grows up with it. In the first sense, then, one may say without hesitation and with piety, "You were angry, and we sinned," since the wrath at the stage of deliberation exists before the sin. In the second sense the saying is neither pleasing to God nor consistent, for we do not sin because of wrath; rather, because we sin, we draw wrath upon ourselves. It would come to much the same thing if someone took this as his starting point and set it out in a gentler and more plaintive sense: "You did not check the impulse when our will was moved toward wicked deeds. Instead, you foresaw what would come to pass as if it had already happened (for your all-seeing eye beholds even what we have not yet carried out), and at our plotting of evil you allowed your wrath to begin to stir. While it hung over us, sin leapt upon us all the more boldly and found an easy way in. For when your love for us gives way to your hatred of evil, and compassion yields to justice, the prey becomes easy for the enemy to catch. If we had had some means of turning your wrath, once stirred, into kindness, sin would have shrunk from boldness into cowardice, and we, helped and strengthened, would have thrown off its assault rather than falling into its snares." But perhaps, even if it does not soar with loftier ideas, the meaning comes closer if "You were angry, and we sinned" is taken as "You were angry because we sinned," that is, "Because we sinned, you did not hold back your wrath against us."

For the conjunction that binds together words and thoughts in sentences, namely "and," is often used in a causal sense, both in our sacred Oracles and in Attic style, and the examples are known to all. I have no leisure to list the instances from Greek writers. I will mention two of ours and leave the collecting of the rest to your zeal, if you care to do it. The sacred psalmist and forefather of God, David, says: "Give us help from affliction, and vain is the help of man." Here the "and", which can stand for countless other examples, is enough to show that it is used causally, as if he said: "Give us help from affliction, for vain is the help of man." And Isaiah himself said (it is more fitting to show the conjunction "and" taken causally from the same voice and the same ground): "Woe to those who take counsel in secret, and their works will be in darkness." No one would dispute that "and will be" is said causally, and this is why the "woe" is launched against them. In the same way, "You were angry, and we sinned" will be understood without trouble or forced argument. The ready usage of Scripture lets it slip into the right meaning through an untroubled hearing, and in place of the initial difficulty it keeps intact the commonly held and God-pleasing confession. For it is a common notion, especially among the pious, that the Divine is angry when we sin. And one can see that the more modest this explanation is than the elevated one, the less it needs the roundabout words that squeeze the meaning with subtleties, and the more than sufficient it is. Still, we must not shrink from inquiry. Our sacred Oracles are a spring of saving waters that profit the soul, and the deeper we dig into them with our reasoning, the more abundantly the graces of their meanings will flow. The saying "You were angry, and we sinned" seemed perplexing when it was taken simply and heard as applying to the whole of human nature. For how could anyone escape sin if divine wrath sends it upon him? How could there be a just exaction of penalties for sins, if those who suffer this abuse are dragged against their will into what is unlawful? And where is free will? There are countless other such difficulties, and is it not the saying that is seen to cause them? But if someone applies it to the common axiom

[?] and thinks it is said of the whole of human nature, [he runs into these difficulties]. But if one does not force it into a universal sense, and instead keeps it within its own proper bounds, it will be seen to be free of most absurdities. What, then, do I mean? That the Prophet uttered the saying about the nation of Israel and not about all human beings without distinction. The very title of the prophecy bears witness to this and leaves no room for dispute: "The vision," it says, "which Isaiah son of Amoz saw, which he saw against Judea and against Jerusalem in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah." Even where he mentions other nations and reveals visions about them, his account of these too is for the most part directed at the people of Israel. At one time the foreigners serve as a scourge for the Israelites when they walk contrary to the Lord's ordinances. At another, divine favour puts power and victory into their hands when they hold fast to the Master's commandments. Indeed, shortly before the passage in question (to pass over the rest), the prophet makes it indisputable to all that "You were angry, and we sinned" is said of the people of Israel, speaking roughly as follows: "Where is he who led Moses by the right hand, the arm of his glory?... And he led them through the deep like a horse through the desert, and they did not grow weary... So you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name. Turn back from heaven, and look down from your holy and glorious dwelling... For you are our father, though Abraham did not know us and Israel did not acknowledge us." It would perhaps be tiresome to list everything. Since it has become perfectly clear, then, that "Behold, you were angry, and we sinned" is said of the people of Israel, the next question is [?] why it was said. They had enjoyed many marvellous and supernatural works. They had seen Egypt scourged with ten plagues for their sake. They had seen their pursuing enemies destroyed in utter ruin without hand or spear. They had seen the watery element offer its back dry for them to cross on foot, a pillar of fire blazing by night to show them a straight path, and a cloud of light keeping off the sun's rays so that the journey would be less painful. They had bread from heaven, harvested by the tongue of Moses. Sea and land set before them a table of ready-made sacrificial meat (55). Water from a rock- [NOTES. (33) "preparing" in the plural number [?]]

[?] rock gushed forth in unfailing springs. Israel enjoyed all these benefits and gifts beyond reason and imagining, as though everything that concerned them had been set apart as something exceptional and not according to the providence and care shown to the rest of mankind. So Israel utters a cry like this: "He who gave us these things freely, out of sheer goodness, would not have let us sin either, had he not allowed his great and indescribable concern and care for us to be turned into wrath." Israel would be saying and thinking these things as a lament, not as a declaration. He is not laying down doctrine but bewailing his state. He is not clearing himself of the blame for sinning, but mourning and accusing his own wilful wickedness. That is why he weaves into his other words things that are apt to stir affection and mercy: "You are our father; Abraham did not know us... from the beginning your name has been upon us," and whatever else is joined to these that can draw sympathy and kindness. It is as if he were saying: "Alas! In return for such a wealth of gifts, and glory proclaimed throughout the world, I am convicted of being caught in such sins, and of having become a reproach and a laughingstock!" Moreover, Israel is everywhere seen to be divided into two portions. Some of them make a calf and abandon God, while others punish their audacity with slaughter and death, carrying out the sentence of Moses, or rather the just judgment of God. Some serve God as priests, while for others a chasm in the earth becomes a ready-made grave. Some are consumed by flames sent from God, which exact the penalty for their grumbling, while others flee to mercy and gratitude and become spectators and witnesses of that astonishing sight. The bodies of some fall in the desert, and they are judged unworthy of the promised land, while others do not lose the promises. And there are countless other instances. Since the tribe of Israel is thus divided into two portions, the grateful and the ungrateful, nothing prevents us from saying that the thoughts and confessions of the grateful are these: "Our lawlessness is great before you, and our sins have stood against us; for our lawless deeds are within us, and we know our iniquities; we have acted impiously and lied... and we have turned away from following our God," and whatever else belongs to the same confession and contrition. But the blasphemies of the grumbling, thankless and ungrateful are these: "Behold, you were angry, and we sinned," and, if you like, also: "Why have you made us stray

from your way, and hardened our hearts so that we do not fear you?" and all such offshoots of the same desperate mind. What is said later in the passage could be settled [?] by other arguments and fitted into the sequence of the context and into uncontested agreement. Nevertheless, the method I have described is enough to scatter the mist of speculation and dissolve the cloud of doubt. There is no doubt that these blasphemous words belong to the ungrateful disposition. Those who make up the ungrateful, hardened and incurable portion are in the habit of grumbling against God and his servants and rising up against them. It is their custom [?] and practice, above all, not to regard themselves as the cause of all their evils, but to lay the blame on the source of all salvation, the cause of all good things. But what has been said has been said. I yield the judgment to those who have been graced with the gift of discernment by the power of the all-holy Spirit, and leave it to them to accept and embrace whichever explanation is better than the rest. At the end of my discourse I happened to remember the version of Symmachus. Had it occurred to me at the start, we would not have needed so many arguments and elaborate theories to reach a solution. For he rendered the saying like this: "You were angry with us when we sinned." This leaves nothing ambiguous and no [?] question, but sets out a meaning that is clear and too plain to be puzzled over. For we know, we all clearly know (57), that the Divine is angry at our sins. It is also plain that this version not only suffices by itself to resolve the difficulty, but also shows that not a few of the solutions given earlier are more secure [?]. It does not conflict with the others, but leaves them standing to serve their own purpose.

QUESTION 43. Why is it that, although our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ taught the mystery of baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, his apostles and disciples did not baptize in this way, but into the name of the Lord Jesus? 1. Some of the holy men can be seen confronting this difficulty, not with arguments that resolve the question, [NOTES. [?] in my version [?] was missing; [?] however has only "for we know clearly."]

but with arguments that dismiss the charge by granting pardon to those unable to keep the commands. They admit that the disciples did not baptize in the way they had been taught, but baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, acting on a principle of accommodation and foresight. They fitted their judgment all the more to the occasion and its urgency, managing this mystical and sacred act so that it would be beneficial and readily acceptable to those coming to the preaching. Whatever they saw, more than anything else, standing in the way of the crowds and troubling their minds, that above all they made it their business to treat and prepare for in advance. And what stood in the way and was thought hard to accept was confessing Christ as Saviour, and especially as Son of God and God, and obeying his precepts. So what they saw as most in need of teaching, they put before everything else, and they thought it right to initiate the crowd of those coming forward on that basis. That is why, when they baptized, they did not baptize into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Instead they invoked the Lord Jesus, and by the washing of rebirth they cleansed the baptized of their defilements. They consecrated the gift by calling on the name of the Teacher, and they taught that through him those found worthy of the cleansing are enrolled in adoption as sons. Only he, they taught, can make people sons of God by grace, for in him by nature and from eternity the dignity of sonship and divinity was present. Through him, too, the oneness in kind of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is seen and revealed together. So those who believed that they received adoption through the Son would not be slow to agree that he who grants it is God. This, then, is how some have undertaken to resolve the difficulty. 2. But I cannot see how anyone could try to tie a knot instead of untying one more effectively than by these arguments, weaving a difficulty no weaker than the first (59). For this would rather confirm the disciples' disagreement with their teacher and supply a reason for it. A reason for disagreeing does not remove the disagreement. On the contrary, it attaches a deliberate judgment to it and implies that the Master's own intent was set aside [?] on purpose. What could be more urgent than the theological proclamation that reveals, in a few names, the oneness of nature and equality of power of the Trinity? And this mystery was not imparted to them at the beginning, while the disciples were still imperfect, nor when the voluntary and saving sufferings were about to be accomplished and the crisis of the moment overshadowed the precise teaching that demands judgment [?]. It was imparted after the cross, after the burial, after the kingdom of Hades had been despoiled and

the enemy of our race had been handed over to unbreakable bonds. When he had risen from the tomb and inaugurated the common resurrection, then, then indeed, he who by nature, in his divinity, has authority over all things on earth and in heaven, and who also received it in his humanity, engraved this royal and saving law. He did not engrave it on tablets of stone, but on tablets too excellent to share in earthly matter: the minds of the apostles. Through them he spread out over the whole world, as it were, edicts and proclamations according to which those coming to piety were to be initiated and perfected. "Go," he says, "and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe (clearly, and before all else, what is now being introduced) everything I have commanded you." 3. What could be more urgent than this sacred and saving command? What need is there for human judgment, when the Master's voice proclaims the doctrine in sacred words and sets his verdict upon it more securely than any seal? Even if both had been equally urgent and equally needed, I mean the saving law and the disciples' judgment, and no other consideration had stood in the way, even so it would have been intolerable to put the serving tongue ahead of the Master's own teaching of the mystery. And if the disciples' practice entails setting aside the Teacher's command, how does the gracious pardon not turn into an audacity that does it outrage? It would mean considering the Master's judgment not urgent and the servants' idea urgent. It would mean neglecting what no one could admit to neglecting without madness, and cherishing and preferring a course whose judgment condemns the one who made it. But if they themselves so openly neglected and transgressed the force of so great and weighty a commandment, if they were truly guilty of the transgression, how could they urge the hearers of the sacred teachings to obey the Master's commandments, to conform to them, and to order their own lives by them? For trying to make people keepers of commands by setting commands aside is like demanding obedience from them while transgressing oneself. What better opportunity could the enemy find than this to embolden him to corrupt the teaching and heap the ultimate outrage on the preaching? 4. These and many other such points arise from pious and impartial reasoning. They discredit the supposed solution and prompt us to look for another account of the question. By it the difficult approach to the problem can be widened into the smooth and level ground of understanding, and the mist of doubts will be scattered. For that the all-holy and perfecting acts of piety of the holy apostles, when they administered baptism, are said to accomplish it in the name of Jesus Christ, none of the

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople

[?] … no one with sound hearing will venture to contradict. But what meaning such words and names unfold and express is no longer something everyone can understand. Peter, the chief of the apostles, urging the Jews toward repentance and announcing pardon for their bloodguilt, says: “Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins.” Again, when divine inspiration moved him to baptize the centurion, he counted Cornelius himself and those with him worthy of regeneration, and performed for them the gift of forgiveness in the name of the Lord. At Ephesus, too, there were disciples who had been baptized only with John's baptism. The history records that after they heard Paul teaching, and the Apostle laid his propitiatory hands on them in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, they received the heavenly gift of adoption and enjoyed the coming of the all-holy Spirit. Countless other passages of this kind, phrased about baptism in the same pattern of words, can be found without effort. Yet, as has been said, the obvious interpretation often sinks beneath the depth of the sacred meaning, and unless it is put to scholarly testing and study, it will not be freed from obscurity and from conflict of opinion. Indiscriminate assent to sounds, and acceptance based on the mere echo of words, have often given birth to many other absurdities in many matters. Here too such an approach would not only cut the awesome mystery of regeneration into two rites, but would display countless others, multiplying through the division. It would take the first addition as a starting point for those that follow, thinning the single and undivided character of piety, and the uniform, single mode of initiation, into a multitude. And once that uniform rite was set aside [?], not even the first rite that crept in and adulterated the prerogative of the Lord's command could escape being set aside along with it.

[?] … decreed, to confirm this and to perform regeneration according to it, a rite that is holy and beyond all reproach?

6. And I have not yet mentioned the irresistible force of the refutations: those who have abandoned the Lord's rite of initiation from the start will be forced, even against their will, to admit countless rites of the one adoption, and will expose the gift to mockery. They will baptize no longer with the priest pronouncing the divinely fitting invocations of the initiation, but with the candidate himself seizing the act of initiation before he is initiated, and then cleansing not others but himself with the washing of regeneration. For in the holy Acts of the Apostles themselves one finds that Ananias was one of the disciples, and a divine vision commanded him to bring into the company of the apostles the persecutor and dread enemy of piety who had not yet become Paul. When the initiator had removed, by the touch of his hand, the bodily darkness from the eyes of the one being initiated, then, at that very moment, Ananias said to the man who had been changed from darkness to light in both mind and eyes: “And now why do you delay? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.” “You calling on,” not someone else initiating him or chanting the theological invocations. What are you saying? The candidate performed the initiation before he received it? The one who needed regeneration himself brought about the regeneration? The one who was to be perfected by the priest's hands and lips seized the priest's dignity and conferred perfection on himself? Yet the superficial reading of the letter, on the strength of which they set aside the Lord's command, requires them to believe exactly this, even against their will. So here is another mode of initiation, agreeing with none of those already mentioned. And when the chief of the apostles, writing his catholic exhortations to the Jews of the dispersion, excelled [?] with both hands through the speed of his tongue and the swiftness of his pen (40), he pronounced baptism to be that of a good conscience, not consulting a prophetic tripod but speaking sacred words from a soul possessed by God. Would you not, then, seize on this expression too, proclaim the introduction of yet another initiation, and inaugurate a washing that cleanses sins, performed not in the name of the Lord Jesus, nor administered according to any of the other formulas mentioned, but consisting in “the pledge of a good conscience toward God”? Do you see to what absurdities they surrender themselves, those who prefer the unexamined utterance of names to the truth of the realities? But why should I add yet another point, no less offensive than those already mentioned, not to say heavier than them all? Paul, the loud-voiced trumpet of the Spirit, the man raised on high, trumpeted forth loudly and plainly that we were baptized into the death of Christ. You hear this, sir; but he said before

these words: “All of us who were baptized into Christ.” So, on the hypothesis of those who teach that the names are used indiscriminately, there are two initiations at once.

7. What, then, must be said? An impartial weighing of the refutations has the unanswerable power not only to refute those who invent the tale that the disciples practiced initiations different from the Lord's. It also seems to show that it is by no means blameless, while the Lord's sacred formula stands, to insert other expressions that do not preserve exact identity with it in every respect. But in fact there is nothing of the kind. These expressions do not legislate against it, commanding action contrary to its rule and decree, nor do they draw its prerogative to themselves. Rather, they refer the principle of regeneration to it alone, and signify and proclaim it through a variety of names. What, then, must be said? What else, besides what has been said, than to say by way of illustration that everything which signifies regeneration is like lamps shining with light, kindled from that divine source, pure and ever-flowing. They themselves, however, are not the purifying fire, nor is rebirth accomplished by them. That one thing alone bestows grace and adoption beyond reason, while these point to it, some more clearly, others more enigmatically, and mystically and concisely intimate to us one and the same initiation. For to those who love contemplation and have received from the Spirit the grace to understand the sense of names and words, each of the expressions used here and there proclaims baptism into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. But those who admit the sound of a word only as far as the gate of the ears, and leave the inner faculty of judgment mute, would stumble into countless errors.

8. Nor is it only in the present subject that many abandon the realities and sit idle beside bare words; they do so in countless others too. It is through these that the heretical tares which have sprung up beside the Church cultivate no nourishing fruit, but sprout poisonous drugs. Piety is not like this. Being everywhere of the spirit rather than of the letter, it harvests the fruit of piety and enjoys its nourishment, with no dragon's seed sown among it and no trace whatever of the ancient serpent showing through. How, after all, could one say that baptizing into Christ is a different law of baptism, or that baptizing into Christ's death is yet another? If each of these were a law of initiation, they would legislate against one another, and whatever means one used to overturn one would overturn the other as well. Likewise, if such expressions had the prerogative of introducing laws, the Lord's initiation would, not unreasonably, be

thrust aside as something superfluous and useless; and it, in turn, would bring about the abolition of all of them with more brilliant force and dignity. Therefore also from the [?] of the many words spoken against one another [?] to dispose of. But what else does he say than this: “For this reason I did not make baptism my principal work, so that I might not attach glory to myself by the number of those baptized, and so give a pretext for slander to the envious [?] and to those who make it their business to assail the finest things out of envy, as though I were trading in the salvation of the reborn and insulting the gift of the Spirit with praises of myself”? And from countless other passages one can see that glory, praise, and honor are signified by the word “name.”

9. Through these considerations, then, such reflection also passes on to the particular names. These distinguish and differentiate the persons. At times they announce an imitation and likeness of some magnificent act of each person; at times they prescribe the keeping and observance of commandments. It is in this sense that the Israelites are said to have been baptized into Moses (14). Imitating him, as it were, they crossed the watery element on foot, their feet unwetted. Making him the leader of the action and placing all their hope in looking to him, they proved stronger than the plot of the Egyptians. In the very streams that did not so much as wet their feet, they watched their pursuers go under, and they delighted in a double joy: the extraordinary, utter destruction of their enemies and their own deliverance beyond reason. A similar logic governs what the Teacher says [?]: “All of us who were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death.” By “were baptized into Christ” he proclaims both his initiation and the rite handed down, and that we accomplish the rebirth. By “into his death” he does not mean that we perform the washing of regeneration by invoking the Lord's death. God forbid! Such a transgression was dared by Eunomius the Anomoean (15). He means rather that those baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit imitate the Savior's death, as in sacred symbols and hidden mystical figures, and sketch and represent what he willingly endured. By the triple immersion [?] they portray his three-day sojourn in Hades, and by the equal number of emergences his resurrection on the third day, through which the restoration [?] and the renewal are portrayed as well. For indeed this very “being baptized into Christ,” and “into his death,” and “into

[?],” and “into the name of Christ,” and the like, show no great difference in the form of the names and words; but in the meaning they signify, and in the way they distinguish and express the reality, they display the greatest possible difference.

10. That the word “name” also signifies, in another way, the power of the proclamation (45), Ananias, Paul's initiator, makes clear, when he feared he would suffer what one would naturally expect Saul to do. To the one directing him to initiate the persecutor he says: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem.” Then: “And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” Yet it was not the work or concern of any of the faithful merely to shout the bare name of Christ, or to make the invocation a mere utterance of the lips, apart from correct doctrine and the faith into which he had initiated them. Rather, he here calls “those who call on the name” of Christ all those whom faith in him adorned, who could be seen to be lovers of his initiation, and whose struggle was for precision in piety. And what else was this than to think and proclaim that the Savior is the Son of God and consubstantial with the Father? “For I and the Father,” he says, “are one.” And indeed also that the all-holy Spirit proceeds from the Father (44) and is not estranged from his glory and divinity. For what proceeds from the Father's essence by nature, or rather by a supernatural and ineffable principle, knows how to bear in itself the glory, authority, and power of the one who sends it forth, and to preserve unaltered the stamp of that essence beyond reason. It is clear, too, that the Son, being the radiance of the Father, bears in himself everything with which the Father, in begetting him, adorned the form of his offspring by the rays of divinity, proclaiming their kinship. In such a theological initiation, then, the multitudes of believers were perfected. And they could rightly be said to call on the name of the Savior, because they preserved the orthodoxy of the doctrine of which he was the teacher.

11. No less will the discourse, as it proceeds, show through other passages as well that this view is consistent. For the one who gave the oracle, recalling Paul's initiator from his great anguish and fear, says in effect: “The very man you are amazed at and fear as an enemy of the saving proclamation is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel.” That is to say: not only has he leapt away from the ranks of the enemy, but he will also be revealed as a champion of the piety now under attack.

For when the God-fearing proclamation is besieged and shaken by the impious, he will lift it up, support it, and render it unshakable. This is what the force of the word “name” signifies here: the true faith, the mind of piety, the proclamation of theology, the mystery of the Word's incarnation. For what difficulty would there be, and what support would be needed, simply to address the Lord with a single word? Even the demons themselves sometimes cried out the Lord's name, and with some addition. But it is clear that here by “name” he means the proclamation announced through Paul and the reverence directed to God, for whose sake the former persecutor gladly bore countless deaths every day, teaching, exhorting, initiating, proclaiming the faith in accordance with the initiation the Savior revealed to him. “For I,” he says, “will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

12. Notice the repeated use of the word “name.” Why? So that the persistence of the word, signifying and making plain the same reality again and again, might through the hearing, as it were, imprint the mystery of piety on our thoughts; so that, bearing it in our minds like a royal seal and keeping our eyes on it, we might not turn aside onto many roads shaped by differing words. It was for this mystery and for precision in the faith that Paul suffered things beyond remedy. It was not for a bare name, nor for a word that confines the awesome greatness of the faith within a short combination of syllables. That is why one may hear the sacred words teaching once more: “Is this not the man who ravaged in Jerusalem those who called on this name?” For how could a word be ravaged, a word bounded by a brief stroke of air, which of itself opens onto no meaning or theological doctrine, which cannot implant precise doctrine in human souls, and whose existence lasts no longer than its utterance? It is clear that here by “name” we must understand not the ordinary sense current among everyone, but that which proclaims and signifies the mystery of all piety and the precision of the proclamation running through the whole of our theology. Such a name, that is, the perfection of the faith, sinks deep into our minds and takes a foundation firmly grounded in the God-loving disposition of believers and the steadfastness of their conviction. It was this name that Saul, as he once was, besieged, and that Paul, as he later became, carried before Gentiles and kings, showing it to be unalterable and invincible through his own struggles [?], and converting many of the nations from impiety and initiating them into this piety. Therefore, whenever the sacred Scriptures say that the disciples baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, or use some other construction of similar wording, we must understand it consistently with the formula of utterance laid down, and in a manner worthy of God. And of the

disciples we must suspect nothing unworthy, but confess that the apostles performed the rebirth in accordance with the Savior's proclamation and teaching, and that the others who initiated did likewise, neither thinking, nor saying, nor doing anything outside the Lord's command.

13. But perhaps it might occur to some to argue, not to say to wrangle: if the disciples baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, why are they said to baptize into the name of Christ, or the like? This has already been sufficiently shown by what has been said. Instead of much else, it would have been enough to trace the reason back to the usage of our sacred Scripture, to show that this way of speaking is characteristic of it, and to rid oneself of idle curiosity rather than philosophize. For in every kind of discourse many idioms can be observed by which it is characterized; and no one who recognizes an idiom lets his mind wander off into some other inquiry. This can be seen not only in God-inspired writings but also in what the Atticizing tongue takes pride in adorning. Still, nothing prevents us from explaining the idiom more fully as well; and indeed the discourse did not overlook this earlier, since the idiom is not without its reason. For the faith that he taught to the disciples, and through the disciples to the world, might justly be referred to him through the phrase “into the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” and similar expressions, in which, despite the difference of words, the meaning is the same and one. The name indicates this because he himself became the author of piety toward the divine, and because we are taught that in the remembrance of Jesus as Lord the whole mystery of the Word's dispensation for our sake is summed up and displayed together. Each of the pious can unfold it and through him be guided toward the perfection of the knowledge of God, not compressing and narrowing the sense of the doctrines to the brevity of the word (for that would be to utter a bare sound), but being enlarged and perfected in faith and in the fullness of piety. And, if you like: the Son is inseparable and undivided from the Father and the Spirit, since he is of the same superessential essence, power, and authority. Yet the Son, having taken up our flesh, was seen and touched, and became visible to our eyes and tangible to our touch. “For what we have beheld,” he says, “and our hands have touched, concerning the word of life, and the life was revealed.” Through the one person, then, who out of love for humankind became for us, as it were, an ineffable ocean of knowledge [?], and who initiated us into mysteries beyond reason, we have been illumined with the consubstantial, superessential, and single nature of the almighty Trinity, and have been led by his hand to the rest of the contemplation of the mystery. Fittingly, then, whenever we do anything in fulfillment of the doctrine handed down, we think it right to refer it to the one who handed these things down.

14. This also makes clear that Paul too proclaimed the name of Jesus, and in which sense of the name. Or rather, no one whose heart the grace of his words has touched can fail to see it. At one moment he showed forth the awesome love for humanity in the incarnation, both initiating others into the mystery and proclaiming it. At another he spoke boldly about the Trinity, proclaiming along with it the rest of the power of the mystery [?]. But nothing compares with hearing the man himself: “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance” (that is, the Father's), the Son “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped.” For he did not receive the inheritance of the Godhead by succession. Nor did he put the power on himself by attacking another and seizing it from him. From the beginning he was of the same essence and nature, and by nature [?] in no way subject to its removal. For this reason, apprehending no difficulty at all, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” And again: “One God and Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.” In just this way he proclaimed the economy of the Word and confirmed the theology of the Trinity. He took the unity away from none of the three hypostases, but referred them to it with equal honour. And he did not have one rule over and care for all things while another did so for only some. Rather, all three alike and with equal honour hold the creation of all that exists, together with lordship and providence. 15. Do you see how the teacher of the Church bore the name of Christ? Look further: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David.” Here again the Trinity is proclaimed, God and the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, and the incarnation of the Word is proclaimed along with it. Having said “Son of God,” he adds the things by which the Son is marked out. He was recognized, he says, and marked out by many other properties that belong to no one else. He was marked out especially because he became the author of his own resurrection, something that had never happened before. Not least, he was marked out by the work of the all-holy Spirit. At the birth the Spirit overshadowed the consubstantial Word and worked with him as he came forth from the seed of David. At the baptism the Spirit became a witness to his true sonship and consubstantial divinity. I think my hearers would find me tiresome, and fond of piling up what is superfluous, if I wrote out every passage in which the divine Paul set forth the Trinity and proclaimed the mystery of the incarnation, bearing the name of the Lord before Gentiles and kings. So we shall be content with what has been said. It will be no labour for anyone who wishes to collect the rest as well. The divine company of the other disciples clearly preached and taught in the same way. As they preached, so they baptized, and they preached as the subsistent Wisdom had taught them to speak of God and to preach. One of these teachings, which was

no less important than any of the other doctrines, was this. They were to perform the washing of regeneration into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by invoking them bring the baptized to rebirth. In this way the God-chosen assembly of the apostles initiated people into the gift of forgiveness. In this way Paul baptized those whom he baptized. In this way he bore the name of the Saviour before Gentiles and kings and spoke out boldly. It is in this sense that he cries: “I appeal to you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing.” 16. Would you like the chief of the apostles to appear as a witness for you too? In the wording of his phrases he may not seem to agree with the [teacher] of the Church and with [?], yet in truth he

is the one whose power healed the incurable disease. He taught that the name here stands for the sum and the confession of the faith. See what he says: “The God of Abraham and Isaac has glorified his servant Jesus.” Then, making his meaning plainer, he adds: “And by faith in his name, his name has made strong this man whom you see and know.” Pay attention: “Yes, and the faith that is through him has given him this perfect health.” As he begins to speak of the miracle, he declares that the name of Jesus Christ itself performed the healing. Then he moves from the name to the faith, which is the mystery of godliness. After that he calls the name [?] faith in him once more, as if afraid the hearers might forget that he had used the name to mean faith. Then he adds, “And the faith that is through him,” that is, the faith he preached. Do you see how the name here stands for faith in him, and the faith for the godliness he preached, and how that preaching makes the lame man's feet strong? So even if there were no other testimony, the testimony of the chief apostle alone would have been enough to show brilliantly what the sacred Oracles mean when they say that those who come are baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, and so on. Peter said these things as he displayed the divine work. The beloved disciple taught the same doctrine, Luke

wrote it down, and Paul taught it. The company of the other apostles proclaimed it along with them, for it is quite unthinkable that they went astray on essential matters. Thus the name of Christ is faith in Christ. And faith in Christ is the theology that he handed down to the eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, together with the mystery of the economy. 17. But if you want more arguments on this same subject, you will not be disappointed here either. First, no solution to the original difficulty could be more reasonable than the one already given, which clearly lays out an understanding of the question. Second, the solution that some have devised is not beyond reproach. It has already given many openings for criticism, and it would give you more if you wanted them. If merely saying the name of Christ put off those who first came to the faith, how could it have been right for those baptizing to bring it forward, of all things? Putting forward what pained them would not have healed what troubled them. It would only have made their minds harsher and more inflamed. Something painful soothes those who resent it when it is left unsaid rather than spoken. And it would have inflamed them to anger still more if the apostles had kept silent and passed over what most of the Jews already knew, I mean the Father and the Spirit, and instead brought in the title of the Son, which they could not even hear without pain (45). Brought forward in that way, it would have put them off all the more. Placed alongside the names they honoured, it would have left the hearer divided between what pained him and what pleased him, and he would have been troubled by only one novelty, the addition. But if the familiar and honoured names were passed over in silence, and only the offensive one were proclaimed in their place, would it not have been more natural for them to leap away at once and stop their ears? They would have been struck by two novelties, or rather many, and the arrow of pain would have struck them more bitterly and sharply. That would have made them utterly hostile and left them quite unable to come near the preaching at all. 18. “The Jewish nation,” he says, “could not bear to confess Christ as God. That is why the company of the apostles baptized in his name.” But how does it make sense to soothe with what inflames, or to heal by means of the wound? Would not the opposite argument be more reasonable and more sensible: the apostles did not baptize into the name of Christ, for those being initiated [would have taken it] hard… (45) The manuscript reads τὴν προσθήκην (“the addition”).

…[if the practice had come from] the disciples' own invention, as the contentious argument would have it, it would already have spread throughout the world and become customary for everyone being initiated. Before the innovation in baptism had spread widely, it would not have been so hard to establish the Lord's ordinance. But once it had reached the ends of the earth, who would have been able to drive out the rite that had taken hold and to call back the one given at the beginning but entirely silenced? The saving command found no room because the hearers were reluctant to accept it, even when no other initiation had yet taken hold of their ears or been written and stamped on their souls. How then could it find a way in once they had been taken hold of and initiated by the rite of the apostles, when the rite already holding unchallenged power would be clashing with it and rising up against it? Do you see how it is shown from every side to be impossible that the eyewitnesses and true ministers of the word (whose whole life and course was to seal their love for the Lord with their death) did (not) keep his decrees unbroken and unaltered? 19. What would you say? Who would not be seized with trembling and fear on hearing the sentences threatened by the apostolic ordinances? Not one or two of them, nor several one at a time, but the whole company of the disciples together declared them, confirming the Lord's command [?]. [?] We must hear the very words that have been ratified by a heavenly decree (46). They cry out loud and clear: “If any bishop or presbyter (pay attention, sir! Or rather, no special attention is needed here, for the Lord's tradition is plainly confirmed), if anyone, then, does not baptize according to the Lord's ordinance into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, let him be deposed.” Nor do they stop the condemnation there. Even if those who baptize try to use other names while in no way reducing the

number of the Trinity, even so they do not escape paying the same penalty, for they too insult the Lord's teaching just as much. Suppose they keep the names as handed down but do not join to them the proper form of immersion. Suppose they complete the baptism with one immersion instead of three, or rather, to put it more fittingly, finish the baptized person off. Suppose they carry out the rest of the command but baptize into the death of the Lord. None of them is acquitted of the charge. They fall under the same judgment and the same accusation, for transgression in like matters brings like punishment. Those who have dared to baptize in some other way are drifting toward setting aside the venerable command just as much as those who have decided to perform baptism by invoking Christ or his death. 20. Do you hear, O Paul? But bear with it: even after your crowns [?] you must strip once more for the contest! You are ravaging the Church again. You are taking letters from the Jewish high priests again. Having been Paul, you have fallen back into Saul. How can you, who taught these things, say again that all are baptized into the death of Christ? One moment, with your fellow apostles and fellow contenders, you demand penalties from those who dare to baptize in any of these ways. The next, on your own, you not only say it, and not in a corner, but proclaim it. And you do not only proclaim it without writing it. You put the message in writing, above all when writing to the Romans, and you raise to unassailable strength the teaching that the baptized are baptized into the death of Christ. But the herald of the truth would silence those who introduce the innovation in baptism and accuse him himself of voting for their opinion. He would answer them like this: 21. “Yes,” he says, “I confess that those who were baptized were baptized into the death of Christ. But I do not confess that baptism is performed by invoking his death. Far from it! This gift of forgiveness is performed, as the Saviour himself handed it down, into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. It is, however, a symbol of his death. Through the threefold immersion and rising up out of the water it pictures and represents his three-day burial and resurrection. That is why I did not simply say, ‘We were baptized into his death.’ I first put, ‘As many of us as were baptized into Christ,’ and then added, ‘were baptized into his death.’ By setting these different ideas and names side by side in one sentence, I taught that baptism is performed by invoking neither of them. Otherwise I would be caught thinking and saying contradictory things, and at the same time. By saying ‘We were baptized into Christ,’ I indicated that we were baptized according to the rite he instituted. By

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. saying ‘We were baptized into his death,’ I indicated that saving baptism bears the figure and image of his death, from which immortality has flowed for us. It is one thing to say this, which we also hold. It is quite another to say that the mystery of regeneration is performed by invoking his death, which we condemn. So we have not changed sides, nor gone back to the Jewish letters that we condemned. The heavenly doctrines were written once for all, not on tablets of stone, but on the soul's tablets, which are firmer than any and cannot be broken. Yet these people try to turn Paul back into Saul, and they disparage the rest as well, though they are ashamed to admit it. They have taken it upon themselves to twist and slander my words. I too cherish and ratify the common decrees of my fellow apostles. I would show no leniency whatever to those who dare to baptize in some other way and not according to the Lord's rite. That holds whether they use names equal in number to those of the Trinity, or falsify nothing else but complete the baptism with a single immersion, or are guilty of neither of these but baptize into the name of Christ or of his death, or devise some other notion that tampers with his divine and saving tradition. On the contrary, let no one catch me failing to record as liable to the same condemnation anyone convicted of any one of these things, or of anything like them. Changing the kind of names used does not make the offence a mild one. Transgressing the command brings the same condemnation on all who are guilty of it.” So speaks Paul, the orator of the Church. He defends its custom and its practices, strengthens the saving command, silences all who have tried to lean the other way, and sets his seal on the decrees of those who preceded him in election and apostleship. But what do you say [?]? Is it possible to accuse others of transgression and yet become teachers of transgression oneself? Or to exact penalties from others for transgression while thinking oneself not answerable for the same daring act? Indeed, for whatever others did wrong, if they did wrong, it is these men who ought to pay the penalty, since it was they who gave the others the occasion. But I think this too is enough. 22. It is now time to look back over the many arguments by which the solution to the original difficulty has advanced. It advances, first, by an argument that distinguishes the meanings of the word “name” and clears up the confusion. We can then know clearly when “name” means the proper name itself, when it means the glory and honour of the one named, and when it means his teaching and preaching. The solution is also supported by recognizing that a likeness in the form of the wording is not always matched by a likeness in meaning. Being baptized “into the death of Christ,” being baptized “into Christ,” and indeed being baptized “into one body” will not convey the same thought just because the expressions have the same form. Rather, as much as these

come close to one another and resemble one another in the sound of their words and names, so far do they stand apart from one another in the difference of their meanings. In addition, there are the absurdities shown to follow from the other solutions. Further, if the disciples had tampered with their teacher's legislation, it could not have been recovered from anywhere else. That setting aside of the command would have prevailed to this day, and the order now held sacred in the Church would have had no way in. Moreover, Peter and Paul, the chief disciples, stand as witnesses to this solution. And there is the awesome and fearful point that the inexorable synodal sentence of the apostles falls on those who dare to perform baptism in some other way, contrary to the Master's law, and to legislate against his lordship. This is why the Church throughout the whole world, which baptizes into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit in succession to the acts and preaching of the apostles, is accustomed to sing in a melodious and ringing voice, once the baptized have been cleansed by regeneration: “As many as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (48). By this it proclaims no less clearly that the apostles did the same. Now we say that those baptized into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit have been baptized into Christ and have put on Christ. Likewise, when the company of the apostles performed the washing of regeneration with the invocation of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, they were said to baptize into Christ, and in the name of Jesus Christ, and so on (49).

QUESTION 44. What is meant by the saying, “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not be lacking on your head,” and “The wise man's eyes are in his head”? Those who lived by the ancient ordinances took the wearing of white as a cherished symbol of sacred joy and of a holy state. They also made anointing the head with oil a sign of the same disposition. That is why our Lord, turning us away from imitating the Pharisees, said, “But when you fast, anoint your head with oil.” In other words, do not weave anything gloomy or downcast into the good work of fasting. Since, then, the

white garments and the oil adorned the body for those under the Law, and showed a life lived in joy, the Word uses these outward examples to urge us to keep the soul itself bright and beautiful. It would be bright and beautiful if its garments too were white. They would become white when they shine and glow with the purity and brilliance of the virtues, with no vice darkening them. Without these, not even piety toward God can exist. For it is piety that puts forth the virtues and makes them well up. It makes their company harmonious and in tune. It weaves the wedding garment worthy of the heavenly bridal chamber and prepares the soul to be clothed in it. And it brings about salvation. For all this, the anointing with oil is especially laid down and prepared beforehand. So the word says, “And let oil not be lacking on your head.” By this he depicts almsgiving toward our neighbours and the stream of earthly oil [?], and he bids that our head never lack it. Someone who showed mercy once has not thereby achieved mercy. If he often overlooked someone in need, he has turned his earlier good deed into his accuser. He cannot avoid being exposed as one who scorns virtue and almsgiving [?], and his conduct shows that the deed came not from virtue but from some passing circumstance. See how deep and carefully considered the wording is: “Let not the oil be lacking on your head,” he says. Even if someone has often been anointed, he says, the moment he stops being anointed this becomes a lack in what he did before. Besides this, the expressiveness of the wording opens up a further insight. One who uses this oil does not confer as much benefit on those who receive mercy as he lays up and secures as gain for himself. That is why he calls neglecting mercy toward those who share our nature a lack in one's own anointing and benefit. And it is not simply the loss of some ordinary part of the body, but of the most sovereign part, the one that holds the rest together: the head. Lacking what the head is anointed with is just what has been described. Many people admire neither possessing the oil nor using it, but they take on a craving for the glory and reputation it brings. Some give away a few of their possessions, and things they do not even value, wishing to collect the name that comes from oil, that of being merciful. Others do it so that the crowd will think them above money and contemptuous of what most people eagerly seek. Others do it for some other reason that has nothing to do with virtue. With these people, even if mercy seems to flow out, it does not come from the head or go to the head. It does not spring from sound judgment and uprightness of mind, but from a wavering purpose and from indulging the passions. This oil could have been poured out and lavished to the great advantage and salvation of the one who empties it out. Instead it is poured away [?] to his loss and peril, and those who empty it out get in return not even a drop of benefit. But one who gives mercy solely to relieve the poor, to make atonement for his own soul, and for the sake of virtue truly pours out the gift from the head

…and of right judgment, and he does not deprive his own head of the anointing that strengthens the soul's governing faculty and makes it cheerful. It is clear that other virtues grow up and blossom together with the achievement of almsgiving. For who truly carries within himself the precious treasure of mercy, unadulterated, and will cast an envious eye on his neighbour, or will look upon [?] a tyrant's hand, when his own hand has not yet stopped stretching out the mercy that pours forth from it? Who will rob other men of their marriages while he is drenched in oil and softened in his mind? And how will this man exact interest from debtors, when he shares out among the needier even what his father's inheritance has brought him? So through one virtue, the one that pours out mercy, once he has secured its leadership, he will draw up the others as its kin and attendants, as a phalanx and as allies for himself, and will make them his own. And one who has achieved mercy with zeal and wisdom would also have his eyes in his head, that is, the habit and faculty that oversees and tells the worse from the better. For those who hold back from the practice of mercy and compassion, the eyes and discernment are no longer in the head, nor able to give light and guide the one who uses them. They are in the loins or the belly, or rather they have become a footstool for the feet, trampled and made useless, and they leave the man blind and wandering in deep darkness. And if the head of man is Christ, the saying urges us always and continually to look toward him, and to fix and lift up in him all our watchful and contemplative care: “I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.” And again: “As the eyes of a maidservant,” it says, “look to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God”; and what a gain this is: generous and rich gifts come upon us [?]. Moreover, while our eyes are always turned to the Lord, the snares that the enemy spreads beside our steps are idle and useless and have no strength to hold our feet. For he himself, the Creator and Provider, through whom we have trusted and believed that we see, will pluck our feet out of the enemy's snares with invincible strength, and will make the road of our salvation smooth and level. We have now explained how “Let not oil be lacking on your head” ought to be understood. But if instead of “let not be lacking” the saying is read in the text as “shall not be lacking” (for this reading of the words is also found), nothing prevents it. Then “Let your garments be white,” as was said before, is taken as a symbol of the virtues, and “Oil shall not be lacking on the head” means this: when good deeds shine around the soul, and it is clothed with the intelligible world and the brightness that comes from them, the precious oil and ointment, which signifies the grace and gift of the Holy Spirit, will not fail to water and

anoint your governing faculty, and to fill it with every holy and blessed contemplation and perfection. Christ is also called, and believed to be, the head of the Church, that is, of the faithful; and in another way he makes the poor his own and takes the alms given to them as given to himself: “For inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” So through the words before us the Preacher urges us not to neglect anointing our head with oil, which means giving alms to the poor without ceasing. For through them we offer up mercy to our head, Christ. But enough of this. I know, however, of some people who enjoy considerable esteem in many matters and who hold that Solomon, in the words before us, points to the regeneration that cleanses away the defilements we bear from birth and the filth of our attachment to matter, this purifying and saving regeneration. For, they say, he foresaw the coming of Christ and the mystic rites instituted through him, and so urges man to prefer above everything else this pure and radiant shining garment and the whiteness that sinks deep, even into the soul. In this rite the head too is anointed with oil, the ointment consecrated through the Holy Spirit, and the senses that the head governs, as it supplies from itself the stream of perceptions [?]. Nearly the whole wording fits the proposed interpretation as a shoe fits the foot, and its [?] interpretation of all the other explanations leaves no one in any doubt that it has been well and most accurately considered. But I do not know how one could reconcile wearing white garments at every time, and the head never lacking the anointing with ointment, with rites that have [?] a set time for being performed. Moreover, I do not know how one could easily clear of futility the idea that an exhortation was being given at that time to no one, to people who could neither understand it nor bring themselves to put it into practice. Perhaps, though, “wearing white at every time” could be understood of one who after the purifying baptism wraps himself in the brightness of the virtues and drives the darkness of sin entirely away, so that it cannot come near him. Such a person is clothed in shining garments at every time; and such a person would also never lack the ointment on his head, since he always sets his mind on the things of the Spirit and is watered by the streams of grace that come from there. And if Solomon also possessed the prophetic gift in full, as he set out things divine and human, then he spoke beforehand the word whose fulfilment in deed was to come in later times.
Question 45. How should “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” be understood? For many have made it an occasion for stumbling. It is no wonder if someone who is unsteady in judgment

stumbles at things in which salvation and benefit shine out for many. The wonder is rather that the light [?] bears to shine around the understanding even of those who wilfully blind themselves, and to lead them by the hand, and does not disdain [?] to let them see the truth. For our Lord and Saviour too became a stumbling block to those who are perishing, a rock of offence, and the rejected stone that was laid as the head of the corner. He did not himself become these things; he only seemed to have become them to those who had gone astray. Here too, then, when the Saviour uttered the saying “Who is my mother?”, he was not disowning his mother, as the godless thinking of the impious would have it, nor did he hold her who bore him in low esteem. When he was at the less mature stage of life and was still known by the law of nature, he was subject to his Mother and everywhere upheld the privileges due to her who bore him. How then, once he had reached full maturity, could he have behaved toward his Mother in a less mature and more ungrateful way? So the words are not those of someone disowning his Mother (far from it!) but of someone conveying some other meaning. For how would it be consistent, how free of contradiction, that he who out of love for mankind deigned to come forth in the flesh from her, and was pleased to fashion for himself a mortal form from her immaculate blood and to clothe himself in it, should disdain to acknowledge her as his Mother and deny her kinship in words, when he had already established, secured and granted that relationship in fact and in truth? And if he was going to deny her (oh, what idle chatter!), why did he take her up at all in the first place? Why did he put on a form whose shape he thought an outrage? For their tongues have pushed their audacity even this far; but their madness proves its own refutation, both by this and by many other things. Perhaps someone not [?] shaping his view from the indications of the Gospels will say that the Saviour spoke these words without curtailing his Mother's honour, and still less denying his natural relationship and affection for her, and without in the least withholding the privileges fitting for her who bore him. Yet, he will say, the Saviour put ahead of his attention to her the salvation of mankind and the teaching that leads to that end. For their sake came the Mother and the birth, the emptying from the Father's bosom that left it never empty, his life and conduct among men, the voluntary cross and the death of a criminal, and then the burial and resurrection. Such a person would try to strengthen this idea by arguing that Jesus could not have acted otherwise without departing from this order and chain of providence. For along with his other saving lessons, the Saviour also taught people not to prefer father or mother or wife to his teaching, which benefits the soul, and to devotion to himself. “For whoever,” he says, “does not leave father or mother, etc., is not worthy of me.” That is, whoever does not prefer my saving exhortation and admonition, and love for me, has fallen away from the never-ending good things, and has fallen away from the blessedness which is enjoyed forever by those who preferred, above the bonds of kinship,

my laws and divine love. And to make the commandment easy and readily achievable, the Saviour himself carries it out first and puts teaching his hearers ahead of his mother's need and the favour she asked, all but saying: “Just as I, in teaching you and being occupied with your salvation, have put attention to my mother second and chosen your salvation, so you must free yourselves [?] from every relationship and sympathy that arises from bodily ties, for the sake of your own salvation and of keeping and observing my teachings and laws.” This is why he did not allow the man who asked to go and bury his father. He was not giving people a pretext to despise their mothers (God forbid! and least of all his holy Mother), nor to disown their relationship to their fathers and insult that affection. Everywhere he was urging that the salvation of the soul be preferred to every bodily attachment and disposition. Someone might perhaps set all this out, as has been said, believing that he does not deprive the mother of the privileges of her honour but preserves them intact, and that he keeps the respect and reverence due to her. And yet the comparison explains how the thing compared came down to the lower rank, but it does not free it from being lowered. I also know of some of our blessed Fathers, whom I have often admired and accepted in many things but would not admire in this opinion. In refuting the impious view, they came down to this notion: that the Mother of Jesus felt something human. She took pride in her Son, and she wanted to be openly recognised and to overflow with exultation, because she bore the name of Mother of so great a Son. That, they say, is why she approached while her Son was teaching: so that, as he was naturally being glorified for his teaching, she might share in the glory and have her part of the praise. And therefore the Saviour, who cleanses others of the passions of the soul and wished to free his Mother of such failings, uttered a saying with the force of a rebuke: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” Well, those to whom it occurred to say this have said it. But if we examine the sequence of events, first of all we do not see the Mother displaying anything of the kind or showing a haughty spirit. She did not present herself uninvited while he was teaching. She did not come into the middle of the gathering, interrupt his teaching, or say anything lofty or boastful. She stood outside with great reverence and merely made her presence known, or rather she did not even make it known in words, but wisely let the sight of her deliver the message. How is this a woman eager to be glorified, a woman seeking to be exalted and to pride herself on her son's greatness? What else would even a servant have done, if need called him to come to the Lord? So Jesus' words were not a rebuke to his Mother, nor any way of censuring and correcting a fault. For there was no fault anywhere. Rather, he was silencing a Jewish

jibe that had been uttered. For the spiteful and ungrateful Jews used to say, to slander and insult the Saviour, “Is not this the carpenter's son? Are not his mother and his brothers here among us?” And again: “But we know where this man comes from.” And at that time too, as he was teaching and setting forth the salvation of souls, they envied him and begrudged him the crowd and were burning to slander him. Finding no way to do so, they fall back on their usual abuse and drag out his mother and brothers again for scorn and contempt, all but saying: “Whom are you teaching? Who do you make yourself out to be? Aren't you the son of a poor woman? And your brothers are no different: they live by the work of their hands. Look, they are standing outside looking for you.
