Stop teaching and run off to your relatives. Lead the same kind of life they do, instead of climbing up to the dignity of a teacher.” While they were scheming in this way, as was their habit, the Saviour answered them, opposing them with patience and gentleness, and said in effect: “I am so far from being ashamed of my mother and brothers that I do not turn away from the mother whom nature gave me or from those whom common opinion counted as my kin, nor do I consider them a shame or a reproach. More than that: all these people you see here, listening to the sacred words of salvation, I do not disdain to call fathers and brothers, if only they do my Father's will, even though neither nature nor opinion supports these affectionate relationships for them. Who then is my mother and my sister? Why do you twist these names into an insult and reproach against me? I am so far from being ashamed of them that I have chosen to bind even my true disciples to myself by these names and relationships.” From this one can see that the words in question not only had nothing ungrateful in them and showed no neglect of his mother, but even establish for her the greatest and most fitting honour. He grants her such reverence and privilege, and such a claim to his affection, that he raises those who fulfil the Father's will, and have been lifted to so great a height of virtue, to the relationship and name of mother, as to something great and exceptional in glory; and it is through this that the title of brothers now enjoys honour as well. For if he had judged that relationship fit to be cast off, if he had thought that name fit to be set aside, how could he then have conferred and bestowed it as the crowning summit of all good things on the heirs of the kingdom of heaven? It has therefore become perfectly evident, I think, as was said before, that the words “Who is my mother, etc.” are not only no insult to his mother's affection and dignity, but even gather fitting glory and praise to her from every side. In this way they would be turned, for the senseless, to the opposite of what they were snorting about, and directed toward the pious and proper wisdom about God. So too with “Woman, what have I to do with you? My hour has not yet come.” For if anyone carefully

studies the setting in which these words were spoken, with divine grace working with him and helping him in his study, he will find that they bestow glory and honour on his mother rather than show any disregard for her at all. For in the matter of miracles the Mother and the Son had nothing in common. Working miracles belonged to the Godhead in itself, but to the human nature not in itself, only because of the Word who had assumed it. Yet even in a matter where mother and son had nothing in common, see how he shows the surpassing greatness of her honour within that very difference. When his Mother asked him to work a miracle, he pointed out that this was not something she and he had in common, and added that the time had not come for him to perform divine signs. Then he showed that his reverence and honour for his mother had more power than both the time and the difference in power, so that his words, far from lessening his mother's glory, made it many times greater. For to regard her as having more authority than the time, and as rising above the laws that govern the order of miracles, and then to do what she proposed: how many times greater does this make her honour and reverence? Or if these things had not been said and shown [?]. For through what he said and did he all but shows it, saying: “Sharing a nature does not mean sharing in working wonders. Woman, what have I to do with you? Nor is the proper time for divine works here yet. But so that you may know, you and all whom need has brought together to see and hear, that your rights as a mother remain unaltered [?], and that I myself am the one who laid down the law that children should show their mother reverence—and further, that I put my reverence, obedience and glory toward you ahead of both the order observed in nature and the suitability of the time—look, I am changing the water into wine, because your request has made those things secondary.” For “What have I to do with you?” is not said here in the same sense as when it was said to the man who wanted him to act as arbiter of his father's inheritance. There he said, “What have I to do with you? And who made me a ruler and judge over you?” He confirmed by action the refusal in his words and did not choose to become the judge of a dispute over petty, material gain; but the refusal in words, the rejection [?] through deeds

Here, however, though he used that form of expression, he did not dismiss what his mother had in mind about the miracle, nor did he suggest that her request was rejected. Instead, having taught, within their shared nature, the difference that concerns divine works, he showed clearly that the deed matched the request. As has been said, he showed many times over that his mother's affection and glory carried more weight with him than the suitability of the time and the special nature of miracles.

Question 46. How does this not contradict itself: “It was said to those of old, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’; but I say to you, do not resist the evil one; but whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well”? First, because the one who said, “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it,” is himself the one who pronounced both rulings. No one, not even an ordinary person, let alone a lawgiver, contradicts himself at the same moment. Nor would one who says he does not abolish the law put forward words that abolish it, and certainly not in the same words and in direct sequence, as opposed to at different times and in different phrasing. So these sayings are not opposed; far from it. The commandment that has the character of legislation regulates and trains the judge to keep his mind impartial and his verdict unbending, and to give the litigants an evenly balanced eye of justice. But the commandment not to resist the evil one amounts to not prosecuting or retaliating against the one who started the unjust violence, for his wicked deeds. It no longer looks to the judge, but summons the injured party to forbearance and reverence. This shames the wrongdoer and turns him from boldness and madness to repentance and dejection, unless perhaps he is a beast wearing human form; and it adorns the injured party with the crown of gentleness and philosophy. For the law gives him the right to exact justice from the one who has hurt him. But whoever turns that right into love for mankind and takes pity on his fellow man, directing his just anger only at the author of evils and the ancient enemy of our race, truly ennobles the free will of human nature and has the common Master cancelling human debts. For a nature grapples with nothing but its opposite; the battle advances through the same means by which [?] each advances. You have received the power to punish the wrongdoer by law. If you punish him, it is unclear whether you would have leapt to take revenge on your neighbour even without that power, and preferred getting in first to avoid suffering over not doing harm, and whether you carried out the act without a humane and brotherly mind. But if you do not punish him, you have set up an indelible monument to humanity and gentleness, and left to life an example of living humanely and gently with one's kin. Above all, it is the loveliest and most blessed thing to be raised through such an act to the imitation of divine goodness, and to be called and known as a son of God by grace, as Wisdom and Truth in person affirmed: “Be merciful, as our Father [thus the manuscript] is also merciful.” But if you still wish to [?] the laws

…to philosophize, you will see from this how they agree. The commandment that requires the judge to put out an eye for an eye checks the boldness to do wrong, plainly through fear of suffering what cannot be escaped. The virtue of not retaliating, on the other hand, proclaims the wronged person superior to a passionate disposition and to the human urge to pay back pain for pain, and worthy of admiration. In either way one can see love for humanity advancing and pure mercy poured out on those of the same race. And if love for humanity and gentleness are established by either course of action, it is clear that neither commandment fights against the other, and neither is abolished by the other. Otherwise, how could both alike bring about the salvation of human beings? The one cuts short the impulse of those who raise unjust hands. The other sets the wronged above all pettiness of soul and does not let them be enslaved to the passions that outrage arouses. And the one shows what kind of man struck what kind of man with the blow, and how the one who deserved to suffer took vengeance on his better [?]. Many other things also converge into one and are brought to completion together through both of these saving and beneficial commandments.

QUESTION 47. When the Lord says, "You are of your father the devil," we ask whom he calls the devil, and who the devil's father is. Those before us have put forward differing opinions on this question. Some say that the father of the devil is the one who has driven on to the very extreme of wickedness, multiplied the offspring of the evil one within himself, and often given birth to many deeds of a kind the evil one had not dared before. If so, nothing prevents the father, surpassed in begetting by what came from him, from taking the rank of the son. Meanwhile the one who outdid him in wickedness, and in a sense begot his own begetter, passes over in turn into the relation of father. Take Cain, if you like. He gave birth to many devils at once. That is, he conceived and brought forth the devil's deeds, which had never before had the boldness to break into labor. He tried to cheat with a lie not just anyone but the One who knows all things even before they come to be. He went after his brother with deceit. He stretched a snare against his dearest kin, hidden under the guise of affection. He contrived murder with a brother's right hand. He was the first to outrage the earth with human blood, and he inflicted an incurable wound on his parents. And [?] to demand the reward of their childbearing, that they should not rejoice in a second child, convicting what had gone before with madness and harsher contradiction [?]. And there are other things of that kind. One may also see like things by analogy from their opposites. The one who has come to the summit of virtue through the visitation and working of the All-Holy [Spirit], who multiplies grace within himself and becomes beneficial and saving to many by what he brings forth, is said to give birth to the Spirit of God: "For through fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and travailed, and brought forth; we have conceived the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." In just the same way, the man who has driven on to the extreme of wickedness, conceiving the seeds of the evil one within himself and mul-

-tiplying his offspring and the brood of wickedness, might reasonably be said to give birth to the devil and to be called his father. Others approve neither of these views. They think it is the serpent that is called the father of the devil. Why? Because the serpent first conceived that slander and brought it forth with its tongue. Before man was fashioned and the serpent came into being, the one who fell away from the good sense and rank of the angels was not yet doing the works of the devil. He was seeking to be evil, but he had no opening to slip in. So the reptile, the serpent, having become pregnant with diabolical thoughts and [delivered them] with its tongue, might reasonably be called the father of the devil.

These and other such things have been worked out by others to explain the saying, both who is called the devil and who his father is. As for me, I am not much inclined to admire the solutions mentioned, nor [?] the labors of learned men. Those who are better equipped to see into such matters would have the better right to pass the better verdict on them. But whatever may occur to me, as perhaps to someone else, without attaining full perfection in this matter, I will now set out in words.

First, nowhere in our sacred Scripture have I been able to find anyone called the father of the devil. I have not found it in the older parts of the Law, nor in the parts where grace flashed forth the light of godliness more brightly. Nowhere at all, although many passages often make mention of that wicked and accursed will. Instead they teach that the primeval enemy of our race is called Satan, devil, apostate, Assyrian mind, ruler of the passions, wielder of authority over the spirits of wickedness, and such names. And sometimes the one who has conceived the devil's wretched seed within himself and been adopted through the birth of error is called a son of the devil. That is why the divine Paul named Elymas a son of the devil. But a father of the devil, up to now, I cannot affirm that our sacred Scripture either recognizes or names. So this is one point: nowhere in the idiom of the oracles of the Spirit is a father of the devil either known or named.

Second, not even where people think he is mentioned can they offer a secure basis for the supposition. The people of the Jews nowhere strove to trace their descent back to a father of God [?]. Rather, they were eager to inscribe God as their father in word, and to call themselves children of Israel. And it was not the aim of our Creator and Savior to show that the Jews were called children of the father of the devil. For then they would have been boasting of one [father], and he would have shifted and transferred [the charge] to another, for whom they bore as yet neither reproach nor accusation. That would not keep the logic of the argument. Plainly he named them children of the devil himself. Even if they agreed with him in disposition and in imitating his deeds, to hear themselves named as related to him was heavy and abhorrent to them. Since, then, the Jew inscribed God as his own father, and the Savior was eager to show through their works that this was fal-

[?] …the people of the Jews [said], "We have one father, God," he says: Do you then dare, and are you not ashamed, to name God as your father? Or are you not of the devil, whose commandments you want to do, showing yourselves to be his sons? For whoever is formed and moulded according to someone's commandments may justly be called that person's son. And what commandments were the Jews eager [to keep], or through which [?] the devil…? They received glory from one another. They devoured their neighbors with false accusations and spoiled the finest things with envy. They contrived murder against the Savior and plotted his death with tongue and mind. They put falsehood ahead of truth, and made deceit, slander and love of money their way of life, and whatever else is like these. Through these things they plainly made themselves kin to the devil, the founder and sower of them.

After these words comes the saying that is added and joined to them. On the one hand, it knows nothing at all of anyone, I mean, being named father of the devil. On the other hand, it suggests that the devil is proclaimed both to be and to be called the father of the Jews. For it says, "He was a murderer from the beginning," meaning the devil, not some other father of the devil. To whom else will you apply "murderer" and "from the beginning" and "not standing in the truth at all," except the devil himself? He sharpened his tongue against the Creator with falsehood, sweetened it with deceit, and offered it to the first-formed man. Having bewitched him stealthily with words, he set up [?] a workshop of death in the paradise of life and everlasting delight, in the very place of immortality. For God did not make death. Rather, the transgression of the first-formed man conceived the serpent's counsel and gave birth to death. So the devil is a murderer from the beginning and does not stand in the truth. And they, seeking to kill the Lord and always choosing falsehood before truth, preserve the form of their begetter without counterfeit. It is clear from what has been said that the devil is named the father of the Jews. But of a father of the devil one can find no nature and no name indicated in any way, not even in thought. However, the

final clause of the passage proposed at the start may perhaps seem to point to a father of the devil, at least to those who think it gain to dwell on nothing deeper. Yet it establishes the very opposite and agrees with the arguments that precede it, since it too shows the devil to be the father of the Jews. The arguments of the whole passage approach the matter in two ways. At one point they show the imitation of the begetter from the wickedness of the begotten. At another they present the likeness of the begotten by way of the begetter. Then, passing again from the begotten to the begetter, the passage publicly exposes the unvarying likeness and shows that their kinship carries nothing spurious. So he says: when the Jew speaks the lie, as he does now when he calls God his father, he speaks from his own. For the father's wealth is the inheritance that belongs to the son. The Jew therefore speaks from his own, having entered upon his father's inheritance, for he too is a liar, just like his father. It is clear, then, that this section of the passage not only does [not] chime [?] with those who invent a father for the devil, but also marks out the devil alone as the father of the Jews.

Let these things, however, be treated as a kind of exercise, an argument that is wary for now of being called doctrine. Then a higher account may appear, one that is doctrine in its meaning and that carries the verdict by its strength. It may also fulfill the desire of those who philosophize all their lives, and show that they do not reach out in vain toward the search for a meaning beyond the grasp of the many.

[QUESTION 48.] How many are the women who anointed the Lord with myrrh? I do not find the same opinion put forward by those whose concern it has been to investigate these things. Some, more simply and superficially, not to say more ignorantly, divide up the persons of the women according to the different names of those who recorded this story. They say there are four, paying attention, I think, to no deeper reasoning than the number of the evangelists. Others reduce the persons to two. One, they say, is the reverent and chaste woman, the sister of Lazarus and Martha. The other was recorded differently but is also one woman. She passed from an indecent and promiscuous life, out of impurity, to the struggles of virginity. Matthew and Mark, and Luke as well, dealt with her and recorded the same story, telling it in different words. Still others bring all of them together into one, though they give the opinion no secure footing. Nor does such a supposition gain any respectability from the standing of its authors, for Apollinaris and Theodore of Mopsuestia are its fathers. As for me, I am not allowed to say that there are even two. Neither the Savior's words, nor the actions of the [?] women, nor the difference in time, nor even the opinion of those who saw and heard the deed

…nor other things no less weighty than these [allow it]. They teach that there are three, neither more than three nor fewer. First, then, is the woman recorded in Luke. She was taken into the historical record before many of Jesus' deeds and teachings. After this he sends the disciples out to preach, the miracle of the five loaves is worked, the disciples' opinion about their teacher is put to the test [?], and the deed of the Transfiguration, beyond mind and word, is divinely accomplished. "For it came to pass," it says, "about eight days after these sayings, that he took Peter and John and James and went up the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face became different, and his clothing became white and dazzling," and so on. Moreover, the seventy disciples are appointed after these events, and parables are woven in with admonitions. Clearly the Passion was not yet at hand, and the plot of the murderous Jews had not yet gained force through counsel and deliberation.

From the time alone, then, anyone who wishes can see clearly and beyond doubt how the woman in Luke differs from the others. For the accounts recall each of the other two at a time when the Lord's Passion was already being set in motion by the schemes of the Jews: the one six days before the Passover, the other two days before the Passion. The deed of the first of these is recorded by the beloved and virgin disciple. She was called the sister of Lazarus and Martha. She was known as one of those whom the Lord Jesus Christ loved, and as one admired for the dignity of her life. Six days before the Passover she performed that sacred rite and made her house a holy palace [?]. After these comes the third and last, who anointed the Savior two days before the Passion. Matthew and Mark composed the narrative about her. So the account reasonably proclaims three.

See [?] it from this as well. The first is simply called by the name of wickedness, "sinner." She sees Jesus in the house of the Pharisee, not of Simon the leper, reclining there at his host's invitation to share salt and table. She pours out tears before the myrrh, wets Jesus' feet, wipes them with the hair of her head, and gains the courage to kiss them. From there she grows bold and anoints his feet with the myrrh. All who are present keep silent at the deed, and no one rebukes the poor woman in any way. Only the Pharisee was then known to be displeased at the deed within himself. For he says: "If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, that she is a sinner." Then Jesus trips him up and muzzles him with his own words. But he exalts the woman's deed, honors it with fitting praise, and as reward to her

for her [?] he gives in return the great gift, the forgiveness of sins. He does not stop there, but also credits the woman's salvation to her own disposition: "Your faith," he says, "has saved you." So the woman in Luke is set apart from the others by these many differences.

The one in the beloved disciple's account has a clear [?] difference. She came of an illustrious family and a notable household, and her life was admired. She had received back her brother, just risen from the gates of Hades, so that he was even reclining at dinner with Jesus while Mary herself served. That was when she brought the myrrh, and she too wiped his feet with her hair. She did not offer this godly deed in exchange for some reward. Rather, she meant it as an offering of thanksgiving for the divine work done for her brother. Here all the disciples welcomed the deed in silence, perhaps reflecting on the surpassing greatness of the miracle concerning Lazarus and holding the woman's piety in reverence. Only the slave of avarice, the huckster of betrayal, grumbles at the deed. And Jesus, bringing into the open the disease that had mastered him and made him act this way, said to him: "Leave her alone; she has kept it for the day of my burial." That is: You are eager for my death, and that is why the price of the myrrh means so much to you. But by what she has done she publicly exposes your lawless deed. And she teaches you, even if you have been hardened against learning, that the one you are eager to betray she reveres and offers sacrifice to as equal to God. Such, then, is the sister of Lazarus.

The remaining third of those who poured myrrh on the Master is the one Mark and Matthew told about. She is named from the defilement of fornication. She comes to the house of Simon the leper. He was not leprous then. He had long been held by the disease but had by then been cleansed through Jesus' love for humanity. The harlot knew this, and knew from what abomination his skin had been restored to what appearance. So she took up good hopes of being freed from the disease of her soul, and gained the boldness to approach Jesus. When she approaches, she does not touch him with her hand or wipe his feet with her hair. She did not dare to touch the Savior's body with any part of her own, but kept it untouched by her defiled skin. Instead she steals the chance to honor him and offer sacrifice by means of the myrrh. Breaking the alabaster jar, she pours all the myrrh at once over his head. Then the ones who are indignant are not the Pharisee, nor the traitor alone, but quite a few of the disciples. The indignation arose in different ways and was not fanned by the same mind. Simon imagined nothing lofty about his healer and Savior. Judas was mastered by the passion of avarice. The disciples were overcome by pity for the poor. This was not because their affection and reverence for the Master took second place, but because they knew that he too preferred mercy even to sacrifice itself. "For I desire mercy," he says,

[?] "and not sacrifice." Besides, out of reverence for their teacher they thought it a dreadful thing for the woman to pour the myrrh over his head. So Jesus, drawing the disciples away from their indignation against her, says: "She has done nothing reckless; she has done a good work." That was for the right-minded among the disciples. But to Judas, once more bringing into the open the betrayal he was planning, he says in a riddle: "By pouring this myrrh on my body, she has prepared me for burial." He means: You are indignant that the myrrh is poured out. How much indignation, then, does the one deserve who plots betrayal, death and burial against his Master and teacher? You care for the poor? Then how can you [plot] the slaughter of one who has no home and not even a place to lay his head? It costs you nothing of your own, yet you find his company heavy and unbearable. Where you ought to spend much of your own to relieve the poor's need with mercy, how could you bear their company without vexation and with kindness?

Going over it again, then, without any preconception or bias, we can see and say truthfully the following. One of the women who anointed the Lord with myrrh came well before the others in time. The others performed this sacred rite around the time of the Passion, one six days before the Passover, the other two days before the Passion. One is a sinner and another a harlot, known by their passions rather than by their proper names, while the other takes her designation from her brother. The first, in the house of the Pharisee, anoints the Master's feet with myrrh, washing them first with her tears. The second, in her own house, knows no occasion for tears. Rather, she welcomes with a table and festivity both Jesus himself and the man whose tomb the saving voice showed to be a workshop of birth and a place of return to life. She too empties the myrrh on his immaculate feet and wipes them with her hair. The remaining third comes into the leper's house, she too carrying precious myrrh. But she does not touch the Savior's limbs at all. Suddenly she breaks the alabaster jar and pours the myrrh over his head, using skill and haste to get ahead of anyone who might think of trying to stop the deed.

The first has the city as witness of her licentiousness, for in the city she was called a sinner. The second has the village. The third dwelt in the chambers of the palaces of chastity and purity. At the first, only the Pharisee is indignant. At Lazarus's sister, only Judas. At the last, some of the disciples and, once again, the traitor, that spoil of avarice. To Lazarus's sister no reward is promised for pouring out the myrrh. A benefaction and gift beyond words had been bestowed on her beforehand, so what she gave was a thank-offering owed [?]. Here too only Judas's betrayal and rashness are brought to light and exposed. The woman in Luke finds forgiveness of sins as recompense for both the myrrh and her faith. To the woman in Matthew and Mark is promised a memorial proclaimed through the ages to the whole world. [?] So the recompense differs for each of the

…of the women he makes a promise. Yet the reward given to one does not leave the other without honour. Both found forgiveness of their sins, and both are proclaimed throughout the whole world for this sacred act. Both have been granted a memorial for all time, crowned with praise. What was said to each was the promise that suited her, to comfort her and to show that her deed was accepted. The apostles rebuked the one for misusing the ointment and wasting it for nothing. About the other the Pharisee muttered that she was a sinner under condemnation and yet dared to do such things. He also thought that the Teacher did not know what kind of life and conduct the woman was known for. So to this one the reward announced was forgiveness of sins. To that one it was proclaimed that her deed would be spoken of everywhere and that all would call her blessed. To the sister of Lazarus, however, neither of these is given in return. She was not laying down a pledge for a benefit and favour she still hoped for. She had already received, beyond all reason, her brother back from the dead, and in his new life he had made a beginning of putting death itself to death. For this she was honouring her benefactor with thanksgiving, and she paid him honour as far as her will and her means allowed. Besides, the other women were imperfect and weighed down by the burden of their sins. They needed some encouragement and assurance that their act had been accepted and that their hopes would not be disappointed. Therefore the Saviour of our race gave them promises suited and fitting to each. But she was more perfect. She had already seen the astonishing sight with her own eyes and needed no greater promises for the time being. She was content with that astonishing sight and with the Master's promise, common to all who believe, that whoever believes in him will hold the inheritance of eternal life and never lose it. But why is it that in the case of the woman in Luke none of the disciples, not even Judas, is indignant? In the case of Lazarus's sister only the traitor is indignant, and in the case of the harlot quite a number of the disciples are. Perhaps none of the disciples, not even the traitor, is indignant in the first case for this reason: Judas had not yet been fully overpowered by the disease of avarice, and Satan had not yet made his heart a fit instrument of betrayal. The other disciples were not moved to indignation because they did not yet carry the Teacher's words about almsgiving firmly fixed in their souls, and concern for the poor had not yet taken such hold of them. Moreover, they saw the woman weeping, and she was not pouring the ointment on his head but anointing his feet. Nor had they yet been taught that the Saviour's passion was at hand. All of this was enough to keep them from indignation. And even if none of these reasons had applied, any indignation that sprang up in one of the disciples would have been checked before it came into the open. For the Pharisee got there first, received the refutation of his rebuke, and so taught silence

[Running head: Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople] …to the others, and he was seen to be both their correction and the cause of it. In the case of Lazarus's sister, the right-minded disciples are not indignant. They were held back by the woman's reverence and restrained by the miracle that had just taken place. She too did not pour the ointment on his head but anointed his feet with great reverence. Only Judas is indignant, since he was already beginning to burn with avarice and to be besieged by thoughts of betrayal. In the third case, as has been said, both the other disciples and Judas above all murmur, though from different motives. Judas was already fully in the grip of the betrayal. He could no longer bear the flame of avarice that was consuming everything within him, nor bear to see the Teacher held in reverence and honour by the others. The other disciples, as has often been said, already had a great regard for almsgiving and love of the poor, and they thought they were in no way at odds with the Teacher's mind. For they thought it quite reasonable that a harlot should not be allowed to pour ointment on that spotless head. Besides, they saw that the Teacher disregarded everything and was hastening toward the cross [?] and death, for he was by now continually foretelling his passion to them. They probably reasoned like this: "If our Teacher is preparing for death, what gain is there in pouring out the ointment? What benefit will he get from it, when the death of criminals awaits him shortly?" Therefore the Saviour corrected their thinking with its very opposite: "She has done this for my burial," he says. It was as if he said: "The very reasons you give for not pouring out the ointment are that I disregard everything and am preparing for death. Those same reasons show all the more that the woman's deed was worthily done. For she has done this for my burial." To the right-minded disciples the Lord's word would apply in this sense, and to Judas in the sense given earlier. For the indignant group was divided by different thoughts. So the Master could [?] offer a word suited to both views, and each hearer could apply the verdict to his own conscience. But enough about the women who were counted worthy to anoint the Master with ointment. [Question 48.]

QUESTION 49. How should we understand the saying: "Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to men, but whoever blasphemes [against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven], either in this age or in the age to come"? Our blessed Fathers said what was fitting to say in their own times, and

no stain of heretical opinion found any pretext to mark what they said. Now, however, I will say things that carry no less force than the first explanation and are even further removed from the second [?]. Those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit are not forgiven their sin because they have left themselves nothing through which they could be counted worthy of forgiveness. For forgiveness of sins is given through the Spirit, as the Saviour himself testified when he said: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven; if you retain them, they are retained." He clearly teaches that the forgiveness and condemnation of sins belong to the authority and power of the Spirit. The cleansing and acquittal of sins, then, is performed as a sacred rite through the Spirit. But how could someone who blasphemes the Spirit, and so throws away his own salvation, be cleansed through it, or be acquitted of the punishment and penalties he owes? I think that those who examine the matter carefully no longer have any question about how one who blasphemes against the Spirit will not find forgiveness of sins. The bath of regeneration, too, is performed through the Spirit, and the gift flows from there and springs from the grace that is there. Some mock this and blaspheme it as unable to provide any benefit or gain: "For how can water and oil touching the flesh bring release from the brands that sin has burned deep within, and from the passions of the soul?" Whoever is carried away into such madness that he devises this blasphemy against spiritual rebirth, a gift second to none of the finest gifts, and therefore will not consent to be perfected by the spiritual gift but mocks and ridicules it, will not find forgiveness for his blasphemy, either in this age or in the age to come. This applies to him and to everyone else through whom blasphemy creeps. For the Saviour also said in solemn confirmation: "Truly, truly I tell you, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven." Moreover, "Spirit" is used not only in the more specific sense of the all-holy Spirit, but also more generally of the Holy Trinity ("For God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth"). So it is clear that whoever blasphemes against the Spirit will by no means find forgiveness, either in this age or in the age to come. That is, whoever lets loose a blasphemous tongue against any one of the transcendent and consubstantial hypostases of the almighty and superessential Godhead is in this position. He may seem free of any charge of insult or slander touching virtue and conduct, but he is held and judged for the far greater sin. Consider also the following. The Saviour is called Son of Man because he truly became man and is said to have willingly submitted to human passions. In them human nature, as it was seen in him, received the blameless and

irreproachable state. So by these words the Saviour says something about a person who blasphemes and mocks him on account of the human actions of the Son of Man, that is, on account of his blameless passions. Such a person takes offence because he hungered and thirsted, because he was in agony before his passion, because sweat poured down him, because he called himself deeply grieved when troubled by the fear of death, because he prayed, because he begged to be spared the cup. Whoever takes offence at these human things, by which the Saviour allowed himself to be known as truly Son of Man, can more easily throw off the stumbling block, escape blasphemy and receive forgiveness of his sin. For he sees the blind having their eyes fashioned by a word, and the lame refuting their affliction by running. He sees the man four days among the dead laughing at the power of death, and all the other divine works the Saviour was seen to perform. Each of these has invincible power to free the one who takes offence from his error and his blaspheming disposition, if indeed he does wrong willingly [?]. And if they are all carefully pondered together in the mind, how could they fail to move him quickly to true theology, though he had been dragged into blasphemy by the lowly human things? But another person maliciously turns these God-befitting and transcendent works into blasphemy and strives to make evil out of good. Now, seeing him drive out demons, he says, "He has a demon." Now he says, "He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons." Now, when with clay and a word he forms eyes for one whom birth had deprived of sight, he heaps abuse on him, drags the miracle into insult, and says, "This man is not from God." This person is made no better by the more divine and transcendent works. Instead he is carried toward worse and driven into madness. The very things that should have led him to marvel at his benefactor and sing his praises are the things through which he insults and blasphemes him. Through what else, then, could he turn back, sing a recantation, take refuge in repentance and receive forgiveness for his impiety and his war against God? Clearly through nothing else. So the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, that is, against the divine signs, and has not put away his earlier slander even because of them, can be corrected by nothing else. And if he is not corrected, how will forgiveness of his sin follow? Therefore the saving Word, the fountain of forgiveness, reasonably and in a manner worthy of God declared unworthy of any pardon the one who was determined to turn the divine works into blasphemy. He has left himself no pretext for correcting his insults and blasphemies against the Spirit, so he is very far from being counted worthy of forgiveness. You saw him eating and drinking, and for this you call him a glutton and a drunkard? You saw him welcoming sinners and tax collectors, and this led you to charge him with friendship with tax collectors and sinners? But the lofty things are still left to you. Through them you can turn away from these insults too, take refuge in repentance and find forgiveness. Because he talked with a woman, and a Samaritan at that,

and asked her for water, you were led to think lowly things of him? You took the Samaritan woman as a pretext for a lower opinion and view of him. How is it that you did not also take her as your teacher of the higher one? "Come," she says, "see a man", and she turned the whole city and called them, "who told me everything I have done." Do not even these things make you a beholder of what is more divine and lofty? Or because he asks the disciples, "Who do people say that I am?", do you foolishly seize on the question and think him just one among many? And how do you not rise to a view worthy of God when you hear him say to the one who gave the answer, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God": "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven", and, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it"? Are these human things, or do they belong only to the all-powerful Godhead that loves mankind? "But these are only words," you say. "Sight has not yet received them as witnesses, nor have deeds come at once to back them up." Yet you saw the blind after their birth celebrating the rebirth of their eyes and driving away, by the clearness of their sight, the affliction they had had from birth. You saw the deaf hearing, the steps of the lame set straight by a word, and the dead rising. You saw rocks split at the Lord's passion, and the sun darkened and clothed in darkness instead of its rays and great brilliance. You saw tombs emptied, and the dead foreshadowing the common resurrection with the living and celebrating it together. When you saw these things, how did you not turn away from everything by which you had gathered stumbling blocks for yourself and wounded your judgement? Why did you not run in great haste to repentance and show amendment, so that through it you might gain forgiveness of your sins? But not even by these things do you allow the burning of your heart to be softened. Instead you strive all the more to strengthen your madness and your war against God. At one time, with an over-curious and ill-timed zeal for the Sabbath, you disparage the divine signs that are above the Sabbath. At another, when the Sabbath offers your blasphemy no retreat and you see people freed from demonic affliction, you take refuge in Beelzebul. And when you are at a complete loss to invent even this pretext [?], you decide to make death and bloodshed your helper and ally. The man whom death could no longer hold though he had been dead four days, you stretch out murderous minds and hands to send back to death again. "For the Jews," it says, "sought to kill Lazarus also." Finally you condemn the one who worked these wonders to the cross and death. You ask for a guard, and you set [?] seals on the dead man and the tomb. And most shameless of all, exceeding all godlessness and leaving no room whatever for pardon, you steal the resurrection with the invention of a theft. You were not shamed and changed even by the miracle, which surpasses all the marvellous

and transcendent works ever done since time began. Instead you plotted mischief against it, all the more because it surpassed the others. Consider the person who showed no change or repentance in response to any of the things that brilliantly flash forth the dignity and invincible power of the Godhead, that is, the spiritual operations and deeds. Through the human things he had disfigured and branded himself with base and soul-destroying opinions, and these he did not repent of. He even made the divine things a further occasion for greater madness and war against God, on top of what he had already dared. It is plain and perfectly evident that such a person has left himself nothing through which he might choose the better over the worse, and with fervent and swift repentance cancel the debts already incurred. He will not be counted worthy of remission at all, either in this age or in the age [to come].

There are some who take "either in this age or in the age to come" in another way, and offer a simpler and readier solution to the difficulty. The Mosaic law, they say, punishes with death the one who blasphemes the Divine, and grants him no pardon or remission. This shows that the blasphemer is not forgiven in the present age. They say, then, that it is reasonable to understand the saying this way. Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will pay the penalty from God in the age to come and will have the punishments for blasphemy exacted from him. But in the present age too he is subjected to the most extreme punishments. For the Mosaic law commanded that whoever lets loose a cursing tongue against God, that is, whoever insults the Divine with blasphemies, should be stoned and driven from life. And the Spirit also belongs to the essence and lordship of the Divine. So the Spirit is plainly proclaimed to be God, even if the enemies of God do not think so. It was by the Spirit that the Creator of nature divinely performed works beyond reason, saying, "By the finger of God I cast out demons." He calls the Spirit the finger of God because they do not differ in essence and because the Spirit's operation is sovereign in its own right. ("By the Holy Spirit," it says, "he casts out the demons.") This is not because he could not do it of himself. Rather, in all his works befitting God he was showing [?] that the operation of the Father and of the Spirit is present together with him, since they are consubstantial, of the same nature, and inclined to one and the same will. That is why he said, "My Father is working until now, and I am working", and, "I do not speak on my own", and, "By the finger of God I cast out demons." The same holds for all the other sacred sayings that declare and teach their sameness of nature and power and the unity of their operation and will. I also know of some who said that at the time when the Lord's verdict was pronounced, its force was limited. At that time the resurrection had not yet come and the ascension into heaven had not yet been shown. Nor had the Spirit yet made the fishermen [?] into spontaneous preachers to the whole world. Since these most transcendent things had not yet happened, whoever blasphemed the Son of Man and stumbled at him as a man would find forgiveness. For still

at that time his dignity was overshadowed for them by the flesh. But to the one who blasphemes against the Spirit, forgiveness of the sin will be given neither at that time nor in the age to come. For such people had nothing in the way to stop them from seeing the operation that is beyond reason and the rays of the Godhead flashing out through it. Others draw the words toward the following sense. The bath of remission, which is performed in the Holy Spirit and fire, had not yet been openly proclaimed, they say [?]. So one who had blasphemed the divine Spirit could not find forgiveness, because it was not yet possible to share in the regeneration and the cleansing that comes from it. Therefore, reasonably enough, whoever blasphemed the Holy Spirit obtains no forgiveness at all, neither in this age, and for that reason not in the age to come either.

QUESTION 50. The blessed Mark the evangelist says: "And when his own people heard it, they went out to seize him, for they said, 'He is beside himself.'" How, if one fits the wording together, would they not seem to be at odds with the gospel narrative [?]? We have found this passage given various interpretations. One may take "They said that he was beside himself" as the evangelist's way of saying, "They said that he wanted to leave them, that he intended to abandon them and move on to others." Those who champion this sense bring forward the sacred Luke in support. They say that he relates the same story and says: "And the crowds were looking for him, and they came to him and tried to keep him from leaving them." Others, however, insisted that the story the inspired Luke records is different from the one the divine Mark relates, and so went looking for another explanation. They say: "Here Jesus was in a house, and the crowd itself was learning divine things and being healed. Because the crowd kept pressing on them, they did not even have time to eat bread. And his own people went out to seize him. There, on the other hand, the crowds came to him and tried to keep him from leaving them." Since the stories differ so much, they say, how could one claim that both deal with the same event? But one may answer them that the story is not different. Rather, the ambiguous passage is uncovered and cleared up, so that it becomes distinct, by the one that is not in dispute. The latter shows why the holding back and seizing took place: so that he would not depart and withdraw from them. It shows that they planned to detain him because they longed for his teaching and revelled in the enjoyment of his wonderful works. For the loving Jesus often left this place and the crowds that pressed on him there, taking to others the salvation that came from his teaching and divine works. These interpreters, however, take "to seize him" to mean "to stop him from speaking and teaching", and "he is beside himself" with reference to the natural powers and the settled condition,

…since toil usually brings on a state of being "beside oneself," they offer the following interpretation. Because of the length and continuity of his teaching, they say, "those around him" thought that he had reached the point of immeasurable toil, and that his vital tension and innate strength had given way to collapse and weakness. What they themselves had perhaps suffered from long and unbroken listening, from the press of the crowd and the uproar, they suspected that the teacher had suffered too. That is why it says "those around him," meaning those more closely attached to him, "went out to seize him." They had great care for him and thought for his relief and the easing of his toil, and they meant to separate the teacher from the crowd and give him food and the other kinds of care by which the body is freed from fatigue. Perhaps they went out from some place suited to rest and quiet, to which they had withdrawn to recover themselves. This second explanation does not agree with the first, and this is how it seeks to clarify the gospel saying. There are others who look to the wickedness of the Jews and their blasphemous and malicious bent, and take "he is beside himself" in its obvious sense: that is, he was out of his mind and carried away from his settled state. For such is the Jews' hatred of Christ that they do not shudder at fabricating every insult and slander against the Saviour. They were continually goaded by envy and malice and were no different from madmen. They had truly suffered the utmost derangement of their innate judgement, and they threw their own affliction back upon the one who had freed many from such diseases. He worked divine works beyond reason and thought, and they branded him an enemy of God because he showed the Sabbath to be a day of salvation and a feast of miracles. They saw him free his creature from demons by a word, and they blasphemed that he cast out demons by the ruler of demons. Such people would not have thought it too bold, in the face of his endurance and patience as he taught and healed the crowds, to accuse him of derangement of mind and to make people witnesses of their blasphemous words [?], while they raised insolent and reckless hands against him. So these interpreters say that nothing conflicts with their view, not even "Those around him went out to seize him." For not even his so-called brothers were disposed toward him with affection and piety. They too were scandalized, not being free of Jewish ingratitude because of their upbringing and way of life among the Jews, and at the beginning they often gave many occasions for unbelief in him. They showed a disposition no better than the other Jews, even if afterwards they redeemed themselves by the contests of martyrdom, and proclaimed to all with their blood and slaughter the divinity of Jesus, which before they would not even acknowledge with their tongue. For my part, I am not unaware that those reputed to be the Saviour's brothers were scandalized and did not at first hold a conception of him worthy of God, both because of his assumption of the flesh and because of the

condescension of the Word that passes understanding. They could not lift and raise their minds to match its paradox and greatness, and the venerable Scriptures teach me this. But that they went so far in wickedness as to accuse him of having a demon, of being beside himself and of sickness of mind, I am not able in the same way to accept or concede.

QUESTION 51. Why did God plant paradise when he was about to expel Adam from it at once?

As for things that are ineffable and too lofty to be searched out and grasped, it was neither impossible nor dangerous for Paul and those like Paul to reach up to their contemplation. But those of us who are dragged down by the flesh and the weight of its desires can travel safely on the path that leads to something higher and beyond us when others stretch out to us a kindly and guiding hand. That is why the exhortation says, "Do not seek what is too hard for you, and do not search into what is too strong for you." Yet the Wisdom and Goodness [of God], welcoming us with kindly promises, has commanded, "Ask, and it will be given to you; knock, and it will be opened." Trusting in this promise of the hypostatic Truth, we have both knocked and asked; whether it has been given and opened, the discussion will show. We say that God planted paradise without intending to drive Adam out of it at once. When he formed Adam with his hands, he neither intended nor aimed to make him an exile at once from the plantings of paradise and from the blessed life assigned to him. It was Adam who broke the law of the commandment by transgressing it, and so he turned his joy into grief and brought about his own expulsion from paradise. Just as God did not make death, but fashioned man with a pledge of immortality, so he did not banish him from the sacred place or from its blessed delight. The first citizen of paradise himself, on the serpent's counsel, preferred transgression to the commandment and so brought on himself both death and expulsion from paradise. Second, even though the Divine foresees [?] the offences of human beings, it does not withhold from them the wealth of its benefits and gifts, nor is it accustomed to exact the penalty for offences before the reckless deed has been carried out. So too, though he knew that one of the incorporeal powers would desert his providence and goodness, and the company that deserted with him, he nevertheless brought them forth in goodness. He created the deserter as a morning star, and he did not deprive him of creation or of brightness on account of the darkness of ingratitude into which he later sank [?]. But when he saw him desert and fall like lightning from heaven, he let the penalty

be exacted for his pride. Such is the Creator's economy and discernment toward his creatures. So even if Adam was going to sin and be expelled from paradise, it was nonetheless fitting for the Creator's goodness to bring man into being as a rational creature, and to make the paradise in which he lived in blessedness, rather than hold back the finest of earthly works because of Adam's transgression and the penalty it exacted. For the Divine always does what is its own. It makes the streams of kindness and goodness gush forth unceasingly, and when sin is dared, it brings punishment, because it will not let the wound from the offence stay incurable or allow the wounds to spread through the man. In this case the transgression was foreseen and the expulsion was foreseen. Even so, paradise, the finest masterpiece among earthly works, was not kept from existing because of Adam. So God brings it forth and settles Adam in a delightful way of life. But the impartiality of justice did not allow him, once he had transgressed, to remain there still and enjoy the delight he would have enjoyed had he kept the law. Third, even if after fashioning Adam he settled him in paradise, he did not create so great a masterpiece for him alone. He created it no less, if not more, for all of Adam's descendants who have preserved the surpassingly beautiful and comely form of Adam and the inviolate and untarnished stamp of the divine image. Where, then, would be the goodness, and where the wisdom, in depriving so great a multitude of paradise for the sake of one transgressor, by not creating or bringing forth that sacred place, especially when he himself is not deprived of the common enjoyment in later times? Besides this, we must not overlook the following. Adam, the first-formed, had to have charge of some action and activity that did not degrade him, so that man, the rational creature, would not be idle and thoughtless. Success in it would bring crowns and glory, and neglect of it would bring punishment and dishonour; and when he inclined to the easiest course, punishment followed. So one could raise the same objections about this as about paradise and the expulsion: why, someone will ask and wrangle, were the crowns woven and made ready? If this is so, it is no longer only paradise, Adam and the exile that are being called to account [?]. Those who call such things to account would subject everything that the kindly and creative Goodness chose to bring into being to the same meddlesome inquiries, even if they do not admit it, because they are not satisfied with the wisdom of the Creator. One may also consider this. If he had not been exiled from life in paradise, what enjoyment that the senses can judge would Adam have known he had lost after his sin? Without that knowledge, how would grief and pain have taken hold of him? And if nothing distressing had struck and afflicted him, how would he have recognized how great his sin was? How would he have come to repentance and entreated the divine favour, so as not to be deprived of pardon and release completely and for ever?

Someone might also wish to reason as follows. God established paradise, even though Adam was going to sin and be driven out of it, so that he would not seem to have fashioned man mortal from the beginning by never creating a place suited to immortality and free from grief, toil, thorns and sweat. He did it to show that everything he does and arranges befits him and proclaims the wisdom of his ineffable providence. Moreover, through one of the material creatures he prefigured in deed and announced beforehand that at his second and awesome coming the whole creation will be changed into a better state, since the unsuitability of matter in no way resists the creative and divine will. For the chief of the disciples taught us that heaven and earth will be renewed for the better, confirming the truth of this teaching by his teacher's promise. Even these views would not be far from a God-loving understanding. Besides, it was not right for the finest of all earthly works to be created last; it too had to be laid down at the beginning together with the whole of creation. That it should come into being was necessary, since a dwelling and a choice inheritance had to be allotted to those who have triumphed over demons and passions. And the Divine is always accustomed to set out and lay down the rewards beforehand: "Come," he says, "you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." So paradise too, whether our forefather was soon to be expelled from it or not, had to be laid down before the contestants and the contests whose prize it was seen to be. It had to be laid down together with the creation of the world, so that it would not seem to be the work of afterthought and regret, but of the judgement and goodness that from the beginning established all things wisely.

QUESTION 52. The divine Paul exhorts: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him with bread; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire on his head." How shall we understand "you will heap coals of fire on his head"?

The anagogical sense calls the apostles of the Lord and the martyrs "coals," since they have been kindled by the divine fire that purifies and that burns up and consumes all wickedness. "For our God is a fire," and a fire that consumes wickedness. So also the Psalmist says, "Coals were kindled from him," when he bowed the heavens and came down and put on our flesh like an unfulled cloth wrapping around the lightnings of the divinity. Again, he calls "coals" the burning and consuming punishments and bitter torments, as in the saying: "The sharpened arrows of the mighty, with

desolating coals," that is, with annihilating and desolating punishments, which have irresistible power to consume the guilty. In many other places too one can find the powers of punishment called "coals." So in this second meaning he calls punitive blows and penalties "coals," transferring and carrying over the name from the coals that kindle the visible flame which consumes earthly matter. He exhorts us, then, to feed the enemy when he is hungry and give him drink when he is thirsty, that is, to benefit him and do him good in many ways. For "feed" and "give drink" sketch the whole of beneficence by naming a part. Then he says: by benefiting your enemy and being kindly disposed toward him, "you will heap coals on his head." Since "you will heap" divides into a double meaning, it implies that the sense also runs in two directions. In one, "you will heap" would mean "you will gather together upon," and this governs the rest of the interpretation. The wages of enmity, he says, were going to overtake the enemy piece by piece and over time. But you did not rise up to repay evil for evil. Instead you welcomed the one who wronged you with kindnesses, which make us like the Divine, and so you prepare the just Judge, whom nothing escapes, to heap all the punishments and penalties at once on that arrogant and ungrateful head. "For vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." How then is he humane? How compassionate? How a benefactor, if he plots and contrives these things against his enemies and shows kindness for the sake of the other's punishment and chastisement? Or is it that he himself did not ask for these things, but did them in order to keep the divine commandment and repay the enemy with kindnesses? If justice, being outraged, provoked the Judge to vengeance, then anyone who accepts the judgements of Providence would no longer coyly shrink from that vengeance, but would marvel at the Judge's impartiality and sing its praises. To do good and at the same time seek to obtain punishment from the enemy is incompatible. It is the mark of a confused mind leaning toward both opposites, and it dissolves the gain of the good deed into vanity. But [to show] kindness out of a forgiving mind and sympathy for one who shares our nature, both for the sake of the commandment and

[for the sake of] the enemy, [removing] the coals that are spreading over his head and would quickly destroy it unless someone took them off him and contrived his release—in this one will find great gain and a means to the salvation of the soul. For by calling his neighbour back from bodily harm and destruction, which passes still more into the soul, he rises to the imitation and likeness of the Master. For one who saves a soul, it says, is like the one who created it. How are the coals gathered up and swept off the quarrelsome head by kindness? Because when the enemy is welcomed with food and drink and simply treated well, he ceases from enmity and gives up plotting, even if not for the sake of the good itself, then at least for his own comfort and enjoyment of good things. Little by little he sobers up from his passion and lays aside the burning and inflammation that enmity has caused in his thoughts, and he will come to love and cherish and acknowledge his benefactor. From there, little by little, he grows accustomed to shun a slanderous tongue and the deeds by which a neighbour is harmed, and he becomes a lover of virtue. And who would look for a greater reward than this for feeding the enemy and giving him drink? What could be more profitable? But if after so much kindness the one who receives it refuses to turn from his wickedness and baseness, such a person would be a beast rather than a sharer in human nature. Yet you have nonetheless swept away, by your intention and zeal, the coals that were devouring his head, and you have received no less a reward. Nor have you in any way defaced the stamp that joined you to likeness with the Divine. He, on the other hand, has dragged himself off and thrown himself into the punishing and unquenchable fire. Some, however, have taken the "coals" to be the deeds and exhortations that kindle and warm the governing faculty and change and dissolve the long winter of enmity into peaceful calm. By heaping these on the head of the hostile man, they say, the benefactor drove out through them the deadly [?] and freed him from a great and fatal disease.

QUESTION 53. How should we understand what God said to Moses: "See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh"?

The interpretation of what is asked comes from the words that immediately follow, for he adds: "And Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh." Just as God used Moses to carry out the plagues against Pharaoh and the Egyptians, so Moses used Aaron. Moses, who received commands from God, himself gave commands, and he used his brother as his minister toward Pharaoh. The action kept an exact correspondence in its proportion: as God dealt with Pharaoh through Moses as intermediary, so Moses performed the divine signs before Pharaoh through Aaron as intermediary. In the wilderness of Horeb God commanded Moses to throw down the rod, and it was changed into a serpent;

again, in Pharaoh's presence, Moses commanded Aaron to throw down the rod, and the wood was turned into a living serpent. In short, all the wonders Moses was entrusted to perform he committed and handed over to his brother, and he accomplished through him the miracles he had been commanded to work. So it has become clear what "See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh" is meant to signify.

QUESTION 54. How should we understand the apostolic saying, "But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another," and what goes with it?

There are holy men, graced with the gift of uncovering the meaning treasured up in the depths of the apostle's words, who have unfolded the present text. We accept their interpretation, and your diligence in these matters persuades us [?]; but we will not neglect to draw off anything else that springs from Paul's words. Paul, whose tongue was the instrument of the all-holy Spirit, said, "You were called to freedom, brothers." He taught that the children of grace are not subject to the slavery of circumcision, and are not obliged to be held and worn down by the toilsome and unbearable yoke of the law. But he did not want them to think that freedom also permitted them other things they should not do, or to turn the occasion of freedom into insolence, cutting freedom down and handing it over to the flesh and to the passions that sprout and grow from the flesh. For this reason he added, "But through love be servants of one another." It is as if he said: "You have been called back from harsh slavery into an unexpected and blessed freedom. Flee the dominion of the flesh, through which slavery weighs you down, and do not bow to its laws." The slavery of the flesh is clearly the maker and craftswoman of many other passions and vices, and it schemes to defile the beauty of virtue and freedom. Above all, it tries to drive love out of human souls. "So," he says, "leaving aside for now the other revolts of vice, which are the offspring of the flesh and of the carnal mind, contend nobly against this plot and blow that comes from that source against you—I mean the one that kills love. Do not give this soul-destroying arrow of sin any pretext for finding a way in among you. This will be neither laborious nor hard to accomplish; it will be both easy and saving. For if through love you serve one another, every weapon of wickedness hurled against you will be useless. It strikes the shield of your mutual concord and friendship and is quickly shattered all around; it is beaten off and falls as a blunted dart, and besides this it covers the thrower with the shame he deserves. For mutual service through love secures as a pledge the alliance from above, achieves pure and blessed freedom through peace with one another, and settles in your hearts the hypostatic Peace, our Lord Jesus Christ." Then he adds that the summary of the law too is

…to love one's neighbour as oneself, and how lofty and beneficial this love is, which he establishes and demonstrates with sacred arguments. Then, by setting out what attends human life, he tightens and reinforces his teaching. Most people are less willing to be brought to their senses [?] by laws and threats that bring punishment only after a long time than by things that are visible and perishable and show punishment drawing near. So he does not shrink from exhortation drawn from these things either. He all but says: "If the longing for freedom does not shame you, and the gain from serving one another does not move you, and it means nothing to you that this is the desire of the Spirit and the opposite the desire of the flesh, or that the achievement of love is the fulfilment of the law, then at least beware of destroying and ruining one another. For to bite and devour one another with envy, slanders and false accusations, through which envy too speaks openly [?], how could that not be abominable? How could it not be shunned? How could it not be abhorrent even without anyone urging it?" Therefore one must take care not to fall away from love. To slip away from it is to be swallowed up in fights, factions and quarrels; it makes people arm themselves against one another, and these things together bring about your destruction and ruin. And notice how he brought love in here, although his discourse was chiefly urging that circumcision be set aside. Even though that was his main concern, he still weaves the good of love into his purpose. Why? So that those who took pride in circumcision, being at odds with one another, and those whom Paul's exhortation had won over, would not split themselves apart in factions, rivalries and quarrels, from which being bitten and devoured by one another is quickly seen to follow. He, who in my judgment at least reasoned best about deliverance from these things, teaches it by his words as well as by his deeds, so that those near him might [?] share in that wisdom.

QUESTION 55. [?] the sacred oracle [?]: "Truly, truly I say to you, wherever this Gospel is proclaimed, what this woman has done will also be told in memory of her" [?]. If someone takes "this Gospel" [?] to mean the woman's [?], it seems not to escape the charge of idle talk [?]. But if one takes it to mean the whole Scripture of the disciples who composed the [?] teaching of our common Saviour, this too is not thought to keep the sense coherent, for these things had not yet been set down in writing. To approach this difficulty more sharply, then, [?]. Yet it is not laborious, nor does it need much attention, to see both the coherence of the divine sayings before us and that they stand far above giving any pretext for a charge of idle talk. First, even though the Gospels had not yet been written down, the divine works of Jesus were still being proclaimed to everyone by unwritten word. And if, even before each thing came to be,

…he is the one who knows clearly, what prevents him from [calling] "Gospels" [?] what was soon also to be received in Scripture? So where could anyone find room for incoherence in the words "Wherever this Gospel is proclaimed, what she has done will also be told"? And if someone understands "the Gospel" to be the woman's pious act itself, even then the reproach of idle talk could not attach to these words at all. For he did not simply say, "Wherever it is proclaimed, it will be told," but "Wherever it is proclaimed, it will be told in memory of her." That is, it will raise up for them an ever-remembered glory as her memorial, and will make her love of God resound everywhere and be admired. The sacred Oracles usually use "memorial" for splendid praise, and to signify a glory that flourishes and grows to its prime with the passage of time, as in "The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance," and "Their memory has perished with a noise," and many similar passages. It is fitting that he brings in glory when he foretells the woman's sacred act. Those men had heaped blame and reproach on the God-loving deed of the chaste harlot and rebuked her. For this reason the Saviour passed over the other things connected with the deed and set praise and glory against their reproach: the fame of her work would be spread abroad everywhere. With their rebukes they had cast gloom over her and troubled her soul, so he had to comfort and restore her with the very opposite, to make her spirit rejoicing and exultant again, and at the same time to rein in the rashness of her accusers. The saving Word all but cries out: "The work you want to bring under accusation is not only acquitted of every charge but will be proclaimed everywhere. From the shoots of a harlot a flower of chastity has sprung up, lovely and unfading. It will show a marvellous mind, a spirit too lofty for a woman, that recognized God and honoured with sacrifices him whom a human form clothed. Therefore the ends of the earth too will be seen bringing her their blessing and praises as gifts."

QUESTION 56. What consistent and harmonious meaning can be traced out and understood in David's words: "Against you alone have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged"? There is a solution that applies to this difficulty in particular. It brings into harmony with David's wisdom what seems incongruous in the words and rather inclined to contradiction. It runs as follows. The clause "so that you may be justified in your words" is not the counterpart of "Against you alone have I sinned," even though it was placed nearer to it in the order of the words. It is construed more fittingly and wisely if it is taken as referring back to what comes first at the beginning, namely: "Have mercy

on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my transgression, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged." The rest is a parenthesis and will not break the sequence of either the sense or the construction. And what are the words through which God, in showing mercy, is justified? "Declare your sins first, so that you may be justified"; and "I will by no means desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn from his wicked way and live"; and again, "I do not desire the death of the one who dies; turn, and you shall live." These words justify God, since he confirms them with deeds of kindness and fulfils them with compassionate mercies. Even if they come later in time than David's sin and repentance, they do not come later than the prophetic knowledge that was in David. For the psalm itself records, as on a monument, David's repentance and confession and the mercy shown for his transgressions, and no less does it foretell the later captivity of Israel. In the figure and form of one who prays, it foretells that they would be found worthy of mercy and kindness. With prophetic discernment it declares that they would be made to hear joy and gladness, that the humbled bones would rejoice and be established by a guiding spirit, that Zion would be blessed by divine good pleasure, and that the ravaged and ruined walls of Jerusalem would be rebuilt. So if David's words are construed straightforwardly with one another rather than as a transposed order, nothing, as has been said, is found at odds with the correctness and intelligence of the prophetic words. They call down mercy and kindness from above, through which God's righteousness and truth shine out all the more. In this way it is easy and effortless to see how the disputed point has been cleared up by the related sacred text. It has not corrupted the prophet's divine wisdom and virtue, nor does it put into our thoughts any doubt or any notion unworthy of God. But David's saying admits a particular arrangement and an easy solution, while many other sayings raise the same question and are not resolved by the same method. So it is better to go back to the more general principle that [?] and sets these passages in order, and from there, by judging them all together, to make plain as far as possible their coherent meaning, one worthy of sacred things. There are passages that take on the same figure of construction and need to be unfolded into the same natural, unfigured manner of speech. To set out a few out of many: "I will stretch out my hand to strike you and your people, and you will be wiped off the earth," says the Lord to Pharaoh through Moses; and "For this reason you have been preserved, so that I might show my strength in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth"; and again, "I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that my signs

[?] may come upon them, so that you may recount my signs in the ears of your children"; then, "And Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and my wonders in their land." Each of these, and all the others brought forward in similar expressions, is phrased in the form of a purpose clause. They are spoken according to an idiom of our sacred Scripture. But when they are turned into the natural form of speech, they unfold their pious meaning and shape our understanding in keeping with our divine wisdom. Ancient custom has established the practice of often announcing in this form things that will certainly come to pass and cannot be cut short by any failure of fulfilment. For whatever is expressed as a cause [?] ranks among things whose existence is acknowledged [?]. The idiom of Scripture works like this. Pharaoh disobeyed and was hardened, and the extraordinary plagues and scourges followed, exacted as the penalty for his disobedience and hardness. These became famous and spread through the whole earth, proclaiming the power of God and making people marvel and be astounded at God's mighty hand. This outcome was certain to follow from his hardness, so Scripture set it out shaped as a purpose, using that figure to proclaim that the outcome could not be changed. In general, Scripture wants even statements of cause to be framed and interpreted as expressing the inviolable course of events. So Pharaoh is punished not in order that God might be glorified, even if the form of the wording and construction gives that impression, but because he disobeyed and had to pay the penalty for his disobedience. The punishments did not aim at this, nor at his becoming a slave to disobedience.
