Yet they followed hard on the wretch's heels and punished him, and through these extraordinary divine signs of scourges and plagues, as has been said, the power and glory of God grew and flourished. So it is not unreasonable that the narrative is given the form and shape of a purpose clause, since the foreknowledge of the Oracles testifies to and announces what will certainly come to pass even before it has happened. By the same approach, David's words, which earlier received their own particular clarification and resolution, may also be brought to the same complete understanding as the passages just discussed. David sinned, and committed the greatest of sins. He did not sin so that God might be justified, for no one's sin, absolutely no one's, adds righteousness to God. Rather, he did sin, but he did not increase the sin either by hardness of heart or by premeditation [?]. Instead he took refuge in repentance and tears, striving to wash himself clean of the sin. And God, in his love for humankind, grants pardon, displaying to all his own justice, splendid and conspicuous and greater than human understanding. For this reason David, having said, "[?]

…so that you may be justified," added "in your words." Repentance followed transgression, and love for humankind beyond reason followed repentance, and in that love for humankind was the justice that flashes out in the words and sends forth rays of all compassion and goodness. The words here might also be thought of as God's, as he condescends to human weakness and enters into argument and judgment. For he says, "Come, let us reason together, says the Lord." Let us set side by side the gifts and benefits David enjoyed and the lawless deeds into which he slipped. From a tongue of reed that made an art of piping without reason, he became the tongue of the Spirit and the instrument of wisdom and knowledge beyond reason. From a youth who was mocked, he became an improvised general of the war and of the whole battle line. Alone, without arrows or weapons or any other equipment or experience of combat, he carried off the victory as a trophy and was crowned with mastery over his enemies. From hardship in the open air he came to the splendours of houses of two and three storeys, to more splendid ways of life, and to a luxurious life under a roof. The villager became lord of many cities. Instead of a shepherd's pail and bag, he had a sceptre in his hand and the band of kingship around his head. From a herd of cattle and a pipe that charmed their ears with its sound, he became a proclaimer of oracles about works beyond reason, teeming with gifts of prophecy. From the sheepfolds and the care of flocks and a staff propping up his little body weighed down with toil, he came to a royal throne and purple and bodyguards and a crown. In short, from a common man he became a prophet, from a fugitive a king, and he was allotted invincible might over his enemies. Such were God's gifts to David, and those left unsaid are far more. Now for what belongs to my weakness, and to David's. He was overcome by a woman, taking desire as an ally in the war [?]. Adultery and murder danced against the greatness of the benefits. The flesh outraged the spirit, and lawless desire ran riot over the graces of the gifts, and so much more of the kind [?]. The prophet and king became a huckster, not mixing wine with water but mixing the gifts beyond reason with the passions and wild leaps of the flesh, and so adulterating them. When God is judged and pleads his case with David on these and similar arguments, can anyone say how far he surpassed in justice and showed his goodness to be unsurpassable, above all by not even subjecting to punishment the man who repaid so many good things with evil? For punishment would have cut short God's unspeakable mercy and its splendour, whose greatness no word can declare. When a wronged party exacts penalty and punishment, he settles many of the debts [?]. So the custom of the sacred Oracles, which announces in advance what will certainly come to pass, expresses David's words of repentance and confession, and every similar saying, in the form of a purpose clause, and by this figure it portrays the kinship of what will come about without hindrance

…establishes [?]. Therefore he who [?] by the custom of the Oracles and [?]… QUESTION 57 [otherwise 56]. Why did John still baptize when the Saviour's disciples were baptizing? Because he kept the same purpose unswervingly until he was put to death, the purpose for which he had appeared at the beginning as a minister of baptism. Then he baptized so that he might proclaim to the crowds who came to him the common Saviour of the human race. Later he baptized so that he would not be found slackening in such God-pleasing testimony and saintly resolve. So the Saviour's disciples baptized, proclaiming the Redeemer of the race, and John also baptized. He had become the first instance and pattern of their sacred work, and he joined them in their labours and made himself a fellow worker in this saving work of preliminary purification. For while baptizing he cried out, testifying to all that Jesus was divine. This is what their heavenly Bridegroom wanted and was eager to bring about: he who is far greater than all, he who was sent from God, he who speaks the words of God, he who received and possesses the Spirit, not by measure, through a share in his gift and working, as all the prophets did, but by right of kinship and the dignity of being of one essence, beyond all essence. Yet the baptism of John and that of the Saviour's disciples differed in nothing except the persons who performed it. Each prepared those being baptized to be fit to receive the baptism that would be accomplished through fire and Spirit, but neither of them conferred the grace and working of the Spirit or the complete forgiveness of sins. Such a gift beyond reason [was given] after the distribution of the tongues of fire and the coming of the Holy Spirit through them upon those being baptized

QUESTION 58. Why does Moses in Genesis, in [the account] of the chieftains of Esau [?], simply run through the bare names of the others, but of Anah [?] he says, "This is the one who found the Iamin in the wilderness, when he was pasturing the asses of Zibeon his father" [?]? What is it that he found, and why is it thought worth mentioning? The Syriac word Iamin, or Elmein as some say, means "spring." Springs and wells were highly prized by the descendants of Abraham. They were shepherds and made their whole living from the

great number and thriving of their flocks, so they set great store by springs and wells, since drink no less than food fattens the flocks and keeps them in good condition. So we see Abraham too, though he had received other favours from Abimelech, did not think it ungrateful to reproach him over the seizure of the wells he himself had dug. Nor did Abimelech scorn the reproach. He pretended not to know of the deed his servants had dared to do. With the seven ewe lambs Abraham took care to secure Abimelech's acknowledgement that the well was Abraham's work and labour. An oath and a covenant followed, and the spring took its name from the event and was called the Well of the Oath. Later, when Isaac was living as a sojourner in the Philistines' land to escape the famine in his homeland, the Philistines plotted out of envy to drive him out of their country and stopped up his father's wells, knowing that shepherds could not live if they were deprived of the use of wells. And Moses drove off the shepherds who had begun unjust violence and let the daughters of Jethro water their flocks sooner than on other days, [?] to their father, and he became master of a household instead of a stranger. Countless other examples can be found showing that the descendants of Abraham regarded wells as a highly prized and great possession. This is what Anah, or [?] (for he is called by both forms of the name), found without toil, and so he gave the God-seeing Moses a subject for his history when he set out the genealogy of the tribe of Esau in his account of the origin of the world.

QUESTION 52 [?]. What is meant by the words written in Deuteronomy: "If you build a house [?] for your roof, and you shall not bring bloodshed on your house"? Those before us have spoken about this saying in a way that lacks nothing in clarity or correctness. But since you like to hear from us even things that are easy to learn from others, we too agree with them, especially with those who have seen something better than the rest, and we offer an explanation in harmony with theirs. First, we say, one must know that the conjunction "and", like many other words, often stands as a redundant word in the ordinances of Moses. So the saying could be read more straightforwardly if the conjunction at the beginning were removed. The interpretation divides into two senses. One keeps to the letter and is guided by things perceived by the senses, while the other seeks rather to be raised to contemplation. The first proceeds by what the wording and sense perception chiefly govern, and it unfolds the meaning roughly as follows. "Suppose you have set out to build a house, and you have dug the trench, as one would, to lay the base and put down the foundations. You must not leave the pits open, without a proper enclosure and protection, before you have finished the work, so that someone who does not know what you are doing [?]

…you will be shown guilty of bloodshed: he fell into the pit because he knew nothing of the new works, and you took no care to prevent any such thing from happening. It is no surprise that many animals too fall into a pit and die. But some people as well have been driven to their ruin instead of to the use the pit was made for. The old layout of the place, their habit of walking through it, and the short time since the change all hid the new works from them, and deceived them into suspecting no new or recent danger. For all these reasons, then, we must leave out no safety measure in what we do, so that we may keep our kin and our own people free from all harm and loss. It is lawless and cruel to look on while our kin suffer the worst of misfortunes and pains from the very things from which we reap the benefits. But when the forethought we owe is shown here too, and none of those passing by is swept into the pits, there will be no bloodshed in the newly built house. The enclosure and parapet built around the pit have shown the house clean of bloodshed. By displaying to all plainly one's forethought for one's neighbour, they win many fine praises for the one who took such care, and they have stored up the reward of that care for whoever laid them down beforehand, in like works and like mishaps. They have also confirmed what is most pleasing to God in the legislation: its power, its saving purpose and its claim to reverence. That, then, is the plain meaning of the present passage according to the senses. The meaning that lifts the mind rather to contemplation, and that seeks to bind action firmly to exhortation, would be this. Those who practise a newer philosophy that stands above the many, and pursue a life set apart from the common way of living, have laid a new foundation. They have set out to build a new house that conforms in nothing to the crowd and does not fall back into the tracks of the customary way of life. Once they are in the very midst of the work, they ought not to slacken the strain of their struggles, nor through laxity in the labours that remain let the masterpiece so well begun be built rotten and ready to fall. Through this house they could firmly beat back the snowstorms of temptation even when they burst down like rainstorms, and shut out and check the burning ray, that is, the heat of the passions. This house, so brilliantly begun and advancing so far toward a sweet wonder, must not later be allowed through slackness of mind to fall into ridicule, to come away gloomy and disgraced, and to lose its former glory. Rather, having begun to be built in a new way, it must keep up its achievement in the same manner. A parapet must be set around this delightful and beautiful dwelling, that is, one must practise to the very end the exactness and diligence that lead to the crowns. For the crowns belong to those who compete lawfully and to the end.

For, says the herald of the Church, “no one is crowned unless he competes lawfully.” And whoever has kept the new covenant ever newer by those same new ways of life knows that progress and perfection in Christ is a new creation. “For if anyone,” he says, “is in Christ, he is a new creation,” and he is “to be renewed.” That is: in everything, keep yourselves being renewed in the newness that has been ordered wisely and beyond reason, bringing in nothing old and no disease of rottenness. If the parapet of good deeds is not set upon the dwelling that is being renewed, that is, if we do not keep up to the end the youthful, new and noble contests that win us the crowns, then there is bloodshed, and the most grievous bloodshed of all, in the rottenness of the building. For it brings down with it and buries even the one who at the start of the building's newness had laboured so eagerly. Would that he had not done it in vain! Consider the man who has been so wretchedly turned around that after so many labours and sweats he insults, as if in regret, what he achieved before, and becomes a slave of the passions and the enemy's prey. For him, never to have chosen the new way of life at all would be no worse than to have chosen it and not carried it through to the end, but instead to have chosen what is opposite to what he had zealously pursued. That gives those who hate us the means to revel in mockery and reproaches. [?] Nor is it right to pass over in silence the divine Cyril [?].

QUESTION 60. Why is it that, although the law forbids anyone to touch a leper (or else he is unclean until evening), the Saviour touches the leper when he heals him, even though he was able to heal him by a word? First of all, one must know this. At times the Saviour judged it right to keep the law; at other times he showed it to be inferior to better and superhuman works. But even when he approved of keeping the law, he did not keep it as one subject to the laws. He did so, rather, for two reasons. First, he was fulfilling the dispensation. As one who had not disdained to take on human nature, he was showing that he too does not despise the things by which human affairs are already ordered, but even observes them whenever nothing better draws his providence away and turns it toward itself. Second, he was stopping the blasphemies and unbridled mouths of the Jews. Their God-fighting madness did not shudder to fling impiety and lawlessness, as it were, at the Master, and he turned these back upon their own heads. So when the disciples were accused because, walking on the Sabbath, they plucked ears of grain and, being hungry, made an improvised meal as a remedy, he showed them blameless and untouched by any reproach. He did this by other sacred arguments, and especially by bringing forward examples that, with their force and authority, put the matter beyond dispute. Indeed, he openly proclaimed that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath and not a slave to its observance. That is why, when he was present, the privilege of the Sabbath gave way, just as when the master stands by…

…the slave's freedom to speak falls silent and he is directed by his master's nod. Where he was working human salvation in a divine way, the laws that act as tutors to human beings kept quiet, for they understood that the very work of salvation was far greater than their own tutoring. But where keeping the laws neither put off the working of miracles nor neglected human salvation, then they too asserted their proper claim. Or rather, that claim was always preserved together with them by what the Saviour did. Even when the laws were first introduced and seemed to be at their height, they did not count it an insult or an overthrow of their strength that the priests cut wood, lit fires and divided up meat. Instead they took it as an adornment and a mark of dignity to give second place to these things. Nor did they reckon it a weakness in their own authority that an ox or an ass was untied from the manger and led away to drink, nor did they regard it as their annulment that in these matters one was not enslaved to the commandment. And what need is there to speak of a sheep pulled out of a pit, an ox or a son of man drawn up out of a well, and how many other such things? The Sabbath laws, guarding their own authority, were content with these and even took pride in them, since these exceptions were introduced together with them from the beginning, and the laws were bounded by the inclusion of many other works and by the definition of the acts permitted within them [?]. These and similar things, then, the Saviour brought out into the open when the ungrateful Jews loudly denounced his miracles and his healing of incurable diseases as a breach of the Sabbath. He set the works that are beyond reason against acts done by hand and showed how great the difference between them was. Not even the shameless Jews could deny that the saving acts were far more honourable and wonderful than cutting wood, dividing meat, drawing a sheep or an ox up from a pit or a well, and anything else of that kind, even though they did not turn from their impious and God-fighting mind. But you, observe the incomprehensible wisdom of God and his ineffable providence. The law, I mean, was destined in later times to be wholly annulled and to give way to the power and decree of grace. So when it was first introduced and established, it was bound up with annulment from the start. In this way, when the complete annulment arrived, it could point to the partial annulment with which the law had come forth and show that what had happened was nothing new or strange. It could also shame and muzzle the disobedience of the Jews and their untimely zeal for the law. For the law was not only now moving toward annulment. It had come forth with annulment from the beginning. It was constituted together with annulment, and from the very start it did not exist as something that could not be annulled. And this annulment kept within its own bounds not only the legislation about the Sabbath, but also the rite of the Passover. There it divided up the appointed time, and by a partial postponement it secured the fulfilment of the rite in full. Yes, and the setting apart of a single temple for the sacrifices foreordained that for the Jews scattered all over the earth the sacrifice…

…would remain in every way unoffered and without favourable sign. In part this was because they could not all gather every year from every quarter into the same temple; in part it was because the temple was soon to be overthrown by hostile hands. So too in countless other cases, so that from every side one can see that the old legislation was destined in the end to grow old. The very symbols that made it up proclaimed and announced this in advance, not so much in words as in their very workings and acts. And indeed it had been from the beginning a prelude and a preparatory exercise for another way of life, loftier, more divine and admitting no annulment, for whose sake it came into being at all, and only for a time. Our Saviour, then, heals the leper by touch both for these reasons and to show that he was Lord. He was Lord of introducing the law and equally of not introducing it; and as he could decline to introduce it, so he could introduce it for others without introducing it for himself. For the lawgiver is not obliged to keep the laws, since keeping them belongs only to those for whom they are laid down. A king who makes laws for a city and its government does not subject himself to the measures by which he orders and governs [?] the state. He proclaims them for the sake of those he rules and arranges for them to revere the limits of his decree. But he himself sits above the civic order and its service, and holds the state together and preserves it by his commands. In the same way the Creator and King of all the world gave laws at various times to those in the world, so as to reorder and reshape them for the better. He himself, however, had no need of such provision and was above it, though he generously enriched his subjects with it so that they might take up what it supplied. For our Saviour did not introduce his legislation as other lawgivers do, who lay down their laws with many others judging with them and voting in agreement. He introduced it as God and Lord of all, having taken to himself the authority over the whole of the legislation. It is necessary, therefore, that those for whom laws are made be subject to them, but every argument exempts him, since he stands far above all others [?]. But come, consider this with me as well. The law calls unclean the one who touches a leper. It does not mean the one whom it knew would cleanse by his touch the person gripped by the disease of leprosy. (For there was not yet any hope of grace having come, nor even of its preludes, which revealed a man working divine deeds and superior to suffering, and made this manifest above all to the one seeking healing.) It means the one who brings no cleansing to the leper, the one it saw would rather catch the disease than free the sufferer from his uncleanness. But Christ our Saviour, the physician of souls and of bodies, cleanses the leper of his leprosy through touch [?], and at once drives out the disease in a way beyond all words. How then would it not be absurd for him to shrink from the touch as a cause of uncleanness, when he knew that through it he would show the man oppressed by leprosy to be cleansed? And how would it not be unreasonable for the one…

…[the touch] did not strip away the authority of the Godhead; rather, the man who was assumed made his own the power of the one who assumed him). He touched the leper also because the lawgiver in the proper sense, the one who legislates in his own right, subjects those under his hand to the legislation but is not himself brought under it or carried along with those for whom the laws are made. He did so also because the old law came into being with annulment built into it, and its security took shape alongside that annulment: neither did away with the other, but the legislation took its form from both. Again, the law does not forbid those who cleanse a person of uncleanness by touch to touch him. It forbids those who cannot put the one disfigured by uncleanness in any better state. Finally, by what he did the Saviour rather honoured the legislation, showing that it does not oppose the divine signs but is instead taken up in harmony with them. For all these reasons, then, so far as I can know, our Saviour and God, in healing the leper and joining touch to word, showed him cleansed in a manner beyond all words.

QUESTION 61. What is meant by: “A living dog is better than a dead lion”? According to the letter, the meaning is obvious, but it does not seem to lead to anything useful or necessary, for it is known to all. Not only is a living dog better than a dead lion; everything that has a share in life is better than what has lost it. Even if the dead thing is a lion, and even if it was granted a superiority beyond all measure in the nature and strength of lions, the living is still deemed worthy of a far better lot than the dead. So it is better to proceed from the letter to the spirit and to be lifted up to the contemplation of intelligible things. We have learned, then, from the sacred Scriptures that “dogs” are those called from the Gentiles, while the royal and chosen people, whom the lion might represent, is the one called the Jewish people. And so the Preacher says (for to him God gave the gift of wisdom, to broaden and stretch out to things present, to things past, and indeed to things to come), he says, I mean, that the dog, that is, the man from the Gentiles (for we are taught through the Canaanite woman that he is called this), if…

…a life of virtue does not altogether forsake him, would offer greater hope of not falling away from goodness than one who comes from the royal and [?] race of the Jews but lies dead in respect of good deeds. For the one who shares in the better life holds out hope that he will also rise to perfection in good deeds. But the one who carries the working of the virtues dead within himself, and so is numbered among the dead, boasts of being a lion in vain, since he bears no trace of true life. Indeed, the one regarded as an unclean person, since he is soiled with sins and deprived of the purity that comes through the virtues, has often washed away the mire of the passions with tears and repentance. He has then been found better than the one who appears great and is so elated by his virtues as to think lofty and royal thoughts, for he too has wiped away the scars of his sins by constant treatment. But the one whom the colours of the virtues have painted as a lion is often puffed up by the swelling of his pride, broken down from his arrogance, and made dead, when sin receives him into its death-dealing tents that carry off corpses. And if you like, consider also the one who has been reborn through baptism into the life that is in Christ. Even if a dog's shamelessness once shaped him, even if he was moulded into some other trait of the irrational beasts, he nevertheless offers hope of being transformed toward goodness and being called good. But the one who has fallen away from this rebirth and is deprived of the life that comes from it remains no less dead, even if he seems to pride himself on some virtues and to exult in his elevated way of life. He is far worse than one who was once a dog but has not lost his share in life-giving grace.

QUESTION 62. What does Solomon's saying mean: “Send out your bread upon the face of the water, for in the multitude of days you will find it”? Scripture often signifies the practice of almsgiving through many things, but especially through the providing and sharing of bread, since the need for bread above all sustains human life. So, starting from bread, the most sustaining part, it takes in the whole good work of almsgiving. It is written, then: “Break your bread for the hungry.” And now Solomon, in saying “Send out your bread upon the face of the water,” signified almsgiving. One must supply it to those in want, whose hope of livelihood looks only to a generous hand. This almsgiving, he says, one ought to offer from a compassionate disposition that goes out with tears, and not seize on a neighbour's misfortune as an occasion for display and boasting. Such a person has not let his bread go upon the face of the water. He has flung it down, insulted by his boasting and defiled by his vainglory. For mercy poured out with pomp, self-love…

…and display becomes an insult to the one in need rather than a comfort. A right-minded person will consider not overlooking a brother who is wasting away in want and perishing in poverty to be a debt, and the most unavoidable of debts. He will hasten to pay it and will by no means let it fall overdue. But to hunt for glory and to put on the dignity of a benefactor through such an act belongs to the unfeeling, who know how to pursue what is good only in a bad way. Therefore the first will find the bread of his almsgiving “in the multitude of days,” that is, in the age to come, receiving mercy in return. The other will not find it, for it has already been spent on vainglory and the trade of display. Through these same words you could also pass to another meaning. What sort? Scripture likes to call the multitude of people “waters.” For “Rescue me,” says the one who sings in the Spirit, “from many waters, from the hand of foreign sons.” The teacher of sacred lessons, then, ought to share out the bread that nourishes the soul, which God has entrusted to him, among the multitude of his hearers without any delay or postponement. He must never deprive of this supply those who are in need of it. And what is the reward for this generous work? Clearly the one repaid “in the multitude of days.” And since water can figuratively signify various kinds of things, one would not be unreasonable in contemplating the present passage this way: one ought always to practise almsgiving, fixing one's gaze on the ever-flowing springs of water and carrying over their working to mercy by imitating them. One should not pour out mercy at one time and hold it back at another, but should make continuous and unbroken streams gush forth for those in need. For we hear David singing, “All day long the Lord shows mercy and lends.” And if “he who has mercy on the poor lends to God,” how could anyone who loves God and preserves the nobility of being made in his image think it tolerable not always to make God his debtor, but to cut himself off and deprive himself of the contribution of so great and so rich a gain? Clearly such a person will find it always, but especially in the multitude of days, for the sharing of his bread has stored up for him an unending reward. Moreover, the mystagogue also sends the daily and mystical bread upon the face of the water of regeneration. He offers it to those being initiated, who need heavenly food that strengthens the soul. For after the divine rebirth through water, the heavenly and life-giving bread is offered to those who have been reborn. Whoever distributes it with wisdom and dispenses it worthily has found the bread that truly came down from heaven and gives life to the world. It always gives him life, strengthens him and nourishes him, but especially at the time when what each has done in life is repaid. There are, however, some who take this meaning too from the…

…they think the saying implies this: one should not pry into the circumstances of the person being fed or shown mercy. For these interpreters too, the water is plainly taken to mean the human community. So, they say, a person should not first calculate whether the one who needs alms deserves mercy and kindness or not. Instead, when someone asks for compassion, one should give it without doubts and second thoughts. Someone who casts his bread on the sea throws it into the unknown and does not know where the current carries it, yet it is clearly seen by the One who knows all things and is held within his all-sovereign grasp. In the same way, someone who gives mercy to those who ask for it, without discriminating or hesitating, does not know now who received it. But "after many days", that is, in the age to come, he will know. He will find that bread in the hand of the Master, who shows it and says, "I was hungry and you gave me something to eat." Plainly he will be filled with every joy and gladness, because he finds not only the bread he sent out on the face of the waters but finds it made far more precious and profitable to him.

Here he calls plotting against one's neighbor a "pit", and he calls destruction a "ditch", as it is written: "He dug a hole and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the pit he made"; and: "The sinner was caught in the works of his own hands." So whoever digs such a pit and destruction for another falls into it first himself. In contriving these things he destroys his own soul before he harms his neighbor. If he inflicts harm on the body of his fellow man, he has [?] often helped that man rather than destroyed him, while he has thrust himself into the pit of the soul's ruin. And whoever has contrived the destruction of his neighbor's soul has destroyed his own beforehand all the same, whether he caught his victim or not. The incorruptible judgment reckons the wrong according to the person's eagerness and intent. Even if the intended victim often escapes the one bent on harming him, it still exacts the penalty in full. With these words, then, the Preacher urges anyone who wants to be kept free from harm and injury to stay away from all wrongdoing. Indeed, whoever contrives evil against his neighbor will not escape the punishment of the law. If he has knocked out an eye, he will have his own gouged out; if he has pulled out a tooth, he will lose his own as well. No wrong that injures a neighbor fails to hand the wrongdoer over to punishment. So whoever digs a pit for another, that is, seeks to destroy him, will not escape falling into the pit of punishment, which he deepened for himself while digging the pit against his neighbor.

How should we understand what is written in Ecclesiastes: "Whoever splits wood will be endangered by it. If the iron falls off, he too has troubled his face, and he will strengthen forces; and the advantage of the courageous man is wisdom"?

…is not wholly separated from philosophy. Even in ethical teaching one can find some transmission of insights about nature and about divine things, though to a lesser degree. Likewise, in the philosophy of divine things one can find moral guidance scattered throughout, and an understanding of nature as well. And in the study whose task is to examine the order and harmony of nature, one can find not a few things that raise character up [?] by way of exhortation. That is why the Preacher here draws on something from nature. Through this example he leads the hearer to the exhortation by which one may pass through the present life free from harm and be kept in prosperity. He says: "Whoever splits wood", making this his craft and livelihood, "if the iron falls off" (the iron with which the wood is split), or if after the first split it does not separate further from [?] and finish it in its proper shape [?], "he will be endangered by them", that is, deprived of the benefit that comes from them. "And he will trouble his face": instead of a face bright with cheerfulness, he takes on a gloomy one. "And he will strengthen forces": the forces that envied him, which put on his weakness and helplessness as their own strength. His courage does nothing to help defend him; it dissolves into something superfluous and useless because the iron has fallen off. So when the iron falls off for a woodcutter, many misfortunes follow and overtake a man who could have lived self-sufficiently by splitting and working wood. The same is true of the teacher. He uses the word of teaching like an iron, a tool for dividing. With it he opens up the divine Scriptures, which are bound and knotted together by their obscurity, in a fitting and suitable way, as the grace of the Spirit wills, and he divides them part by part through interpretation that benefits the soul. In this way he preserves the spiritual life for himself while guiding and urging his hearers toward it. But suppose the precision of his teaching, its sincerity and its sharp edge for piety, slips away from him unnoticed and fails him [?] in dividing and clarifying the Scriptures. Suppose he does not interpret their meaning by orthodox doctrine, but lets the saving word fall into some heresy and corrupt opinion. Such a man truly confounds and troubles the face of orthodox [?] teaching that he put on at the beginning, and he fills the souls of his hearers with harm instead of salvation.

And he has strengthened the forces that envied him when he prospered before, which sought to plot against him and strove to oppose him. He has shown himself weak and cast down, and has exposed his once-admired wisdom as brought down to superfluity and vanity. But consider the man courageous in mind. He repels the proud reasonings of the heretics that besiege his right belief. With the cutting word of the Spirit he cuts off their crooked insertions and their twisted sophisms. He also cleanses the true belief, which honors God and holds fast to virtue, of whatever overshadows it, and separates from it anything spurious that the enemies have rubbed onto it from outside. From such a man the iron will never slip away unnoticed, and no one will convict him of having lost it through betrayal. He will keep his original face unchanged and free of all disturbance. And he will strengthen the natural powers within him by adding the powers that come from grace. In this way he truly shows how far the wisdom of the courageous man surpasses the sloth of the coward, who is easily caught out in his deeds because he is so utterly unfeeling.

QUESTION 65. What is the point of the saying "A generation goes and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever"? Solomon has spoken of human pursuits and of the constant labors that people spend on the enjoyment of life. He said that these are frittered away [?] in vanity. The one who toils and labors finds no more gain than the one who gives none of these things a thought. He is subject to the same bodily passions, his body is just as liable to change and decay, and he travels toward the same end and sinks down to it. He showed this by saying, "What advantage has a man in all his toil at which he toils under the sun?" Here "what" is used to mean "none". That is, a man gains no more benefit from all his toil under the sun than if he had not worn himself out and strained himself over any of these things; nor is he shown to be any better off than someone free from such vanity. Having said all this, he therefore urges his hearers to withdraw from eager pursuit of these things and from their vanity. By "under the sun" he usually means whatever serves generation and decay, since such things are carried along by the sun's course. For the creative Word ordained summer and winter, and between them spring and autumn. The sun's course plays a great part in producing the seasons, and the seasons in turn give rise to many changes and alterations in bodily and human things, for worse or for better. So it is fitting that he names eager care about such things in this way, bearing witness that those devoted to them wear themselves out.

He has first discussed these things with regard to individual people. Now he says that each of them gains nothing from their constant distractions and labors, as they devote unceasing eagerness and care to things that flow through generation and decay. And he adds that the same empty eagerness can be seen no less in a whole generation. Of the generations, one holds to what is better and another leans toward what is base. The generation that has toiled under the sun finds its going gloomy and full of misery when it departs, and when it comes its road leads to nothing useful. On the contrary, toils and labors press hard on it, and instead of bringing it benefit they mock it for its vanity. The other generation pushes aside, with sober reasoning, the things in generation and decay, that is, the things under the sun, and takes no account of them beyond what the bond of nature inescapably demanded. Instead it seeks and pursues with wisdom the things above the sun, that is, whatever is by nature better than the things in generation and decay. These are purity of soul, and mercy toward one's neighbor, which cheers and soothes the blows of poverty. If mercy frees him from those wounds entirely, it is the most blessed and godlike of all. This generation drives out licentiousness by love of self-control and dances in the chorus of the other virtues. This generation, then, and the whole company of those who make it up, pursued none of the things under the sun and was not swept around and sunk along with the things in generation and decay. Plainly it looked far beyond the others toward what is better, having exchanged a wandering way of life that drains away into vanity for an abiding and steadfast one. Having set this out in riddling and concise words, he adds: "But the earth stands forever." By "forever" he means the time in which the sun and moon, the dance of the stars, and the heavenly vault itself, moving in opposite directions, unroll their orderly and harmonious motion to divide and restore days, nights and seasons. He brings in the earth, in turn, to rebuke the eagerness of those who have worn out their thoughts and spent their will on vain things, when they ought to have devoted themselves to the things of salvation and worked hard for spiritual gains. It is almost as if he were saying: "What have you gained, O man, from all this trouble and eagerness? Are you not just like the others, who underwent no such turmoil and were not tossed by such storms? Do you not come, just as they do, when you come, and go when you go? Yet you wretchedly rob yourself of all the blessedness that is enjoyed by those who seek and pursue with wisdom the things above the sun. And what is hardest of all, you have found the outcome of your many toils and labors (alas for the unbearable and inconsolable loss!) dragging you and yours toward the worse and lifting you toward nothing better. For see: compared even with this lifeless, motionless ground of the earth, common to all and lying beneath all, not even compared with this, through all

that empty eagerness of yours, have you managed to extend your own span of time, nor have you found any pretext by pushing your way through [?]. You labor in vain and turn everything upside down, yet you pass away all the sooner. Trembling and helpless, you sink down toward things one would think unbearable even to hear about. You do not add even the briefest time to yourself, let alone stretch your life out to match the duration of what is lifeless and motionless. Meanwhile the very ground that is trodden underfoot, a nature without sense or motion, stands and endures, not only many [?]… You have driven it to take up the role of accuser. It accuses your empty eagerness and your haughty thoughts by remaining and standing there for so long. It accuses you also because it was seen to change nothing of what Providence granted it. But you, who were honored with reason, have done the very opposite of what the Creator's care intended, through your eagerness and contention over vain things. You have been carried with unchecked force toward what divine laws forbade and what the laws of nature, laid down from above, abhorred, since they found your empty eagerness and your headlong rush toward vain things an unbearable outrage. So through them the charge is brought before the One who created us and provides for our affairs with all wisdom and love for humankind, than whom nothing more loving or better can be expressed in words or conceived in thought." But for you, perhaps, this is enough. Some, however, can be found who take the generation that goes out and is cast away to be the Jewish people. They take the generation that comes and remains to be the children of grace, who sprang up from the divine seed and the husbandry of Christ. And they take the earth that stands forever to be the Old and New Scripture. In them, they say, the fruitfulness of the virtues can be seen flourishing, together with the everlasting firmness of the laws and promises. The promises they assigned to the righteous, and the others [?] to sinners and those who have offended without repenting…

What meaning does this saying unfold: "There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is an ungodly man who remains in his wickedness"? Scripture also says, "The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and he will be multiplied like the cedar in Lebanon." Both expressions announce the gain of righteousness and the abundance and plenty of good things, namely through "will flourish" and "will be multiplied". This righteous man may be scourged, he may be racked, he may suffer the most painful things; he may be led to slaughter, to death, to the cross. Yet he flourishes like a palm all the same and will be multiplied like a cedar. He finds enjoyment many times greater than his toils and sufferings, and he delights and thrives in indescribable good things. Who, then, is the righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and in what way does he perish? Or clearly

as with the man who has blasphemed against the Holy Spirit, that is, against one of the supernatural, life-originating and consubstantial hypostases of the all-sovereign and creating Godhead. Even if such a man seems to be free of guilt for the passions through his love of the virtues, his sin will by no means be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

QUESTION 67. How should we understand "But if our unrighteousness commends God's righteousness"? The divine Paul uses the word "commends" here without teaching that our unrighteousness is the originating cause of God's righteousness, or any cause of it at all. How could any reasoning that has not been robbed of free will, and has not outraged the divine image, think this of the divine Paul? Rather, "commends" has been used here in the sense of "renders [?]";

that is, it makes something known to all. Nor does the word here mean bringing something into existence. God's righteousness is not the fruit of our unrighteousness. Nor, as some might think, is there any room for raising the point as a genuine difficulty, for even when framed that way it ends in mockery and is carried off into futility. When a genuine difficulty is raised, deeper investigation usually clears away what stands in the way [?] and brings clarity [?]. But whatever plainly shows its own absurdity brings a ready and obvious condemnation with it. Such things cannot even venture to be framed as a difficulty; they are exposed as the work of nonsense and idle talk. That "commends" has been used in the sense of "makes evident", that is, makes something plain for all to recognize, the herald of truth himself stands as his own witness, and his testimony gives us the clearest teaching on the point. Writing to the Romans, he says: "I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a deacon of the church at Cenchreae." Clearly "I commend" is used here in the sense of "I present": "I want her to be recognized; I urge you to get to know her." Why? "So that you may receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints." Here "I commend" does not mean "to cause to subsist" or "to bring into existence". It means that the blessed Phoebe should be known and recognized and made manifest to those in Rome. So too in our passage. How, then, does our unrighteousness commend God's righteousness? In the way that darkness set beside light makes the light shine more brightly to those who look at it. In the way that something bitter, set beside something sweet, makes the sweetness taste sweeter. In the way that something rough, which jars the touch, makes us more aware of the evenness and smoothness of what is smooth. In the way that falsehood, by comparison, makes truth plainer, more desirable and more worth choosing. When two things stand far apart from each other through opposing differences, the one exposes more fully the baseness of the worse, and the other makes plain the goodness of the one who judges. Those who pass from one opposite to the other perceive, from the worse, how far the better excels, and from the better, how base its opposite is, just as the senses perceive their objects. So it is, then, with the all-wise Paul as well, even though he puts it in the form of a hypothesis raised as a difficulty: that our [?] unrighteousness commends God's righteousness. That is why, after linking to what came before the words "Is God unrighteous, who inflicts wrath?", he adds: "By no means!" Why? Because our unrighteousness did not display his righteousness by testifying to it and proclaiming it while we were grateful and seeking to serve God. It did so in the way just described, in which goodness is made more evident through wickedness. The rest of the passage is hard to understand and will perhaps not lack its own separate solution, if divine [?] watches over us more kindly [?]. ¹⁷ Rom. 3:5. ¹⁸ Ibid. 6.

QUESTION 68. "If a man begets a hundred children and lives many years, however great the number of the days of his years, and his soul is not filled with good, and his name will be covered; and it has not seen the sun nor known it; this one has more rest than he." What distinction [?] can this saying show? People in the world pursued having many children very ambitiously, as a great prize, and long life likewise. Indeed, in many places long life is held out as a reward to those who keep the Lord's ordinances. So, says Solomon, suppose someone far surpasses other people in the number of his children and has his life stretched out by great length of years. But in other respects he spoils his life with wickedness. He does not fill his soul with the enjoyment of goodness or adorn it, and perhaps for that reason he is not even granted burial. Such a man would rightly be reckoned much worse off than the stillborn child. The stillborn child did not see the sun; it did not have the means by which it might have seen [?] the things that exist and chosen the better course of action. The other man was honored with all these things, gladdened by a multitude of children, and enjoyed long life. But he did not share in goodness, and while living in luxury he did not hold back from baseness, and the burial he deserved followed upon these things. So it is fitting that he, rather than the stillborn child, should be reckoned to have the worse lot. For this one [?] the sun [?] speaks entirely truly; but nothing, I think, [?] having embraced [?] by proclamation [?].

Question [69?]. What is meant by: "Live in good, and in the day of evil, see. See, God has made this too in accord with this concerning speech, so that man may find nothing after him"?

"You," he says, "prepare your life to look toward virtue, and set it in order for the enjoyment of the good things of the world above. Once you have equipped yourself in this way, and have trained your mind by pious reasoning to gain the power of judgment, you will be able to see without difficulty that the things held to be evils in the day are also [in accord]": that is, the human misfortunes and griefs by which the day of human life, tossed and stirred up, is made evil, and which trouble and afflict those who pass through it along with it. For we are accustomed to call such things "evils" too, as in the saying, "There is no evil in a city which the Lord has not done." And you will be able to see that even these do not befall us out of harmony with God's goodness and providence. This is what he made clear by saying, "See, this too is in accord with this." That is, even what seem to be trials and bodily afflictions do not [?] divine care, nor do they oppose his love for us. For some of them are brought on us for discipline and correction, and others are permitted, and through both an ineffable and wise dispensation can be discerned by one who has been given the grace to judge such things. Now God did not ordain that the things which befall people should be spoken of by every tongue, nor that everyone should know beforehand what is coming. Why? So that a man, having learned and discovered them in advance, might not grow more careless about virtue. Sometimes he would expect that many evils and grievous mishaps were going to overtake him afterward (for what regard should I have for virtue when so many and such great evils are expected? Despair is accustomed to drive the many to this); at other times he would expect that no great or heavy pain was going to befall him. For a faulty judgment about what must be done is apt to trip a man up from either side, and so he would think he needed neither much watchfulness nor care for the virtues. For this reason, then, God made speech about future things unknown to the many. He did not want a man who discovered what hardships were to overtake him in the times after him to give himself up to helplessness and despair in the harder cases and so turn not at all toward virtue. Nor did he want him, in the moderate cases, to grow sick with disdain, as though [assured] of the enjoyment and luxury of what he desires, expecting that no hindrance would be set against it, and so put off his zeal for good deeds. Besides, one who has a judgment cleansed of passion and impartial sees that health and sickness alike bear on people's harm and benefit, and likewise wealth and poverty, strength and weakness of body, glory among men and obscurity, and things like these. For whichever lot each of these belongs to, for one who knows how to live wisely it becomes an occasion of salvation;

but for one who gapes only after what is pleasant and titillating, the pleasant things become a pretext for harm, and the painful things too slide down and are dragged into the same evil. For the one who needs to be purified through such things does not bear them gratefully; instead he is turned toward madness and indignation by the very things that should have chastened him.

Question 70 [or 69]. How the garments of skin which Adam and Eve put on after the transgression are to be understood.

I know of some who declare that the garments of skin which Adam and Eve put on after the transgression are the body, out of which, and [?] from which, the Fashioner constituted the human being, the rational living creature, from the beginning. But these people, striving to say what follows from the assumption that had already taken hold of them, corrupt the truth with an incoherent opinion and knowledge. For in their hands paradise is fashioned in word but overthrown in deed. The plants of paradise, the eating, the bringing forth of Eve through the rib, in short the whole creation of things and its progression, the loving and wonderful care of God for man, and the beginnings of generation and its succession: all these they refer to an intelligible stage, and so they have shown no reverence even for their own existence and being. From there they [?] the whole tragedy according to their own design and act it out, moulding it into whatever shapes and notions they [?please]. They forswear the coherent course of what truly happened and existed, which is seen and known even to this day, and they bewitch the ears of the many with charming and seductive words. For most fictions, being shaped for [?] and for pleasure, are apt to tickle the ears of the hearers and dispose them to the relaxation of pleasure; yet the architects of such things can offer no benefit either to themselves or to those who believe them. But let Origen and the Origenist chorus keep these people. Our Gregory, whom his theological and God-given boldness concerning the Spirit proclaimed "the Theologian," does not give the name "garments of skin" to what the Origenist myth invented. He was as eager as anyone to bring people over from the Origenist opinion, but he knew how to manage his words wisely and with discernment. So he pursues a neighbouring interpretation in order to re-teach them, [?] and lets loose a sharp and effective strain against that vainglory. He does not, as has already been said, call the body "garments of skin"; far from it. He was never found uttering any such word. Rather, he means the grossness and mortality of the body, and a disposition opposite and contrary to the former blessed one. For truly, after the transgression, instead of a body that was impassible, blameless, not weighed down by [?] and mortality, and superior to the motions and titillations of [pleasure?], Adam after the transgression

put on the opposite of these, as it were a garment spotted with the passions just mentioned and soiled by them. This holy man, then, drew those who had sprung from Origen gently and humanely and brought them over to more pious reasoning. He suggested that the garments of skin were things of this kind, and not without an adverb of hesitation. And what do you say? Perhaps at first you laugh, or perhaps you are rather annoyed to hear the truth being smuggled in under a myth; but I think you would not despise the Theologian's dispensation and method. He was not ignorant of the fig leaves with which Adam and Eve covered the shame of their nakedness and made it decent. Nor was he ignorant that the fig leaves came first in providing a refuge for modesty, and that the garments of skin later took their place and met the same need. For after the first covering, the fig leaves, God made them the garments of skin. How then should one suppose that this most theological and God-seeing teacher was ignorant of these things? Should one not rather say that he was managing the matter and devising the salvation of others, in ways that, when the occasion arose, left no heretical sowing or crookedness behind? For whether the fig leaves showed Adam and Eve revering their modesty, or God afterward made them garments of skin as a consolation for their shame, it is no less pious to say that after the transgression Adam put on a coarser and mortal flesh, dragged down by the weight of the fault and of [?], set against God and contrary to him. "But where," you will go on to ask, "did the garments of skin come from?" When you hear that God made garments of skin for Adam and Eve and give it your attention, I think you will at once find the solution running alongside the difficulty. For he who brought man forth from nothing so generously and lavishly could also make garments of skin from nothing and prepare a covering for him with the greatest ease, and this would rather plant an undoubting faith in our reasoning. And if reasoning has raised the idea that they were made from the hides of animals (for these already existed to meet their need for a covering), with God making them wise enough to bestir themselves for their own decency and safety, this too is not far from divine care, nor unworthy of his great goodness toward our race. But this is as much as a summary treatment allows. There are some, however, who will not look to any of this and do not care to, and they have supposed that the garments of skin were the outer layers around the bark of trees. They treat the hides of animals as though they gave a poorer or less honourable covering, and yet hides are pleasanter to the touch and softer than any bark, and, in a word, more suitable by a great many degrees.

Question 71. To what meaning will [?] direct us: "If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly"?

The present passage can be subjected to various interpretations, partly because the reading admits two

different forms, and partly because the statement can naturally take various figures of construction. Moreover, the words "His turning is to you" may also properly be taken of different matters. The difference in reading divides the saying into an interrogative and a declarative form. As a question it runs: "If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, is it not known to you and beyond doubt that you have sinned?" And, in keeping with God's loving wisdom, this seats the sinner himself as judge of his wrongdoing, so that, finding his own thoughts bringing condemnation on him, he may run more readily to repentance and draw forgiveness to himself more quickly. And the answer, which plainly puts forward assent, fulfils the questioner's intent no less through silence: by not daring to open his mouth and utter a word, the sinner is shown to confess his sin even against his will. For in questions where the confession and assent of the one questioned follows plainly and without doubt, silence is apt to carry no less force than a voice announcing assent, but rather more. And it makes the rebuke, if that is what the questioner wants, sharper and more forceful. When the saying takes the form of a question, then, it conveys the meaning just set out. But when it is shaped in the declarative form, it is not uttered with one and the same character of voice, since it can proceed by different modes of the construction by which the words are fitted to one another. For the one making the declaration either declares that "you would not have offered rightly, since you did not divide rightly," that is, that you did not offer rightly because you did not divide rightly; or that, since you did not divide rightly, you sinned even if you seemed to offer rightly, for the rightness of the offering did not correct the sin of not dividing. As for "you sinned," the question delivers it in connection and continuity with the words placed before it. In the declarative readings, however, each version adds "you sinned" to what precedes after a break. Therefore the one who did not divide rightly sinned no less, even if he seemed to offer rightly. For what was done rightly does not so much remove the sin that came before; rather, the sin passes over even to what seemed to escape sin and drags it along into guilt. For often, when good is joined with evil or the worthless with the better, the better does not share its own beauty with the worse; for the most part it is debased along with the worthlessness of the worse. And according to the man whom God taught the genesis of the world, the clean, by touching the unclean, does not [?] impart its purity; and with him too, the profane, when it touches the holy, drags it into profanation rather than partaking of the holiness of the holy. In this way, then, "If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned" may be clarified. As for "Be still," and also "His turning is to you, and you shall rule over him": "Be still," he says, "after the evil already done. Do not add sin to sin, and do not make the evil incurable by adding evil

to it. Rather, in calm and untroubled judgment keep silent for your part and grasp the greatness of the sin. For why do you [?] the reverence due to God into the madness of your own pleasure [?]? Become a man of repentance, and through sincere piety and right feeling make atonement for the offence, raising yourself up from the fall." As for "and you shall rule over it," one interpretation runs: "Your gift, which was not accepted, is not passed on to another, nor does its rejection bring you any loss; it returns to you again. You will have authority and lordship over it as before, suffering no loss from the offering except what the sin has damaged." If someone wishes to take the saying "and you shall rule over it" of the thing offered, he will find some such explanation. But if, by another approach, it is taken of Abel, who both divided rightly and offered his gift rightly and drew acceptance from above, the interpretation would proceed as follows. "You have lost nothing," he says, "of the privileges of your birth because your brother's sacrifice was preferred; nor has any penalty come upon you for your bad division to drag down the standing you had in life before. You were not made to forfeit your birthright for your offence, nor condemned to be subject to your brother; the rights of your birth remain yours, and the dignity of the firstborn's honour. And your brother's turning will be to you. That is, when harm approaches him he will set you before himself as his refuge and helper, and you will have rule over him, as far as the firstborn is granted it. Only be still after your offences. Do not bring into life the tragedy of an unpardonable offence, and do not strive to make the birthright of your birth the firstborn of the greatest and most destructive fault. Otherwise you will deprive yourself of everything that nature granted you through the Creator's love for mankind, of the good things in which, by repenting, you would have flourished, and of the enjoyment throughout your life of the manifold benefactions of providence."

Question 72. What would you say of the words of the divine Paul: "And Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and came into transgression; yet she will be saved through childbearing," and so on? How is "the woman will be saved through childbearing" [to be understood]?

Paul, who became all things to all, had laid down that the woman must be subject to her husband and must learn rather than attempt to teach, and from many other considerations he showed that this exhortation is both just and beneficial. Here too he gives a reason: "because," he says, "the man was formed before the woman." Then comes the greater reason: "And Adam was not deceived, but the woman." She snatched at the bait, was pierced on the hook of deceit, and passed on to her husband the blow and the harm it caused. Teaching is therefore unsuitable for a woman, for when she took it upon herself to teach, she cast the founder of our race out of paradise. For this reason it is said that Adam was not

deceived. First, because it was not he but Eve who, after the serpent, became the enemy's first instrument and led the way in the deception. Second, because he did not himself receive the deceitful and flattering words of the serpent, and was not persuaded that the compassionate Master and Provider begrudged them both their other happiness and their deification. It was Eve who seized on this lawless counsel against the Creator with both ear and will, ate of the forbidden tree, and invited her husband to the same table. He, thinking, as one would expect, that food vouched for by his wife excelled in sweetness and pleasure, and that his helper was urging him toward what was advantageous and beneficial, partook of the plant and fell into transgression. So for this reason too it could be said, not unreasonably, that Adam was not deceived. For many who commit the same abominable deed, but not with the same or a similar intention, are very different. The one who turns aside to the worse through deliberation and discernment and contempt of the better, and chooses the base part, makes his offence unpardonable. The one guilty of none of these, who merely slipped into sharing the deed, can draw mercy from many quarters and need not be driven away from pardon. So it is here too. Eve, having sharpened her thoughts by deliberation and by slandering the commandment, went over to the opposite side "bare-headed," as the saying goes. Adam outraged the law he had been given in none of these ways; he was merely dragged into its transgression. For these reasons, then, it might be said that Adam was not deceived. It might be said no less because he obeyed a voice of his own kind and familiar to him, one that had in many things proved not at all misleading. She, on the other hand, was found to be the slave of a foreign voice, one not even accustomed to enter into conversation, and became the prey of its wickedness. So the saying that Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and came into transgression, admits this reason as well. For both transgressed, but here too the woman's transgression was [greater?]. Indeed she was found guilty of a double transgression: her own, and the one into which she pushed her husband. What then will someone who champions the female nature say to me? "[What has] Eve's deception and transgression [to do with us], [?] that, although the nature of man and woman is one and equal, we have been condemned to take second place, always to hold the rank of learners, and to be wholly deprived of teaching?" To such a person the argument that follows would reply: just as, when Adam was condemned to mortality, death passed to all who came from him, so too, since the woman was not only deceived but also came into transgression, and indeed led her husband into the graver sin on both counts, the race that succeeds her is neither wholly released from the charge nor seen to be brought by a change to a better condition. That Adam was not deceived has, I think, been clarified through these points, and not carelessly. But there are some who take the phrase in the opposite sense. They say Adam was not deceived, not because he sinned less than the woman, but because he sinned more, and they claim that the Apostle too used

the phrase in this way. For she, enticed by stealthy and sweetened words, was carried into disregarding the command, whereas he embraced it rather by judgment and will. Nor is the woman [?] to have deceived him with words in the way she herself was deceived. She even rose up to contradict the serpent, and then, melted by the greatness of the promise, gave way to the deception. With Adam neither of these things happened. He neither contradicted the woman nor was he carried away by the greatness of any promise; yet he was found no less ready to partake of the food than she was to share it. So he might fittingly be understood to have fallen into transgression not through deception but rather through desire for the food. Well, if this argument has a place elsewhere, let it keep it; here it has no entry. For the herald of the truth, by placing Adam above the woman, preferring him to her and urging her to subjection, showed that his exhortation has irresistible force on account of Adam's not having been deceived, just as it does through his other arguments. Thus, I think, it has been clarified in what way Adam was not deceived. As for "the woman will be saved through childbearing," this means the nature of women; that is why the saying changed "Eve" into "the woman." Some say that by "childbearing" the Apostle meant the care and zeal devoted to children, through which the children themselves, established in faith and love, will achieve sanctification and self-control, while the mothers who train them in virtue will clearly be practising and accomplishing the same things, and so dissolve the charge of the transgression. This is what the teacher of the world said: "She will be saved through childbearing." For the training of children, and a God-pleasing provision and care for them, is by its nature a great righteous deed, able to undo Eve's misleading teaching of Adam. "Did I teach my husband wrongly? But I bring up and nourish my children rightly. Does that condemn me? How would this not, especially before a just and loving judge, be a ground of pardon, and, as a good deed set beside the fault, release me from the penalty?" Therefore the female nature, by holding fast to this childbearing and being zealous for it, dissolves and lays aside the charge and penalty that came from the deception. That the Apostle is accustomed to call the saving care of children "childbearing" and "bringing up children" is clear from the following. When he admits women who have lost their husbands to the order, honour and support of widows, he says, "Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old." Then he states what she must contribute as the price of such a rank: "if she has brought up children," he says, "if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has relieved the afflicted." And see how he has ranked and counted zeal for children and their training in virtue together with the service and welcome of the saints and the splendid achievement of almsgiving. These, then, understand "bringing up children" and "childbearing" in this way

Perhaps, though, it is not amiss to take as "childbearing" the following: piety conceives right reason and brings forth, through pure and undefiled birth pangs, the offspring of good works and upright deeds, and multiplies it as a truly most noble progeny, through which every earlier defect is restored. Indeed, the women who are delivered of such birth pangs have borne many sons and daughters. In this kind of adoption the barren woman too is known to bear seven, and to surpass the one who was renowned for her many children. These women also apply to themselves, in a manner more fitting to God and more proper, the words "Be fruitful and multiply," and show the Lord's blessing flourishing in themselves. Such childbearing does not limit the undoing of the deception to women who bear children through union with a man. It extends the correction of the fault to the other women as well, and especially to virgins. For all on whom the ancestral defect had spread are saved through such childbearing. They cast off the shame and burden of the deception by splendid righteous deeds, and they multiply the children of the Church by their own offspring. Shining with faith and love and the sanctification that comes through self-control, they lead those who look on them and consider the beauty of their works to glorify the Father in heaven. In this way these interpreters, not badly, I think, draw the letter up to contemplation. Others, however, more reverently and more fittingly for God, take the childbearing to mean the birth of our Savior from the Virgin, through which childbearing not the impiety of women [?] and [?]

Question 73 [72]. How should we understand the words "Whoever eats this bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," and what follows?

1. The partaking of the Lord's body and

blood is a kind of spiritual food that strengthens the powers of the soul. Since it is offered to a living being made of soul and body, it too holds spiritual grace and sanctification within a bodily substance. So when it passes through the mouth into the hidden chambers of our nature, it is distributed through the whole living being and sanctifies the whole of it. Or rather, it lavishes the working of grace and sanctification on the soul itself and on the mind. Those who are about to enjoy this sacred and spiritual food, then, must not be ignorant of its power, or of the benefit and gift, surpassing all understanding, that is given through it. It is this: the pre-eternal Word, who was in the beginning, who was with God and was God, the creator of our nature, borrowed flesh from virginal blood. He who is rich in divinity deigned to become man for our sake and dwelt among us. He who was in the form of God took the form of a servant, and in his one hypostasis he preserved the boundaries of each nature unconfused and undivided. So he emptied himself for us without being emptied. Having become like us in all things except sin, he did more than go on doing good and healing our infirmities. Even when he was blasphemed and met with ingratitude, he did not hold back the abundance of his gifts, which are beyond reason. Though he endured insults and mockery from those he was helping, he did not turn away from his ineffable love for humankind. He even bore the cross and death, in order to free those who insulted him from death and corruption, and through his own resurrection to refashion our mortal and corruptible nature and raise it up to immortality and incorruption.

2. As a pledge and foundation of all these good things he laid down the partaking of his own body and blood, so that by sharing in it we might believe that we have within ourselves the first beginnings of the heavenly and immortal life. For the Truth in person says, "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life," since by partaking of his immaculate flesh we become one body with him and are counted worthy of incorruption and immortality. So whoever turns his thoughts to these things, stands firm in them and goes over the wealth of his benefits clearly ought to make himself pure and free of evil deeds when he is about to partake of this mystical and undefiled food. He is about to receive into the chambers of his soul, through the presence of his body, the King and Master of all, who mingles with us in an ineffable way and with a love for humankind beyond comprehension, and grows together with our body. But suppose someone has not first cleansed himself of the defilements and passions that ruin and pollute both soul and body, and approaches the mystical and immortalizing table with a filthy life and filthy thoughts to partake of it. Such a person partakes

of none of the grace. A rotten vessel cannot hold ointment, and a pearl is not entrusted to the mud. By insulting and dishonoring what is beyond not only insult but even honor, this man has made himself liable to a judgment from which there is no appeal. For he has outraged the Lord's body, which the audacity of the Jews had already outraged by hanging it on a cross. That is why the one who burns and is weak on behalf of those who stumble and are weak in the faith, setting out the magnitude of the sin, was not content to say once that such a person is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. He testified a second time that whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and [drinks] judgment on himself.

3. This is what he said, the beholder of things unseen and the speaker and teacher of things unspeakable: whoever dares to eat and drink it unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. For why should I do this? It is possible to cleanse myself and scour off my defilements by repentance, and so approach the most pure One, or rather the One who pours forth cleansing beyond all thought. Yet I take no care to weigh this in my thoughts and pursue it. Instead, so as to seem pure to onlookers and worthy of so great a grace and enjoyment, I insult my own salvation and do not shudder to make sport of things into which angels long to look. Truly, those who receive glory from one another neither seek the glory that comes from the only God nor believe in the greatness of the mystery. Our Creator, who loves humankind, counted us worthy of things beyond reason, unworthy as we were. We have been counted worthy of these things and of being called one body with him and sharers in him, if indeed we are willing to receive strength and grace and rise to so great a height of dignity. If, then, we do not make ourselves pure with all diligence, how can we avoid making ourselves liable to a double condemnation? The first is that we rejected so great an abundance of good things when we could have gained them, and deprived ourselves of so great a benefit and of salvation. This alone, even without any further penalty, is the greatest condemnation, as the Lord also said: "Whoever does not believe in the Son is already judged." That is, he already has his punishment. What is it? The very fact of not believing in him. The second is that we despised the gift, insulted the grace and treated the benefactor with contempt, using the mystical food, which makes us one body with his immaculate body, as if it were an ordinary table. Such people, then, are in no better state than the Jews who dared that dreadful and unthinkable deed, hanging the life-giving body of Christ on the wood and draining it of its blood with the spear. That is why the teacher of the whole world rightly condemned such people as guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

Question 74 [?]. The Lord said to the Samaritan woman: "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews," and what follows. By what approach shall we grasp the force of these venerable words?

The Samaritan woman was putting all her effort into exalting the Samaritan belief and ranking it above the customs and doctrines of the Jews. That is why, when the Savior promised to give her living water, she retorted, "Are you greater than our father Jacob?" The Savior knew how to manage everything wisely. He was well aware that exalting the Jewish ways and calling himself the greater one straight away would at once strike the mind of a woman held by a prejudice to the contrary, who as yet could imagine nothing higher than the things of the senses. So he stored this up in silence. Besides, it would have been petty and unworthy of the majesty of Jesus even to declare that the master is greater than the servant. For in a comparison of master with servant, the difference tends rather to dignify the servant with second place while it magnifies the master with the first.
