So he leaves these things to silence and sets out his meaning in other words, which could establish the point no less well while avoiding pettiness, and were better suited to soothe the hearer. He does not himself bring in the comparison or the difference in glory. He leaves the woman to infer the vastness of his superiority from what he is about to say. "For whoever drinks of this water," he says, "will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again." See the wisdom and force of these words. "Will thirst again" needed no proof from elsewhere, since he had the woman herself as a witness who had come of her own accord. "Will never thirst again," by the greatness of what it announces, rouses her to long for the promise. Through both he leads her to consider a more divine understanding, all but saying: If you hold Jacob in high honor and regard it as a marvelous achievement that he gave you water, though whoever drinks it returns to the same thirst, what must you think of me, who am able to give water

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople.

that does not merely ease bodily thirst for a short time, but can become in the one who drinks it a spring of ever-flowing water, and can provide streams of salvation that water those who draw from them and win for them eternal life? "For the water that I will give," he says, "will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." Water cures thirst and cleanses the body of outward defilement. In the same way the spiritual and human [?] streams of Jesus' teaching, and the more divine understanding of him, put an end [?] to the thirst that comes from unbelief, which has consumed all the vital, sustaining moisture of the mind's activity. They also cleanse the soul of the filth with which the defilement of sins and the gloomy reasoning of impious opinions have soiled it. So the Savior handled, in this extraordinary way, his answer to the question that made Jacob seem to hold first place and to be magnified. See how its effect flashes forth at once. It immediately enlightened the woman's mind and brought her to believe the promise, startling as it was, and to grasp that the Lord is far greater than her forefathers. Leaving behind in her mind the water of her father Jacob, she hurries toward this water and says, "Sir, give me this water." Why do you disdain the ancestral water? "Because it stops thirst for a little while, yet lets one thirst again just the same, and it brings me toil." "So that I may not thirst," she says, "or come here to draw." Enjoying your spring, I shall no longer need the ancestral well. Her mind was now illuminated in this way. So when he also spoke to her about the men with whom she had welcomed fellowship in secret and rather [?] relations, she at once proclaimed him a prophet. Yet she asks him nothing about everyday matters. She does not seek to learn or receive any of the things that sustain the body or concern it. Instead she stirs up an old question and rises to learn its solution by asking. "Our fathers," she says, "worshiped on this mountain." By "fathers" she means [?] Abraham, for an ancient account relates that Abraham offered up his son on that mountain. Then she says: "And you say that Jerusalem is the place where one must worship." Two forms of worship, she says, and two places of worship, each an altar and sacred precinct for the service of God. Which of them, then, does better, the Samaritan or the Jew? Here too the Savior, who loves humankind, answers the woman who was seeking the solution of a lesser question

by bestowing a far greater grace. He teaches a more divine doctrine, leading her up from her love of argument to contemplation fit for a philosopher. For he says, "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth." It is as if he said: You ask whether the Jewish belief or the Samaritan view carries off the prize as the more honorable and divine. But I am revealing to you a hidden mystery: "The hour is coming, and now is, when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem." Through the Savior's words the woman passed to philosophy more quickly than a woman usually would. She was no longer eager, as she had been at first, to show that her own ways were perhaps to be preferred to those of the Israelites. She was yielding, improved by the saving teaching, and sought to learn what was better. That is why she says, "Our fathers worshiped on this mountain," for this was what most raised and exalted the standing of the Samaritans' belief. Since a prophet was present, inspired by the Spirit to discern what is hidden from others, she sought to learn from him which belief was truer and more perfect. That is also why, when she began on the subject, she said, "Sir, I see that you are a prophet." Jesus, who loves humankind, first foretells the end of both forms of worship, so as not to grieve her by preferring the Jewish worship. For why should she be distressed that a worship was preferred to her own belief, when it was shortly to come to the same end? Then he states the difference between them: "For you worship what you do not know; we worship what we know." How did the Samaritans not know what they worshiped? On the one hand, not a few of the inhabitants had been brought back from captivity among the Babylonians, still living by the customs of that place and corrupted in the Israelite religion. On the other hand, the bulk of them were of Babylonian and Median race and worship and had been resettled in Samaria. They regarded the God of the Jews as the local god of that land from of old, holding oversight and lordship over that nation alone. So while they offered worship to him, they did not on that account stop serving the demons. The Jewish nation, though not as a whole, at least those of them who chose to remember the Mosaic laws rather than forget them, were entirely free of this abominable notion. They acknowledged the God they worshiped as the creator of all creation, and likewise as its overseer and provider. That is why he says, "We worship what we know; you worship what you do not know." He says "we worship" because he counts himself among the Jews, for he did not yet

Colb.: "only."

let all the rays of the divinity within him flash forth. That is why he asked for water to drink, endured weariness from walking, and relieved the weariness of the journey by using the ground as a makeshift seat. Moreover, he was speaking with a woman who had formed a reverent opinion of him, but who still took him for one of the prophets and for a Jew, dearer to God and holier than others. This, then, is why "we worship" was said. One difference has now been stated, the one by which Jewish worship surpassed the religion of the Samaritans. What is the other? "Salvation," he says, "is from the Jews." How is salvation from the Jews? Is it because, when the error of idols was spreading over the human race everywhere, the knowledge of God shone from there upon other people, and because the very fact that the Samaritans worship God at all began with the Jews? Or rather, we may understand the salvation that came forth from the Jews as the coming of Christ himself, the recall of the human race through him from the ancient fall, and its restoration, no longer to be stolen and corrupted by the plots and envy of enemies. And "the hour is coming, and now is" indicates what follows surely and swiftly. It is as if he said: The prophetic oracles reached their fulfillment at a later time, but it is not so here. The word spoken about me is already present and already at hand, bringing with it the testimony of the works.

Question 75. How is the Divine said to be in the universe, and how can we resolve the difficulties that some raise against [?] this proposition?

Many of the sacred contemplations about God, not to say all of them, have shown by experience something about those outside our doctrine, who were not initiated into the mysteries of piety, even though they surpassed their peers in strength of mind and in knowledge of material things. In their case, the power of contemplation proved weaker than its own grasp [?]. Not only that, but even for those whom the doctrine of piety and purity of life appointed to discern the deeper things, the discovery of the more divine truths does not usually come easily. And why do I speak of discovery, when even the inquiry itself does not proceed for them purely and as reason requires? This inquiry too, being for the most part more subtle and set above the minds of the curious, is eager to be recognized [?]. So what is about to be said must not be heard as though it had grasped the matter with complete precision and left nothing more for the understanding of the subject. Rather, as far as possible, we should kindly hear and accept those who, with all reverence and with anguish, apply human thoughts to things beyond human apprehension. The Divine, then, is in the universe, which is the question you put forward for us to examine together, but not as any being is among beings. Otherwise what is above all beings

would be one of the beings, and the one who brought forth and created all things would be counted as one of the things he created. For this is what follows from a communion with the creative principle that is of the same kind and the same rank as the relation among beings, whenever someone insists that beings relate to one another in exactly the same way as the Creator relates to his creatures. Therefore the Divine is not joined to its creations, nor does it come down to them, as one of the beings. It is distinguished by a disposition and an economy of its own, and adapts its relation to beings accordingly. The Divine is wise and at the same time beyond wisdom, mighty God and beyond God, being in the proper sense and beyond being, likewise goodness itself and beyond goodness. In the same way it is said to exist both in the universe and above the universe. For in the case of the ineffable, many-named and supernatural nature alone, the affirmative form of names carries a meaning that agrees with the formulations that express the intent through negative or privative terms. So "in all" is not a denial of "above all" but rather its harmony and confirmation. Nor, for that matter, does "above all" acquire any departure from the mystical theology more wondrous than what the contemplation sacredly expressed in the words "in the universe" conveys. So whoever is puzzled whether the Divine, if it is in the universe, could not be above the universe has failed to notice his own ignorance of how the sacred words are used of that nature. He imagines nothing higher or more divine about immaterial things than our ordinary talk about material things. But how is it in the universe? It has been said: in no way as any of the beings. If, however, we must not shrink from the height of more contemplative doctrines, the Divine is in everything both by activity and by essence. Do not ask me how. It has been said already: in no way as any of the beings. How, then, is it in things by essence? In the same way as you understood it to be there by activity. Other things are sometimes in potency and sometimes in act. But the Divine, as a discerning mind would perceive, is always act. It does not advance from imperfection to perfection, and its very essence is nothing other than its very activity. Clearly, then, it is present by essence in the same things in which it is present by activity. For it acts by holding beings together and preserving them, and it gives being to and sustains the nature of the things it created. How, then, is the Divine in the universe essentially, and yet no single co-essence and nature [?] is formed from them? Because even when you think of it as being in the universe by activity, and say so, not even then will there be anything complete and having the character of a nature. Nothing will be able to fulfill the requirement in full, that is, to come together, from the universe and from the divine and higher nature, with something else into one self-complete hypostasis. And how could what exists in something by essence (for it seems reasonable to ask this further) [not] be thought of as completing one hypostasis together with it? But this is not hard to resolve. "To exist in something by essence" is said in two senses. One of its meanings, in the

[?] it shows: to become part of the compound and to complete the perfection of the hypostasis, as the soul does for the body. The other, however, could never become part of the mixture. Nor is it exchanged in its properties, as though what is proper to each of the natures were made common. Nor is it completed by either of the things combined. Rather, its coming together constitutes and preserves the conjoined and self-complete hypostasis, in the way that (to use a very brief image taken from ready experience) the helmsman's art stands to the ship. These things, however, are not set out by a dogmatic and unshakeable argument, as the arrangement of the preface has already shown. They are sketched by an argument that conjectures and exercises the mind. Still, let them stand until something better comes to light.

What is meant by the saying of the Lord to the [? disciples] in the Gospel: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand"?

The saying whose meaning you have asked to learn is recorded by the four evangelists, and it was foretold by Isaiah the prophet. Three of them weave the saying in by way of paraphrase, in their own words, while the divine Matthew introduces it as a citation, in the form of testimony. For when Isaiah was found worthy to become a beholder of the Lord's glory, and his lips were cleansed with the coal by one of the seraphim, he then also heard that divine voice saying: "Go, and say to this people: Hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have shut their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them." These prophetic words, which are taken up and used in the Gospels, show the obstinacy of the Jews of that time. No less do they foretell those of them who later stamped themselves in their likeness and were not persuaded by the Savior's teaching, when with wondrous works and supernatural words he put both their hearing and their sight to the test: the one willingly deaf, the other blind with the rheum of unbelief. And neither to so great

a benefit from his words were they willing to open their hearing, nor did they wish to unfold their eyes to such godly radiance of miracles. Therefore the prophet too testifies that their deafness and blindness came about from nowhere else than from their own wickedness, when he says, "The heart of this people has grown dull." And since they had made their heart dull, for this reason they also heard heavily with their ears and shut their eyes. Then, to show that they did not even wish to recover from their self-inflicted maiming, he adds: "Lest they should ever see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them." So they grew dull in heart, and for this reason they heard heavily and shut their eyes. And they shut their eyes and made their ears heavy, lest they should ever see with their eyes and hear with their ears. They willingly submitted to the maiming of these organs so that they might not turn and obtain healing of such great afflictions. In this way the prophet plainly attaches the cause of the blindness and deafness to the mind and choice of the Jews. He by no means brings in a decree of God inflicting these things on the Jews. The prophet was pillorying the obstinate among the Jews of that time. He said that they were unwilling either to open their eyes or to lend their ears to hear what concerned their salvation and the godly teaching. Instead, because of the sins they habitually committed, above all conceit and boastfulness and leaning toward error rather than piety, they closed their eyes and stopped up their hearing, and so made themselves blind and deaf. And, what is worse, in this condition they thought they saw better than others, and were inflamed with the passion of self-conceit. For they seemed learned in the Law, and they carried the words of the prophets about on their lips, which made the charge against them all the heavier. In this way they made their disease incurable. Hence the Savior, after he had shown the man blind from birth seeing, and they had set their God-fighting tongues moving to insult instead of to offer sacrifice, says: "For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." And when the Pharisees retorted, "Are we blind too?", he says, "If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now that you say, 'We see,' your sin remains." For the one who knows that he is blind from ignorance recognizes his affliction. He goes all the more quickly to the physician, seeks the enjoyment of the light, and hastens toward it. For this reason he is found worthy of the loving providence, and is illumined by its radiant beams

in his mind and led up to saving contemplation. But the one who is darkened by hardness of heart and yet thinks he sees has brought a double blindness on himself: first because he does not see, and second because, though he does not see, he thinks he sees more sharply than others. For self-conceit, being a deep darkness over the eyes of the soul, only intensifies the disease of the dimness that already held them. Now that the prophetic words have been examined in this way and the holy oracles clarified in this way (even if some part of them has not been included in the clarification), the saying will no longer, I think, give the hearers the same occasion for inquiry, or so great a one. For it is clear that it was given to the disciples to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, since they neither grew dull in heart, nor heard heavily, nor closed their eyes. But to the rest, whom he also calls "those outside" (for they had placed themselves outside salvation), it is no longer given. Since they had walled themselves off from all salvation and benefit through the passions described, it is reasonably not given to them, because they had not made themselves fit to receive it. That is why it was fitting to speak in parables rather than set forth the mysteries of grace bare. For it is neither profitable nor a mark of impartial judgment to place the worthy and the unworthy in the same rank of teaching and salvation, just as one should not throw pearls before swine or cast holy things to dogs. From what has been said, then, the words "so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand" also find a way to being understood. For "so that" is here akin to "because", and the one is naturally taken in place of the other. Likewise "not" here holds the place of a negation, not a prohibition. That it is more than conjecture to take the words this way here has an incontestable witness in the meaning of the prophetic words, from which the Lord's sayings also proceeded. The holy Matthew is a witness too: with the same sense in mind he used "because" instead of "so that", and reported the passage as a negation instead of a prohibition. For he introduces the Lord saying: "This is why I speak in parables, because seeing they do not see." So it has become plain that the "so that" in the other evangelists is used for "because", and that the prohibitive particle has taken on the force of the negative one. In this way the Jewish nation took on as its own the madness and obstinacy of their forefathers, and counted it gain to deprive themselves of the Master's teaching and benefit. For it was not so much the springs of their bodily descent that they traced back to those forefathers

as their hardness of heart and the ingratitude of their minds. The Israel of old crossed the wet waves of the sea on foot. A pillar of fire and of cloud made their road free of hardship. The one kindled a torch by night and at the same time led the ungrateful people by the hand. The other sheltered them from the painful blaze of the sun, in place of the roof of a house, and made the day of their journey a day of gladness. In short, though they enjoyed benefits beyond reason and were overflowing and fattened with all the good things of life, they kicked back instead, and raged into insult against the Divine, exchanging faith in the Creator for the worship of idolatrous defilements. And those who sprang from that mind no less than from that stock acted in the same way at the coming of our Savior. They became spectators of similar [?] supernatural miracles being performed: now incurable bodily afflictions were driven out by a word, now his creature was set free from demonic harm and plotting; wounds of the soul were healed by his teaching, and the good news was proclaimed that the power of Death was already being put to death. They were found worthy of many other gifts and benefits besides. Yet they had no mind to perceive any of these things or to repay their benefactor. They were roused only to use their God-fighting tongues. They seized the dignity of those who see and hear and put it on themselves. Yet they would not hear the Master's words, which called them to salvation more loudly than a trumpet, gathered many of the nations to it, and taught the knowledge of the truth. Nor were they willing to see the miracles performed before their eyes. They armed both their minds and their tongues for blasphemy alone. Therefore it was only reasonable that the mysteries of the kingdom were not entrusted to them. Apart from the other reasons, a greater condemnation would have come upon them had they been entrusted with them. For the greater the gifts a person is found worthy of, if he turns toward the worse instead of changing for the better, the more he is liable to a double condemnation: for his prior wickedness, and for the choice that made the benefit an occasion for increasing his depravity. That it was not by allotment that the disciples were given to know the mysteries and the others were not has already been shown. The Savior establishes it no less himself when he calls the disciples blessed because they see, and hearing they hear. For a beatitude, in the Scriptures and especially in the Lord's sayings, does not come from a necessity that imposes what cannot be escaped; it comes from the choice of the better. ("Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly"; and [Editor's note: … μιασμάτων for βιασμάτων. I write ἀμείψασθαι for ἀμείνασθαι, unless you prefer ἀμεί-]

"Blessed is the man who has pity on the lives of his beasts.") And the Savior, joining many beatitudes one after another, assigns none of them to things in which allotment holds sway. He gathers them all upon those whose virtue is the fruit and harvest of their own choice. So it was not by allotment that the disciples were given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, nor was ignorance of them so given to these obstinate Jews. Rather, because they willingly made themselves blind and deaf, the divine and impartial judgment showed them to be unworthy of these mysteries. How, then, the beloved disciple, the instrument of theology, can say, "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart" is no hard task to understand from what has already been said. If he did not call Isaiah as a witness to his statement, or if he brought forward the same words on another subject, there would be some ground for perplexity, and a search for some other solution beyond those already given. But these words too are brought forward from the prophetic passage, whose meaning has shone out most clearly and brings no perplexity, and whatever was disputed in the other evangelists has also been settled. So it is clear that whatever was going to be puzzled over in these words has also been resolved in advance. For the first to record the Master's deeds can equally [?] explain "he has blinded" and "he has hardened" through the words, "This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear." But suppose someone takes "he has blinded" and "he has hardened" not as afflictions that came first but rather as ones that followed, a kind of recompense for what had gone before. He too would not miss the mark, and this would bring him not far from the truth. For since they willingly shut their eyes and stopped their ears, those afflictions came first. Blindness and deafness then became a penalty for them, following on the willfulness of their wicked minds, and part of that penalty would be that it was not given to them to know the mysteries of the kingdom. One may also hear Jesus saying a little earlier, as the son of thunder himself wrote: "The light is with you a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you"; and, "Whoever walks in the darkness does not know where he is going." For the true light shone when the Savior of the world came. But they would not fix their gaze on it, nor walk in the radiant [Editor's note: … it reads: "The righteous man has pity on the lives of his beasts." (17) In the manuscript thus: "For equally the first," etc. There]

[? light] of his teachings. Therefore, as a consequence, darkness overtook them, exacting the penalty for the wickedness that had already taken hold of them. And this could rightly be called being blinded and hardened. Just as the one who chose to walk in the light also knows where he is going, so the one who refused to walk in the light ends up walking in darkness and wretchedly travelling the road of the blind and the hardened. It has also been said before that the lightning flash of the Master's saving teaching pilloried the Jews as blind and hardened, and made the rheum and sightlessness already present in the eyes of their souls all the more manifest and evident. For just as this [? visible] and most beautiful sun, sending out the bright rays of its disk, exposes those whose eyes are diseased, so too the intelligible sun, the light that never sets and knows no evening, Christ our God, came to dwell in the world. Through godly miracles beyond reason he flashed out the splendor of his divinity, and so exposed all the more the darkness and sightlessness that already gripped the eyes of the soul of the obstinate Jews. Yet the sun in the world is not the cause of blindness when it exposes the sightlessness of those who have the disease. In the same way the supramundane and intelligible sun, the exact and true radiance of the Father, when he pillories the existing blindness of those caught in the affliction, could by no means be thought its cause, even if he might be said to have blinded them. For the darkened state of their reasonings rather made a public show of a maiming that was not hidden even before. If the brilliance of the divine light had not flashed out so greatly that even the minds of the nations sitting in darkness and shadow were lit up and recovered their sight to know God, the Jewish race would not have been shown to be so blind. But the overwhelming excess of the radiance that went forth through his works, the operation of his illuminating power, and the recovery of sight among the nations became a clear proof against those who did not run to the light of truth and were not illumined to piety. It proved that they had brought their blindness upon themselves willingly, and [?] the salvation of the whole world out of surpassing madness

QUESTION 77. Various problems concerning genus and species, in which their solutions may be found.

1. The subject of genera and species has often been investigated by us, and the settling of the old

disputes has gone forward, leaving nothing unresolved, as it seemed to those who were inquiring together at the time. The Platonic Ideas received a special examination, since they cannot even be predicated of individuals. I will not now argue that to presuppose types and likenesses of things yet to be produced belongs to a craftsman, but to one too weak to create what he wills by a simple act. Nor will I argue that, on this view, seeking patterns for the things that exist necessarily carries the procession of things formed on to infinity. The first is wholly unworthy of our conception of the Divine. The second, taken by itself, brings with it the abolition of the things fashioned in thought. But even if one should grant that particular things receive from there the impress of the types of each property, one will find no consistent argument for bringing them under predication by those types. For what is sealed would not be the seal, nor is what has received a likeness by participation the same as what provides the likeness. Nor could the things in the divine [?] mind, which enjoy an unmoved and unshakeable stability (if they exist there at all), ever be said to be predicated of things that are forever borne along in flux and outflow. The difference is very great, and it appears even from the very relation that provides some kind of connection. For the principle of cause and effect, especially when it operates in the creative and exemplary mode, plainly shows a difference of existence within the conjunction of the relation. Now in cases where the things signified seem to be joined by the likeness of their names, this relation still makes the distance between them admittedly great. How then could things be brought together into one when they offer no word of connection and give no occasion to show union, since they are not of a nature to come together, not even where a connection could keep its own proper due [?] unadulterated? With such considerations the Platonic Ideas were examined, and many older arguments also bore on our purpose.

2. The genera and species other than the Platonic Ideas, even if they had their origin and arose from a different notion and approach, do differ in their constitution. Those who philosophized more elegantly were keen to call some of them "after the many" and others "in the many". But as regards being predicated, they differ little in their use, and so the same testing and discrimination by means of examining arguments sufficed for each of them. As for incorporeal hypostases, there was not even an ancient dispute, and it was quickly agreed that the genera and species predicated of them also share in the incorporeal nature. But much contention arose about the three-dimensional hypostases, which are bodies and are called bodies: must their genera and species be called bodies, or should they be placed in the domain of the incorporeal, as being superior to sense perception? At that time, however, these questions were discussed with precision, and the hearers did not think they needed a second inquiry. But since your

holiness has now seen fit to request that a summary outline of these matters be put out in writing, nothing prevents us from treating the same matters briefly.

3. The definitions of incorporeal things, at least those that define the subject, are clearly incorporeal. So too are the genera and species contained in them, and examining them would raise no difficulty for anyone. But how could the definitions of bodies be bodies, even if the ready analogy suggests it? For definition and body have refused any communion with each other. And if a definition is by nature something other than a body, how will the genera and species that complete the definition not demand the same otherness? And how could the incorporeal be predicated of bodies? Or rather, the genera of these would not be incorporeal, nor would the species. Yet they would not be bodies either, for they are not subject to bulk or to matter, in which the fullness of dimensions subsists. They are, however, wholly corporeal and are said of body, for they interpret and announce a body as their subject. Thus "man" is corporeal, because it names Socrates or Plato, who is a body, and by unfolding their essence it distinguishes them by name from things of the same genus. But if man is not a body, and Socrates is a man, how will it not be concluded that Socrates is not a body? This, and any similar problem, seems to be the strongest of the difficulties. Yet it is not hard to resolve. For anyone willing to look, the major premise in the first figure is taken as indefinite; put forward in this way it does not depart from the truth. But if one converts it into a universal, it changes along with it from truth to falsehood. For it is plainly false to say, "No man is a body," since, according to the argument stated earlier, it is true that man is a body. Someone might bid farewell to the logical structure and not think it wise to busy himself with drawing a syllogistic [?] conclusion. He might say outright that it is crude either to say or to think that man is a body, even without [?] concluding that Socrates would not be a body. How the division of substance into body and incorporeal could then go forward as the primary things distinguished from each other is a matter to be considered later. Meanwhile let the argument not depart from the sequence of what has been said. For what has been said applies to such predicates not only in the negative figure but also in the affirmative, for those who wish to put forward a conclusive argument to strengthen the difficulty. Suppose we say, "Man, or animal, is corporeal," and then, "Socrates is an animal, or a man." Would we not be compelled to call Socrates [?] corporeal too? For this is the conclusion drawn, while the major premise here too remains true, since the premise is put forward as particular. But if it were raised to the universal form, it would immediately be detected

[?] …presents the falsehood. For how could one say, "Every man, or every animal, is corporeal," when the proposition "No man and no animal is corporeal" is expressly true? Further, how could those things not be corporeal which the underlying body makes known? And how could it be estranged from the corporeal name and constitution? It stands apart from the incorporeal nature, and it has withdrawn from corporeal properties. What lot among beings could it then fall to, if someone were to place it beyond even the bounds of the corporeal? But if anyone wishes to look at the matter another way, he will find the difficulties no less easy to resolve. Socrates is a man, or an animal, in himself. But man, or animal, is corporeal not in itself, not from above and not by nature, but because it announces and indicates an underlying body and embraces its relation to that body. There is therefore no argument that requires Socrates to be called corporeal. Such an argument is woven out of premises of different kinds that do not resemble each other, so that they cannot even be called two parts of the same argument. Rather, one premise belongs perhaps [?] to one thing and the other to another, and they keep up their lack of anything in common. It is reasonable, then, that nothing could be concluded from such an alien interweaving and confusion. 4. But consider with me this further point as well, which is sharper than the one before us. Suppose that Socrates, who is both what is immediately predicated and what properly announces the subject, could not be required to share his own properties with what is signified. And this holds even though the major premise here, if one wishes to compose a syllogism, can somehow move into the universal figure. For no one will call the thing that the word "Socrates" signified something that announces or indicates the subject, [?] since he has no reasoning that slides away into harm [?]. If this is so, will not every argument all the more refrain from dragging the consequences of what is predicated through the mediation of Socrates, which are not predicated in themselves, onto Socrates as well, and from transferring them to him? 5. The division that splits substance into body and the incorporeal would not fall outside a theory that resolves the question, if one gives as the reason that it makes the cut with a view to the last and final subjects. Even if the work of division seems to proceed from above, reason still works busily from below. It brings the senses as helpers to its judgment and gathers from them an unerring knowledge of particulars for itself. Running up in this way to the more general theory, it looks down on the lower things as if from a lookout, with greater experience and wisdom, and so it brought forth the method of division. This method is evidently later than the one mentioned before, as is the one they like to call analytic. But other arguments could also be used on this point, for one can see that most people blink at this loftier and more philosophical account of causes. For many

things whose explanation goes deep refuse to fit themselves to people's ready ears and superficial minds. Such things naturally take up residence above all through methodical experience and leisurely judgment. When that is absent and there is no demonstration, the argument seems weak, turning the minds of the hearers toward itself [?]…

6. Some raise the difficulty that, if one grants that the genera and species of bodies are bodies, then three-dimensional extension [?] will follow for them, along with circumscription in place, being judged by the senses, body passing [?] through body, and anything else of this kind that the over-curious have pursued so eagerly. I might not unreasonably wonder at these people. They search into such matters and think their arguments serve their own purpose, so how is it that they did not say before everything else, "If genera and species are bodies and individuals, they will certainly be particulars too"? They did not blush to raise the properties of individual bodies up to the genera and species of those bodies. How, then, were they careful not to conclude the particular and individual as well, that is, Socrates or Plato, of the genera and species? Having once inverted the order of predicates and decided that the properties of the ultimate subjects should be predicated of the genera and species that are themselves predicated, they are justly liable to explain why they did not also try to predicate the particular and individual itself of the genera and species. They should also explain why they did not think they could refute those who hold that genera and species are bodies more effectively through this absurdity. For this is what the whole design of their clever arguments is aiming at. 7. But let these be dismissed as the leaps, I think, of youthful cleverness. It is youthful to dart about and to be eager to overturn the proposition before one. When the proposition escapes their grip, it draws to itself a firmer reputation for existing than it had before. Before it has been put to the test of contradiction, its strength is uncertain, because no refutations have yet been offered. But once people have tried to refute it, the pressure makes it stronger, and it gains much more than the reputation it had before, both of [?] and of truthfulness

8. Some say, "When the species and genera of bodies are taken in thought, they must be both considered and named incorporeal, but when they are fastened [?] onto the subjects, then it is proper to call and reckon them bodies." I would gladly ask these people whether they took them as incorporeal and then thought about them in that way, or whether they bestowed this nature on them in the very act of thinking. If they took them as incorporeal and changed nothing by thinking, the difficulty remains no less than before, and indeed more boldly. But if they took them as bodies and moved them over to the incorporeal, then bravo for their marvelous and so speedy craftsmanship! For concepts, insofar as

[they are concepts, are] entirely incorporeal. But who could transform bodies into the incorporeal by conceiving them? And do they fit them to the subjects just as they conceived them? Then how do they avoid predicating incorporeal things [?] of bodies? But if they fitted them to the subjects again just as they took them at the beginning, then the mind labored for them in vain, changing what cannot be changed and fashioning shapes of fantasy for us. Then again, they fit them, as they say, to the things themselves and for that reason do not take them away from bodies. Do they attach them by conceiving them, or do they improvise this conjunction idly and however it happens to occur to them? Either option, I think, is perilous. The first destroys its opposite, the claim that bodies change through thought into incorporeal substance. The second belongs to triflers and is laughable. 9. What, then, is the account that escapes all these traps? It was stated somewhat suggestively before, but let it now be said more clearly. The genera and species of bodies are corporeal, but they are not bodies. They indicate the subjects, but they are not the things indicated. They unfold the existence of the subjects, but do not give them subsistence. They announce the [?] of the parts within them, but do not supply it. They are names that signify the hypostases of the subjects through corresponding and appropriate concepts. They do not supply from themselves, to things that exist and are entirely self-sufficient, what those things do not need. The same is true of "good," "wise," "just," "benevolent" and similar predicates, even though some of them indicate an activity or passion of the subject, and others its existence and substantial being, or its passions and activities. Suppose each of the predicates in either of these classes brought from itself to the subjects a heap [?], either one conceived through bodies or one derived from the property of qualified things. Suppose each of them placed into the individuals ranked under a category either natures of bodies or, if you like, natures of incorporeals, and loaded them with additions. How would an opinion that accepts this differ from monstrous fabrications and phantoms? But someone may delight in the word "body" and, without departing from the corporeal concept, wish to call the genera and species that are said to be predicated of individual bodies "bodies." We will not quarrel with him. "Body" spoken in this way has cleanly escaped all the traps described above. And to humor, by conceding a word, the mind of someone who wishes to philosophize would not, I think, be considered unreasonable, where benevolence is the judge. 10. Such, then, in accordance with your request, is my summary sketch concerning the subordinate genera and species that are said to be predicated of individual bodies. It puts forward a theory, I think, no less elegant than the one the man whose allotted fatherland was Stagira, and who turned all Greece to sweet wonder at his wisdom, propounded about them. After much (26) Vat. reads μεταποιήσῃ. (28) Cat. reads πρὸς θήκας. [study] of genera and species

and practice, he called these "twitterings," as though he were eager to exact insult from them as a penalty for the many labors spent on them, and he also cast such a great pursuit away as worth nothing. However, the immediate and direct predication of the ten genera of the things ranked under them received a different and more precise examination. That predication also contains something deeper, I think, than the opinion and philosophy of the ancients. This examination took place while we were still occupied with dialectical studies, when our discourses were in labor with many children and brought them to light from a theory that had for a long time been [obscured?] by the devices of lawless men. So from that source and that training, what escaped the zeal of many before is now easier for those who philosophize as offspring of that sacred birth. And may those who come after us be able to say, with just reason, of a [theory] flourishing and in its bloom [?], something far from boasting and indeed not deserving reproach.

QUESTION 78. Difficulties and solutions of polemical and dogmatic sacred questions, from the second oration On the Son of Gregory the Theologian. (variant: [?])

1. I did not think it right that you should seek to learn the meaning of the Fathers' words. Your age, your diligence in logical method and your study of the sacred Scriptures set you above others as a teacher of many fine lessons. Children who love their father, even when they already discern accurately by themselves what is to be done, still look to their fathers because they wish to lean on paternal counsel. In the same way, though you are quite able to resolve the logical disputes that arise, you nevertheless judged it right to look to our [judgment?]. So I thought it best not to slight your filial love, and I chose no less to honor the affection due to children. That is why the extreme difficulty of the times and the lack of scribes had less power to force me to act against your request. 2. The question put to you [?] is clear and, I think, needs no interpretation. But the construction of the sentence is somewhat compressed and needs examination to untangle it. Both "God" and "Father" might be said with reference to the incarnate Word. But he is properly "Father" of the Word, and properly "God" of the assumed nature, just as he is not properly "God" of the Word, nor "Father" of the assumed nature. [Hence?] "properly" and "not properly" are found applied both to "Father" and to "God." Another [copy] begins: From the second [oration] on the Son. "For he would be called God, not of the Word but of what is seen [?] — for how could he be God of him who is properly God? — just as he is also Father, not of what is seen, but of the Word. For he was [twofold?]. So that 'properly' applies to b-

[-oth] properly, with "Father" joined to the Word and "God" to the assumed nature; but "not properly" applies the other way round, with "God" assigned to the Word and "Father" to the assumed nature. As you see, the meaning presents nothing unclear. But how could the construction of the sentence [?]? Or [?], if we take it through "so that," the "properly" applies to both, not [?] in part. Neither "God" nor "Father" is taken of any single one of the subjects, nor of both. Rather, each of them is taken with each of the subjects, "Father" being assigned to the Word and "God" to the assumed nature. In the same way, with "not properly" too, no one of the predicates is taken definitely of any one of the subjects, nor of both. Instead, both are taken with each of the subjects, but by the principle of interchange, as compared with what was said of "properly." For "God" predicated of the Word and "Father" predicated of the assumed nature carry the meaning of "not properly." And the meaning of "properly" and "not properly" here seems to be the opposite of how we use these terms in our own case. In the ineffable union of the Word and the flesh, "Father" is said properly of the Word, and "God" not properly. But in our nature it is the reverse: "God" is said properly, and "Father" not properly. And this is what you asked about: the force of "than" (ē). It does not indicate disjunction or any other of the senses into which it naturally divides. It takes on a clarifying, comparative character and does the work of "compared with" (para). The sentence would be framed more clearly if one chose to rephrase it this way: "so that the 'properly,' taken from one of the pairings, and the 'not properly,' taken from the other, are the opposite of what holds with us." For "properly" and "not properly" arose from a particular combination of predicates and subjects, and are understood along with them directly. He took both the "properly" and the "not properly" (for this contemplative man is fond of brevity if anyone is), referred the hearers' minds to the pairings formed from them, and added "are the opposite of what holds with us." The sense of "are the opposite of what holds with us" is clearly meant to embrace each combination formed from "properly" and "not properly." This turn of phrase [?] means to teach that nothing prevents both "properly" and "not properly" from being said of the Word, since with us too both are observed, though opposite in meaning. There "God" is not proper, but "Father" is; here "Father" is not proper, but "God" is. 3. What has been said would become clearer on a diagram. Place "Father" and "God" above. Below them place the Word under "Father" and the assumed nature under "God." Draw lines in parallel that join the Father to the

Word and God to the assumed nature. Then draw other straight lines from the beginning of each parallel to the end of the other. These form a kind of chiasm with each other and stand diagonally to each of the parallels. From this it is clear that, following the parallel position of the lines, the Father as Father of the Word and God as God of the assumed nature would be said properly. But following the connection of the chiasm, God as God of the Word and the Father as Father of the assumed nature would be said not properly. If you take one line from the parallels and the other along the diagonal, and do this for each pairing, you will see "properly" and "not properly" arising together in both cases. The Father is properly Father of the Word, but God is not properly God of the Word. Again, the Father is not properly Father of the assumed nature, but God is properly God of it. So four pairings are observed in doubled sets [?]. One consists of the parallels and another of the chiasm. Each of the remaining two is produced by combining one of the diagonals with one of the parallels. It is evident that "are the opposite of what holds with us" applies to each of these last two. In them the Father, joined to the Word and to the assumed nature, fits the Word properly and the assumed nature not properly. Likewise God is declared to be properly God of the assumed nature, but not properly God of the Word. So when we examine it in this way, one member of the pairing will appear as "properly" and the other as "not properly." This does not happen in a single way, but in a doubly varying relation and conjunction. And it is clear that, in each of the pairings, both "properly" and "not properly" are the opposite of what holds with us. The names "God" and "Father" were yoked together through their appropriation by "properly," and no less yoked through their connection with "not properly." They are also, if you like, applied to the same hypostasis, though not in the same way. For these reasons, this passage has given the heretics a pretext to strengthen their impiety behind a mask. They steal away the "properly" and the "not properly," and, having plundered the text, they bring forward "Father" and indeed "God" as they please for each of the natures united in the hypostasis, in order to build up their own blasphemy. But this is as much as the account of philosophical theory sets out on these matters. [?] Father God

4. Concerning the saying "Now I am lying" and [?]… [some] make bold to rank the Word of the Father as later and among created things. The divine Gregory conceded that the argument put to him proceeded by contradiction. In fact it did not [?]; both parts of the antithesis were framed affirmatively, even though one of the expressions had the simple form and the other the form produced by transposition. But he passed over this, so as not to seem to give these technicalities an entry into matters of God and theology, or to let them pride themselves against it. He sets the siege-engines of truth against their very citadel, and with the evidence of the realities rather than a verbal counter-objection he cries out: "It is not necessarily so, O [?]. Your refuge of contradiction does not require us to concede one of the premises." It was through this refuge that their boldness against piety seemed invincible, and its way of deciding was not impartial. Having put forward this objection, he sets out examples, such as "Now I am lying" and "You were present at your own coming-to-be," and others like them. He shows that it is not necessary in every case to concede one side of the contradiction. Sometimes, as in the cases before us, it is possible to deny and dismiss both and look to a third, in which the truth is seen to spring up. If the Theologian had been dealing in technicalities, he could have distinguished which contradictions allow a decision between true and false and which do not. But his purpose was to speak of God, not to pride himself on the art, and to refute the heretics, not to initiate disciples, to whom the dialectician [?]… : "But if it seems necessary to you, according to your dialectical assumptions, that one side is true in every case, answer me a little question. Is time in time, or not in time? If it is in time, in what time? What is that time besides this one, and how does it contain it? If it is not in time, what is this surpassing wisdom that introduces timeless time? And as for 'Now I am lying,' grant that only one of the two is true [?], for we will not grant both. But it cannot be done. Either in lying he will speak the truth, or in speaking the truth he will lie, by absolute necessity. What wonder is it, then, that just as opposites coincide here, so both are false there, and so for you

…[?] is celebrated with orgiastic frenzy. It was fitting, then, to be content with using these examples to pillory those who presume to reduce the nature of God to a technical method, carried away into a boldness far worse than superstition, and to show that this much-vaunted instrument of theirs, contradiction, does not have invincible force even in ordinary matters, much less is it a criterion of the supernatural essence and of the majesty that is beyond reason. There may be many expressions that keep the form of a contradiction but no longer serve in the same way to discriminate. For example, if someone asks about a living man whether he will rise from death or will not rise: for neither answer is something a sensible person ought to accept. And yet the present construction of the statement seems to offer somewhat more security, for the negative particle was joined to the predicate verb and did not pass over to the subject. Of the same kind is this: “Do human feet grow lions’ claws, or do they not grow them?” Or of someone already being carried along in the very course [?] toward the finish of the race: “Did he make the beginning of his motion in the very act of being carried, or did he not begin at all?” For how does such a fracturing of words distinguish truth from falsehood? Or this: “Does fire that moistens and cools bodies display this activity according to nature or not according to nature?” This one plainly, like the question put forward by the heretical invention, has the shape of the question counterfeited. Or: “A man carried aloft from the earth: is he released from his motion through the air, or is he not released?” This is free of the cause just mentioned, but it no less transforms and counterfeits the form of contradiction properly so called. Or: “Time, flowing like streams of water: will it stop its flow or will it not?” It is clear that this combination of words too, imitating [?], has come forth through the same trickery. And if you like, also this: “Did incorporeal nature, when it put on bodily form, have its composition from matter and form, or from neither of these? For if from matter and form, how is it incorporeal? But if from neither of these, whence did it get its bodily form?” Again: “Does motion take place in motion or not in motion? For if in motion, what is it, and in what, and which of them, and what is their difference from one another? And how will that one in turn be in motion, and will not the infinite slip in? But if not in motion, how will immobility hold motion together, and how will rest, joined to movement, not be moved along with it? Or, if it is not moved along with it, will motion [?] in rest?” “The whole creation that is superior to creation: was it brought forth by some activity, or is it known as not having been brought forth at all? For if it was not brought forth, how is it said to be a creation at all? But if it was brought forth, how did it come to be superior to creation?” And how much of such babble and ignorance dances around the form of contradiction! [Notes: (51) “Neither” in the manuscript; [?]…, though the manuscript [?]. (56) Latin [?]: “will be moved along with.”]

6. And look, if you will, at something closer than what has been said. Did God bring forth the age as already existing or as not existing? And does it subsist or does it not subsist? For if as existing, how is the bringing forth not in vain, how is it not nonsense? But if as not existing, where is there room for extension in things eternal? And if it does not subsist, how is it among beings at all, or whence is there an age? But if it subsists, whence will it come to have its unboundedness and its being impossible to traverse? Do you want to see the absurdity at still closer range? Did the Father become Father being Father, or not being Father? For if being so, then one thing in him is prior and another came after, and how has the unchangeable been changed? But if not being so, the account of change no less does away with unchangeability, and stands even more strongly against eternity. But these things belong to the babblers of heresy and are the crops of its first sowing [?]. 7. Very well. But perhaps another heretical argument might act boldly and, removing the cause arising from transposition by which the contradiction was adulterated, might contrive to put the question in some such way as this: “Did the Father beget the Son as existing, or as existing did he not beget him?”, and will demand that one part of the antithesis be given as the answer. But this refuge too has been shown by the examples already given to be rotten, its sanctuary thrown down and outraged by justice. Still, nothing prevents us from stating the refutation now, directly and briefly. “As existing he did not beget” divides into a double meaning. The one leads simply to “he did not beget,” attaching nothing else of what ought to be joined to it; the other brings in the consequence as well: “he did not beget him as already existing.” One who shuns all trickery and connects the argument fittingly will say this, because the one begotten has his existence concurrent with his begetting. The heretical argument, then, frightening the simpler folk with bogeys through the first sense, persuades them to flee and not to turn to the second meaning, the one proper to the argument. For if one fixed one's mind on that one, he would give, as you see, a very easy and orthodox

answer. For to declare “as existing he did not beget,” because the begetting is concurrent with the existence: what is laborious about that, what is difficult? How is it in keeping with the heresy, or rather, how is it not opposed to it? And what does it lack with respect to piety? And if it should be necessary to come down to a humbler level of argument, and from there to receive the contemplation still more fully unfolded with respect to the loftier inquiry, you may consider it from this: for example, “Did the begotten one lay aside eternity, or did he not lay it aside?” For to reply simply “he laid it aside” did not block the sophist's road to mischief: seizing on the word, the sophist will seem to conclude, “So he does not have eternity with himself.” But if someone, adding what is lacking, declared “He did not lay it aside, because he never had it” (for laying aside belongs to things previously possessed), he put a strong muzzle on one whose art is the practice of idle chatter. And from this, if you cultivate it in your mind, countless examples will spring up for you by which the babble and boldness of heresy are muzzled. 8. But these things have been said to you in passing about the technical use of contradiction and the prattle of heresy, since the aforementioned work, which has long spoken freely in dialectical discourses, is quite sufficient to provide more complete teaching and contemplation. For the rest, farewell; and consider our slowness in meeting your requests to be due to the lack of copyists rather than to any neglect of your requests.

QUESTION 79. Why did Moses keep silent about the angels in his account of the creation of the world? And what does this mean: “For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head”? Both these questions you can find solved in other writings of ours as well, in a solution that I would say falls short in nothing of precision and is in no way deficient in force. But since it is dear to you to have the contemplation and recollection of them in a more particular form, even though you yourself are graced not only to know such things but also to enable others to learn them, we did not refuse the request of your understanding. We say, therefore, out of what the great throng of memories and thoughts, of trials and afflictions, did not take away but left as some remnant still remaining, that Moses, for various reasons, when he undertook a plain narrative of the creation of the world, made mention neither of the essence nor of the coming into being of the angels. For these are separate from the sensible creation; and for those of Israel, who were only just being led up to a more divine contemplation away from, above all, the Egyptian superstition, in which they had spent a long time, if not held fast by the error, at least living among those held fast by it,

it was neither easy nor simple to bear being led up to learning about incorporeal and godlike minds. And no less, if not more, than the reasons mentioned, it was because he was going to bring laws not to angels but to human beings, for whom there was both coming into being and a passage from non-being into being. And the author of Genesis, offering necessary teachings that also provide what is useful, introduces the coming into being of heaven and earth and the other things, because these came to exist before the substance of man, and because man was to have his way of life among them, and because they were to supply the other necessary needs pertaining to sense for those receiving the law. For of God they had in their souls some notion and image, of whatever kind, even if not raised to precision; but of angels none at all. Indeed, even the nation of the Jews, after many generations, thought fit to confess God, yet considered it intolerable even to admit angels and spirits by hearsay. That the account of the incorporeal minds was passed over at the beginning by Moses, who saw God, because of the weakness of those receiving it, is clear from the fact that at the end of the rest of his history, and after many words, he came round to mentioning them, though even then not introducing their coming into being but the gladness of the heavens and the worship of the angels, saying: “Rejoice, O heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him.” David, however, the ancestor of God, declared their substance to be of fire, and their creator to be the one who is also acknowledged as the creator of all the rest of creation. Such, then, is what the occasion allowed us to say about the angels. As for “For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head,” it means: you will gather up the coals that are consuming and destroying his head. For they would quickly work it to ruin, unless you quickly drive them away from it and free it from the passion that creeps over it and devours it. How would you not be seen to be the best physician of your neighbor by acting thus? For the enemy, welcomed by you with a table and friendly hospitality, even if not because he loves the good and is a lover of virtue, yet at any rate because of the comfort whose enjoyment he has from you, how would he not take up the thought of departing from his enmity, and rise up to depart from his plotting? And, sobering his thoughts and turning the burning and inflammation in them, which anger had kindled, toward withering and calming, would he not be led little by little to recognize and love his benefactor, the beneficent and kindly right hand having sweetened all the bitterness of hatred, and having dissolved, by respect and affection, the soul and, through the body, also [Note (44): The same, in place of “maker of heaven,” of which the latter [?]]

the head's hostility against the benefactor? But if, after so great a kindness, through which the beauty of goodness is portrayed, the one possessed by envy and hatred of his neighbor should not wish to look toward anything better, nor toward change and correction, such a one would be a beast and not a man, and such an evil is rare in human nature. But you, no less even after such great madness, indeed all the more heaping up by your care the coals that are consuming his head, would fulfil the imitation of the Master by your kindnesses; while he, most wretchedly, has shown his own sin to be stronger than all kindness and likewise than all pardon. But if someone wishes to understand “You will heap coals of fire upon his head” also according to the ready interpretation, the one that exhorts the many not to make enmity worse by enmity and retaliation, neither would this miss the mark of the aim for which it is designed; and the persuasion that urges the many not to retaliate is better able to draw them to assent. It runs thus: The one who has taken up enmity against you without cause does not stop moving his arrows. It would be better, considering the common Fashioner, the right hand that fashioned you both, and your shared nature, to conquer the one who hates you by kindness of disposition, because he perverts through enmity what is of one nature with him. If not, but you wish to retaliate against him and grieve him, and not fail at all in this, feed him, give him drink. How and why? Through these things you make the common Master your avenger; and by your kindnesses you will move him to vengeance; and you would quickly see your enemy burning and consumed as if by fire by his judgment and sentence, and perishing together with his own enmity and plotting. [On gno]mic wills in Christ [?].

QUESTION 80. What are we to call gnomic wills in Christ, and in what sense can we speak of a human, hypostatic will in Christ himself? The account of gnomic wills in Christ is in one respect difficult, in another easy. Since none of our notable and God-bearing Fathers, so far as I know, has handed down anything notable on this subject, clarified so as to be distinct, except Maximus the Great, truly the champion of piety, the difficulty of speaking about it creeps in for this reason. For to rest so great a doctrine on one man would not make it fearsome and unapproachable to those wishing to attack it. But since, again, from the very chambers of piety and from concurring reasonings many proofs come forth to guard the right doctrine, in this way it remains the easiest thing to speak of, or [?] loftier than comprehension. And you, most beloved of priests, if the offspring of this discourse appears to you worthy of your request and your hope, cherish it as something common to the one who helped deliver it and to the one who bore it. But if it is imperfect and deficient compared with what has already been brought to completion for you in your contemplations (and I would pray for this, if the desire to win possessed me, for it is much sweeter to win in the person of a friend than in another; for we do not, as the proverb has it, run the risk on a Carian, but we think it wise to seek the genuineness of victory in our own blood), nevertheless take up the offspring as one exposed, and having nourished it and brought it to completion with your own labors, do not begrudge making the joy and enjoyment of it common. The powers of the soul, then, are twofold, as was long ago distinguished (for we must retrace our steps a little): the cognitive and the vital; and for the present subject it is rather the vital, that is, the appetitive, that is needed. There is sown in the soul, then, an appetitive power for what is according to nature, one that holds together all that belongs to it essentially, and this is called willing. Therefore they also define natural will as a natural and rational willing [?]. Therefore they also define natural will as a natural and rational appetite

dependent only on natural things. So willing is itself the vital and rational appetite, the simple power of all that constitutes the nature. For the appetite of irrational beings, not being rational, is not called willing. What willing is, then, has been stated. Wish is a particular natural willing, that is, a natural and rational appetite for some thing. For the power of desiring rationally lies in the human soul; and when this rational appetite is moved naturally toward some thing, it is called wish; for wish is a rational appetite and longing for some thing. Wish is spoken of concerning things in our power, that is, also concerning impossible things [?]; for we wish even not to die. Wish is of the end, not of the means to the end. For the end is what is wished, such as being healthy; the means to the end is the way by which we must become healthy. After wish come inquiry and consideration, after which comes deliberation. For deliberation is an inquiring appetite concerned with things in our power; for one deliberates whether one ought to pursue the matter or not. Then one judges, and this is called judgment. Then one becomes disposed toward and loves what one has judged, and this is called disposition (gnōmē); for if one has judged but is not disposed toward what was judged, that is, if one does not love it, it is not called disposition. Upon disposition follows choice, as it were a selection. After choice follows the impulse toward action; then use, after which the workings of appetite cease. In irrational beings, then, impulse follows immediately upon appetite, but in rational beings not always. For irrational beings are led by natural appetite, which is why the appetite of irrational beings is called neither willing nor wish. But in human beings natural appetite is led rather than leading; for it is moved freely and with reason, since the cognitive and vital powers are yoked together in man. Freely, therefore, he desires, and freely he is impelled, and the rest freely.

In the case of the divine, blessed, and superessential nature, we speak of wish, but we do not properly speak of choice, just as we speak neither of consideration nor of deliberation. Nor even in the case of the Lord's soul do we speak of deliberation or choice. For it had no ignorance, even though it belonged to the nature that is ignorant of the future. For being united to God the Word hypostatically, it had knowledge of all things,

not by grace but by nature, because of the hypostatic union; for the same one was God and man. Therefore it did not have a gnomic will either. For it had the natural, simple willing, which is seen alike in all human natures; but his holy soul did not have a gnomic willing contrary to his divine will, nor any other besides his divine will. For disposition is divided along with the hypostases, except only in the holy, simple, incomposite, and indivisible Godhead. For there, since the hypostases are in no way divided or separated, neither is the thing willed divided; rather, the gnomic is as it were united to the natural, and [?] subdivided by the law of its own circumscription. And there, since the nature is one, the natural willing is also one; and since the hypostases are undivided, the thing willed is also one, and one is the movement of the three hypostases, for the immaculate and supernatural union does not permit itself to be insulted by the division of some material imagining. But among human beings, since the nature is one, the natural willing is one too; but the hypostases are separated from one another and stand apart in time and place and in their disposition toward things and in many other respects, and for this reason both their wills and their dispositions are seen to differ. But in the case of our Lord Jesus Christ, since the natures are different, the natural willings of his divinity and of his humanity, that is, the volitive powers, are also different. But since, again, the hypostasis is one and the one who wills is one, the thing willed, that is, his gnomic will, is also one; clearly because his human willing follows his divine willing and wills those things that his divine willing willed it to will. Gnomic wills, then, and hypostatic, personal, and elective wills would signify the same underlying reality. One must know ([?] lovers of learning), for the sake of a clearer completion of the terms, that “will” sometimes signifies the willing, that is, the volitive power, and is then called natural will; and sometimes the thing willed, and is then called gnomic will. And according to the holy Maximus, gnomic will differs from natural will in that the former both is and is called hypostatic and personal, while natural will is not. And it differs further in that the simple and indiscriminate

impulse and longing for the things that constitute us according to nature is natural will; whereas the particular and varying movement and appetite for things that contribute to pleasure is gnomic will, which is recognized also in the intensification both of the good and of what is not such. And the first meaning is not wholly alien to the second; rather, they share in common a property of quantity [?], in the same way as the meaning of “nature” when taken in the case of man. For here “nature” is twofold: one sense signifies simply and universally each of the individuals ranked under “man”; the other, not [?] the whole, the innate power that gives strength for actions, according to which, among the company of these particular men, one is more naturally suited to geometry and another more apt to be perfected in music, or some are known as workers of gentleness and others rather of temperance. Choice, then, differs from natural will, by sound reasoning, in that it is a deliberative appetite for things in our power; and further in that natural will depends only on natural things, while choice depends only on things in our power. “But that the one will of Christ is natural and elective,” he says, “none of the Fathers dared to think or say,” knowing truly that choice belongs to things that move in [opposite] directions, I mean toward good things and toward bad, which it shows a want of right judgment either to think or to say of Christ. Further, if there is a hypostatic will in Christ, it will certainly differ from the gnomic wills seen in each human being; and it will likewise differ from the will seen in the Father and the Spirit. What, then, is it, that is neither a human gnomic will nor wholly a divine will? For no one will call it something composite, since it is not possible even to conceive of a composition of will, as one can see a composite hypostasis. Nor would anyone say that this argument does not allow any other human being to have a gnomic will either. For every gnomic will of someone is not the same as any of those seen in the gnomic will of individuals, but altogether different; so that even if it were human, it would fit none of the individuals under “man” as human. For if the gnomic will belonged properly to one of the individuals, it would be human; but it is no longer human, because neither Socrates, nor Peter, nor anyone else, insofar as he is by nature a man,

[?] has a gnomic will; or else the argument is sophistical that distinguishes the individual from the others of the same nature in each particular. From the admission that the individual in question is the same as none of the other individuals, either in hypostasis or in its other properties, it goes on to strip them of their common nature as well, and to deny that its gnomic will is human. For on many grounds this fallacy will cut off and separate the common nature from the individuals that fall under it and are included under its name. That is why this argument is not on the same footing as the one that refuses to admit a gnostic will in Christ. In the case of human beings, it takes one of the individuals, who admittedly has a gnomic will by reason of his difference from the others of the same species, and then rules out the common nature. That is sophistical, and an inference that does not follow. But in the case of our Lord Jesus Christ, we first ask whether we should say at all that a gnomic will belongs to him, and it is not possible to find hypostases included under the name of Christ. Further, in the case of human beings one can say that the gnomic will present in them is not the same in one as in another, insofar as it is distinguished by the hypostases, but that insofar as it is brought together into one nature, nothing [prevents] it from being called both human and the same. In the case of Christ no one will be able to say anything like this, for in Christ there is no one common thing to be found: two natures make up the hypostasis, not one. Nor can one say of the gnomic will that insofar as it is this one, it is not the same. For Christ is one, and his person is one and his hypostasis is one. He has no hypostases of the same rank and the same name ranged alongside him as Christ, and nothing is said of him in common that could also apply to others. So the difficulty that follows remains unsolved, the question of what the gnomic will could possibly be, since it can neither be nor be called human or divine. This, then, is the second argument stated: that we must not say that there exists in Christ a gnomic will, that is, [?] a human hypostatic will. The third: if a human will is spoken of in Christ
[?] ... That is why this argument is not on the same footing as the one that refuses to admit a gnostic [read: gnomic] will in Christ

[?]. The hypostatic will is said to belong to the natural will, for the gnomic will is a qualified natural will. So the gnomic will in Christ, too, would depend on a natural will and be put forth from it, though not from a simple natural will but from a composite and mixed one. For if anyone were to suppose at all that a hypostatic gnomic will belongs to the composite hypostasis, it would have been put forth from a composite natural will. Then there would be a composite nature in Christ, which has been condemned by the unanimous vote of those who accepted the authority of the two natures as beyond dispute. Further, the gnomic will is preceded by deliberation and by a disposition toward, and assent to, what is being judged. Of these, the first is a passage from ignorance to knowledge and discernment, and the second is a kind of turning and change of disposition, for the disposition has been turned to affection from not feeling affection. None of these may be thought of Christ. It is therefore intolerable to say that a human gnomic will exists in him. Besides what has been said: if those who use a human gnomic will are in the habit of fighting against the divine will, how is it possible at all to conceive of a gnomic will in Christ?
