To put it more generally: if the gnomic will inclines equally to either kind of action, I mean the base and the better, how is it not reckless to introduce a gnomic will in Christ, and to make him who acts with uniform goodness, and is in the proper sense most perfectly good, out to have an inclination evenly balanced between the worse and the better? This is enough for now to show that the human gnomic will cannot properly apply to Christ.

We must now ask whether we should not speak of a divine gnomic will in Christ either, just as we should not speak of a human gnomic will; or whether the human is not allowed while the divine is not forbidden. Of the arguments stated in that discussion, the third and the fourth in particular have force in the same way on the same points. For the word of truth, by the same approach, both distinguishes and brings together [?] the divine and the human gnomic will. And apart from what has been said, if anyone supposes that a divine gnomic will is spoken of in Christ, let him say whether he thinks it is the same as the divine natural will or different. If it is the same, what is the point of the name, which would bring in a fanciful picture of notions

split into difference? But if it is different, how would it not also be different from the will contemplated in the Father and the Spirit? That is absurd. For the natural will in God, being common to the three thearchic hypostases and undivided among them, is seen to fit them as equals and without variation. What cannot be found in human nature can be perceived in the essence that is beyond divinity and beyond being: its natural, more-than-divine will is marked by identity of mind, unity of concord, and invariability of assent. How then could the common and invariable will of the nature be narrowed into a hypostatic gnomic will? In the proper sense, then, a divine gnomic will could in no way be spoken of in Christ, since no one speaking properly would dare to say this even of the Holy Spirit. For how could what is common be hypostatic? Nor [?] ... If someone were to misuse the word metaphorically, borrowing it from human hypostases, but without corrupting the sense that befits God, he might not forfeit the indulgence allowed in matters of words, since he would be found [?] to incur strangeness of words, not of doctrines. It would also be fitting to set out the sacred words on which they rely when they think they are establishing the opposing will, and, by offering clarity and right understanding, to show that this pretext too has been taken from them. They say, then, that it was said: "I did not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." Clearly, they say, it is the gnostic will that is meant here. To this it is easy to reply: if in saying "the will of the Father" he did not mean the gnomic will (for no pious person can declare that there is a gnomic will in the three thearchic hypostases), then clearly in adding "my own will" he also meant not the gnomic will but the natural one. So the saying not only fails to establish a gnomic will in any way, but rather overturns such a supposi-

tion. For natural is of the same order as natural and answers to it, just as gnomic stands in the same rank and relation as gnomic. There is also another reading, more fitting than what they say, if the force of the words is taken as a negation: "I did not come to do my own will," because my will is not at all another will besides the will contemplated in the Father and the Spirit. But if someone thinks the expression is not a negation but a comparison, which is rather what the plain sense of the wording suggests, it could reasonably be understood like this: I did not come to do the natural will of human nature, but the divine will. That will is not gnomic either, but single, and seen without variation in the three thearchic hypostases, although in human nature and in all the other things that he brought into being by his creative wisdom it could in no way be seen, since it does not even come near the divine and more-than-divine property. But if someone is attached to the expression "gnomic will" and refuses to look to any of the solutions given, let him take the present explanation as a consolation. What the Lord's words now indicate could be understood as the gnomic will of Christ, not of one thought of as a man, but of the one contemplated as Christ. Having become wholly of the Godhead, this will is brought to perfection and refers its own limits to the divine and supernatural infinity. And surely we shall not again find two gnomic wills cropping up. To speak of one thing and another brings in a doubling of the subject; but to speak of the same thing in one way and in another brings in a variation and alteration of relations, and in no way a cutting and dividing of what was one from the beginning. The first did not let even the many escape the hunt; but for the second, without leisure and practice in argument, it is not possible even to [?] the tracks of the quarry rightly

The same meaning would apply to "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will." To fear death belonged to human nature. But it belonged to the divine nature not only to be in no way disturbed by what was at hand, but even to take pleasure in these things for the salva- [Notes:] Read: παρὰ τὸ τοῦ. ³ "Will crop up" (προσανακύψει), as the Colbert manuscript has. Read: τῷ.

-tion of the human lump. Again, "I will; be clean" is not evidence of a gnomic will, but a declaration of the divine, innate and undivided will, which belongs equally to the Trinity, beyond being and of one nature. For just as their almighty divinity, authority and providence are common, so too the will for our salvation, both of body and of soul, is common, admits no cutting, and is divided by no difference. That is why "I will; be clean" is the will of the supernatural Godhead. For providence over human beings depends on it; it manages the care of bodies and of souls and is known to vary according to what is beneficial. Nor does "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" hint at a gnomic will. Rather, through the question the apostles are getting rid of their ignorance, taking care not to do anything concerning the Passover that would not please the Teacher: as if to say, "Where would it please you to eat the Passover, and which house would seem suitable to receive the supper?" Besides, this very utterance expresses the ignorance and supposition of the disciples, not a judgment of the Savior, and it introduces no doctrine. The same is true of "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." These are the words of the one who needs healing, not of the one who provides it; and nothing prevents us from saying that here too the will of the supernatural Godhead is implied. As for "What do you want me to do for you?" and "If you wish to be perfect," these clearly do not look to the hypostasis of our Savior Jesus Christ, nor do they refer to it, but to the person who is subject to the exhortations and who longs for healing. In neither of these is the gnomic will signified. And elsewhere, wherever there is talk

of will without the word "natural" or "gnomic" being attached, it will easily be told apart by being referred to one of the interpretations given above. Other points could be added to what has been said, through which the argument that sets up a gnomic will in Christ is seen to be no less [?]. For if the hypostatic Word of God became man for our sake, then as man he had the natural human will, and as God the natural and divine will. Now the contentious argument says that he also had a gnomic, that is, a hypostatic, will. It will surely have to say, even against its will, that he had his gnomic and hypostatic human will insofar as he was a human hypostasis, and the divine gnomic will insofar as he was a divine hypostasis. For along with the picture and outline of a gnomic will, the personal character is also brought in, since the two notions belong together. Just as, where there is no person, no gnomic will is granted to be present either, so [where there is a gnomic will] the presence of a hypostasis follows without doubt [?]. But the first of these is the madness of Nestorius, to teach and imagine a human hypostasis in Christ; the second belongs to the Arian mania, which walled off the three thearchic hypostases from one another by other essential differences and likewise by gnomic wills. But the mind of the Church, just as it rejects as impious those who say that there is in Christ a human hypostasis stripped of the Godhead, so too charges with godlessness those who divide up the common will of the triune Godhead. "For," they say, "it was by gnome that Adam fell from the commandment, and by it [?] that he suffered the passion; and it was to this that the best of physicians applied the remedy and the cure." Not even this: it is not necessary that the gnomic element of man be taken up together with the human lump by the Savior and physician of our souls.

But one can say to them that if failing in gnome and falling from the commandment is the cause of the assumption, then for those in whom sinlessness has not been assumed, neither is the gnomic [mind] assumed whole [?] ... it will easily be told apart ... being referred. That is: [?] the contentious argument says that he also had a gnomic, that is, a hypostatic, will; it will surely have to say, even against its will, that his gnomic and hypostatic human will [?] insofar as he was a human [hypostasis] ... sinlessness has been assumed, neither is the gnomic mind assumed whole. But according to them they assign the property of the rational soul in man by halves. For if it was assumed because it sinned, then what had not sinned [read: τὸ ἡμαρτηκός] would surely not have been, because it was not assumed [?]. That is: they [?]

mind, but according to them they assign the property of the rational soul in man by halves. For if it was assumed because it sinned, then what had not sinned would surely not have been assumed [?]. Further, if the natural will is above all what constitutes the essence of man, and he is characterized by it, and the perfection of man is also seen through the natural will, and if the Word does not endure the insult of a gnomic will, as being sinful, why then should we not shrink from saying that Christ assumed a gnomic will rather than the natural one, which is common to all men and brings with it the perfection of nature? Further, if the gnomic will is laid down together with birth, then infants still clinging to the breast and finding there the liquid table of their food would have to show their nature by a gnomic will, and to settle their doubts altogether, though they do not yet have the power to make a choice among them. Further, if Christ became an infant and was made like us in all things except sin, and the gnomic will was not implanted in infants, then clearly it was not implanted in our Lord Jesus Christ either. But if its assumption happened in some other way, let them say where they learned of a double assumption, and therefore of a double incarnation, especially since Adam, in transgressing, served not the natural will but the gnomic one. But they are eager to creep along through the tangles of contradiction, though they have often failed to submit to correction [?]. And they say: if in all things that subsist in nature, the nature surely [Variant readings:] "For just as, where there is no person, there is no [?] of a gnomic will granted to be present." "The Word (as a sinful gnomic will) does not endure": the Word does not endure the insult of a gnomic will, as being sinful. That is: [?]
contains individuals of the same species, and in Christ we speak of a natural human will, then there would reasonably be, belonging to this natural will, a hypostatic and gnomic will as well.

Further, if the gnomic will is nothing other than a qualified natural will, and Christ, having the natural will, did not merely act in general but did this or that particular thing, then a gnomic will is to be found in him as well. But each of these arguments depends on a sophistical tangle. The first, because it makes the descent from the natural to the hypostatic by cutting the nature up into particulars. But the pious account of Christ does not make the cut and the descent from some one nature to particulars, for there is no single nature here that is being cut up. Rather, it unfolds from the hypostasis into the duality of the natures. In the other case the natural will will have hypostatic wills, because many hypostases by nature fall under it. But in the mystery that concerns us, since only one common thing was seen under the sun, and Christ's hypostasis is one and undivided, the nature cannot contain anything hypostatic at all, nor can one nature be conceived at all. The second sophism of the heretics builds its mischief on the fallacy of the consequent. For the gnomic will is always both hypostatic and qualified; but the qualified is not always hypostatic. The common natural wills, too, differ from those of other kinds by a natural quality, yet for all that they are not gnomic wills. But even if the fallacy drags the consequent along with it, the falsehood was nevertheless not shaped by that. For one can say that if quality is seen to be twofold, one in the natural will and the other in the hypostatic, nothing prevents us from saying (rather, the argument will lead us there) that since the quality is twofold, and this one is not natural (for that is common), it would be a hypostatic and gnomic will. So it would have come round to the same point, even if the construction of the argument, the contrivance of the heresy, had not proceeded by the fallacy of the consequent. What then should we say? That Christ, though he was one hypostasis, is not seen to have used any qualified hypostatic will. He willed to partake of food as fulfilling the natural will, but of sweetened or astringent or otherwise [?] ... is always both hypostatic and qualified. But the qualified is not always hypostatic. For the common natural wills, That is: [?] qualified, because it is not natural. "Nothing prevents us from saying (rather, the argument will lead us there) that since the quality is twofold, since it is not natural." That is: Nothing [?]

[no] longer. In the same way, by the principle of human nature, he willed to take drink; but fragrant wine and strong drink or anything of the kind had no will to provoke or urge him. Christ our God, one according to hypostasis, partook of food and drink simply, by the principle of human nature, as has been said; but he was in no way carried away by his will to the special property of food or drink that flatters the senses beyond what is necessary. That is why, when he was confirming the truth of his human nature after the resurrection, and showing that he had not laid it aside, he did not ask for this or that kind of food, but simply said, "Have you anything to eat here?" The saying perhaps also brings in another meaning, but no less, if not more, it brings in the one that teaches us that Christ, being one hypostasis, undivided and inseparable, had and kept the natural human will, but is nowhere shown to have received a gnomic will. No doubting thought will trouble anyone with sense, since many holy men too, often distinguished in ascetic contests, do not refuse with their will to take food simply suited to nature, for the natural replenishment of what the body innately loses. But they pay little attention to seasoned dishes that bewitch the gullet and other such refinements, which sprout and grow from the gnomic will. Yet they do not altogether despise these either and wrap themselves in a lack of appetite. Some resolve [?] to live blamelessly and to partake blamelessly; others do both sinfully and dangerously. You have Isaac as an example of the first kind: he desired game, obtained it, and partook of it with all reverence and moderation. [?] ... by the same principle of human nature he willed to take [read ἡδύνουσαν, as a little above] ... and flatters the senses beyond what is necessary, the property of food or drink [?], he was in no way carried away ... altogether despise [read ὑπερορῶσι] these and ... …and bequeathed to him much of the inhabited world. But his son Esau, being in the grip of desire, did not will or desire rightly. For a brief pleasure he bartered away great glory and an honor confirmed by law, setting up his gullet as judge of his actions in place of his mind; and from this he brought dissensions and countless evils down upon those caught up in it. Yet the opposing argument grows still more shameless and says that this very willing—to be earnest, raised above the way of life of the many, and not to be mastered by the belly and its foods—is a gnomic will. For if it were natural, all would have to do it. But then, my good sir, if the will to wear oneself down with toils and hardships, and to be among the afflicted rather than among those who live at ease, is gnomic— First, he will not be able to bring forward any particular case as an example that compels assent (as the argument showing that gnomic will is not present does). Instead he will take refuge in some common and negative name, and, by setting aside the particular and hypostatic will, he will try to shore up his own nonsense. Second, the locusts and wild honey are not the product of a gnomic will, for it is something done by force: 'From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.' John's food, then, was a matter of force, and lay not only outside gnomic will but outside will altogether. If someone, still more contentious, should say that the forced itself belongs to gnomic will, many absurdities will follow. The most obvious is that he has unwittingly introduced some common species of will, not gnomic will. For such a will would be a forced will and an unwilled will—a fabrication that the champion of gnomic will did not wish to admit into his construction [?]. The same argument holds for everything else that gnomic will can be taken to cover. But if, as regards the human, gnomic and hypostatic will found no place in Christ, it could hardly be imagined in the divine nature of the Word, especially since neither to the Father, nor to the Holy Spirit, and therefore not to the

[he] will dare. It could hardly be imagined in the divine nature of the Word, especially since neither to the Father nor to the all-holy Spirit (and therefore not to the Son and Word either) could any pious reasoning attach anything distinguished by a quality and set apart by a property—the gno-

3 and Word, anything distinguished by a quality and set apart by a property; indeed, no pious reasoning could attach the gnomic will to them. Yet perhaps it might occur to some to say that there is nothing impossible in speaking of an unforced forced thing and an unwilled will. [?] … would be one who has not perceived [?] … impossible. But if something is forced in one respect and unforced in another, unwilled in one respect and willed in another, how could the absurdity creep in? For, to pass over the rest for now, the martyr who suffers incurable torments for the sake of piety both felt pain and endured that unendurable violence; in this he would be hard pressed by force. But since he would not bear to escape the tortures by turning aside to idolatrous error, he was unforced in what he did, bringing so great a violence upon himself. From the same image the unwilled is also made clear. Or else this argument is an unfolding and clarification of words that seem to conflict, but it has no power to shake the demonstration establishing that there is no gnomic human will in Christ; or it concludes the contrary [?]. For something forced in one respect and unforced in another, unwilled in one respect and willed in another—this he has so far in no way contrived to attach to the gnomic will. Whether or not it has been stated is something one who knows clearly and philosophizes impartially ought to consider. But if what exists by nature has been overlooked as though it did not exist, and if, through failing to perceive the nature contemplated by reason, people also fight against its name, then it has not been stated. Yet its existence does not prove false when it is investigated. Or else this argument is an unfolding and clarification of words that seem to conflict, but it has no power to shake the demonstration establishing that there is no gnomic human will in Christ; or it concludes the contrary [?]. For something forced in one respect and unforced in another, unwilled in one respect and willed in another—this he has so far in no way contrived to attach to the gnomic will. Whether or not it has been stated is something one who knows clearly and philosophizes impartially ought to consider. But if what exists by nature has been overlooked as though it did not exist, and if, through failing to perceive the nature contemplated by reason, people also fight against its name, then it has not been stated. Yet its existence does not prove false when it is investigated. It is not to be said, therefore, that it has been stated because it is among the things that exist; but not because the many pass it over in silence is its existence also struck out. For many things, before a more precise

essence. It [must] therefore be stated, since it is among the things that exist; and its existence must not be struck out because the many pass it over in silence (I would prefer the reading παραγράφεσθαι). id

investigation is applied to them, are spoken of simply, and their name is plain to everyone. But when they are unfolded and examined in detail, they take on a certain complexity and call for a name suited to the concept. Take, for instance, the natural and acknowledged human will: when closely examined, it would be seen to display differences. These differences constitute distinctness, yet they do not cut the common species up into new kinds. For example, someone wants to eat and drink, but one person has this appetite more strongly throughout life and another less. The more and the less do not divide the natural will or narrow it into a more specific will, since the more and the less are not by nature able to produce an inherent alteration of any species or common nature. Someone will therefore say, cut short by sound judgment [?], that this natural will, insofar as it extends equally over all human beings, is not divided into subordinate species; but insofar as it admits variations of more and less, it preserves a certain analogy to things that are divided, yet the division does not give rise to a new species. Nothing, then, prevented us both from simply confessing the natural will of man and, when this is closely examined and, as it were, distinguished by differences, from [designating it] with more varied thought and more varied names [?]. One will find the same thing observed in countless other questions. But why do I speak of remote things, when I can confirm the argument with a closer example? Paul shaves his head and purifies himself, and he circumcises Timothy. Did he will these things purely and without admixture, with nothing of the unwilled woven into his will? Then how does he count the things of the law as loss and refuse, and being circumcised as rendering Christ of no effect [?]? No argument could deny that these things were involuntary and unwilled, and that they were a mode of economy resting on, and interwoven with, what was quite unbecoming and unwilled, together with the will. Will anyone, then, begrudge us the names, when he sees that things involving such interweaving need fitting and appropriate words? What is absurd—or rather, how is it not necessary—in naming it, since an unwilled will is evidently found to exist, and force slipping in under the voluntary? And to those

[?] … to announce these things and make them known in words as well? One ought therefore to consider not whether the names happen to be ready to hand for you, but whether the nature of the things demands to be signified by fitting names. But the champion of the opposing side will say that these points cut the other way, overturning the demonstration by which it was established that gnomic will must not be ascribed to Christ. 'But no one demanded,' the truth might reply, 'either that one should not investigate the nature of the matter proposed, or that, once it is found, one should let it run wild in silence and hide it, or that one should dissolve the reality of things because of a poverty in the use of names.' No one proposed or blamed any of these things. The complaint was rather this: when the gnomic will was put forward for inquiry purely and without any foreign admixture, he ran past it and slipped away as though it had never been spoken or conceived at all. Then, by lumping together the voluntary with the forced and the unforced, and wrapping the meaning of the simple term in this complicated notion, the man who makes contradiction his way of life thinks he escapes his hearers' notice. Besides, we do not at all deprive holy men of gnomic will—God forbid! For being human, and not yet having laid down the burden of the flesh, they often made use of human gnomic wills. But this is what we say: if in them, still bound to flesh and blood, gnomic will was often at work, [?] … being present unhindered—who would not be ashamed to think or say that gnomic will exists in Christ? Nor indeed does the continual contradiction of the argument that establishes right doctrine [?] the demonstration of the truth; on the contrary, it shows it to be still more irrefutable. For to devise every hold against it, and yet for it to

break them all easily, and to stand beyond every slander and abuse—how does this not reveal its unsurpassable strength? And even if this argument had met with an objection not so easily resolved, the opposing case would not be strengthened even so. For the remaining arguments present the truth so very plainly that even one ready to dare every kind of daring would not attempt to look it in the face at all, even if he carries off shame from every one of them. For those over whom the arguments brought forward prevailed proclaim the victory unassailable; and those who were astounded merely at grappling with them bore witness that the strength of these feats is not even in doubt. Besides, the best argument is the one whose radiance of truth flashes out so brightly that no one even [ventures] to quarrel with it, nor attempts at all to overshadow its brilliance with contentions. Again, the strongest of arguments is the one that has escaped all the holds devised against it by its opponents and has won the victory in every contest, its rivals finally thrown down. So how could the argument that combines both in itself—the unassailable strength of the one and the inalienable prize of the other—and is able to shine with the exceptional and incomparable virtue of each, such as the present one, fail to display the most perfect and unsurpassable strength of the truth? It was for this reason that the inquiry into the subject brought forward these points and the objections: so that you might clearly recognize that, though briefly, yet not perfunctorily, it brought the nature of the matters to light. The present discussion, then, aiming not much less at shared exercise than at knowledge of the nature of things, has gone through these matters in this summary way. But if anyone has learned from the sacred Oracles or from our God-bearing Fathers some more elegant contemplation, more elevated toward the truth, and should reveal it, he would quickly see us taking the rank of disciples rather than seeking to be thought teachers.

QUESTION 81. What is meant by the passage in the Acts, 'When this sound occurred, [the multitude came together]', and so on? Did the mockers understand the apostles when they spoke in tongues, or not? For if they did not understand, how did the apostles speak to all? But if they did understand, how did they dare to allege drunkenness, when the refutation lay at their very feet—the perception of the very people who heard and understood? This is how someone might put your difficulty in sharper form. But I would say the opposite: that if they had [not?] understood, they would not even have slandered the miracle as drunkenness. For why would anyone even try to slander something that [?] … not even of those who [?] … him? No, they did understand, but they were displeased. For those men were speaking the mighty works of God, and the ill-disposed, stung by this, tried to turn the miracle into a mockery. That is why blessed Luke says, 'Mocking, they said'—as though they were dragging it down [?] and slandering it, contriving to overshadow the working of the miracle. How, then, could they understand and yet attribute what was said to drunkenness? Out of great and surpassing folly. For it is the habit of such people, when what is said is not to their liking—even if it is otherwise saving and beneficial—to blame derangement for what was said, or to charge the speaker with drunkenness or even a demon, and to claim that neither he himself understands what he is saying nor does the hearer, even though the speaker is speaking without stumbling, and the one who mocks and blames him is perfectly sound as far as hearing and understanding go. And they dared all the more to speak of drunkenness because they heard in their own language and supposed that the others, because of the difference of tongue, did not understand; so they thought they had found a ready occasion [?] for their slander. For they themselves understood, but they guessed that the others present, on whose account they were dragging the miracle down to drunkenness, were far from understanding. And there is nothing surprising in this. For just as, when the Master's authority was driving out demons, they understood and saw the marvels, yet when they ought to have sung hymns and worshipped, they were carried off into blasphemies; and seeing every disease and every affliction put to flight, they turned the surpassing greatness of the miracles and of the beneficence into fuel for envy, slander and murder—so now too, unable to deny the extraordinary and marvellous character of the tongues, they were nevertheless stirred up by envy and were not ashamed to spread the charge of drunkenness over the miracle. And consider the excess of malice, matched by an equal folly. Since it was implausible—especially at the third hour—that the apostles should give themselves over to drunkenness, being men who were heralds of virtue and caught in the midst of fears and dangers, they fall back on the [quality] of the drink

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. (although the grapes were not yet in season, but were only just turning the moisture of the earth into blossom), and they weave their insult into the quality of the drink, saying, 'They are filled with new wine.' For in those whose recklessness of mind is unrestrained, the only aim set before them is not how to say something fitting and not ridiculous, but by whatever means come to hand to give full vent to the madness and perversity of their soul and to console themselves in their helplessness at what they see. That is why what they thought they were saying out of cleverness ends in great folly and senselessness on their part.

QUESTION 82. How is [?] taking the name of the Lord and God in vain [?]? They take the name of the Lord their God in vain. Those of the Old [Covenant] do so by attaching and applying it to idols, by outraging it with a perjured oath, and also by dragging it into jests or other idle talk. (For each of these people uses God's name as a vain thing.) Those of the New do so whenever, contrary to the law laid down, they subject his name to an oath. For those in grace must have something more perfect than those before it. Then there are those who estrange the Son from the Father's essence and rank him with the creatures, and then again, as if out of remorse, adopt him into the name of the Godhead. For in applying the divine name to a creature, these people make it absurdly vain. And there are also those who, in [?] contests, toss it here and there as though it were something ordinary, turning it around and sounding it out as though they were playing at dice—which is what those especially do who trifle in heretical chatter. Further, those also take the name of the Lord our God in vain now who dare to call the image of Christ indifferent, no different from that of the Antichrist or from the idols of pagan worship. For all such people, as far as their daring goes, declare the Master's name vain and useless. One must in every way regard the divine name as awesome and venerable: one must neither delight in oaths at all, nor outrage it with perjury, nor attach it to idols; nor, after the disease of Arius, deify creation against the Creator; nor regard as indifferent what has been deemed worthy of this name and what has received the opposite lot; nor play dice with it in heretical word-battles; nor mix and knead it together with superfluous idle talk. Rather, only in our sacred prayers and rites and in fitting teachings [should one use] that saving and wondrous

QUESTION 83. What is a spirit of Python? Our people of piety have very aptly named 'ventriloquist' the evil and unclean spirit that lurks in the human belly and is fit to dwell in the receptacle of dung. Among the Greeks, most call it 'entrail-diviner', while others name it 'belly-diviner'. Sophocles and Plato, it seems, were ashamed on the demon's behalf of its dwelling in the belly. The one, being a poet with a tongue that enjoyed much licence and independence, granted it the chest instead of the belly and renamed it 'chest-diviner'. The other, perhaps to avoid an obvious falsehood but disguising the insult by another method, calls the belly-dweller 'Eurycles'. Someone of that name, they say, lived long ago and was notorious for this affliction, and from him they assign the name to those who came after. For this tribe of demons seems to love lodging in the dung of the belly, not only of women but of men as well. It leads the people astray and brings utter destruction on those who have been persuaded to heed it. Many of the Greeks also call it Python. I think it was this that lodged in the belly of the slave girl of the Philippians and paid over the proceeds of error to her masters, as though they were its masters too through her. With malicious intent it planned to worm its way even into the favor of the divine Paul by praising him with encomia; and as the wage of its flattery it found banishment from its unjust and beloved dwelling.

QUESTION 84. 'Because all sinned'—the phrase which the divine Paul spoke and which you asked to understand. Some have explained its meaning by supplying 'in whom', namely Adam; others by supplying 'in which', namely death. To me neither seems right. Nothing needs to be supplied, since the phrase is complete in itself. For 'eph' hō pantes hēmarton' here does not point to a person, nor to anything like a person; rather, it sets forth a cause: 'because all sinned', that is, 'for the reason that all sinned.' This construction is found countless times even among outside writers, but the divine Paul will suffice, as the interpreter of his own words. For he says elsewhere, 'For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened,' and then, 'because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over.' From this it is perfectly plain that he used 'eph' hō' to signify a cause; that is, 'for this reason we gr-

-oan: not because we wish to be unclothed, but because we wish to be clothed over.' To put it more broadly, the sense of the phrase is this: 'We groan while we are in the tent, being burdened.' What then? Do you wish to strip off the body that God's hands fashioned, and to which he joined a soul, a divine inbreathing? 'No,' he says, 'God forbid. For I do not groan because I am not stripping it off, but because I am not being clothed over it.' By 'clothing over' he means being clad with incorruption over the body, and being refashioned [?] as a kind of firstfruits. That is why he immediately adds, 'so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.' So: 'I groan, not because I do not lay the body aside, but because I am not clothed [?] with incorruption and eternal life.' Not only from this passage is it clear that 'eph' hō' signifies a cause for him, but also from the very sense of the passage before us. For he says that when Adam had sinned and was then condemned to death, the race descended from him was also made to pay the penalty of death. Yet he does not say this simply or without discernment, but 'because all sinned'—that is, 'because all sinned, as did the one who begot them.' For this is what made them sharers in the punishment as well: sharing in the deed drove them into sharing in the condemnation.

QUESTION 85. What does it mean not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers? What you asked—what is meant by 'Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers'—has, I think, a double sense. Either it means that you must not lean the other way toward unbelievers and heed their myths rather than the teaching of the faithful. Or it means that you must not yoke yourselves to unbelievers as though they were your own and [?], and so plough the same furrow of impiety. The old law also decrees this when it says, 'You shall not mate your cattle with one of another yoke,' or, 'You shall not put your cattle under one of a different kind.' By these words it commands that one must not join one's own animals with animals of a different kind, either for breeding or for any other work: the latter is impractical, and the former overturns the ordinances of nature. But through this legislation about irrational animals it enjoins still more that rational beings should in every way flee fellowship with those who are of a different kind in faith. They should neither come together with them in marriage nor take them on as fellow workers in spiritual work. For such a person will corrupt his fellow labourer rather than help him grow. And why should the nobility of your piety be mixed up with bastard breeds? The sense of the phrase, then, though double, as we said, puts forth the same kind of benefit. The difference in meaning, however,

[?]… — this will evidently also determine the spelling. The first form will have a short syllable after the initial one, while the second will have it lengthened in sound. Farewell in the Lord.

I am most surprised that you, a student of grammar who spends time on the works of the poets, should think that *enkombōsasthai* (“to tie on”) is a barbarian word and not a Greek one. The blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, was not at all concerned with choosing Greek words, yet he took this one into his letters. He did not care about the sound and art of words, or the noise of fine phrases and the clatter of language that some people use to tickle young men's ears and win applause for themselves. What he cared about was planting the salvation of souls in his hearers. You, of all people, remembering Epicharmus and Apollodorus of Carystus, who are your own authors, should have welcomed the word instead of objecting to it. Epicharmus uses it in many places and in various moods: “*enkekombōtai*,” he says, and in the infinitive, “*enkombōsasthai*.” And the Carystian, in *The Woman Who Leaves Her Husband*, says (let me give the quotation for your sake): “Folding the shoulder-cloak double, I tied it on from above.” With these in mind, you should not accuse the herald of truth of barbarism. You should admire him all the more. He looked down on such concerns as child's play, yet on occasion he wrote his letters by the standards of the judges of Greek diction. This lets us see that if the sound and charm of words had mattered to him, he could easily have won great admiration in that field too. And if he had seen any salvation of souls coming from such effort, you would see that his words, through the natural beauty they still have, surpass the spells of Plato, the elegance of Demosthenes and the grand style of Thucydides by as much as those writers are said to surpass the Asiatic orators. (For your sake I would rather not call them “the affected ones.”) He would have managed it with ease. He received far greater, supernatural gifts for the salvation of mankind. If any such gain had grown from this kind of ambition, he would not have fallen short even in this youthful contest. Here too, without even entering the contest, he would have been declared the master of all.

QUESTION [?]. Why, you ask, did the Cherubim appear to the divine prophets in the forms of oxen and lions, eagles and men? As for the

[Notes: Cod. M.: “will have the syllable after the initial one short … into a diphthong”; read φροντίδι, and so Hoe[?]: th[?]]

reasons given by those before us, I think you know them already. I also think you disregard those who said that the Cherubim use those shapes to hint at the principles over which they were appointed as overseers. These interpreters put the Cherubim in charge of oxen and men, eagles and lions, for what reason I do not know. In doing so they bring in the Platonic Ideas under other names, which is more Platonic than pious as a treatment of the question. I would say that the shapes do not display the things the Cherubim oversee. Far from it, for there is one Creator and overseer of all. What the figures do show clearly is this. The one who established the earth, the air and the heaven and everything in them is the very one who gave being to the supercelestial powers and brought them into existence. (These are the places where the creatures shown in the vision live and come to be.) Second, the account teaches through these figures that man, ox, lion, eagle and the other creatures came into being easily, by a word alone. In just the same way that blessed nature was brought from non-being into being at the Creator's [?will]. To display forms and shapes like these in that bodiless and shapeless nature is simply to show that there is one and the same Maker of all. It also shows that the bodiless and intellectual nature came into being with no more labour than the other creatures, since the divine will of infinite power acts in all things alike and with equal strength. If you like, the likenesses in the Cherubim teach a third thing as well. Man, eagle, ox and every other creature obeys the Master's command and shrinks before what he orders. In just the same way the whole supramundane and supercelestial essence yields to his nod and readily carries out every command. Perhaps, if you think it over yourself, you will find other reasons in what has been said, and I would be glad to read them.

QUESTION 88. You ask how we can say “God the Father, God the Son, God the Spirit” without being forced to confess three Gods instead of one. I will tell you clearly and briefly. Truth itself, for which our divine Fathers strove, supplied them with many and varied examples to resolve this difficulty, and they set these out as the need arose. Anyone who wanted to recall them all would end up writing a whole book instead of a letter. I think that would be superfluous anyway. For why [do so,]

when one can readily turn to the ancients? But you (I can find no less offensive way to put it) want new writers in place of what was well written long ago, writers who make their own what came before them and belongs to others. [?] Without those, then, here is a brief and clear answer, [?] without arguing you into it. Listen carefully. It goes like this. When you call the Father God, do you cut off his hypostasis and separate it from the common Godhead that is in him? You would not dare to say so. To honour and name the Father as God in that way would be worse than the gravest insult. It would make him a torn-off piece, an offshoot of the whole and superessential Godhead, the Godhead from which divine union, cohesion and connection come even to things whose lot is to exist in division and flux. You see how you can rightly conceive the Father as God and declare him so. So when you name the Son God, you will not separate him from the same Godhead either, unless you were pretending to declare the Son God in one sense and the Father in another. The same goes for the Spirit, of course, since the same wrong thinking would follow. Each of the three, taken by itself in the mind, is rightly called God, and God, and God. Yet none is in any way cut off from the one Godhead contemplated in it. It follows that, taken together, the three will be glorified not as three Gods but as one God. If each, conceived by itself, were called God because it belonged to a Godhead of its own and of a different kind, then together they could fairly be named three Gods. But each of the three is called God because all are gathered into the same, single Godhead in equal honour. So who can force us to speak of three Gods when they are in no way divided from the Godhead that is contemplated in them and makes them complete? Rather, we must call the three one God, since none of the three is ever divided from the unitary, uncut and undivided

1. As far as I know from memory and from the sense of divine Scripture, the name “God” has three meanings. The first is the One who properly and primarily Is, in whose hand are all things and who rules over all: “For all things are your servants.” 2. In second rank, and by sharing in the first cause, a man too might be called god. This is the man who shapes himself into an imitation of God through the practice of the virtues, as far as a begotten nature can. For the divine and all-[?holy] nature is good in the proper sense, but by participation so are those men who through purity of life [have received] that

[Variant readings: 1. Erroneously for εἷς (“one”). Cod. Man[?]: “the three are one God.”]

[nature's] radiance and been lit up by it. In the same way, “God” is not only the nature that rules over all and holds authority over all things. Men too can be seen counted worthy of this name. The first to receive the title was Enosh, son of Seth. The people of that time honoured him with the divine name for his piety and goodness of character. From him the whole race came to be called gods and sons of gods, as it says somewhere: “The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” By “sons of God” he evidently meant those descended from Enosh. They had relations with the women descended from Cain, corrupted the race and were swept together into impiety and wickedness. To say that angels, a bodiless nature, fell into love for women truly belongs to people who have themselves fallen into mythical notions that are not far from impiety. So from that race, and from other men, all who strove to draw near to God by cultivating their character, and also those who rose to the dignity of just judges and the rank of rulers, received the divine name. “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken,” it says; and, “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High”; and, “God has taken his stand in the assembly of the gods”; and, “In their midst he judges gods”; and, “You shall not revile gods, nor speak evil of a ruler of your people.” These passages make it clear that divine Scripture calls “gods” both the friends of virtue and the friends of justice.

3. There is also a third meaning besides these. In one way it is connected with the second, but in more ways it differs from it. In this sense Moses is made god to Pharaoh. This use of the title is taken by analogy. God told Moses, “Throw down your rod,” to confirm the promises. In the same way Moses ordered Aaron to throw down his rod, to bring about what had been threatened. Moses carried out God's commands, while Aaron carried out Moses' orders toward Pharaoh by scourging Egypt. Aaron became his brother's prophet, just as Moses was God's. That is why Moses is not called simply god, but god to Pharaoh. He did everything as if with [?sovereign] power, with Aaron serving him. This use of the name shares two things with the one before it: it is applied to a man, and to a man who has virtue. But it differs in many other ways, and especially in these. The title proper to Moses becomes his alone and is not shared, as the other is. And in the other case the one who received the title was accepted as god simply, not as god of someone. Here, on the

contrary, he is god of Pharaoh. [?] the sense; but the way in which Moses was called god of Pharaoh, as we said, is clear from what has been said. The case of Aaron proves it no less. He was a man, he practised virtue and, if you like, he presided over the wonders, yet nowhere is he called god of Pharaoh. 4. So the divine title is applied to three different subjects, to one properly and to the others by homonymy. One can also find another meaning of the word, which does not reflect true belief and comes only from the usage of divine Scripture. Scripture is accustomed to call the objects of Greek worship gods. Often it does so ironically: “[Go] and cry to the gods you have chosen for yourselves, and let them save you.” Often it does so simply to identify what is meant: “You shall have no other gods besides me,” it says, and, “You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver and gods of gold.” The examples are countless. Now that the meanings of “God” have been distinguished as four, one must understand the passage set before us for study: “A man who curses god shall bear his sin,” and what follows. Some take “God” here as the true God, God in the proper sense. Others take it as one falsely given that name. Since they start from different premises, they also interpret the rest differently. Those who take “god” here to mean whatever object of worship each of the impious holds explain the sense like this. One must not insult, it says, even what a devotee of Greek religion worships. That object deserves every [?contempt], and it is right for each of the pious to regard it as an abomination and call it one. Still, the man who regards it as a god and then blasphemes it is guilty of sin. By his own judgment and decision such a man is caught blaspheming God, and he makes himself accountable for impiety. Why do it, when he could either not worship it or not revile it? You are combining things that cannot go together, reviling what you worship. If you have condemned it, abandon it. Or do you still come to it as a god while you have not stopped reviling and cursing the thing you serve? “A man, then, a man who curses his god, shall for this bear his sin.” This is not because he cursed a god, but because he let loose a reviling tongue against the one he worships as his god. Then comes: “And whoever names the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death.” If anyone dares to curse and blaspheme the true God and Master of all, death is his penalty. Such a man is caught in a double offence. He has reviled his own object of worship, and he has poured out insult against the Saviour and Creator of all, who is far

above all praise and glory. The first man is guilty of sin, that is, he owes the penalty for drunken abuse and insult. So is the man who curses his own object of worship, even if it bears the name of deity falsely. But the man who drenches the Creator and God of the universe in insults and dares to curse him owes a double and manifold punishment. That is why that blasphemous head deserves to be removed from life by stoning [?], paying the penalty for its unbridled tongue. 6. This is how the first group explains the passage. Those who came after them expound the sense this way. “A man who curses his God shall bear his sin”: the meaning, they say, is plain on its face. Whoever curses the true God, or insults him in some other way, is guilty of a sin that ends in inescapable punishment. And “Whoever names the name of the Lord God” means the following. The Jews were forbidden to utter God's name through their lips at all, meaning the name used alongside the word “God.” It was utterly ineffable and unspeakable, except that it was reserved for the high priests alone, out of honour and reverence for the Divine. For this reason it was not even written in their own letters. They marked it with certain foreign and altered letter shapes, as more mystical symbols, and so hinted at it. There were four letters, and that is why they also called it the Tetragram. So among the Jews, they say, it was equally grave to curse God and to name him, that is, to bring his ineffable name through the lips, and especially into the hearing of ordinary people. That is why death was laid down as the penalty for either act. 7. That is how these people interpret it. This name was engraved on a gold plate and fastened with bands to the high priest's headband, where it guarded and adorned his forehead. It made him appear awesome and venerable to those who saw him. At the same time it charged him that his high-priestly mind must always be united to God and never be torn from that union and blessedness and dragged down to earthly things and to vanity. What this name is, the God of all himself teaches. When Moses asked what his name was, he said, “I am He who is.” Then, confirming that the name he had already declared was his, he says, “I am the Lord; I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob,” and then, “and my name I did not make known to them.” It is as if he said: I have counted you worthy of greater honour than the patriarchs, your forefathers. My name, which I did not make known to them, not even to Jacob when he begged for it, I have made plain to you by declaring, “I am He who is.” Among the Hebrews this is called Aia [?],

and among the Samaritans Iabe [?]. It is written with these letters: yod, aleph, [?]vav, [?]he. These signify that God has no beginning and no end. “He who is” shows this too. The phrase indicates that nothing properly is or exists at all either before him or after him, and this establishes that he always is and is eternally. So whichever interpretation you follow, I think you will fault neither for lack of clarity, nor for straying from the passage. Farewell.

What a fine difficulty you raise! You write that if the divine name is unspeakable and beyond knowledge, how could death be the penalty for uttering it? No one could utter it, however much he wished. But if it was possible to bring it forth with the lips, how was it unspeakable and inexpressible? I think you have the solution already written out for you, and very clearly. The superessential God said, “I am He who is,” and said that this was his name. Moses heard this word. He did not only hear it but told it to the high priests. He did not only tell it but had it written on a gold plate [and] made known [?]. All this makes it perfectly clear that by its own nature the name was both knowable and speakable, and that some people knew it and could speak it among themselves. But it reached neither the ears nor the knowledge of the many, and those who knew it were bound not to pass it on to others. That clearly allowed it to be called unspeakable and inexpressible. So the divine name was unutterable and unspeakable, not because by nature it could not be spoken with words and tongue (that is clear, since anyone who wishes can now speak it), but because it was not speakable or knowable to all. Even those entrusted with knowing it could not, for fear of death, tell it to others or make it known in any other way. There you have it, my excellent friend: how the name of God was unknown and inexpressible among the Jews, and yet how some of them, if they wished, could say it themselves and teach others to know and pronounce it as they did. They would have done so, had the fear of the punishment hanging over them not been greater than the desire of those who sought to be initiated into such things. As you see, there is nothing difficult here, nothing that forces us into any perplexity.

QUESTION [?]. What is meant by “I have often intended to come to you”? “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often

intended to come to you, and have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit,” and what follows. You wanted to learn the meaning of this passage. It can be taken as a hyperbaton, so that the order runs: “I do not want you to be unaware that I have often intended to come to you, so that I might have some fruit among you too, but I have been prevented until now.” Arranged this way, the construction of the passage is clear and gives the sense of the sentence. Someone might object: if their faith was being proclaimed in the whole world (he bore them this witness a little earlier), what fruit did he want to bring by coming himself? We will answer: a great deal. They had indeed come to believe, and because of the city's fame the report of their faith had spread to everyone. Still, they lacked much. This is clear from what he said a little before: “so that you may be strengthened.” Who needs strengthening, if not those who are wavering? It is clear again later in the letter, when he urges them not to judge one another and to avoid dissensions and stumbling blocks. Throughout the whole letter one can see many such things, which show that they were still incomplete and newly established. So there is nothing improbable in their faith being proclaimed while they still needed much help from Paul, and the watering and fruitfulness that his words would bring. Notice how he says, “so that I might have some fruit among you too.” On the one hand he shows that their fruit was counted as Paul's own fruit. So he rejoiced in the good deeds of others as another man rejoices in his own achievements. “So that I might have some fruit,” he says, treating their fruit as his own. On the other hand he makes clear that he was setting out on the journey to them for their benefit. Besides, if one looks closely, their fruit truly is Paul's fruit. The salvation of men was his work, his zeal and his field to farm, and so was presenting them bearing the fruit of piety and the virtues. So he rightly says, “so that I might have some fruit.” In a few words he makes both points plain, completely and elegantly: that they bear the fruit of faith in their good deeds, and that he [bears fruit] in them. For in their fruitfulness Paul's farming was brilliantly displayed. So if one takes the passage as a hyperbaton, the sense unfolds as above. The great Paul uses this figure often, as he also uses ellipsis, periphrasis and the construction *apo koinou*, and he handles every kind of style. Yet it is also possible not to read it as a hyperbaton but to keep the order as it stands, and draw out a sense like this: “I have often intended to come to you.” Why, then, did you not come? “I have been prevented,” he says, “until now.” For what reason? “So that I might have some [?]

"…that I might have [some fruit] among you also." That is, he was hindered for this reason: so that he would not come too soon and find you still without fruit. Had he found you unripe, he would have blamed himself for untimely haste, and you for slowness where there ought to have been none. "Therefore I put off my coming, hoping for the harvest of the cultivation." While it is not yet even looking toward budding, and is already falling short even in its flowers, one is reluctant to be present, though one longs to enjoy it [?]. But when, after the budding and the flowers, it shows itself and comes to maturity, then the journey toward it is filled with joy and gladness. Such a journey does not know how to count its labours, nor to divide its zeal among other things. What then? If they are bearing fruit, what need is there for Paul to come? A great need. For he was not expecting all the fruit, but some: "That I might have some fruit," he says, "among you also." It is superfluous and pointless to urge someone who already bears fruit perfectly to bear fruit. In the same way it is laborious and disheartening to urge people on to perfection when there is not even good hope of reaching it. And even if there was some fruit among them, and that fruit perfect, not even so would that winged and lofty man simply have been held back from coming. He both knows himself to be, and calls himself, "a debtor, not to Greeks and barbarians only, but also to the wise and the foolish." With his eagerness he did not stop seeking more than what already existed. So even if they grew weary in their works [?], he himself did not cease doing his own part, but pressed on, seeking to add still greater things. So much for this interpretation of the passage. But the meaning can also be seen another way. This explanation is perhaps simpler, but I think it is more suited both to Paul's intention and to his wording. "Often," he says, "I purposed to come to you, but I was hindered until now." Why? "That I might have some fruit" — as if you were to say, "There was some fruit standing in my way, which I had to gather first, and only then come to you." What, then, was that fruit, and among whom was it being gathered? He will tell us himself. At the end of the epistle, as though summing up for himself what he had said in the preface, he says: "Therefore I was hindered from coming to you" — which amounts to the same thing as "I was hindered until now." Then: "But now, having no more place in these regions" — that is, having clearly finished the work — "I will come to you." You see that what kept him from coming was the fruit being gathered in those regions. To leave his labour there unfinished was not in keeping with Paul's soul and zeal. And notice how this unfolding of the passage needs no figure of hyperbaton and meets no counter-arguments. Rather, it fits both the words and the aim of the divine Paul better than the other explanations. Nor does "among you" stand against it in any way, for it is the beginning of what follows,
