and is not joined to "That I might have some fruit." It means, as it were: "Among you also I am a debtor, as among the rest of the Gentiles, to Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish." He says this so that they would not object: "Why then did you make it your concern to gather the fruit in other regions, but take no account of us?" "Yes," he says, "among you also I am a debtor, as among the rest of the Gentiles. This is what I hasten toward, this is what I seek. I am in debt to all, and there is no one for whom I am not held fast by great concern." But enough of this for now. The method of a commentary is different from what the form of a letter requires. So it is not possible to do either cleanly, as the rules of the art demand, while interpreting in the form of a letter. If the occasion grants the freedom to interpret properly, then perhaps, God willing, I will have the grace to speak more fully, and you to hear.

QUESTION [?]

You wonder whether the letters of the divine Paul are composed with such stylistic forms. Do not be annoyed with me for telling the truth: you have not yet looked down into the depth of the wisdom in that man. If a more diligent study of his words should take hold of you, with favour from above evidently looking kindly on you, you would rather wonder how so great a grace of wisdom had escaped you, and how the beauty of his native eloquence had not found in you a warm lover. I am not yet speaking of his wisdom in doctrines and faith. Not even you, I think [?], dispute that with us. I mean all the power and strength of speech that makes him admired. How then was he "unskilled in speech"? In the same way that he was "the first of sinners"; "the least of the apostles," "one untimely born" of them all; "the refuse of the world"; "not worthy to be called an apostle"; "the offscouring of all"; "a spectacle to angels and to men." Who is this? The one who could have stood on his authority as an apostle of Christ. The one who laboured more abundantly than all. The one who was set apart for God even before he loosed his mother's birth-pangs. The beholder of things unseen and hearer of things unutterable. The fragrance of Christ to God. The one who carried about in his body the dying of Jesus, and his life as well. So this man, so great and so eminent, was "one untimely born," "offscouring," "spectacle," and "refuse" — and in just that way "unskilled in speech." Some of these titles reflected the opinion of those who did not grasp the depth of the preaching. Others he conceded himself, bearing them with the moderation and gentleness of his character. What then? Does our faith rest on the wisdom of men? God forbid! It rests on the power of God, through which even the unskilled are made wise. Is the wisdom of God, then, the wisdom of this age and of its rulers? Who would say that? For that kind of wis-

dom has instead been abolished by the foolishness of the cross. I mean the error of impious doctrines, the persuasive speech that comes to its aid, the intricacy and art of malicious sophisms. The soul is mortal, they say, because it shares and suffers with the body. The world has no Creator, because, unlike fire, [?] neither does water tend to be carried [?]. Marriage should be held in common, because the city is more united in mutual love that way. The living come from the dead, since we also sit down after standing. There must be many gods, because the things that need providence are many, and there is a danger that a single god would grow weary from being occupied with the common care. Or else necessity compels the first to produce something inferior, so that he is not stripped of the privilege of being the first principle, and the second in turn produces another lower still, and so on to infinity. These foolish notions go beyond the last extreme of insanity. They are worthy of a soul that is truly mortal, and of hemlock. Paul, truly wise in things divine and human, drove this wisdom of the age out of the world through the wisdom of God in a mystery, and kept the minds of the faithful closed to it. Such wisdom is foolishness with God. The reasonings of those who are wise in it are vain, and caught in their own craftiness, they are seized by the simple word of truth. As in the past, so now every pious mind spits upon it: its long drivel, its pitfalls for the soul, its snares of the Evil One, its great workshop of perdition. But correctness of words, and of the way they are put together — how does that harm piety? What damage does it do to those who use it? Into what error, small or great, does it trip them? If the Fashioner of nature is himself also the craftsman of tongues, how does it not follow that the disciples of the Word should above all use fitting speech? Did Christ not take unlearned disciples, then — and I would even say, most unlearned, and if you like, more voiceless than the fish they used to catch? Yes. But just as he took unlearned men, so he took tax collectors and fishermen. Did he leave the tax collectors collecting taxes and the fishermen fishing? Where would there be anything in that worthy of wonder or of Christ's power? And how could anyone escape the refutation that their works provide? So neither did he leave unlearned those whom he took from that condition. Instead of fishermen he made them fishers of men: "Come," he says, "follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Instead of tax collectors he made them saviours of storm-tossed souls. Instead of unlearned men he made them teachers of the world. He filled them with divine and heavenly wisdom, and showed them lacking in nothing of human wisdom either, wherever need called for it. Otherwise, how did they engage in argument with Stoics, with Epicureans, with countless other errors that had left behind a great name for eloquence? How did the rush of his speech and the easy flow of his words, coming together with the miracle, lead his hearers to take Paul for Hermes? And had he not been quick to tear his garments, the sacrifices due to the gods would have been offered to him publicly as an honour.

I pass over for now the rest of his power of extemporaneous speech: in churches, before the people, in court, in the synagogues of the Jews, in the marketplace, as he taught, refuted, exhorted, made his defence and bore witness. I pass over how great it was with individuals and with crowds, before judges and before slanderers. I pass over how by his speaking he won over the king of the Jews. That man would very nearly have gone over to the Christians, had not the swollen pride of rule and of the purple got in his way and kept him from the full precision of the preaching — something that has often ruined many at the decisive moment. I pass over how he restrained those who were murderous against him and thirsting for his blood: by addressing them he persuaded them to take up the care of his safety. I pass over how he went up to the Areopagus into the midst of men puffed up with eloquence. That is the Areopagus where, as Greek myths love to tell, gods both received and gave judgment against one another and against men. Standing there, he had to answer not to one speaker but to all the learned among men — if indeed the Athenians then surpassed other men, and those of the Athenians who held power in the Areopagus surpassed the Athenians. Even so, he so shook their souls with his words and so transformed them that many of them hung upon his tongue and his words, cast everything away, and turned for the whole of their lives to piety. They were seen as imitators of the man who had engraved deep in their souls the doctrines of virtue and of right worship. Were these and similar things done without fitting speech? Who would have paid any attention to him if he spoke barbarously and could not even pronounce the words correctly? How could what he did not even know how to say have seemed to others to be soundly thought out — let alone have persuaded them to share his mind? "But grace from above was at work." I say so too, and above all: grace from above, not art. What comes from art is human and common, but what comes from grace is heavenly and belongs to the apostles. Grace was at work. But the first thing it worked was this: that its ministers should utter nothing unworthy of it. For this too, no less than anything else, leads opponents to perceive the invincible power that strengthens them. Somewhere it says: "Now when the Jews saw the boldness of Peter and John." What boldness, if not clearly their boldness in speech, with which they silenced their shameless questioning? Then: "And perceiving that they were unlettered and unskilled men, they marvelled." We see fishermen as orators without letters, men with no art, pouring wisdom from their lips. What is this? Where have these superhuman gifts come to them from? We know one thing: "that they had been with Jesus." You see how the strength of their words roused their enemies to wonder no less than the miracle performed right before them, and

brought them forward, had they been willing, toward the knowledge of the truth. See from another passage, too, how much they feared their power in speech. They ordered them not to speak at all. What are you saying? If the unlettered man only moves his lips, your reputation immediately collapses? An old doctrine that has held sway so long gives way to unskilled speech? A people raised on the ordinances of Moses, fixed in its resolve to live and die by their antiquity, goes over to a new tongue? "Yes," he says. "For the unskilled man does not utter unskilled words but words of wisdom. Nor, as an unlettered man, does he utter barbarous ones, but graceful and clear words, like someone who has gone through every art. A native persuasiveness sits upon their lips. By it whole nations of orators and herds of the unlearned are drawn to what is preached to them, as if bound with unbreakable bonds. That is why I forbid them to speak. I see that with a few words many have left their ancestral ways and gone over to them. Often with a single discourse, even those who always stood with us against them, and were their bitterest enemies, are now ranked among their followers and well-disposed disciples. This forces me to order them to be silent. For this reason I do not allow them even to open their mouths: because of the boldness of their speech, its strength, its native persuasiveness." You see how far the teaching speech of the apostles made the Jews cower and stand dumbfounded. Yet in Paul this grace shone out more abundantly still. Shall we call the chief of the apostles as a witness to the wisdom in this man? "Just as," he says, "our brother Paul wrote, according to the wisdom given to him." He both knows and testifies that Paul's wisdom is a divine gift. Then, as if hailing the depth and density of his writings as divine and extolling them, he says: "in which there are some things hard to understand." As if to say: the reader of Paul's writings needs a sharp mind, divine help, wise teaching [?], and steady understanding. That is why the ignorant and unstable not only gain nothing, but trip themselves up and perish besides. Paul was also rich in the gift of tongues to which he was not accustomed and which he had never even heard, and even in these he yielded first place to no one: "I thank my God," he says, "that I speak in tongues more than you all." If, then, he had invincible power even in foreign tongues, because the inspiration of the Spirit made him wise, how could it be reasonable for him to corrupt the Greek language, which was already familiar to him [?]? Would he excel in the tongues by which he was to win many to piety, but give cause for laughter and mockery in the one by which he was to win nearly all mankind? And indeed, not even his enemies thought him so careless in speech. As for the testimony from enemies that points to his praise, there is no one

Notes: ἐκείνῳ: C. M.: ἐκείνοις. ἐπιπνοίας: C. M.: ἐπινοίας.

who would not be put to shame by it, however proud he might wish to be of being contentious about everything. Pay attention to me, then, to the testimony. The Jewish nation thirsted for Paul's blood, because once the heavenly light had shone around him, he went over wholly to the one he had persecuted. And they were inflamed all the more toward murder when his preaching left their synagogues empty. Every art of slander and every device was set in motion. They armed their fellow countrymen for the man's slaughter, not only with silver spears, as the saying goes, but also with lies, deceit, anger and audacity. In their hopes their hands were already dripping with the warm defilement. But their hopes deserted them, leaving their leaping and rejoicing in vain, because the champion proved stronger than all their devices in his defences. At last, at a loss before his power in speech and his invulnerability, they hired an orator for pay to plead for the slanderers. They thought the accused could no longer escape that man's arts and the intricacies of his words, even if he were ten thousand times innocent; they did not even consider it in doubt. But Paul, truly wise in all things divine and human, confronted even a man so equipped by art and by pay. Through the wisdom and grace clearly supplied to him from above, he so withstood him in argument and fought it out that he routed and shamed him, art, fee and all. He filled the high priests and priests, and all who had plotted his murder together, with astonishment and helplessness. So they not only regretted their attempt, but, though more savage than ever in their rage, imposed silence on themselves as a sentence for two whole years. You see how the power of the champion's words forced the most hostile, against their will, to bear witness. And if Paul's wisdom in deed and word has been proclaimed even by his enemies, how will it not be honoured exceptionally and worthily by those who were initiated into piety by it? Do not suppose that by wisdom, strength and power of speech I mean this overworked, affected kind. That kind adulterates the native beauty of speech with cosmetic drugs and flowers, and with artificial colours turns the youthful and dissolute toward itself. Nor do I mean the kind that puts on a sullen, unsmiling air for no good purpose. It sits beneath a deep darkness of obscurity, confuses and overawes the ignorant and vulgar with the gloom around it, and preens itself as it drags blind lovers after it. Nor do I mean the kind that breaks its neck chasing the licence of the poets, consorting with newfangled impulses and playing the fool. I mean the kind that is sober in its expression, plain in teaching, foremost in instructing, unique in persuading, and

clear in unfolding the nature of things through thoughts suited to them. Where emphasis is needed, it reveals the truth of hidden things in a deeply mystical and initiatory way. These are the marks of the native, orderly wisdom of speech that profits life. The others belong to the kind that delights irrational sense. It rejoices rather in deviations and a novelty-seeking character, looks to no benefit, and dissolves into applause, flattery and endless drivel. So it was not in keeping with Paul's high-mindedness to imitate, even remotely, the author you carry on your very head for his power in speech and all but worship: the man of "ἦ δ' ὅς" ("said he") and "ἦν δ' ἐγώ" ("said I"). Someone, I believe, even used to praise him for these, as though they were among his special glories. I would add, quite reasonably, "ἐπεπόνθει ἐγώ" ("I had suffered"), "ᾔδει ἐγώ" ("I knew") and "ἠκηκόει ἐγώ" ("I had heard"). I do not know how anyone could go through his works without soon falling into a long fit of disgust. He grew so soft and effeminate in his novelties of wording that he would no longer leave the verbs even a mark of person, but forced their character into a counterfeit form that shows no person at all. I pass over for now the man of "the fatnesses of the eyes" [?], who was suffering in his soul rather than speaking. I pass over the one who loved "the trusty hopes and stable conditions of the flesh" — more to his misery than to his gain — and who wantoned in many such chatterings and evil follies. I would by no means make the wonderful Paul an imitator in speech of either of these, or of anyone else like them — far from it — any more than in deeds or in reverence. Nor, for that matter, is the Gorgianic play with its jingles [?], almost on a par with the leaps of dancers on the stage, fit to express the depth and steadiness of Paul's lofty thoughts. He took as the rule for his tongue the kind of words that could convey the meaning of such great matters worthily, neither falsifying anything nor running riot. "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!" And: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?" Or: "Who has given to him first, so that he will be repaid?" "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us." For this wisdom, through which he uttered such things, I revere the teacher of the world as divine. I would pray for the daring to revere him as he deserves. He sets out the thought in clear and steady diction, and offers its benefit to all alike. What would you say on observing the purity of his language? It is not only in correctness of diction and in the symmetry of harmoniously compact periods. It shows also in whatever is directed to narrating events, where he drags in nothing needless from outside, both in the figurative use of words and in

Rom. 11:35. Gal. 3:[?]

…he turns away from harshness and, with good judgment, dismisses it. Yet he has blended clarity with grandeur throughout, as well as anyone else, or rather as no one else has. I do not yet mention that he varies his style with deliberative and legislative speech, or that his discourse concerns divine matters and the things most honoured among people, or even that no one can imitate the brilliance and radiance of his expression. “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me.” “So I run, not aimlessly; so I box, not as one beating the air.” And: “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave; therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” And: “For our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we also await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.” These passages are exceedingly wonderful (how could they not be?), and among other reasons because brilliance and purity come together in them to the highest degree. But what is he like when he speaks in maxims and [?] makes steady pronouncements, when he refutes where he must, rebukes as he must, and solemnly warns? “For by whatever a person is overcome, to that he is also enslaved.” “Bad company corrupts good morals.” And: “This I say, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption.” “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” And: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked.” And: “Look, I, Paul, say to you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.” And: “I testify to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is obliged to keep the whole law.” And: “Does any of you, having a case against another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous and not before the saints?” Collecting the instances of his grandeur would amount to reading his writings through from beginning to end, so thoroughly is dignity itself blended through all his words. But what of his character? “Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” And: “For I am the least of the apostles, and am not fit to be called an apostle.” “Remembering your tears, I long to see you, so that I may be filled with joy, being reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice.” “I wish that those who unsettle you would even cut themselves off!” And: “Without us you have become kings, and indeed I wish that you had

become kings!” And countless other passages. Does he, then, fall short of any of those who have worn out their whole lives on these things? He did not, I think, bother with their pursuits even so far as learning their names, but with an untaught tongue he [?] the orators. Or perhaps his character and clarity, blended with grandeur, are thus outstanding, but he lacks speed? Yet who is so naturally gifted at using vigour in such a well-blended way? “It is God who justifies; who is to condemn? It is Christ who died, or rather who was raised.” “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial; all things are lawful for me, but not all things build up.” “What advantage, then, has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, because they were entrusted with the oracles of God. What then, if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means!” And: “What then? Are we any better off? Not at all.” And again: “When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we speak kindly.” Why should anyone attempt to measure the open seas by drops? To submit those to a count of drops and to try to set out Paul’s wisdom in words come to the same thing. For he did not even pass over adornment, though he disregarded it entirely. Rather, he stripped it of the artifice with which one might have embellished oneself, clothed it in what is natural, something one would scarcely hope for, and so brought it forth to be admired, so that this very thing stands before those who can see it as the rule and pattern of true beauty, far surpassing what is sophisticated and contrived for prettiness. But there is nothing like hearing him himself. “How then will they call on one in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in one of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things!’” Again: “If then there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation of love, any affection and compassion, make my joy complete.” Then: “Affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope, and hope does not put us to shame.” Thus the style of the Epistles of the great Paul gives form to the ideas of every excellence in speech and is adorned with fitting and appropriate figures. It deserves to hold the place of an archetype and model and to be emulated, and sensible people, at least, have no right to describe it as written in imitation of others. Nor is it easy to find anyone it could be said to portray, since Paul’s words are the fruit not of study but of a supernatural conception: the wealth of wisdom, the pure and translucent spring of truth, gushing with saving delight. This is a brief gleam of the fearful lightning from above, leaping from the apostolic lips; this is a measured outflow of the divine power that is made perfect in weakness, [?] the world,

watering it; this is the work of the grace that operates in earthen vessels. O incontestable testimony to awesome and wondrous mysteries! Wisdom dripping from a layman’s tongue, a standard of eloquence from an untrained mouth, the art of rhetoric from unlearned lips! And what do you say? Does some doubting thought or perplexity about Paul’s wisdom in speech still trouble you? Or rather, will you still quibble over whether [?] he shaped his Epistles with figures? Or would you not instead condemn your former views, since the gift of such great graces escaped your notice? And what would you say if you looked more deeply into the other side of his power in discourse: how he handles the arrangement of the main points; his intelligence as he introduces and manages his material, raising objections and answering them; what he is like in the invention of arguments; the fertility of his elaboration; how ready he is to persuade, how rich in comparisons and examples, how great in enthymemes; and all the other power akin to these? If you were granted the chance to go through these, even if you chose to devote your study to nothing else, they would move you to a truly keen love and a sweet wonder: the man’s handling, in these respects, of the question of food sacrificed to idols; the passage where he sets out to purge the arrogance of those who were puffed up because they spoke in tongues; and indeed how the law was bound to give way to grace. But enough about these things, and that within the limits of a letter. If we are ever together (and we shall be; a divine message foretells this to me), then we will discuss these matters with you more fully than now.

25. However, the passage, “Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, whether prophecy according to” [?]

the proportion of faith; or service, in serving; or the one who teaches, in teaching; or the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, with simplicity; the one who leads, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” This passage would be a splendid example of amplified speech. For it has the particulars following immediately on the general: on the one hand, prophecy and service following “gift”; on the other, following service, its more particular forms, teaching and exhortation; and, if you like, following exhortation, giving, leading and mercy. For the one who gives, the one who leads and the one who shows mercy all serve as a kind of comfort and encouragement to those who benefit from them. Moreover, it is amplified in another way as well, for to some of the gifts he attaches their cause. And it is not only amplified but also varied by the figure of the word “taken in common”; and it also displays what is specifically called ellipsis. For “having” is carried in common over “whether prophecy, whether service,” but in what is called zeugma it is split off at “whether the one who teaches, whether the one who exhorts,” and in the following parts of the sentence. For although “having” was spoken at the start in the plural, we understand it in the singular with “the one who teaches” and “the one who exhorts” and the rest. Again, the same passage hangs entirely in suspense, with no resting point at all, unless some verb is supplied in thought. For unless we supply “let him abide” with service, teaching and exhortation [correct to παρακλήσει], and before these with “whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith,” adding “in prophecy”; and unless, again, we attach “let him give,” “let him lead” and “let him show mercy” to what follows, we would have made the whole passage incomplete and defective. So the passage was shaped by three figures at once.

26. Next, again, the elliptical figure appears. For in “Let love be without hypocrisy,” “let it be” is lacking, and so on in what follows. [?] Another period takes up [?] “Abhorring what is evil”; it runs to a very great length [?] and extends into a long breath-period, nor is it free of amplification either. For “abhorring what is evil” finds its completion in “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.” For the end and, as it were, the summing up of all the other virtues is to extend goodness and love even to enemies and to those who hate us. It is by this practice, the saving and unerring word assured us, that men on earth are made like the Father in heaven.

But there is a great multitude of such examples in the writings of the divine Paul. Of these I have set out a few, for the reasons I gave at the beginning, to which I attribute the causes, and also why I have not gone through the other figures he used, nor discussed at all the origin of figures, their differences, their number and their use, where figurative speech came from, and for what reason the Greek language adopted it. For I would not think it right either that you, a man of such stature, should need any instruction at all on these matters, or that we should show off by teaching about them. Some of these things are elementary and suited to beginners; others have become clear and easy to understand through the examples we have given [?]. The character of the apostolic writings, then, is naturally formed [?] by the figures mentioned and by many others. But I would not gladly say, as I have often disclaimed, that he wrote these things by art and study. I do not so belittle that heavenly man, who by his preaching made the whole inhabited world into one house or one city. Rather, he did it by the innate power of his intellect and his energy in all things, or rather by the grace of the Spirit [?], which never failed to supply him throughout with the wealth of innate knowledge and a sagacity beyond the human, and through which he had for effortless use and command what others barely attain [?] through labor and study. As for you, illuminated purely by the rays of truth that come from there, may you, just as you have gained sight in the contemplative part, so too have your practical life ordered throughout by the commandments that come from there.

603 [?] What is the meaning of “Let your light shine before men,” and what follows? To your long and elaborately contrived difficulty we offer a simple and brief solution. “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven” is clearly an exhortation to virtue. But “Do not do your almsgiving before men” [forbids] love of glory, and that is the removal of vice. How then could the removal of vice be in conflict with the exhortation to virtue? On the contrary, the cutting away of the one rather establishes the existence of the other. For the man who disregards human glory for the sake of the divine laws is the ardent lover of virtue, and he has the Divine to make his works public and cause them to shine like light. But the man who pursues mercy for the sake of human glory is the one who carries off, plainly, also the [?] of display. As far, then, as the divine verdict differs from human zeal, so far does a man who practices virtue and pleases God differ from a man who puts forward his action as a hunt for human praise. The saving word commands all who are eager to have God as witness and herald of their works to flee the imitation of such a man, and not to put their own devices ahead of the testimony from above.

QUESTION [?]. What is the meaning of “My Father is greater than I”? Our Fathers have understood this saying of the Gospel, “My Father is greater than I,” in different ways, though no interpretation does harm to the truth. Some say that he is called greater by reason of cause; and this presents not a difference of essence, but rather identity and sameness of nature. For every father, since he precedes his son as cause, rather binds together and maintains through himself the unity of essence, even though the separation of the hypostases, which is so great, especially among created beings, flowing and multiplied from countless circumstances, is forced into otherness. So the Father's being greater than the Son by cause belongs to sameness of essence and sameness of nature, and in no way to difference of essence. Others have taken “greater” with reference to his humanity. For they say that just as “going to the Father,” and “I will no longer speak much with you,” and “the ruler of the world is coming” and, searching, finds nothing at all

How is there no conflict between “In my Father's house there are many dwelling places” and “If I go, I will prepare a place for you”? There is no conflict in meaning between “In my Father's house there are many dwelling places; if it were not so, would I have told you, ‘I am going to prepare a place for you’?” and what is said next, “If I go, I will prepare a place for you.” For in providence and foreknowledge, or, if you like, in essence and existence, the places were certainly prepared beforehand by the God of all for all who have lived worthily of heavenly glory. But as for inaugurating them and showing them to be truly dwelling places, if indeed they are properly called dwelling places, in which those who abide take up their lodging, no one anywhere showed this until the saving cross, the descent into Hades and the ascent of the Master into the heavens. But he himself, having ascended into the heavens with the human nature he had assumed, and having inaugurated for us “a new and living way,” as the blessed Paul says, made the dwelling places there truly more ready and all but visible to the worthy. So the dwelling places are with the Father, and the Son, having gone, prepared them.

[?] the cause of right deeds [?]. [?] swelling pride and [?] drawn down to moderation. [?] “Do not rejoice that [?], but that your names

just as these belonged to the assumed human nature and not to the Word, so too does “My Father is greater than I”; for this saying stands among those and is spoken in the same way as they are. Others granted that “greater” refers to the Word, but not simply or according to essence. Rather, since the incarnation is the utmost self-emptying and humiliation, in which the Word emptied and humbled himself, “taking the form of a servant,” it would follow that, compared with one who never underwent self-emptying and humiliation, he is said to have taken the lesser part. For in this very respect the one who was not emptied, being in greater pre-eminence, is greater than the one who was emptied, who, without lowering his own pre-eminence in any way, passed in the human nature even through the most shameful sufferings, I mean the cross and death.

One might also, not unreasonably, take the saying as spoken with reference to the disciples' understanding. For since they were still imperfectly disposed toward their God and teacher, they thought the Father much greater: partly because the Mosaic laws proclaimed the Father to them more plainly than the Son, and partly because the Savior kept turning them toward the Father again and again. Since such an opinion was fixed in them (that is why they said, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us”), he takes his stand addressing their supposition and says something like this: that they were acting inconsistently with their own professions by giving themselves over to grief “because I said, ‘I am going to the Father.’ For if you loved me,” and you think the Father is greater, “you ought to rejoice that I am going to the one who is greater; for you insisted that if only I showed him to you, he would suffice in place of everything.” Indeed, if someone understood the Father to be called greater than the Son in this sense as well, he would not stray from what is fitting. And perhaps nothing prevents us also from taking this as a word of condescension, shaped toward the lowlier because of the weakness of the hearers. For there is much such accommodation in sayings of this kind, for the gain and salvation of those not yet able to bear more perfect things, as in “I will ask the Father, and he will send another Paraclete,” and “I thank you that you always hear me,” and countless others. How then is it clear that these were shaped for weak hearing? The Savior himself, the fount of wisdom and the abyss of understanding, taught it, interpreting his own words when he said: “I knew that you always hear me, but I said it because of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.” But for a letter, I think, this gives sufficient instruction on the question asked.

…was written in heaven. And: "Many will say to me on that day, 'Did we not do many mighty works in your name?' And I will say to them, 'I do not know you.'" For this reason Paul too is allowed to wrestle with certain trials, so that, as he himself says, he may not be too elated, and so that the surpassing greatness of the revelations, which brings with it [?] a need for every kind of discipline, might be checked, and the skittish leaps by which human nature is carried away toward conceit might be cut short. And if you like, there is another reason. Afterward the chief of the apostles was to bear those [?] threats, the bitter persecutions and the countless slaughters with an unshaken and unwavering mind, and in this way he would summon his tormentors to marvel at the Lord's help. Seeing that the man who had fallen at the voice of a servant girl now stood so immovable against such great sufferings, he might draw them over and, through this, lead them from Jewish lowliness to the great mystery of godliness. And third, it seems to me a splendid and great example for the guidance of souls. For the generations that followed, what is more splendid than the chief of the apostles, whenever someone who has grown weak is caught and wishes to restore [?] what is perfect? The chief of the disciples had seen some mighty works and performed others himself. He had received so much teaching and had such long and varied experience of the Teacher. Yet after denying him three times, he not only cleansed the sin through repentance and hot tears but was restored to the very dignity of apostleship. If so, then I must not grow slack and give up when I slip through weakness. I must rise quickly to repentance and, considering the riches of the Lord's kindness, dedicate myself wholly, in contrition [?] of heart, to him who bore our diseases and our weaknesses. For these reasons, then, I think, and others like them, Peter was allowed to be caught in the sin. But it was not because the Teacher foretold the denial that Peter was forced by some necessity of foreknowledge into what he did not will. Otherwise you would soon be attributing the cause of all wicked deeds to the source of good things. For he also foretold the betrayal to Judas and the bloodguilt of the Jews. And even where he did not foretell, he certainly foreknew that the first man would choose contempt for the commandment he had been given over obedience [?] to it; and he foreknew the fratricide of Cain [?], the hardness of heart of Pharaoh and the lawlessness of Saul. But why should I go through them one by one? It is not only these. The deeds of whole cities and entire nations are also encompassed by foreknowledge: the unspeakable deeds of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the idol-madness of the Greeks, the Egyptians and nearly all the barbarians over many ages. But why mention these? Consider the very sower and architect of evils, and the powers that were torn away with him from the lot above. Was [God] ignorant of his arrogance and his plotting against human beings, of their unsurpassable wickedness? What… [Variant readings: "hardness"; C. M.: "lowliness." Photius, Questions.]

…then? Since the wisdom that works good was ignorant of none of these things, shall we for that reason remove the blame from those who, with a will bent on evil, exchanged the better for the worse, and condemn the one who foreknew? Where does such an idea have any place? Suppose I see someone rushing toward a cliff and then recognize that he will be destroyed. Or suppose I see someone drawing a sword against his neighbor, so that I am not ignorant of the murder. Is it then just for me to pay the penalty instead of the one who did it? If this is laughable and senseless, how is it not madness and effrontery, instead of demanding justice from those responsible for wicked deeds, to drag slander against divine foreknowledge? And if foreknowledge is not answerable for the guilty, is foretelling liable? For a thing was not done because it was foreknown or foretold. Rather, since they were going to do what they ought not to do by a self-chosen inclination, they could not escape the unescapable, all-seeing eye of God. This is why blessed Peter, too, did not deny because the Lord foretold it. Rather, because he was going to slip into the denial, it was foreknown by the Teacher and proclaimed in advance. I will give you a brief solution to the difficulty. Read "If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true" as a question. By it the Savior, first of all, refutes and repels the supposition [?] of the Jews. But take "Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true" as the Lord casting his own vote and pronouncing judgment, and the pretext for the difficulty will find no way in. Or, if you prefer (for the power of truth is not at a loss for solutions), our Lord Jesus Christ was twofold, being of divinity and humanity. We will understand "If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true" according to the law of human nature, as we do many other things. For no human being is trustworthy when testifying about himself. But "If I testify about myself, my testimony is true" is spoken with the dignity and authority of the divinity. For the nature that is highest of all and Lord of all needs no testimony or confirmation from elsewhere. It not only puts forward its own trustworthiness from within itself; for all other things that come to be trustworthy, it is also the source of trustworthiness, just as it is the source of their being and existence. But as a summary I think this is enough. There are also quite a few solutions of the passage that range more broadly than the present ones. Since it is easier for those who read the books of the Fathers to come across them,

I see no need to take on [?] the labors of others myself when the matter is so easy; I willingly pass over them for now. But one should know that the saying "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing" leads us into no dispute either. It can be read as a question, or understood as spoken according to the laws proper to human nature. When the Lord says, "Where I am going you know, and the way you know," the disciple's reply is neither inconsistent nor contradictory: "Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?" For the Lord's saying was not spoken simply or absolutely, nor without some premise going before it. It has a preceding statement to which it is joined: "I am coming again, and I will take you." Having said this, he adds a clause with "so that," dividing the purpose of the taking into these three: that the disciples may be where the Teacher is, that they may know where he is going, and that they may know the way. For he says, "I am coming again, and I will take you to myself." Why? "So that where I am, you also may be; and so that you may know where I am going; and so that you may know the way." The "so that" plainly serves all three purposes, as it often does. So he was not saying that knowing the way and where he was going were already theirs, any more than being with him in heaven. These things were stored up for them for the time when he would return and take them. Since three things were promised to the disciples at his return, Thomas marveled at the greatness of the promises. He had not yet grasped even the lesser, so he naturally questions how they will come to share in the greater. For it is a lesser thing simply to know where a place is than to know the way leading there, and that in turn is less than already living in the very place that is sought. The disciple's question, then, is consistent and in no way conflicts with the Teacher's words. For the Lord did not say that they already knew the way, or where he was going, or that they were already with him in heaven. He said that these things would be theirs once he had returned and they had been taken. The Lord's return may be his appearance to the disciples after the cross and the resurrection. At that time they truly recognized him as God and learned both the way and where he was going. They no longer had any doubt that they would be with him among blessings beyond description, but rejoiced as though they were already with him in their hopes. So either "I am coming again" and what follows means this, or it means his return at his second and awesome coming. Then they will know, through experience itself and for all eternity, both the way and that blessed
place, and the enjoyment of the good things in it.

Question 100. Why did the angel not come to Joseph before Joseph fell into perplexity about the Virgin, but came to him only then? When Joseph was at a loss in his thoughts, the angel appeared and resolved the conflict among them. That he was at a loss about the birth and entirely helpless is clear from what he was thinking and what he was on the point of doing. "For he wished," it says, "to dismiss her secretly." He would not have thought of sending her away, secretly or at all, if he had been convinced that the swelling of her womb came from illegitimate conception. Rather, since he was a great lover of justice, he would sooner have handed the offense over to the law and its punishment. But he was not convinced of this. The unsurpassable virtue of the betrothed woman and the fitting watchfulness of the man to whom she was betrothed walled off every impure suspicion. Nor, on the other hand, did he understand that the conception was the work of divine power, for the event lay beyond human thought. So he was tossed about by his thoughts, at a loss as to what he should do in order to do what pleases God. When he was being shaken by these thoughts, then, most opportunely, the One who was miraculously working the swelling in the virginal womb sent an angel to confirm him in that in which he ought to remain unshaken and steady. That is why the angel says, "Do not be afraid to take," and so on. "You," he says, "are planning to send the virgin away secretly, afraid to keep her because she is carrying a child whose origin is unknown. But I command you to take her and keep her with you. 'For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.'" And this child not only proves her who carries him blameless, and not only fills her with glory and splendor beyond what is human, but is born as Savior and Redeemer for the whole world. Fittingly, then, the angel does not appear to Joseph earlier, but only when doubtful thoughts were troubling him. For when the storm is fierce, then the calm is sweetest. And "your wife" is said in place of [?] "your betrothed." Since she had cast neither her eye nor her thought toward another man, she had preserved for you the standing of a wife, safe and untouched, and had not loosed the ordinances of betrothal even in thought. Besides, it was an ancient custom to call women "wives" whom only the bond of betrothal bound, even if the law [?] of intercourse with them had not yet been known.
Question 101. What is the meaning of "Sell your possessions and give to the poor," and so on? Your difficulty, in a more bitter and more pointed form,

I know was once worked up [?] by Julian the Apostate. So I will write to you what I said in my replies to him, which memory has preserved, and I think that this will supply a sufficient solution. As though celebrating his inventions against the Truth, he said something like this: "Hear an excellent and statesmanlike precept: 'Sell your possessions and give to the poor; make for yourselves purses that do not wear out.' Who can name a more statesmanlike commandment than this? For if everyone obeyed you, who would be the buyer? Who would praise this teaching? If it prevailed, no city, no nation, not a single household would hold together. For once everything has been sold, how can a household or a house be held in honor? And it is obvious without being said that, if everything in the city were being sold at once, no buyers would be found." With such reasonings the Apostate pours his mockery over the divine commandment and thinks he is doing something wise and noble. But the word of Truth gives a sort of slap to the childishness and rottenness of his arguments. First, it says that there is nothing surprising here. The very commandment that brings great benefit to the sensible, and a sweet wonder that rouses them to hymns of the Lawgiver, brought the apostate harm instead of salvation, loss instead of gain, and blasphemy instead of gratitude. For one can indeed see that, because of the way human beings are disposed toward it, the good is surrounded by these two: choosing it and fleeing it. The first leads those who choose it up to a better rank, making them all the more beholders of its beauty and genuine lovers of it, adding to their love as it adds to their grasp in contemplation. The second drives its own followers as far away as possible into exile and carries them over cliffs and crags and through countless wanderings. Once it has turned them away from inclining toward the good and produced a deep forgetfulness of that beautiful sight, it accustoms them to delight only in the gloom of vice, and leaves them blind, and no less enemies of their own salvation. In this way Julian too, his whole soul muddied by the darkness of apostasy and deprived of the eyes through which what truly is is grasped, shows himself hostile, an enemy to the commandments that lead to what is best. He did not refrain from barking even at so great an exhortation, but strove to bring into reproach what is worthy of all praise and wonder. For "Sell your possessions and give alms": what occasion for compassion, or for true goodwill toward one another, does it lack? And self-control, and temperance? What teacher of philosophy is greater than this commandment? Does it not grant freedom from all the passions that love of money knows how to breed? For where is theft once avarice is abolished? Where is robbery? Where is brigandage

among people who are seen to be eager even to distribute what is their own? And strife, fighting and contentiousness: do they not vanish at once along with the free spending of money? Will a licentious and dissolute life find a way in when almsgiving prevails? Almsgiving spends every surplus on the needs of the needy. It does not allow a person to run riot into a surfeit of luxury or other self-indulgence, from which the more shameful passions of touch usually spring up as well. How, then, will benevolence and generosity, and readiness to show mercy to the destitute, overturn cities, nations and households? How will the abolition of seizure, of brigandage, or simply of all injustice and tyranny be the overthrow of human society? Consider someone who has not spared even his own possessions for the common good, who gives up his own advantage for his neighbors, and who bears himself wholly above attachment to material things. How could he be caught by any of the passions mentioned? Rather, being pure of all of them, how would he not gain for himself above all the goods that truly are? And how would he not be a great benefit to his fellow citizens, not only through the help he gave the destitute but also through his own personal way of life, set before them as an example of a philosophical and lofty life? Such men set out what they have for all to share. They stretch out right hands full of mercy, drive out all violence and honor justice. In short, they treat their neighbors as equal to themselves. Will a city founded [?] of such men be close to ruin? [?] …than all the cities that have ever measured their prosperity by many years, [?] it will have a better and more lasting duration and [?]. But the [?] Julian, it seems, does not want this. He wants his citizens to put forth a heavy hand that gathers wealth for them from the labors of others, and to spare neither a brigand's daring nor secret or open plotting. Even if they have to make an attempt at tyranny, even if they have to act, and be seen, more cruelly than Phalaris, even if they have to outdo [?] those notorious for every vice, they are to refuse nothing whatever in order to increase their possessions. Having prepared and stored up an abundant supply for every pleasure and desire, they may thereafter luxuriate and revel without fear, living for the belly and the genitals. And they define the glorious and enviable life, prolonged to the greatest length of time, as nothing other than the life they themselves lead. For of course the counsel is not good that comes from him who founds cities by his care, and whose deep and great providence holds nations together and establishes households, he who, judging by what he saw fit to say, instead of lovers of [Variant readings. C. M.: "of seizure"; C. M.: "abolition."]

humanity [would supposedly be] bringing in lovers of money; instead of people who love one another, [?] slaves; instead of the merciful, the merciless; and in short, instead of people who are best in everything, people who are worst in all things. For it is clear that, just as a character free from avarice draws the other virtues along with it, so the disease of avarice drags all its kindred vice along with it. But, as I was saying, this fine counselor and mocker of the Lord's commandment advises people to choose the worst instead of the best. Consistently with this, he declares that no city, no nation and no household could live happily in any other way, or even last very long, unless they choose to be wholly wicked rather than wholly good. To such an end, both for his counsel and for his idea of society, has he been brought by his audacity against the divine commandment, by his [?] tongue, and by his clever arguments for overthrowing it. And yet, if nothing else, you should have remembered your Cynics, the "dogs" you admired, and felt shame before Diogenes, Antisthenes, Crates and the rest of the chorus of your admirable dogs. Even if, by the showiness of their manner, they counterfeited the stamp of true poverty, they at least appeared to hate the love of wealth, and they made a great point of seeming to embrace a simple life free from love of money. It is to them that you should rather have said, instead of treating them as divine: "If everyone obeyed you, no nation, no city, not a single household would hold together. For if all people imitated you, how could a household or a house still be held in honor?" That is your clever objection to the commandment, full of everything nauseating: "How can a household or a house be held in honor?" But how is it that, instead of rebuking your dogs for these things, you admire them beyond measure, while you tear apart these sayings, which introduce a way of life far better than theirs and free from all wickedness? And why did you display the sharpness of your reasoning and the depth and force of your nature, so good at hitting the mark, on this teaching alone? You could have babbled the same nonsense about many others. "Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." But if everyone shines, who will be left to see, and to honor God with glory for what they have seen? "Give, and it will be given to you": if everyone chooses to give [?], who will receive? "Forgive, and you will be forgiven": if everyone forgives, who will there be for them to forgive? "Love your enemies": if everyone loves, where are those who are hostile? If everyone, when struck on the right cheek, also offers the other to insult, where are those who will strike? And countless other examples. Or rather, so to speak, no divine exhortation, in the actions of one person toward another…

[?] …against which one cannot see this irrational and foolish insolence making any headway. For when a commandment has its existence in a pairing of persons, whoever splits these apart from their connection and relation to one another, and then insists on pushing everyone into one side of the division, namely the side from which the action proceeds, will certainly find it easy to use the remaining side to overthrow the commandment, since he takes as his conclusion what follows from the false and absurd premise he has made up himself. And he will ask, very solemnly, with irony and empty bluster: “If everyone acts, who are those on whom the action is performed?” Since, then, this lofty and vigorous assault of yours could easily be brought against almost the whole teaching of the Spirit, why did you not unleash so great a test, if not on all of it, at least on most of it? Why did you, out of great caution, confine it to one single commandment? For then we would have admired the resourcefulness and depth of your arguments all the more. But this too was a device of malice rather than of folly. For he knew, he knew, that if he brought the same denunciation against all the Lord's commands, his trickery would be easily detected, since even an ordinary person could see that not all the saving precepts would give the same grounds for being overturned by their own terms. With one, however, he hoped rather to escape notice, if he kept his slander within limits, and he hoped that his own malice would thus find a better way in to turn round into blame of what is blameless. So by the very means through which he planned to escape notice, he himself put on public display how malicious and rotten his own words are. Yet, having given himself over to such chatter and mischievous sophistries, he ought not to have passed over the insolence that could be aimed through the other side of the persons either. With the same quickness of mind and nimble wit he should have raised the further difficulty and said: “But if everyone chose to buy instead of selling, who would the sellers be?” For what difference is there between driving everyone into the ranks of those in the market and then looking for buyers, and, conversely, turning them all into buyers and then searching about for those willing to sell? But let that pass. What about you? Do you want all people to be fine and good, and above failings? Or does that displease you? But if everyone is fine and good, where is the need for laws? Where is the toil, the zeal and the forethought of lawgivers? And yet it was precisely in their concern that people should be fine and good that they laid down the laws. And will not justice turn out, on your account, to be a goat-stag and a nonsense word? For where is justice when there is no lawsuit? And where is a lawsuit when no one does wrong? And who does wrong, when everyone has changed over to the better? Will not gentleness also be gone? For to whom is one gentle when there is no one to provoke him? Where is the provoker, whom does he provoke, and for what cause? For a good man has nothing over which he could provoke another good man, even if he wished. And clearly he will not even wish

[To Amphilochius, Question 101] to. So by this utterly wicked nonsense of yours, whoever wishes people to be fine and good is liable to a great and serious charge. For if that teaching prevailed, the greatest of virtuous achievements would be gone, and the laws themselves would be something futile, a superfluous crowd. And I do not yet say that through it the destruction of the good is brought about, nor that the choice of the best is shown to be the introduction of the worse. For your reasonings are not wise or full of political theory, you who brandish politics at us and say, “Can anyone name a commandment more unpolitical than this one?” And yet you all but worship the constitutions of the Greeks [?], which teem with countless licentiousness and countless contradictions among themselves, which are most hostile to every human polity, and which have remained nonexistent and insubstantial through all [time?]. You who keep them in memory and pride yourself on them, ought you not to have been ashamed even to bring the very word “polity” out past your lips? Yet you dared even to mock this commandment. And so energetic are you that what you strive to blame you praise without noticing it, and what you labor to praise you [disparage?] without perceiving it. But I let this go for the moment. In your great wisdom, then, you supposed that the Savior had political [science?] as his principal aim. Then why do you not bring charges against him (lover of accusations that you are, breathing insolence) that he laid down nothing about generals, or armies, or [tactics?]; nor how one must advance against enemies through [?], nor when to make truces; nor even at what [price] grain and other goods should be sold; nor about market inspectors and judges and lawgivers, what sort they should be and [?] — why are you not annoyed that he introduced none of these? Blind and abominable man, so deep was the sleep you were sleeping (and that while you spent your nights sleepless in your futile labor against the divine [oracles]) that you did not even become aware of this: that our Savior and God [did not make] the [political?] forms and their ordering his principal aim. For he knew, he knew, that [experience?] provides sufficient preparation for learning these things, since need and necessity offer easy instruction every day, and the failures of those who went before are enough for those who come after to bring in correction in similar cases. [?] … and in this too one has erred [?] … correcting what has been established by changes [?]. But the Savior's principal concern is the salvation of souls and the introduction of a philosophical life and a higher way of living. For through this comes the freedom of [souls], and the [ascent?] to and union with the first Good, not the care of political conduct or of bodily happiness. That is why the exhortation [seems?] [?] to lovers of the flesh and the body, just as it does to you [?] … [harsh?] and averse to virtue. But if indeed

there was any reasoning in you, you ought, even while practicing slander, to have kept to consistency. You should not have sneered in ironic language that the Lord's commandment is not political, but rather that it is not philosophical, nor the foundation of a philosophical life. But you, finding fault with it on grounds for which it does not deserve blame (and even there you have already been convicted of idle talk), and not daring even to mention the grounds on which such a commandment might be blamed, have refuted with irresistible argument the fault-finding, malicious and rotten character of your own judgment, and have borne witness, though against your will, that the commandment is above all fault and slander. Next, see how, having himself posited the impossible, he thinks he can draw the resulting absurdity against someone else. For when he says, “If everyone sells, who will buy?” he drags in the absurdity by an impossible premise of his own. Yet he thinks the charge belongs not to his own trickery, but that the commandment he insults supplies the cause. For it is not, it is not possible — even if Christ were to urge this many times, even if he were to bind it with countless threats, even if he were to hurl lightning and thunder and thunderbolts and chasms in the earth along with his words — it is not possible that everyone should choose to sell at one and the same time, and that no lover of gain and wealth should be left. For there are, there are at every time both the one kind and the other. Virtue is never accessible to everyone at once. One must be content if even the majority reach it, and by turns. But not even this is easy, nor can it be seen in the case of any virtue, for its lovers are always fewer than the lovers of vice. Yet this is no reason for the one who cares for the human race to take away words of admonition and abandon his teaching, just because he would not have everyone obeying. Rather, because in many people they produce flight from the worse and choice of the better, for this reason all must be summoned to virtue. One may also consider how this clever man, so quick in speculation, foreseeing nothing of what follows, says: “How will everyone sell?” Are all people rich, then, and no one poor? Is no one even among those who live with only enough to get by? And yet we see that most people are counted among such. The rich are far fewer than the rest. Where, then, did you find all people rich, and ready to obey and sell their possessions? But it seems you collected them from Plato's Republic,

[?] … might be thought. So your arguments have been overturned and made a mockery of by your own, while ours not only are not touched [?], but also furnish a refutation of the folly and audacity with which he rushed to slander. “But if everyone should sell, what house can be held in honor?” O the precision and cleverness of your dialectic! Bravo for the persuasiveness and sharpness of your rhetoric! O you who are so great at seeing consequences, and from far off! O you so haughty in your words and so irresistible in your refutations! O you who reproach us with the talk of the crossroads! Would not an old woman at the crossroads, coming from the all-night festivals of your gods and soaked in wine, utter things more adroit and witty than these? “What house can be held in honor?” And what, tell me, is more honorable than equality for those who have been allotted a nature of equal honor? What is better to choose, for those whose lot is to live in the same city, than to enjoy common and equal [conditions]? But perhaps greed and tyranny are what you count honorable, or frauds and the accursed schemes and tricks of hucksters and dealers against their neighbors. For nearly all wealth has these, recent or older, as the sources of its origin, the things by which the Transgressor decided to dignify what is honorable. But he was wholly ignorant, as he was of everything, of what is truly honorable before God and what is not. Human beings, and those of the herd at that (for those who have kept their love of philosophy pure would not do so), gape at one thing only, wealth and the luxury and glory that come from it, and they consider its possessor honorable and blessed even if he teems with countless evils. But God honors the pious and grants good repute to lovers of virtue, even if no mass of money puffs them up, and no pride and luxury from it make them conspicuous. Indeed, those whose glory comes through these things do not even want the toil of virtue or the zeal of piety to survive. It was necessary, then, it was necessary, that our Lord Jesus Christ, being God, who emptied himself for the salvation of our race and shared in flesh and blood as we do, should not look to what is sweet and pleasing to those who set their minds on earthly things, nor overlook the things that breed vice and let them send down roots and their seeds spread into fruit. Rather, he had to make law and precept of those things by which the passions are cut off root and all, and the perfection of every virtue and of pure contemplation is achieved. Of these the present exhortation lacks none; rather, as has been said, it holds the power of more. But perhaps, someone may say, the commandment as spoken escapes every absurdity and has proved too lofty for any verbal attack, but in practice it has not turned out the same way, and its existence in deeds falls short of its consistency in words? Yet it has so turned out that through the deeds themselves it has given its reality the clearest proof, and has shown that its consistency in words agrees with its realization in practice. For ever since this saving exhortation came forth from the Lord's spotless lips, from then until now one cannot find a time in which it is not to be seen in human

souls, taking root and growing deep, and increasing in breadth and length, and increasing and perfecting the other virtues along with it. For at that time three thousand and five thousand, and then a multitude beyond counting, came together, gave up what was their own, and put their goods in common. And there was no one poor among them (O wondrous lot, not even hoped for before it came about), nor anyone rich. “For as many,” it says, “as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid them at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as anyone had need.” Do you hear, Julian? “As many as were owners” sold. Not all? But at that time, from the very beginning, the commandment, thus fulfilled in a multitude, advanced brilliantly and came to real existence in its workings, flourishing. And from then until now it has not only kept unfading the flower of its prime, with which it adorns human souls with blossoms, and, while the rot of the passions breathes out a great stench, draws them to the saving and life-giving fragrance of the virtues. It has also embraced and traversed all the ends of the inhabited world by its workings, not merely person by person, but now whole peoples and communities beyond number of those who are truly solitaries, establishing a heavenly life even for those on earth, and spreading it; and through the deeds themselves it shows how great is its consistency in words, or rather, through its consistency with reason it brilliantly displays its reality and abundance in deeds. Not only that, but through itself it also makes the efficacy and power of the Lord's words no less admired. For by turning human souls, as many as are worthy, toward itself, and by sowing the seed of the word in them and making it grow deep, it has found ample means for the tree to be known by its fruit, and through them, in turn, for the strength and wisdom of the gardener to be hymned. And not even in these things, great as they are, is the full greatness of its nature displayed, but in this: that it surpasses the other virtues and achievements and holds their very existence together. How could anyone fail to admire exceedingly the lofty and saving power of its nature, unless he were to be convicted of wandering blind in [the light?] and so paying the same penalty as Julian? For those who trace out the heavenly polity through the life they live on earth — these, these one can see laying down this very thing first as a foundation, as it were, and a base: “Sell your possessions and give alms,” and so building the other virtues upon it, as though without this no other virtue had the power to subsist in purity. So, having first sold their possessions and distributed them to the needy — how could anyone worthily hymn the divine and

God-working and loving-kind character of the exhortation? Thus stripped from then on of money and of every other earthly attachment, they enter upon the contests of asceticism, stretching their mind toward one thing alone and setting their desire on what Paul speaks of: “to depart and be with Christ.” Through him — O blessed sight! — the more perfect knowledge of the Father in the Holy Spirit, a knowledge without mirrors, is unveiled together with the first Good and makes it shine forth for the enjoyment of those who behold it, and bestows the summit of all desires. Thus, thus this saving and Lordly commandment has not only preserved with great power its reasonableness and consistency as something spoken, routing by force and [overthrowing] every opponent raised up to war against it. Much more, through the conspicuous working and reality it has throughout all the world under the sun, it has shown more perfectly and more wonderfully the coherence of its words and the irreproachability of its intent; and, beyond what the strength and nature of arguments could do, it has made those who dared to insult it undergo the gloomy blush of [shame]. So much, then, has been said against the Apostate, who acts maliciously and behaves insolently toward our religion. But for you, a lover of learning who celebrates divine things in a manner worthy of God, I think even a few of the things said will suffice to resolve the difficulty.

QUESTION 102. What does the ephod signify? The ephod, which you asked to learn about, we have found from our reading to signify three things. One is the priestly and holy vestment, which it was lawful for none but the priests alone to wear. Through it was revealed what was to be done in matters where human judgment was too weak to see what was advantageous, for instance, whether to make a truce with enemies or to commit the decision of the war to the spear, and anything else of that sort. This, then, is the first meaning of the ephod. The second somewhat resembles the one just mentioned in form, but is common and not priestly; David is seen wearing it. “David,” it says, “wore only an ephod.” Some (since it was made of byssus, and byssus is a plant) named it after its material a “byssus robe”; others, deriving the name from the way it was worn, called it a “shoulder-piece” and an “over-garment.” Besides these, a third meaning can also be seen. For the worshippers of idols, imitating the priests of God, assigned special vestments to their own priests in the shape of the ephod, [copying its outline?], and, borrowing the name from there, they too called it an ephod. And they used the imitation to consult the demons through it, they too, in order to learn what they should do. And there is nothing new in this. For just as the name “God” signifies the One who truly is, yet was also applied to the falsely named demons, so too the ephod is divided into opposite meanings. And not only is the name “God” divided between opposites, but also “holy” and [?]. For each of these signifies both the One who properly is and the One who is properly holy; and it was also transferred by the worshippers of demons to honor the objects of their own worship, in the same way as the ephod was

QUESTION 103. How is “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” not contrary to “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well”? The legislation that orders the penalty of “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” is not contrary, as it has seemed to some who are not of sound mind, to the counsel “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well,” and to others like it. For the former regulates the judge and is addressed to him: it lays down that he must be impartial toward those he judges and must avenge the one wronged, exacting an equal penalty from the wrongdoer. The latter, however, is not addressed to the judge, nor is it a law — far from it, for then it would indeed be contrary. Rather, it exhorts the one who has been wronged, anointing him for gentleness and compassion, making him stronger than anger and rage, and offering its counsel in a highly philosophical and beneficial way. For what one has been deprived of cannot be recovered; or, if one does recover it, one has nothing more than what one had from the start. But the one who has overcome his enemy through gentleness and a compassionate mind not only wins a brilliant victory and raises an ever-memorable monument to virtue, but also makes the common Judge propitious and kind toward himself, since he has made himself worthy to receive what he himself has shown to his neighbor.

QUESTION 104. [?] Let the more ineffable and deeper account of the cause be left to God. But from what he has allowed human understanding to grasp, we say that the reason he permitted Abel, who was righteous, to come to death before Adam, who had sinned and received the sentence, was this: so that the one under sentence, learning in his innocent son how fearful and inescapable the penalty was, might take in greater grief and show repentance, and so depart owing less for his transgression. And further, it was so that the foundation of death, having first received one who was wronged, might become rotten. For just as, if it had first received the guilty, it would have laid a [firm] foundation for itself, so, by snatching the righteous man, it unwittingly set its own base rotten and easy to overturn. But consider with me also whether the doctrine of the resurrection is foreshadowed and mystically taught through this. For if God is good and just, or rather the very source of goodness and justice, he would not have let righteous Abel depart unrewarded and before his time. And why do I say unrewarded? He would not unjustly [have let him suffer] the greater instead of [?]; one who had been shown to be dear to God he would not have overlooked as he was slain, unless there is another state after this, and another life

…was laid up, in which he keeps in store [?] the requitals and recompenses for what is done, having prepared them with the ineffable wealth of his providence. So you will no longer dispute why Abel, the first to become a friend of righteousness, was also the first to pay service to death. And if you look to Enoch as well, who was most righteous, you will have still more reason not to ask how death came to rule over the righteous rather than over the guilty. For he, by his virtue and by the generosity of God (and so that your perplexities might not be left with something hard to make out), was declared to be above the snares and the tyranny of death.

QUESTION 105. On circumcision. Circumcision seems to me to accomplish three things. The first is that it marks off the descendants of Abraham as with a sign and seal, and separates them from the other nations. The second is that it prefigures and proclaims in advance the grace and power of divine baptism. For just as in former times the one who was circumcised was enrolled among the people of God through the seal, so the one who is baptized, having had the seal of Christ imprinted on himself, is enrolled for adoption as a son of God. The third is that it is a symbol of the faithful who are established in grace. They cut away and put to death the uprisings of the pleasures and passions of the flesh by the cutting word of faith and by ascetic labors. They cut not the body but the heart, and are circumcised in spirit, not in letter. The divine Paul, the initiator into such mysteries, testifies with a clear voice that their [?] praise needs no human judgment but depends on the verdict from above. Some also hold this view: that Abraham was of the race of the Chaldeans, and that the Chaldeans mingled with their mothers, daughters, and sisters by a lawless custom. So, they say, that neither he himself nor the race descended from him might be defiled by these ancestral customs, he cut off the foreskin in repudiation of such unspeakable practice. For him circumcision became a separation [?] of his own flesh and a turning away from close kindred, at least in the matter of marital union. And indeed, after circumcision no one of Abraham's blood could be caught entangled in such unspeakable practices, although Chaldean incontinence went on enacting such things fearlessly and shamelessly for long ages, even afterward. Let each person think about this as he pleases. Still, the race of Abraham had to be set apart. First, it was not to mingle with the other nations, little by little slip into their ways, suffer a perversion of its own piety, and serve their abominations. Next, it was so that the fulfillment of the divine

promise might be shown plainly and made known to all, as the seed of Abraham multiplied and grew into a countless multitude. For if they had been mixed up with the other nations, the truthfulness of the promise would not have been recognized in the same way, nor would the marvel of their great number have been admired, as it was when they had a way of life of their own, set apart.
