The third reason, which one can see is the most important of all, is that it had been promised to Abraham, beloved of God, that in his seed all the nations would be blessed. This could come about through no one else but through the very One who formed them, and who extends and pours out the ineffable gift of his providence even to the things on earth. For only the common Maker himself is able to bestow a common blessing too. But this greatest work of his providence toward us called the Provider to become man (for so it had been foreordained from above, before the ages, by divine and ineffable decrees). For this reason the race of Abraham was set apart and kept from mixing with the other nations. So when the Creator and Master took our nature from it, and shared in flesh and blood as we do, the truthfulness of the promise would be fully evident and plain to all. It would also be clear that Christ our God, in whom all the nations have been counted worthy of the blessing in grace, did not disdain to take the first, human beginnings of his birth according to the flesh from that man's loins. These, then, and others like them, are the pious lines of reasoning. And this too, I think, is clear to you. The divine Abraham did not have circumcision as the cause of his faith, nor did it hold the rank of faith. He believed first, and received circumcision only as a seal of the faith that already existed in him. Some say that he was circumcised so that, once stripped of the coverings that nature provides, the organ of child-begetting would be clean of the filth that gathers there. I know that the children of the Greeks and some of the Jews have babbled this. I could say countless things against them, since the absurdity of their opinion supplies refutations in abundance, but I will say only this. I would gladly hear them say it if I saw them first bringing the sword against the very source of the seminal flows, or against their bellies, which they have made into channels for more and fouler impurities. QUESTION 106. What does the redundant use of “am” mean? The redundant use of “am” after the pronoun “I” placed before it in the same expression is customary in divine Scripture, but that gives no ground for charging it with solecistic language. If you dispute this, consider expressions such as “themselves” (sphas autous) and “he went away having” (apēlthen echōn), which are redundant in Greek writings. Consider also how “some” (tines) used with “certain” (enioi), and “sphas” used with

“autous,” signify nothing but what the words placed before them [?] already indicated. From such cases it is plain that this is a recognized kind of redundancy and a figure of speech, not solecistic ignorance. “Having” (echōn), too, is often attached as a subordinate word to “you went away,” “you walk,” “you hurry,” and many others, and your own sophists use it to signify nothing at all, simply as a redundancy. If you want to be silenced by examples closer at hand, I will not leave this out either. Recall the infinitive mood of “to be” (eimi) itself, joined with the participle “willing” (hekōn). Few of the Atticists do not count the phrase hekōn einai as a brilliant ornament of their writings. I know well that you will blame yourself, since you spend time with their works and see that “to be” is plainly redundant in them in many places, yet you never once dared to reproach them with solecistic speech or to suspect them of it. Were you not ashamed? On account of the redundancy of “am,” you brought a charge of solecism that would apply equally to both (if this really were a fault in the Greek tongue), and you brought it against our divine and most holy Scripture alone, as if by some barbarous decree. But I know the impartiality of your judgment, and so I am hopeful about the future. I expect that you will no longer regard such things as faults. I also expect that if others dare to make the same error, you will easily win them over and teach them better about the things whose ignorance was giving them wings and goading them on to go astray. For ignorance is the mother of rashness.

QUESTION 107. Why do the poets place the horn of Amalthea in the hands of much-enduring Heracles? Know that the poets place the horn of Amalthea in the hands not only of much-enduring Heracles but also of eloquent Hermes. So do not give yourself wholly to military campaigns and bodily labors and keep away from fine learning, thinking that the happiness of life flows to you only from there. Our noble Muses differ from the Greek ones as much as free natures differ from slaves, and truth from flattery. Allow them, at least in turn, to charm you with the solemn and sweet strains of their songs. For the self-governing tribe of poets readily grants the horn of Amalthea even to the river Achelous, because it flows around the land below it and makes it bear every kind of crop. But it is nothing great for a human being to obtain what even lifeless things have by nature. True and divine happiness is the kind that befits a human being, and compared with it the [?] Amalthea is found to be sickness and poverty. That happiness can be reaped only from the divine Oracles and the cultivation they make possible.

…the divine Paul has taken it here not in the sense that the obvious meaning of the words suggests. On hearing “to have authority,” some may perhaps understand it to mean exercising authority over others and being lord. But here he says the woman “has authority” in the sense that she is placed and ranks under authority. To make the point clearer, together with the solutions to the other difficulties you raised about the same passage, we must begin from here. The teacher of the world commands that men keep their heads uncovered when they prophesy and pray, but that women keep theirs covered. He gives two reasons for this command. “The man,” he says, “has his head shorn and shaved, but it is not right for a woman to do either of these.” So even if the man keeps his head uncovered, a woman must not dare to do so. He keeps his head uncovered so as not to disgrace it, for it makes no sense to remove the hair that nature gives and then devise a covering from outside. For the woman, however, the veil is a duty. She disgraces her head by leaving it uncovered just as she would by having it shaved and shorn. Nature provides the one covering and modest shame the other, but both are coverings of the head. Just as the shaved woman has put off the natural covering, so the uncovered woman has stripped off the garment of modest shame, and in this respect she becomes the same as the shaved woman. This, then, is one reason why she must be covered and he need not be. Or rather, someone examining it closely would say that this is not so much a reason given as an overturning and refutation of those who try to find fault with the legislation. They hold that women should act as men do in these matters too, because they share a common nature. But whether it is a reason or a refutation of the fault-finders, such would be its meaning. He gives a second reason, as follows. The woman, he says, is by nature under the authority of the man, for she took the first bodily beginnings of her coming into being from him. The man has authority over many other things too, but the most glorious and honorable part of his authority and rule is the woman. This is what he means by “The woman is the glory of the man.” Since the woman, then, is the most glorious and distinguished part of the man's rule, she is bound to do everything by which subjects honor the man as their ruler. She would do this by having his authority upon her head and by showing her subjection in covering her own head. She would regard him as her head and devote herself wholly to him, referring herself to him as to her head. For it is shameless and ungrateful not to acknowledge him as the source and co-cause of her existence, and not to render him the honor due to a ruler. There are many considerations she might weigh, but suppose she takes none of them into account. Suppose she feels no shame before any human being while she rejects her ruler and declines to be subject. Yet before the angels at least, he says, who oversee and witness her origin and coming forth from the man, it would be right for her to feel abashed and ashamed. For that reason she should be subject to the man and wear the covering on her head as a symbol of her subjection. This is what he

made clear when he said, “For this reason the woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels.” The man, however, is not subject to the same law of subjection, and so he has no need to cover his head. “But surely,” he says, someone might object, “the man has Christ as his head and is the most glorious part of His rule. For he is called the image and glory of God, just as the woman is called the glory of the man. Why then does he not cover his head as well?” One can answer him that for this very reason he ought rather not to cover it. In this way he too is shown to bear the image of the common Master, ruling and exercising authority rather than ranking under others, and bearing his head uncovered is the sign of this. No one disputes that God rules and is Lord, since he has been revealed as the head of the man, and not of man only but of all things. So there is no need of symbols to show subjection to him, for his power over all and his lordship as Master are acknowledged by all. But it is not equally clear to all that a woman must be placed under the authority of the man. She above all ought to know it and to display it by symbols. For some women, even while wearing the symbols, rise up against many, abandon their proper order, and fill with tumult and disorder not only households but even cities. What would have happened if this were not so, and she had not been commanded to keep her subjection? It is reasonable and beneficial, then, that the blessed Paul laid down his other rules too, and argued, with wise and natural and also civic reasoning, that a man should have his head uncovered and that a woman may not go uncovered.

To lovers of learning I am, how shall I say it less invidiously, obliging. So you will find the solution to your difficulties both brief and easy. These words were spoken to the founder of fratricide: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still.” Know that they can admit different interpretations. One reader takes them as a statement, and would see a sense like this in them: “You could not offer rightly, since you did not divide rightly.” That is: since you did not divide rightly, neither did you offer rightly, for right offering depends on right division; therefore you have sinned; be still. Another reader takes the saying not as a statement but as put in the form of a question, which is quite possible. He will find this sense: “Even if you offer rightly, if you still do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” It is as if to say: “Did you think, then, that you had not sinned [?] because you offered rightly, although you did not divide rightly?” For perhaps nothing prevents someone from offering rightly, if he sacrifices to no other but to the God of all alone, and yet from not dividing

rightly, if he does not keep the rule proper to division. But the one who serves divine things blamelessly must both divide rightly beforehand and likewise offer rightly. If the passage is read as a single period, then, it would admit interpretations of this kind. But someone might take it not as one simple period but as one made up of two shorter ones. He could read it as a statement, keeping the period, with one part spoken elliptically and the other complete in itself. Even then he will do no harm to the nature of the truth. For example: “If you offer rightly, would you not be approved? But if you do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” For just as offering rightly is pious, so not dividing rightly makes one liable to the charge of impiety. Such, then, is the account of the syntax of the text and of the meaning that emerges from it. “To offer rightly” is evident in itself, but “not to divide rightly” perhaps needs clarifying. The one who divides rightly is the one who does not bring God just any gifts. He divides and discerns with right judgment, and offers to him those gifts that far surpass the rest. For surely it is fitting to set apart the things most precious of all and to offer them in sacrifice to God, the Creator and Giver and cause of all good things. Abel was shown to be such a man, grateful and loving God with a pure love. For it is said of him that “he offered of the firstborn and of the fat portions.” That is, he offered those that excelled the rest both in being firstborn and in being, as one might put it, fattened and rich. “Of the fat portions” means of the well-fed and fattened animals, which through much care yield what is choicest and best. Both of them took care to offer, but they did not take the same care to divide and select the better things. Abel, as he divided rightly, so also he offered. Cain, on the other hand, either did not offer rightly either, because he did not divide at all, or else, if one grants that he offered rightly, he still went very far astray in setting apart and selecting. For he offered not the better things but those that were not such. This is clear both from the fact that “God did not look upon his sacrifices,” nor consume them with divine fire as he did Abel's (for some have interpreted it this way), and from the penalty he paid for his wrong division. So much for “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” “Be still” is as if you said to someone who has sinned: “Calm yourself, examine closely how wrong your act was, and make amends for the sin by repentance.” For in stillness and calm of thought what was overlooked is better seen and judged. Perhaps he was also checking in advance the impulse that Cain wretchedly went on to carry out. “You have sinned,” he says, “be still. Do not add another wrong to this one. Let your madness stop at the offense against me. Keep not only your hands but also your mind clean of your brother's blood.” And “Its turning is toward you,

and you will rule over it.” Either this is said of the offering itself, as if to say: “It is unworthy of my acceptance, and so it turns back to you, and you will be its master, just as you were before it was offered.” Or the saying refers not to what was offered but to the very fault committed in the offering. That is: “You, and no one else, became the cause of the sin. Therefore its turning and its reckoning will come back to you, and you will rule over it, since you have been shown to be the originator of neglect toward God, from which all other sins proceed.” Someone might say that this was spoken as consolation, for Cain was grieved, not because he had sinned, but because he came off worse than his brother in the sacrifices. Even this is not far from God's boundless and inscrutable love for humankind. A loving father might speak this way to a son who has sinned: “Do not lose heart or be swallowed up by grief because your brother outdid you in his gifts. He has justly been preferred for what he did piously. Yet he will turn back to you, and you will again hold the privilege of the firstborn, for your authority over him will not be taken away,” which [?]. But for a letter I think this is enough. I know that some of the most ancient Jews, who were thought more learned than the rest, have written something else. They say Cain was said not to have divided rightly because he offered his gifts from lifeless things and not, as Abel did, from living ones, since lifeless things fall far short of living ones and are much inferior to them. That is why, they say, the God of all was pleased with Abel's gifts because they were living, but disregarded Cain's sacrifice because it was brought from lifeless things. But if that were so, Cain would have been reproached not for the division but for the sacrifice itself, because he did not offer animals instead of fruits. Yet the divine voice nowhere appears to have found fault with this. It found no fault with the gifts at all, but brought its reproach against the division. Besides, from the beginning one of them took up farming as his way of life and the other shepherding. Is it not absurd, then, to suppose that Cain was blamed because he offered from his own goods and not from someone else's? One might add this too. On their view, the one should have been disparaged for choosing to farm, and the shepherd accepted, not at the offering of the sacrifice but at the very beginning, when they chose their ways of life. For, as these interpreters supposed, the difference in their pursuits was the origin and cause of the one erring by sacrificing fruits and the other being preferred by making animals his gifts. And how is it that later, in the laws, fine flour, ears of grain, and the bread of the Presence were counted as offerings to God? Moreover, the creating Word said “very good” not of some created things but of all of them, and so they were made. What reason, then, would there be for their Creator to dismiss the fruits of the earth, which are more truly human food, as without honor and as an abomination? So the interpretation considered earlier is to be preferred to an approach like this one. For this approach seems somehow to sing in harmony even with those who are ignorant of the meaning of our pure and bloodless sacrifice. From such reasoning Julian, the [?] apostate, also [?] against the [?]…
…writing of [?] piety, writing things strange and foolish, nevertheless thought it something wise and hard to refute to accuse Christians of not honouring the Deity with animal sacrifices.

QUESTION [?]. The Saviour shortens the time of his promise because of the disciples' faintheartedness, and appears to them in Jerusalem itself before they reach Galilee. This is surely no breach of his promise, far from it. It is rather a swift fulfilment that comes from his great love for humankind. Someone may still be unreasonable and try to force the truth into falsehood. He may say that it is not the mark of a truthful person to promise to show himself in Galilee and then grant the sight of himself in Jerusalem. Let him rather understand this. Suppose the Saviour had said that he would give the disciples the enjoyment of that blessed sight in Galilee and then had not granted it at all. Or suppose he had added that he would not be seen by them in Jerusalem, and then was seen there. In that case it would not be very foolish to suspect him of falsehood. But he foretold his appearance in Galilee and fulfilled it, and he also granted the appearance in Jerusalem. Then where can falsehood find any way in, even if only as a bare [?] appearance? Indeed, is this not, so to speak, a double fulfilment of the truth? He kept what he promised, and he also gave what he had not even promised. Consider this as well. Suppose he had simply foretold that he would be seen by the disciples in Galilee, and was then seen somewhere else first. Let that be granted, and even so falsehood has no place. But he said that they would see him once they had gone there, and they had not yet set out. The wonder of the resurrection was not yet firmly established in them, so that they would leave Jerusalem and expect to see the risen one in Galilee. How then is the slanderous charge of falsehood not utterly senseless? Besides what has been said, we must especially observe that the Saviour stood among the disciples in Jerusalem and was seen by them, yet they did not properly behold him. How could they see him when they thought they were looking at a spirit? Even when they later believed, it did not amount to much. What did they learn, except that "a spirit does not have flesh and bones," and that the one who had been put to death had also risen? That is why he rebuked them and said, "Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts?" These were not people firm in their judgments, nor did they reason about the truth with an unshaken mind. But in Galilee they truly beheld and saw him. There it was revealed to them and made clear that the one they saw and looked upon was himself "the one who despoiled the power of death." He was the one who had received all authority and lordship over everything on earth and in heaven. It was then too that they were invested with the great and lofty dignity of the apostleship to the whole inhabited world. Therefore, in Galilee

the disciples truly beheld their teacher [?]. For then, more than before, they were taught and came to understand that he was Lord and sovereign of the universe, the giver of the grace of the all-holy Spirit and the steward of every other good. So Christ spoke with complete truth and in a manner worthy of God when he said that the disciples would see him once they reached Galilee, even though he had already shown himself to them in Jerusalem.

QUESTION [?]. "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands." What, then, of the vessels for libation in Christian worship, the chalices, the censers, the figures of the cross and countless other things? I will not even mention the symbols of the Mosaic sacrifice. Are they not silver and gold, wood and paints, the works of human hands? God forbid! They are not silver but made of silver, not gold but fashioned from gold. Nor are they wood or paints. These things have matter, but something else is made out of them, brought to completion as something wonderful. Nor are they the work of human hands that play about with matter and, without any divine working, shape whatever happens to come into their minds. So the idols are nothing but the matter itself, put to shameful use, together with the heedless and senseless labour of human hands. Our sacred objects are given form in matter, and a hand serves in making them, but that hand is moved from above. It serves inspirations from above and wise thoughts that are guided by pious judgment. Pay attention, Iconoclast, and do not be ashamed to learn the things that will free you from dreadful shame and show you how to escape an inescapable judgment. Our vessels for libation, our chalices and censers, our figures of the cross and the like are not gold or silver, nor the material of wood or paints, nor the works of human hands. In the same way, the sacred representations in our icons are not silver or gold or bronze, nor yet paints, nor (God forbid!) the works of human hands. For the divine and unerring proclamation of the apostolic and patristic tradition from of old acts like a living wisdom. It takes up the matter, works it according to its own sacred ordinances and shapes it with skill, and so it makes images and gives them form. It does not allow the disorder of matter or human meddling to assert itself freely in them. It displays and declares the whole work as its own, and in the venerable icons it presents to us the reflections of the prototypes, pure and unadulterated, in a holy manner and in holy form. Here, then, I think, you have in brief the means by which you will show yourself bearing more fruit of the piety of our forefathers, and will silence the heretics. As far as matter and substrate are concerned, the table of God and the table of demons,

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. divine sacrifice and demonic sacrifice, the orgies of the pagans and the mysteries of the Christians, and many other things that stand in the most extreme opposition differ only a little. But in use and name, in invocation and consecration, and in countless other respects, the distinction between them is beyond words. So it is, then, with the idols of the nations and the icons of Christians, the temple of God and the altar of idols. So it is too with the vessels used in the Hellenic sacrificial smoke and the sacred vessels of our pure and bloodless sacrifice. In each pair, though the two belong to opposite ranks, there is matter, and sometimes the matter differs in no way at all. But in what forms them, gives them their shape and naturally makes them different, the estrangement between them is seen to be boundless and scarcely expressible in words. Matter that has not been changed into anything better, but has received a large share of what is worse, might justly be called wood and stones, gold and silver, or the works of human hands. Such things are profane, accursed and unclean, and they get these names partly from their matter, partly from their maker, and partly from those to whom they were impiously and godlessly dedicated. That is why an idol is reproached for its dumbness even though it has a mouth. Though it has feet and hands, it is reproached for not moving. Though it has ears and nostrils or anything else, it is reproached for its lack of feeling, its inactivity and its emptiness. Their archetypes are either nothing or wretched and accursed. Their maker, along with the impious worshipper, is even more wretched, and their whole worship is still more hateful to God. How could such things ever come to have any grace, glory, power or more venerable name? The venerable sacred vessels of the Christians, our sanctuaries and icons and the other symbols of our divine worship, may have no different matter underlying them. Yet they have been transformed into something far better. They have been sanctified and perfected by their use, their name and the sacred rites, by the divinity of the models whose features shape them, and by countless other things. Therefore they can no longer be thought of or called wood or stone, silver or gold, or paints stripped of the power and grace that give them form and attend them. They are rather holy, precious, glorified and venerable. They have come to share in the power from above and in those to whom they are dedicated, whose name and form they bear. They carry our mind across to those beings, and they convey to us from there a good and divine favour. So it would not be reasonable to name them from their matter, or from any other unfitting property that suits their opposites. They are named from what they share in and what they are directed toward, from what they serve and are consecrated to. It is from these that the truly pious know them and name them, very rightly and justly.

…death threatened; not a promise of life; simply not the things there, not the things here. How then does he willingly stand apart, and that for the sake of his kinsmen according to the flesh? He not only endures the separation. He even desires and prays to be separated from Christ: "For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh." This is how someone might sharpen your difficulty. What then? How can things that cannot be reconciled be reconciled? First, one may say that these things are not in conflict at all. Undivided longing for Christ is not opposed to loving one's neighbour so much that one counts the neighbour's salvation as no less than one's own good. These things rather agree with each other. Whoever loves his brother fulfils the Master's commandment and keeps his affection for the Master pure and undefiled. "By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another"; and again, "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." For love of God and love of neighbour are the head and bond and root of every other good deed. "Yes," he says, "but here he puts his kinsmen first and prays to be separated from God in order to win them. Yet Christ said, 'Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.'" But how is this loving them more than Christ? If Paul had cherished them for some other reason, the argument would have force. But if he cherished them so that they might become Christ's, I cannot see how his kinsmen were preferred to the Creator. For what else did loving them mean than bringing them into submission and joining them to our common Master? How then can it be loving them more than Christ, when he was drawing them into obedience and love toward Christ himself? Rather, anyone who examines this with impartial judgment will clearly see in it the torch of divine love that always blazed in Paul. He was not content to bring himself alone. He hastened to bring others with him, not only by his tongue and his hand that worked signs [?], but by his life, by his whole conduct and by every method. "Fine," he says, "if he were not separating himself from Christ. To want others to be brought to Christ deserves no blame. But to separate oneself from the one to whom one was bringing others cannot escape blame." What then do we say? That he was in fact not separating himself? For he did not say, "I pray to be separated," but "I could wish." That is: if it were possible, if it could happen that a godly longing were overcome by a divine longing, if a love worthy of God could surpass a divine love, I would have striven to undergo even this. For Paul did everything in order to win all people for Christ, but above all the Jews. They were his kinsmen and had been brought up under the laws, and to them the promises had been given from of old through the fathers. But they also opposed the preaching more than the others. That is why the struggle over them,

the zeal and the toil were greater. He wanted to prevent the law from seeming to have contributed nothing to grace, and from seeming to have made the souls it trained no better prepared. He did not want the promises to the fathers to be thought false or vain. He did not want Christ to be blasphemed by those who ought above all to worship him. And when his nearest kin were behaving outrageously toward our common Master, he did not want to seem to share in their outrage himself, through his share, and that a very great one, in the same blood. Such was Paul's soul. Through every means he wanted complete glory and worship to be brought to God: through himself, through those of his own race, through the Gentiles. He could not bear to present the ministry of his apostleship lacking in any part. Most of all, the unbelief of his kinsmen grieved him, and he burned with concern for them. To show this he said, "I could wish that I myself were accursed." It is as if he said: "This is how the goad of longing drives me to speak. This is how the flame of affection that feeds on my heart forces me to cry out. This is how my love for Christ, and my eagerness to consecrate everyone to him, persuade me to think. I would wish it, if it were admissible, if it were allowed. I would wish it if there were some saving separation that granted union with God, some separation that bound more tightly, some estrangement that united more perfectly. For the sake of Christ's glory and the salvation of my own people, I would not have passed over even this way." He had already shown his love for Christ from everything that exists. He said "I am persuaded," and confirmed his faith by both words and deeds, "that neither death nor life, nor rulers nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." He went through everything that exists, listing it part by part and summing it up, yet the course of his longing had not yet come to rest. So he goes on to add things that neither exist nor have ever come to be but are only supposed. He is like a lover who knows no satiety, who always thinks he falls short of what he owes and strives to make up the rest. He all but says: "I would have laid down hope itself, the race itself, salvation itself, if Christ were glorified more by such an act and the Jewish nation turned and was saved." But to think and speak like this is no separation (how could it be?) and no division. It is rather a wonderful and supernatural union, a most novel kind of joining. It is the clearest proof of an incomparable affection for God and for human beings, and truly the one unmistakable mark of that blessed and heavenly soul of Paul. This, then, is the first solution to the difficulty, and I think it does not stray far from the apostle's mind. But Paul's planting is not of a single kind. Sometimes it has many stems and varies, so that from one field of the text ripe fruits of

meaning spring up. Come, then, let us gather the rest of the fruit [?] as well, and anything else from that field that is worth harvesting. We see that the divine Paul does not simply say that he wishes to be separated from Christ for the sake of his own people, nor [?] to stand apart for ever, which would perhaps be more fearful. He does not say, "From now on I pray to become accursed," but "I could wish to be." This amounts to saying: "I would have thought it better, if only you had run to the preaching of Christ, that I should linger a little longer at the gates of the letter of the law and sit in its shadow, than that I should have run ahead and hastened along the course of faith and then see you so hostile to grace and unwilling to turn to it." And indeed, even if he had lingered, he would have fallen behind in nothing [?], even though many had started before him. But why should one cautiously say that he fell behind no one, instead of boldly stating the truth, that he outran everyone in his course and his zeal? For Paul himself, delay would have led to nothing harmful. But he felt no small fear for those so badly disposed toward the faith, that they might suffer the same hardness of heart all their lives and bring eternal destruction on themselves. That is why he puts their salvation ahead of his own speedier entry into salvation. Note too that divine Scripture often uses "anathema" to mean bodily affliction and punishment. Then you will easily understand that with these words the divine Paul was praying to suffer what evildoers suffer, so that his kinsmen might be saved. And not only this, but to suffer it at the hands of Christ himself as judge, pronouncing the sentence of punishment. That is what "from Christ" would mean. This is great and wonderful, how could it not be? Yet it brings in no separation from the longing for Christ or from union with him, and it gives no foothold to the difficulties raised above. For wishing to suffer the extremes in one's body for the salvation of others does not diminish divine affection at all, even if it draws a sentence from above. I would rather say that it increases it. So the divine Paul offered himself. He prayed to undergo bitter and heavy punishments, if only he might see his own people lay down their envy and their war against Christ, shake off the heavy and ancient burden of the law, and come under the kindly and light yoke of grace. It remains to observe the following. Suppose someone takes nothing into account beyond what is written. He approaches the words as they stand, without any over-subtle reasoning, and entrusts the verdict about them to impartial judgment and, to use the divine Apostle's own term, to "spiritual examination." He will find nothing difficult or puzzling in them [?]. I will pass over the patriarch's wonderful Rebekah, who boldly [?] drew a curse upon herself so that by skill she might secure for her son the inheritance of his father's blessing [?]. But [?] Moses, the one who saw God [?], said the same things on behalf of the Jews before Paul, in a few words. Will that not suffice, in place of everything else, to resolve the difficulties raised against the Apostle's words? For what does he say? "If you will forgive them, forgive them; but if not, blot me out [?]"… but how [?]; truly akin [?] … will suffice [?].

the soul of Moses [?] to the soul of Paul. "From the book of life," he says. What else does this mean than: "If you will not be reconciled to my kin and join them to yourself" (O mind drunk with undiluted care for those of its own blood!), "separate me too from yourself"? For clearly whoever is blotted out of that book is also condemned to separation from God. It makes no difference whether one says, "Blot me out of the book of life," or "Separate me from yourself." O boldness that won not only freedom from condemnation but also renown, through God's generosity and through its own labours as well! For that voice rescued his people from a just wrath, and God did not blot the speaker out of the register of the ever-living. Moses is wonderful for saying and doing these things. So too Paul, shown to be even more vehement in the same kind of things, is to that degree more wonderful. Or does he not seem to you to make himself anathema for the salvation of his kinsmen, and in a way to cut himself off from grace, when he circumcised Timothy? Or when he, the brilliant preacher of the Gospel, went through Jewish vows? He shaved the hair of his head and offered the customary sacrifices. He did this not for himself alone but also for others who were purified with him, and he paid the costs and expenses of the sacrifice. To what end? So that he might win everyone for Christ, bring more people to him and by all means save some. For this reason he becomes a Jew to the Jews, behaves as one without the law toward those without the law, and is weak with the weak. Yet he is none of these things, either in his judgment or in fact [?]. He "becomes all things to all people, so that by all means he may draw some up out of error." To put it in a word, he was a skilful imitator of our common Saviour and Master. Our Lord suffered everything for us with the unspeakable wealth of his love for humankind and his self-emptying. For our sake he did not refuse even to be called and considered sin and curse, though he is the source of all blessing and the destruction of all sin. The disciple, truly genuine, set him before himself throughout his life as a noble example. He never stopped copying that wonderful and much-loved image of Christ's way of life into his soul and stamping it there. As for the question that puzzled you, receive these solutions. I do not know whether they fall short of what you need, but they certainly run longer than a letter calls for. Farewell.

QUESTION [?]. On the tabernacle of witness. You ask why the lawgiver commands the tabernacle of witness to be covered with coverings woven of different colours. He calls such fabric spurious and turns those he was instructing away from wearing it. Yet the tabernacle was where God appeared and where the holy of holies was kept. You may hear an explanation that applies both to this and to similar cases. In laying down such laws, the divine Moses was making clear that one must not attend upon bare

…by the wording of the letter, nor to hold fast to the obvious sense of what is apprehended; for those who stubbornly insist on reading it that way will never be able to capture the meaning of what is commanded. Of this kind is the command to do no work at all on the Sabbath, while the priests are permitted, for the sake of the sacrifices, both to chop wood and to slaughter victims, though they above all others, as the standard and, as it were, the model for the people, ought to have kept the legislation inviolate. So too is the command not to build altars of hewn stone because they are defiled, giving the tool as the cause of the defilement, since it had been laid on the stones in dressing them; and yet with a blade they perform what is most honoured and greatest among the Hebrews, circumcision, and indeed all their sacred rites are carried out and completed with blades. And then there is this: whoever touches a corpse is unclean and is then cleansed by the priest; but the priest cannot cleanse him except by means of victims, which he himself first puts to death and touches, and with the blood of the dead animals, or with the ashes, he sprinkles the man who comes to him because he has touched a corpse, so that he may be cleansed. To anyone who stays with the letter, this looks like nothing but a riddle. Of the same kind is the absolute prohibition on Israel's making any likeness, while the very one who laid down this law first had the ark itself made after the pattern and in imitation of what had been shown him on the mountain, and then had images and likenesses of the cherubim carved and chased, and woven and embroidered into the curtains, and likenesses of pomegranates worked onto the sacred vessels, and countless other things. And who would not marvel at this, if he lingers only at the porch of the wonder and does not lift his mind to what lies hidden within? The man whose body is spotted with newly arisen leprosy, but whose whole surface has not yet been ravaged by the disease, the law declares unclean and defiled; but the man whose whole body is gripped by the evil, who has become an abomination [?], and [?] near to having even the natural bonds of his body come apart, this man is judged clean and worthy of the congregation? And if you wish to look also at this among those who lived under the law: no one was permitted to dare to sacrifice anywhere other than at the tabernacle, for the penalty of blood awaited the transgressor; nor, after the temple was built, to perform sacred rites outside it. Yet the wonderful Samuel set up an altar while the tabernacle was still standing, and leaving the tabernacle aside he offered his sacrifices there. And not he alone, but the holy Elijah too, while the temple in Jerusalem stood in its splendour, raised altars on Carmel and offered sacrifices. And none of these men was, I will not say spared from blame, but was even warmly accepted by God, who through Moses had forbidden that any such thing be dared,

and the burnt offering of their victims was made by heavenly fire more conspicuous and more marvellous than all the other sacrifices whose performance was directed by the law. Then again Samuel, raised to the height of the high priesthood and of prophecy, slays Agag with his sacred hands; and before him Phinehas, for a double slaughter, of a kinsman and of a foreigner, carries off the priesthood as an everlasting gift. Moreover, still earlier, those who had filled their hands with the blood of their own kin were counted worthy of a splendid blessing and of greater honour, even though the guilt was shared by those who were punished and those who exacted the punishment; yet these men were honoured with such rewards for shedding blood. But King David, who was compelled to go out in wars against those who opposed him, was for that reason prevented when he was eager to raise up the temple in Jerusalem. And Saul and Ahab, because they looked with humane eyes on the enemies they had captured, were punished with the loss of their kingdom and paid the penalty of death by the sword; while David, because he subjected such people to a juster judgment, was judged unworthy of building the temple. And if you wish, this same man is shown to be worthy again: he raises an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan and offers a wonderful sacrifice, heavenly fire joining to make the burnt offering acceptable, and by propitiating God he stays the unrestrained fury of divine and just wrath that was consuming all Israel; and yet this same man, for having been unrelenting toward the blood of enemies, is shut out from building a temple to God. How, then, will reading these and similar things according to the letter free them from charges and contradictions, and display the fitting coherence that is to be seen in them, rather than fill them with great confusion and perplexity? Besides this, what sense would it make that God permits marriage and counts it worthy of his blessing, yet by the divine statutes calls unclean the one who has had intercourse in the mysteries of nature, and decrees that he may not approach holy things unless he is cleansed? Again, that an earthen vessel, when it touches anything unclean, is to be broken, as though what has been defiled could no longer be freed from its uncleanness; but if it is bronze or wooden, it is easily rid of the uncleanness by water? And that the bones of Elisha, by the common law of the dead, lead to uncleanness, yet the dead man who came near them received from them pure rays of life and was brought back from the gloomy gates of death to the light of life? What then? Will you call unclean those who, by coming near the bones of a dead man, were cleansed of the uncleanness of death? Or will you offer for them not a thank offering for their raising but a purification offering for the [Variant readings: a. C. M.: "subjected similar ones who had been captured." b. Another reading: "shut out"; C. M.: "call." c. Another reading: "be washed off"; C. M.: "be freed."]

touch by which they were raised? And how would the apparent sense of the written words here not be great ignorance and [?]? And the jawbone of the donkey, a source of threefold uncleanness, how did it pour forth streams of clean, drinkable water for the thirsty Nazirite, becoming renowned for wonders as great as its uncleanness? For it was the bone of a donkey, and of a dead one, and third, an instrument of killing; and it did not lie in the ground near water, nor would any moisture secretly seeping into the bone have [?] it, but it was carried in the hand of a fighting man as a weapon against enemies; and it gushed out so great a spring of water that the man who had grown thirsty through so much toil and weariness, and over so long a stretch of time, had a share of drink unstinted and abundant, beyond his need. Such, then, was the miracle that the bones of the unclean, dead and murderous animal served. As for those who make "Jawbone of a Donkey" the name of a spring, and bring the water to the thirsty man from there, they do no harm at all to the present argument; for it is plain that they too, in saying this, are tracking far from the letter. But as long as faith in miraculous works stands firm, I would not gladly agree with them. And why should one go on enumerating such things? For almost through the whole letter of the law such a storm of enigmatic meanings has been poured out. But, as I said at the beginning, through these and all such things the wise lawgiver clearly shows that the announcement according to the letter and the obvious sense of what is written is one thing, spread out like a veil over hidden truths, and that the divine wisdom of the spirit, concealed in the depths, is another; and the multitude of the Jews and of the Judaizing heretics, standing far from it [?], do not cease from a long and grievous wandering.

Question 111. What causes you so much perplexity, as you write, does not seem to me to involve much difficulty. For in the first place, the Son, who exists in the form of God the Father, having appeared in human nature and form, mostly conversed with his disciples as a man, showing that he had taken on our nature. And what is so perplexing if the one who grew tired and sweated and rested in sleep, who, to put it all in a word, sustained the flowing nature of the body with food and drink, this very one should also take on ignorance of the coming day, and should not decline to set limits to the measure of human knowledge, just as he did with the other human things? For as Creator of all and God, he knew all things together with the Father; but as man, he did not reject even the ignorance that befits human beings. For he who chose to take on the whole, how would he have refused to take, or to be believed to have taken, any single part of it?

[?] Second, even if someone says that the sense of the words looks to postponement, and to his not wishing to tell the disciples what it was not yet profitable for them to learn, the method of loving providence does not reject this either. It might be carried out by an ignorance assumed by way of dispensation, and by his preferring to seem not to know rather than grieve the disciples, who were seeking to learn what he knew, by not teaching them. For how else would it make sense that he should know the things before that hour and teach them with great precision, yet not recognize the hour itself, which follows upon them and is the smallest part of all? How could any existing thing escape that divine mind from which nothing is hidden? Or what reason would there be that he should have [?] the knowledge of the things brought into being by him, while the time alone lies beyond his comprehension; that the power of the judgment should depend on him ("for the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son"), while the discernment and determination of the hour escapes his wisdom and lordship? And why do I say these things? Will he who knows the Father, as the Father knows the Son, be ignorant of a day and an hour, small and easily bounded intervals? Is it not plain that he will not [?]? He who knows all things even before they came into being, the enhypostatic Wisdom of the Father, who has everything that is the Father's except unbegottenness, was certainly not ignorant of such things either; but, deferring a knowledge that was unprofitable for the disciples, out of love for mankind he made their ignorance his own, and framed his answer to them so as to cause them no grief. Third, one might also see this: that the Son yields the prerogatives to the Father as the cause. For it befits a Son who loves his Father, the Creator and Lawgiver of every nature and of all good order, to honour the Father also with the privileges of being the cause, and to ascribe to him the knowledge of that day and hour, just as he ascribes many other things to him; not depriving himself of it (far from it!), any more than of any other honourable and good thing, but giving the Father precedence in this too. And surely no one who makes the Son's grateful reverence a pretext for ingratitude, and then fastens ignorance on him, taking refuge in the syllables of the wording, will be acquitted of blasphemy. For not even the precise wording, as will be shown later, gives anyone a pretext for not wishing [to think] rightly

…described a theory. He said that knowing is twofold: one kind by understanding, the other by experience. By understanding, then, the Son knows that day and hour just as the Father does; but by experience not yet. For the Father had come to experience and had acquired such knowledge when he gave all judgment to the Son; for the Father had then judged it right to hand over all judgment to the Son, and, as far as concerned his own decisions, his own judgment had been put into effect and brought to completion. But the Son, plainly, has not yet judged, nor has he yet brought into actual practice the work of which the Father proclaimed him Lord. Therefore the Father knows the hour also by experience; but the Son, though he knows it by understanding as the Father does, does not yet know it by experience as well. He will know it when he delivers the judgment, his knowledge by understanding then passing over into knowledge by experience. I have set out this interpretation for you, not for whatever truth it contains, but to show how a man of such great simplicity took care to work his way into so intricate and elaborate an idea. That the words themselves offer no refuge to those who make ignorance a ground of slander is easy to learn from what follows. The holy Matthew, recording the Lord's saying, writes: "No one knows the day or the hour, not even the angels, except my Father only." Consider, then: first, that having said "not even the angels," he does not go on to add "nor the Son." For the wording would perhaps have offered a retreat for the impiety if he had added the Son to the angels and then gone on, "except my Father only." But as it is, he does not speak that way anywhere; having extended the ignorance as far as the angels, he does not bring the Son under it, so that the Father, mentioned next, has no room to be set in contrast with the Son as they would have it. Rather, ascending from below, from the disciples, and reaching the angels, he goes no further; enclosing the ignorance there, he removes the supra-essential and creative essence far from it and places it above it. For the question was asked by human beings, the disciples, and the answer was "No one knows," that is, no human being; then, "not even the angels": [?] this rank, the nature of the bodiless beings, is second after the human. What then of the Son? If, as is indeed the law of sons, he is heir of his Father's glory and nature, you gape for ignorance in vain. If he does not have that, he will fill for you the third rank of creatures; and then how does the saying leap over him and pass on to the Father? For if he held not the Father's rank but a third rank, the saying ought first to have said of the Only-begotten, "nor the Son," and only then ascribed the knowledge to the Father. But as it is, having gone through human beings and bodiless minds, he does not carry the ignorance over to the Son, but at once bears witness to the Father's nature, of which the Son is the true heir, as having the [Variant readings: a. C. M.: "the Father … the judgment to the …" b. C. M.: "the ignorance and the." [?]]

knowledge. Where, then, did you get the ignorance that you fabricate as an insult to the Son? Unless, perhaps, for you the Only-begotten and Lord is to be ranked with the angels and servants, something no impiety has ever yet been seen to devise. But if you do not dare this, and you exempt the Son from the angelic essence, even though you do not yet grant him equality with the Father's, then, since the words so plainly declare the ignorance of the angels, you will surely have no way of fastening it on him, even if you force him ten thousand times into some other rank apart from his paternal inheritance. And so, again, even against your will, the Only-begotten, joined with the Father in a knowledge that even by your own account is supernatural, supreme and paternal, will make a mockery of your banished third ranking. Where, then, does it appear here, either in the wording or in the sense, that ignorance pertains to the Son, as the heretics in their madness leap to claim? "Yes," he says, "but he added, 'except my Father only.'" Very well and wisely said, so that you would not think that the ignorance, having run through the bodiless minds, had room to advance even as far as the first nature itself. For from this nature, this alone, the creator and sovereign of all things, he casts ignorance as far away as possible, just as he does all the other things by which the created order is recognized. And if the word "only" still stirs up confusion, let him understand rather that it is in contrast to those whose ignorance he mentioned, and from whom he distinguished the Father, that he also set the word "only." For what sense at all would it make, after attributing ignorance to the angels, to leave them aside and suppose that "except my Father only" was said to distinguish the Father from the Son, of whom he had said nothing? Further, if "only" is troubling, let the trouble be dissolved by "my Father." For it is plain that he did not use "only" to set himself apart from the one with whom he proclaimed his natural kinship by saying "my Father," but in contrast to those whose ignorance he declared along with it. How could he be thought to distinguish himself in saying "except my Father only," he who cries out equally in word and deed, "I and the Father are one," and "All that the Father has is mine"? For it is plain that knowledge too is one of the things, and the smallest of them, that the one who begot him has, along with countless others. And apart from what has been said, [?] the Only-begotten, who assigns ignorance to them and knowledge to the Father, what [?] is this, that he who counts himself worthy of the greater things, and of what is always proper to God alone, should declare himself unworthy of the knowledge of a matter that will later be revealed to all, good and wicked alike?

Is it not clear from every side that ignorance will in no way come to the aid of the heretics? For the common teacher and Saviour of our race, teaching those he had set apart as disciples to understand their proper limits and to keep away from inquiries that make life

no better, but that for many might become an occasion of conceit and empty swelling pride, and arranging to introduce what was beneficial to them without grieving them, and by persuasion rather than by force, brings the angels before them as an example: so that, not receiving knowledge of the things which even the bodiless beings, who are above us, do not have, they would neither be distressed nor have any complaint against their teacher for not choosing to teach them what even the bodiless nature, which is above them, did not know. What then? Was this not enough for the disciples, both to make the failure of their request as painless as possible for them and to set their minds in order so as not to search into anything beyond them? Must the enhypostatic Wisdom, the Son, also be drawn into their ignorance, as it seems? And what consolation or what encouragement is the ignorance of God to his worshippers, who need his providence and wisdom? Rather, how is it not an abyss of despair, an impiety besides, deep darkness, utter dejection and an error deserving no mercy, to have a God overcome by ignorance, and to confess that he needs to learn and needs another's providence in order to come to know what until now, like the rest of creation, he does not know? For if one accepts the ignorance as pertaining to his humanity, it has been said already that there is nothing difficult in the source of wisdom, who both knows and has all that the Father has, taking on ignorance just as he took on the other human things. But if one refers the insult of ignorance to his divine and undefiled nature, how is the impiety not grievous on every count, and beyond pardon? Consider this as well. The Saviour said somewhere, "No one knows the Father except the Son." What then? Because of "no one knows" and "except the Son," will you exclude the Father from knowledge of himself? And how would that not be plain madness? Rather, you will understand these words as distinguishing him from all that comes after the first nature, and in no way as directed against the Father, who is instead understood together with the Son and brought in along with the mention of him. How, then, when you hear "No one knows the hour except the Father," do you not keep the same rule, understanding the Son together with the mention of the Father, and assigning "no one knows" to rational creation? Yet here he even listed the natures of created beings by kind, so that it was more natural to take "no one knows" as referring to them; whereas "No one knows the Father" carries an unrestricted expression, with nothing in the preceding words to which it might be confined. If, then, in "No one knows the Father except the Son" you shrink from blaspheming the Begetter, do not in "No one knows the hour except the Father" be turned to insulting the Begotten either. But if you dare the second, you have dared the first all the more; for it is more ignorant not to know oneself than not to know another. Why not

…is not the former even more dreadful as an insult than the second? And if that one leaves no one any further extreme of madness and impiety, what could anyone say about this? Again he says, "No one knows the Son except the Father"; and no one would condemn the Son as ignorant of himself unless, on top of the other absurdity, he also made the Son's knowledge of the Father inferior, if indeed the Son has grasped that knowledge but has not yet attained knowledge of himself. So if, in "No one knows the Son except the Father," they in no way exclude the Son from knowledge of himself, neither in "No one knows the hour except the Father" will they exclude him from foreknowledge of that time. And if they drive him out of this, they have already driven him out of that, even if they have not yet dared to lend their lips to the service of their impious reasonings. For the form of the statement, on which above all they built up their deception and kept up their hopes of impiety, is exactly the same. And as for knowledge of the Son, they would not rave so far, nor would they themselves deny, that it is far more divine and exalted than foreknowledge of that hour. Such, then, is the saying of the holy Matthew, and such is its meaning in these words. But the blessed Mark was inspired by the same Spirit, rich in the same grace, and entrusted with the same word of preaching. Plainly, then, even without examining the text, he would never say anything that conflicts either with his fellow hierophant and fellow initiator into the mysteries, or with the truth into which they initiated us and which has been brilliantly shown through many things [?]. Nevertheless, an examination of the text will make their agreement, and their common striving for the truth, all the clearer. Observe with me, then, how this divine man takes care to leave the heretics no pretext at all, but shakes their contrivances from the foundations. He did not attach to his own writing even the word "alone", which they would have found lying there, a vain refuge for their impiety but a refuge nonetheless. Instead he removed the word, and with it he took away their pretext for wickedness. Like his fellow hierophant, he too ascends from the lower ranks, and having reached as far as the angels he closes off there, completing the ignorance together with the period of the sentence. Then, starting again from another beginning, he not only attributes no ignorance to the Only-begotten, but on the contrary plainly testifies that he has the Father's knowledge. And not only the knowledge: he also teaches us the manner of that knowledge, declaring in his theology that the Father, the source of the Son's other natural and divinely fitting dignities, is also the cause of his knowledge. For what does he say? "Nor would the Son know, were it not for the Father." That is, the Son's knowledge springs from the same place as the cause of his begetting. For he is not without beginning and without cause, as the Father is. He is referred back to a beginning, and has the one who begot him as his connatural cause.

…"Nor would the Son know, were it not for the Father." What testimony could be more brilliant or weightier than this? What the Father knows, the Son also knows. If anything escaped the Son, he would draw the cause of it from the Father; but nothing escapes the Father's knowledge, and so nothing escapes the Son's either. The nature is common, the divinity is common, the essence is common, and the communion in these makes their other divinely fitting dignities common and undivided as well. "The Father gives life to whom he wills," and again "the Son gives life to whom he wills." No one comes to the Father except through the Son, and no one comes to the Son except through the Father. The Father knows the Son, and as he knows him, so the Son knows the Father. Whatever the Father has, apart from being unbegotten, the Son has entirely; and whatever the Son has, apart from being begotten, the Father has entirely. "For what is mine," he says, "is yours, and what is yours is mine." The divine Mark had been initiated into this theology and initiates us into it. Defining his teaching with precision and brevity at once, he cries aloud, "Nor would the Son know, were it not for the Father." Having stated the conditional premise of the argument, he left out the minor premise, since it is evident to all of itself and disputed by no one. For there is not, and never will be, anyone who would refuse to attribute to the Father the knowledge of that day and hour. Not even the architect of evil himself would belch such a thing from his lips into anyone's ears. Whoever grants this, however grudgingly, will be bound to concede, however unwillingly, that the same knowledge is in the Son. For "nor the Son, were it not for the Father," since the Father knows, brings the Son by an irrefutable argument into the same knowledge. So it is not possible [?] to say otherwise: in the most precise and God-befitting way, the text proclaims that the knowledge in the Father is shared by the Son. Now consider with me the wise and manifold economy of the all-holy and divine Spirit, and how, working in each of the evangelists through different phrasings, it brings them to the same conception of true piety. The holy Matthew adds "alone" to the words and nowhere inserts "nor the Son", so that the heretics could not claim he separates the Son from the Father's glory and drives him down into the rank of the angels. The divine Mark puts "nor the Son" first and makes it the beginning of a second period, and he removes "alone". If that word stood here too, it would become plunder for the impious, and "nor the Son" would no longer be taken as the start of a new period but would be fraudulently made the end and completion of the preceding one. Read in Mark's way, the Father's knowledge was established as common to the Son and complete. Through the fraud, however, ignorance is admitted, and the Master and Creator is assigned the rank of angels and servants, which is exactly what the fighters against God are striving for. To cut out their malice, the evangelist cuts away and destroys in advance the pretext of "alone". So, seeing how through each of these inspired and sacred-speaking men the mouths of the heretics are stopped, and the solutions to your difficulties, through…
…both turns the malice of impiety aside more firmly [?], and shows him to be a more ardent lover and champion of true piety.

QUESTION 115. On the wisdom of Solomon. Man of God, what has come over you? What were you thinking of? After so long a time, after so deep a forgetting of us, after so dreadful and unheard-of an oblivion on the part of those who once loved us, after trying so many hardships, after so long a silence imposed by condemnation (I do not say what kind), you have decided to put forward the sort of questions that are usually pursued by those who prosper in the present life and practice philosophy with greater vigor. But our very life has long since withered away in misfortunes, and we are dead in the greater part of ourselves. Now we wander about in this wretched bit of flesh (how long will you cling to life?) like some faint image of our old way of life and love of learning, an image barely even recognizable. Only one thing do we philosophize about: death. And even death grieves us by its delay, because it does not take us away more quickly from the afflictions that hold us without pause, for those who press upon us never let up. However, if for some reason I do not know it has become a pleasure for those in whom prosperity flourishes, and whose tongues herds of rhetors delight to serve, to listen to a voice from the tomb as well, then my phantom will speak, for in present circumstances that is the more fitting way to put it. Perhaps writing too lies in ambush for my silence and seeks a pretext for another tragedy. And if it also lies in wait for words, we have long had experience of those who lie in wait. So it will speak rather than keep silent. But it will speak briefly and humbly, as is fitting for those in such a condition to answer. The first question, then, concerns "Solomon was wiser than all men, and than Ethan the Israelite," and so on. First we say this: we have nowhere found "Israelite" written, as you have quoted the passage, unless our afflictions have already taken our very memory away as well. Instead of "Israelite" we have read "Zarahite". For "Israelites" is the whole race of the Jews, and the nation bears that name in common. To characterize particular persons by a common term, to which their descent refers all alike, cannot escape just censure. The reading would be correct if "Israelite" were replaced by "Zarahite". As for Ethan, some of the copies call him Gaethan, perhaps indicating the same man by two names. The rest of the passage splits into two texts and is varied by a double interpretation. If the text reads "Heman and Chalcad and Cardala", it indicates ancient men born to wisdom, who prophesied in Egypt before Moses had yet come forth into the light of the sun.

These would then be descendants of Zerah, who was born to Judah of Tamar. Along with prophecy and wisdom of other kinds, their nature had also been richly endowed for the composition of songs, so that some of the psalms carry their name in the title. So the divine Scripture says that Solomon surpassed in wisdom not only other men but these men too. But if, according to the other form of the reasoning, Solomon is said to have outshone all men and to have been wiser than Ethan and Heman, one should know that Ethan and Heman did not merely leave their glory preserved in memory, as Chalcad and his companions did. In the very times when Solomon was astonishing everyone with the wonder of his wisdom, they too were seen to excel all their kin, partly by greatness of nature and partly by wealth of wisdom. And what else did they do but proclaim the king's glory all the more brilliantly, by holding second place to him, while they themselves possessed an invincible power of making his fame resound to the ends of the earth [?]? Besides the things for which they were admired, they were also psalmists like the others, singing the wonders of God with lyres, harps and cymbals. Ethan's ancestor, I think, was Merari, who held third place in the list of Levi's sons. Heman was the son of Joel and the grandson of the prophet Samuel, whom the Oracles connect with the kindred of Korah. Korah and his sons were kinsmen of Moses the lawgiver, cousins' children, so that Heman's bodily descent also came from that line. That is enough on the first question. As for David, we know that he was anointed once but proclaimed king twice. He was anointed by Samuel the prophet. He was proclaimed first by the vote of the tribe of Judah in Hebron, and seven years later by the remaining tribes, who approved the earlier decision with unanimous judgment. The Oracles, speaking more loosely, call both the earlier and the later proclamation by the people an "anointing". David appears to have put on a royal crown, as far as I remember, when Joab had first made war on Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, their royal city, and brought it near to capture, and the king arrived and finished the siege. Then, holding as spoil the crown of Milcom (for he too was king of the captured), and having won an uncontested and brilliant victory over him and his whole people, David placed it on his own head. It was adorned with precious stones and weighed a talent of gold. The "thigh" is rendered "shin" in the edition of Aquila. Strictly speaking, it would be the "leg", which is also denoted by two other names, I mean the limb after the thigh and the extremity beyond the thigh. For the word "shin" wanders across various things. People are accustomed to call "shin" the front of the leg rising into the muscle, as the back is called the "calf"; and also the whole thing composed of the shinbone and the fibula,

together with the flesh that covers them. [?] Some of the copies read "from the people", others "beside the others". If it is "from the people", it means, "I have set this before you as a testimony in the presence of the people." If it is "beside the others", it means, "I have bestowed the honor on you as a special portion, chosen above the others." These limbs of the body might also carry an image of kingship. Though they are shorter than many of the animal's limbs, they nevertheless support it and bear up the whole bulk of the composite body. In the same way the firmness of a king, though concentrated in one man, holds up and supports the whole body of the state even when it is shaken, and does not let it collapse and be shattered. But these things are perhaps too elaborate for the voice of a phantom. Farewell in soul and body, and no longer put such questions to those in Hades. Put them to those whose life runs smoothly, whose mind, words and hands have not been paralyzed. On the homeland of Paul. Paul, the divine apostle, by his burning longing of love for Christ and his unsurpassable course of preaching won for himself the Jerusalem above as his homeland. By lot, from his ancient ancestors and his bodily descent, his homeland was Gischala, which is now a village of Judea but was formerly a small town. But his parents, together with many others of the nation, were captured by the Roman spear, and that event gave him Tarsus as his homeland, where his mother gave birth to him. "For I am," he says, "a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia." Then Roman munificence, vying with the greatness of their power, extended its generosity even to foreigners, and permission was granted to rise to the Romans' noble standing in citizenship and name, sometimes as a gift and sometimes for a great deal of money. So in this way, by a few syllables and human laws, Rome and the Roman commonwealth became a homeland for the parents of the inspired Paul as well. This is what that divine man indicated when he said to the tribune who boasted of a Roman kinship acquired by purchase, "But I was even born a citizen." That is, "Roman kinship comes down to me as a paternal inheritance, and I did not come forth into the light from my mother's womb while my parents were still [?]

but when Roman blood was already dignifying them in the registers." So the orator of the truth is found to have not only two homelands, as you yourself argue, but a third besides. One of them, Gischala, is reckoned to the portion and jurisdiction of the tribe of Benjamin. Tarsus was the gift of captivity. And the enrollment of his parents among the Romans makes him a Roman, together with the paternal rank that passed to him by inheritance.

QUESTION 117. The same difficulty and its solution. The renowned Barnabas, truly a vessel of gentleness and compassion, was a Jew by the blood of his ancestors but derived his Cyprian origin from his homeland. The eloquent Apollos, who reached Ephesus with his preaching and crossed over to Achaia, was of Jewish stock as far as the nature of his parents goes, but through residence was registered with Alexandria as his homeland. In the same way the holy Paul, though sprung from the Jews and traced to the tribe of Benjamin, acquired Tarsus as his homeland, because his parents had settled in that Greek city. Again, the tribune stood as far as possible from the Roman race by his parents and his native land, but with money, as he himself admitted, he was admitted to their distinction. The city of Philippi, the metropolis of the province of Macedonia, had no claim to kinship with the Romans, yet it was able to shine with their name. For the masters of the slave girl from whom the spirit of Python was driven out were enraged against the heralds of the truth, since the healing had driven away their trade along with the affliction. Dragging before the magistrates those who had rid her of the demon's fabrication, they said, "These men are throwing our city into confusion. They are Jews, and they proclaim customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans." You see how the Philippians pride themselves on the name of Romans. Again, at a later time Josephus, sprung from genuine Hebrew seed, with Jerusalem itself as his allotted homeland, descended from priests and a priest himself, nevertheless took the name "Flavius" in addition to the Roman name, a privilege that Vespasian's family name conferred on those who boasted of Roman kinship. And in calling himself both Roman and Flavius, Josephus was never convicted of being an alien, even though many attacked him out of envy; nor was he even brought to trial [?]. And, if you like, the city of Jerusalem itself, which in later generations received the name Aelia from Hadrian's family name,

[?] slipped, as the saying goes, into the Roman race. All these, though foreign in nation and homeland, were enrolled as Roman citizens. In the same way the parents of the inspired Paul did not live in obscurity within the Jewish commonwealth but had some advantage over the many, and through enrollment they were judged not unworthy to be counted members of the Roman fraternity. And so the wise Paul was well aware that Roman nobility had come down to him from his father by right of succession. From now on, let your concern be no longer merely to raise difficulties, but much more to seek out and value solutions that suit the question. Someone who tries to resolve dialectical problems from immediate, primary and per se principles while granting the [?] does not escape the charge of falsehood. Someone who demands geometrical necessities in rhetoric, and someone who tries to bring forward civic and superficial proofs for mathematical theorems, falls into something similar, not to put it more harshly. In the same way, those who expect to learn the truth about historical questions not historically, but from another kind of reasoning, fall into the same error.

QUESTION 118. Why was Christ circumcised? The deeper purpose of Providence, for which Jesus Christ our God received circumcision in the flesh, withdraws from human understanding and sinks into the unsearchable depth of his judgments. But what we can see, taught by our blessed Fathers and examining it ourselves, we do not find beyond reach. First, he is cut in the flesh to refute those who slander the Old Testament and hurl insults at the one who gave its laws. For the good and true God underwent the circumcision given from there, as not even they would deny. By these very deeds he bears witness that the lawgiver of circumcision is good, a giver of good things, and shares the same nature. If the lawgiver were of a contrary nature, the fountain of goodness would not have displayed the drops of the law from there pouring forth through his own flesh. So to muzzle the unbarred mouths that spoke blasphemy against the Father, or indeed against the Son himself ("For all that is the Father's is the Son's," and "whatever the Father does, the Son also does"), he is cut in the flesh of the foreskin, and with it he cuts away the occasions of many impious heresies. Second, consider this. The impious Apollinarius once dared to make the fantastic claim that the flesh that was assumed shared one essence with the divinity that assumed it. He fashioned flesh to suit himself, not such as human nature knows, but such as the fantasy of deranged reasonings created. So the cutting of the flesh, and the

…brilliantly proclaims that the Godhead is of another nature, and shows that what is consubstantial with our flesh is also there. Third, besides what has been said, the children of the Manichaeans make it a dogma that Christ took on flesh only in appearance. But, as you see, the circumcision walls off this blasphemy too in advance. An appearance does not admit of cutting and suffering and a visible flow of blood, nor does a phantom straightforwardly admit the works of reality. Again, Valentinus talks emptily, saying that the flesh united to the Word was not formed from the virgin's undefiled blood. Having fallen down from piety, he brings the body down to him from somewhere above. But this man's audacity too, as is clear, is cut off from afar by the circumcision. Besides these things, he is circumcised in order to show the [?] of the commandment that had been given. For together with the blamelessness of those who observed it, he establishes that its inviolability remained until his own coming.
