If he who had no need of circumcision at all nevertheless undergoes it, hardly could anyone under the law who disregarded it be found not liable to penalty. Again, the people of the Jews, being most fond of finding fault and clever at inventing pretexts that do not exist, would have had a plea to seize on if he had brought them salvation without undergoing circumcision. What plea would they not have thought to grasp at as they thrust the teaching away? "How could we accept as savior someone who is uncircumcised and who overturns every ordinance from the very hearth?" So, to shut off every retreat for them, and so that they might have no room to turn their own sin onto the one who was blameless, he is circumcised in the foreskin, and at the same time he cuts away every specious argument of the ungrateful. Consider this too, I ask you. If he had put an end to the practice without being circumcised, the Master might perhaps have been suspected by some of having contrived the abolition of circumcision through his disciples, as though to free himself from blame while championing his own purpose. But since he both is circumcised and puts an end to the practice, he removes this suspicion of the fault-finders in advance. And do not pass over this either: circumcision was a type and symbol of baptism. So as long as the truth had not yet been revealed, the type had to prevail; but once the truth had arrived, the type had to withdraw. Therefore the hidden part of the flesh is circumcised while the circumcision of grace has not yet been revealed. But once that circumcision illumines all things by the Lord's baptism and displays the truth in brightness, the things of shadow and riddle find no place to speak openly. Apart from what has been said, we must also recall this: that in the seed of Abraham all the nations will be blessed. God, swearing an oath by himself to the righteous man, makes his tribe the chosen one out of all nations. As though sealing it through the head of the tribe with circumcision, he both marks the faith of the patriarch

and at the same time keeps the race set apart. So if all the nations had been blessed through Christ, the common Savior alone, and he had not borne the mark of Abraham's seed, which was circumcision, the oath would have given grounds for a charge of breaking it. So that the promise might reach its gracious fulfillment for Abraham, and that he might dissolve any suspicion of perjury against the Truth (and the Truth is God, for "I am," he says, "the truth and the life"), he is cut in the flesh of the foreskin at the first-fruits and introduction of grace. And this is the calling, the blessing, and the adoption of the nations, by which he at once brings the way of life under the law to its limit and fulfills it. One might observe many other such things at leisure. But since neither the rule of a letter nor your own intelligence finds it agreeable (for what is there, among the things passed over in silence, that could not be hunted out from what has been said?), setting them out has been judged superfluous.

Question [119]. "No one has ever seen God." Your fine diligence and zeal for such wise and divine studies rouses not only me to attend to them. It also, I think, moves to wonder, and to words worthy of praise, everyone in whom no rival passion has dissolved the charm of noble things and set indifference in its place. This is especially so because, though you have been entrusted with so many cares [?], over which you keep watch each day as you provide for them, you do not turn aside to rest and recreation from your labors. Instead you turn your thoughts still further, toward effective action and what will benefit the fatherland. Nor do you cease searching the depth of such wonderful and philosophical speculations until, as far as possible, you succeed in running up to the very summit of truth. I count blessed those who see and hear these things in you. And then I become aware of the malice of my enemies, and of what a fine and most delightful sight envy has robbed me: the sight of philosophy dancing in public life, and our philosophy at that, whose fruit is heavenly things. As for us, then, like the Aegians we are "neither third nor fourth," for our affairs have come to this lot. I do not know the tribe [?]. I know the potsherd; I do not know whether the pebble is dropped into the urn through the funnel; I do not know anything else. For the Pythian oracle,

anyway, let it go, since it has nothing to do with us, except that something like what was said, as you yourself would put it, has brought our life to its present state. When your letter came, a severe illness was scourging me. Because of the pains pressing on me, it scarcely granted me leave to say anything at all in reply to your request. Still, as one weighed down by illness, I would say this. In its own superessential and incomprehensible essence, the divine escapes not only human sight and thought. It also escapes the very highest powers that draw near to it, which far surpass our nature. This is true not only in the present time, in which we are bound to this much-suffering flesh, but also in the ages to come. Then, when we have put away much of the riddles and mirrors and have put on incorruption instead of corruption, the truth flashes forth more purely and perfectly. What need is there to say it? Moses ascended to such a height of virtue that, among his other wonders, he had the grace to work them himself: he tilled the heaven with his tongue as though it were a field, and from it supplied ready-made food to many tens of thousands. Elijah had the nature of fire divided into horses and chariots to serve his ascent to heaven. Yet neither of them, nor the choir of the divine and blessed prophets, indeed no one at all, was able to come to a comprehension of what the supernatural and pure nature of the Godhead is, and how it is. That it is and that it subsists, it granted us to comprehend, though it shines its radiance more on some and less on others, in proportion to each one's attainment. But what it is, or how it is, it has unveiled to none of the [?]. Even to Moses, the foremost of the saints, who longed for it, it did not grant what cannot be seen. As a consolation for his failure, [?] of the incarnation, and even then the mystery is unveiled through symbols and types. To others, in [?] and likenesses, as far as a human being can see, the divine flashed forth its own glory. That no one among men has seen God or will be able to see him, the old and sacred [books] are full of testimony, and so is grace. A whole book would be needed to set out the oracles that bear witness to this knowledge. Moreover, there is the initiate and disciple of the words of the divine Paul. He was an orator in his words and a philosopher in his thoughts. Or rather, he distills from his mouth and tongue the grace from above and pours out for us the [?] of divine wisdom. This great Dionysius brilliantly and keenly pursues the point that the divine, whatever it is, is never in any way subject to human comprehension. [?]

And indeed, from the great champion of piety, who made his whole life a contest (I mean the divine Athanasius), one can take many sayings. They proclaim that the divine, without some veil, covering, or likeness, is wholly incomprehensible to the human race, as far as its essence and nature are concerned. Then there is the royal robe of the Church, the wonderful and great Basil, at once the best and the sweetest physician of souls. Who does not know that, in mixing the remedy against the madness of Eunomius, he set forth this very point as one of his Paeonian antidotes: that the divine and ineffable nature is incomprehensible and inconceivable? Moreover, there is the man who received the title "the Theologian" from the divinity of his words more than from his name (I mean Gregory). He wrote whole [?] discourses on this subject, tracking the truth with very dense and keen arguments. And indeed there is the orator of the Church, or rather the one who after Paul civilized the whole earth by the words of his preaching and the rest of his instruction, the very one whose words made his mouth known to the world as golden. He has a discourse that flows with great persuasiveness together with the truth, entitled "On [the Incomprehensible?]," which strives for and demonstrates nothing other than the point before us. At leisure, one might find countless others of our divine Fathers who cast their vote in agreement with those mentioned. If the bitterness of my illness had not intensified the pain, I might perhaps have shown their opinion in their very words. But it is easy for you, once reminded of those mentioned and of those still remaining, to gather their testimonies into one and behold how wonderful the harmony of them all is. For now it is enough for us to set out only the voice of the incorporeal beings. The choir of the apostles, seeing our common Master and God taken up together with what he had assumed, were astounded and amazed. Then these beings declared to them plainly: "Why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." He was going, clearly, to be enthroned in the Father's bosom together with what he had assumed, just as earlier on earth he bore the flesh as a covering and was clothed in the human form.

So the sacred oracle confirmed that the common Master would appear again in the same form and nature, and would come within knowledge and apprehension. And then notice, I ask you, to whom. Not to ordinary people, nor to those who surpass other people by a small measure in divine inspiration, in the height of contemplation, and in the other virtues. It was to those very men who from the beginning had been chosen by the Creator himself, out of all human nature, to become eyewitnesses and ministers of the word. As for you, fare well in all things. Keeping soul and body pure for God, may you cross the waves of life with cheerfully blowing breezes and swim above their brine.

Question 120. What does the apostolic saying mean: "Always, and now too, Christ will be glorified in my body"? The words of the orator of truth, "Always, and now too, Christ will be glorified in my body, whether by life or by death," pour forth from a reverent and holy longing. They rest on a hope that does not know mortal nature, and they suggest the following sense. Christ was always magnified in Paul's body. He was magnified both when he allowed Paul to suffer hardship in bonds and scourgings and to be thrown down at the gates of death, and when he drew him out and snatched him from the midst of his distresses. For through the trials that Paul was permitted to contend with, and as he grappled with what led to death, the preaching of piety was confirmed and strengthened. Those who saw Paul's bonds and afflictions were amazed at his endurance in them and were roused by the wonder to turn to God. They reasoned that if what he preached were not something divine and wholly true, he would not gladly give himself up to countless unbearable evils, when he could stop and be rid of his pains and not summon death to the contest. Rightly, then, Christ was magnified through these things, as the preaching came to be confirmed for the many and spread wide in people's souls. Again, when he drew Paul out and snatched him from deadly dangers, he was magnified by that very fact. For it was not by any human contrivance that the contestant was often released unharmed from the midst of a murderous hand and of evils thirsting for blood. It was a divine and superhuman grace that rescued his servant beyond hope and dissolved the dangers. How were the bonds loosed? How did the chains fall off? Who kindled the light in the cell? How did it shine all around and fill the whole place with radiance, with no material serving the flame?

How was the prison alone shaken? How were the doors opened? How did those countless astonishing things come about, unless the power of the all-ruling hand was being displayed? Through both, then, Christ was magnified in Paul's body. He was magnified when his herald endured bitter and deadly tortures, and through the means by which, supernaturally and against expectation, he made his contestant uncapturable by the bloodthirsty plots of those scheming against him and showed him to be so. So both through life, that is, through what gives and preserves life, and through the blows and tortures that bring death, Christ our God, the fount of wisdom and [?], was magnified in Paul's body. Nothing prevents the teacher's words from also sketching a prediction. He stood before Nero's tribunal a second time. The first time he made his defense and was released; the second time, as Nero's cruelty rushed against everything with unchecked violence, he departed this life by the sword. So this would be what he is now saying: Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life, as now when he snatches me from a murderous and bloodthirsty hand, or through death, as will happen later, when the president of the games does not deprive me of the crown of the contests. For it was necessary, it seems, that the athlete should not grow weary before the end. His superhuman course was not to be cut short by the common death of nature; rather, his very departure to the one he longed for was to be a prize and a contest beyond earthborn nature. This, then, is what he foreshadows and teaches his disciples in advance: he who lives not for himself but for Christ, who both becomes and is all things to all. He does so in order that afterward no confusion and turmoil, caused by the unexpectedness, should shake their souls when his martyrdom was suddenly announced. For Paul's life was truly a great thing, the first means of salvation after God. Nor should it cast them into helpless despondency, overturn all their hope, and make them slack toward piety. One can also hunt out another aim of these words, if nothing else, then at least one lying right at hand in the saying. What is it, then? "As always," he says, "throughout the whole span of life, Christ was magnified in Paul's body, as he suffered bravely and loved living in a way higher than ordinary life, and as he was delivered in ways strange to hear and too great to believe, so now too he will be magnified, even at the very end of my contests." He will be magnified both by his shield-bearer's not suffering and, likewise, by his suffering. For when this noble man came to the very last stretch of his contests, he was first released from death and slaughter. He had dissolved the charges by the word of truth and a God-fearing judgment, or rather, the almighty right hand had shown its generosity there. So clearly Christ was magnified in Paul's body. Then came the second occasion. For it was no longer necessary

to see only a miracle of the Lord's generosity concerning Paul; his own deeds too had to shine forth more brightly. So from then on he goes to meet everything for the sake of the preaching, disregarding the sword itself and the slaughter itself. He pursues a single aim: to prove that everything comes second to the truth, and to depart to the one he preached while his blood flowed. Through this, clearly, Christ was magnified once again.

Question 121. What were the things lacking in Christ's afflictions, which Paul filled up? The passage of the apostolic words put before us admits two lines of interpretation. Some take "what is lacking" quite simply, as the [?] of the word readily suggests. They say the divine Paul said, "I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ," and meant: "If Christ left anything lacking in his suffering, I fill it up in my body." To support this sense, they say: just as it was given to the apostles to perform greater signs than Christ did, and again, just as Paul himself [?] accomplished something higher than the Lord's commandments (for though he was entitled to be supported by the Gospel, he did not accept support), along with certain other such things, so too he filled up in his own body what the Master had left lacking. That is how some have understood it. Others think it grievous at the outset to say that Christ fell short in anything in his suffering. For what [?], what did he not undergo? He was abused and mocked; he endured plots, ambushes, outrages, and reproaches, from his own people and from outsiders; and finally he endured the cross and a criminal's death. He suffered these things although he could easily have fled, and he suffered them all freely and as a gift for our sake. So how could he be said to have fallen short in anything, or to have left out at all anything he had to suffer? As for the apostles receiving power to perform greater wonders: if Christ himself were not the one who supplied the power, this would not only foster the interpretation mentioned but would also fan into flame a far more absurd blasphemy. But the growth of these wonders (for they spring from the same root) is rightly referred back to the one who led the way. It is not those who receive the power of wonders but the grace of the one who supplies it that deserves surpassing admiration. As for the fact that, though he was entitled to be supported by the Gospel,

he did not accept support, it was a praiseworthy and blessed deed. He refrained from using his right so as not to give a handle to those who were seeking to find a charge against him. But here too he was guarded by the Master's commandment. Even though by law and by nature we are free to do many things, the Master set against this freedom the stumbling block it might be to our neighbors, and by his own deed urged us to leave our right unused. "So that we may not cause them to stumble," he says, "go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you." Paul's action is praiseworthy (how could it not be?), but it offers no guarantee that Christ fell short in anything. For the reasons mentioned, then, some are not content with that explanation and take the saying in another sense. They say that "what is lacking" here unfolds the following meaning. Things that are done fall into three classes: some are greater, some are middle, and some occupy the last place. So when the divine Paul says, "I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ," they say it means: "The last of Christ's afflictions, those holding the lowest place, these I fill up in my body." That is: "My sufferings are so far from being comparable to Christ's that I dare not compare them with the greater ones, nor even rank them with the middle ones. I am content to be counted with the last and lowest. For however much a man may [?] for Christ and suffer, nothing is equal to what he himself [suffered] for us, or even near it."

Many things, they say, would agree with this interpretation. "For I am," he says, "the least of the apostles, and not fit to be called an apostle"; and, "I press on, if only I may lay hold of it"; and, "carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in his body." How could anyone be said to fill up what was lacking in the one who did and suffered everything freely and as a gift? And there are many other such passages. The form of the second interpretation would be quite fitting, were it not that "lack" occurs in many places in both the Old and the New Scripture. "Did you lack anything?" he says; and, "Those who fear him lack nothing"; and, "For I reckon that I have fallen short in nothing"; and, "[?]"

…in no way was I a burden to anyone; for the brothers supplied what I lacked.” Since the word occurs in many other places as well, it is not easy to draw out such a sense from it. Rather, as was said before, we see that in the usage of Scripture “lack” expresses the need of the thing signified. Since both of the senses mentioned are open to doubt, a third might emerge between them onto undisputed ground and, having found a way from there to escape the objections on either side, it would be something like this. Holy Scripture must be allowed to use “lack” in its customary way, and nothing new must be introduced regarding the word. How, then, does Paul “fill up in his body what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ”? This remains for me to examine [?]. It does not mean the things that Christ ought to have suffered but did not endure. Certainly not! For he fell short in nothing at all; on the contrary, his grace overflowed toward us. What lacks, then, does Paul fill up? Whatever the Savior would have suffered while teaching, if he had still been dwelling in human life at the time when Paul was preaching and still caring for his creature by his presence. Those are the things Paul now suffers, and so fills up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ. This also comes closer to the force of the word. For he does not simply say “I fill up,” but “I fill up in turn.” That is: “In place of [?] the Master and Teacher, I, the slave and disciple, have taken up his ministry, and I fill up in turn what is lacking in his afflictions. For what he would have endured if he had not entrusted the ministry to me, I fittingly fill up in my body as what is lacking in his afflictions, since I have received that ministry.” That the disciples were appointed successors of the Lord's ministry is not hard to see from other passages too, but here Paul will be enough to speak for himself: “For all things,” he says, “are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.” And: “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making his appeal through us; we beg you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God.” So, just as the disciples received the word of reconciliation as their lot and are ambassadors for Christ, they also fittingly fill up in turn, in their own body, whatever he would have suffered had he still been carrying out the ministry himself. Paul did so most of all, when, confident in his works, he says, “I am in no way inferior to the super-apostles.” And notice how this interpretation offers nothing contrived. For the word “lack” is not forced, but [Notes: (61) So the Colbert manuscript, instead of “will fill up all things.” (69) The Coislin manuscript wrongly reads: “who, confident in his works, to say.”]

Scripture's usage is allowed to stand. Paul fills up the lacks, but not whatever was simply lacking, nor does he do so because the Savior was lacking in anything, which would be offensive. Rather, he fills up whatever the Savior would have suffered and endured if he had not entrusted the ministry to Paul and the other disciples, in the same way as he did before, when he was preaching and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of heaven. But let this much be said by me to discharge my duty to your fine diligence. If anyone, even among those born later, should perceive something new, that too would be dear to me.

QUESTION 128. “For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” He called the evil spirits of the air “rulers and authorities.” This is not because they have any rule or authority over us from themselves or from above. It is because we have handed ourselves over to sins, of which the demons are the sowers and prompters, and so we have granted them the rule and authority through which we do their will. For the same holy man says: “By whatever someone is overcome, to that he is also enslaved.” Since we are overcome by their provocations and suggestions, and are carried toward whatever works of sin they wish, we fittingly make them rulers and authorities over the passions that spring up in us from them. We have been stripped of the freedom of the Holy Spirit and of mastery over our own free will, and have enrolled ourselves as slaves of sin and answerable to it. For this reason he does not simply call the spirits of wickedness rulers and authorities, but also world-rulers of the world. Here, as is Scripture's custom, “world” does not mean the creation brought forth from heaven and earth and what lies between them. Far from it! “World” means those who have taken up worldly and fleshly ways of thinking and are excited by the things that charm the senses and make them soft. In this sense the Savior also said of the disciples “that they are not of the world.” It is obvious that they too belonged to the creation, as does the whole human race. “But they were not,” he says, “of the world.” That is, they were not among those excited by the perishable and short-lived things of worldly vanity and deceit. As for “in the heavenly places,” some prefer the more obvious [?] reading. Altering the beginning of the word, they read not [Note: (70) So the Colbert manuscript, instead of ὑποσπορεῖσθαι.]

“heavenly” but “under heaven,” although our holy Scripture does not read so. They say that the demons, that is, the spiritual forces of wickedness, are called beings “under heaven.” For whether they dwell about the air or about the earth, they could equally be called beings under heaven. But although their interpretation is not impious, their alteration is not pious. For one must never, not even in a single letter, falsify the holy words. This is especially true here because, as I said, the sense of the passage proceeds without hindrance from the unaltered word. For the things within heaven, such as the air, are also customarily called “heavenly.” Nothing prevents those that dwell in the air, that is, the spiritual demons of wickedness, from being named in this way after the place where they dwell. They are called “spiritual” because they have no share in flesh and blood, but received from the beginning an immaterial and fleshless substance. One might also say, more in keeping with the subject at hand, that here he gave the name “heavenly things” to piety and the virtues. For through these we inherit the kingdom of heaven. Our struggle “against the spiritual forces of wickedness” takes place in the virtues and in piety: we are eager to achieve them, while they oppose us in whatever way they can and take up every kind of war. Therefore the teacher of the world said wisely and fittingly, “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness,” that is, against the demons who are bound neither to flesh nor to blood. And then, in what and over what is the struggle [?]? “In the heavenly places,” he says, that is, in the things that win us the heavenly dwelling. As has been said, these are piety and the chorus of the virtues. If someone wishes to take “in the heavenly places” in its more obvious sense as the heavenly dwelling itself, the pious meaning still holds. For the struggle against them is also for this: we strive to obtain the heavenly inheritance, and they strive to deprive us of the inheritance from which they themselves have fallen.

QUESTION 123. Why is the book entitled Acts of the Apostles, even though it does not contain the acts of the twelve? At the beginning it contains miracles and a little teaching of the apostles, but after that the whole narrative moves on to Paul. The book is entitled Acts of the Apostles, he says, even though it does not contain the acts of the twelve

but at the beginning contains miracles and a little teaching of the apostles, and after that the whole narrative moves on to Paul. It is entitled Acts of the Apostles, however, because, as Paul says, “When one member is glorified, all the members are glorified with it.” So the author made the acts of Peter and Paul common to all, and entitled the book Acts of the Apostles. And if the whole body is included in the head, they reasonably called the acts of the leading apostles Acts of the Apostles. Besides, the shared teaching of the apostles is contained in these acts. Even if the account of it extends only a little way, it still provides a reasonable ground for the title. Some say that the author of Acts is Clement of Rome, others Barnabas, and others Luke the evangelist. Luke himself settles the question. First, his preface shows that he had already composed another work containing the acts of the Lord. Second, he is distinguished from the other evangelists in this: none of them carried his composition as far as the Ascension. He alone recounted the Ascension in detail and then made it the starting point of Acts. For Matthew's Gospel ends with “the eleven disciples went…” and finishes with “to the end of the age. Amen.” It adds nothing about the Ascension. Mark mentions it, but only in passing, saying: “So the Lord [?] … and sat down at the right hand of God.” He included neither the manner of it nor any other of the essential points of so great an event. John's Gospel gives no account of the Ascension at its end, but it notes that “Jesus did many other things as well; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that not even the world itself could contain the books that would be written.” As has been said, Luke alone recounted the Ascension at some length at the end of his Gospel and begins Acts from it.

QUESTION 124. How many times did Christ appear to the apostles after his resurrection from the dead, and where, and when? The Savior was seen by the disciples over forty days, but he presented himself to their sight only eleven times. And fittingly so: since the disciples were eleven, he made eleven appearances. Where is the proof that he appeared only eleven times? It comes from what follows. First he appeared to Mary at the tomb and to the other women. Isaiah foretells this when he calls the women and says: “Women coming from the sight, come, an- [?]

-nounce it to us.” Then he appeared to Peter, then to Cleopas and his companion. He appeared to them both while they were walking along the road to Emmaus, when they did not yet understand, and at the breaking of the bread, when he revealed himself to them. Then he appeared to the ten, when Thomas was not present, as it was evening on that day. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, as Paul notes, adding that most of them remain until now. Next he appeared to James; this too Paul teaches. He appeared not only to the twelve, for Paul said earlier, “He appeared to Cephas, then to the eleven,” and then added “to the apostles.” Then he appeared to the seven at the Sea of Tiberias, that is, Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, James and John, and two others of his disciples. Then he appeared to all the apostles, that is, the seventy. Then he appeared on the mountain in Galilee where Jesus had directed them, and on the Mount of Olives, when [?] the Ascension also took place.

QUESTION 125. Why did Christ command the apostles not to leave Jerusalem, and when did they hear the promise of the Father? He commanded them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, “which you heard from me.” That the Savior spoke of it is clear. For he said: “I am going up to my Father, and I will ask him, and he will send you the Paraclete.” But where did the Father make the promise? The Father's promise is not found in the Gospel. Is it not clear that it is found in the prophets? Paul also testifies to this when he says: “Paul, a slave of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son.” So, having promised the gospel beforehand, he also promised to give the Holy Spirit. And God says through the prophet: “In the last days, says the Lord Almighty, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy.” There is the promise! And here is its fulfillment: the Holy Spirit, in the form of tongues, rested on each of the disciples, and they spoke of the mighty works of God. That it is the Father who says these things, and not the Son, is clear from what follows. “And I will give,” he says, “signs in the heaven above and on the earth below.” The blood, which counts as a marvelous sign, is the blood that flowed from the Lord's side after his death. The fire is the fire that was divided among the apostles, as was said before.

“And the sun too,” he says, “will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes,” that is, the day of the Son. That these words were spoken by the Father and not by the prophet is shown by the beginning of the passage. For it reads: “In the last days, says the Lord, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh,” and so on. Clearly “the Lord” is not the prophet, who is our fellow slave, but the God and Father who sent him.

QUESTION 126. When were the apostles baptized, and by whom? We find that before Christ's passion the apostles received the baptism of John. Before the passion the Savior did not give a different baptism. He did not want to undo John's preaching, or to give the Jews who opposed him an excuse to claim that he had brought in his own baptism to insult the Baptist. But he supplied what was missing by baptizing not in water but in the Spirit. As he himself says, “But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now,” namely ten. A waiting period of ten days was given to exercise the apostles' faith. While grace remained quiet and none of the things promised appeared, their faith was exercised, and their hope gained time to bear the fruit of unwavering confidence. To be baptized in the Holy Spirit, then, is the same as to receive the Holy Spirit. So the apostles were baptized in the Spirit, and in water before the passion. That washing was for the forgiveness of sins, but not for a share in the Holy Spirit. The Master makes it plain that John baptized the apostles when, at the time of the washing basin, he says to Peter, who was refusing: “Whoever has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet.” By these words he showed that not only Peter, but the others too, had been bathed with John's baptism, since he washed only their feet. The Savior, then, did not set aside the baptism of repentance that John performed for the forgiveness of sins. He even perfected it by adding the gift of the all-holy Spirit.

The Savior says, “Remain in [?] … when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” How, at the time of the Lord's garment, do we put on a servant's one? But clearly both garments are of equal honor, and they show one and the same sovereign source of kindness and grace. The Holy Spirit is called the garment of the faithful, not as a cloak is a garment, but as iron puts on fire: it is not wrapped around from outside, but is penetrated through and through. In this way we put on Christ and the all-holy Spirit. We do not put them on like a cloak lying around us from outside. Rather, our heart and our thoughts are filled with light, and our face with grace. That is why those who rose up against Stephen, gazing at his face, saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

“And they were gazing into heaven as he was going.” He no longer says “as he was being taken up,” but “as he was going.” For in the flesh he was [?], but by his own sovereign authority he went. The angels call the disciples “Galileans” to honor them, for “Galileans” means “those who have been revealed.” Indeed, Christ performed his first sign at Cana in Galilee, and there he manifested and revealed his glory. Hence the prophet Isaiah cries out beforehand: “The land mourned, Lebanon was put to shame; Sharon became marshland. Galilee and Carmel will be made manifest.” At this point one must add: “Why do you stand looking?” Elijah, as a slave, was taken up into the height of the air, as if into heaven. But the Master, as Lord of all, was taken up not as if into heaven, [but truly into heaven]. The Master's going, or being taken up, into heaven is noted a third time. The threefold repetition of the word shows that the event was certain, true and no illusion. For our holy Scripture knows this figure of speech as a mark of confirmation and assurance.

QUESTION 129. Whose saying is “Who is this King of glory?” When the earth saw the Lord and Savior with divine power, commanding the winds and the sea, it said in amazement: “Who is this [Notes: … his, and not ‘being taken up’? Then in the margin: (93) ‘but as’ — ‘the Master into heaven’ in [?]]
that even the sea and the winds obey him?” In the same way heaven, seeing the Godhead in the flesh, says in amazement: “Who is this King of

Some ask: Why is our season of fasting limited to forty days? Why is it neither extended to fifty or sixty, nor confined to fewer than forty? This is not only handed down to us. Our common Master and Savior himself, the lawgiver of those under grace, is seen to have fasted forty days when the tempter [was about] to attack him and he stripped for the contest. Before the Master, the prophet Elijah is recorded as completing the same number of days in fasting. Earlier still, Moses did so on Mount Sinai, when he was preparing to receive the tablets from God. That, then, is the question. Perhaps someone else, raised up and lofty in contemplation like the men just mentioned, could give a deeper, more hidden reason, one more sublime and divine. We shall state what has come to our understanding. In six days God created this present, visible world. On the seventh day he rested from his works and brought his craftsmanship to completion. This seventh day is counted together with the days before it, just as every beginning and end of a period of time is included when counting the intervals between them. The present age is completed by the week as it continually comes round again. The eighth day signifies the age to come and the passage from the present into another, more divine lot and state. This is called the eighth, the first and the one. It is called the eighth because it is a different period beyond the time that is completed by the week. It is called the first because it is the beginning of another lot and of a more divine and better way of life. It is called the one because no other period of time follows it, but it exists and endures without end. With these points considered first, we turn to those who choose to pass [?], week by week, this fleeting and perishable time, which is measured out and flows along with fleeting and corruptible things. Such people have stained all their senses with sins and with the mist of the passions. They have filled their hearing with harlots' songs and all that goes with them, and their sight [?] with soul-destroying spectacles. Their touch, taste and smell, so that I do not lengthen my account by naming each sense one by one, linger where it is not lawful. Yet they could have occupied themselves, without condemnation, with what nature provided and divine law did not forbid. Since our [?] senses have been so soiled and defiled by the passions and by the flux we take on in this flowing time, their cleansing and restoration to their original state [is] not in one

…might be not after the pattern and imitation of time that flows away and loves sin, but rather according to the order, the training and the imitation of that time which is free of passion, does not flow away, and has no end. A little earlier our discussion taught us to call that time the eighth, the first, and the one. Our five senses, multiplied by the octad, make up the number forty. Through the five senses we live and carry out our actions, both the base ones and those counted among the virtues. So it is fitting that we purify the senses over forty days, and we have been taught to apply every kind of healing to them, so that we may live by them as the octad would direct, and not let the flux of the hebdomad command and give orders. Holy John of Constantinople also shows his agreement with this view of ours, and bears witness to it in advance, in one of his discourses, the one entitled On Fasting.

QUESTION 131. What is meant by "magnet"?

1. The magnet you asked about is the stone that draws iron. It is called this because, they say, men of Magnesia, who wore stones on their feet, first discovered it and came to know its power. Apparently they wore shoes studded with stones, and when they happened to walk slowly over iron-bearing ground, they felt themselves held back by a heaviness and difficulty in moving, as the pebbles clung to the iron. The wonder of it struck them and stirred them to look for the cause, and this led to the discovery of the stone's power. It is called not only the magnet but also the Lydian stone, the Heraclean stone and the siderite. Since you take such pains over these matters, we too must make an extra effort. It is called siderite ("iron-stone") from the effect it has on iron, or, if you like, from its appearance, for in color it looks something like raw, unrefined iron. It is also said to have been found originally mixed in with iron ores. Some have thought it is called Heraclean because its pull is so strong and powerful. It would be truer to say that it takes the name because the thing first appeared, as they say, near Heraclea. Some writers record this as the Heraclea in Pontus, while others think it was the one in Samothrace. Some people regard the siderite as a different stone from the magnet, and say that it is entirely bright and translucent and streaked with silvery glints throughout its whole body. It may also be called Lydian, perhaps after the distant homeland of the people who discovered its power. Or someone might find occasion to gather some other explanation from the sea of ancient history.

2. As we examine this stone's power of attraction, its sympathy, and the kind of love that nature has placed in it toward iron, we should rejoice in God, the supreme craftsman of creation. We should also be ashamed by the way these senseless things cling together and hold to one another, since we, who have been honored with reason, do not keep the bond of affection and love even as well as they do. Yet we are clearly taught that even if we possessed every form of virtue, without love for one another, that spiritual love-charm and bond, everything slips away from us and is lost. It is said that there is another stone whose nature is the opposite of this one, though we have not yet come to know it from experience. They say that iron brought near it is pushed away. This too applies to us. We ought not only to be united and bound to our own kind by the bond of spiritual love; sometimes we must also push people away and turn from them. This applies when they have entered on a life of stumbling blocks and offenses and try to stand in the way on the paths of piety, or to trip up and turn aside those who run the course of the virtues. This is also what the Lord's saying commands. Someone may be among our closest friends and kin, even working with us in our contemplation and conduct of life, as dear as a right eye or a right hand. Even such people we must cut off and turn away from with all our strength.

QUESTION 132. Whom should we call "little children," whom "children," and whom "sons"? And what does Peter mean by "We have the prophetic word made more sure"?

There are three things that bring human beings to perfection. The first is cleansing from sins. The second is a faith that is pious and free of doubt, which does not change to accept anything empty or new. The third is the struggle against the passions and the devil, and victory over them. The cleansing of sins is a kind of spiritual birth, or rather a rebirth, which renews the person who has grown old. That is why Paul said, "My little children, for whom I am again in the pains of birth until Christ is formed in you." Through this rebirth we are also adopted as sons, although we are servants of Christ our Master. So those who have been found worthy of this grace may fittingly be called "little children" and "children." Those who champion the piety proclaimed from the beginning have already gone gray in mind. They admit into their thoughts nothing empty, nothing new, nothing that is the brash invention of human ingenuity, and by a just verdict they show themselves worthy of a spiritual title. In addition

to these, there are those who have fought nobly and bravely against the passions and the enemy and have done the real work of soldiers and athletes. In all these deeds they have shown a spirit that is young and at the height of its vigor and desire. Will they not also share in the name that fits them? I think, then, that what has been said gives you a clear solution to your question: "I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name's sake. I am writing to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I have written to you, children, because you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one."

People are made "little children" and "children" by the rebirth that grants forgiveness of sins, and by the dignity of adoption. Through these we have received the power to recognize in our deeds the One [?] as Father, and in the same way we have also taken on a debt. People are made "fathers" by the gray hair of piety that comes from the beginning, and by knowledge founded on what is firm. They are made "young men" by mastery over the evil one and the passions. This is the meaning of the apostle's words. As for the repetition of the words, the first set would count as a statement and the second as a reminder. Repetition usually makes hearers more attentive and engraves the meaning of what was said more deeply in the memory of their souls.

If you look at it rightly, you will not find what was said by Peter, the chief of the apostles, puzzling either. He said, "And we heard this voice borne from heaven," and then added, "And we have the prophetic word made more sure." He does not mean "more sure" for himself. Far from it, especially since he had already declared, "Having been eyewitnesses of the majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ, we made known to you his power and coming." What could be [more sure] than seeing with one's own eyes, opening one's own ears to receive the voice from above, and being illuminated by the Father's testimony? He means "more sure" for those he was writing to. It is as if he said: If anyone has doubts about what we testify, let him look to the prophetic word, which is certainly more sure than the disputes of the many about us. For the prophetic word does not come from human opinion, as some might all too easily suppose about other words [?]. He teaches more clearly, as he goes on, that he did not mean "more sure" for himself. For he adds, "to which you do well to pay attention" ("you," he says, not "I"), "as

QUESTION 133. What does the Apostle mean by "peripsēma"?

Here the word "peripsēma" ("offscouring") can simply mean something held in dishonor, something lying underfoot, so to speak. But a meaning closer to the mark would be a ransom, a kind of sacrificial victim offered for others. Ancient usage tended to give this name to such a victim, and it gives the following reason for the name. In old times, when people experienced some wrath from above and realized that they were being made to pay for their misdeeds, the whole people would gather around one of their number. This person was to be offered in sacrifice for all and become their means of purification, either because the lot had set him apart or because he volunteered out of his own eagerness. They would wipe him all over with their hands (peripsōntes) and touch him, saying, "Become our peripsēma."

Paul often wisely took many things captive to the obedience of Christ, and the words of outsiders no less than other things. He did not take what was elegant in style and pleasing to the ear, but what was genuinely suited to express and convey his subject. He took this word from that source too, and writing to the Corinthians he says, "I have become the peripsēma of all." And he really did suffer and endure hardship constantly as the peripsēma of all, and was stretched on the rack of terrible trials. I pass over the rest, for I find one saying of his that outweighs all the others: "By the boast I have in you, I die every day." You see how he was the purification, the victim and the "peripsēma" of all. He was set on fire within and burned, and suffered countless things from without, not for the Jews alone, nor only for his own kin, but for Greeks and barbarians and simply for all people, if only, as he himself cried out, he might save some. So what happened to him every day he also declares in words, saying that he has become the peripsēma of all.

The words that immediately follow in the passage confirm this meaning. "I do not say these things to shame you," he says. That is, I am not reproaching you with my kindness or my favors. What then? "I admonish you as my beloved children." For children ought to remember a father's kindness, and he calls them not just children but beloved children. That is: I count you so much my own, and I burn with such love for you, that I do not refuse even to become your peripsēma, to be offered as a sacrifice, a victim and a purification for you.

Indeed, the correct construction of the phrase also inclines the word toward this meaning rather than the one first mentioned. Grammatically, something dishonored and spat upon would rather be said to be such "to all," not "of all." But the wise and inspired Paul does not say, "I have become a peripsēma to all," but "of all." Moreover, the passage just before these words also agrees with this meaning. For having said, "When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat," he added, "We have become like the perikatharmata of the world, the peripsēma of all, until now." That is: Why should I list one by one the labors, afflictions and struggles I undergo for your salvation? To put it in a word, "We have become like the perikatharmata of the world, the peripsēma of all, until now." The word "perikatharmata" ("refuse") might also be used of something loathed and to be avoided. But here it would fit better to take it as meaning the purifying and atoning victims that are customarily sacrificed for others.

However, since neither meaning does violence to the truth of what is signified, nothing prevents each reader from choosing whichever he prefers. If Paul was sacrificed as a victim for his disciples, he was imitating his Master and Teacher. If instead, while teaching, exhorting and doing everything for their salvation, he was regarded as dishonored and loathsome, he was again looking to that same Master in suffering these things. For the Master was reviled and insulted and endured every kind of mockery, yet did not cease to care for the salvation of those who insulted and abused him.

This brings to mind, opportunely, something you asked long ago: what is meant by the Gospel's words, "And they buffeted him (ekolaphisan)"? In a general sense the word means "they mocked." Buffeting is a kind of game. Usage has changed the β into φ, as in many other words, for the Attic dialect pronounces the word with β. So the bloodthirsty and ungrateful nation of the Jews was so enraged against their benefactor that they did not merely raise their hands to kill him. They thought they had achieved nothing great if any kind of mockery, sneering or outrage escaped them that they did not heap upon him. So they mocked him with the crown of thorns, the reed, the title of king and things of that kind. Here the lofty and great John, as if passing quickly over the outrage, says, "And they struck him with their hands." But the inspired Mark and Matthew, whose wording differs only slightly, give both the name of the outrage and the act itself: "For they buffeted him, and began to cover his

face and to buffet him." Then: "And [?]." This is what the literal meaning of "they buffeted" conveys. The wise Luke in particular is astonished, and notes that the Jewish nation could never get its fill of outrage and insolence. After saying that they struck his face and blindfolded him, he adds, "And they said many other things against him, blaspheming." But I think you now have enough on "they buffeted," "peripsēma" and "perikatharma" for the scope of a letter. As for you, keep the sufferings of Christ and of Paul in mind, and stand firm and nobly against insults and trials. Better still, rejoice in them, remembering which choir you are enrolled in and who leads it. Do this against every assault of hardship, whether it comes from demons or from men who wear human form but play the part of demons in attacking you.

QUESTION 134. How many beginnings of the year should we recognize [?], and which are they?

1. Rome extended its spear to the ends of the earth and made the inhabited world the measure of its power. It delights to glory in a number of names, and in the same way it grants the year three beginnings. It has three names: a mystic name, a priestly name and a civic name. The mystic name is Amor, which means "love." The priestly name is Flora, which means "flowering." The civic name is Roma, which reversed spells the mystic word. The priestly name could be shared with the people, but any priest who divulged the mystic name paid the ultimate penalty. So, as we said, Rome was honored by three names and dignified the year with three beginnings. One of these it called priestly, another

TO AMPHILOCHIUS, QUESTION 134

ancestral, and the remaining one cyclical. The priestly beginning comes when the sun passes through Capricorn and the days begin to lengthen. Strictly speaking this falls in the month called December, but in people's perception, and especially for the Romans, it carries over into January. The ancestral beginning was assigned to the month called March, when the Romans began to move and prepare their arms. The cyclical and civic reckoning, which your diligence asked about, declared September the beginning of the year. The Greek language calls this the epinemesis, and the Romans the indiction.

In ancient times this cycle came round every five years, a period they called by the native name lustrum. Later, they say, they honored Ares, their ancestral god. Since this star completes its own circuit in fifteen years at its shortest course, they decreed that the epinemesis, or indiction, should be completed in the same span of time. That is the reason as their ancient tradition would give it, set out in their theological and secret manner. Not far from this is the explanation that Augustus, sole ruler of the Romans, learned that the equinoctial hour is marked off in roughly fifteen parts, and so decided to limit the cycle of years to the same number. Others give a more political explanation: for that many years he shared the consulship with Antony and the management of public affairs; then he joined battle with him and won the victory over him, when, at the beginning of the month of September, Egypt fell to his spear.

At each beginning of the year they performed special sacrifices and rites, honoring and appeasing those they believed to be gods. But in the month of September especially these were carried out with greater splendor and lavishness.

2. The new Rome then succeeded to the inheritance of the old and came to share its power, and it changed erring worship into the pious worship that befits God. Along with this it changed the demonic rites and sacrifices into pious holy services worthy of God. For this reason it laid down a law that on the first of September God should be appeased with public litanies and other prayers of atonement, and that the high priest should attend the celebrations and lead the sacred rites and offerings of atonement and salvation.

As for the name of the yearly cycle, the Roman word means "announcement," since the beginning announces the period; this is what they call the indiction. The Greek name, epinemesis, describes the thing it names. In ancient times taxes were not fixed on subjects as a set and unalterable burden. Instead the size of the harvest made the assessment humane. When the harvest was scarce it lightened the levy [?], and when it was plentiful it did not weigh people down, and

it shared out the proportionate amount among the taxpayers without causing them distress. The tax was collected only when need called for it. When there was no such pressure the tax was not collected at all, and the whole fruit of their labor became profit for those who had farmed the land. So, because the assessment was distributed (dianemesthai) among the subjects, the yearly cycle was given the name epinemesis. Those who make up a derivation of the indiction from the victory at Actium seem to me to force the word into a sense that is most jarring to the ear and far from convincing. These are my answers to your questions, given as they came readily to memory. If you draw up anything from deep study of history and point it out, and add it to what has been said, that too will be very welcome to us.
QUESTION 135. How is it not a contradiction to say, "If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well," and "If [?], why [?] me?"

The Savior laid the foundation of a gentle and peaceable way of life when he gave this commandment: "If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well." Yet when he himself received blows on the face from men, instead of turning the other cheek he answered, "Why do you strike me?" Overcurious reasoning might twist this into carelessness on his part. But he by no means overturned his word by his deeds. In a way, he rather confirmed what he had said even by this action. There, his exhortation cut off retaliation, through which strife goes on without end; that is why he commanded us to refrain from the first counterattack. And here he did the same thing. He did not exact punishment for the outrage from the hand that struck him by fighting back with his own hand. He simply exposed the injustice by pleading his case in words.

The supposed contradiction might be brought into harmony more aptly as follows. There he forbade us to resist those who wrong us in the body and in bodily matters. Here, however, he was being prosecuted on a charge of deception and of harming the people he was guiding and saving. The false accusers were trying to establish this charge by their blows. If he had not stood up to refute it, at least in words, he would have released them from guilt and spurred them on to even bolder impiety. And he would not have cleared himself of the slanderous and false charges they had impiously heaped upon him. So where is the contradiction or conflict in this? Do not strike back at the one who has struck you; but the one who charges you with deception or impiety, or who accuses you, the preacher of salvation, of introducing destruction, him do not

…allow these things to be fastened on you, nor submit to them [?], neither by word nor by silent disposition, nor be to blame in any other way? But for the lover of beholding the truth, what has been said leaves no further pretext for dispute. The sayings "Do not do your almsgiving before men," and "Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing," and "When you fast, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do," are so far from conflicting with "Thus let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven" that, in my judgment, they actually establish the closest possible agreement with it. For display and the hunt for glory are a vice, and they rightly provoke indignation and censure [?] from serious people. But fleeing vainglory is a virtue and the mark of a dignified character, and among intelligent people it is apt to produce thanksgiving to God, because they see the hunt for glory dishonored and virtue honored. How then do those who make a display of themselves hunt for glory from men, when what follows them is rather censure? And how do they "have their reward"? Not from the God-loving and serious, certainly, but by leading astray the many, the herd, who are able to examine nothing beyond appearances. If, then, vainglory makes people base and stirs up indignation among men, while fleeing it does the opposite and directs the more reasonable to glorify God, how is "Thus let your light shine before men" not found rather to commend not making a display and not seeking vainglory? But how will the light shine before men if they know nothing of what is done in secret? This has already been answered, but it may be put better thus. The Father who sees in secret is himself able to make the radiance of the inner lightning shine out into the open. Besides, the serious man is marked out by two traits and painted chiefly in two colors: by the choice of virtues in the likeness of the Creator, and by flight from vice. Now the flight from vice certainly shines before men, even if one keeps its brilliance within as far as one can. For not to have a hand that does evil, whether in violence or in matters of money, nor an unbridled tongue given to slander, to oaths, or to such things, and simply in all things

to give no handle—these and the like flash out a great and brilliant light to men, even though we in no way wish it. This is what the divine Paul says when he lays down for Timothy the laws of the priesthood: "He must also have a good testimony from those outside." Moreover, being without offense to Jews and Greeks and to the whole Church of Christ is something that the flight from vice establishes and secures. Fasting, pity for the poor, a tear from the eyes, and intensity in prayer love secrecy in their practice; nonetheless they have the flight from vice as a loud-voiced informer and a piercing herald, which, having first shone out before men, is apt somehow to draw along with it and make shine together with it the gleam of hidden virtue as well. There are indeed, there are some virtues which it is fitting to practice in public, especially for those in authority: justice, I mean, and piety, and courage, its champion, and all that assist them. That is why the Savior does not command these to be confined to concealment, but fasting and almsgiving and anything similar. In all of them, however, he banishes display and vainglory, and this is what he means by secrecy and by the right hand not knowing what belongs to the left. He who has a mind that is pure and above passion, whether he does good at home, in church, or in the very middle of the city, is a most exact keeper of the Lord's commandment. For he does not perform the act for display or as a screen for vainglory, and by his deed he turns those who see it to the glory of the Father. But since we do not see many such people (because the very loftiness of the achievement tends to lift the doer up along with it; for vainglory shoots its arrow violently from below, and is often able to pierce even a firm character and turn it downward), working in secret is found to be far safer, especially for beginners. For those who have got entirely beyond the arrow's reach, working done openly and in public is no hindrance. Thus the Savior too sometimes performed miracles in the midst of people and in the synagogues, but at other times would not allow them to be made public. The first because, just as he was wholly beyond the reach of the other passions, so he kept vainglory out of reach as well; the second to give us a rule and a standard, so that we might flee display and repel the misguided praises of the many. Public action, then, is more perfect and belongs to the perfect, as we said, but hidden action is safer. For in the former vice often slips in unnoticed along with virtue, whereas in the latter, in the hidden action itself, its entry is completely walled off. [Editor's note: I would prefer αὐτῆς, that is, "of vice," or αὕτη [?].]

Thus the legislation is in no way contrary to the Lord's words. You could also see the point made in another way, no less. For the Savior, rebuking the Pharisees and reshaping their affected and festering manner into decency and goodness, forbade them to live for men and bade them pursue whatever serves God. So, freeing from their disease those sick with vainglory, he says to them, "Do not do your almsgiving before men," and "Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing," and the like. He cleanses the passionate of their passion, drives the hypocrites off the stage, and calls those who live in darkness and error to the unerring and pure life of virtue, from which dispassion shines forth, and true glory, and the radiance of the soul. Thus the divine and sacred Oracles are not contrary to one another; on the contrary, none of one's works could flash out its brilliance unless it first scatters the darkness of vainglory and removes it from

Moreover, if not giving offense to one's neighbor goes together with—or rather comes before—illuminating men by one's works, and not acting for display is contained within not giving offense as a part within a whole, then fleeing vainglory becomes a preparation for shining before men through one's works. But the Lord's sayings, at your request and for your sake, have been shown by various approaches to embrace agreement rather than to be at odds. It is also in imitation of the Lord's laws, and takes its origin from them, to treat by several arguments problems that seem to be in conflict with one another. For the common Creator, Teacher and Savior himself is seen to be the author of this rule by what he did. Perhaps it would not be unwelcome to unfold for you at the same time the consideration of the third question as well. When the ungrateful and shameless nation of the Jews charged the disciples with gathering grain on the Sabbath, he muzzled their spitefulness in more than one way. First he set necessity against them. This is established by the deed and example of David, who ate the loaves of the Presence, which it was not lawful to eat, and is acquitted of blame. Second, from the place, that is, from the privilege attached to the place. This argument is also by example, but deeper than the first. For just as an action [?] performed outside the temple

[?] brings one to judgment, but in the temple itself lets him go unaccountable, so too gathering grain on the Sabbath makes some people liable in the ordinary case (let that be granted you), but frees from all accusation the saviors and teachers of mankind, who are with the very Lord and lawgiver of the priesthood. For what is here is far greater than the temple. Further, he pillories their madness on the ground of mercy as well. For if sacrifice is greater than keeping the Sabbath, and your law puts mercy before sacrifice—"For I desire mercy," it says, "and not sacrifice"—then those who see the disciples pressed by hunger and want of food, and instead of turning to mercy demand punishment for lawbreaking, are caught in a far graver transgression while championing the shadow of the law. Not only that, but he slaps them down with a fourth argument, saying that man was not made for the Sabbath, but conversely the Sabbath exists for man's need. Indeed, he lays the scourge of his words upon their folly even to a fifth stroke, rebuking them now more as a master and with authority: "For the Son of Man," he says, "is Lord even of the Sabbath." And if the Son is Lord, and the disciples are above all sons and heirs (for they were the first to be born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God, and were counted worthy of adoption from above), they will no longer be slaves of the Sabbath but will be its lords. Strengthened and grounded, then, by this method [?] of the Lord's, and by others like it, we have, as you asked, brought the seeming discord of the venerable Oracles by various arguments into an undisputed concord. But so much from us to you. If the quickness of your understanding, the intelligence of your thought, your wealth of sacred contemplations and your rhetorical skill should go on to contemplate sweeter and loftier things—and contemplate them they would, if only you wished, unless I do not know my friend—I would have received the fullest return of favor.

Question 104. Why does Paul the apostle put his own name first in his Epistles? The divine Paul puts his name at the head of his Epistles because he does not wish to open his mouth without remembering the Lord's benefaction. For grace renewed even his name, changing Saul into Paul, altering his words as it altered his ways. That is why he says "Paul," since he bears, as it were, even his very name from the Lord's munificence. [Note: "we have brought into an undisputed concord" (εἰς ἀστασίαστον συνηγάγομεν συμφωνίαν), from the Colbert manuscript.]

He who was enriched with everything by Christ—his name, his faith, his longing, his course, his apostleship, his way of life—is fittingly, then, also "a slave of Christ." For one who received so much as a free gift, having laid down nothing beforehand, how is he not a slave, and whatever else besides, of the one who honored him with so much? All are slaves, even against their will, whom the creating Word brought from nonexistence into being: he compels them to look to the Master and [?] the power of the Creator. For the creature must of necessity be a slave and subject to the lordship of the one who created it. Also a slave is whatever enjoys the providence of a higher being, and, just as it has the existence of its life from there, so too the continuance of its survival. And grateful slaves would be those who, freed by a great ransom from bitter tyranny and harsh captivity, have resolved to enroll their redeemer as their Master. But the divine Paul did not make much of subjecting himself to Christ in these ways; for these are common and show nothing exceptional or wonderful. Rather he adorns himself with other ways, and shapes himself into a slave by more and greater ones, and brilliantly displays the purity of slavery and what is truly free. First, by the gifts given to him by the Creator, in which he could take a special pride. Second, by his love for him, fiery and surpassing that of other men. And third, by his unhesitating service in the apostleship and the unflagging course of his slavery he shows, with a free spirit, his truly noble birth. And in addition to these, by the exactness and purity of his conduct, through which he presented himself as a slave to Christ—body, soul, thoughts and everything—nowhere shaming his election nor making light of the vote from above, but everywhere rather showing it to be truly divine and confirming the judgment by his works, and leaving—why need I say it—none of the commandments unfulfilled, when one may see that he even surpassed them? So the wonderful Paul is shown to be a slave in one way as the masterpiece of the creating hand; in another, as held in existence by the providence from there; then as one bought by the Lord's blood; and beyond these, in the ways peculiar to himself. For he does not stop even here, nor confine his slavery to what is common, but, clothed with a wealth of graces, he yokes himself under the yoke and manner of another slavery, striving to repay with unaccustomed services the one who honored him with newer graces. Indeed, he loves the Master above all things, falling short in no excess of affection, and more than one could reasonably marvel at [?]. And he counts all things as refuse, so that he may gain Christ, the one he longs for. But also [Note: "For he who received so much as a free gift … how is he not a slave" I have taken from the Colbert manuscript. Colbert reads οὐδ' ἐν.]

he is sent forth as a herald and fills the world with his preaching, running from Jerusalem as from a starting post to all the ends of the earth, and trumpeting the Gospel as far as the very streams of Ocean. Such was the slavery Paul knew, and on top of these a seventh mode of slavery is completed, by which he fulfilled and kept the ordinances and statutes of life in Christ purely and earnestly, as no one else did, either then or later, pummeling his body and enslaving it, lest having preached to others he himself should be disqualified. These are the wondrous forms of slavery, better than any freedom; by these he breathed, in these he never ceased to serve, in these he contended and took pride. That is why, when he writes, he enrolls himself as a slave of Jesus Christ. This, he says, is my rank; this is the badge of my ruling authority; by this I wish to be known to all. Those who live in the world wish to be designated by worldly ranks, signing themselves consuls and generals and tribunes and the like. But for Paul it suffices for greatness of glory, rule and rank to be a slave of Christ, and to be known by that rather than by anything else. Let this, then, be our account of why Paul puts his name at the head of his Epistles and always describes himself as a slave of Christ. As for "declared Son in power," and what follows, it seems to me to have some such meaning as this. "Declared" means, as it were, recognized, come to the knowledge of men. For we are accustomed either to grasp things by a name or to arrive at knowledge of them through defining statements. So here, by "declared" he does not mean that he was taken into adoption by someone—far from it!—nor that he acquired the title of Son of God by some act of adoption; but "declared" means made manifest to us through the properties that belong to him, and come into our knowledge and comprehension, so far as that is possible for human nature. From what, then, and from what sources is the Son of God marked out, and by what properties is he characterized when he comes to our knowledge? From the prophetic oracles, he says; for he shows this by saying, "which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." Second, from the mighty works which he performed beyond nature: "declared Son of God in power," he says. Then from the Holy Spirit, whom he supplied to those who had believed in him. And also from the fact that he rose again, he who was born of the seed of David. For the concurrence of all these [Notes: From Colbert, in place of οὗτός τε. The same, in place of κοπιάζων. I write ἰδέαι for ἰδίαι. … the words [?]: "of the declared," "of the recognized" [?].]

marks him off and sets him apart from all the others who by grace have come to be called sons, and shows and teaches everyone that he is truly and by nature the Son of God and God. Hence it would be possible, not only by rearranging the words but by stringing them together in their direct order, to define and set forth the uniqueness of the sonship of Christ our God, and to give the faithful a clear and pure knowledge and understanding of him. For example, if someone asks, "What is Christ?" it is easy and no labor to answer: Christ is he who was proclaimed beforehand through the prophets and was born according to the flesh of the seed of David; who benefited the human race with supernatural powers and with an abundant and lavish supply of the Holy Spirit; and who through his own resurrection put death to death, despoiled Hades, and raised with himself the dead of all ages. This is the Christ, this is the Son of God and God. For his Gospel Paul was set apart; this is what the phrase "declared Son of God" presents. Add, if you wish, for further unfolding and clearer exposition: through whom Paul also received the grace of apostleship to persuade the barbarian nations and prepare them to obey the faith of Christ—that is, to believe in him and worship him alone as true God and Son of God, abandoning their ancestral customs and their old superstitious error. As for the saying of the holy James, "Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation," it does not mean: let him talk big, let him swagger, let him brag. None of these. These words are indeed customarily used in that sense, and the obvious meaning of the expression points that way. But here "to boast" stands for "to take courage, to hope." For let him not lose heart, he says, because he is lowly, as one worn down by poverty or insulted by obscurity among men. For our Lord too chose the lowly and mean, the poor and the beggars, leaving the rich and those proud of their glory and birth to snort in their arrogance. So no one ought to lose heart because he is lowly; let him rather be filled with joy, considering that through his meanness and lowliness he is a partner and sharer in the apostolic choir. But perhaps someone will object that what has just been said would suit not those who were then beginning to believe, but rather the faithful of today. For to them the rank of the apostles was not yet so brilliant and admirable as to call others by their example to imitation of and zeal for virtue. But this is no obstacle. For even then the greatness of their virtue escaped hardly anyone, since people even [undertook to honor] them with sacrifices [Notes: Acts 9:15: "for he is a chosen vessel of mine." I would read μηδείς.]

[?] … and undertook to honor them. And Paul himself says boldly, "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." The exaltation of the humble-minded man, then, is his humility, in which he ought to take comfort, to be cheerful, and to fill his soul with joy, just as if someone else were clothed in all the world's wealth and human glory and held it in his hand. For one who is lowly in this way and in these things has God exalting him and setting him on high: "He who humbles himself," it says, "will be exalted"; whereas one who on the contrary exalts himself will find God set against him, humbling him and casting him down to the ground, puffing and empty bragging and all. You have seen exaltation as the cause of the utmost humiliation; you have seen humility bearing one up to heaven. How then would one not be cheerful, and fittingly boast—that is, rejoice and take courage—in the exaltation of his humility? What then? Are the rich deprived of this ascent and exaltation? I do not say that, since the common Master does not cast the rich out of the kingdom, but only those who are melted into their wealth and wholly bent on it and agitated by their cares, who have bound all their concern to their treasures and keep their souls buried and fettered in earth and gold as in a prison. Censuring their folly the Savior said, "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." To such rich men the heavenly commonwealth is inaccessible, and "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle" than for them to enter the kingdom of heaven. How then will the rich enter, and the heavenly commonwealth become their portion? If they imitate Abraham, if they imitate Job, if they prove good stewards of their wealth and not petty tyrants, shutting away behind many bolts and bars the relief of the poor, which is no less their own salvation than that of their fellow men. And how will the rich man arrive at this practice? What is the cause of this achievement? Humility, he says.
