For if he humbles himself and is not lifted up to conceit, nor falls into madness, exulting and swelling over his gold and wealth, he knows that none of these things is his own, that all are God's, that it is easy for them to be taken from him and transferred to others, that they were given not so that his neighbors should go without necessities, but so that they might share in them through the one who received them—and countless other things besides. Knowing these things and turning them over in his thoughts, he gives thanks to the Giver. He knows himself a debtor; he obeys the laws of the one who formed him and enriched him; he manages his own goods as another's and administers them—or rather as most truly his own, both reckoning and making his own whatever [he bestows on?] his fellow [Note: εἰς γῆν ("to the ground"), Colbert, in place of ὀργήν. [?]]

…has gained the strength to care for the faithful and for those of his own kind, supplying the needy so gently, so humanely, so prudently, as one appointed by God to be guardian and steward of what is held in common. Do you see how humility makes even the rich man splendid and exalted and worthy of the kingdom? That is why he says, “But let the rich man boast in his humiliation.” In this humility, he means, let him place his hope; in this let him take courage; through this he will be exalted. For if he does not gain this from his wealth [?], he says, what else will he have from it: from earth, from clay, from such tiny pebbles? Or rather, as the holy James puts it, he is no different from the flower of the grass, which blooms for a season and often delights the senses, but when the sun burns down on it, it withers and vanishes, leaving behind not even a trace of its former beauty. Just as the flower of the grass decays and perishes even while it is putting forth its loveliness, so the rich man too withers and perishes in the very flower of his extravagance. Indeed, you will find him even weaker and feebler than the grass. For the grass blooms in its own season and withers in its own season. But the rich man is often struck at the very height of his prime, when pleasant things sprout and bloom for him on every side, things that seem splendid and enviable, and when, swollen with pomp and conceit, he is a terror to many. Then, at that very moment, he is often seized suddenly by the law of death and vanishes from among men, or a shipwreck sends him beneath the waves. And what is strange and unexpected, sometimes it does not sink the man himself, but his gold, which is his soul and his life. Or else the hand of a tyrant, or of someone more powerful than he, seizes his wealth and leaves him bereft both of his haughtiness and of his life. Then there are the plots of servants and the ambushes of robbers. Who could count and number all the things by which such a man is caught and destroyed? So such a man is more wretched than a flower, and readier to suffer its fate. But these are the matters you asked about, and this letter has discussed them with you. As for you, show yourself a servant of Christ our true God in deeds and in doctrine, and manage your wealth well. Put your confidence in such humility, and be of good cheer. Farewell in soul and body and in all else.

Question 137. To the same Amphilochius. A clear synopsis of the ten Categories.

1. Of the things that exist in some relation and association with one another, some are homonyms, some synonyms, and some paronyms. Besides these there are certain others, of which some are called polyonyms and others heteronyms. In a way, polyonyms are the opposite of homonyms, and heteronyms the opposite of synonyms.

2. Homonymous things, then, are those that have the name in common but differ in their account, whether the account given is a definition or a description. For example, both a man and the image of a man are called a “living thing” (zōon). These, then, are homonyms, for they share only in the name, namely “living thing.” Nothing prevents us from calling the image a zōon as well, since we call those who paint such images zōgraphoi. But they differ in their account, for each of them admits a different definition or account. The one is an animate substance capable of sensation, while the other is plainly neither animate nor capable of sensation, but

something produced by art through imitation, or a work of art brought into being through imitation. Homonyms are described as follows: homonymous things are those that have only a name in common, while the account of the substance corresponding to the name is different. Here “name” must be understood simply as any word whatever, and “substance” simply as the subsistent existence of each thing, whether it is a substance in the proper sense or an accident. This, however, is the account of homonymous things. It would not fit the homonymous word itself, whose description would rather be this: a homonymous word is one that signifies several different things according to different notions. So much for homonyms.

3. Synonyms are things that have both the same name and the same account. For example, both a man and a horse are called a living thing. These, then, are synonyms, for their name is one, namely “living thing,” and their account in respect of “living thing” is the same. Synonyms are described as follows: synonymous things are those that have the name in common, and the account of the substance, that is, of the subsistent existence, corresponding to the name is also the same. And just as homonymous things admitted one account and the homonymous word another, so it is with synonyms. The account just given would not fit the synonymous word as well. Its proper account would rather be this: a synonymous word is one that indicates several different things according to one and the same notion. Just as in the case of synonyms and homonyms the accounts of the things were shown to be different from those of the words and names themselves, so one may examine the case of paronyms, polyonyms and heteronyms too. Distinguishing and understanding these is easy from what has already been said. To discuss each of them in such minute detail is perhaps too lowly and simple a task, and would be superfluous even for beginners. So we leave this distinction to them and tell them to work out the rest for themselves from what has been said.

4. Paronyms are things that share in part and differ in part, both in name and in thing. Take, for example, grammar and the grammarian. The grammarian plainly shares

in grammar, but also differs from it. Grammar is knowledge, while the grammarian is a living being in whom that knowledge resides. In the name, likewise, they both share and differ: they share at the beginning but differ in the final syllable. To put it more completely, paronyms are described as follows: paronyms are all those things that, being derived from some thing, have something in common with it and something different, both in the thing and in the name.

5. Polyonyms are said to be things that admit the same account but have different names. Examples are man (anthrōpos), merops and brotos. These obviously differ from one another in name, but they do not differ in account. Each of them admits the same definition, namely a rational, mortal living being.

8. Further, some of the things that are said are said in combination, that is, joined together, as in “a man walks” or “a man runs.” Others are said without combination, such as man, ox, horse, walks, conquers, runs. Of those said without combination, some are substances and others accidents, and of these, some are universal and others particular. Accidents are called “in a subject,” since they have their existence in some substance. Their definition is as follows: what is in a subject, that is, an accident, is that which exists in some thing, not as a part of it, and cannot subsist apart from the thing that underlies it. Substance, on the other hand, is called

“not in a subject,” for substance is never found in something else that contributes to its existence.

9. The universal is said to be “said of a subject,” for the universal is always predicated of some subject that underlies it. Particulars are said to be “not said of a subject,” for particulars, that is, individuals, are never said of any subject. Now substance is called “not in a subject” and the universal “said of a subject.” So “not in a subject” and “said of a subject,” taken together, will indicate universal substance in every case. To give an example in outline, take universal man. Universal man is said of a subject, namely of some particular man, such as Plato or someone else, but it is not in a subject, since it was accidents that were said to be in a subject. Again, an accident was called “in a subject” and the universal “said of a subject.” So “in a subject” and “said of a subject,” taken together, will indicate a universal accident in every case. To give an example in outline, take universal color. Universal color is said of a subject, namely of some particular color, such as this white, but it is also in a subject, in a body such as snow or something else. Further, the particular was called “not said of a subject” and substance “not in a subject.” So “not in a subject” and “not said of a subject,” taken together, will indicate particular substance in every case. To give an example in outline, take a certain man or a certain ox. None of these is either in a subject (for that was shown to be an accident) or said of a subject (for that was shown to be the universal). Further, the particular was called “not said of a subject” and the accident “in a subject.” So “in a subject” and “not said of a subject,” taken together, will indicate a particular accident. To give an example in outline, take this white or this black. This white is in some body, but it is not said of any subject, since what is said of a subject was shown to be the universal. But enough about these things.

10. When one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, that is, synonymously, everything that is said of the predicate will also be said of the subject. For example, “man” is predicated of a particular man, and “living thing” is predicated of man. Clearly, then, “living thing” will also be predicated of the particular man, for the particular man is both a man and a living thing. But when something is predicated of something not synonymously but homonymously, it is not necessary that whatever is said of the predicate should also be said of the subject. For example, “white” is predicated homonymously of a body, for a body is called white. Yet the account of white will never fit the body, for its account is “color” and certain other things, and a body is obviously not a color.

11. One must also know this: things of different genera, which are not ranked under one another, also have differentiae that differ in kind. Take, for example, living thing and knowledge. The differentiae of living thing are “walking” and “aquatic,” but none of these belongs to knowledge, for one kind of knowledge does not differ from another by being two-footed.

12. Further, of the things said without combination, each is either a substance, or a quantity, or a quality, or a relation, or a place, or a time, or a position, or a state, or an action, or an affection. Substance is, for example, man or horse. Quantity is, for example, two cubits long or three cubits long. Quality is, for example, white or literate. Relation is, for example, double, half, greater. Place is, for example, in Athens or in the Academy. Time is, for example, yesterday or last year. Position is, for example, is sitting or is standing. State is, for example, having shoes on. Action is, for example, cutting or burning. Affection is, for example, being cut or being burned. Each of these, when said on its own, signifies neither truth nor falsehood. But when they are combined with one another, they signify truth or falsehood, as in “a man walks” or anything else of that kind. For “a certain man walks” must be either true or false.

Question 138. On substance.

1. First we must speak about substance. Substance, then, is not called substance according to one and the same notion. The word is one of those said in many ways, even if

this has been overlooked by many of those who have chosen to say something about substance. In one, entirely different way, the supersubstantial substance that brings beings forth would be called substance; but contemplating it belongs not to the present inquiry but to first philosophy. In another way, matter is called substance, and in yet another, the form that shapes matter and gives it its species. Each of these two is called substance, yet neither of them is, properly speaking, a thing that exists by itself. Matter needs the form-giving substance in order to exist and be manifested. And form, though not in the same way, still also needs the material substance, on which to find a seat and a base. To examine each of these belongs to the natural philosopher. Further, substance is also the name for the existence and “substantiation” of each being in whatever way, which has non-being as its opposite. And again, in civic usage, substance means the estate and holdings of each person's property and money. Since substance, then, has been shown so far to be said in all these ways, not one of the senses mentioned can be, or be named, a category. The supersubstantial substance that holds beings together is established as far superior to such words and notions, or rather as exalted and enthroned above them in ineffable transcendence. Matter and form are graspable by the intellect alone and can be contemplated only in composites; they do not subsist on their own in actuality and existence. Of the other words, one is perhaps proper to politicians rather than philosophers, and the other signifies nothing ordered or defined, but indicates everything homonymously. And a category is far removed from a homonym.

2. Besides the senses already mentioned, everything that subsists by itself is also called substance. One might fittingly give its account by saying that it is a thing that exists by itself and needs nothing else in order to exist, such as man, ox, fire, earth and the like. Such substance could also receive the name of a category, whereas clearly none of the senses mentioned earlier could. Of this substance just defined, one kind is composed of matter and form. The other is foreign to matter and form, but has its nature fitted together from things analogous to them. Of this latter kind, one acts by direct apprehension and all at once, like the nature of angels, and then intellect as well. The other carries out its activities with some movement, like the soul. And although their activity and their existence are distinct, they have this in common: they both are, and are called, incorporeal. Whatever has withdrawn from matter and from enmattered form has passed over into the class of the incorporeal. For even if, compared with what is properly and primarily incorporeal and supersubstantial, these things are content to be, and to be called, bodies, still, having escaped the enmattered and corporeal

grossness, they are joined to the nature of the immaterial and are counted among the incorporeals. But that belongs to another and deeper discussion. Of the substance composed of matter and form, one kind is uniform, which we usually call simple; the other is multiform, which we specifically call composite. Of simple substance, again, one kind moves in a straight line and the other in a circle. Of the kind that moves in a circle, one moves from east to west, like the so-called starless sphere and the sphere of the fixed stars itself. The other moves the opposite way, from west to east, like the so-called spheres of the seven planets. Of the kind that moves in a straight line, one is carried from the middle, that is, from below, upward, and the other the opposite way, from above downward. Air and fire move from below upward, and of these, fire differs from air by its dryness. Water and earth move from above downward, and their nature differs by moisture. So much, in outline, about what is called simple substance. Of composite substance, one kind is capable of sensation and the other is not. The kind capable of sensation is that which is naturally fitted to use the senses. The kind incapable of sensation is that which is governed without any sensation. Of this latter kind, some does not even have the nutritive power within it, such as stones, wood and the like. Some is governed and held together by that power, such as plants, shrubs, grasses and the like. The kind whose nature is to use the senses also admits differences. Either it puts forth the power of moving from place to place and makes up the nature of animals, or it lacks this power and constitutes the substance of zoophytes, such as oysters, sponges and many others. The kind that has acquired the power of moving from place to place in addition to using the senses, and has thereby been given the form of an animal, is divided into rational and irrational, and produces two distinct species. I mean the rational animal, which is man, and the irrational, which admits still more differences. Of these, some walk and some swim, and each of these is divided again, and the division goes further still. But let me be brief, lest I be blamed for writing a natural history of animals in a treatise on the categories. This, at least in my own view, is the distinction among the meanings of substance, and the division of substance as a genus cut into species. How this theory escapes the objections that catch those who have tried to divide substance differently, and how far its usefulness extends, you will perhaps recognize for yourselves, either right now or as you make progress. But the division of substance, the account proper to it and the distinction of its meanings are contained in what has been said.

3. The definition just stated fits both universal and particular substance. But Aristotle, when he defines particular substance, which [?]

he sets out as substance in the Categories, speaks as follows: “Substance, in the most proper, primary and chief sense of the word, is that which is neither said of any subject nor in any subject, such as Socrates, Plato and the like.” Universal substance, which he also calls secondary substance, he defines as follows: “Secondary substances are the species in which the things called substances in the primary sense,” that is, individual substances, “are present,” such as universal man and universal animal. For the particulars, such as Plato and Alcibiades, are included in these. He calls the particulars first substances because they are better known and clearer to us, and because everything else is predicated of them and, as it were, has its seat in them. Some things are predicated of them synonymously, like the universal substances, and others homonymously, like the accidents. So if particular substance did not exist, then in a sense neither universal substance nor accidents would subsist. For these reasons, he says, it would be fitting for particulars to be called first substances. Do not let this escape you, though it has escaped nearly everyone: individuals, called first substances, and universals, called second substances, do not bear the name of substance synonymously, either with each other or with the substance whose account and division have been given. Insofar as they are called substances by the common account of generic substance, however, they are named synonymously both with each other and with it. That things taken as second substances and first substances are not called such synonymously, either with each other or with substance [?], is something I could say much about. For the sake of brevity, I will for now say only this. The very fact that they are not simply called substances, but are called so with an addition, the one “first” and the other “second,” is clear proof that each of them is called substance according to a different notion, and all the more so since each in turn takes the lead in a different respect [?].

4. Whether Aristotle did well or not in calling one substance first and the other second, we have discussed elsewhere, and not in passing. But one must know something that nearly slipped past us: there is another meaning of substance besides those enumerated, one that is ready to hand in common usage. This is the species closest to the individuals. In this sense, although this man and this horse are of one substance by the common account of substance, we nevertheless refer them to that meaning, and so we regard and name them as being of different substances. We are also accustomed to call this very thing nature, and in this sense

[?] Ch. [?]. …we say that Socrates is of the same nature as Plato, but that a given man is of a different nature from the horse (39). So the meanings of substance that have emerged so far would be nine in number (40). But the others will be treated more precisely elsewhere.

5. Now substance, whose definition and division have been given, and which is able to receive both the notion and the name of a category, has [?] (41). First, it is not in a subject. This property belongs to every species of substance, but not to substance alone (42), for it also belongs to the essential differentiae. These, such as "rational" and the like, are clearly not in a subject, since they cannot be accidents either. The second property of substance is that nothing is contrary to it (43). This property too fits every species of substance, and not substance alone. No substance, insofar as it is substance, has anything set against it as a contrary. Yet neither is anything contrary to quantity: clearly nothing is contrary to ten, or seven, or the like. The third property of substance is that it does not admit of more and less (44). No substance whatever could be called more or less a substance than any other substance, at least according to the very definition of substance taken simply. This holds whether you take particulars and compare them with particulars, or universals with universals, or even particulars with universals. How could anyone say or think that Socrates is more a substance than Plato, or man more than horse, or, if you like, [?] animal? Neither is more a substance than the other. Nor is Socrates more a substance than man or animal, nor indeed are these more substances than Socrates, and the same goes for all the rest. So it would be a common property of substance that it in no way admits of more and less. The fourth property of substance is that, while remaining the same and one in number, it is receptive of contraries through its own change (45). This is a property in the strict sense, because it is convertible: substance alone, and all substance, both remains substance and, as it changes in its qualities, becomes…

Whether something of this kind also happens to substance considered as matter is not something to decide at present. Those who say that this property also attaches to a statement and to an opinion (48) hold a falsehood that is easily exposed. They argue this way: the statement "Socrates is sitting" remains the same insofar as it has its being as a statement. While Socrates was sitting it signified the truth, but once Socrates stood up it is found to have taken on falsehood. So the statement too is receptive of contraries. The same applies to opinion: while he was sitting, the opinion that he was sitting was true, but when he stood up the same opinion came to be receptive of falsehood. That is how those who raise the difficulty argue. But they should understand that the statement did not become receptive of falsehood and truth through its own change, nor did the opinion. It happened rather through the alteration of the thing that the one believed and the other reported. Had Socrates not changed by standing up from his seat, the statement that Socrates is sitting would never have become false, nor would the opinion (49). So from this too it is clear that the property given is above all a property of substance. Substance not only receives contraries by nature through its own change, but by changing (50) it also causes other things to seem to become receptive of contraries. Statement and opinion, then, even if it is granted that they are receptive of contraries, could not be said to be so at all through their own change, as substance is. Rather, it is through the change of substance, and because substance receives the contraries, that they are shown to share in its effect and so to seem receptive of contraries.

6. Aristotle, however, treating substance rather offhandedly, not to say rather carelessly, posits two further properties of substance. One is to signify a "this something", which would be a property not of substance taken simply but of what he called primary substance. The other is to be predicated synonymously (51), and this would be a property of what he called secondary substance. But signifying a "this something" belongs to primary substance alone, since only the particular, pointed out with the hand or by some other such means, is said to be a "this something" (52). Being predicated synonymously, however, does not

…[things] that are unmoved remain entirely so in every respect. But when the thing is moved, [the statement] is said to be now true, now false … For a statement and an opinion are said to be receptive of contraries not because they themselves have received [them], but because the affection has occurred in something else.

belong to secondary substance alone, but to many other things as well. The essential differentiae are predicated synonymously: "rational" is predicated synonymously of Plato and of Socrates, since Socrates and each of the others is called rational and truly is rational. In quantity, quality and the other categories too, one can see clearly as one goes on that genera are predicated synonymously of the species under them, and species of the individuals under them (53).

7. Other properties of these substances can also be stated, drawn from what Aristotle himself said. Of the particular, it is a property that it is said to be more a substance than the universal. Of the universal, it is a property that it is said to be less a substance than the particular, and not only than the particular but also than itself. That is, not only are universals less substances than individuals, but genera are also less substances than species. Animal, for instance, is less a substance than Socrates, and not only than Socrates but also than man. So secondary substances are less substances than particulars. Each of these properties would be most strictly and especially proper to its respective substance. Nothing at all among beings could be called more a substance than universal substance except the particular, and again nothing could even be conceived as less a substance than particular substance except the universal. From this one can also see clearly that universals and individuals, when called primary and secondary substances, are not called substances synonymously, either with each other or with substance taken simply. And one who says "Bucephalus" has indicated Alexander's horse more clearly than one who says "horse" or "animal". In the same way, within universal substance, the species is more a substance than the genus. First, because the species is nearer than the genus to what is most of all substance, namely the individual

This belonged to fire from the beginning (27) and contributes to the constitution of its substance, so it clearly did not arise from an affection, yet it produces one (28). Likewise the sweetness of honey did not arise from an affection (29), but produces an affection in the tongue. Or again, it arose from an affection but does not produce one, like the qualities that subsist in the soul, such as manic frenzy, anger and the like (30). Such a quality arose from an affection (31), but does not produce an affection in the

(15) Mon.: "then, having this as a state, came to possess it." (16) Mon.: "in actuality." (17) Mon.: "and is [?]." (18) [?] (19) [?] are. …seeing or touching. A passive quality differs from an affection in the same way that a state differs from a disposition. If the affection remains for a longer time, so that the one who has received it is named paronymously from it, it is called a passive quality. If it passes away at once, it is called only an affection. 4. The fourth species of quality is figure and shape. These differ in that figure is properly used of inanimate things and shape of animate things. Besides these there are other species too, such as straightness and curvature and things like them, which are also set apart from figure and shape. These are not brought under figure, as some have unreasonably thought, since figure is the boundary of any bulk whatever, or, as some say, that which is enclosed by some boundary or boundaries. Nor, likewise, are they brought under shape, since shape is the boundary of the whole form. Rather, they are species in their own right that are brought under quality, just like roughness and smoothness, rarity and density, and anything similar. 5. Quality is predicated in four ways: paronymously, homonymously, heteronymously, and without a name. Paronymously, as "grammarian" from "grammar." Homonymously, as a woman is called "grammatical" (grammatikē) from the science of grammar (grammatikē). Heteronymously, as "good" (spoudaios) from virtue: the good man is so called from virtue, but not paronymously, as he would be from "zeal" (spoudē). Without a name, as with the man apt for running and the man apt for boxing. No names have been given to the qualities by which these men were qualified. The word "running" (dromikē) is not the name of the capacity by sharing in which the man apt for running is called apt for running. It is the name of the art, and from the art it is not the man apt for running but the runner who is paronymously named and derived. Likewise "boxing" (pyktikē) is not the name of the capacity by sharing in which the man apt for boxing is called apt for boxing. It is the name of the art, and from the art it is not the man apt for boxing but the boxer, that is, the one skilled in boxing, who is paronymously named and derived. Such a thing is found in only a few cases. In most cases quality is predicated paronymously of the things that share in it. Just as quality is not predicated in the same way of the things that have shared in it, [Note 33: Mon. reads "remains." Note 34: Mon. reads "the affection."]

but of some paronymously, of others homonymously, of others heteronymously, and of others without a name, so too the things that have shared in it are not qualified in the same way, either in what they are or in what they are called. Things that have shared in a quality but have undergone no change in the position of their parts are, and may be called, qualified in the proper sense. But things whose parts have changed position would rather be said to have position, not to be qualified. The grammarian, then, and the just man, the ruddy man, and the like would be qualified in the proper sense. Each of them, having received its own quality, was altered in some other respect but underwent no change in the position of its parts. But the rare and the dense, the rough and the smooth, the curved and the straight, and anything similar change the position of their parts as soon as they share in the paronymous quality. Sharing in the quality did not primarily alter anything else in them. It changed the position of their parts, and so it made what received it not qualified in the proper sense but something that has position. For that is and is called dense whose parts lie near one another, and that is rare whose parts stand somewhat apart and are separated from one another. Again, that is smooth whose parts lie in sequence with one another and differ neither by projecting nor by sinking relative to one another, and that is rough whose parts project beyond one another or fall short. So much for these. 6. Quality has three properties. One is having a contrary, for justice is contrary to injustice. But this property belongs neither to quality alone nor to all quality. Not to quality alone, since it belongs also to acting and being acted upon, as will be said later. Not to all quality, since pallor [?], though it too is a quality, has no contrary. The second is not admitting the more and the less. Grammar is not more or less grammar than grammar, nor is justice more or less justice than justice. A just man, however, is said to be more or less just than another just man, and a grammarian more or less a grammarian than another grammarian. This property does not belong to everything that is qualified, nor to it alone. Not to it alone, since it belongs also to acting and being acted upon. Not to everything, since the square and the triangle, though they are qualified, that is, have been given quality, are not more [Note 52: The codex reads "synonymously." Note 53: … [?] as above. Note 54: Mon. reads "whose parts have some distance or loose spacing; and smooth that whose…," as above. Note 55: [?] adds "as if on a straight line, appearing neither in projection nor in deficiency." Note 57: Mon. reads "the parts thus" [?] … Mon. reads "are not … one another [?] … less." The rest [?]]

or less. If you compare the triangle with the square, neither is said to be more or less, for these are not compared at all insofar as they are triangle and square, since things that are compared must share the same name. And if you compare triangle with triangle, or square with square, even then neither will be said to be more or less than the other. These are indeed compared, but squares share equally in their name and definition, and so again do triangles. For this reason one square cannot be said to be more or less a square than another, nor one triangle more or less a triangle than another. The third property of quality is that things are called like and unlike in respect of it. This is a property in the proper sense, for a thing is called like in respect of none of the other categories mentioned, but only in respect of quality. 7. One should know that all the most specific qualities, such as grammar and justice and the rest likewise, are brought under quality. The more generic ones, however, are also brought under relatives. Knowledge is a relative, for knowledge is spoken of in relation to the knowable, and so is a state, for a state is spoken of in relation to what is had. This, then, is what there is to say about quality. On relatives. 1. Relatives are things whose being is the same as being somehow related to something, that is, whose existence lies in their relation to something else. Examples are the double and the half. The double has its being in its relation to the half, and the half in its relation to the double, and likewise in the other cases. Certain things fall under relatives. Some of these are spoken of by sameness, some by inequality, some by generation, some by participation, some by subordination, some by affection, some by judgment, some by position, and some by reference to the genus. Examples: by sameness, as a friend is the friend of a friend, an enemy the enemy of an enemy, and the like is like to the like; by inequality, as the greater is greater than the lesser and the double is double of the half [or by equality, as the equal is equal to something]; by generation, as a father is the father of a son; by participation,

as what participates participates in what is participated; by subordination, as a master is the master of a slave; by being affected [?], that is, by undergoing, as the striker strikes the one struck and the one struck is struck by the striker; by judgment, as knowledge is knowledge of the knowable; by position, as the right is right of the left; by reference to the genus, as grammar and music and the like. None of these is brought under relatives on its own account, but by reference to its genus it might perhaps be brought under them. Their genus is knowledge, and knowledge falls under relatives, so these too fall under relatives through their genus. But this point is treated more fully elsewhere. 2. The account of relatives given at the beginning properly describes their nature. The one we shall now state appears rather to be a kind of concomitant. It runs as follows: relatives are all things that are said to be just what they are of other things, or in relation to something else in some other way. I said that such an account does not reveal the nature of relatives, because not everything that is said to be of other things is a relative. A hand is called someone's hand, and a head someone's head, and the other parts likewise, but these are not relatives. They are substances, and no substance is a relative. One should know, however, that some relatives are expressed with the genitive, as the master is master of a slave; some with the dative, as the knowable is knowable to knowledge; and some with the accusative, as the striker strikes the one struck. This is why, in the concomitant just mentioned, he added "or in some other way" to "are said to be of other things." By "are said to be of other things" he meant to indicate relatives expressed with the genitive, and by "or in some other way" those expressed with the accusative and the dative. 3. Relatives have four properties. The first is that contrariety exists among them, for ignorance is contrary to knowledge. But this property fits neither all relatives nor relatives alone. Not all, since nothing is contrary to the double. Not relatives alone, since something is also contrary to quality
…is said; for knowledge is also the genus of each of these. These, then, are the things that fall under relatives as [?]…
[Note 89: Mon. reads "which we shall state." Note 91: Mon. [?] reads "as we said, that this account does not reveal the nature of relatives; for a hand is called someone's hand."]

…is contrary. The second property is admitting the more and the less, and this fits relatives in the same way as the property before it. The third property of relatives is being spoken of in relation to correlatives. The slave is called the slave of a master and the master the master of a slave. The double is double of the half and the half is half of the double. The greater is greater than the lesser and the lesser is less than the greater. Knowledge is knowledge of the knowable and the knowable is knowable to knowledge. Perception is perception of the perceptible and the perceptible is perceptible to perception. The other cases are similar. This property belongs to all relatives and to them alone. The fourth is being simultaneous by nature. The double and the half exist together: when there is a half there is a double, when there is a slave there is a master, and when there is a master there is a slave. The others are similar. They also do away with one another together: if there is no double there is no half, and if there is no half there is no double, and likewise in the other cases. This property belongs to all relatives and to them alone. The perceptible and perception do not contradict it. Fire, water, and the other elements did exist before animals, in which alone perception is found at all (for every animal is composed of the elements). Still, they did not exist beforehand as perceptibles but as bodies or substances. When there was no perception, because no animal yet existed, the elements did not fall under anyone's perception, and if they did not fall under perception they would not yet have been perceptible. They became perceptible when perception grasped them. And if someone claims that the stars existed before human beings came into being and says they were knowable when there was not yet any knowledge, he will be overturned by the solution of the difficulty already given. The stars did exist, but not as knowables. When no knowledge yet contemplated them, how could they be knowable? Clearly they became knowable when they were grasped by knowledge. And indeed those who define [?] them as coexisting from eternity with the heavenly body [?] and with man, clearly not even…

[Note 5: Before this Mon. has: "For the more and the less belong neither to all relatives nor to them alone." Note [?]: Mon. has "and," as also the words "to relatives" [?] … "belongs to relatives and to them alone." Note 10: Mon. … "property of relatives" … Note 11: "and masters" … [?]. Note 14: Mon. "belongs and alone" [?] … saying that it does not belong to all relatives, [?] …]

[?] … that the elements or the stars existed before knowledge [?] they will concede; but in reason and theory alone [?] … to place simple things before composite ones [?] … they will [?]. So it belongs to all relatives to be simultaneous by nature. But enough has also been said about relatives. On the remaining six categories. Aristotle, perhaps not teaching but merely indicating the teaching, if indeed the saying "published and not published" has been falsely ascribed to him [?], … [?] covered, among other things, the six categories as well, and rather briefly. We, however, have gone through the four categories at moderate length and with the clarity proper to teaching, and we have thought it right to keep the same pattern of teaching for you in the remaining six as well. Therefore we say that, before everything else, one must know that each of the categories under discussion is something simple. Each of the six categories is brought about when two things are coupled together. Still, it is clear that we do not call the coupled things themselves the category, which would make the category composite. They are not taken as its parts, nor as some underlying matter, nor as the elements of a composite. Friendship is a union of two, yet it is neither of the friends, nor is it composed of them in any way, but is entirely simple. Mastership is brought about and appears when certain things are coupled, yet it is entirely simple. In the same way each of the six categories appears when two things come together, yet it is neither of them, nor is it composed of them in any way. In this sense, then, these categories are distinct from the four, yet simple just as those are. Being simple is common to all the categories, but being produced and appearing when two things have come together is especially proper to the six. Having stated what belongs in common to the six, let us examine each of them separately. First let us take acting, sketching its description, its species, and its [?] … [Note: "and similarly in the other cases."]

Question 143 [?]. On acting. 1. Acting, then, is being active in any way whatever. It has two primary species: acting upon something else, and acting not upon something else. An example of acting upon something else

is striking, burning, teaching, and the like. Examples of acting but not upon something else are contemplating, playing the cithara, and the like. Each of these has four differences. A thing acts either by nature, as fire is said to heat and an animal to make sounds; or by choice, as in enriching, praising, and glorifying; or by art, as in building a house and the like; or by chance, as when a falling stone strikes or hits someone, or gives off an echo. Further, some acting leaves a product behind after the making, as the house remains after the building, while some leaves nothing. After playing the cithara no product of the playing remains. Further, acting takes place either in the body, or in the soul, or in both together, or with respect to external things. In the soul, as teaching someone a virtue or habituating them to a virtue or a vice. In the body, as burning or cutting. In both together, as healing, for this belongs to both together and not to the soul or to the body separately. With respect to external things, as enriching and the like. Further, acting is either perfective or destructive. Perfective, as healing. Destructive, as making the body sickly. Further, acting either makes something such as the agent itself is, as what heats makes something hot, or not such, as what cuts makes a cut. And if this is so, and acting is coordinate with the agent, then acting too will have this difference. 2. Acting admits the more and the less, for one can heat more and less, and cool likewise. But this does not happen in every case. One cannot build more and less, though one can build better or worse. The second property of acting is having contrariety. Heating is contrary to cooling, and paining to pleasing. But one would not see this happen in many cases, for nothing is contrary to cutting or burning or the like. The third property is being said alike and unlike. We speak of heating alike and unlike, of healing alike and unlike, and of building alike and unlike. This property fits nearly all acting, though not acting alone, for it fits being acted upon as well. The fourth property is that the things brought under acting are not brought under it in one way. Heating is brought under acting primarily and is acting in the proper sense. The thing that heats is said to be brought under acting because it is brought primarily under the agent, which is coordinate with acting. Likewise the thing that has heated is said to be brought under acting because it is brought primarily under what has acted, which is itself also coordinate with acting. The other cases are similar. From this you have as a corollary that the categories are not in every case predicated in the way genera and species are. Otherwise, how could one say that the thing that heats and the thing that has heated are brought under acting? That the things mentioned are brought under this category is clear to anyone who runs through the other categories. The thing that heats is neither

substance [?], as is immediately clear, nor quantity, nor a relative (for it does not have its being in relation to something else), nor yet quality. The hot is a quality, but the thing that heats is not called heating because it is qualified in some way, but because it does something. That neither the thing that heats nor the thing that has heated, nor their coordinates, can be brought under position or any of the remaining categories, it would perhaps be pointless to go through. Yet surely no one will say that these are not brought under any category. Nor will anyone say that the agent and what has acted are each a category of its own [?], for such a person would multiply the categories without end and know no limit to knowledge. The property, then, is reasonably assigned. A corollary has emerged that was unknown to many of our predecessors, not to say all of them, and it has been examined philosophically and in accordance with truth. To you the point has been handed on even more clearly and precisely through our select [?] conversations. This property belongs not only to acting but also to being acted upon and to position. The fifth property of acting is that it does not occur without motion. Heating, burning, cooling, teaching, and the like do not occur without motion. The sixth property is a property in the proper sense, and it is also convertible, since it fits nothing but acting. I mean that acting is brought about both from the making and from that from which the making comes. So much about acting.

Question 144. On being acted upon. Being acted upon is not different from acting in its subject, even though their being differs. So it will take on roughly the same species and properties stated above. That acting and being acted upon are one in subject, even though their being differs, is clear. The motion is one, but together with the agent it is called acting, and together with the patient it is called being acted upon. Its property is that it is brought about both from the undergoing and from that in which the undergoing takes place. This is its property above all, and therefore it is also convertible.

Question 145. On where. 1. Where, then, is being in a place. It is divided [?] … [?] being acted upon. Acting and being acted upon are twofold: they are either in the body or in the soul. In the body, as cutting and burning. In the soul, as paining, [?] … and being acted upon [?] … in [?], as being pained, and [?] being cut [?]. Further, acting is perfective or destructive. Perfective, as teaching, [?]. Destructive, as acting impiously [?]. Likewise being acted upon is either perfective or destructive. Perfective, as [?]. Destructive, as being cut or burned. It has

…[is divided] first into six species: being above and below, on the right and on the left, in front and behind. Each of these is either far or near. Further, it is either in a primary or in a secondary [place]. I say that a body is in a primary place when it is in a place equal to itself and not contained in a larger one, and in a secondary place when it is in a larger one, as we say, for example, that Socrates is in the house or in the city. Again, when 'where' is taken specifically, one kind is said to be so by its own nature, and this is always understood as the same, as the heaven's being above (for its place is ordered relative to one thing only, which alone is called 'below'; I mean, relative only to the place of the earth). Another kind is not by nature but accidental, as a living creature is said to be above with reference to the roof of a house; for these things can be called both above and below, though taken in relation to different things. 2. The properties of 'where' are three in number. One is to co-signify place: being above is properly a case of being 'where', but it also co-signifies a certain place, namely the upper place, and this property belongs to every species. The second is to co-signify a local relation. Local relation is twofold. The being-contained of the body, according to which it is said to be contained, would be a local relation, and so likewise would the containing of the place, according to which it is said to contain the body. Since local relation is taken in two ways, as has been said, both of these are co-signified by the category of 'where'. But it seems to co-signify being-contained rather than containing: it co-signifies being-contained primarily, and the containing is signified along with it. This property too belongs to every 'where' and to none of the remaining nine categories besides this one. A third property is that a certain position follows it inseparably. Whatever is somewhere certainly has some position: what is above, for instance, has the position of its parts, or of the whole, arranged this way or that, and so likewise does what is below, and similarly with the others. So this property would accompany every 'where'. A fourth property is that it is the result of a body and of the place containing it: being above results from the upper place and the body in it, and being below likewise, and similarly with the others. Let us not overlook, however, that 'above' is taken in one sense of place alone, and then it belongs among the relatives; in another sense it is something in a place, and then it falls under the category of 'where'. This [?] more broadly [?]. The present property belongs to every species, to it alone and always, and therefore it is also convertible. There are many negative properties, I mean not admitting contrariety, not having a contrary, not admitting more and less, [Editor's notes: (26) The manuscript reads τεταγμέναι. (28) Perhaps read προσημαίνειν, 'to co-signify', 'to signify in addition'. (31) [?]]

not being called like and unlike, and countless others. But we shall have to content ourselves with those that have been stated and found affirmatively, steering clear of what is unphilosophical and superfluous.

QUESTION 146. On being-in-a-position. [?] …is properly called also standing; another comes from different [elements], such as reclining and sitting. If this is so, then being-in-a-position results either from a non-composite position or from a composite one. Further, one kind of position belongs to the parts only and not to the whole, such as rarity and density, roughness and smoothness. Another belongs to the whole only, such as reclining and sitting, for it is not a part that is said to sit or recline but the whole. Another belongs to both the whole and the parts, such as standing in the proper sense, which is the uprightness of both the parts and the whole. Indeed, what is in a position is either upright in every respect and is said to stand, or upright in one respect and bent in another and is said to sit. These would be species of being-in-a-position: reclining, standing and sitting. Yet these would not be the only species of being-in-a-position; there are countless others. For instance, the rare and the dense and the like, which are said to be in a position, are said neither to stand nor to recline nor to sit. These would fall under that sense of being-in-a-position which indicates the position of the parts relative to one another only, and not the position of the whole. That rarity and density and the like are not positions of the whole is clear from this: one and the same whole cannot have two positions, yet rarity and standing are found in one and the same thing. Just as all the parts can have a shape of their own besides that of the whole, so they can also have a position of their own besides that of the whole. Of things that are in a position, some are so by nature, like the rare and the dense; some by choice, like a man's sitting; some by art, like a statue's standing; and some by chance, like this stone having fallen and lying thus. 2. It is a property of being-in-a-position to be named paronymously from the position: 'to sit' is named from 'a sitting', 'to stand' from 'a stance', 'to recline' from 'a reclining', and likewise with the others. That is why, where the positions have no names, the species of being-in-a-position have no name either. A crow's posture of this or that sort, say, or anything else's, has no name, because there is no name for such a position either, and the augurs' boys will not quarrel with us over this. For in giving names, out of great ambition, to the postures of animals, they have either given names to the positions as well, or they are liable to be caught out [?] by

us. But of these things elsewhere. A second property of being-in-a-position is that things are said to be 'alike' with respect to it: we say that people sit alike and unalike, and recline alike and unalike. A third property is that the things brought under it are not brought under it in the same way. Sitting is brought primarily under being-in-a-position and is being-in-a-position in the proper sense. The one sitting, however, is said to be brought under being-in-a-position because it is brought primarily under 'what is in a position', which is coordinate with being-in-a-position. In the same way the one standing and the one reclining are said to be brought under being-in-a-position because they are brought primarily under its coordinate. From this too it is clear, as was said before, that the categories are not in every case predicated as genera are. A fourth property of being-in-a-position is that it is the result of the position and of that whose position it is. This would be a property in the strict sense, since it is also convertible: whatever is being-in-a-position [results] from the position and from that whose position it is [?], and whatever is these is being-in-a-position. So much, then, about position. As for the negative properties, since they are very many and of little use, and besides are easily supplied, let them be passed over here too.

QUESTION 147. 'When' is being in time. Its species are as many as one supposes the species of time to be. If one also counts the 'now', there are three; if not, which is in fact true, there are two: being in the past and being in the future. Further, what is said to be in time is said to be either in a primary or in a secondary time. It is in a primary time when the time is neither greater nor less than the motion of the thing said to be in it. It is in a secondary time when the time is greater than the motion and extends beyond it. We say, for example, that so-and-so was born yesterday, although the whole of yesterday was not stretched out over his birth: a short interval matched it, and the rest of the time extended beyond it. Further, one kind of 'when' is definite and the other is not. The definite kind is like yesterday, today, tomorrow, last year and the like; the indefinite like long ago, very long ago, just now, hereafter. These too would belong to 'when': I mean 'when', 'then', 'earlier' and 'later', 'at the same time', 'already', 'slowly' and 'quickly'. One must know that 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' and the like are homonymous. In one sense they signify time only and are species of time; in another they signify something's being in time and are species of 'when'. This has escaped not a few of those in former times who were thought to be philosophers. Co-signifying time belongs to 'when' most of all. A further property of it is to be the result of time and of the things that are under time, for it receives its existence in a certain relation of these to one another. This would be its property most of all, for it belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. But so much about 'when'; [?] here too.

How many Sibyls have there been? There have been ten Sibyls. The first of them was named [Samb]ethe [?]. The ancient accounts call her Chaldean, or rather Hebrew, and say that she was joined in marriage to one of the sons of Noah and went into the ark with him and the others. They say that she also prophesied about the building of the tower and what befell those who dared to build it. They say that, since she lived before the division of tongues, she uttered her oracles in the Hebrew language. Not only that, but she also foretold the affairs of Alexander of Macedon, and Nicanor, who wrote the life of Alexander, mentions her. The second was the Libyan, whom Euripides mentioned in the prologue of the Lamia; but they do not make her name entirely clear. The third [?] was born at Delphi, and Chrysippus wrote about her. The fourth was the Italian, who had her dwelling in the wilderness of Italy. The fifth was the Erythraean, who also foretold the events of the Trojan War; Apollodorus of Erythrae gives an account of her. The sixth was the Samian, whose proper name, they say, was Phyto. The seventh was a Cumaean by birth, named Amalthea, though others say Herophile, and among some she bore the name Taraxandra. Virgil, the Roman poet, calls her Deiphobe. The eighth was the Hellespontine, who was born in the village of Marmissus near the small town of Gergitha, which at one time lay within the territory of Troy. The ninth was the Phrygian. Last of all, the tenth was a Tiburtine by birth, named Albunea. They say that these women, being out of their minds [?], prophesied the future; and since those who took

down the oracles in writing were not skilled enough to write down what was prophesied without error, and especially since their hands could not keep up with the rapid rush of the words, it came about that many of the oracles fell into limping meters and were never corrected. For the women who gave the oracles were in a state of ecstasy when they foretold what was to come; and once they had stopped prophesying, they had no awareness at all either of what they had said or of what the oracles meant.

QUESTION 151. On the quotations from outside sources found in our Scripture. Jude the apostle, in his Epistle, cites this passage from the so-called Apocrypha of Moses: 'When Michael the archangel, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him, but said, "The Lord rebuke you."' In the same Epistle he quotes another passage, from the Apocrypha of Enoch: 'Behold, the Lord came with his holy myriads to execute judgment on all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds which they committed, and of all the harsh things which ungodly sinners spoke against him.' Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, presents the blessed Paul citing to the Athenians, in his address, part of the heroic verses of Aratus, where he says: 'As even some of your own poets have said, "For we are also his offspring."' The blessed Paul, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, quotes this saying from the so-called Apocrypha of the prophet Elijah: 'What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.' In the same Epistle he recalls a popular Laconic proverb, which Isaiah the prophet had used before him and included among his own words: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.' Again in the same Epistle he quotes Menander the comic poet, who himself records maxims of certain ancients [?], saying: 'Bad company corrupts good morals,' and so on. And in the Epistle to the Galatians he used the following saying from the Apocrypha of Moses: 'Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation; and as many as walk by this rule, peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.' And in the Epistle to the Ephesians he quotes from the so-called Apocrypha of Jeremiah: 'Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.' And in the Epistle to Titus he cites the oracle of Epimenides the Cretan seer, which Callimachus also mentions in his own poetry: 'One of them, a prophet of their own, said: "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies." This testimony is true.'

QUESTION 152. What is the obscurity of Scripture? The obscurity in the divine Scriptures has many causes. First, every language, when it is translated into another, loses its proper flow. Second, words with the same form among the Hebrews caused ignorance in the translators, like [?] with respect to accent and meaning, and 'oros' and the like. For kalós, with the acute on the last syllable, signifies what is beautiful and comely, earnest in virtue and fit; but kálos, accented on the next-to-last syllable, signifies a ship's rope. Again, hóros, accented on the next-to-last syllable, is either the definition of a thing or a hill and high place; but orós, accented on the last syllable, is the watery part of milk. Third, there are Hebrew words which cannot be rendered among the Greeks as they are by nature, but have been left as they stand, as in Jeremiah 'the enclosure sinoch'. Fourth, punctuation too often causes obscurity, as in 'the good will be inhabitants of the earth', unless 'the good' is marked off by punctuation. Fifth, a difference of accent does the same, as in 'The beginning of wisdom: seek wisdom', unless we accent 'arche' on the next-to-last syllable and take it as a verb. Sixth, many words among them indicate both singular and plural in one form, as 'God' and 'gods'. Seventh, many things shift between persons: the words to Abraham, 'Now I know that you fear God', were said in place of 'you know'. Eighth, they also use the genders the opposite way, for they speak of the moon and the sea as masculine. Ninth, they often leave something out, as in 'they go up mountains and go down plains'. The word 'as' is missing, so that it reads 'they go up as mountains', for the passage is about waves, 'and go down as plains'. Tenth, during the captivity, after the books had been burned, the people in Jerusalem and those in Babylon sent the oracles of God to one another, and others lay in wait and seized the books. So they wrote again in symbols that strangers could not understand, and from these came the obscurity, until later Ezra, under inspiration, recalled all the books and handed them down in writing.

QUESTION 153. The same, more clearly. One cause of the obscurity of the ancient Writings is the brutishness of the hearers. Paul bears witness to this when he says that the same veil remains at the reading of the Old Covenant, not taken away, because it is abolished in Christ. A second cause is that Moses, [Notes: Chrēstós, accented on the last syllable, means 'useful'; Chrêstos, with the circumflex on the next-to-last syllable, is the proper name. (56) Scholion: For 'archē', accented on the next-to-last syllable…]

the lawgiver, wore a veil over his face, and correspondingly the legislation also brought obscurity with it, like a veil. Neither of them is to blame; the weakness of the hearers is the cause. Moses put on the veil because they could not bear the glory of his face uncovered, and the law likewise, in place of a veil, wrapped itself in obscurity for this very reason. For laid up in those writings, as in treasuries, were the more perfect and loftier doctrines, which announced beforehand Christ, I mean, and his Covenant. But for them, the imperfection and sickliness of their minds stood in the way of any profit from that source, while for us it was kept as a treasure, so that when Christ had come, what was treasured up might be unveiled through turning to him. See to what dignity the coming of the Master [?] has brought us: it has placed us in the rank of Moses. Besides, prophecy of future things, even if no obscurity is drawn into it from any other source, is still not as clear as the narration of present things. But when the things prophesied reach their fulfillment, the obscurity also changes into clarity. When the Saviour foretold, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,' it was not only the other Jews, in their disobedience and recklessness, who failed to perceive or understand the prophecy. Not even the band of disciples, who were more intelligent than the rest and enjoyed the Lord's teaching, understood it. They too needed the outcome of events in order to grasp what had been prophesied. Therefore the Jew is not liable to blame for failing to understand the prophecies about Christ before his coming. That is why the Saviour said, 'If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.' For even if the oracles foretold him, they were overshadowed by the absence of the one they proclaimed. But once he was present, they were no longer overshadowed from any other source; they were veiled only by the wickedness and malice of those unwilling to receive them. In addition to these, a cause of obscurity is that the Old Scripture was not delivered in the Greek language but passed into it from Hebrew; and a language translated into a foreign one naturally brings obscurity and difficulty of understanding with it. The Mosaic legislation was spoken in Hebrew at the beginning because at that time only the Jewish nation was devoted to the knowledge of God, while the rest had become brutalized into idolatrous madness. But when Christ was about to come and call the whole world to himself, and the Greek language prevailed among the nations more than the others, then the Hebrew speech was also changed into that of the Greeks, no more than a hundred years before the Saviour's coming, when Ptolemy himself

was reigning over Egypt. For it was fitting that the oracles that foretold the common Saviour should be announced beforehand through the very language by which most of the nations were to be guided to the knowledge of God. The languages were divided into many tongues because man, having received one language from the beginning, was lifted up to folly and godlessness. Since they used the one speech harmfully, a multitude of tongues was fittingly brought in to replace it. Yet the profit and use of the one language were displayed and restored long years after its division and dispersion by the disciples, when, their mouths sharpened by tongues of fire, they proclaimed the mighty works of God.

QUESTION 154. How many editions of Scripture have there been? The first is that of the seventy-two translators. These were Hebrews, chosen six from each tribe, and they translated the divine Scripture under King Ptolemy Philadelphus, 301 years before the birth according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ. The second is that of Aquila. He came from Sinope in Pontus and, being a Greek, was baptized in Jerusalem. Then he rejected Christianity, went over to the Jews, and he too translated the divine Scripture, under the emperor Hadrian, who became leprous, 430 years after the translation of the seventy-two. He did not set out his translation with right reasoning, but in hostility to the Christians. The third is that of Symmachus. He was at first a Samaritan, but not being honoured by his own people, he ran over to the Jews out of love of power and was circumcised a second time. He too, with an eye to hostility against the Samaritans, translated the divine Scripture, when Severus was reigning, producing his own edition 56 years after Aquila's translation. The fourth is that of Theodotion of Ephesus. He had belonged to the heresy of Marcion of Pontus, and in anger at his fellow heretics he made his own edition of Scripture while Commodus held the Roman empire. The fifth translation has no known author; it was found hidden in jars at Jericho under Caracalla, emperor of the Romans. The sixth, likewise anonymous, was discovered in a similar way: it too was found hidden in jars, under Alexander the son of Mamaea, at Nicopolis near Actium [?]. After all these, a translation of the sacred Scripture was made by Lucian, who is numbered among the saints, the great ascetic and martyr. He examined the editions written before him, diligently read the Hebrew texts, and carefully scrutinized them; what was lacking or superfluous with respect to the truth he [corrected?] [?], and he produced a distinct edition for the Christians who shared his faith. After his martyrdom this edition and

…the persecution that took place under the tyrants Maximian and Diocletian, was found in Nicomedia, written in his own hand. Constantine the Great was reigning at the time. The book was found among the Jews in the wall of a small tower, sealed over with plaster for safekeeping.
QUESTION 155. What did the shepherds see that made them make known what had been told them about the child?

They had seen the good news with their own eyes, and they were seized by the wonder of the truth, so they did not hide the reason from those who asked. They revealed and proclaimed to everyone present all that they had first seen and all that they had heard, both from the angel himself who announced the good news as herald and from the rest of the angelic host that sang hymns. They reported the things beyond reason that they had seen not only to Mary and Joseph. After them, they told their story to everyone else they could meet and so made them sharers in those supernatural sights and sounds. At once the city of Bethlehem, which was nearby, was filled with the truth of the saving birth and the certainty of the testimony from heaven. Those divinely wise shepherds eagerly told everything and planted the awe of the wonder in people's souls. For it says: "All who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds told them." How could anyone not be amazed to see on earth the one who is in heaven, joining earth to heaven through peace, while heavenly things made the earth their own? Or rather, that ineffable infant joined heavenly things to earthly ones, the heavenly by his divinity and the earthly by his humanity. Out of this union in himself he brought about a marvellous peace between them, a peace beyond reason. Seeing this, the heavenly hosts sang in a spiritual dance, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace." But here the work of the shepherds ends, both their proclamation and their running. "But Mary," it says, "kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." What words? The words of the archangel Gabriel, of Zechariah, of Elizabeth, and of the shepherds, in which the angel had brought them good news. She also kept the words of the ranks of angels, whose hymn-singing made faith in the good news more secure. But what did she compare these words with in her heart? Clearly, with the events she had experienced herself: the conception without seed, the pregnancy without labour pains, the birth without corruption. So, comparing the words with the events that had happened to her, she embraced the right judgment that she should confess as God

the one who had been born. Finally the shepherds, having [?] the marvels they had seen and filled their souls with joy, returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, just as it had been told them.

QUESTION 156. [?] … our [?] … Jesus Christ, having received him in his arms [?]

Symeon was not a priest, but he far surpassed the priests in [virtues?]. So the priest performed for the infant what the law commanded, and he carried out these duties. Symeon, however, was advanced both in his other achievements and in the grey hair of old age. In accordance with the divine oracles, he was granted the joy of seeing the child. He recognized the one who had been foretold, he saw the truth of the oracles, and he carried in his arms the one who carries all things by his word. He became an eyewitness of the salvation of the human race and was filled with a more divine delight. So he no longer clung to life. Since salvation was now at hand, he longed at once to leave the flesh and to announce the salvation to those in Hades as well. And he blessed God, that is, he offered him praise and glory. Among other things he blessed him because the promises made to him had come true, and because he had been allowed to see with his eyes the consolation of Israel and to carry it in his hands. Filled with holy [joy?] at this, he said: "Now, Master, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word." He means: "Now that I have the fulfilment of what was announced, let this perishable life also have its end. For your word foretold these things to me. Long ago you yourself gave me the good news that I would not see death before I had seen your Christ. Since what I longed for has come before my eyes [?] and I have what I craved, now you dismiss your servant. I am not troubled at the experience of death [?], nor disturbed by doubtful thoughts. I go in steady peace and [with] great gladness [?]. For [my eyes have seen] the salvation of all the peoples." And see how precise the divine and holy elder is [?]. Before the blessed sight [?] he was waiting for the consolation of Israel. But once he had come to the [fulfilment] of his hope [?], he no longer cries out that he has seen the consolation of Israel. He cries out that he has seen the salvation of all the peoples: "For my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples." So brightly

did the ineffable radiance, beyond reason, that he saw in the infant shine around him that everything which would be unveiled little by little as time went on came to his knowledge all at once, even then. And so that no one would have any room to think that by "all peoples" he meant only those of the Jewish nation, he adds the words that follow: "A light for revelation to the Gentiles." This means: "Let no one now suppose that I am speaking of the whole Jewish people. With this word I point to the entire human race. For this child, whom I have seen and carry in my arms, will be the salvation and redemption of all." He was not content even with this. Distinguishing Israel from all the nations, he adds: "a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel." It is as if he said: the infant carried in my arms is a common salvation for all the nations and for Israel. For the nations he is light, because he leads them out of the darkness of idolatry. For Israel he is glory, because the ordinances given to them were being cleansed of the mist of idolatry [?], and he will change them into glory and perfection. In another sense, too, the one born is the glory of the Israelite people, since he became man from the seed of Abraham. A little before, the prophet Isaiah also proclaims the same thing in advance: "Behold, I have set you as a light for the nations, to open the eyes of the blind." That is, he will grant them sight and the power to tell light from darkness, truth from falsehood, and piety from error. That is why David, applauding this salvation as though dancing and proclaiming it, says: "Clap your hands, all you nations, for the Lord Most High is awesome, a great King over all the earth." Israel is called Christ's people and is Christ's people, and in this it is set apart from the nations. It is certainly set apart from them by the Mosaic laws. So it is clear that this people too belongs to Christ, even if it had not yet enjoyed grace or been counted among those within it. And if the people of the Old Testament is Christ's people, how are the lawless mouths of the followers of Mani not silenced, since they assign this people to another first principle? Now while the elder Symeon was uttering these words of divine teaching, "Joseph and his mother," it says, "were marvelling at what was said about him." This was not because they were only now coming to know things beyond reason. It was because they were adding these to what they already knew in a supernatural way. For whenever the knowledge of supernatural things brings the one who knows them back to memory of them, it renews the wonder in the mind. Then, having completed

his hymn of praise to God, the elder turns his words to blessing those who had brought the infant. From there he turns his speech to the mother alone. "And Symeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother." Note that it says "to Mary his mother," not "to Joseph his father." He gives both of them a share in the blessing. But he addresses the more secret matters to the mother alone. Through the shared blessing he does not strip Joseph of the role of parent, while through his words to the mother he sets the Virgin apart from Joseph and proclaims her the true mother. What, then, does he say to the mother? "This child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against." Do you see how he prophetically lays the whole economy of the mystery before the Virgin, and how she [hears?] its account? If you would also like to go through what follows, the solemn sayings of holy men will lavish on you the complete solution to your questions [?]. The text is: "This child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against," and so on. Since you have quickly asked for the solution of the remaining points as well, we will give you this one too, trusting in God. By "fall" he means here the fall of those who fell away from faith and piety toward him. By "rising" he means the rising of those who recognized that the Saviour had come. Isaiah also foretold this when he said: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." Those who have not believed in him would fall. And those who have fallen away from the idolatrous error and the other errors in which they were formerly [entangled?] are led by the hand to the rising of the soul. He also indicates the cause of the fall and the rising. What is said about the economy becomes rising and salvation for those who assent to it, but fall and destruction for those who speak against it. And what are the things spoken against?
