All [the faithful] have believed that a virgin gave birth and remained a virgin. But those who have sunk into materialistic reasoning and know nothing of what is above nature are not persuaded to agree with this. They will not admit that he who fashioned her a virgin wholly can also keep her a virgin, especially if the one who fashioned her undertook to be born of her. Other signs concerning the economy might also be spoken against. (Note 57: I read "solemn sayings" [semnologēmata] instead of "solemn saying" [semnologēma].)

For example, those who have risen take it as a supernatural teaching that the one born is truly God and man. But those who look to human weakness and refuse to be lifted at all above it will not agree that the same one is both God and man. Many other signs of the Saviour's ineffable coming have also become matters of dispute. When the holy Symeon had gone through these things with the Virgin, he added at the very end the suffering the Virgin herself would endure from grief. He says: "And a sword will pierce your own soul too, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." "Your own" means this: "You have learned every detail of the mystery exactly, yet even you will not be spared the suffering of grief. No one knows better than you that you conceived without seed, that the birth was without seed and the pregnancy without labour pains. No one knows better the good news of Gabriel, the stories of the shepherds, and the countless other extraordinary wonders. Yet the lovers of error and accusers of the truth will not only [deny] these things. They will also slander you yourself over the conception and the birth. That slander will pass through your soul no less than a sword, biting and wounding it. But when they have insulted you in this way, then all the more will the thoughts of many hearts be revealed and dissolved." How, and in what way? The slanderers would not give up their slanders, and those slandered took refuge in the ancient test and judgment of the law. And what is this, if not the trial carried out with the water of conviction? An old story has gone around that when the ever-virgin Mary was slandered, she agreed to submit herself to the trial by water. The water brilliantly displayed and declared her purity and spotlessness. As a result, the slanderers were put to shame. Those who had earlier doubted her virginity and the incorrupt birth were made certain by testimony no one could dispute. And the Virgin was freed from the dejection and grief that the slander and accusations had caused her. Now, we have received from history that the water of conviction sends up its springs near Gaue [?], a mountain of the Palestinians. The old law also knows this test, which distinguishes women who do not corrupt their chastity from those who outrage their womb by intercourse with strangers. But this perhaps undermines the story's credibility. For it is recorded that the water of conviction was brought against the Virgin before the infant had appeared. At that time the circumstances gave reasonable grounds for doubt, and the

trial was not being drawn into absurdity. But once the birth had taken place and the infant was known, what occasion was there for the water of conviction? Nonetheless, this has been told according to the story. I know, however, that many of our holy Fathers have taken the sword that passed through the soul of the ever-virgin Mary to mean the bitter and painful anguish over her child that seized her at the time of the saving Passion. By her unsurpassable grief and the extraordinary rending of her heart, she showed a mother's natural compassion for her Son. And through this maternal compassion the thoughts of many hearts were revealed. It refuted those who spin fables that our Lord Jesus Christ wore flesh only in appearance, and those who shamelessly claim that he brought his flesh down from heaven and did not take it from the Virgin. It would also be quite in keeping with right reason to say that a sword passed through the Virgin's soul when they left the boy behind. They had gone a long way before they found he was not with them, and they turned back to search for him as though they had already lost their treasure. For then too the thoughts of many hearts were revealed. The Virgin said to the child, "Your father and I have been searching for you in anguish." The subsistent Word, who had also put on flesh, replied, "Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" By this he meant the famous temple, which was called the shrine and house of the Father. When the Son clearly proclaimed his own Father, the thoughts of those who say that he is not the son of the carpenter, nor of any other earthly seed, were clearly revealed. He is the Son of the one who begot him before the ages. As for the account that says the sword that passed through her soul was doubt, as though the crucified one might not be God, it may have been put forward by some, but I would never say it. "And there was," it says, "Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher," down to, "and she was a widow of about eighty-four years." Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel: these details distinguish her from the mother of the Virgin. She shone in every virtue. She did not leave the temple, and she served God with fasting and prayer night and day. From this it is clear that the whole remaining choir of the other virtues was present in her as well. Her mind was purified by these virtues, she had become a vessel of the all-holy Spirit, and she received the impressions he gave. So "coming up at that very hour she gave thanks and spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem." "Coming up at that very hour," it says. What hour? The hour in which the Mother and Joseph

were presenting the child in the temple. And see how she, who was close to Symeon in virtue, also shares prophecies close to his. They were present in the temple at the same time, and they were granted the grace of prophecy at the same time. Symeon went first in uttering oracles. Anna held second place, yet her oracles were not second-rate. She called the infant Lord and gave thanks to him, and she spoke of him to all who were looking for redemption in Israel, proclaiming the redemption and salvation of the race. Perhaps one might give a sacred interpretation of why Symeon went first. He bore the type of the law, for his name signifies obedience. Anna bore the type of grace, for that is what her name means when it is unfolded. Christ lay in the middle between the two of them. He released the one, who was ending together with the law, and kept the other, who for the time being lived on with grace. The Virgin and Joseph, having offered their shared hymn of praise to God, returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. After forty days the events of the magi and the star took place, and then the flight into Egypt and the return from there.

QUESTION 158. Why does Christ choose Mary Magdalene, from whom [he had cast out] seven demons?

We find that Scripture uses the number seven both for virtue and for vice. It was fitting, then, for the Saviour to choose Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons, so that through her he might drive the ruler of wickedness out of human nature. It says that the histories teach that this Magdalene remained a virgin all her life. An account of her martyrdom is also in circulation, in which it is said that her extreme virginity and purity made her appear to her torturers like clear glass. It says that after the falling asleep of our Lady the Theotokos, Mary the myrrh-bearer went to Ephesus to the beloved disciple. There she completed her apostolic course by martyrdom, not wishing to be separated until death from the

virgin and evangelist John. Just as Peter, the first of the apostles, was named for the unshakeable faith he had in Christ the rock, so she too, it says, became the leader of the women disciples. Because of her purity and the love she had for him, the Saviour called her Mary, by the same name as his Mother. Just as the band of disciples followed the Master, so the band of women disciples followed the Lady and Mother of the Lord. For the disciples once marvelled, it says, that he was talking with a woman. Clearly the Lord was not in the habit of doing so. But the Mother of the Master was completing the course of the Gospel together with her Son and Creator. These women followed her together with their common Master, and they ministered to the disciples with what they needed from their own means.

QUESTION 159. What is the meaning of "I do not speak on my own"?

The false christs spoke on their own. They spoke not from the law and not from the prophets, but from their own opinion and impulse. The Saviour, however, did not depart from the law and did not abandon the prophets. At one time he said, "Isaiah spoke well," at another, "Is it not written in your law?" and countless other such things. Those who came before Christ wickedly took his name for themselves and put forward their errors from their own madness, not from the sacred Scriptures. Because of them the Saviour says: "I do not speak on my own," as they did. For to speak on one's own is to speak outside the sacred Scriptures. God says through the prophet Ezekiel that speaking on one's own is the mark of false christs and false prophets: "I did not send them; they spoke on their own; they utter what comes from their own hearts." The false prophets preached on their own, and he wanted to clear himself of the charge of such madness. For the ungrateful nation of the Jews slandered him as a deceiver who was leading the world astray. That is why he said: "I do not speak on my own," but from the law and from the prophets, whatever I have heard from the Father in the law and in the prophets. He says this in the person of the flesh, to dispel the impious suspicion. "But you [do] what you have heard from your father the devil." A father's goods become the children's inheritance, and so what is his becomes the property of his heirs. Here, then, speaking on their own and speaking from their father the devil are seen to be equal and to amount to the same thing, (Note: the same manuscript wrongly reads "planōn auton.")

Just as Christ, when he came, became the fulfilment of the law and the prophets, so the Spirit too is the fulfilment of the Gospel. When Christ came, he confirmed what the Father had spoken in the law and the prophets. That is why Paul says: "Christ is the fulfilment of the law." The Holy Spirit fulfilled what belongs to the Gospel. Whatever is in Christ's teaching, the Spirit fulfils. Whatever is in the teaching of the law, Christ fulfils. This is not because the Father is imperfect. Christ is the interpreter and perfecter of what is the Father's. In the same way the Spirit clarifies and makes plain what is the Son's. For he says: "I have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now; but when the Holy Spirit comes, he will guide you into all the truth," and so on. Note that the Spirit does not speak on his own, for he does not contradict the Son. He fills out what is the Son's, in the same way as the Son fills out what is the Father's. Note also that in this discourse, toward the end, you will find Chrysostom showing that being sent makes neither the Son nor the Spirit less than the Father, since the Father himself is sent by the Spirit and by the Son. He says in these very words: "If I show you the Maker of heaven and earth being sent by the Spirit and by the Son, what will you do? Either deny Christ and throw away the Scriptures, or, as a servant of the Scriptures, submit to the Scriptures." "And where," he says, "is this said? Hear God speaking through the prophet Isaiah: 'Listen to me, Israel, whom I call.'" He sets out the whole passage up to the words "And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." He insists that it is the Father who says these things, and he confirms the argument from what comes before. So he makes it clear that the one speaking here is the Father, who is sent by both the Spirit and the Son.

…whose divinity. “Though Jesus had done many signs,” it says, “the Jews did not believe, so that the word spoken by Isaiah might be fulfilled: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” He himself, then, is also righteousness: “For my righteousness draws near to come.” He himself is both Savior and arm. That is why Paul too gathers everything together and refers it to one person, saying: “Who was made for us from God wisdom and sanctification and redemption.” He has risen for us as a righteous dawn. “For behold,” it says, “I will raise up for the house of David a righteous dawn, and a righteous king shall reign.” The dawn is one, but its rays are many: rays of love for mankind, of healing, of peace; rays of righteousness, and of countless other things. That is why David too sang prophetically: “In his days righteousness shall dawn, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away.” This dawn, then, rose both from on high and from the earth: from on high according to his divinity, from the earth according to the economy of the incarnation.

QUESTION 164. What is the meaning of “Because the creation itself will be set free from bondage,” and so on? Creation served man: sun and moon, stars and earth, and all that is in them. It did so not because he was worthy (for he was a transgressor and liable to judgment), but because God commanded it to serve, so that the image might not be utterly insulted by everything, even though it had transgressed. So, when the whole of creation was in revolt, God commands creation not to throw off the reins. The sun is to provide its rays, the earth its fruits, the sea its fish and its commerce, and each of the creatures the use and benefit that comes from it to mankind. Laying this meaning bare, the Apostle says: “For the eager expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope; because creation itself will also be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” What I mean is something like this. When God saw that man had fallen, and that creation was balking at serving the one who had sinned, he bridled it even against its will. He commanded it to serve as before, when man kept the commandment and so preserved his royal and ruling dignity. For creation was ashamed to have the captive of transgression inscribed as its lord and to wait on him, seeing that he had become the slave of sin. But the Creator commanded it not to disown

the transgressor, but to display the unstinting grace of the common Master and the unchangeableness of his kindness. And he promised creation too that when the corrupted and captive man was renewed and set free, it too would be renewed. It is as if he were saying: “The image has fallen and slipped through transgression, and is being corrupted through disobedience. Bear with serving the corruption of the corrupted one, so that when I renew him, my image, the corrupted man, I may renew you, the creation, along with him, and make you share the throne of his glory. You were dragged down with him in his misery; you will rise with him in his glory.” But what does it mean that creation flees man’s lordship? For it says, “Creation was not subjected to futility.” To what futility? Whenever man turns away from God, he is called futility. Hear David singing: “Surely all things are futility, every living man.” Every man who abandons God and pursues futile things is futile. God appointed angels over the regions of the inhabited world, each to have charge, as Moses also says, of a particular nation. And he appointed them to bridle inanimate creation, so that sun and moon, sea and earth, and all that is in them should serve man’s enjoyment. Yet the angels were worn down by serving men who were unworthy and liable to judgment, especially when they saw them attaching the Master’s dignity to idols and dedicating things to them. The earth bore the wine, and the altars received the libations; and the other fruits too they offered to idols. That is why the angels were distressed, seeing things that do not exist honored in place of the One who is. This also explains the other problem, the one concerning the prophet. “There came to him,” it says, “the angel Gabriel, and said to him: Daniel, servant of God, from the day you set yourself to afflict your soul before the Lord, your prayer has been heard, and I have been sent to announce these words to you. But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians withstood me, until Michael, the prince of your people, came to my help.” For one might be puzzled. If the angel in charge of Persia has been appointed by God to that charge, and Gabriel likewise has been sent by God to bring Israel back from captivity, how can the prince of the Persians withstand him? The difficulty may be resolved as follows. The world had been filled with idolatry, and the angels set over the nations were indignant and distressed. But Daniel, carried off captive to Babylon with his kinsmen, proclaimed the knowledge of God. So did the three youths, whom the fire refreshed when it exchanged its burning power for cheerful breezes. And so, by turning many away from the error

of idols, they brought them to worship God. The angel set over the realm of the Persians therefore rejoiced, seeing God worshiped in his territories instead of idols. He saw Nebuchadnezzar, who had once compelled people to sacrifice to idols and subjected those who would not obey to the most extreme punishments, now speaking splendidly of God and saying, “Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego, servants of the Most High God,” and many such things. Now, blessed Daniel was praying to God, since the seventy years fixed for the captivity had been fulfilled, that he would bring Israel back from captivity, and Gabriel was sent to make the proclamation known to him. Then the overseer of the Persian realm withstands Gabriel. He is grieved that the land he oversaw would turn back again to its former impiety and error once the teachers of piety were carried back from there. But he resisted not by fighting but by pleading his case. “What is the hurry for the return?” he said. “When Israel lived in its own homeland and prospered, it often slipped into idolatry. But now they not only worship purely, they even contend for piety, and many of those in error are turning to the true God. Nothing more profitable for the soul will follow for those who receive this favor, and it will again make those who began to be pious because of them subject to the ultimate evil, impiety. How much better, then, not to bring Israel back from captivity for the present, and to keep in that same piety those who have just recovered their sight to the light of the knowledge of God! You were sent, you say, to restore the people to their homeland. What homeland? The one they defiled while they lived in it, with the smoke of sacrifices offered to demons and with their mad devotion to idols. Jeremiah denounces this, saying: ‘As many as your cities were your gods, Judah; and in every street of Jerusalem you sacrificed to Baal.’ Back then they were deluged with countless good things from God, yet did not turn from wickedness and impiety. Now they endure countless evils, yet do not stand apart from God. What, then, will be the gain of the return?” So the resistance was not of evil against good. For it did not say “he fought,” but “he withstood.” Often there is a resistance of the just against the good, just as love for mankind often withstands law, and law withstands love for mankind. The law punishes the sinner, but a king’s clemency often pities the sinner and snatches him from punishment. So here the contest is not of opposite against opposite, but of kindred against kindred. For neither is the just found apart from goodness, nor the good apart from justice.

It says that creation, as was said before, was in this condition. It was indignant that it had to provide its services to the transgressor even unwillingly and wait on him. The angels were vexed at the ingratitude of the one receiving their benefits, and the whole world had been harmed by lawless deeds. “For God saw the earth,” it says, “and it was corrupted, because all flesh had corrupted its way.” Creation was no longer such as God had established it for them from the beginning. The heaven was no longer lit by the stars without any defilement, as before; the earth no longer yielded its fruits undefiled, as before; nor was the sea, nor anything else in creation. For the transgressor, entering it, defiled and muddied everything. He defiled it with blasphemies and with God-opposing and shameful utterances, the earth with murders, the sea with pirates and robbers, and the springs and rivers with idolatries, attributing them to nymphs and demons. Men fashioned the whole of creation into gods, and nothing so defiles and debases creation as its being deified. The Savior of the world entered it through flesh, freed it from these countless defilements, and renewed it. He set it free from harms and sufferings far more grievous than bodily corruption, and so renews creation through his first coming. This is so that you may learn that he is the one who also fashioned it in the beginning. It is not the work of one to create and of another to renew what has been corrupted; both belong to the same wisdom and skill. He renews creation at his first sojourn so that no room for unbelief may be left you, as though at the second coming it would not be renewed, and you along with it [?], into incorruption, into freedom from passion, into ineffable beauty. For Christ was willingly in weakness of flesh, in sweat, in sufferings, and slandered as a deceiver and a Samaritan; yet even then he cleansed creation of so many great and long-standing passions and defilements. When, then, he comes as judge of the living and the dead, escorted by myriads of angelic ranks, as Master and Lord of all, when all things shudder and tremble, how can the change from corruption to incorruption not be seen to be the easiest thing? It is also consistent, and fitting for God, that the Savior comes with the prophets proclaiming him beforehand. Otherwise someone might think that God is like a man who fails in his first plan and remedy and moves on to a second. So that no one might suspect this, the prophets foretold his coming from of old. They showed that God does not find what is beneficial by deliberating, but foresaw everything from the beginning. For we humans deliberate, and if we fail in our first attempt, we move on to another; but God is not

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople] so. He gave the law, then the prophets, and after these the Gospel. He did not learn in the course of time what was beneficial, but knew from the beginning that creation, and the man within it, could not otherwise have come into being, or been educated, or taken up the dignity of incorruption, except in the way that his ineffable providence and love for mankind arranged. Some say: if God foresaw that Adam would sin, why did he bring him into being at all? There are many very fine solutions to this difficulty. The divinely wise John Chrysostom, for one, says: “I say not only that he foreknew it, but that he would also raise him up when he had fallen, through the economy.” He did not see the fall before he had planned the rising. He knew that man would fall, but he laid up beforehand the remedy of the resurrection, and permitted man to come to the experience of death, so that he might learn what he enjoys through himself and what through the grace of his Maker. He knew that Adam would fall, but he saw coming forth from him Abel, Enosh, Enoch, Noah, Elijah, the prophets, the wonderful apostles, the nobility of nature, the God-moved clouds of the martyrs dripping with piety. He saw all this. Where, then, would it have been good, or just, or fitting for God, to refuse to bring Adam forth from non-being because one man was going to sin? To cut off the line of so many men, of whom the world was not worthy, not even of any one of them? To reap at the root so great a growth and beauty of the race, and to let loose excision and wrath against it? And all this at a time when the one who would later choose sin had neither sinned nor even contemplated sinning, since he did not yet even exist? If prudent men do not exact penalties for sin from someone who has contemplated sinning but has not sinned, surely all the more does it befit God not to demand the penalties of sinners from one who has not even contemplated sinning. This is all the more so since the sin, though grievous (for how is breaking the Master’s commandment not grievous?), would not be incurable for the ineffable love for mankind of the Maker, and the first-formed man was going to be brought back to his ancient nobility. So if the first ancestor had not been brought into being because he was going to sin, the Divinity would have shown itself punishing one who had not sinned. It would have deprived him of his later recall and salvation, and left creation bereft of so many fine and good men.
QUESTION 162. What is “Firstborn of all creation”? Since the divine Paul said, “Firstborn of all creation,” the heretics, it says, not understanding which

creation he is speaking of, foolishly bring the Son down to the level of a creature. But creation is twofold: one is the creation that has come into being, the other the creation that is being renewed. For Paul himself cries out: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” And to show clearly that he calls Christ firstborn of the renewed creation, he adds: “Firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might be preeminent.” He is first among those being renewed, those called to incorruption, those raised from the dead. He is first not according to his divinity. Far from it! It is an insult to God to call him the first of creatures, since he transcends and is enthroned above all nature by an ineffable principle and an inconceivable preeminence. Rather, he is first according to his humanity, having become our leader in the resurrection and in the transformation from corruption to incorruption. Elijah raised the widow’s son, Elisha raised the Shunammite’s son, and the Savior himself raised Lazarus on the fourth day; yet none of them rose to incorruption and immortality, for death again became lord over them. But Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him. Nor will it over those whom he will raise at his second coming. O our wicked and senseless judgment! Christ came to us, gave us his Spirit, and took up our body, and so the exchange took place. He took our lump of clay, exalted it, and seated it at the right hand of the Father. And ingratitude insults the benefaction: we received the Spirit from him, and we insult the Spirit by numbering it among creatures and slaves.

QUESTION 163. What are petition and prayer? [What is petition and prayer?] Petition, it says, is the word used when someone asks God for something. Prayer is when one hymns God. Thanksgiving is when someone acknowledges his gratitude to God for what he has experienced. Intercession is when someone appeals to God against those who wrong him, calling on him to avenge. And to appeal, it says, is not to supplicate but to ask a question and receive an answer. So God says to Elijah, “What are you doing here, [Notes: (91) ‘transcends and’: from the Colbert manuscript. [?] (‘εἴη’ [?]). [?] ‘calling on’. The same shortly after reads ‘still’ [?].]

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, 852] Elijah?” And the prophet, when asked, answers: “I have been very zealous,” and so on. [Gallandi, p. [?]–750 [?]. Rom. 1:16–17.] Paul says: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel; for in it the righteousness of God is revealed.” How, then, is the righteousness of God revealed in it? How? The first law had been given to the Jews alone and not to the rest of mankind, although they shared the same creation and nature. The Gospel, by contrast, was given equally to all who share that nature. So it is fitting that the righteousness of God is revealed in it, and that it is called the Gospel of righteousness. In the Old Testament, then, the calling was not righteous, for it did not call and enlighten all alike, but only the Jews. So it was not righteous but a dispensation, preparing the way for righteousness. I do not say that this one is righteous and that one unrighteous. Rather, that one was the way to this one and its preparation. The Jews supposed that the Gospel too would be given to them alone, just as the law had been. But the outcome went beyond their hopes. That is why David also says: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple,” and then, “As is your name, O God, so also is your praise.” Not in the midst of your people only, but to the ends of the earth. And to show that showing mercy to the ends of the earth is a matter of righteousness, he adds: “Your right hand is full of righteousness.” “The Lord has become king.” How is it that “the Lord has become king”? As though he had recently received the dignity of kingship? If he had said, “The Lord is king,” his eternal [?]

authority would have been what he was expressing. But by saying “has become king,” he speaks of his economy through the flesh. Through it our nature shook off the domination of the devil, of sin, and of death, and recognized its Maker as the true King, the giver of incorruption and of resurrection. David, then, brings good news to those who had long been ruled by sin, by death, and by the devil: that yoke has been broken, that power dissolved, and the Lord reigns over all. As he himself said after the resurrection: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Before this, death and sin reigned over us. “For death reigned from Adam to Moses,” and so on. And the Savior says of the devil: “If Satan casts out Satan, his kingdom is divided.” So before Christ’s sojourn among us Satan reigned over our race, and so did sin. For Paul again says: “For just as sin reigned in our mortal body, so also grace reigns through Christ.” “The Lord has become king”: the power of sin has ceased, and that of death and of the devil. Let the earth rejoice, then: the earthborn nature, once led astray, now glorified; once in tombs, now on thrones. It says that most things in the Old Testament were matters of dispensation, not of what pleased God and of his primary good will. They were types and shadows of things to come, not the realities themselves. One can see that in them the outward forms are one thing and the meanings another. For example, God certainly does not take his rest in blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen. For God demands purity of souls, not the bloom and splendor of bodies; but in bodily brightness he sketches the image of the virtues. If he truly took his rest in those vestments, why did he not clothe Moses before Aaron? Why did he dress the priests in a robe that Moses never put on? And Moses was not [?], yet he washed them with water. Why? So that you might learn that these things were not of primary importance to God, that for the perfect man virtue is adornment enough, and that these things were a type of virtue, not virtue itself.
QUESTION 165. Why did the high priest wear a turban [?] on his head? Because the one appointed as head of all, according to

…he had to have authority over the head, and to know that, though he was set forward as head of the others, he himself is also under a head: the common Master and Ruler of all. For authority that is unrestrained and answers to no one is unbearable and harsh. This is also why, under grace, those being consecrated to the high priesthood receive the Gospel upon their heads, so that the one being ordained may learn that he is receiving the true tiara of the Gospel, and that, although he is consecrated as head of the others, he himself is nevertheless made subject to these laws, and while he rules others he is ruled by the law. The tiara showed authority: both the authority he himself held over the people and the authority of God, to which he himself was answerable. The golden plate, on which the name of God was engraved, lay upon the breast, and it bore a figure [?] of the movements in the heart, and showed that these must be regulated by inclining toward the Divine and referring all things to it. On the shoulders were two emerald stones, bearing six tribes on one side and six on the other. These were a symbol of the high priest's appearance. For the emerald stone has both a comely greenness and a translucent purity, and displays the power of a mirror. The priest, too, must be sober in his ascetic discipline and offer his life as a mirror to those under him. The emerald is on the shoulder because it is a sign of action, for the power to act depends on the shoulders. That is why God says to Jerusalem: "Set your heart upon your shoulders, honored daughter, for the Lord is creating you for salvation." For Scripture takes the hands and the shoulders to mean actions, as when it says of David: "And by the understanding of his hands he guided them." Set in the oracle on the breast were also the twelve stones, signifying the twelve tribes. Now notice: above, on the shoulders, the stones were of one kind, the emerald, but below, on the breast, there were twelve. The text is hinting that from above we all came forth from one nature, but as time went on we were divided by differing wills. It assigns the one to will and the other to nature. Under the hem of the priest's robe, the so-called fringe, hung pomegranate flowers, golden pomegranates and bells. How could these things please God in their first and literal sense? Rather, he allowed the virtues to be portrayed in the priest's vesture: the flowers and fruits below are the accomplishments of the virtues, namely almsgiving, righteousness, love for humankind, and the matching choir of the others.

…that, he says, you must not alter the words of the living God. You were baptized into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Why do you abolish the living names and bring in names produced by reasoning, speaking of "offspring" and "unbegotten" and "begotten," "ever-existent" and "not ever-existent"? Does God put up with these empty words? Once he came close to destroying prophets because they altered a single word. And see how precise he is about a small word. Some people, out of inexperience, called the words of the prophets "the burden of the Lord." God says through Jeremiah: "If the people, or the priest, or the prophet asks you, 'What is the burden?' say to them: 'You are the burden of the Lord. For I will take you up as a burden and dash you down, so that you no longer say "burden."'" God threatens this so that a single word will not be altered. And you, who are twisting the whole precision of the doctrines, think you will escape the hands of God?

QUESTION 166. How is Christ [?] [an ambassador?] from the [Father]? Answer: Christ, he says, came from the Father to humanity as an ambassador. The ambassador was slain, and then peace was made. But ambassadors, when they come, both bring gifts and receive gifts. What gift, then, did he come bringing, and what did he receive in return? The gift is extraordinary, just as the ambassador is extraordinary. He came bringing his blood as a gift. He came bringing his body as a gift. And what gift did he receive from me? Faith. And what did he give me in return for it? Grace. I believed; he gave grace; the enmity was ended. When an ambassador comes to a nation, he does not deign to talk with any of the market crowd or the poor, but goes straight to the king. This ambassador, however, came and at once talked with a harlot, a robber, a tax collector and magi. Do you see the ambassador's love for humankind? He did not come to one person or two, but to our common nature. And he came clothed in my garment, so that he would not frighten off his prey by appearing in naked divinity.

QUESTION 167. [?] the saying: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." Answer: The Hellenists say, and the Judaizers too: What does Paul mean when he says, "The old things have passed away; behold,

all things have become new; if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation"? For I, he says, see nothing new. — That is because you do not have eyes to see these things. Come, and I will make you eyes, and you will see. — You make eyes? — Yes. — So you are a creator? — Certainly. — Are you out of your mind? — No. — Then do you make eyes for the body? — No, but something greater: eyes for the mind. — And you will make eyes for me? — By all means, for you do not have them. — I do not? — But do you have them? — Yes. — How? Tell me. When you go into a temple and see there a bare wooden image or an unhewn stone, and you say, "This is God," do you have eyes then? What use are the outer eyes when the inner ones are blinded? Do you see that you need me to make you eyes, so that you may [see] the stone as stone and the wood as wood? Do you have eyes when you [carve?] wood and worship it? And I, taking it, [?]…

…the walls, and gilds the ceiling, would you not have said to him, "Man, get the sick one back on his feet! Why are you decorating the house? Help the one lying ill"? Christ, too, came into this world, where he found my nature lying sick, and he takes on the whole struggle to heal it, renewing it and setting it upright. Why, then, do you blame the physician for not doing those things, and then turn around and find fault with Christ for doing these? This is how the old things passed away; this is how all things became new; this is how there is a new creation. And one could [say] countless other such things…

QUESTION 168. Why does the Apostle call Christ's death "death" when he speaks about Christ, but call ours "sleep"? Answer: Why is it that when Paul speaks of Christ he calls his death "death," but when he speaks of our end he names it "sleep" and not "death"? In the same passage he mentions human death three times, yet nowhere says "death"; he calls the departure "sleep." He does not use this careful choice of words casually, but is building up something wise and great. In Christ's case he calls it death in order to confirm the suffering; in ours he calls it sleep in order to console our grief. Where the resurrection has already taken place, he boldly calls it death; where it still lies in hope, he calls it sleep. By this name he consoles us and holds out good hopes to us, for whoever sleeps will surely rise. Indeed, death is nothing else than a long sleep.

QUESTION 169. Why does [Isaiah] leave the vision and address heaven and earth? [?] Answer: You announced the vision you saw, but he says, "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken." You promised one thing and say another? At the beginning you said, "A vision against Judea and against Jerusalem," and then, leaving [?] the account, you talk to heaven and earth. You have left [?]…

…and you even talk to the irrational elements? Yes, he says, because the rational beings have become more irrational than the irrational ones. And not only for this reason, but also because Moses, when he was about to bring them into the land of promise and foresaw what was going to happen, speaks like this: "Hear, O heaven, and I will speak; let the earth attend to the word from my mouth." "I call heaven and earth to witness against you, Jews," says Moses, "that if you enter the land of promise and forsake the Lord God, you will be scattered among all the nations." So Isaiah came. The threat was about to be fulfilled. He could not call Moses, who was already dead, nor those who had heard him then. So he calls the elements, since Moses too had called them when he solemnly warned the people. Yet Moses could have called Aaron as witness, and many others. But I would say this is why he did not call them: they were going to die and would not be present as witnesses when Israel turned aside to lawlessness. "Therefore I call to witness the elements, which endure." Isaiah does the same, not only for the reasons given, but also because when he spoke to the Jews and found that they would not listen to him, he turned to the elements and took them as his witnesses. "Hear, O heaven," for you brought down the manna. "Give ear, O earth," for you provided the quail. "Hear, O heaven," for you supplied them with things beyond nature: above, you remained as you were made firm, and yet you did not disdain to imitate a threshing floor. "Give ear, O earth," for you were below, and you set an improvised table before them. This is also why another prophet, seeing a king raging, idols being worshiped, God being insulted and everyone else cowering, addresses none of them, but turns away and says, "Hear, O altar, hear me." Why then do you talk to a stone? Yes, he says, because the king is more senseless than a stone. "Hear, O altar: thus says the Lord." At once the altar split, broke apart and poured out the sacrifice, but the man did not listen. Instead the king stretched out his hand, wanting to seize the prophet. And what does God do? He withered his hand. But he did not wither his hand at the start, so that the king might come to his senses through what happened to the stone. God wanted him to be corrected without punishment falling on him. "But since even the stone split and you were not corrected, I will turn my just wrath upon you."

…to seize authority over created things, he wants the affairs of the divine economy to lie under the Savior's providence. That is why the parable also presents the younger son taking his father's property and setting off for a far country. The distance was not measured in miles; he removed himself by his way of life. For the sinner becomes far from God not in place but in manner of life. Having taken his father's property, he squandered it by living prodigally. He received the sun to enjoy, and worshiped the light [?] as God. He received springs for refreshment, and made a god of the gift. He ignored the giver and glorified the gift above him. The creation is the same, the father's property, but not everyone sees it alike: one person used it well and another badly. [?] this one and that one, though different. The pious person sees the beauty of heaven and from that beauty sings the praises of the Creator: "For I will behold," he says, "the heavens, the works of your fingers." The impious person saw it, but did not raise [?] his mind to the Creator. He stayed with the beauty of heaven and imagined that the thing made was a god. The pious person does not treat the creation as sacred, but reserves worship for the Master. He honors the creation, but as a fellow servant. He does not take the reverence due to the Creator and attach it to the creature. He praises the work of art, but does not transfer the artist's glory to it. The impious person, on the other hand, did not see wrongly, but worshiped wrongly, and overturned the whole order. That Scripture often calls the devil a dragon and a crooked serpent. That is why the Savior says, "Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions," and so that you would not think he meant creeping things, he added, "and over all the power of the enemy." The devil is a dragon and a serpent, not as the root of evil, as the Manichaeans say, but as the ruler of the demons, who became their leader in the fall.

QUESTION 171. The greeting from above; the conception without seed; the pregnancy beyond words; birth pangs without labor; the seal of virginity; the release from the pangs (for the birth was without corruption, and the mother remained a virgin even after giving birth); the one born, God in the flesh; a choir of angels making the wonder their song. Where so many and such great things come together, how could anyone dispute it, even if he devoted all his

effort to disputing [?] that she was a virgin, or that she remained a virgin to the end? If some find a pretext for blasphemy in the words "He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son," let them know that the truth of the immaculate Scriptures wanted to set forth what was extraordinary, supernatural and beyond comprehension, namely a birth without knowledge of a man, and left what came afterward to be understood as following from it. For that she who remained a virgin in giving birth should remain a virgin for the rest of her life is neither new nor in any way extraordinary; rather, it follows of necessity from what went before. Besides, Scripture also chose for the moment to silence the blasphemy of the Jews, who slandered the seedless birth as the result of fornication. So it takes a stand against their malice with the words by which it clearly proclaims that the mother was untouched. Let them also realize that they did not wish to understand even the very words of which the divine oracles are made. Otherwise they would have learned that "until" is sometimes used to contrast with the time that follows, but sometimes to point out great works befitting God. So it is here: it is not used to contrast with some other time, but on the contrary to indicate an endless span. Examples are close at hand: "In his days righteousness shall spring up, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away"; and "Sit at my right hand" (it is written that the Father says this to the Son) "until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet"; and "Behold, I am with you" (again the Savior says this to the disciples) "until the end of the age." It is clear that here "until" does not introduce a boundary or limit in time. Rather, the word also points to the greatness of divine things and sends the reader's mind toward an unlimited extension. And not only this; one can also see a third meaning of the word, in which nothing great or vast is indicated, but simply that what comes after "until" is no different from what came before. For example: "The dove did not return to Noah until the earth was dried"; and "Until you grow old" (he says elsewhere) "I am God"; and countless others. From these it becomes plain even to the most willfully obtuse that the word is used to mean "continually" and "forever." So when these all-daring people show that after the moon is taken away, the righteousness of Christ our God sinks into nonexistence, and the abundance of his peace dwindles and turns into enmity; and that after his enemies are put under his feet he gives up [?] the seat at the Father's right hand (may this blasphemy fall on the heads of the shameless!); and then that after the end of the age, when his closeness to them is greater, he departs from the disciples; and that when the people of that time grow old, God no longer exists;

or, if you like, that the dove returned to Noah after the earth was dried — then let them raise the question whether, after the ineffable and virginal birth, the Virgin had relations with a man in mind. If I were not writing in the form of a letter, I would have set out more proofs for you, God willing. But these are enough for those whose mind has not also [?] along with their ignorance. For the rest, [be well] in soul and body [?]. QUESTION 172. On providence. 1. If none of those who do wrong, or sin at all, had punishment overtaking them close at hand, and all who practiced virtue spent their lives in misery, then your argument about providence would not be so very unreasonable and lame. But many who pursue vice have been seen to pay the penalty in the very act, and many whose lives are ordered by virtue are known to prosper. How, then, is the notion against providence not foolish? If what provokes you against it is that not everyone receives their wages here, know that by the very things with which you thought to fight it, you instead proclaim that it is unassailable and also wise. For suppose that in the present age everyone, without exception, either paid the penalty for their sins or, for having chosen what is better, enjoyed glory, honor and happiness. Then the judgment of the world to come, which belongs to the supreme wisdom and care of God, would have been set up in vain. And flight from evil would have proved to be forced and involuntary, since those who had resolved to do wrong would naturally fear immediate punishment, and they would be drawn away from vice not by the choice of a good will but rather by cowardice. Indeed, the practice of virtue would then be a matter of working for hire, not of virtue [?]. There would no longer be any distinction between the earnest and the worthless. Nor would it be that some practice virtue, and exercise it out of divine love, in order to gain the kingdom to come and keep the Master's commandments, while others do so in order to pass the present life in enjoyment and happiness. 2. Besides, and finest of all, the contests, I mean, for which the righteous are especially crowned, would be abolished [?]…

…for that is the act of one who [abolishes them?]: that none of the righteous would want to suffer the toils of the present life. Not only that, but it would also be the act of one who increases punishment and is excessively angry with sinners. And this point is no weaker as proof than any of the others. Both of these things are foreign to God's love for humankind. For to take away crowns and to devise the bitterest, undiluted punishment are far removed from a governance that is good in nature. And how could punishment not be prepared for sinners as, in a sense, utterly inexorable and undiluted to the dregs, if God's kindness overflowed so far that they could live better and enjoy both comfort here and good things there, and even so they did not choose the better over the worse? So the fact that not all the earnest have a prosperous life here, and not all the worthless a miserable one, comes from God's supreme love for humankind and care for human affairs. Some of the earnest, then, are chastised here so that they may receive crowns, and so that the divine love in them may be shown to be all the more wonderful, revealing how great it is when it flourishes even in afflictions. And also, if you like, so that, as the divine Paul says, they may not be exalted beyond measure, nor be thought by some to be greater than what they are seen to be. 3. Understand with me, if you please, also this: since they delight in the great and pure pleasures that come with virtue, and are relaxed by them, it would be right for them to keep company with afflictions as with an astringent, tightening medicine. Moreover, the grace of God shines out more brightly through their weakness and is admired. It is also for the complete shame and downfall of the evil one, when, though drenched with the sweat of temptations, they neither slackened the tension of virtue nor grew soft in their wrestling against him. But not all are handed over to temptations, so that the thoughts of the weaker may not be thrown into confusion against providence. Of the worthless, too, some are punished for the cleansing of their defilements, namely those who have sinned somewhat more moderately. Others are punished to prolong [?] the reckoning for the lives they have lived, which is surely laid up for them, more bitter, in the world to come; and so that even the foolish may become aware of God's hatred of evil. But not all are punished, so that the honor of free will may not be shown to be in vain [?]; so that the benefit of the commandments' legislation may be shown to be pure and undefiled by compulsion; and because the common judgment of all remains in the world to come. Again, many of the righteous live in comfort, set before their neighbors as encouragement, consolation and a common good, and as a pledge of the enjoyment to come, and so that people may believe that the eye no one escapes watches over things here too. But not all, so that the grace of virtue may not seem [limited] to a temporary reward

…to be dissolved; and so that the punishment of those who have slipped might not, in a sense, be made ready in its heaviest and most undiluted form, since their sin would then stand wholly beyond any defence [?]. For what can you say? When it was possible to live at ease both here and there, you chose punishment on both sides and exchanged the better for the worse. Nor should anyone think that an excess of kindness was a device for an excess of penalties. 4. In the same way, for many of the unjust too, present affairs flow along with the current. This is so that if any trace of goodness has ever been done by them, they may receive their reward here, since the deed is too weak to reach as far as the repayment in the next life. It is also so that they may not seize on misery as an excuse for wrongdoing. But prosperity does not attend all of them. Otherwise the road of wickedness would grow still wider and drag many into the pit. Lovers of sin would sink still further into insensibility, and they [?] would think the divine verdict a joke. There are countless other things through which one can behold the beneficence and wisdom of providence, which surpass human judgment, method and inquiry. Meditate on these and similar things and train your thoughts on them. Then recover yourself from the irregularity and confusion that present affairs seem to show, and let neither our sufferings nor the unbroken run of trials arm you against providence. Perhaps, as we pray, we are being cleansed through them of most of our filth. Then the surpassing wisdom and love for humankind of providence shines out all the more brightly. Or perhaps, as you yourself think, we are undergoing contests and struggles. Then do not begrudge us the crowns to be won there; rather, extol providence and recognize its beneficence and majesty in all things. May our sufferings, through the compassion of Christ our God toward us, be one or the other of these two things, and not the prelude to a heavier punishment that admits no consolation.

Question 170. On the Trinity. To confound the Trinity abolishes the persons; to divide the essence imagines an estrangement and a cutting-up of the Godhead. Flee the precipice on either side of the royal road, and, according to the Church's definitions and ordinances, … [Variant readings: "have slipped"; "For what? When it was possible."]
…worship and adore one essence and Godhead in three hypostases and persons, and proclaim the theology of Christians, summed up in these terms.

Question 171. How should we understand what was said by Job: "Cursed be the day on which I was born"? Job curses the day of his birth for several reasons. Not the least is that he was tossed about by anxious thoughts. Perhaps, he feared, he had gone so far in wrongdoing as to stir up so great a wrath of God against himself. That is: "I have run so far aground from the Master's commandments that the magnitude of my evil escaped my notice. Yet I have provoked the long-suffering and benevolent God so far that I was judged liable to such wrath and required to pay such heavy penalties. Cursed be that day!" So the curse was not so much an expression of indignation [?] at what he was suffering. It was a lament and a pitiful complaint over the things by which he thought he had grieved God. The Master's voice makes this clear when it says to him: "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?" That is: "The sufferings to which you were handed over are not an exaction of payment for your sins. They are an exercise of virtue, and they win you a recompense of prizes and crowns greater than your pains and wounds. So it was not in an outpouring of wrath that I allowed you to be subjected to such penalties. It was so that your virtue might be displayed more brilliantly, and you might be shown to all as a champion who wins trophies against the common enemy of our nature." He curses the day of his birth, and not without reason. On that day he used to entertain with splendid feasts those bound to him in friendship, as well as his kinsmen. It is likely that, living in luxury, they amused themselves with the delights and pleasures of various spectacles and performances, which please both ear and eye. When kings feast together, such things were very likely brought in along with the banquet. That is why anxious thoughts troubled him, lest these things had become hateful to God and stirred His wrath against him. So he curses the day of his birth, the day on which he let the tension of his soul, gathered and turned in upon itself, flow out into luxury and smile at these shallow pleasures. He also uttered the curse aloud, perhaps so that he would not seem to the many to bear that dreadful calamity without feeling. There is nothing unreasonable in supposing this. For he utters the curse not against something that exists, but against something that, once it had happened, no longer existed at all. Such a curse would make plain both the magnitude of his suffering and his awareness of his pains, and it would show that the one cursing was guilty of no offence, since his indignation was directed at things that do not exist. Someone might also say that he spoke these words remembering the Master's sentence, and he would not stray far from a view pleasing to God. Which sentence? The one He pronounced against Eve, when she made Adam a partner

in her deception. For then, Scripture says, He yoked human childbirth to griefs and pains, together with the curse. Thus He fortified with gloomy sorrow the very thing from which hopes of joy ran ahead. So Job turns his mind to this sorrow and all but marvels at the sentence and praises the Master. "Truly," he says, "cursed is the day on which a human being, releasing his mother from her birth pangs, comes out into the rays of the sun."

"By myself I have sworn, says the Lord." Where can one find that God has sworn, whether by Himself or by anyone else? How could God have sworn, when through the Gospels He forbids everyone to swear any oath, and bids them guard themselves and not use the tongue in the service of sworn speech? For the Son is in harmony with the Father in all things, and what He says He has received from Him. What then does "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord" mean? It means: "Among human beings, the force of an oath confirms what is promised. In the same way, my promise cannot be broken." For often, after an oath has been taken, either an unsteady intention dissolves the oath into perjury, or, even when the intention is firm, the flux of matter and the instability of earthly affairs cut short the fulfilment of what was sworn. But with a bare promise of God, nothing of this sort can even be imagined, much less believed. God therefore takes no oath, since the divine promise is more powerful than any oath. He is accustomed to add "By myself I have sworn," or rather to place it before His own promises, whether they bring gloom and punishment or joy and gladness. So those who are reckless with oaths take refuge in this turn of phrase in vain. For nowhere has the Divine been seen using either oaths or the adverbs of oath-taking.

Question 176 [?]. What is the meaning of "And a sword will pierce your own soul too"? A sword passed through the soul of the all-holy and ever-virgin Mary at the very moment of Christ's saving passion. This was not because she was struck by doubting thoughts or wounded by the darts of unbelief, nor because she exchanged her joy for grief. It was because, while her Son was being crucified, she gave her mother's heart over to its natural compassion to do what is proper to it. For what would a mother not suffer at seeing her son, and above all one who lived beyond the measure of human nature, undergoing the punishment of criminals? For the all-immaculate Mother of the Word, this suffering was more bitter and piercing than any sword. She had many grounds for knowing that her Son was God made flesh, yet He did not suspend the laws of nature in every case. He also allowed nature to show itself within its own proper bounds. Therefore

Question 177. What is the meaning of "Do not groan against one another, so that you may not [be judged]"? How is it possible for someone who is insulted, or driven from his own property, or beaten, not to groan against those responsible? Not to retaliate or strike back is difficult, but it is still possible for those who practise philosophy and are secured by the divine commandments. But not even to groan against those who have wronged one — how can that find a place in a nature that is fluid and mortal? Or is it in fact much easier than the former? When one has the power to sate one's anger, to hurt in return and to recover the whole loss, [it is hard to refrain]. These things are great and demand a very noble soul, one able to overlook them and rise above human attachment and the urge to retaliate. We know that they often wrestle down and overcome even those who strive to be high-minded, though the love of philosophy and the fear of God have raised many above these passions. If, then, you have been able to master these unruly passions, how much more will you drive groaning away from yourself, a thing so paltry and able to bring no gain? Besides, consider the one who groans. If he groans because he is eager to exact justice and cannot, he has already repaid the wrong by his own impulse and judgment and by the lack of restraint in his urge. If one may say so, he has repaid it even more heavily, since he counts it a misfortune to fail to hurt the one who hurt him. But if he groans and does not wish to take revenge, then within a manly mind he is acting out a scene of womanish faintheartedness. He need only become sober and turn back to himself, and the scene is over. So the exhortation of the Lord's brother overflows with wisdom and ease, and, if you like, with profit and salvation.

Question 178. What is the meaning of "Adulterers and adulteresses"? The Apostle divides the inclination of sins toward the passions into two kinds. An adulterer is not only someone who has cut himself off from divine affection and union with God. He is also someone who has set out to tear away from there the soul betrothed to Christ, the true Bridegroom, and by uniting it to himself has wrapped it in the charge of adultery. For divorce from God makes the one who departs an adulterer, and makes the soul that followed his deceits an adulteress. In the proper sense, the adulteress would be the soul that has been separated from the divine works and commands and has turned aside to worldly pleasures, whether someone deceives her or she is driven by a goad from within. For this soul was joined to Christ through baptism and was brought as a bride into the ever-virgin and undefiled bridal chambers,

so when it takes up the deeds of an adulteress, it rightly receives the name that fits the deed. Both the adulterer and the adulteress take many forms. If someone prefers love of money to Christ and tries to urge others to the same conduct, he is an adulterer, and the one who is persuaded is an adulteress. Glory in this life, or other fleeting pleasures, or some other need or delight may bewitch the soul's free will and subject it to the mind of the flesh. Then such a wretched soul is an adulteress, and it owes the penalties of the adulteresses whose deeds convict it. There are many adulteresses, and slightly fewer adulterers. For many people may, through inattention, choose to do what they should not. But to incite others to the same conduct, to lead them on to lawless imitation, and to make one's own sin an example to others without blushing at all is not the work of the many. It belongs to those who have reached the extreme of hardness of heart. That is why the Apostle says, "Adulterers and adulteresses," placing the adulterers before the adulteresses, since they hold first place in wickedness. Every teacher of sin, compared with those who keep their sin to themselves, has a double charge entered against him: the sins by which he himself perished, and those by which he tried to destroy others along with himself.

Question 179. What does the Apostle's saying mean: "Submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake, as free people"? This saying is connected with what comes before, so that "Submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake, as free people" means: not because of the fear that hangs over you from the civil order. Those who submit in that way take the rank of slaves and show their submission as slaves do. They fear their masters' blows, they fear the threats of the laws, and dread drives them to submit. But the one who submits for the Lord's sake, that is, who obeys the Master's commandments, is free from all earthly fear and free from the anxiety that threatens punishment. He ennobles his soul by his longing for the Master and by keeping the commandments, and so he bears his submission to human authority willingly. There is another point. Christ, having once redeemed us with His precious blood, declared us free from the tyranny of the devil. So that no one may say, "If we have become free, how can you subject us again to worldly rulers?", [he says, "Submit as free people"; submit] [?], that is, willingly, from your own intention and by choice. Just as what is involuntary, compelled and unchosen belongs to slaves, so what is voluntary, uncompelled and self-chosen belongs to the free. So when we submit willingly, obeying the Master's laws, we strengthen our freedom all the more, and we present and show ourselves worthy of this gift. For by the very things in which we honour the Master, being led gladly by His laws,

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. …we acknowledge [?] that we have received the gift and we admire His generosity. By these things we offer reverence to the Giver without excuse. How could it fail to be salutary, besides, to keep one's station in civil life by a willing intention and to render to superiors what is due to them? Such people truly keep their souls free from all disorder and faction, and they show themselves to all as worthy of the freedom given us by God. Others hold up freedom as their slogan with a wicked intention and an evil boldness that delights in disturbances, and so they break up good order by faction. Holding up freedom as a cloak for wickedness and arrogance, they are slaves of irrational passions, slaves of tumult and uproar. They bring accusations against freedom, and so they are unworthy of it. By this exhortation the Apostle wants us to make ourselves obedient to the laws in all the transactions of life and in other civic matters, so far as they do not defile divine love and faith. He also wants us to be well disposed toward those entrusted with the authority and care of the laws, and not to despise our superiors, even if they have turned aside from the worship of the truth to its opposite. Why? One reason concerns those who have turned aside into impiety. When they see our good disposition and the nobility and docility of our character, they may at once blush before our way of life and our conduct. At the same time they may consider our refusal to obey them in matters of worship to be not the work of arrogance or the habit of a stubborn mind, but the work of a love beyond reason and of divine power and working. And at the same time, through our gentle and reasonable conduct, they might be able, if they were willing, to look up to the inexpressible beauty of our worship. Winged by love for it, they might come to abhor the demonic frenzy of idolatry and exchange it for union with and longing for the Church, the bride of Christ. This is the first reason for the apostolic admonition. If you want a second, it is this. When those who honour the religion of the Greeks persecute, banish and punish the faithful, they should have no other cause to point to for the persecution. They should not be able to bring them to trial as seditious troublemakers, but only for their piety itself, and for refusing to drag divine worship down to matter and created things. He himself showed this when he said: "So that, though they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God on the day of visitation." And again: "For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people." Does some pagan or Jew charge you with sedition? Show your peaceableness. Does he slander you as disobedient and unruly? Muzzle him by your submission. As boastful and [?]? Refute his loose tongue by your humble and gentle mind. As one who breaks up civil order? Expose the slander by never acting unreasonably in these matters. This is how a foolish man can be muzzled. This is how a servant of God is glorified. This is how he conquers the world, even if he is scourged, even if he is racked, even if he is impaled, as long as he keeps the trophy over sin [?] unviolated
with himself. Whoever lives according to these precepts keeps his deeds and words purely free, and, before these, his very…

Question 180. Questions on theology, addressed to the same person. The Divine is ineffable, just as it is incomprehensible. Nothing prior to it can be grasped, not even by bare concepts, through which reason might advance and pass on knowledge and comprehension of that blessed and inexpressible vision. Yet, though it is ineffable and incomprehensible, we can still receive certain conceptions befitting God from the things that come after it. Some illumination from there, however faint, comes down into these things and prepares our mind, through them, to gaze toward that inaccessible beauty. Those who sit wrapped in thick darkness still receive a brief and faint gleam of the sun's rays. In the same way, those clothed in flesh can be led up to some notion and conception befitting God by drawing shadowy rays from the radiance of the intelligible Sun, as if through a kind of mirror made of longing and inquiry. So the relation that the sun holds among sensible things gives, as an image, the kind of conception one might offer of the Divine among intelligible things, and

We are also led up, by denying all beings, to contemplate the essence and Godhead that transcends beings. For what is none of all things, yet greater than the whole, would be God. He brought the whole universe from nonbeing into being and exercises providence over the continued existence and harmonious motion of what He has brought forth. And even before this, the knowledge that God exists has been sown in common in all human minds. The radiance from there rouses our mind as if through reflections and enlightens it, if not to know what God is, at least not to be ignorant that He exists at all.

Consider multitude: everything that is called continuous, or is bounded as discrete. Just as it can be divided and scattered to infinity, so too it can be carried off into corruption. It has surely been kept from suffering this the moment it came into being by participation in some one, and so it enjoys permanence… [Variant readings: "The Divine is ineffable, just as it is incomprehensible." [?] "shadowy … of longing and inquiry." "Greater than the whole … we brought forth from nonbeing."]

…[?] of cohesion. It holds together by participation in the one that is one in the proper sense and beyond essence. Otherwise things divisible and scatterable [?] would belong to a nature that is wholly flowing and corruptible. Instead they hold together by participation in a one. Anyone who called this one a faint shadow of the One that is one properly and beyond essence would come close to a likeness that portrays nothing rash. Such is the one found among us. Multitude, as has been said, participates in this one. It is divisible, scatterable and fluid, yet it has not flowed away altogether in its course, just as it has not been cut [?]. In this way multitude itself, which is indefinite [?] and formless in its own nature, is bounded and given form through that one. For the tetrad and the pentad, the decad and the triacontad, are like images and projections of the one among us. They unify multitude, give it form and bound it. In the same way with what is unified: no thing unifies itself; it is unified by unity. So the unified, too, is preserved by participation in the one. Here too, however, this is not the One that is properly one and beyond essence. It is, as has been said, the one that enjoys the [illumination?] from there…

Further, among beings one can find what rules and what is ruled. And what rules, when it takes on the rank of what is ruled, is clearly not ruler in the proper sense [?], since being ruled brings it down from its rule. Is there not, then, some principle set far above all, itself without beginning, from which what rules has received the faint shadow of its likeness, and so has drawn its relation to rule and its name of rule? Look at it another way. Just as there is some last thing that is only ruled and does not rule, so one can see, conversely, that there is a supreme principle without beginning, exalted above all others. This principle would fit the Godhead and divine rule that are beyond mind and beyond every conception. Again, one can find good in the nature of beings, or rather many and various goods. For whatever enjoys no goodness at all, but has come to the extreme of wickedness, cannot subsist at all. It would at once be scattered and destroyed, if corruption and scattering belong to evil. So it is clear that the…

…some sharing more and others less in the good. And if some share more and others less in the good, there is no doubt either that those which receive a share are made good by those that shared first, or second, or in some other rank. All of them bear the grace of the good within themselves through the bounty and enjoyment of some goodness that lies above them. If this is so, there is then a goodness beyond good, from which those made good receive the gift of being made good in proportion to what they can receive. From what has been said, then, it is clear that one can hunt out a line of contemplation showing both that God exists and that he is a One beyond being, a beginning beyond beginning, and a goodness beyond good, as the fountain of goodness. Other things too can be gathered, as images, from what comes after, as was said at the outset. Through these one may gaze upon that inconceivable and inexpressible beauty of the Godhead beyond being and beyond nature, especially since it is not hard to collect such things by the method already described. For the present need, given the lack of scribes that besets us and the captivity of our books, this too is enough for you.

QUESTION 18[?]. [?] neither [?] nor further [?]

The account that dwells among things unspeakable and surpasses the knowledge we have in mirrors and riddles would belong to other bounds, kept in the inner chamber of a more God-seeing and heavenly initiation. But as for what can be seen through the curtain and taken in by ears of clay, [?] even if we cannot hunt down what is sought, tracing the later things through the first, we shall not be answerable to [?]. One of these, then, and the more sacred to state, is this: the mystical, never-silent hymn of the Cherubim, gathered through the threefold "Holy" into one lordship, sketches the threefold perfection of the Godhead. The simplicity of the names, set in plain succession with nothing introduced between them, and the unvarying sameness of the word, image no less the simplicity of the [nature] beyond being. Likewise it also teaches [?] that [none is] merely ruled and not ruling [?], [nor does] the ruling one take on the rank of the ruled;

the inseparability of the hypostases from one another, their sharing one nature, and their being unvaried in essence. Further, beginning, middle and completion belong fittingly to perfect things. Of all the numbers, three was the first to be allotted these; and so the ineffable and inconceivable Godhead, providing for our knowledge of it [?], fittingly did not disdain to show forth, from things known to us, certain symbols and traces through the theology of the Trinity. Further, again, whatever we behold in God as befitting God we find, they say, to have been summed up from the beginning into three, gathered into neither fewer nor more. And what are these? Essence, power and activity. For it is not holy to take power away from the Godhead, nor yet activity, and much less essence. Nor can these be gathered into one and the same hypostasis and given one and the same definition, whether of power and essence, or of power and activity, or of activity and essence. Yet neither is anything lacking from their sum. Since, then, there are three things into which the other names and properties befitting God are summed up and referred, it is fitting that the divine is neither confined short of the Trinity nor extended beyond it.

How the names might be referred, and which of them belong to each of the three notions spoken of in theology, is neither hard to discover nor, once discovered, hard to share with others for their benefit. For instance, "beyond being," "the good," "without form," "the one," "without quantity," and the like, would indicate the essence, some directly, others with some intermediate considered alongside. "Self-determining," "self-ruling," "Lord," "creative," "almighty," and the like, are included in the consideration of power. Creation, providence, salvation, the distribution of gifts, bestowal and the like speak in sacred terms of activity, in various and mystical expressions. And if some of the names and notions befitting God reach not into one of the three only but run through the whole Trinity, not one of these conflicts with the account of truth or with the contemplation of the theology of the Trinity; rather, it confirms all the more how secure and irreproachable they are. It also gives a starting point for further reasonings, by which the [?] is shown to unfold reasonably into a threefold compass. Likewise, if someone by another approach should show that the names

and notions befitting God are bounded within a threefold count, he would not on that account take this as cause for introducing a sixfold number — far from it, not even remotely — nor a multitude or any other plurality. On the contrary, the inviolability of the Trinity, confirmed by various demonstrations, will show still more clearly that theology cannot be moved or altered. For when the supernatural Trinity's freedom from contraction and expansion is grasped not by a single line of contemplation, but its immovability and firmness are revealed from many sides, how would this not be an irrefutable confirmation of the reason given at the outset? If the threefold summation were shown by various lines of contemplation on one subject after another, and not on the same, single Godhead, nothing would prevent the Godhead, which is not multiplied, from being multiplied along with the multitude of arguments. But if, as often as we are granted the grace to consider the same Trinity, good beyond good, we grasp this sacred number, which is beyond number, neither contracted nor overextended, how would the multitude of arguments not rather teach us, unassailably and most truly, that the theology of the Trinity is unmultiplied and cannot be taken away?
