There are, then, other things too by which the Trinity is shown, after the likeness of the reasoning already considered: such as mind, the intelligible, and intellection; then Word, and Spirit, and that from which these proceed. Then also beginning beyond beginning, first and innate beginning, and [the beginning] of those things of which, by reason of their shared nature, it has been established as beginning; from which also, among all beings, beginning proceeds, by reason of shared nature, into mastery and lordship. Then begetter, begotten, Spirit: for the fountain and cause of all that is begotten is not barren, nor is the supplier of all breath without breath. Nor is it poorer than its own creations, since it first and primarily gives life, in a manner beyond nature, yet according to its own innate property, which is beyond reason. For the nature and life of what is beyond nature and beyond being, which is before every beginning, must precede the things brought forth and given life by the principle of creation and mastery, of which all other nature and life has been established as a radiance and as imitations; since even in earthly things nature is set up and presides before art. And by necessity, again, [a nature] that is not self-ruling nor without beginning,

[being referred] to another nature, the creator of all natures and set apart from them by unutterable superiorities, [?] is made and constituted an image of generation. Many other things too could be arranged toward the same contemplation. I know that some have spoken of yet another [?] contemplation. The divine, they say, weighs the providence of all things with virtues [?] and the balance of justice. Now the instrument that people have devised for judging equal and unequal they call, in the proper sense, a balance. In it the two ends on either side hang from the beam at the middle. By its threefold [?form] the distinction of the hypostases is indicated; yet their judgment and activity are one, and in this way it images within itself a contemplation both threefold and single. God, the judge and weigher of all, did not count it an insult to be wrapped [?], through words familiar to us, in the knowledge of himself, which is beyond comprehension. Nor, if you consider [?], can one find in any other number but three the extremes joined to the middle with unvarying and uniform equality. Since, then, among numbers it sketches equality, sameness and [?] inseparability without confusion, and mirrors a sacred image of our theology, the mystagogical usage of the Church has fittingly made it its wisdom to teach, through this rather than any other number, the unfolding of the threefold monarchy. But one must also take the following as a guide [?] toward understanding that the Trinity can neither be multiplied nor tampered with. What is this? If each of the things brought from non-being into being is made of matter and form, or at any rate of an elemental dyad analogous to matter and form, then the immaterial nature beyond being, the creator of this universe, must have risen above the twofold count of created things, as earthbound and material. If this is so, it is fitting that the divine in no way endures to be completed in a twofold count. And in the theology of the Trinity, leaving matter and material things below, it does not admit the count beyond it, which would insult it, lest

it be brought down to the diffuse and unsettled, flowing away from its first compass and scattered among every human notion. God is a Trinity and not a dyad, lest, bearing within himself the cause and beginning of cutting and scattering, he should insult his single, uncut nature, the fountain of all unity. Much less is he four, for that is a double cutting, one [?cutting] the generation, the other cutting and dissolving what has been compounded from it. Nor would five have any place in our consideration, nor the numbers after it: partly because they come after the Trinity and fall below its notion of indivisibility, partly because the further they advance into composition, the more they share in scattering, cutting and flux. Fittingly, then, theology takes up the Trinity to manifest the hiddenness in the nature; and the One because nothing else so well expresses and shows the hiddenness of the Godhead, which is beyond mind, as the one, and because the divine is hymned as the fountain of all shared nature [and] unity. Further, the dyad, first and above all, bears within itself the traces of non-being. For it, before all others, is the source of dissolution, cutting and scattering, and the cause of all things' bearing within themselves the preludes of corruption. But the Trinity is the first to image the uncut and unscattered, and whatever else shares in the undivided and unscattered nature is recognized as having received it from the Trinity. Therefore the divine fittingly rejected the cause of flux, dissolution and corruption, and deigned to make known, through the Trinity that images it, its freedom from flux, scattering and dissolution. For to disdain the cause of cutting and flux and the passions of like rank is proper to the Godhead; but not to let the human mind wander into perplexity — by not disdaining the Trinity, which is the first to image all that is opposite to those passions — belongs to the love for humanity that befits God, and is a most conspicuous display of his providence toward us.

QUESTION 182. How do we say that the divine is one and three?

We speak of the divine as one and three, and our theology speaks sacredly of the one and the three as belonging to the one supernatural Godhead, not taking the one or the three properly as numbers, as with things that are by nature and properly

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE

counted. For the Godhead, the source of good beyond every beginning, is set entirely, by an ineffable measure, above every number and above the units that make up the parts of number and of every other quantity. Yet by the one it symbolically allows its hiddenness to be unfolded: what in its nature is unutterable and undeclarable [?], and — how might one put it — gathered into itself and kept in silence, beyond all mind and intellection. The three sacredly initiate us into its manifesting goodness, its procession and expansion, and reveal it, not shining forth its whole radiance, but as much as human nature can receive; through these the Creator, and the self-subsistent power and providence, shine out together and appear together in the activity that gives life to the universe and holds it together. For as its abiding in the inexpressible [?] of hiddenness, its complete immobility, is hidden away as in the chambers of silence, so too it has withdrawn from all thought, since none ascends to what is beyond mind. In the former, then, the imagination befitting God beholds abiding and rest, immovability and sameness, and, as far as human nature can receive the rays of the illumination that lie above, the unity of abiding, rest and immobility. In the latter it sees, ineffably and without any flux, in a manner befitting God, the otherness that is one in form and works divinely, and the undivided motion in unmoved hypostases. The divine, then, is one and three, but not by the reckoning of arithmetic. This, indeed, is what the great Dionysius before us, the initiate into things unspeakable, initiated by him who reveals the inexpressible, said in riddling fashion: that the cause of all that is intelligible, by its preeminence, is neither one nor unity, setting him above all that is honored among us. And it is clear that before the rest [?] of counting together; and again we see the Godhead sacredly hymned as monad and unity, because of the simplicity and unity of its supernatural indivisibility, from which, as from a unifying power, we are made one, and as our divided othernesses are folded together in a manner beyond the world,

we are joined into a God-like monad and a God-imitating union; and as Trinity — note this: for he does not speak of it as a number, but because of the manifestation in three hypostases of the fruitfulness beyond being, from which every fatherhood in heaven and on earth exists and is named. And there are many such things in that divine beholder of the unseen, worthy of Paul's initiation. That the Trinity is not among things properly counted can be seen from what has been said, and various other arguments show it too. With things properly counted, such as men, say, or angels, or countless others, we can say "a triad of angels" and "a triad of men," and also "three angels" and "three men." But of the Trinity, holy beyond holiness, beyond all mind and number, no pious person would say "a triad of gods," nor "three Gods." Again, the persons understood in the supremely holy and consubstantial Trinity clearly preserve their properties undefiled and pure as they indwell one another. The Father fills all things, the Son fills all things, and likewise the Holy Spirit. And conversely, where the Spirit is present, there too are the Father and the Son; and in those in whom the Son is present, the Father and the Spirit are present with him. But with things properly counted there is nothing of this kind, nor

Further, with things properly counted there is both addition to and subtraction from what is counted; but with the Trinity beyond being and beyond comprehension, how could this be conceived at all [?]? And one could consider many [other arguments].

QUESTION 183. On the same subject, to the same person.

The one and the three, spoken in theology of the one nature of the Godhead, are not properly number, nor the beginning of number. Rather, the one is a symbol of the hiddenness that cannot be conceived, and expresses in a riddle the ineffability of its existence. The three unfold its manifestation, and lay bare to divided beings the knowledge of the undivided and incomprehensible Godhead. For the essence that is beyond mind and all comprehension is manifested, unfolded [?] in the names of Father and Son and Spirit, just as by the one it is drawn back into what is hidden and inconceivable, not deprived even in thought of its supernatural hiddenness. And while the names stand apart from one another, the [ineffable] and indivisible conjunction of the
"as of a number," he says. That is: "For not as [?]" … of hiddenness. And while the names stand apart from one another, the ineffable and indivisible [conjunction] through them

903 PHOTIUS [?] … is spoken of through them, and the unmultiplied [?] of the unity proceeds without multiplication, united to the Trinity; and the three put forth [?] what belongs to the simplicity and conjunction of the one [?] and incommunicable [?], truly God; for there is nothing like this among creatures. But if he were only one, or only three, the divine would be pressed to have countless sharers, and [creation?] would show the Creator joined to its own [members].

QUESTION 184. If God and the Godhead are in all beings and pass through all, what wonder is it if he is also among men as a man?

That he is in all things we know, among other things, from the account of creation. That he is among men we know from his assuming the creature out of love for humanity, and from participation and communion in the birth which he himself established, [the creature] enjoying a second honor after the first: the creating hand bestowed the one, and he himself, coming forth, bestowed the other. Just as, because he brought beings from non-being into existence, we call him Creator, even though his procession is far greater than creation; so too, because he benefited men with a providence set apart from all others, even though the birth from the Virgin, that inexpressible birth, is greater than human birth, we say that he who is before every beginning was born, and that the fashioner of nature was called a man. We do not make a man into God (far from it! for that is truly impossible and cannot withstand the judgment of reason); rather, we confess that God came forth as a man. This is both easier for God, who fashioned nature, and proclaims an abundant [display] of love for humanity.

QUESTION 185. How is it possible at all to conceive of the divine as incarnate?

I do not think anyone is so empty of God or of divine illumination as not [to have grasped] that
(61) [?] And participation and communion in the birth which he himself established, [the creature] enjoying a second honor after the first. That is:
[?] Just as, because he brought beings from non-being into existence, we call him Creator, even though his procession is far greater than creation. That is:

the divine is present everywhere without being divided, and fills all things; this he has grasped by an innate and common perception. And if God is present to all beings, and his supernatural nature is in no way altered along with his creations by his presence among them when they are altered, nor diminished along with the deficiencies by which, in their descending order, one falls short of another, nor insulted by the stains that spring up in creatures, but, set above them in the inexpressible and inconceivable preeminence of his blessedness and impassibility, he is somehow present to beings, and holds them together and governs them — how could it be impossible, or bring any insult, for him to be present to the human lump and to display his ineffable love for humanity and his providence through the incarnation? Rather, how is it not good? How is it not fitting? But the argument,

someone might perhaps object, proposes that we think not only that the divine became man, but also that it entered the nature of all other creatures and took it on into its own being. Though I welcome the nimbleness of your mind, noble sir, I do not welcome the rest of your approach, because you did not quickly recognize or notice that you are violently denying the thesis you began with. For he who contends that it is impossible for God to become flesh and take on human form appears, through his second difficulty, to concede it so far that he declares God did not take on the nature of any of the other creatures either; and he who sees impossibility in one case has voted for possibility in all of them together. So it will be found, even by you who argue about impossibilities, that it is possible for God to become flesh.

QUESTION 186. Why did God become incarnate?

Since it belongs to very few, through mind and contemplation, to [ascend] to

he declares God did not take on the nature of any of the other creatures either; and he who sees impossibility in one case has voted for possibility in all of them together; so that, not even by you who argue about impossibilities, will it be found that it is possible for God to become flesh. That is:

[?] …to rise to a conception of the Divine that is worthy of God. This is clear from the fact that even those who are thought to have reached the summit of human wisdom disagreed very widely both with themselves and with one another. For this reason God became man. He did so in order that not only those thought to have somewhat more knowledge than others, but also the great mass of humanity, who are led by the senses rather than by reasoning, might be able to make their way back, through what they see and hear, to a pious and saving understanding of the Divine. They would rise through the things of the senses to the things of the mind, and from the divine works performed through the medium of the flesh to the contemplation of the supernatural and incorporeal Godhead. This is clear from what has actually happened. Ever since God became man, and accomplished his marvellous and supernatural works while bearing our form, humanity has cast off its strange and endlessly wandering fantasies. It has bidden a long farewell to long-winded nonsense and to the fabrications of idols. It confesses and worships the God who appeared in the flesh as the true God. It was granted to learn this Godhead by sight and hearing through his presence in the body and through his works that surpass reason, and through such knowledge it was led up to the recognition and contemplation of the immortal nature. That is one reason. The second is that the strong man would never have been bound unless one mightier had undertaken this contest and this struggle. Third, teaching that is set before our sight and hearing is more compelling and more precise than teaching announced from afar and through other intermediaries. And, if you like, there is a further reason: for many people the practice of the virtues by imitation is easier and can readily be carried out, compared with a practice that is demanded without any example. But no imitation that lifts up human life would be possible for human beings unless someone practised it in a human way. And how could there be such a human practice if the Word had not become man? It was therefore out of love for humanity and unsurpassable providence that the Word became incarnate and that he lived his deifying life and conduct among us. Why was it the Son, and not another hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, who took on our nature and became flesh?

Why, when the Trinity is proclaimed to be of one nature and equal in honour, is the Father said [?] to create through the Son and the Spirit, but not the reverse? 1. Some say that certain people are brought into perplexity on this point. The all-holy Trinity has been allotted the same nature and equal honour, and divine Scripture above all makes this plain. Why, then, does that same Scripture glorify and proclaim the Son as Creator more than the Father? For even if the Father is also found to be called Creator, the Son is called so more often. Again, how is it that the Father is said to create through the Son, but not conversely? The Son is not said to create through the Father, and the Spirit is not said to create either through the Father or through the Son. Or is it possible to understand that they act through the Father? This is a paradox to hear, but not a paradox to understand. For even if the Son and the Spirit do not create through him, they nevertheless act in other works by sending him. So is the paradox not without discredit? And who is it who leads us to this belief? No other than the Father himself, who is sent. For he uses the prophetic voice of Isaiah and says: "Hear me, Jacob, and Israel whom I call: I am God, the first, and I am also hereafter, and besides me there is no God. With my hand I laid the foundation of the earth, and my Spirit made firm the heaven." See how, when he creates, he creates through the Son and the Spirit. "I gave command to all the stars." The God of all said these things through the prophet, and through these words he made himself manifest: the one who says them is the Father himself. For his right hand is the Son, and his Spirit is the Holy Spirit. 2. O hidden words! Or rather, O meaning that is not evident, but easy to grasp once it is made evident! He goes on: "And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." So the Spirit, like the Son [?], though itself sent forth by the Father, now sends the Father. For he said, "And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." From this it is clear, even to those who are not especially sharp-sighted, that being sent does not lower the Son to an inferior nature and honour, nor the Spirit either, since even the Father himself is said to be sent by each of them. The Father sends the Spirit, and the Son sends the Spirit too. The Spirit also sends the Son: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me." And it sends the Father as well. So the Spirit is not diminished by being sent. Not only does it send, but it also anoints the Son. How then could being sent lower [?] the Spirit? Not only

…to speak from himself. At that time he also made the sending of the Spirit his own: when he himself was being sent, he also took on the role of sending. Do you see that all these words belong to the economy of salvation and not to sovereign origin? Understand what belongs to the economy, and distinguish what belongs to the authority of origin. Being sent does not undo consubstantiality, and sameness of nature is not turned into otherness. When the Son came forth from the Father and arrived, then he also sends the Spirit. There is no separation in the coming forth and no division in the sending: he came forth while remaining, and he sent while keeping the Spirit with himself. The Spirit raises Christ, not as though the Godhead in him were powerless, but so that you may understand that the activity of the Spirit is not foreign to the Godhead in the Son. Further, the Spirit sends the Father, but not often. It does send him, so that, contrary to the babbling of the heretics, the Spirit may not fall away at all from the same equality of honour and Godhead. But it does not do so often, so that the causal principle in the Trinity may not be thought common to all three. For this reason the Father is often said to act through the Spirit, and likewise through the Son. This is said often, so that being the cause may be confirmed as belonging to the Father. But the Spirit is not often said to act through the Father, nor the Son either. Otherwise, if the Spirit and the Son were often said to act through the Father, the ill-scheming and many-shaped madness of the heretics might force the hypostasis or the glory of the Father down into a lower rank, or, what is more readily done, strip away his honour as cause. The Father sends both the Spirit and the Son; the Son, too, sends both the Father and the Spirit. Here you see the equal honour of the nature. But it is the Father who sends often: here you see what is distinctive of the cause. So within the unvarying identity of the essence the Father's property shines forth, and it allows the sameness of nature and equal honour of those who have proceeded from him to shine forth along with it. 4. Now it is said not only that creation came into being out of nothing through the Son, but also that he is proclaimed the lawgiver of the Old Testament. For divine Providence long ago was muzzling the madness of those who dare to trace the Old and the New back to two opposing principles, and tearing it up by the roots. The Church clearly confesses that the Son delivered the ancient oracles and that the same Son

became the author of the New, and that before these he gave being to the nature of created things out of nothing. Even so, the Christ-hating and God-fighting race of the Manichaeans and the Marcionites do not shudder to trace the gospel proclamation back to one principle, and the Mosaic writings to another principle opposed to it. What mass of blasphemy would they have stopped short of, then, if the Father had been proclaimed exclusively as the lawgiver of the Old Scriptures, and the Son exclusively as the lawgiver of grace? But these matters belong rather to another occasion and another subject. We must return to the original difficulty: how the Father creates through the Son, while the Son does not in turn create through the Father. The solution already given clearly resolved part of the difficulty, but it rather sharpened the rest. Still, it is better not only to rely on reasonable reflections, but also to make them secure by using the Oracles of Scripture and their teaching. For when our arguments are supported by the oracles of the all-holy Spirit, the more force they gain, the more they are raised to prevail over criticism.

QUESTION 189. Why do we confess the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, but do not agree that a Father or a Son is ascribed to the Spirit? The Godhead of the divine-principled hypostases is beyond all principle and beyond God. For the most part it is wrapped in incomprehensibility, and likewise in ineffability. This is so not only in the contemplation of its nature, but also in the inconceivable hiddenness of its properties, which is seated above all. Still more has it withdrawn from the minds of earth-born beings who try to give reasons for it. Yet out of love for humanity the radiance from on high flashes its rays upon us as through a mirror, and we are illuminated with knowledge in proportion to our sincere longing and the clarity of our faith. For what is altogether beyond contemplation is also beyond love. It cannot cast down even a spark of desire, or kindle that desire into flame, and it offers nothing suited to drawing us towards itself. But such knowledge is a rare thing. It belongs to the inspiration that comes down from above and supplies a loftier learning, and it requires a purified mind, withdrawn from the opinions of the many. Since, however, the weakness of our nature does not allow us to behold what proceeds from above, God's benevolent goodness has deigned to grant us the grace of being led up, from the things familiar to us in our own world, to a contemplation of that nature which lies beyond conception. Through these things it leads us by the hand and raises us to a conception of Father, Son and Spirit that is worthy of God. Through analogy it beguiles and fills to the point of knowledge our divine love, which is cramped by complete ignorance. For this reason we do not hesitate to call the all-holy Spirit the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. For even in the things of our own world we see that both a father and a son have a spirit, and we know how to acknowledge it.

But we neither allow it to be said, nor accept it in our reasoning, that a spirit has a son or a father. So, being led up from the analogy of what is acknowledged in our own world to the sacred discourse, beyond us, about the superessential and beyond-divine divine-principled hypostases, we are rightly taught to say "Spirit of the Father and of the Son"; but we do not consent to learn that the Spirit has a Father or a Son.

QUESTION 190. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are consubstantial and of equal rank in power, will and lordship. Why, then, does the Father hold the first place when they are enumerated together? 1. Someone else, perhaps, who is carried along by more theological thoughts, and who through perfection in the virtues has made himself better fitted to receive the rays of the radiance from above, may display an understanding raised to a loftier contemplation. He will give an account of these questions, to which it is not easy to ascend for those who have not been freed from earthly ways of living. As for me, I am conscious of nothing loftier in myself, and I have not yet moved my thoughts away from the conduct of this earthly sojourn. Yet whatever has accrued to me from the study of the Oracles and from exercise in them, with providence from above assisting us, I will not neglect to set out with equal eagerness for the common benefit of all who share a common piety and zeal for it. Father, Son and Spirit are of one nature, and one can see in them an unvarying identity of will, power and kingship. The same holds for the other divine and supernatural names by which the Thearchy, beyond principle and beyond God, is named. Nevertheless, the Father is the cause of those who are from him: of the one by generation, of the other by procession. Both are referred back to him as to the principle of a connatural bringing forth that has no beginning apart from him. This explanation reasonably shows why the Father is ranked before those who are from him, but not also why the Son is ranked before the Spirit. The account would appear to proceed by a more general method if it arranges the enumeration of the all-holy Trinity according to the order in which they became known [?]. For the Father first came to human knowledge, then the Son, and through the Son the Holy Spirit. It is true that knowledge of each was revealed to human beings by the divine hypostases through one another. The Father pointed out the Son from heaven, and the Spirit bore joint witness by its descent. The Son in turn glorified the Father and spoke of him as God more plainly, and he also sent the Spirit to the disciples. Moreover, the Spirit calls the Son Lord: "For no one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit."

2. So the manifestation and comprehension of each of them comes through the others. Through these too we have a clear path for leading the mind up to the unvarying sameness of their common nature. And those who have been granted to know one of the blessed and creating hypostases purely and sincerely also retain the knowledge of the others along with it. For whoever knows the Father knows the Son as well. Whoever has come to know the Son, with the perfection of knowledge possible among human beings, is not deprived of a like knowledge of the Father. The same is true of the Spirit, which searches the depths of God and reveals to human beings the hidden and more perfect teachings. Whoever has received pure instruction from the Spirit is not estranged from the divine wisdom that speaks of the Father as God, nor from the wisdom that initiates us together into the Son. Nevertheless, although these things are interwoven and unfolded in a harmonious connection, it is plain that the word "Father" became known to human beings earlier in time, and was familiar to their ears more than the word that designates the Son. The word "Spirit" was taught by the history of Moses even more than the name of the Son. Still, unlike the title "Son", it could not bring with it the sense of self-subsistence, since its meaning tips both ways. For the word can equally be applied to things that subsist in themselves and to things that fill the role of a part of a hypostasis. So far did the name "Spirit" fall short of conveying a teaching about the Spirit worthy of God that no small portion of humanity, having grown old in the laws of Moses, could in no way bring itself to confess the hypostasis of the all-holy Spirit, just as it could not confess the nature of the angels either. Thus the readiness with which the Mosaic writings speak of the Spirit by name became useless even to the Jews themselves. As a result, on this very point not only is the Son ranked before the Spirit, but also whatever can be gathered under the name of the Son and referred to it finds grounds for a higher rank, though not a higher nature. For none of the Jews disputed them: the Word, I mean, and the right hand, and the power, and the like. None of them was seen to deny these, or shamelessly refused to admit that they are rightly said of the Father, even if not all agree [?] that what these terms put forward and sum up is the person of the Son. In this way, then, it is with good reason that the Son, and not the Spirit, holds the second place in the enumeration. 3. Moreover, the pure teaching about the Spirit came forth after grace had expressly proclaimed the Son as God. For when, by the descent of fiery

tongues from heaven, the Spirit created voices in many languages for the apostles, and made unlettered men into improvised orators for every nation, then, then above all, the human race came to be raised to a more exact knowledge of the Spirit's Godhead. The word "Father" was known to human beings first; grace proclaimed the Son as God; and after these the dignity of the Godhead of the all-holy Spirit was revealed through its divine activity in the apostles. It is therefore fitting that they keep the same order in the enumeration as well. The knowledge was arranged to come forth in this way so that people devoted to the error of idols, on hearing plainly and all at once of a Trinity of persons, would not become hard to draw away and hard to lead up from their slide into idolatry. Even when the Trinity was taught gradually in this way, and at first through riddles and veils, humanity barely moved away from polytheism. If it had been proclaimed openly and all at once, how would their superstition not have despised and rejected all teaching and exhortation that led them by the hand to the one sovereign principle? Would it not have preferred the ruin that gripped it to the salvation being preached? So it was fitting that knowledge of the Father was revealed first, and then, step by step, knowledge of the Son and of the Spirit. From there the sacred and God-befitting character of our initiation, which follows the order of knowledge, consequently drew along with it the same privilege in the enumeration. 4. Besides, to call God our Father is neither offensive nor grievous to the ear. It comes readily to hand and is not ashamed of its boldness. But to declare the Son or the all-holy Spirit our son is not tolerable even in thought: such an expression brings absurdity along with impiety. So the human mind finds no difficulty in accepting the name of Father, both from customary usage and from its innate grasp of it. Knowledge of the Father came first, and so it set out the teaching of the sacred Oracles advancing in due sequence. Starting from familiarity with the word, it made provision for the learning of supernatural things to enter us without difficulty. And, if you like, consider it again [?]: neither innate reason nor customary usage would ever have the Son come before the Father [?], nor the Spirit either. It always knows the reverse, and it does not shrink from teaching those who are persuaded. Hence the enumeration, too, received the teaching that puts the Father before the Son and the Spirit, and did no violence to it. For this reason, then, the Son is called the right hand, the word, the power and the wisdom of the Father, and the like. But the Father, although his nature does not differ from the Son's, would never come to be regarded or spoken of as any of these things of the Son. For he is not referred to the Son as to his principle and cause, and he does not take as his own the things that the Son makes his own by being referred to the Father. Hence, when we speak of the Father as God, we say that he does through the Son, or also through the Spirit, whatever the blessed and beyond-divine nature

is wont to effect. But we do not accept saying the reverse, for we are not initiated into teaching that either the Son or the Spirit acts through the Father. 5. Apart from what has been said, not only to the Jews but also to all whose worship is the error of idols, it is sweet and pleasing to call God their Father. To pass over the license of the poets, one can hear Ariston's son, together with many others among the Greeks who took up the same pursuit of philosophy, hymning God as the Father and Maker of this universe. He taught that it is a labour to find him, and that once one has found him it is impossible to declare him to everyone. For the Jews too the word was ready to hand and sweet, and a ground for self-importance. That is why they raised their eyebrows when they ought to have blushed and checked their arrogance, and said, as though exulting in the word, "We have one Father, God." Do you see how sweet and charming it is to human nature to call God its Father? But concerning the Son or the Spirit, what such word could anyone find to use, or say without blushing? For this reason, then, at the beginning it was not as easy to proclaim the Son as it was to proclaim the Father. Instead, the teaching about him was handed on to those who were not unworthy through other expressions of equal force: arm, I mean, and right hand, and wisdom, and other terms that suggest a similar meaning. But the title "Son" was kept hidden within the bounds of silence. Why? Because the word "Son" in itself immediately brings with it a distinction of person, and this trips up the weaker, or those keen on contention, and sends them towards polytheism. But "right hand" and similar terms almost balance the scales. They hint at a distinction of hypostases and also draw them together into one and the same. So they no longer gave those who gaped after idolatry an occasion for the same harm.

Moreover, the word "Spirit" can be applied both to what subsists in itself and to what exists in something else. So, unlike the name of the Son, it does not compel those who are unwilling to accept him as a complete hypostasis in himself, and it does not bring them over to assent. It still requires argument and confirming judgement drawn from reasoning. For this reason, even though at the beginning the Spirit was proclaimed less clearly than the Father but more than the Son, the order of proclamation does not give it the same position in the enumeration. For when the Father and the Son are proclaimed, they introduce self-subsistence unambiguously. The word "Spirit" can equally indicate self-subsistence, but it cannot equally be applied to a hypostasis alone, and so it does not retain the dignity of being ranked first. Further, if the Spirit was sent to the disciples through the Son, the sending in no way diminishing the nature but preserving its unvarying identity, the order in the enumeration

[?] …the [?] of the properties that belong to each hypostasis could at once distinguish and proclaim what is unchangeable and unconfused. And this is also because we have learned the theology of the Spirit above all from the Son. He taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and has been raised to the same rank as the Father and the Son, and that the Spirit is called the teacher of the things that are more perfect. Human weakness could not yet receive the more perfect things, so the Saviour did not initiate his disciples into them, but promised that the Paraclete would become their teacher in those things. So we see that the Son, when he came to dwell among us, led the way into this pure theology of the Spirit, to which human nature could not raise itself. 7. The knowledge of the Father came first, and both the Son and the Spirit have their procession from him. They can be said to have come forth from him, but he cannot be said to have come forth from them. Among human beings the name of the one is customary and familiar, and they apply it to themselves, but no one can conceive of the others in that way. The one name is sweet and pleasing for a creature to bear, but the others admit no such approach. For these reasons and for the others already given, the Church has received this order of enumeration for them, though they are consubstantial and of one nature, and preserves it as a general rule. So far, however, this is only an elementary account of the enumeration of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. A more complete and precise examination requires and awaits a treatment of its own. QUESTION [?]. Why the restoration of the race came about not through any of the bodiless powers, nor through a mere man, but through the self-emptying of the Word [?].

1. I know that some studious people ask why the correction of the common fall did not come about through one of the human race. After all, someone of the same nature is more persuasive and better able to win conviction. But it is not hard for them to see now, even if they did not before, that this advantage too is included in the incarnation of the Word. The riches that belong to that marvellous self-emptying, however, could not be found anywhere if one of the human race had undertaken to free humankind from the tyranny that held everyone. First, the one who undertook such a great deed, accepting the task of working the salvation of all by the riches of his wisdom and his unsurpassable love for humanity, ought not himself to be one of those who need salvation and restoration from someone else. Yet every human nature is liable to sin and needs a great deal of the same providence and cleansing. How could one who stands in the same
need of healing administer cleansing to others and be the provider of [?]

2. Second, how could a man accomplish a work of God, a divine work, something new under the sun? Suppose someone were to make the ambitious attempt, though it could not succeed [?]. The fall would then quickly and easily either return to itself or grow worse. It would return, because those who had enjoyed the benefit would not think it a great evil to drag down, out of ingratitude, a man subject to the same passions as themselves. It would grow worse, because they would rush to attach to their saviour the honour that belongs to God. Consider Moses. The people often grumbled against him and treated the salvation from the evils of Egypt, which came down from above through him, as worse than those evils. Even so, they planned to proclaim him a god after his death, as mystical and sacred writings teach. That is why his tomb has remained hidden [?] and unrecognized by the eyes of the Jews to this day, for the enemy is quick to turn to mischief and to deceive humankind with weapons on the right hand and on the left. If they did this to Moses, how would they not have proclaimed as God the one who freed them from a greater tyranny, even if they knew he was of their own nature? I pass over for now how Paul was made a god by the Greeks [?]. Clearly this would not have been a raising up from the fall but a worse and irreparable falling away. Perhaps it would not even have seemed unreasonable: just as created things owe their Creator reverence and worship as God, so too the saved would owe it to the one who saved them, and those who were refashioned [?] to the one who refashioned them. That is why not even the angelic nature takes on the salvation of our race. Instead, the very one who formed us is seen as Creator and also of the

3. Besides, it does not belong to slaves or creatures to annul the commands of a king and lord, and in the same way it does not belong to them to raise those commands to something better. Yet when Christ became man, along with his other good gifts, or rather before many of his other benefits, he reshaped toward greater perfection the ancestral laws that had been better suited to the Israelites of that time. "It was said to those of old," he says, "'You shall not murder,' but I say to you this. 'You shall not commit adultery,' but I say this. 'An eye for an eye,' but I say this." And the countless other laws that had been given long ago to suit the imperfection of their hearers can be seen raised to something better by the Lord's judgment. He did this for countless other reasons, and also because, if the old laws had remained wholly unchanged, the same way of life would necessarily have been preserved along with them. That way of life did not shine with anything supernatural or [?] higher, nor was it rich in the power to receive such things. Countless lawgivers and prophets and many other sacred teachings had trained it before, and yet the undertaking would never have reached its end

[?] but it would have proved vain. If human life had remained as it was, the effort and undertaking for salvation that went forward would have been exposed as futile. Human ambition achieves nothing great: it is impossible for the servile creation to try to rearrange the laws of the Creator and Lord, and it cannot do so without incurring the charge of presumption. But for the one who works the salvation of his creature out of the depths of his mercy, rearranging the Lord's laws is fitting, since he has the Lord's authority by nature, and renewing the way of life for the better is easy and appropriate for him. 4. Moreover, we have known the proof of such great love through the self-emptying, for our sake, of the one who cannot be emptied. How would that proof have come to our knowledge, and how would we have recognized the greatness of his providence for us, if he had thought it right for us to receive the common salvation of the race through someone else? Nor does it belong to the angelic nature to work this great and universal mystery. The angels have each been allotted oversight according to the boundaries of the nations, but they were not entrusted with governing the whole race, much less with refashioning it. Still less does it belong to a mere man, even if he surpasses others in virtue. We often see the most illustrious of them entrusted with training and governing a single nation, and not even the greatest nation, and yet failing to carry out even this task blamelessly to the end. Consider Moses, if you like, and Joshua after him, and all the others who were entrusted with leading the nation. Besides this, the greatest of all the marvels of the ages, the truly surpassing marvel, would have sunk into something cheap, a deed that offered no wonder at all. When one creature unites with another and takes on its fellow servant, nothing ineffable follows, and there is no wonder to strike us with amazement at the incomprehensible and at the riches of his love for humanity. What would be wonderful or beyond comprehension in an angel taking human nature as its own? Both are creatures and fellow servants, and both are subject to change. Even if one has been honoured more and the other less, each is still changeable. Once the union had taken place, no one could tell whether the lesser, by sharing in the stronger tendency to change, would be swayed by it, or whether the lesser would prevail over the greater. 5. But I almost passed over the main reason. If an angel or a mere man had been put forward to rescue us from the fall, we would not have enjoyed salvation. Instead, the race would have fallen away from the finest and most precious thing, the ineffable glory. How so, and why? Because we could not have come even close to the things we now delight in since the Word

became flesh, enjoying things beyond all thought. If a human or angelic nature had undertaken the saving plan for us, where or how would our race have been granted the following? To be seated at the right hand of God the Father, to be raised above every choir of angels and archangels, and to enjoy honour and glory so great that even the powers above, who stand nearest to God, long to look into the glory we enjoy through our shared nature, and find that obtaining it is greater than their desire. Suppose the human race had been deprived of this blessed, ineffable and inconceivable portion. Our nature would not have come to enjoy the glory that now shines out, since it would have been united only with a human or angelic nature, and we would not have risen to such strength and power and such exceptional honour. In that case, what daring against us would the enemy have held back? What schemes would he not have set in motion, nursing once more the hope of taking the race into his power and dragging it back under his ancient tyranny? Against whom would he not have risen up to seize power again? Would he not have shown an arrogance greater than before? Would he not have thought himself bold enough to meddle with heaven itself? For these and many similar reasons, then, the Word of God, who is Son and true God, and no one else besides him, took on our flesh with divine wisdom and in a way befitting God, and accomplished the common salvation of the race. QUESTION [?]. Why will the Son alone sit as judge in the age to come? Creation [?] and every act that one of the divine hypostases is said to perform is also a common work of the others, since they share the same providence, the same unvarying authority and goodness, and the same single will. Yet the dignity of the coming judgment is assigned to the Son for many reasons befitting God. This is not because the Father or the Spirit stands apart from the work. Rather, the Son has taken up the judgment and holds the leadership in it. First, he himself is called the Creator and steward both of the created things that came into existence out of nothing at the beginning, and of the renewal and refashioning of the human race after it was shattered. So it was fitting that the one who undertook both the creation and the providential care of human nature, in each of its formations, should also be appointed its judge. Providence is bound up and interwoven with creation, and judgment and examination of those cared for are bound up with providence. Since creating and renewing have been his work, it is reasonable and just that the judgment of his creature should also be referred to him. Second, it belongs above all to a lawgiver to judge those to whom he graciously gave laws to live by

(and these are the human race). The Son is above all the lawgiver of the New Covenant, though there is no division in the communion of the Father's will and cooperation or of the all-holy Spirit. So it is fitting that the Son is appointed judge of those to whom the laws were given. Further, because he took on our human nature, he came to know human nature by experience and acquired a twofold knowledge of those who are to be judged. The divine Paul says this somewhere as he sings the praises of his mercy toward us and his atonement for us: "Because he himself suffered when he was tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted." Nor would this be far from a pious [?] reflection. Perhaps it is also not unreasonable to consider this. The Son humbled himself in an unspeakable and indescribable humiliation, sharing flesh and blood just as we do. For that reason the judgment of all is entrusted to him, raising him up from that great humiliation and splendidly proclaiming his dignity as God. Finally, and not least of these reasons: in the universal resurrection it is not bare souls but souls united to their own bodies that share in the resurrection. In this state they stand before the judgment seat, and in this composite condition they undergo their sentence. So it was altogether necessary for their judge also to preside in that same form. Then those being judged would be able to see the one judging them, the judgment would be conducted in words they know, and the knowledge of the verdicts would come through their ears and minds with the greatest clarity. And we all know that our form suits none of the supernatural hypostases except the Son. In theology, to confess three essences is polytheism, and therefore atheism, while to speak of one hypostasis is Jewish and Sabellian. In the same way, in the doctrine of the incarnation, to believe in one nature and one hypostasis is Manichaean and [?], while to speak of two natures and two hypostases belongs to the Paulianists and is hostile to Christ. What, then, should one do? One should follow the middle and ecclesiastical teaching. It turns away from the blasphemy on both sides and wisely [?] confesses and teaches one hypostasis in Christ but two natures.

…prepared bread of pain and destruction for himself and for those who believed him. But the choir of the orthodox have taken Peter, the chief of the apostles, as their teacher, or rather Peter's Lord and Maker, who is ours too ("Do not call anyone on earth Rabbi," he says, "for you have one teacher, the Christ"). They clearly confess that the two natures, divinity and humanity, are unconfused in the one hypostasis of the Word. The Truth himself taught this. He called himself Son of Man, and Peter, the chief of the apostles, called him Son of the living God. The first he confirmed by his own words, the second by accepting it. And so, as a reward for his right confession, he entrusted Peter with the keys of the kingdom. He also made firm that the Church is founded on Peter's confession and wins a splendid victory over the gates of Hades and over all the reckless talk of heretics.

QUESTION [?]. If one nature were recognized in Christ, one will would also spring from it. But since there are two natures, two wills must also spring from them. And since no nature is without activity, each nature will certainly bring forth its own activity as well. And just as the human nature followed the divine nature of the Word and was subject to it, so clearly the human will was subject to the divine will, and the one activity to the other. QUESTION [?]. On images. The Greeks will not tolerate images of Christ our God, because they do not regard him as divine. The Jews, sick with an even greater madness against him, cannot bear even to hear of the practice. Others, an evil and accursed lot, tell the fable that his body was laid up in the sun. Others dissolve it into the elements from which they claim it was composed. Still others, starting from [?], insist that he did not take on our body at all. For all these it necessarily follows that Christ should not be depicted either. So let the offspring of that much-erring and adulterous seed, I mean the new brood of Iconoclasts, consider whom they claim as their fathers, and which party they choose to be named devotees and disciples of among Christians. QUESTION [?]. On images. Simon Magus and Carpocrates were baptized. For this

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. reason they carried around an image of Christ, but they did not give up their magical trickery and their passions. For that reason they carried around images of certain other people as well. Let the champions of the Iconoclasts be ashamed, then, for they are shown to be more senseless than even those most superstitious men, who went astray in both belief and life. You ask why we have attached shame to the heretics? If I did not expect it to upset you, I would have shown that the question is a foolish one. This much I will say: I will show you, if you like, that they cling to senselessness as well as impiety. The very arguments by which they tried to slander orthodoxy are the ones that most clearly testify to how ancient the making of images is. They did not notice that they were admitting, against their will, that it is as old as Christianity and baptism. And by claiming that even the baptized followers of Simon did not insult images, they forgot that they were showing themselves to surpass [?] those men in want of judgment. QUESTION [?]. On sayings that seem to conflict. "Sell your possessions and give to the poor." You think this command heavy and hard to bear. But I ask you to see in it rather that the yoke of the Lord is truly kind and his burden light. He commands us to lay down a load and shake off the stuff of cares and temptations, not to take it up. He has allowed us to give these things to those in need and in return to be rich in heavenly treasure. Even if we do not give them away, they lie idle and useless for this present life, and when we pass over to the next they are left behind here. So consider instead the Lord's love for humanity and the varied and many-sided working of his ineffable Providence. Things that must happen in any case, even against our will, he accepts as our own labours and fruits once we add our intention to them. Those who contribute nothing but their free choice he receives into the inheritance of his kingdom as though they had achieved everything: "Come," he says, "you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." The sun is not opposed to the stars, nor day to night, nor the sun's rays to the gleam of fire. Neither is mature manhood opposed to youth. Or, if you like, the astringent that prepares the material for purple dye is not opposed to the bloom of the purple [?]. Nor are the mixing of colours and the shaping of a picture opposed to the lines sketched beforehand

and the outlines of the shading. What is the point of setting side by side things that seem opposed? The comparison itself overturns the appearance of opposition [?]. Nor, to answer your own difficulty, is grace opposed to the law. Instead, the law is the guide and herald of grace, in harmony with it and preparing for it, its way and its equipment, and everything else besides. Grace is the completion, and everything that belongs to the completion came before it. The law was shown to be the servant of grace. It guided, announced beforehand and prepared. It became a way and a type, outlining and pointing to the truth within itself. It lacked nothing that a preparation needs. But grace came, and the law fittingly ceased, for it is the nature of what is preliminary to step aside and give way to completion. And so that the people devoted to the law might recognize the God of grace as also the Lord of the law ("Be still," he says, "and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth"), grace came and the law withdrew. It withdrew as the stars do when the sun shines, as night does when day dawns, as flames of fire are dimmed by sunlight under a clear sky at high noon, as infancy comes to an end when one grows to manhood, as the astringent's quality yields when the purple dye prevails, as the lines and preliminary sketches do when the picture is completed. In each pair just named, the one went first as imperfect, and the other came after as perfect. The later is not hostile to the earlier, for there is much harmony and kinship between them, but neither does the earlier remain once the perfect has come. This is the law of nature: once completion is achieved, whatever was taken up to prepare and complete it falls idle. So the law has been set aside now that grace has come, but it has not been destroyed. It has ceased, but it has not been discredited. Christ fulfilled it without removing a single stroke from it, and he made it disappear entirely by bringing it to completion, for there is no need of the tutor when the teacher himself is present. To destroy the law and convict it as blameworthy would be to overturn it from its foundations, paying no regard to any of its ordinances. But to make it cease and fall idle, with fitting praise, is only to carry out what it commanded, then to bring in grace and let the perfect conceal the imperfect. And the one who destroys the law is not the one who does not transgress its precepts but the one who does. Nor does the one who knows that those precepts must cease and fall idle transgress them. The transgressor is the one who does not even know this, although the precepts themselves proclaim in many places that they will fall idle. And it is not the one who, after they have ceased,

[?] knowing them to be useless after grace, but not rejecting them as profane before grace, in the very time when they were in force. The law, then, is holy and just and good. It was truly the herald of one who is good and more than holy, who fulfilled all righteousness in a way beyond nature. But now it is useless; it stands idle and has ceased. For when the Lord has come, what belongs to the guardian [?] must fall silent. No one runs to medicines once he is in full health. No one who enjoys solid food concerns himself with the wet-nurse. No one who is an orator goes around looking for teachers of syllables. Nor would anyone raised to the rank of general long for the lot of the common soldier. Nor would anyone who has received the heavens prefer the goods of the earth, just as no one who has put on kingship would trade it for a private man's tunic and the rank of a subject in place of the rank that rules and commands. I think you now have enough, and more than enough for the space of a letter: ample solutions to a difficulty that is tossed up and down and has often caused great perplexity. By them the Jews, the Greeks and the arguments of Marcion will be thrown into confusion, though they have often thought that with such an array they were rising up against the Church. For Christ fulfilled the law but did not destroy it. He brought it to an end but did not overturn it. He is its goal, not its abolition. He made it idle but did not slander it. Grace and the law are in harmony, not at war. If someone should also say that the Lord dissolved the law in the letter but fulfilled the law in the spirit, he will say nothing unreasonable. But to say that he dissolved the law of the Deuterosis and fulfilled that of the first legislation is the talk of those who [?talk nonsense].

Question 200. Since the Lord says, "Do not cast [your pearls] before swine," and so on, how should one teach unbelievers?

The holy things and the pearls are both the word of the divine preaching and the undefiled body of the Master. They are pearls because they are precious, and because they send out the bright radiance of salvation to those who approach sincerely. They are holy because they are venerable, and because they separate people from error and dedicate them to the truth. The dogs are those heretics and unbelievers who, though often instructed in the word of godliness, not only became no better disposed but displayed their fury against our sacred religion more madly than barking dogs. The swine are those who wallow in the mire of the passions and remain insensible and unmoved by exhortation. To all of these, the divine oracle declares, the divine mysteries must not be set forth, since by what they have done they have made themselves unworthy

of the supernatural salvation and grace. But if they are not to be given to these others either, perhaps someone may wonder: to whom, then, should they be given at all? I say: to the faithful and orthodox, and to those whose life is in harmony with their faith. But among the unbelievers, and indeed the heretics, and also those who are at odds with purity of life and slip away from it, we must instruct by word, and eagerly lead by the hand, those who are like sheep without a shepherd and are in great need of pastoral oversight and instruction. For on these the Lord has compassion, and he feeds them with food that both sustains the body and improves and strengthens the soul. Very well. But how do the swine and the dogs turn and tear those who set before them what is not permitted? Clearly the dogs do it by mocking, laughing at and ridiculing what is beyond all praise, and the swine by profaning and befouling its purity and surpassing brightness with their own uncleanness and incorrigible wickedness. Each of these recoils on those who dispensed the mystery heedlessly and without forethought, and brings about their grievous fall and great disgrace. Pearls and holy things would include not only what has been mentioned, but also the gifts of miracles, and besides these the miracles themselves; and third, if you like, the apostolic and divine dignity, which the order of high priests is seen to inherit by succession. None of these may be set before dogs or before swine. The common law for all of them is the Master's sentence and decree quoted above, but one could find testimonies about each of them individually without much labor. To begin with, there were those who, like dogs, flaunted their shamelessness and asked for a sign when the sight of the signs already shown had scarcely left their eyes. The Savior of our race not only showed them nothing at all but declared that none would be given. Revealing the reason for refusing, he called them an evil and adulterous generation, showing by each of these vices that they were no better than dogs and swine. Again, in his own homeland he did not do many mighty works, because of their unbelief. In many places he is seen to require faith first and only then to perform healings. So the man with the mind of a dog and the ways of a swine [?] is unworthy of the benefit that comes from signs, and if so, much more is he unworthy of the gift of working signs itself. This is plain in itself. Nonetheless Peter, the chief of the disciples, furnished the clearest proof when by his rebuke he shook off the superstitious, wicked and gold-loving Simon. And that no such person deserves a share in apostolic dignity or high-priestly honor the Master himself again shows by deed and word. There was a man who asked to follow him and contrived to slip into the lot of the apostles and its privilege. Not only did the Lord not receive him, but by [?]

exposing the secrets of his heart, he drove him away from discipleship. For he who knows all things even before they come to be saw that this man's heart was a dwelling and lodging for birds and foxes, and that very thing he asked [?]. Full of guile, frivolity and shamelessness, and given over to the passion of avarice, the man dared, before he had driven these beasts out of his soul, to thrust himself into the calling of the disciples and imagine himself a vessel for those supernatural gifts of the Master. So he who draws all people to himself and wills all to be saved sent him away very far from his hope. The vessel of election, too, who ran across the vault of heaven as if it were an earthly racecourse and ran the course of the whole world in the race of preaching, agrees with his Teacher and Master, both in his sufferings for godliness and in what he writes to Timothy: "Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, and do not share in other people's sins," and countless other things. But enough about these matters. I would not hesitate to lead you to another line of contemplation as well, one that borders on what has been said, since such things are your love, your delight and your favorite spectacle. I do so even though I notice that the conventions of a letter are quietly making me cautious [?]. One would not stray from the truth in recognizing and calling the pure thoughts about virtue "pearls," and the precious and venerable element of pious and orthodox reasonings "holy things"; just as one may call the impious and heretical thoughts "dogs," and the pleasure-loving, foul and passion-ridden ones "swine." So we must not throw the pearls and the holy things to these swine and dogs or offer them up for strife and wrangling. Many have set them before such thoughts and made their [?contest] in the reasoning part of the soul into a theatrical show. Because their attachment to the passions left them without impartial judgment, they were [?put to flight] before they knew it and fell a tremendous fall: in them the better was overcome by the worse, and they made themselves a tragic spectacle rather than spectators. If you pass from conflicting notions and thoughts to the opposing actions themselves, and to the people whose conduct matches those actions, you will find this contemplation advancing no less. For an earnest and orthodox life, shining like pearls and holy things, ought not to live alongside heretical, foul and filthy ways of life and be mixed up with them. "Come out from among them and be separate," says the Lord, "and I will welcome you." And: "What fellowship

has light with darkness?" And: "Drive out the wicked one from among you." And: "With such a one do not even eat." And a countless multitude of others. I have taken pains over these things for your sake. But the field of anagogical contemplation, too, knows how to take pride in the breadth and inventiveness of its insights.

Question 201. How should one judge what happens in life?

Some pay the penalty for their wrongdoing in this present life: there you have the clearest proof that there is a Providence that presides over, takes account of and cares for things here. Many who lived more unjustly have not paid the penalty: that is an even greater proof that they have been reserved for another, more bitter and harsher judgment. Many of the righteous have lived happily: take this, in turn, as a prelude and token of the recompense there. But many have also struggled through many miseries: this too silences even the most contentious, for it shows that another life surely awaits us, and another tribunal, where each will receive the reward for what he has lived according to his deserts.

Question 202. How did the apostles, though uneducated men, overcome all the orators?

If the mind surpasses letters, and divine grace surpasses the mind beyond all comparison, do not be surprised that the apostles, who received the greater and indeed the greatest gift, utterly overcame those who prided themselves on the least: I mean the orators and the philosophers.

Question 203. Why did Paul, when addressing the Athenians, argue from their own writings?

Others may well be puzzled. The divine Paul teaches us to compare spiritual things with spiritual. He regarded even the Mosaic philosophy as refuse compared with the surpassing wisdom of Christ. Why, then, did a man who said and taught such things address the Athenians from the inscriptions written on their altar? For it seems unworthy of the divine inspiration in Paul to build up the truth out of myths. I would not much blame the others who are puzzled by this. But you could correct them from countless scriptures and arguments, you ardent lover of dialectic. You I would blame most justly, on the strength of one of your own rules, as having forgotten that wisest and most useful principle of dialectic. Which one? That where the hearers' perception does not accept the truth when it is demonstrated from its own true premises, but is blinded by its radiance and the

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople.] purity of the idea, then in such cases, wherever there are things they are by nature not incapable of grasping, one ought to start from these as far as possible: lead them by the hand, build up the truth for them, and let its brightness dawn gently on their minds.

Question 204. Why is prophecy shrouded in modes of obscurity?

You ask why prophecy is shrouded in modes of obscurity. I answer briefly: because prophecy is not history. The virtue of history, if anything, is to speak clearly and to work out nothing elaborate. It teaches what happened in public, which everyone, good and bad alike, knew at the time and is not prevented from knowing now. But prophecy's task is to reveal hidden things to the worthy and to make them inaccessible to the profane. For prophecy, then, what is shadowed, enigmatic and veiled is most fitting. From this, I think, your difficulty is also solved, which ran: "If we were not meant to learn it, it should not have been spoken at all. If it was decided that we should learn it, prophecy should not be obscure and so nearly equivalent to not having been spoken." For what has been said settles the matter: it was fitting and necessary neither [?to keep silent] nor to speak openly to all, but that it should be spoken clearly to the initiated and kept inaccessible to the uninitiated, and not

Question 205. On the depiction of the form and features of the saints [?].

You said that those iconoclasts who are bold and ill-intentioned, and who take idle curiosity for wisdom, put forward this question. Which of the images of Christ is true: the one among the Romans, the one the Indians paint, the one among the Greeks, or the one among the Egyptians? These are not like one another, and whichever one calls true clearly rules out the rest. But this difficulty of theirs, or rather this wicked contrivance (O you fine ornament of orthodoxy!), can be struck down in many ways and exposed as full of great folly and impiety. First, one may say to them: "Meanwhile, by the very means you have chosen to fight against the making of images, you have testified, even against your will, that images exist and are venerated everywhere in the world where the Christian people are found." So what they try to destroy they rather establish, and they are caught by their own words. Second, without realizing it, through what

they say they are placing themselves in the ranks of the pagans. For what they have said about the venerable [?] images could equally be said about our other mysteries. A pagan might say: "Which words of the Gospel do you call inspired? Which Gospel at all do you mean? The Roman one is written in one set of letter-shapes and forms, the Indian in another, the Hebrew in another, the Ethiopian in yet another." And not only are they written in dissimilar letter-forms and shapes; they are also pronounced with a different and utterly foreign sound and sense of speech. Would such people not then say, or rather, why would you not say, that no one should believe or come to the Gospel because it is proclaimed in dissimilar forms of shapes and sounds and meanings? This audacity too belongs to your way of reasoning. Indeed, not even a pagan would readily put such things to us, for they too have many things similar to our sacred ones. They share with us a common nature, mind and reason, a similar blending of soul with body, and countless other things. In the same way, regarding the notion of the Divine, although they differ from us on most points and the most important ones, there are nevertheless things which, because the common notions are so evident, not even they dare to contest. So not even a pagan would dispute with us about this, but only some other man wholly [?] without religion, who has accepted neither any notion of the divine nor any worship at all. Third, and corresponding to the second point, you will surely ask: "Which cross shall we consider like the original, the one shaped with the title or the one shaped and drawn without it?" For whichever one we acknowledge as the likeness, then by your wise syllogism the making and veneration of the others will be denied, or has already been denied (at least by you, who dare such things about matters so great). Fourth, you will bring forward the difference and dissimilarity in the mystical sacrifices and the other sacred rites, to slander and overthrow our whole undefiled rite and worship. For the wicked scheme you have devised in your minds against the image of Christ shakes the entire sacred rite of Christians and the divine mysteries from their foundations. Fifth, we must state what most clearly holds up their impiety and hatred of Christ to public shame. Why do you stop short at the image and unroll such drivel, when you ought to strip for combat against the one depicted himself, which they keep concealed for now? Why do you not display openly, with your lips and with bare face, what you are laboring with in your minds, your implacable war against Christ, instead of hiding behind the image as a mask? Let them say it: "The Greeks think Christ appeared on earth looking like them, the Romans rather that he resembled them, the Indians again that he had their form, and the Ethiopians, clearly, that he looked like them. Since this is so, which is the true Christ, the one imagined by which people? Must we not then confess or believe that Christ came in the flesh?" For truly, as far as these wretches are concerned, he did not even

come. For the very wickedness they devised against the image they have long before been caught raging against the one depicted, decreeing that because those who imagined him differ, the one imagined must be abolished entirely. You see what their aim is, and what their contrivance against the image was really aimed at. In addition to what has been said, this must be said, not to them, for they are unworthy, but to the faithful and Christ-loving: dissimilarity among depictions does not by any means destroy the nature and truth of the image. For the one depicted is depicted not only by the shape of the body and the form rendered in color. He is also depicted by a particular bearing, by an accompanying action, by the portrayal of sufferings, by dedication in holy places, by the explanation of inscriptions, and by other distinctive symbols. It is utterly impossible that none of these, or not most of them, should be present in the images of the faithful. Through them, no less than if every feature were present, we are led up to the thought and honor of the one depicted, which is the aim of image-making. But this has been said in passing, and in the form of a letter. A precise treatment of the work will, God granting, be reserved for its own proper treatise.

Question 206. Why is human life called a shadow, a dream, smoke and vanity?

It is not to declaim against our worthlessness that divine Scripture has called human life a shadow, a dream, smoke, vanity and other such names. What would you say of the age of childhood? What is more vain or senseless than that? But consider youth too, which might seem to be the very flower of nature. It is full of storm. Much in it is light, hollow and easily blown about. It passes more quickly than any dream, bestowing and providing nothing else. It merely stirs up a great tossing and surge of passions in the soul, and in some it has sunk the very first impulse toward virtue. And what of the borderland between the ages? This too differs in nothing from drifting smoke, darting here and there and settling clearly nowhere. It still shares somewhat in the light and disorderly movement of youth, not yet having fully freed a person from the fog and turmoil of that time. And being close to old age, it is quietly and imperceptibly filled with its soot, and so begins to ebb away and wither. It seems to stand apart from the harm and vice of either extreme, yet it shares no less in the depravity seen in both, and so it truly dissolves into smoke and a dream. And old age itself

what of it? Even if we say nothing, it cries aloud to everyone its own afflictions, its weight and its hardship, and shows that it is more worthless and fainter than dust, smoke, shadow, dream and everything else. How then can one escape these evils? In childhood, by receiving a good upbringing and having sober tutors, which is not in our own power but depends on the care of parents or guardians. In youth, when our own part also begins, by a very strong bridle and by the most exact discipline, training and practice. In middle age, through the habit already formed and imprinted on the soul, which has the greatest power for the achievements that follow, and through equal zeal and care for perfection in virtue. For the one who has managed and steered his life in this way, old age will come as a harbor and a rest from toil. The pleasure of the soul and divine joy will push aside and hide the blemishes of the body, and will show that person to be truly blessed. But you, my child, should not only read eagerly what I write, but take it to heart still more eagerly through your deeds.

"Put your hand under my thigh," says the patriarch Abraham. In giving this command to the servant who was to bring back the bride, he indicates two things. The first is obvious: he exacts the oath on the venerable mark of circumcision. The second is to be understood: he exacts it on Christ our God, who was to be born from him. He binds the servant, makes doubly sure that he keeps his oath, and at the same time makes him more eager. As overseer and witness of the oaths concerning the bride he sets over him no other than the one who promised that his seed in Isaac would be multiplied like the stars of heaven. This is the one who is able to bring his promises to fulfillment and whose gifts and graces are irrevocable. It is almost as if Abraham were thinking and saying: "Servant, you who are to bring the bride for my true-born son, you need only be eager in your service and bring an earnest will. The rest will be accomplished with the greatest ease by the one who is overseer and witness of the oath, and who granted the promises of many descendants." And see how devoutly and fittingly he ordered the one who was to be the go-between for his son's begetting of children to swear while touching the seal that he had received as the sign of a multitude of offspring through faith. It is as if to say: "He who gave me circumcision himself made the Canaanite race, among whom I sojourn, accursed, but made ours blessed. See, then: touching his [?] seal, I bid you swear by its lawgiver that you will act in no other way than as to him who [gave the promise] of many

…to the giver of children, we shall grant it: to take a girl of our own kin as bride for the son.” He seems to me to be doing much what a pious man, one of those who live under grace, might do when he is eager to have some similar matter carried out.
