He might set out the very symbols of divine and saving baptism, I mean the white robe and the other tokens of that gift, and then require the one who had promised to serve his wishes to touch them and take his oath on them. So, as far as a letter allows, you have from what has been said, I think, how reasonable, consistent and pleasing to God were the thought and action of faithful Abraham. These considerations drive away every vulgar, trite and hostile line of reasoning.

QUESTION 213. You are greatly amazed at the hardness of the apostles' hearts over the loaves, and you say: “Did they not see? Did they disbelieve the miracle with their own eyes, and with the hands that served it? How did they not understand? How did they forget?” There is indeed room for perplexity here, though not so much. But it is better to consider the matter rightly and resolve it as follows. They did see what was done, and they did not dispute their own eyes or their own hands or fight against them. They saw these things, they knew them, and they marveled. For they were not disposed like the senseless or the blind, or like the Jews, who fight against everything and have no shame. But they had not yet risen to perfection. They thought that their teacher performed his divine signs like one of the saints and prophets of old, whenever grace from above granted it, and not as God, with all authority and lordship. For this reason, when they had brought no more than one loaf with them and heard him tell them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, they were led off into reasonings about how they would be fed. As we said, they did not yet grasp that he was able of himself, always, and by the power of his own authority, to do whatever he wished. The Master found fault with this: they had not yet formed an opinion of him that befitted God and rose above human measures. So he rightly charged them with hardness of heart.

QUESTION 214 [?]. To the same man, who was perplexed by the words “And they did not understand.” Once again you are perplexed, and you ask how it was that the disciples did not understand when the Master foretold to them, clearly and plainly, the insults he would suffer from men, the blows, the cross and his death. For it says: “And they understood none of these things; this saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.” But consider this. The Saviour, to make his disciples sharper, often

spoke to them in parables. Moreover, what he spoke of was in itself astonishing: raising the dead, promising an eternal kingdom, and foretelling his own death. And there is more. By then the disciples' love for their teacher had grown strong with time and was at its height, and [they wished] [?] him to suffer nothing terrible. What a person does not want, he will scarcely admit is at hand even when it is already present. For all these reasons the apostles thought that what was said about the passion was some kind of parable, and not a prediction of those hardships. That is why they could not understand what was said, or rather would not, even though it was otherwise clear and plain. And if you also wish to take into account the matter of the resurrection, the thing becomes harder than belief. Even when examined on its own, a resurrection accomplished by the dead man himself is beyond belief; how much more when it is set beside, and foretold together with, those other gloomy things that stand diametrically opposed to it. Then it is no longer [surprising] [?] that they did not understand, at all

QUESTION [?]. The saying “God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham” was taken by those before us to refer to those of the Gentiles who have believed. Their hearts were hardened and insensible like stones and rocks; for what is more absurd, in hardness and insensibility, than to worship stones and wood? Yet they broke away from that state and rise up through faith as the seed of Abraham. But if it is not unacceptable to speak more closely to the wording and to the history, this too should not be overlooked. The Baptist wished to show how ineffable, supernatural, all-working and almighty the divine will is, and so he spoke these words. He was implying that just as in the beginning God willed it and formed man from clay, so now too, if he wished, he could even more easily refashion stones, which are akin to clay and made of the same elements, and raise them up as seed and children to Abraham. But consider with me also a third interpretation. I will not say it is closer than those already given, but it is no more distant than the other either. From the very stones which the Forerunner pointed to when he said, “God is able from these to raise up children to Abraham,” one can see, in actual events, children raised up to Abraham and the prophecy fulfilled. For when the passion that saved the world was being accomplished, those stones and rocks were split along with the rest. Then many [?] of both Gentiles and Jews had their hardened hearts broken through by the miracle. They were established in the faith of Christ and enrolled among the children of Abraham, both in lineage and in inheritance. So, as you see, the interpretation has been set before you both by spiritual contemplation and by history. The history is twofold, one part having happened before,
the other afterward. Through both of them we contemplate the creative and infinitely powerful character of the divine will.

QUESTION [?]. To one who asked how the divine Apostle can escape being convicted of lying, since he declared himself both a Jew and a Roman, and said at one time that Tarsus was his homeland and at another that he was born in Rome. Paul, the disciple of the truth, did not lie when he called himself either a Jew or a Roman. He was a herald of the truth, so it was impossible for him to rely on a lie, least of all when he stood before a court and was being prosecuted by the Jews on charges of deceit and wrongdoing, things he himself was destroying. How would he have dared to use a lie and [clear himself] [?] of the slander against him by the very means he used to deceive? Was he not afraid of being refuted at once, or later on? Did he not see that when the drama was exposed he would gain nothing, and would also make himself liable to a double punishment: for the charges the Jewish nation brought against him, and for the lies he told about himself? And how would Lysias, who held office and could easily discover the truth, have refrained from beating him, unless he had been persuaded? How could a prisoner and a poor man have persuaded him, unless the facts of the truth [convinced] [?] him? And how could Lysias, writing to Felix, have insisted that Paul was a Roman? “For having learned that he is a Roman,” he says, “I came with the troops and rescued him.” Was Lysias then deceived and carried away? By what trick? And how [?]? And how did Felix fail to detect the crime, when he was even granting the Jews lawless favors? Was he an eager servant wherever a favor was lawless and unreasonable, and yet sluggish and indifferent wherever a favor could be granted with right reason, not stirring himself even to begin to want to grant a just favor? What persuasiveness or consistency could that have? Then there were the men who were present, breathing murder against him and leaving no stone unturned; I mean the Jews. If Paul was contriving to fend off torture by a lie, how did they not burst out with a cry that filled the theater: “See, men, what a lie he has told! He is an impostor and a sorcerer! He is not a Roman! He found a way to mislead even you and escape the trial of the scourge. But you [?]. He has dared [?] even before us, and we bring our charges with the proofs in hand: this common destroyer [is ruining] [?] the common order of mankind!” But none of this happened. They had nothing to say, and they did not dare to say it, neither then nor afterward. Yet a court was convened for them again,

and their friend Felix sat in judgment. But Paul's truthfulness was so evident and so prevailed in everyone's opinion that it stopped the mouths even of the shameless Jews, who dared to say anything in order to [do harm] [?]. So in many ways the divine Paul is shown to be above all falsehood in calling himself a Roman. “But if he was a Roman,” someone says, “how did he insist, both elsewhere and in the very same speech, that he was a Jew and that Tarsus was his homeland? For he said, ‘I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city.’ How then can both be true together, and the same man be called both a Roman and a Jew?” To this we say that there is nothing absurd about it. By birth, and by his upbringing under the law of Moses, he was called a Jew, and his homeland was Tarsus, where his mother bore him. But because his father had been enrolled as a Roman, by Roman favor or even for money, he too was called a Roman and was one. That is why, when Lysias said to him, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum,” he replied, “But I was born to it.” He obviously did not mean born in Rome. Lysias was not boasting and insisting that he had been born in Rome either, but that he had the Roman name and citizenship, to which he proudly claimed to belong. The divine Paul answered him back, all but saying, as he humbled his pride: “You declare that your rank is recent and began with you, but the privilege of this distinction and title came to me rooted from long ago and handed down from my father.” For this reason Lysias, when he heard this and was assured that he had been trying to beat a Roman, gave up his boldness and anger for cowardice and fear, and drew back. At that time honor was enjoyed not only by those who were natives of Rome, but also by all who held the title itself by right of favor or purchase. So there is no difficulty in the divine Paul being a Jew and also being called a Roman. For both individual men, like Lysias, and whole cities, though [not Roman] [?], took the Roman name for themselves. To pass over the other cases for now, hear how the Philippians prided themselves on being Romans. When Paul drove the spirit of divination out of the slave girl, her masters, who ought to have given thanks, were inflamed with anger and dragged their benefactors into the marketplace before the magistrates, and they said: “These men are throwing our city into confusion; they are Jews. And they proclaim customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans.” You see how the Philippians were both called Romans and

called themselves Romans, having the one name from their homeland and the other from decrees. What then [?]? Or rather, how has it not become plain that the blessed Paul, being a Jew, was also a Roman? From this too it is clear that his claim to the Roman name was not [?] a pretext for a lie. For if he had called himself a Jew to some people and a Roman to others, the staging of a deception might have had some reason behind it. But since he insisted on both before the same people, is it not very foolish to suspect that, having planned to tell a lie, he put forward and admitted in advance the very thing by which anyone telling fabrications would be all the more easily exposed? Rather, it was the mark of a man who truly trusted in the nature of the facts and held the truth, clearer and brighter than any slander, suspicion or falsehood: before the same people and before a whole crowd he proclaimed himself a Jew and named his homeland as Tarsus, and then went on to declare himself a Roman. This is all the more so because he did not add the word “Roman” [casually] [?], or as if trying to slip it past them. He said it twice, and a third time, and he used it to alarm the tribune; and that, more than anything, inflames anger and stirs and rouses even the unwilling to a more exact inquiry. So, as has been shown, we can learn from many points that the divine Paul was a Roman. First, from the truth that was his, and because he was known as its herald. Second, because he proclaimed himself a Roman while standing before a court. Third, because he was being slandered with charges of deceit and wrongdoing, a situation in which not even a very foolish and shameless man would have lied. Then there is the fact that he did not utter this word idly or out of vanity, which one might perhaps overlook, but to rescue himself from torture and to alarm the magistrate. There is also the fact that Lysias was persuaded and refrained from outrage, and that he insisted to Felix that he had rescued Paul, a Roman, from the bloodthirstiness of the Jews. Moreover, it never even occurred to Felix to look into any such suspicion, although he chose to gratify the Jews and was eager to do so. And what is altogether beyond dispute: not even the Jewish crowd, though it was present, shouting and daring everything, dared to accuse him of lying on this point. Besides all this, he told the same people that he was both a Jew and a Roman, which no one would boldly say unless he was very confident in the truth. He put the title forward insistently and persistently. And, if you like, many people, both individuals and whole cities, whose homeland was not Rome obtained the Roman name by decree. From all this, I think, it has been established clearly and indisputably that Paul, if anyone ever did, spoke the truth on both counts when he declared himself a Roman and a Jew. “What then,” someone says, “was he not a Christian?” Most certainly he was. “Then why did he not call himself by this name too?” Here it was superfluous. For this religion and this name he suffered everything

and fought to the end, enduring and rejoicing. And he himself [?], by his teaching, his labors and his sweat, made Antioch the first of all cities to pride itself on the name of Christians. And if we must also listen to some history, a certain account is told that goes back to great antiquity. It says that the tribe of Benjamin, rooted in Palestine, spread its shoots as far as the regions of Italy, and gave the Roman race and Rome itself both their origin and their name. On this account the divine Paul, whose blood goes back to Benjamin, could fittingly be called a Roman. For Benjamin had many descendants, from whom Arad [?] and other cities and lands took their names. Among them was a man named Ros, who went to the regions of Italy, fathered many offspring there, rose to great glory and power, and gave Rome its name, drawn from himself, and the Roman race as well. As for the Greeks' explanations of the city's name, which are many and do not even agree with one another, those who tell this story will not even listen to them. So Ros, a descendant of Benjamin and an ancestor of Paul, fittingly made him a Roman: Paul drew the more remote cause of his lineage from Ros himself, and the nearer one from the Roman body of citizens. But although this history is pleasant and charming to hear, its charm does not bring persuasiveness with it. I would much rather have put it first, as the account given to me from the beginning [?], were it not so ancient, too hoary to be believed, not only now [?] but even by the people of that time, and of no use as a guarantee for rescuing Paul from a beating. With this, then, I have resolved your fine difficulties. They are fine because they spring from a fine mind that is diligent and loves God. If anything else occurs to you, ask with confidence: not us, but Paul, and the common teacher of Paul and of us, Christ our true God. Farewell.

QUESTION 212. Why was the veil of the temple torn? The veil of the temple is torn while the Master hangs on the wood, for many reasons, I think. At that saving passion the earth shook and trembled and all but collapsed, and the ungrateful can attribute this to natural disturbances of the elements. But the veil was torn from top to bottom with no one in particular tearing it, something that could not happen by nature, either before or since. This leaves no escape, even for the most malicious, from admitting that the portent was an act of divine wrath and that what happened was an irrefutable proof of the Jews' bloodguilt. Someone might give a second reason, saying that it was a sign and a forewarning of the overthrow and

desolation, so many years later, of the far-famed temple and of the Jewish rites and mysteries in it. Among these it was a great and earnest concern that no one among the multitude should see what lay within the veil. That is why the fabric was spread across: to keep the sacred things unseen by the people and visible only to the priests. When it was torn, their sight was evidently laid open to all, and the things that until then were [hidden] [?] and [secret] [?] became common, brought out for everyone to see and profane. By this was [foreshadowed] [?] also the complete abolition and cessation of all their other ordinances and of the worship under the law. A third reason can also be discerned, which seems opposed to the one just given but is rather born from it. What is it? The knowledge and worship of God among the Jews was shut up in a narrowly bounded place, Judaea and Jerusalem. Even so, it served as a type and a preliminary sketch of grace. So the worship and knowledge confined to so narrow a space had to cease, and that which was to spread to the ends of the inhabited world through the saving passion had to be established. That is why that frontal curtain is torn, the one that enclosed the Holy of Holies as in a secret and untouchable place. By the deed itself it all but cries aloud and summons everyone to the divine vision and knowledge of the things unseen. It proclaims that piety will no longer be confined to one part of the world and to a nation easily counted, but that all the nations and the ends of the world will come to enjoy what was inaccessible and unattainable to the Jews. But pass on with me to the next reason as well, and consider it this way. The ark, and what was in the ark, were made after the pattern of heaven and of the things under heaven. For it says: “See that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.” So the ark, together with the other secret things, was hidden in the temple, shut off by the veil, and gave access to no one except the priests. This signified and outlined that the entry into heaven had until then been kept closed to human beings, and that no one, not even of those devoted to the worship under the law, had been counted worthy of that lot. So the veil is torn when the Master is crucified, trumpeting and announcing to all of us the entry into the heavens. For indeed, through his life-giving death he opened the entry into the heavens for the whole human race: he who for this emptied himself, took on our flesh and suffered all things for us, Christ our God.

Our fathers have published interpretations of these sayings according to more than four senses, I think: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,” and, “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” Yet you are looking for another one besides those already given, many as they are. I do not know why, for those are enough to satisfy the desire of a soul eager to learn. Still, perhaps there is no harm in considering this one too, since it agrees very closely with the facts themselves. What is it, then? It is this. Some people stumble at Christ our God because of the signs of his humanity: for example, that he ate even with tax collectors and sinners, that he slept, that he grew tired, that he said, “My soul is very sorrowful,” and anything else of that kind. The Word, who wisely governs all things, did each of these to confirm his becoming man and to show it plainly. Those who have stumbled at Christ over such things can, it seems, easily be set right. In a way their blasphemy slipped out of them through ignorance, because they could not see into the depth of the divine dispensation and his unspeakable condescension. So when they see his more divine works and deeds, these people will very quickly change their minds, and in the same way they will be forgiven for their sins. This is what happened to Paul the persecutor. He heard of the cross and the death, and that he ate [?] and drank, and whatever else the Jews brought forward to slander the Master. But when he had a more divine experience and the vision from above, he at once threw off all those blasphemies and became a herald of the one he had persecuted. So too three thousand at once, then more after them, and then a people too great to be counted, were turned around by the divine signs and eagerly came over to the preaching they had once fought against. It is clear from what has been said, then, how forgiveness is given to those who blaspheme against the Son of Man: ready pardon follows on easy change. But there are others who have before their eyes the more wonderful works, works that only divine power can perform: demons driven out, diseases banished, eyes created for the blind by a word, all those supernatural and astonishing things. If they refuse to turn at any of these, as though deliberately blinding themselves to the works of the Spirit and to the light, then repentance is hard or even entirely impossible for them, and for that reason forgiveness too is taken from them. For what could persuade them to change, when they have hardened themselves against things so new and so far beyond nature, and none of these has shamed them into turning back?

So their offense is rightly unpardonable, and their blasphemy is greater than forgiveness. Examples of what I mean are Annas and Caiaphas and many of the Jews. They saw him driving out demons, and when they should have worshiped their benefactor, they reviled him as driving out the demons by the ruler of the demons, a piece of daring beyond all shamelessness. They saw the blind seeing, and the bedridden proving their healing by running and carrying loads, and they said, “This man is not from God.” When Lazarus was raised on the fourth day, they were inflamed to further murder: “For they were seeking,” Scripture says, “to kill Lazarus too.” Then, when they learned that he himself had risen, they tried to cover up the resurrection with money and lies. And when the disciples' mouths had been sharpened by tongues of fire, and they were proclaiming the mighty works of God in foreign languages and leading a countless crowd to true religion by the miracle, these men were not ashamed to mock that awe-inspiring miracle as new wine and drunkenness. Nor were the accursed wretches afraid of being consumed by that strange fire. So none of these supernatural things was enough to change their wicked and perverse minds, once they had made themselves ready to be shameless and insolent toward the very greatest of the spiritual and divine works. It was very justly and wisely said, then, “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” For those who have taken offense at Christ the Master because of his more human and humble traits, the greater and loftier works make change and forgiveness easy. But for those who have behaved madly toward what is spiritual, supernatural and divine, correction is extremely hard or even impossible. That is why no forgiveness for their offenses will come to them.

QUESTION 214. By an ancient custom, people who were glad and rejoicing used to anoint their heads and wash their faces, and these were regarded as signs of joy and gladness. So when the Master laid down the law about fasting, he wanted us to keep the fast with joy and gladness, and he says, “Anoint your head and wash your face.” He did not mean that we should grease our heads with oil or rinse our faces with water. He himself did not use these things when he fasted for forty whole days, and no one can see any gain from them for a person who uses them. He is not, then, commanding us to anoint and wash ourselves with oil and water. He used the very symbols of joy and gladness to lay down that we should rejoice and be glad while we fast. For if we dispose and adorn

ourselves in this way, we will be able to hide what we do from other people, and we will make the struggle of fasting light for ourselves. Where there is eagerness and joy, even hard work is light; and where there is sluggishness and distaste, even the easiest thing becomes very hard. So you too should anoint your head and wash your face, which is what you asked to learn about. Make yourself bright and cheerful while you fast, from the good spirits and rejoicing in your heart, and try in every way to hide your good deed from people, so that God, who watches over hidden things, may be the one who rewards you. And while fasting, you may also generously enrich the ruling part of your mind, which is in your head, with the oil of good deeds, and from there, as from a spiritual fountain, wash your whole self and your face and make them bright and clean (for “by almsgiving,” Scripture says, “sins are cleansed away”). If you do, you will show that the explanation of the divine sayings has come to you to your very great profit.

QUESTION 215. The Savior said in the Gospels, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” He did not say this, as someone might foolishly think, because he was ashamed of being born of a mother, or because he was stripping his mother of a mother's honor and privileges. How could that be? Even before the time for his miracles had come, he turned water into wine out of respect for her. At the very time of his passion, when he was stretched out with wounds, spear, cross and nails, he showed the greatest care for her. And before all this he was obedient not only to the woman who really gave birth to him but also to the man supposed to be his father: “For he was obedient to them,” Scripture says. But why do I say these things? He was not ashamed to live in a womb, and he willingly undertook the act itself; how could it make sense for him to be ashamed of the name? He made honoring parents a law that comes right after the duties owed to God; how could he himself be found guilty of despising his mother? It cannot be said, then, it truly cannot, that our common Creator said, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” because he was ashamed of his mother or looked down on her. Rather, through these words some other, greater purposes are being worked out. In many places he teaches us to put the salvation of the soul ahead of everything else, and to value neither father nor mother, neither children nor brothers, nor even the whole world itself, above it. Here he shows this very thing plainly through his own actions. While he was teaching the crowds and sowing the word of salvation in their souls, his mother and brothers came and stood there, calling their benefactor and the common Savior away to themselves. And quite

rightly he did not turn at their call or answer it. He did not leave his teaching, disregard the salvation of his hearers, and put his mother's request first. By this action he taught that when someone is cultivating the salvation of souls, the soul being cultivated ought to attend only to the one who cultivates it, unless it means to receive the seed along the path, or among thorns, or on rocks. In just the same way, the [spiritual] cultivator is bound to give himself wholly to the work of cultivation, and not to divide his attention toward the rocks [?], not even if it is his mother, or some other close relative, who calls him away from there and tries to draw him off to himself. This is not neglect of his mother, but great forethought and zeal for those who are being saved. For the time for teaching should not, not even [?], be spent in attending to relatives. That is why the Savior drew the disciples closer to himself and said, “Here are my mother and my brothers.” That is: these people, these, who receive the Father's seed of teaching into the bosom of their souls, fill the place of mother and brothers for me. Clearly this is not the act of someone belittling the woman who bore him. For how could he have raised such people, as if to great glory, to a mother's portion? Rather, it is the act of someone who reveres and honors her as she deserves. For, he is saying, the affection and devotion a person ought to have for his mother and brothers, these people too are counted worthy of, when they carry out the teaching and give birth to the good works that grow from it. Consider this as well. He had said before, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” So that he would not seem to be imposing a heavy and difficult command, he fulfilled it first himself by his own example, making it easy to imitate him, and put the benefit and salvation of the many ahead of attending to his mother. It is almost as if he gave his actions a voice to say: Do not think my commandment is heavy and hard to carry out. Though I am under obligation to no one, I am the first to begin the work, and, as you can see, I put your salvation ahead of attending to my mother. I am the Master and Creator of all, and yet I did not hesitate to show you this, and I even put my zeal and devotion toward you ahead of a mother's affection. How much more, then, are you bound to repay me in kind, and to put your love and goodwill toward me, your benefactor, ahead of everything? Yet even this is not for my sake. For what would human longing add to him who turns all things with a nod, and whose fingers made human nature itself, and heaven, and the whole universe? No, I seek this too, like everything else, for your own salvation. So we should not be surprised if Christ, while honoring his mother as was fitting, still did not

put her ahead of our salvation. Indeed, it was for our sake and for our salvation that he took a mother at all. Since he did not even spare himself for us, but endured those countless sufferings and that shameful and violent death so that in place of death he might make us heirs of deathless life, it was not unreasonable for him to value our salvation even above his feelings for his mother. And if you would like to consider another point too (for the cultivation of the divine Scriptures yields a rich harvest and gives much benefit to those who work hard at it), you will see something no less important than any of the others. When the Savior said, “Who is my mother and my brothers?” he was not addressing his Mother. That blessed Virgin was standing outside with dignity and reverence, not presuming to go in to her Son. So she was not interrupting his teaching; she only longed to see him. To whom, then, was the Master's word addressed? Clearly to the man who called out and shouted, rudely and at the wrong moment, “Your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.” That Jew (for the Gospels give us no more precise name for him), when he addressed the Master, not only added no word of respect, but did not even wait for a suitable time. He interrupted the teaching and, with great arrogance and boldness, threw out the words, “Your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.” I think he did this as though he were scheming to mock the common Savior of our race by pointing to his family. Otherwise he would not have so boldly, and in the hearing of the people being taught, made this reproach, to call it by its proper name, rather than an invitation to the Master. He schemed and plotted these things, trying as far as he could to make the crowd less attentive to the teaching, and to cheapen and undercut the teacher's credibility by pointing to his relatives, as he thought he could. For elsewhere too the Jewish nation is seen burning with envy, especially during the time of his teaching and his miracles, and inflamed beyond all bounds to slander and insult the Master. “Is not this the carpenter's son?” they say; and again, “We know his father and his mother”; and, “As for this man, we do not know where he comes from”; and, “Are not his brothers and his sisters here with us?” and many other spiteful words like these. So Christ the Master, exposing this man's lawlessness, and through him the whole band of those who thought as he did, framed his reply with some such meaning as this: “Who is my mother, and my brothers?” That is: Why did you set out to bring up my mother and brothers as a reproach? Your wicked scheme was plotted in vain; your trick will be turned

against you. I am so far from being ashamed of my relatives' humble station that I not only acknowledge as mother the woman who truly bore me according to the flesh, but I do not refuse to adopt as mother and brothers these people too whom you see, humble and without a city, homeless and poor, though they are not related to me by birth at all, so long as they carry out the Father's will through my teachings. She had nothing in common with the divine nature (for what does the human race have in common with the Godhead?), yet by the Father's will I took flesh from her, made her my mother, and preserved all a mother's privileges for her together with her virginity. In just the same way I raise these people too to the portion and dignity of brothers and mothers, though they have no claim on me even from belonging to my tribe according to the flesh, if only I find them carrying out my teaching and the Father's will. From what has been said, then, I think you can see clearly that even in saying, “Who is my mother?” and what follows, our Master and Savior was in no way guilty of disdaining his mother or neglecting her in any way. Rather, these words, like all the rest, show that the Theotokos rightly enjoyed a mother's honors from the one who was born of her.

You asked about the words of the herald, in which he proclaimed, “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.” We find that they have been understood in several different ways. Some have taken “sandal” and “strap” to mean nothing other than what everyone knows them to be in ordinary usage, simply those very things. This view, I think, comes not only nearer to the point but also fits the wording. On this view, the Baptist uses these words to declare that the one being baptized is incomparably greater. He is saying: I know him to be so far above me in greatness and dignity that the gap is not merely that between a slave and his master, but whatever other difference and distance there may be that leaves nothing beyond it. For I do not count myself worthy to be considered even for the very lowest form of slavery, and that is what untying the strap of a sandal is. Others, perhaps more allegorically, suppose the sandal to be the world, and the strap to be those questions about it that are hard to grasp, the bond of ignorance that cannot be untied. They call the world Jesus' sandal because, they say, his Providence runs all through it, holding the whole of it, embracing and sustaining it. Or rather, he guides and carries it with his own foot in perfect wisdom. That is, it does not need much deliberation and forethought on his part; by the very least and lowest exercise of his oversight he preserves and orders so vast and great a work of art. But this

interpretation, the more ingeniously it has been crafted, the farther, I think, it stands from the true meaning. Still others say that the sandal stands for the flesh (for the Word put it on, they say), and the strap for the union of the natures with one another that took place, which the Forerunner did not dare to untie, nor did those who listened to his teaching. For it is neither [?] permitted, through absurd notions, to split off what was assumed from the Word into a separate hypostasis. Others again, besides these, have understood the sandal to be not simply the flesh but the incarnation itself, his becoming man. They take the strap to be not the union of the natures but the knot of perplexities about the incarnation and his becoming man, which go beyond human reasoning. Not only should ordinary people not allow themselves to work at untying and explaining these, but one must also understand clearly that not even those like John, who are lofty and exalted in both action and contemplation, no, not even they, could come to know what is hidden and hard to grasp in those unspeakable mysteries. For he himself, the “greatest among those born of women,” by confessing that he could not untie the strap, shows that not even he would be able to solve such perplexities. And what are they? What is the self-emptying of the Word? How is the Creator united to what he created? How could a virgin give birth, and make the release of birth pangs a seal of her virginity? How did the Savior, who had bulk and a body, run across the surface of the sea? How is he enclosed by a tomb, bars and seals, and then come out of it while these remain undisturbed? And then, when the doors were shut, how does he appear among the disciples with the same body? Eyes and fingers probe the blows and wounds of one who is beyond suffering and incorruptible; and how could anyone explain eating and drinking being done by a body that needs nothing and is subject to no decay? No one, not merely ordinary people of the crowd, but not even someone who had reached the perfection of the Forerunner, will untie any of these knots, and others like them, clearly and cleanly. One person may perhaps tell his hearers something more comforting than another does, some consolation for this great perplexity. But the truth in these matters, without mirrors and riddles, is equally beyond everyone in this life. These, I think, are the most noteworthy of the interpretations I remember, and I have written them down for you. Judge between them yourself and embrace the better. If you are too modest to judge, I recommend to you the first and the last of those I have set out. The first fits both the subject and the words best; the last you will find more suited to contemplation. Farewell.

Question 217. On the difference between images. It does no harm to the image of Christ that the Son is called the true image of the Father, any more than it does that man was truly made according to the image of God. Nor is it harmed when we say that those who have lived virtuously are formed into the true image of Christ. These things are not said to disparage the man-made image, nor to brand it as false, but so that the difference between them may be recognized. When we call the Son true wisdom, we do not banish the wisdom drawn from the divine Scriptures from the realm of truth. When we name him true light or true life, we do not declare the light of the sun, or our life here (not to mention the life to come), to be something unreal. In the same way, when we say that the Son is the true image, we do not drive into falsehood the images that received their origin through imitation. We are showing how far that image surpasses them. Hear, then, the son of thunder, and how, thundering to us from above, he teaches us to understand this way of using words. In saying "and grace for grace," he named both the Old and the New Covenants with the term "grace." Then, setting forth the superiority of the one over the other, he says, "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." Clearly, in saying this he did not strip the Mosaic law of truth or grace, for he was the very one who a little earlier had honored it with the name of grace. Nor did he accuse it of falsehood. It was not to insult and slander the law that he applied "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" to the ordinances of the Gospel (that is what Heracleon and the children of Heracleon would say). He wished to present the Master's generosity as more remarkable and more perfect than the Mosaic legislation, and so he gathered it under the shared title of grace and truth. The divine Paul does the same. When he declares that "the law has a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things," he does not deny that the law is a type and image of the good things to come. By these words he shows that grace, rather than the law, images the enjoyment of the good things to come. And indeed John Chrysostom, so great in the unfolding and teaching of the divine Scriptures, can be shown to use this figure of speech in many places. When commenting on the divine oracles, and on what was said to Nicodemus, [Notes: (a) "man-made"; (e) perhaps "the one".]

[?] he set the tongue of interpretation to work, and, discussing rebirth through baptism and the timeless begetting of the Son from the Father, he says: "For even if this birth is heavenly, yet compared with that true birth, which is from the essence of the Father, it is earthly." You hear how he says "compared with that true birth." Is the birth through baptism, then, not true? Unless you were utterly mad, you would not dare say so. Why then did he say "compared with that true birth"? He was extolling how much higher and more wonderful that birth is, not depriving this one of truth. But why do I say this? Hear him rather saying the same things as I do, not only in thought but in the very words, and showing us that this usage is found even in the Master's own sayings. When the Saviour said to the Jews about the manna, "It was not Moses who gave you the bread, but my Father gives you the true bread," Chrysostom, unfolding the Lord's meaning, says this: "He calls it true bread, not because the miracle of the manna was false, but because it was a type, not the truth itself." And there are countless other examples. Why should I call on this witness or that [?]? Everyone alike, both the nurslings of the Church and the most learned of those outside it, knows this usage, except, it seems, the Iconoclasts, and books are full of this idiom. When there are two or more things that bear the same name, whether by homonymy or in some other way, or that otherwise share certain properties, anyone who wishes to speak of the pre-eminent one among them gives to it in a special way what belongs to them all in common. He does not take it away from the others altogether. He uses it to show how the thing under discussion surpasses the rest. The examples already given will suffice for the argument, I think. But if you want a list of others, go through the books for yourself, and by writing down the examples of such usages you will fill a whole book.

Question 218. What Christ our God said to Mary Magdalene as she approached him, "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father," seems somewhat hard to understand. What, then? Would he rather allow her to touch him after his ascent to the Father? The meaning is this: "You may not touch me," he says. Why? "Because you do not yet think of me as having ascended to the height of the Father and taken up the dignity of the [?] essence. You still think lowly things about me as you approach me, and nothing higher than human measures. And this, far from

making you worthy to touch my glory, actually puts you far away from it." And see how, having said "Do not touch me," he added "for not yet." He was giving her hope that she would not be driven away from her longing forever, but would shortly obtain what she was eager for. It is as if he were saying: "With the attitude you bring as you approach me, you may not approach me, for you would not obtain what you desire. But if you lift yourself above lowly things with higher thoughts that befit God, you will be granted access, and you will enjoy greater things than you hoped for." For the woman wanted [?], as before, to keep company with the Master in a more human way, in the manner of the economy. She did and thought many such things as she sat by the tomb: bringing myrrh, weeping, suspecting that he had been carried off, [?] the resurrection. But he drew her away from this impulse and cleansed her of such suspicions, and showed besides that her attempt was untimely and impossible. "Do not touch me," he says, "for I have not yet ascended to my Father." That is: "It is not right to put your satisfaction ahead of the common providence and the benefit of the world. Nor is it right, to satisfy your longing, to keep overshadowing the Father's divinity that is in me, and to let you still approach me as a mere man. The time before the cross belonged to condescension and to lowlier things. Then you too were allowed to lean on lowlier thoughts, as if resting, so that you would not be forced toward greater things at the outset and all at once, and so lose everything and be swept away. But now the time of higher and divine things has come. Death has been swallowed up in victory and put to death. Hades has been emptied of the dead of all the ages and cast out of its tyranny. Splendid trophies over all enemies have been raised through the resurrection. You too, then, must lift your mind to higher things that befit God. You must no longer seek the former things, the things of condescension, nor linger among lowlier things and be carried down with them. If you achieve this, you will readily find what you long for, and with an unerring mind. Once you have received the right understanding you have not yet received, you will marvel all the more at the ineffable and supernatural manner of the incarnation. And you will go further than what I forbade you: you will take care not to approach and touch me in a lowly way, and you will show a longing and devotion toward me worthy both of my divinity and of your perfected faith." The woman was not forbidden to touch him as a primary matter or for its own sake. She was forbidden because she still meant to touch him with lowly, earthbound thoughts. The women who met the Lord clearly prove this. He greets them splendidly, first of all, with "Rejoice," and his immaculate feet

he allows them to touch, since they were perfected in both mind and hands. But since the woman had for the moment been prevented from touching him, she might have failed in her eagerness and fallen into grief and brooding, for her sex is prone to faintheartedness and suspicion: "How I have been overlooked! How I have been scorned! Alas, what will become of me now?" To keep her from running to such thoughts, the Saviour anticipates her and comforts her. "Go," he says, "to my brothers and tell them." With these words he drives away the turmoil of her thoughts and encourages her to take heart, in two ways. First, he appointed her the evangelist of the resurrection. Second, through her he gave the same command as he gave the disciples. For he says, "And tell them: I am ascending to my Father." It is as if he said: "Do not let it grieve you that I prevented you from touching me. I did not do this to slight you or to insult you. The nature of things, and the ineffable law of my providence and economy, wills that this should hold for everyone. And you will have nothing less, but rather more, even if your eagerness goes unfulfilled. See, I am sending you to the disciples as the herald of my resurrection. And I give them the same command I gave you: to know that I am ascending to the Father. They are no longer to be carried along by their former opinions, imagining lowly and human things about me, expecting to travel with me again as before, to share toils and griefs, and to be constantly in my company and gather with me." Consider, I ask you, how in his words to the woman he also called the disciples brothers. He was preparing her to take courage in every way and to accept nothing grievous. By graciously giving the disciples the name of brothers, then counting her among them and judging her worthy of the same things, he cast out all her grief and all the turmoil of suspicion. Very wisely, too, and in a way befitting God, he said "to my Father and your Father" with a distinction and separation: the conjunction links the syllables, while the difference and otherness of the realities is made plain. By the particular he showed nature; by the common he indicated grace. Nature differs from grace and adoption, and by just so great a measure the relation by essence to the one and only-begotten of the Father surpasses the relation to the others that comes from love for humanity and compassion. Clearly, the Only-begotten is established above the many sons whom grace has brought to birth. So, having said "my Father" and set apart by the particular the genuineness of nature, he added "your Father," setting forth the adoption and enrollment of the apostles that came from his generosity. "My God" and "your God" also look to the same meaning and are meant in the same sense. Through "my God" the kinship and intimacy of the One is proclaimed and included; through

"your God" is shown what the many share in common: servitude, subjection, and having been created. For it is clear, clear to everyone, that just as the word "my" sometimes signifies what is inferior and different, or what is superior, so again the same expression marks what is equal, akin, and most genuine. These things I have sketched for you in outline. The sketch falls short of the subject, but perhaps not of what a letter requires.

Question 219. "He sweated blood" is a proverb used of people who are deeply grieved and in anguish, just as "he weeps blood" is used of those who lament bitterly. If someone should think that the words of the divine Luke, "And his sweat became like clots of blood," are an adaptation of this kind (for the man was not unacquainted with such learning), you have your answer. But if this seems too far-fetched to you, the following is easy and immediate. By saying "like clots of blood," he did not declare that clots of blood were sweated; otherwise he would not have said that the sweat came about in their likeness, and this is plainly what "like clots" indicates. He wanted rather to show that the Master's body was not moistened by some slight dampness, appearing, as it were, for show. It was truly drenched all over with sweat, like thick drops. So he took clots of blood as an image of what happened. He was showing, through the thickness of the sweat, as through the intense prayer and the great agony, that the Saviour became man by nature and in truth, not in show and appearance, and was subject to the natural and blameless passions of human beings. The Master himself demonstrated this very thing by his deeds. He showed that he received the suffering not in the divine nature but in the human, and he prayed, and was in agony, and sweated out those thick sweats that resembled clots of blood. So no longer think it proper that this passage of the Gospel be cut out, even if, as you said, some of the Syrians think so. Recognize that it contains nothing impossible, and is rather entirely consistent. Set it alongside the other divine oracles and read it with an undoubting mind.
Question 220. There is much I could say by which it is possible to recognize clearly

that the Master's saying, "Everyone who looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart," is neither heavy nor impossible, but light and kind. For now I will tell you only what suits a letter. First, we who belong to grace are bound to accomplish something more than those who lived under the law. The strictness of the legislation is not by nature equally heavy for each party. What perhaps seemed heavy to them is moderate and light for us, and what is so for us was not so for them. The law only forbade them what was not lawful to do; it gave them no power to fulfill what it commanded. But we have received great help through baptism and the other gifts. This help lightens almost every difficulty and does not allow the evil spirits to attack us as tyrants. It permits [them] to attack only through our own laxity and, as it were, our yielding. So if nothing stricter had been commanded of us than of them, God's justice and goodness would have been turned into their opposite. The same strictness and the same way of life would have been demanded both of us, who have received the greatest help, and of them, who enjoyed no such help, and equal action would have been required from unequal strength. It is both unjust and most oppressive, at the final reckoning of the work, to demand ten talents from the one who received two. In the same way it is negligent, and on the other side lawless, to approve the one who received five talents when his whole business has come to only four. Each must be required to work in proportion to his strength and to the gift allotted to him. Such is the law of equality and of impartial judgment and decision. It is clear, then, from what has been said, that for us not even to look at a woman to desire her ought to count as not committing adultery counted for those under the law. Not only the truthfulness and consistency of the words testify to this; it can also be seen plainly in the deeds themselves. One cannot find more people under Moses who fled the act than people under grace who have withdrawn even from the things that push toward the act. A great many among us have not only refrained from casting curious, lustful eyes on the beauty of others; they have not even simply gazed at a woman's face, preserving their chastity right down to the bare act of seeing. Second, to those trained under the law, the good things of the earth were held out as the prize for fulfilling the commandments. To us is offered the kingdom of heaven, and "what eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man." So the difference between the prizes also shows how easy and kind the gospel commandment is. It is not equally toilsome to run one

stade and win a wreath of wild olive, and to run two stades and be counted worthy of a golden crown. Clearly the toil of the two stades is lighter than that of the one. The incomparable excellence and splendor of the prize lightens the hardship and does not even let the runner feel the double exertion and the double sweat. Besides this, he did not define this entanglement through the eyes simply as adultery. By saying "adultery in the heart," he tempered with a law of [?] compassion what seems vehement and severe in the pronouncement. "In the heart," he says, the adultery took shape, the adultery produced by the frenzy and titillation that came through the eyes. How could anyone speak more humanely than this? You cast a lewd eye on the face of another man's wife. You reveled, though it was not allowed, in a licentious sight that was not yours. With languishing glances you dripped the venom of passion into softer souls. From there you kindled in your thoughts a flame now fiercer and uncontrollable. The burning passed all the way to the heart, and only opportunity is lacking for the act. How have you not committed adultery in your heart? Another man might perhaps have said that you had even committed full adultery, especially if he perceived that you had done this against his own wife. For everyone tends to make light of the sins he himself has committed against others and to examine them slowly, but to see more sharply the wrong done against himself, and then to become a stickler for strict justice. "You cast your eyes on another's face, sending out lewd rays through them. They were reflected back at you and struck your heart [?]. You drag the creature away captive, and are dragged in turn by the same snares. You were wounded, and you wounded. You were overthrown, and you overthrew. How is this not plainly adultery?" But our God, the lover of mankind, does not speak so. He confines the sin to the heart, where the passion also arose. "You have committed adultery," he says, "in the heart." Do you see how kindly, how gently, he judges everything, and how he spares us? In addition to what has been said, consider this too: he pronounced this judgment not to devise punishment for us but to rescue us from punishments. The man who lingers over such improper sights is close to being plunged wholly into the act itself. So, to rescue us from being punished, he checks in advance the causes of the deeds for which we are made to pay penalties. If you look more closely, you will see that through this commandment he contrives for us no inexorable penalty and no senseless punishment, but rather loving consolation and saving guidance. How? Human weakness being what it is, we are often carried, even without premeditation or curiosity, into

improper deeds. Sometimes, without having planned it or fixed the passion firmly in our thoughts, we slip into such an act through some force, or a sudden seizure, or deceit. When that happens, we should not fall down utterly or throw ourselves into despair. Considering that we were swept into the fall without premeditation, without eagerness, and without the prior consent of our thoughts, we should quickly raise ourselves up from there and run to repentance, having found a great ground for pardon in the fact that we did not fall by intent. The Saviour pronounced this judgment so that, whenever we are caught by a sudden assault, or some trick, or even by force, we can console ourselves with these thoughts and run more eagerly and straight toward amendment. He placed the [?] of sin in the choice of worse things and in the consent of the thoughts, and not in the act alone. This is not the work of one who burdens the conscience of sinners without reason. It is the work of one who lightens and comforts the burdened conscience of those who were caught without premeditation. For those who have gone forward through those incitements, the condemnation is great and hard to bear. (Why did you plan it? Why did you stir up your passions and hand yourself over wholly to the base choice, willingly abandoning the better, when willing the better is easier? "For it lies near at hand and ready for all," as Paul also cries out, "to will the good," and it is no labor to hate its opposite.) But just as the condemnation is severe for such people, so for those not carried away in this manner God's love for humanity anticipates the punishment, granting easy pardon and acquittal through swift repentance. So much for this. But you, I pray, turn away from improper deeds, and refrain from setting up idols in your thoughts through curious and passionate looking, so that you may come to delight in words like these rather than be vexed by them.

Question 221. Of what heresy was Eusebius Pamphili? Eusebius, whether the slave or the intimate of Pamphilus, was caught in Arianism, as his books loudly proclaim. He himself, supposedly repenting and against his will, confesses the disease, but in his very repentance he shows himself rather unrepentant. For in the things by which he seemed to defend himself, he does not show that he has departed from his former false belief, nor to the holy and ecumenical

…of heaven is greater than he.” The saying about the Forerunner, spoken in praise and in the form of a question, “But he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he,” we know that most of those before us took the Master to have spoken as a statement, delivering his own verdict. Of these, some join “least” with “in the kingdom of heaven” and read them together, and so make the one who is least of the others in it greater than John. By “kingdom” here they understand the time after the Lord’s resurrection, in which above all the things of the faith were perfected and strengthened through the cross, baptism and the Spirit. By “least” they understand the lesser of those who live as its citizens, who, even if he has less than the others, still carries off the greater share when compared with John. For the Forerunner, they say, still lived under the law and so is among those born of women, over all of whom he did indeed win the first prize. But the one who lives in grace is also among those born of the Spirit and born again from above. “For to those who believe in his name he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.” Compared with these, they say, the Forerunner is not merely greater than none of them, but falls short even of the least. That is how these read it. Others, however, were abashed on the Baptist’s behalf, and rightly so, I think, at the thought of making so great a man not even the equal of any of those perfected in grace, and even meaner than the least. First, then, they read “But he who is least” separately from “in the kingdom of heaven.” Next, they more readily take “the kingdom of heaven” to mean the Lord’s second coming, and “the least” to mean our Lord Jesus Christ himself. At the time of his first coming the many did not consider him greater than the Forerunner. But at that time he will be recognized by all, even by those who once refused to acknowledge him, with

a fearful and dreadful awareness [?], when he comes as judge and king of all. Yet even these did not all take our Lord Jesus Christ to be called “least” in one and the same sense. Some took it of the time of his birth according to the flesh, for the Lord’s birth came a full six months after the Forerunner’s. Others took it of height, for it is handed down that the Baptist was also taller in body than the Master. Still others took “least” as referring to the opinion of the many. John was thought to be greater because he had been dedicated to God from infancy and had taken up an unencumbered life in the desert from his very swaddling clothes, and because ready reasoning tends to regard the one who baptizes as more venerable than the one baptized. For different reasons, then, these agreed that the one proclaimed was considered by the many to be less than the Forerunner. But they declared with one voice that in that heavenly and dreadful kingdom the Master will be proclaimed greater than the servant. For my part, I excuse myself from arbitrating between these, and I do not consider it my place to judge who spoke better. Nor will I say how those accused of condemning the Baptist to great lowliness might retort that neither have you, their accusers, conceived anything great by declaring the Master greater than the servant. (For what glory is it for the Master to be shown greater than the servant, and that at his ineffable and dreadful coming?) So I have judged that it is not my place to say any of these things. I cherish these men, who were above all high priests and servants of God, and I confess great gratitude for what they said. (Whatever raises objections in other people’s minds does not necessarily give any handle against those who first spoke. One may be content if someone who begins a lofty contemplation reaches the truth to some degree, and our renowned Fathers for the most part revealed the meaning of the divine oracles with great precision.) Still, while I honor and admire these men as highly as anyone, I will not keep silent about what has occurred to me. I see, then, that the Master’s aim here is not to show the Baptist as inferior to himself, or to anyone else, let alone as less honored than the least of all. Quite the contrary, his aim is to glorify him with praises. Of the views mentioned, one is perhaps unprofitable and the other demeaning. If you drive the herald down among the lowest, you will not preserve the loftiness of the one proclaimed either. And to belittle the servant, especially here, is superfluous and does not escape pettiness. The Master’s aim, however, is clearly directed toward praising the Forerunner, and very rightly. That great man was living in prison for the sake of the divine laws. He disregarded the evils that held him. He did not fear the sword or the slaughter, but feared that when death

came upon him, a ruinous belief might be left behind among the living, and the Master’s majesty might be greatly diminished through his own negligence. For many supposed that the herald was greater than the one proclaimed. Even some of his own disciples fell into this through self-love, drawing on their teacher’s preeminence to increase their own glory. When he saw this, he was all aflame, and did everything he could to destroy this wicked suspicion. Many times he tried to lead his disciples away from that opinion with various arguments. But when he saw that his words were being defeated by their attitude and that rivalry was winning out, he looked for another way, and resolved to persuade them by letting them see for themselves. And see how wisely he handles the matter. He sends the disciples to the one they envied, and by giving the message the form of a question, he arranges for them to gain their own salvation through what they would see. In this way the earlier error, once the disciples were corrected, would also be extinguished for the others and dissolve completely. As soon as they arrived, the Savior (who had also graciously granted the Baptist the wisdom to devise this plan) for the time being answered nothing to the question in words. He knew, he knew well, that the one who had proclaimed him in advance from the very womb, by leaping and by his mother’s tongue, and afterward by countless brilliant testimonies and declarations worthy of God, needed no instruction about him. Instead he displayed the incomparable greatness of his divinity through extraordinary signs and wonders, which was exactly what the sender was working toward. He held the envoys spellbound by the miracles before their very eyes, and then sent them back, now obedient to their teacher and heralds of his divinity. So the Baptist, by thus drawing his disciples away from error, contrived through them that other people too should run to the common Master. The Savior, for his part, urged his hearers to emulate the man’s other virtues as well, and welcomed him for so great a zeal and eagerness, and repaid him with praises fitting for the Master to give and justly deserved. For he who had appeared as the free benefactor of all would never have allowed the Baptist alone to be sent away unrewarded for the affection he had shown beforehand and for his burning love even unto slaughter. This, I think, is the first reason for the praises, but the following is no less important. John asked, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?” for the salvation of his disciples. But on the surface, to those who do not look into the ingenuity and wisdom of the one asking, the question suggests that the Baptist asked it out of ignorance. So that he might free him fully from this suspicion too

(for truly the greatest slander and accusation against a herald is ignorance of the one he proclaims), the Lord turns to the praises and weaves them in several ways. For it would truly be absurd if the Baptist should fall from his former glory through the very thing by which he would otherwise have gained. Therefore he offers the first praise from the verdict of the hearers themselves, and the third from the testimony and prediction of the prophets. Each of the remaining two comes from his own judgment as Master. The second way states the praise directly. The fourth weaves the encomium out of the absurdity that follows for those who supposed that the Baptist put the question out of ignorance. The first and fourth ways of praise are woven by refuting things that in no way belong to the Baptist but that some people have wrongly supposed. They are cast in the form of a question, and they call for and teach the opposite of what the question says. The middle ones set down the praise directly, as statements. Take the words “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the winds?” This sentence, cast as a question, does not declare the Baptist to be a reed. On the contrary, it establishes that he stands far from all who waver in their judgment like a reed. In the same way the saying “But he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he,” put forward in a similar manner, shows that not the least, indeed not anyone at all, is greater than the Forerunner. For the Savior would not suddenly have taken back the praises he was weaving, nor flung the one he was praising all at once among the last. Rather, he keeps the same thread throughout and nowhere allows the least in the kingdom to be thought greater than John in his preeminence. The praise woven from the hearers’ verdict, to put it more fully, runs something like this: “What did you go out into the wilderness for? To see a reed shaken by the wind? Or a man dressed in soft clothing? Clearly not at all. For you yourselves, by what you did toward him and by running out into the wilderness, testified to the opposite of this opinion. You believed him to be someone wonderful who had all but passed beyond human limits, as indeed he is. So neither has such a man now, through some change of heart or ignorance, put this question to me through his disciples. On the contrary, by a wise method he arranged for those he had taught to be assured by their own eyes of what he had taught them in words. For what reason could there be for such a man to undergo a change or decline from better things? Every falling away to the worse comes, to those to whom it comes, either through weakness of will, or the passion of love of pleasure, or love of money and the desire for this empty little glory. Through these comes also the slide into the other passions,

to which not a few others fall prey, but especially those dazzled by royal palaces and caught up in that dust. It is not easy for anyone to say how far beyond their reach John was. For he is not, he is not a reed that is tossed by the winds. He escaped, the Lord says, the ways of the unstable and the sickness of those who are blown about like a reed. Nor did he give himself over to soft clothing, or to the other things that weaken those in palaces, enslaved as they are to gold, pleasures and love of glory. No, the desert was at once his splendid home, his paradise and his palace. Camel’s hair covered his body, and a leather belt was around his loins, binding and deadening all the bodily and human stirrings on either side of it. And if you wish to consider his food too, he hardly partook of food at all [?], but only what was bitter and gave no nourishment, and not even that in full measure, but so as to cheat the very necessity of nature. Into such a life how could luxury dare to slip in, or fleeting glory, or wealth, which is a heavy and bitter tyrant both to those who have it and to those who lack it against their will? And not only do his deeds cry these things aloud, but you yourselves, he says, have presented yourselves as no less witnesses, from the deeds that drew your eyes and your minds. For you too bore witness by deeds that the Baptist stands higher than those who are unstable in mind and those enslaved to pleasures, glory and wealth, from which come change and decline for the worse, and ignorance.” This, then, is the type of praise drawn from the hearers’ verdict. What is the next? Clearly the one drawn from his own declaration as Master. Which is this? “Yes, I tell you, you went out to see a prophet,” as though they had clearly agreed to this by what they did. It is as if he said: “I know that you went out into the wilderness to see neither a man easily swayed in judgment, nor one fond of money or vainglorious, nor one overcome by luxury, but someone lofty and exalted, who shared in the gift of prophecy. And you supposed rightly. For yes, I tell you, you went out to see a prophet.” Then, not stopping there, he declares him even more than a prophet. And since judges, lawgivers and kings had also left a great name for virtue, he did not want him to be thought greater than the prophets yet inferior to someone among the others. So by one declaration covering all of them he proclaimed that the Baptist holds the first place, saying: “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist.” This, then, is the second type of the encomia. The third, set among the Master’s own praises, puts forward the testimony of prophecy. “For this is he,” he says, “of whom it is written: Behold, I send my messenger before your face,

who will prepare your way before you.” The fourth and last is the one chiefly under examination. Like the first, it proceeds by refuting a supposition that in no way fits the Baptist. It too takes the form of a perplexing question and proceeds neither directly nor as a statement. From the absurdity that results, it removes the base supposition, and from there it weaves and completes the encomium of the Baptist. What, then, is the false supposition? That some thought the Baptist did not know the one he proclaimed, and for that reason put the question. And what is the absurdity that follows? That he would for this reason have been cast out of the kingdom of heaven. For whom else would the least of all in it be greater than, except someone driven far away from it? Why he would be cast out needs no argument. Whoever is not firmly persuaded that he who was born of the Virgin, baptized by John, attested by the Father’s voice and pointed out by the Spirit who shares his nature is the Redeemer of the world and the destroyer of Hades, such a person is clearly outside the kingdom of heaven. For how could anyone inherit a kingdom who does not even know its Creator, the one who distributes it and allots its inheritance? How, then, is the absurdity refuted? First, from the matter itself: how is it not absurd that the one who proclaimed the kingdom to others should himself fall away from it? But also from what was said earlier. Suppose, then, that John did not know what he proclaimed, that he let what he had heard from above slip into forgetfulness, that he does not know the one he baptized, and that he asks in order to learn who the one expected is. Then clearly he will not be counted worthy of the kingdom at all, not even of the place where the least dwells. But this is among the most absurd of things, for other reasons and also from what was said above. For where is the prophet who does not even know what lies in his own hands? Where is the one who is more than the prophets, if he did not know the very one he proclaimed? And how could one be the greatest among those born of women who is not even worthy of the kingdom? So he is in no way less than the least in the kingdom of heaven. Nor was he ignorant of the one he proclaimed. He shaped his teaching into a question not so that he himself might learn, but so that he might improve his disciples by letting them see for themselves. This, then, is the unfolding of the whole meaning. The Master’s divine oracle, by a pointed and concise saying in the form of a perplexing question, presented the whole sense when he said: “But is the least in the kingdom of heaven greater than he?” This saying strikes us the moment we hear it, and by the sheer extent of its absurdity it does not allow us to be carried off into any unseemly supposition about the herald of the truth. At once we are driven to see the wisdom and usefulness of the question put through the disciples. From there, in turn, we are drawn still more to accept the praises. And we do not judge the Baptist to be less than the least

of those in the kingdom of heaven (far from it). Rather, we agree that he stood above judges, lawgivers, kings and even the patriarchs themselves, as the Truth itself clearly proclaimed. And very fittingly. He was held in prison and in countless afflictions, kept for death, enduring these things as a further contest for the sake of the divine ordinances. Yet his burning love for the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, did not wither. Instead it blossomed all the more, and strove against death to be rekindled further and made immortal. Nor did he cease proclaiming the heavenly Bridegroom with hand and tongue and by every means, longing to join everyone to him and to plant in them a love for the bridal chambers. It seems to me that he even rejoiced at the sword, was distressed that it was slow in coming, and hastened toward those in Hades, so that there too he might be the first to proclaim and announce in advance the one who was expected. Are these not things worthy of praise from the Master’s own tongue? He saw the sword, he saw the executioners, and he made the slaughter a spur to his love for the Master, turning wholly toward him. Truly, “among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist.” He touched the Master’s head. He proclaimed him from the womb. He proclaimed him until death. He drew the world to repentance. I pass over his life in the desert, the extraordinary way of living and conduct that shamed even the shameless Jews, and the more-than-human life that stopped their unguarded mouths. Is he not rightly the greatest among those born of women? Did he not deservedly receive the Master’s praise? Is the least in the kingdom of heaven greater than such a man? From what has been said, therefore, one must read “But he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” not as a statement, but in the same manner in which one also reads “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” And consider carefully that we were not forced to twist “in the kingdom of heaven” into some contrived sense, away from the obvious meaning known to all. Nor did we weave any overly elaborate additions into “least” to make it agree [?] with “greater among those born of women.” We only adjusted the original form of the saying to the interrogative type, and so we have presented the meaning of what is said clearly, even if at greater length than suits a letter.

QUESTION 223. If the Divine is everywhere, how is it a slander against the mystery to say that it is present in a woman’s womb? “Yes,” they say, “[?] present [?] of a woman, as also [?] no [?]; but for God to become incarnate from her, how is that possible?” Then, my good friend, you yourself also, of the [?] against the
[?] this. [?] entirely. [?] of the desert. Then, my good friend, you yourself also, of the [?] against the

…of the mystery [?] of slander, and you departed from it even against your will; and without noticing it you are passing over from the ranks of the enemy into the ranks of friends. For whoever drops the slander and seeks a demonstration of the proposition no longer contends by arguments that would keep him from being drawn away from his opinion, but by arguments through which he himself might come to accept it. And yet for someone prepared for this, it would have been enough to understand that the truth purges the problem of the slander. For if someone sees that what he flees as absurd not only contains no absurdity but even follows by the necessity of reason, how can he fail, once he has cast off the slander, to embrace it? Is virtue impossible? But I have shown that many pursue it. So the possible has been brought in its place, and what was formerly an exile now becomes its citizen. Is courage harmful? But I have shown it to be as profitable to life as anything is. So what seemed hateful because of the harm has become lovable, since it does not have the harm. Is it impossible for God to be present in the womb of a virgin? You agreed that it is rather impossible for him not to be present. What further proof does the proposition need? “But I must learn,” he says, “how it is possible for him to become incarnate.
