Or rather, if being present is God's incarnation, you will soon clothe him in the form of every living creature.” Now you have gone back, no longer to the side of friends but again to the hostility of enemies. But by the same arguments that defeated you before, you will not escape falling here either while you stand in battle array against the truth. So rise up for the skirmish. Does God have a providence for human beings greater than for the herd animals? Would you not say so? For both the creation of these animals and the providence over them exist for the sake of human need. So the presence of the divine is not alike in human beings and in the other animals either. For being one, it is said to be multiplied without multiplication. So your many forms have been reduced to the one form only, that of human beings. You see how easily the champion of unbelief falls. “And what of this?” he says. “Even if the Word has escaped the forms of the other animals, it still remains for us to speak of an incarnation not from one virgin but from all women and virgins.” But, my good man, here too the fall of the shameless is plain in the very things in which they have already been shameless. Nevertheless, since you have risen up again, as it seems, [?] it will be enough for me to throw you down again with wise arguments. For I would say that it is rather impossible for one who has once become incarnate to need a second incarnation. Therefore an incarnation through all the virgins has no place either, but only the one through a single virgin.

QUESTION 224. Do the demons [know? ?] that, if they repent of what they dared, they are released from their daring? Or, having once fallen from divine wisdom, were they also deprived of the knowledge of it? If the former, how did an incorporeal nature,

not dragged down by such heavy weights of flesh, become worse than the nature that is held down by the flesh? For many human beings who had driven on to the very extreme of evil were raised through repentance even above the way of life they had before. But if after the fall ignorance completely seized them, both of their daring and of turning back, and they sleep shut in such deep darkness, how is it that they do not let up in wickedness toward human beings, wickedness surpassing all imagining? For they both provoke people and drag them down with them into unspeakable acts of daring, in cases where often not even premeditation came first. Now if one were to put the many arguments more concisely, the problem, as I think, would amount to this: the demon fell; does it repent? “But it was hardened.” Where did the hardening come from? For the demon is itself the cause of hardening for others. If it has been hardened [?], how was it not hardened [?]? But neither [is it possible?] for those who have been hardened to harden others and to increase the hardening. And how did something fashioned entirely for good not incline toward good at all, but fall toward that to which it was not led, as toward that [?]? And what could that be which received them, if the race of demons had not turned?

QUESTION 225. Chapters, set out as a dialogue between a Hellenist and a Christian, by which the Trinity is established. HELLENIST: Since I know that you are a champion and defender of the Christian doctrine, and moreover distinguished for your fairness, I would not hesitate, if you yourself agree, to subject the meaning of the doctrine honored among you to the scrutiny of reason. For I see much in it that is unpersuasive; and whenever it puts on the appearance of persuasiveness, it displays no less a refutation of itself and overturns what it set out to establish. CHRISTIAN: How so? What argument has persuaded you to think and speak like this? That your opinion is not at odds with us and with the truth, there is no need to learn; and that the purity of piety cannot be seen by those held fast in the fog of false doctrines, this too is not hard to grasp. But tell me what arguments led you to say that the arguments about our piety, while contriving to be persuasive, rather slide off into what is unpersuasive and undemonstrated. HELL.: I will tell you, then, not new or recent arguments, but ones put forward long ago by your ancient Fathers. For these men, bringing in a Son and a Spirit for God (for this is the doctrine and the preaching of you Christians), weave some such tangle in the form of a question: “You would not call God irrational, without a Word. And if you too shun blasphemy, you will certainly say that he has a Word. And unless you suppose him breathless and of the nature of insensible things, he certainly has a Spirit as well. Therefore we must sing the praises of God as a Trinity.” And they weave alongside these some other such

sophisms: “God is not among those deprived of offspring; therefore he is [?] of offspring and has begotten. And he could not be without a Spirit either. So from these premises, again, God would be a Trinity.” Many other such things could be gathered; for those who spend their leisure in the manner of dreamers it would not be hard to collect them and to indulge themselves, though not others, with a speculation that has gone astray on these matters and persuades those who do not examine things to accept what is unpersuasive. CHR.: What argument, or rather what reckless madness, has prepared you to babble so much against piety? HELL.: You have said nothing yet; these are only the outer gates of your fairness and kindness. And do not be annoyed with me; [?] and nothing of what you ought to be [?], but at the proper time we will hide what follows [?]. CHR.: Speak freely, fearing nothing; for you will find nothing inside bolder than the outer gates. Unless you yourself, not yet constrained by the necessity of the arguments, sharpen your tongue to insult piety and raise your eyebrows in the manner of fools. HELL.: I will say nothing base or insulting of my own. But if what pass for demonstrations among you bring such things with them, it is not I who bring them; those who put them forward are liable to the charge. CHR.: Speak, then; the test of truth will not overlook what is mistaken. HELL.: I will say nothing else, but only these very things which I said when I began the discussion. CHR.: How so? HELL.: Those who bring in Christ as [Son?] of God ask whether God has a Word or not. CHR.: They do ask it; but I do not know whether they ask it in the form into which you reshape the question. But for now let it stand, so that another inquiry, taken up before this examination is finished, may not cut off [?] the sequence of your argument and make the whole account unintelligible. But if you ask me what I would say, you will know [?] that your judgment too inclines toward another opinion [?]. HELL.: Whenever I hear this question put forward, I break into a smile and ask the questioner which half of the alternative he wants to hear; for I find it not unpleasant to say either. If I say that God has a Word, I have taken away the Word's being God; for the Word does not have a Word, unless you want to compete with the Greeks in calling on a multitude [?] of gods. And if I say that he does not have one, your question has collapsed at the very starting line. And under the [?] too comes the question whether God is barren or generative and breathing, and all the other such sophisms that are staged as if on a stage. These things are not insult but refutation; they dispel the contrivance or the [?], and expose your mischief.

CHR.: Well done! The whole [argument?] against piety, festering for so many years, has at last and with difficulty been [blunted?]; and if you are willing to come to your senses and look, you will see how much strength it had to ravage what lies within [?]. HELL.: How so? CHR.: I do not think it has escaped you, as has been said, that these things are put forward by the pious, but not in the way you put them. HELL.: Really? In what other way? CHR.: Well, it is not what they ask, but something else. HELL.: Again I am cleared of a just charge and of great blame in censuring things of which not even you are a defender [?]. For by abandoning the things I am charging and bringing forward others instead, however much confidence you have given to what you bring forward, just so much lack of confidence have you assigned to the things attacked by us. CHR.: But how could anyone look on you more kindly, or would you call him noble and good? For having fallen where you deserved, you not only [do not rejoice?] if someone raises you up, but you even demand thanks because he did not leave you lying there [?]. HELL.: How so? CHR.: Because you accused them of what no one puts forward; and seeing yourself, it seems, being driven out of your accusation, you ask [?] for the things in which you went wrong. You do not think that you owe thanks if someone moves you away from your rashness; instead, because you rushed at some things and slandered others, you think highly of yourself. And yet what could be worse than such folly? HELL.: Before the refutations one should not raise one's eyebrows or think highly of oneself; for at what [?] would anyone mock those who give an account or put forward arguments? CHR.: Well said. Now follow my reasoning: they do not put the question, “Does God have

HELL.: How else, then? CHR.: Is there some Divinity enthroned above all beings, creating them and watching over them, or not? HELL.: This has nothing to do with my argument. For if I do not attach to the divine nature the attributes that belong to it, I will not for that reason seem to be slandering the sophists. CHR.: That is not what I mean; but give yourself a little [?] to listening. This Divinity (and I do not mention [?] the hymns), will you call it rational and breathing, or irrational and breathless? Answer me boldly and seriously. HELL.: I would not want to say either. CHR.: But does not either answer lead you away from your earlier insult? If you say rational and breathing, you will not force us to say that the Word has a word or the Spirit a breath. And if you say that that Divinity has no share in reason and in the breath that is the source of life, [?] you plunge yourself, not others, into the utmost impiety. And neither

do you leave [?] any room for the polytheism of Hellenic godlessness against us, nor is the Word cast out [?], nor indeed the Spirit of the Godhead. You see how the same things, when they are not put forward in the same way, stir up a great surge and turmoil for those who have no experience of the wise and irrefutable method. Why are you silent? If you have understood, your understanding should not go soft; and if you have not, nothing, as you see, prevents you from saying again what you think. HELL.: I marvel how the same argument, when shaped differently, gave so many handles for attack, while now, put forward by you, it was clearly shown to be free of them all. And not only this, but what you proclaim seems to lead to conviction. CHR.: It is not only in the thesis we have discussed, my excellent friend, that one can see this, but in many others too: the form of the argument and the way it is presented, when handled deceitfully, turn into perplexity, but when put forward straightforwardly, preserve and guard their proper dignity. HELL.: For example? CHR.: Let us leave aside, if you like, matters far afield; but I must mention one that, together with the demonstration already discussed, also came in for its share of mockery. HELL.: Which do you mean? CHR.: I will not ask again whether God is generative or not, lest by taking away generation you take away the Godhead of the Son along with it, or by granting it you weave us a chain of polytheism. Rather, I would ask something like this: whether the divine (I leave aside for now the hymns that that blessed nature compels us to say)—whether the divine, I say, is generative, or has been deprived of this power. And when the mind of the simple person, instead of inclining toward the absence of begetting, turns toward begetting, we [know?] the Son, neither estranging him from the Godhead nor confessing begetting as a property [of each?]; for these things belong to the whole Godhead, not to each of the persons spoken of in it. What is the meaning of “Where have you come from?” The utterance does not simply, as one might think, present only the form of a question; it also discloses the contemplation of a deeper inquiry. “You,” he says, “who were condemned for your arrogance to have your dwelling among lowly and earthly things, where have you come from, or how have you come to these things, when you have no authority to meddle with the lives of holy men, but have been cast out only among those who, through the offenses of their own way of life, make you an instigator and supplier of absurdities? Where did you come from, then, to set yourself up as auditor of a life that is no concern of yours?”

QUESTION 227. In “God sent forth his Son, born …,” should one say gennōmenon or genomenon, with one n? One must say genomenon, “born of a woman,” just as also genomenon, “born under the law,” with a single n. First, because of the continuous parallelism of the thoughts and the words. Second, because Christ has been born of the Virgin—gegennētai, written with two n's in the second syllable—but he is not now being born, gennatai; for he was born of the Virgin once. And let no one be led into error by the words of Gregory the Theologian. For when he said “Christ is born,” he did not mean that Christ is continually being born of the Virgin, but that the festival then being held happened to be the day of the Lord's birth. In every way [?], then, one must take care not to write or pronounce genomenon, “born of a woman,” with two n's. On nature and hypostasis. What was the visible aspect of Christ, a nature or a hypostasis? [?] of the composite hypostasis of the Word, which is enhypostatic. On hypostasis. Is the composite hypostasis of the Word of the same nature as the simple hypostasis of the Word, or of a different nature, or of the same nature in one respect and of a different nature in another? If it is of the same nature, and the simple hypostasis of the Word is of the same nature as that of the Father, then the composite hypostasis is also of the same nature as the simple hypostasis of the Father. How then is the composite of the same nature as the simple? And how could the Father's hypostasis not also be called composite? And thirdly, the three simple hypostases of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, together with the composite hypostasis of the Word, make a tetrad. If it is of a different nature, a tetrad remains in this case too; and how is it of a different nature from itself, unless one speaks of two separate things, the composite and the simple? And if it is of a different nature in one respect and of the same nature in another, it will follow in this case too that the Trinity is called a tetrad; and it will also follow that we are at a loss how it can be of a different nature from itself in one respect and in another

The absurdities followed from taking the one as two from the start; for it was from this that, on these hypotheses, the Trinity came to be inferred to be a tetrad. For the composite hypostasis of the Word is not one thing [?] … par excellence [?] … Cotelier; the Theophany, Works, vol. 1, p. 615.

and the simple hypostasis another, so that one could ask, as though about two things, whether they are of the same nature, or of a different nature, or of the same nature in one respect and of a different nature in another; rather, it is one and the same. So to those who ask these questions it is necessary and true to answer: it is neither of the same nature, nor of a different nature, nor a combination of these. [?] without flesh (the incarnate hypostasis of the Word [?]) [?] (of which the hypostasis is one and the same [?]). On the Godhead. Are “Godhead” and “God” the same, or different? If different, what is this Godhead, and what is the Godhead besides God? But if the same, and each of the three hypostases is God, then each is also Godhead. Did Christ assume man in general or a particular man? We say that he assumed neither man in general nor a particular

QUESTION 232. What is the meaning of “So we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were appealing through us; be reconciled”? “For Christ” has been said in the sense of “in Christ's place,” since the disciples took over the ministry in place of their Teacher. You might also understand it this way: we too often go on embassies on behalf of worthy people, and by adding mention of the person concerned we make the embassy more deserving of respect. Paul does the same when he says, “We are ambassadors for Christ”: by the greatness of the person he moves those to whom the embassy is addressed to reverence. “It is on behalf of him, then,” he says, “that we appeal—on behalf of the one who reconciled the world through his death.” So we too must be obedient, since otherwise, as far as it depends on us, that great and unspeakable love for mankind shown toward us will remain ineffective and be insulted. Then, exalting the person still further, he says, “For God made him who knew no sin to be sin.” And again there is the addition of another amplification, drawn from the benefaction, Patrologia Graeca 101.

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. … [show]ing its loftiness: “so that we,” he says, “might become the righteousness of God in him.” “Working together with him,” he says, “we also appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain.” In this way Paul makes clear what it means to be an ambassador for Christ. To what end? So that you may not, as far as your part goes, prove his grace, great as it is, to have been in vain. And it is not only we who bring the embassy to you; it is as though God the Father himself were appealing with us on behalf of the Son. Respect the ambassadors, be ashamed before those who appeal to you, revere the one on whose behalf the appeal is made. When the saying is taken in this way, “for Christ” will be understood not as “in Christ's place,” but, as has been said, in its plain sense.

QUESTION 233. What is the meaning of “or, to speak more precisely, which the Godhead is”? Since, he says, the phrase “in which” does not present a single thing—as in “in heaven” and the things in it (for heaven is one thing and what is in it another)—he adds briefly, so that you may not suspect any such distinction here too: “or, to speak more precisely, which the Godhead is.” One can also take an image of what is said. Suppose someone said that kingship is in kings, and then, wishing to put it more precisely, instead of “is in them” added, “I say that they themselves are the kingship.” He clearly attaches the power of kingship to them, but he does not change the nature of the kings into a quality. In the same way nothing prevents one who says “or rather, which the Godhead is” from showing that the Godhead is inseparable from the hypostases and undivided, while not dissolving each of them into the Godhead or into the same nature [?]. Rather, preserving the distinctive property of the hypostases, he shows by these words that they are of one nature, one Godhead and one essence.

QUESTION 234. Why was the person leprous all over considered clean under the [law?], while the one leprous in part was considered unclean? Because the one who was leprous throughout had no hope of healing. For this reason God in his love for mankind did not think it right to inflict a double penalty on him—I mean the leprosy, and also the name that comes from uncleanness and exclusion from the temple. But for the one leprous in part, since the hope of healing lightened much of his distress, it is shown, reasonably enough, that he did not enjoy the same kindness. [?] For the Godhead is one in three, and the three are one: “those in whom the Godhead is, or, to speak more precisely, which the Godhead is” [?] … in three formulas of the three [?].

QUESTION 235. Why is the Spirit called the image of the Son? And what is the tetractys of the Pythagoreans? The Son is called the image of the Father both because he is referred to him as to his cause and because he displays and images the Father in himself, as he says somewhere to Philip: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” But the Spirit is the image of the Son not as being referred to him as to a cause—far from it!—but because it is impossible to come to know the Son in any other way unless one takes the all-holy Spirit as a fellow worker to guide one by the hand. The Pythagoreans honor the tetractys as being an image of the four elements.

QUESTION 236. Why does Jacob anoint the stone? He prefigures the hard, stony heart of the Gentiles: it will be anointed with the Holy Spirit and set apart for God, as that stone was. His anointing of the stone might also be understood in another way: because through unspeakable mercy the flesh that was assumed was to be anointed with the Godhead. And the Lord is [the stone?], the precious cornerstone, joining the two together in himself.

QUESTION 237. Why does he bow down upon the top of the staff? He bows down to the staff of his son—he, the mind that sees God; for this is what “Israel” means. He did so because he was foretelling that the flower from the staff would be worshiped not only by the young but also by the aged Israel. He also does not distribute his blessings equally among his sons: some he places under blessings, others he exposes as sons of curses. For just as he fathered the old people, so the Lord, through spiritual birth pangs, gives birth to the new people and grants them a share in the blessing—not to all, but to those who have made themselves worthy. So Jacob does not distribute the blessing to his children out of favoritism; he makes their deeds the judge of the distribution. [?] … what John the Theologian says about life. [?]

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Question 238. [What is the meaning of] "Against you [only] have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight [?] … that you may prevail when you are judged"? David breaks into another man's marriage and adds murder to adultery, and he contrived to keep the deed hidden. But when God, through the prophet, brings him to be convicted of what he had dared, the man comes to himself and says: "Against you only have I sinned." That is: even though Uriah has been wronged, I have learned from these reproofs that the sin was dared against you, and I run to you for pardon. You did not even let it be counted as a sin against my servant, but as an outrage against you, the Master. Why? "So that you may be justified in your words": that is, so that your justice may prevail over human scheming, and so that no sinner may imagine he can outwit your judgment. This is what "You will prevail when you are judged" means: you prevail because no one can be seen to be righteous beside you, and because by your goodness the all- [?] … [?] Taur. 82.

Question 239. What is the meaning of "I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh"? Paul did not say this of himself. He was taking on the person of human nature. The good does not dwell in our flesh when we have been enslaved to sin by habit and by time and carry the evil within us as something lasting and hard to wipe out. Someone who has been enslaved by long practice of these things finds, even if he wants to run back to virtue, that his intention is hard to carry out and hard to achieve. That is why he says: "It is no longer I who do it." In other words: I know the deed is not mine [?], since I am hard pressed by it. It belongs to the sin that dwells in me, which has made its home there firm and immovable. So I lament, seeking freedom, and cry out: "Wretched man that I am!"

… many of whom stripped for the contest and fought the struggle with no lack of spirit, yet did not let us see the victory as decisive (I will say nothing harsher). Still, we have gathered quite a few points to work from out of the holy and blessed men who came before us, and we have joined to them those that the kindness of divine favour did not refuse to grant us. We pray that your zeal and hope will not go away empty of grace and of a knowledge that needs no other standard from elsewhere, or, failing that, that it will need only very slight further correction. To ask for a treatment that lacks nothing is to force the writing to great length, while to demand brevity is to allow many necessary things to be left out. Nevertheless, as far as I am able, I will try to carry forward the discussion of the fixed term of life, as you have asked.

2. Some people bring forward chasms in the earth, shipwrecks, plagues in the air and other such events that bring death on many different people all at once, and then ask whether these people were destined to come together and meet the same end. They seem to me to be turning into a question what is plainly seen. It follows that they need perception rather than proof, and, without probing more deeply, I would say they lack altogether the judgment that comes from reasoning. To admit that things exist and then ask whether they exist is simply to put on display the weakness of the faculty of the mind, which cannot be put into words. Each crowd is caught within the same limit of death, and this is agreed. And the term is nothing other than the end of each person. So how are they not shown up as asking whether a term has come about, when they admit that it has, by asking whether one fixed term was set for all of them? That is one point. The second is this: why do they take refuge in a multitude [?] from which a single demand for its end is exacted all at once? Clearly because they admit a term for some people but dispute it for the majority. Otherwise they would never have devised the appeal to a multitude dying all at once as their chief weapon. And indeed, if they say there is a term for some but not for all, then the very arguments by which they themselves tacitly accept a term for some allow those who say there is a term for all to force them, and drag them even against their will, into agreement. They hold that some people have a term and use certain arguments to fend off the difficulties raised by those who fight against [?] that opinion. If they were reasonable [?], they would use the same arguments to teach others how to fend off the attacks that they themselves [bring] against those who say that one common term for all has come upon the multitude in question.

3. Moreover, it is not only when some unusual disaster strikes that whole crowds of different kinds are handed over by one term … (Note 6: for "at one", perhaps read "under one".)

… of death. The ordinary human condition of life also shows such things every day and sets such stories before us. There is no day on which old man and youth, child, woman and virgin, poor and rich, subject and ruler are not caught together in the same net of death. Why, then, do they flee from the everyday condition of life and take refuge in the destruction of people that comes from disasters? Clearly because they do not think they can achieve their purpose from the former, while in disasters their difficulty finds room. And yet there too different kinds of people are likewise found handed over at the same time to a single death. They have not dared to press their difficulty from there, and so, by what is taught in those cases, they show that their bold display in these cases is the work of rashness and audacity. It offers nothing at all that is persuasive or compelling to the one who undertakes it.

4. God did not make death. He set life before us, and then death, which lies before us not by natural necessity but by free choice. For sin, when it was full-grown, gave birth to death. Look at Adam: he was destined to live a course of nine hundred and thirty years, and, had he not sinned, [?] it would have been completed in full [?]. Life was ordained by God, but death was also foreknown. So God is not the cause of death, for foreknowledge did not bring about death; the transgression of the commandment did. Enoch is still alive. How so? He received his translation as the prize of piety. And Noah? He was justified and saved the seeds of the world as a second [father], while [the world] suffered death beneath the waters because of its sins [?]. What of Lot, a Sodomite by residence but not by choice? What of Moses together with the Israelite people, when the Egyptians were plunged into the abyss? What of those whose corpses fell in the wilderness, and of those who did not stumble? What of the tribal leaders who joined in revolt and whom the earth swallowed alive? And, to pass over every destruction brought on by sin and by free will, what of the words "If you are willing, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if not, the sword shall devour you"? What of the godless priests whom Elijah burned up with divine fire, and the two companies of fifty, and those of whom [it was said], "I have kept for myself seven thousand men," and the dead man whom he raised? If God spun these and similar things like a Clotho, where is free will, not to mention the absurdity of it? What of the final destruction of the Israelites, the penalty exacted by an Italian spear for the Lord's blood and the gore of the prophets? Did it come from a fixed term, from free will, or from something else? What of the bloody murder committed against Abel … [?] Gen. 5 [?]; Isa. 1:19 [?].

[?] If a term had been fixed, why is Cain, as though he were only its servant, condemned as a fratricide to groaning and finally to the total destruction of his whole family? And how is it that divine law, from Noah until now, deliberately condemns the murderer to death? Or how should the case of Agag be reckoned? If the term set for him had been completed, he would not have died [?], even though Saul did not want to strike him [?]. What of Job's children? Did they die by a term, or at Satan's request? What of Hezekiah? What of the Ninevites? What of all those after them who have been saved, or are being saved, by good fortune? What of "that someone lay down his life for one he loves," of which the holy martyrs are the model? How should Phinehas's deed be classed: as wrongdoing, or as a term? Where does that leave "If you do good, you will live long"? Where does it leave "Sins diminish tribes"? What of those who hang themselves of their own will out of fear of death, or kill themselves in any other way? What of those who suffer death against their will at the hands of others, or from hunger, or surfeit, or extreme cold or heat, or a pestilent disease, or anything too strong for help or beyond cure, not to mention every death that comes through loss of blood? What if someone leaves an artery unbound, willingly or not? Will not the intelligent spirit, which is bound up in the blood, escape with the blood of his life, since blood congeals into flesh? For flesh and spirit go together. And how is this? Because the divine, self-subsistent Word became flesh and dwelt among us, around the one who bound securely [?]. What of land-dwellers killed by earthquake or fire, and those kept safe at sea, while others perish in the waves and others on land come to no harm? What of the dead raised by Elisha? What of those raised by Christ, the author of life? What of Tabitha? What of Ananias and Sapphira? What of the raisings of the dead that the other saints have worked as wonders up to the present day? If the term had been fulfilled, how is it that what was ordained has not been carried through?

5. Does the whole Old [Testament] know any term set by design other than the one alone that comes with the transgression of sin: "In the hour you eat, you shall die"? Whether the Gospel proclaims a term, I cannot say. I know of one supreme term, spoken by Christ. The Pharisees asked him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices, and about those whom

the tower in Siloam fell on and killed, whether they were the worst sinners of all. He said no. And he adds not only "Unless you repent" and the rest, but also sets out the term in the example of the fig tree, saying: "Cut it down; why should it use up the ground?" Likewise the divine Apostle adds a term for those who, as in my own day [?], partake unworthily of the immaculate mysteries: "That is why many are weak and ill, and a good number have fallen asleep." What of David, the ancestor of God, who sets the measure [of life] at a handbreadth, at seventy or, for the strong, eighty years, and links toil to whatever goes beyond that? Then he says: "Bring my soul out of prison"; and again, "Do not take me away in the midst of my days"; and, "Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days."

7. Which of the apostles, or of [?], or of the holy Fathers, writes about a term? If they appeal to Basil the Great, those who think so understand him wrongly. Everywhere he holds that death comes from us and not from God. And what he adds about the term amounts to this. The saint's aim was to show that God is not the cause of evils. Going through the matter point by point, he showed that falling sick is ours and healing is God's, in keeping with the words, "There is no affliction that the Lord has not made."

Question 241. What is the meaning of "You are of the father of the devil," and who is the devil's father? The first objection is that nowhere in our sacred Scripture, neither in the older books of the Law nor in the age of grace itself, can the expression "father of the devil" be found, even though much has often been said about that evil power. Scripture is found calling the enemy of our race, the author of evil, Satan, devil, apostate and the like. Sometimes it calls someone a "son of the devil" when he shows the devil's evil offspring in himself and is shaped by the stamp of deceit, as in blessed Paul's words to Elymas, "son of the devil." That is one point: in Scripture's usage a "father of the devil" is never named. Second, not about the father of the devil [?] …

… but now: "We have one Father, God." Not "We have as father the Father of God." The Saviour leads them away from the relationship of sonship implied in the name, since they had cut themselves off and severed themselves from likeness to him. "Do you dare," he says, "to call yourselves sons of the Father? You are of the devil." Then: "And you want to do his commandments"—clearly not those of the devil's father. For where has such a one handed down commandments, when Scripture does not know him at all? He means the commandments of the devil, who is your father. These are fornication, adultery, theft, murder, lying, and all the other evils of which the devil, by his own will, became the sower, and the leader in daring and doing what should never be dared. And "He was a murderer from the beginning": to whom could this more fittingly be applied than to the devil himself? With his tongue he drove Adam out of paradise and brought about his death and corruption. For God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living. Who else forged death through a lie, and corruption against Adam's inmost being, except the one who handed over the serpent and through it mixed the deadly poison of blasphemy against God for the woman, and through her for Adam? From all these things and others like them it is shown that the Saviour's word is speaking about the devil and names him the father of the ungrateful Jews. For they too were eager to call God their father and to be counted among his sons. The Saviour divides the present saying into two parts and again weaves each into the other. At one point he puts the devil first and the Jews second; at another he mentions the Jews first and then brings in the devil. So, having first dealt with the devil and shown from the kinship and likeness of their works that the Jews have him as their father, he turns again to the Jews themselves, on whose account the whole discussion had begun. And he says: When the Jew speaks a lie, as you do now when you say "We have God as our father" and "We have Abraham as our father," he speaks from his own. That is, he speaks from the belly and not from the judgments of the Spirit. That he is a liar is shown by his own boasting, and it is plainly demonstrated by the one he has set up as his father through the likeness of his deeds. That is why he says: When the Jew speaks a lie, it is because he is a liar, both he and his father. And this father, as has often been said, the Saviour declared and named to be the devil and no one else. (Note 25: Colb. reads "now the Jews".)

[Question 242.] What is the new moon, what are the Calends, and what are the [Ides]? Those who led [?] the Romans divided each month into three parts. The new moon, that is, the beginning of the month, they called the Calends. After that they called the ninth day of the month the Nones. In addition to these they called the third part the Ides. Greek speakers derive the name from the full appearance of the moon, while the Roman priests derive it from a rite of theirs that they called idulis, meaning the sacrifice of white sheep. There is also much other technical discussion about it, which would need more leisure and care.

Question 243. On the divine nature and hypostasis. "The one nature of the Word incarnate" puts forward a single, pure meaning, one that agrees with those who teach two natures united [unconfusedly] according to hypostasis. This is clear from the fact that Cyril used both forms of expression. He neither rejected "one nature of the Word incarnate" nor denied "two natures inseparably united according to hypostasis." And not only Cyril, but all who after him were known to belong to the party of true religion. It is no wonder if, when the expression plainly signifies true religion, the heretical mind takes it captive for its own malice. Those who put mischief before learning are bold enough to twist other sacred expressions too. Yet these men achieve no more than those others did, except to give proof of their malicious mind. If they do not embrace the right meaning, their malicious scheming will surely turn back on them. They will be driven to the blasphemy that God the Word bore flesh only in appearance, as the followers of Mani say; or that the Word was changed into flesh; or that the nature of the body was swallowed up by the invisible, supernatural and incorporeal Godhead. Blessed Cyril and countless other Fathers often use "nature" in place of "hypostasis," and not even the Confusionists are forbidden to do this. So how can they fail to make us Orthodox laugh when they brandish Cyril's phrase "one nature of the Word incarnate"? If one can see that it was Cyril's habit often to use "nature" in place of "hypostasis," then he speaks with us rather than with the apostates. For it is our position both to hold and to say (Note 27: perhaps "Romans".)

"one hypostasis of the Word incarnate." See how they fight against God and are outcasts [?]. Even against their will they concede what they do not say when they plunder [?], and they become accusers of the very things for which they pretend they would undergo countless deaths rather than abjure them. The Acephali, that is, the followers of Severus, split nature into two natures. They call one particular and the other universal, though this notion contributes nothing to their impiety. This empty talk does not support their absurd opinion when they spin tales of one nature in Christ, and it does nothing to oppose the Orthodox. They must be asked this: when they say that Christ is from two natures, from which two do they say he is—the particular ones, as they call them, or the common ones? If from the particular ones, how are they not ashamed to insult Nestorius, whose doctrine they embrace? For what is composed of two hypostases cleverly contrives a composition into one person, but nonetheless introduces and teaches two self-subsistent hypostases and puts this forward as common doctrine [?]. To say that Christ is composed of two common natures puts Nestorius to shame, since what is composed is not necessarily divided into self-subsistent hypostases. But to say that he is composed of two hypostases, as they are forced to say, proclaims Nestorius's mind rather than their own. Whether someone says that Christ is composed of two hypostases, or exists in two, or is two hypostases, Nestorius's war against God is strengthened. In the same way, if someone says that the hypostasis of the Word gave subsistence in itself to human nature, then whether he says "from two natures," "in two" or "two," he equally confesses the hypostatic union and proclaims the true faith. For Christ is composed of God the Word and human nature. The Word, which is a hypostasis, became flesh, and the flesh does not introduce a person but declares the human nature.

Question 244. How [?] is the apostolic saying "He seated us at the right hand of God the Father" to be explained? Divine Scripture has proclaimed that we have become superior to angels through the coming of the Word in the flesh, and also that in the resurrection we shall be equal to angels. "For he seated us at the right hand of God the Father," as the divine Paul cries out, and so on. These statements do not conflict. Because what was taken from us shares the Father's throne, we have clearly risen above the glory and honour of the angels. And because in the resurrection [we shall] no longer [have] any of the things of the flesh [?] … to sit with me on my throne, and so on.

…so that we are neither dragged down, nor swept away, nor at all placed in need of any of the things the nature of the flesh was enslaved to, he grants us kinship with the lot of the incorporeal beings. So we will rightly be both equal to the angels and better than them. We will be better because our nature, in the one who assumed it, has taken its seat beside the Father. And each of us will have received equality with the incorporeal minds through impassibility and incorruption, and through being freed from all bodily things, from passions and leapings, and from material grossness [?]. But we must look closely at the saying, "They will be like angels of God." It does not proclaim an equality of nature. It means that they will suffer none of the fleshly things they suffered before: in the resurrection they too, freed from fleshly things, will live in a way that resembles the impassibility of the angels. Yet we are better than the angels in another way as well: when we slipped, the Son of God took up our nature and saved it, but he did not do so with theirs. And we must look for the reason. It is that they led others astray, while we were among those led astray. They also had many advantages for not sinning: being hard to affect, being nearer to God, and being incorporeal. Humans, by contrast, are tipped toward mercy by their greater susceptibility and by being dragged down by the body and bound to it. And, the greater point, no others have been born after the fallen angels on whose account their fall might have drawn the Lover of mankind to mercy. Those who transgressed remain content with their transgression forever. Further, taking on the nature of angels is nothing like, nor even close to, taking on that of humans [?]. For what would it have profited those who did not fall? And if it were for the sake of the fallen, how would those who had not fallen not be worse off than the fallen? Or must this be worked out further? Further, the Word, made flesh, taught us the lessons of virtue and of piety. Through them, by his grace, when we act rightly, the unending inheritance of the kingdom of heaven that he promised has become ours. But the angelic nature already had knowledge of both virtue and piety. It knew virtue, as is clear from how it dragged toward the opposite and enticed those it tripped up. It knew piety likewise, as is clear from what they cried out: "I know who you are, the Holy One of God," and "Have you come before the time to torment us?" and countless other things. So it would have been in vain for him to enter the nature of the angels. Further, the Word is made flesh to show us, through what he did, the road by which our ascent to heaven will be provided. But the demons have before them the orders of their own kind, from the lot they once shared, which show forth blessedness through what they do. Yet in the madness of their will they neither follow them nor turn

back to them. So it would be pointless for the Word of God to enter the nature of angels. Rather, it would lead them into a greater and heavier punishment, if that is possible, than the one laid up for them. Further, if the Word had meant to enter the nature of angels, how could he have done so with no birth to serve as the means? And if this had simply been granted to the demons through appropriation and a relational union, they had torn themselves away from it. Further, which of them would he have made his own in the fullest sense? If it were those who stood firm, what would the fallen have gained? Even before, while those remained in the better state, the demonic was wretched. If it were the fallen, where is justice? And how would there not then be room to choose what Paul condemned, "Let us do evil"? Further, since birth is not the means of coming into being for the angelic powers, the Word of God could not have assumed their nature as such, only some single individual. And whichever one he took, that one alone would he have saved. So he would have had to put on countless angelic individuals. Rather, there would be no mercy [?] for the demons, who showed themselves instruments of all wickedness.

Question 245. Why do we renounce Satan and not wicked people? We renounce Satan and his works, and not wicked people, for several reasons. First, so that we do not take from this renunciation occasions, however unreasonable, to hate our own kind, turn away from them, shun them and renounce them. Second, suppose we renounced wicked people, and not only we but the teachers and apostles before us. Which sinner would then have been saved? Renunciation breeds aversion, and aversion does away with exhortation and teaching, and with them conversion and repentance are done away with as well. Third, who would the person be who says, "I renounce sinners, or wicked people"? If he called himself one of the sinners, he would be renouncing himself. If he called himself one of the righteous, then, to leave aside everything else, at the very time of repentance and salvation he would be digging for himself a pit of boasting and of Pharisaic ruin. Fourth, it was not a human being who deceived in the beginning, but the evil one. Fifth, Satan cannot be changed from his wickedness. Sixth, the renunciation of Satan's works also includes whatever a person does, since its seed comes from there, from the deception; for it is traced back to him.

Question 246 [?]. Why are Gurias and his companions called Confessors? The martyrs Gurias and his companions might be called Confessors not because they confessed Christ in the arena, for that is a contest common to all the martyrs. It is because they were taken as overseers and guarantors of the solemn agreements that people make with one another. They never betrayed the hopes of those who trusted in them, and they exacted just punishment from those who broke what had been agreed. Since they became fervent and inexorable overseers of the agreements people make with one another, they were fittingly allotted the name of Confessors.

Question 247. Why is Christ crucified? The Word of God, who is God, is crucified after becoming flesh for several reasons. He is crucified to show plainly that the devil acts unjustly, and to display his unsurpassable love for humankind. He is crucified so that the claim that he is God would not seem easy and become an occasion for many to make gods of themselves, so that in abolishing error he would not bring in a ruinous error [?]. He is crucified so that, by setting himself forth as an example of endurance and perseverance to those tried by abuse, plots and mistreatment leading to death, he might prepare them to bear what befalls them nobly and with thanksgiving. He is crucified so that he might reveal more fully how utterly mighty his power is. To overcome an adversary by strength, by hand, by weapons and by allies is praiseworthy, but it belongs among ordinary deeds and shows nothing exceptional of divine working. To abolish and triumph over Death itself, and Hades, and the devil, and the principalities and powers of the world, and to do it through death: that would truly belong to God's almighty power, which is beyond mind and thought. And he is crucified so that, by showing how abundant his good gifts to us are, he might make us debtors of pure love toward him and of a life lived according to his laws. Through these the gain comes back to us ourselves, for it is our inheritance of the kingdom, and a life amid indescribable…

Question 248. How can the apostle's saying, "Signs are not for those who believe but for unbelievers," be reconciled with the Lord's words, "Your faith has saved you," and "He could not do signs because of their unbelief," and others that suggest the same idea? For one who searches with a love of learning, understanding these sayings is not hard. The display of signs is empty and futile in two cases. One is those who have already believed for some time and admit no doubt about our mystery. The other is those wholly in the grip of unbelief, who are not

willing to be led by the hand to piety through signs. But some were raised in unbelief and then slowly begin to rouse themselves to yield their thoughts to piety. For them the manifestation of wondrous works is fitting and useful. For this reason the Lord does not seek faith from those who are utterly faithless, for he knew he would not find it in them. Nor does he seek it from those who have believed sincerely, for he has already received it, since they brought it to him beforehand. He seeks it from those who are passing from impiety to piety and are already in labor with faith within themselves. Signs, then, are not given to believers, for that would be superfluous. Nor are they given to those who stay unchangeably in unbelief, for that would be in vain. They are given to those passing from unbelief to faith, whose faith seeks to be brought to completion and, once completed, becomes the means of enjoying God's signs. So the voice of the divine Paul does not conflict at all with the words of the Gospel. God, who does everything for the salvation of humankind, did not see fit to work wonders for those whose hearts were hardened, and those who had sincerely believed did not need them in order to believe. It remains that the Savior of our race worked miracles for those who had not yet believed and still stood among the unbelievers, but were nevertheless seeking something through which they might believe. Taking the signs as their guide, they passed over into the portion of the faithful.

The question is foolish. The one who said, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," clearly did not say that the earth was eternal. And he said that the earth was not simply [?] there, but that it was unformed: it was still invisible, because the water lay over it, and unformed, because it was not yet adorned with vegetation. And why did he first establish the form of light, and then its substrate, the body of the sun? So that he might work a greater wonder, says the Theologian. For with everything else he first established the matter and then gave it form, afterwards assigning each thing its order, shape and size. Here, more wondrously, he established the form before the matter, for light is the form of the sun.

Question 250. If God created light, who made darkness? For these are opposed to each other. They are opposed to each other, yes, but humans need both. David says this too, when he praises the mighty works of the Maker: "You made darkness, and it became night," and so on, up to "Man will

go out to his work and to his labor until evening." That darkness is necessary is clear. That it is not a substance but an accident can be gathered from the following as well. It is a shadow cast by heaven and earth, and for this reason it vanishes and dissolves into non-being when the light rises. Light, on the other hand, is a substance and has real existence, so when it sets it rises again, and when it departs it returns. One can also see from the following that darkness is accidental. A house without windows is full of darkness, but when a lamp is brought in it is lit up, and the darkness does not move somewhere else but is utterly destroyed by the presence of the light. So darkness is neither an unbegotten substance nor a begotten one. It is a necessary condition arising from begotten things, and it proclaims the wisdom of God. The prophet, accordingly, praises God for this too: "He who made light and fashioned darkness." He fittingly says "made" of light and "fashioned" of darkness, for darkness is an accident that comes together and dissolves.

Question 254 [?]. Why did God make wild beasts and reptiles? Children need bogeymen, and straps and rods: with the first we frighten them, with the others we discipline them. God foresaw that we too would incline toward sloth, so he prepared the wild beasts for us like straps or bogeymen. By frightening us with them he would draw us to himself and prepare us to call on him for help. But just as grown men despise childish frights, so those raised in virtue do not fear the attacks of wild beasts. The beasts stood by Adam before his sin and acknowledged that they were his servants. They lived together with Noah in the ark. The lions lived with Daniel in the pit, though they were very hungry. And the viper that sank its teeth into the Apostle's hand found there none of sin's slackness and looseness, so it sprang off at once and leapt into the fire, as if exacting punishment from itself for having attacked a body that was in no way its concern. And even though we are slothful, God still cares for us. He allotted the beasts the more deserted places and the time of night, and he assigned the reptiles their holes in the ground, so that the human race would not easily be harmed by them. Yet he sometimes permits some people to be harmed by them, so that each of us, afraid of suffering something similar, may flee to God, who is able to save. Besides, these creatures also contribute to many antidotes [?]. So let no one examine the beast by itself and blame the Maker for it; let him look instead for its use. The human body too has much beauty and harmony

and usefulness in its parts. But it also has mucus and spittle and foul-smelling excrement, and no one in his right mind would malign the creature for these things. To live without them is impossible, for the body is watered by them and so flourishes, by blood and phlegm and both kinds of bile. Just as it is held together by these, so it perishes when any one of them is in excess or deficiency. And if someone cut a joint off the fingers, he will see that by itself it is entirely useless. For this reason we too should not examine each part of creation separately, cut off from the whole, but should seek and consider whether it contributes some use to the common good. And the beasts respect human beings because of the authority over them given to humans in the beginning. But when a person has transgressed the divine law, there are times when they despise him.

Question 252. To whom did God say, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness"? Clearly to the Son, who is of the same substance and the same nature, for only of these can there be a single image. Some heretics have raved that this was said to the angels, and, more godless still, to the demons; they are utterly foolish. What fellowship does the image of God have with angels or demons? When things differ in substance beyond all comparison, how could anyone conceive of the same image for them? One might also laugh at the folly of the Jews. They say that God declared this to himself, in imitation of kings [?]. Both "we command" and "let us make" are spoken in the plural, yet they differ greatly from each other. "Let us make" calls someone of equal honor as if to share in the act. But "we command" or "we write," though put in the plural, gives no ground at all for thinking that someone else is being called to share. Besides, "we write" and "we command" are clearly addressed to someone, namely the subject. But here, especially because "according to the image" is added, "let us make" allows us to think of no other person than the Son and the all-holy Spirit. [?] Those entrusted with the great offices were accustomed to say "we command," "we write," "we order," and the like. Yet divine Scripture mostly presents the God of all speaking in the singular: "The time of all flesh has come before me," and "I was grieved that I made man," and "I will blot out man," and "There shall be no other gods besides me," and countless others. Only rarely does it use the plural, to indicate the number of the persons of the Trinity, as in "Come, let us go down and confuse their tongues," and in the passage we are now discussing. For here too God was fashioning the rational creature, which after many generations he would renew when he performed the all-holy baptism with the invocations of the holy Trinity. He was about to create the one that would receive those mysteries,

that is, human nature, and he enigmatically indicated both the identity of the substance and the number of the persons. By saying "God said," he made clear what is common to the divine nature. By adding "Let us make," he revealed the number of the persons. Again, by saying "image" in the singular, he showed the identity of the nature, and by adding "our," the number of the hypostases. The God of all foresaw everything, including the Only-begotten's becoming man and how he would take this nature from the all-pure Virgin. So he very fittingly deemed even the foundation of the race worthy of the greatest honor. First he placed deliberation before the act of creation, to signal in advance that what was being created would be rational. Then he indicated the number of the persons of the Godhead. In this way the human being, as he was fashioned, would receive the riddles of theology, and once deemed worthy of the all-holy baptism, would know clearly that the one who fashioned him also saved him, and the one who saved him also fashioned him. Besides this, by becoming, as it were, the craftsman of the fashioning with his own hands, he showed his greater tender love for this creature. Yet we do not say that the Divine has hands, or that it needs any deliberation or prior contemplation, so that, as in Plato's myths, it builds its work after the pattern it has in mind. Rather, each of these things shows God's greater care for this living creature.

Question 253. What does "According to the image" mean? Some have said that "according to the image" means the invisibility of the soul. But if that were so, the angels would be according to the image much more. Others very foolishly say that the human body was made according to the divine image. They are misled by the way divine Scripture often speaks of God's eyes and hands and the like, and they do not see that God, speaking to humans through humans, measures his words to the weakness of his hearers. Because we see with eyes, Scripture calls his power of sight "eyes," just as it calls his power of hearing "ears" and his command "mouth." Yet one can learn in many places of Scripture that God is uncircumscribed. Some of the teachers, then, understood "according to our image and likeness" in this way. The God of all, having made the sensible and intelligible creation, fashioned man last of all. He set him in the midst of inanimate, sensible and intelligible beings as a kind of image of himself. So the inanimate and animate beings would bring him their usefulness as a kind of tribute, and the intelligible natures, by caring for him, would show their goodwill toward the one who made him. Still others said that man was made according to the image of God with respect to rule. For he added, they say, "And let them rule over the fish of the sea," and so on. Just as God himself has lordship over all things, so he has given man authority over the irrational creatures.

One can, however, find other imitations of God, as of an archetype. Man too, in imitation of the God who made him, makes houses and walls and cities and harbors, models of the heavens, and images of the sun and moon and stars, of humans and of irrational animals. The difference between his making and God's is beyond words, yet in making, man somehow imitates his own Maker, as an image imitates its archetype. An image has the likenesses of its archetype: it has the form of the parts but not their activities, for it lacks a soul, which is what moves the body. So too man reigns and judges in imitation of the God of all. But man needs witnesses and accusers and countless other things in a trial, while God needs none of these, for he knows all things even before they come to be. So too man has been called god, because he was also called the image of God. Paul says: "A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God." But again, God is by nature what he is called, while man, as an image, has only the name. Again, God is properly and truly uncircumscribed, yet human reasoning somehow imitates this too. In an instant it roams over east and west, south and north, and even the heavens and the regions under the earth. But it does so only by the imagination of reason, while God is uncircumscribed in substance, in wisdom and in power. One might also find another, more exact imitation in the human soul. It has within itself both the rational and the vital. The mind begets the word, and together with the word proceeds breath, which is not begotten as the word is but always accompanies it. But these are present in man only as in an image, so the word and the breath have no hypostasis of their own. In the holy Trinity, by contrast, we conceive three hypostases, united without confusion and by themselves…

Question 254. You call God good, so how can you attribute such severity to him? It is cruelty and harshness to inflict such a punishment for a little food, not only on those who sinned but also on those descended from them. First, those who choose to be pious ought to be convinced that whatever the God of all does or commands is holy, just, good and loving toward humankind. Next, one must know that every law, even one that gives commands about small matters, has the same force as a law commanding the greatest things, and this is especially so when the law is divine. Take the law that commands circumcision: anyone who transgresses it does his neighbor no harm. Nevertheless the lawgiver says, "Every uncircumcised male who is not circumcised on the eighth day shall be utterly destroyed"…

[?] and the punishment he had set for murderers and adulterers, he carried out on them. If Marcion and those who share his impiety find fault with the law, and with the lawgiver himself, chiefly because of these things, let them be silenced from the Gospel: "For whoever looks lustfully at a woman is judged by him as an adulterer"; and, "Whoever says 'Raca' to his brother is liable to the council; whoever is angry without cause is liable to judgment; and whoever calls him a fool deserves Gehenna." Why, then, do they call the one good but the lawgiver of the Old Testament harsh? By their own standard these commands are harsher than those. We, however, know that both these laws and those come from one God. The difference was caused by the condition of those who received the laws. Like a wise teacher, he offered imperfect things to the imperfect and perfect things to the perfect. We must also consider this: the first people to break a law are punished without pardon, so that others will see the penalty and not break it. So the first man who gathered wood on the Sabbath was stoned by the whole people. Later, when many had broken the law of the Sabbath, the lawgiver bore it patiently. So too Cain, the first murderer, was struck with incurable punishments, while many later murderers did not pay the penalty at once. It was fitting, then, that Adam, who had received a law, and a very light one (for God had given him an abundance of every kind of fruit and forbidden him only one), should pay the penalty for his offence, for the benefit of the human race. But if God was quick to anger, as the ill-named Marcion said, and imposed the penalty of death for a little eating [?], how is it that when all mankind had run aground in impiety and lawlessness, he did not bring utter destruction, but even gave his Son and bestowed salvation through the passion and the cross? Yet it is clear to those instructed in divine things that God does nothing out of regret. That is a passion proper to beings with a changeable nature who do not know the future. But God sees what has not yet happened as already having happened. So, knowing beforehand that Adam would become mortal by breaking the commandment, he prepared his nature in advance as male and female. Such a formation of bodies belongs to mortals, who need to bear children for the race to continue; an immortal nature has no need of the female. For this reason the Creator brought the bodiless beings into existence all at once, in their full number, but he made the mortal living creatures two by two of each kind and gave them the blessing of increase. Foreseeing these things, God not only formed the human being male and female but also gave them the law about food: "Behold," he says, "I have given you every seed-bearing plant," and so on, "I have given you for food." And this was before the commandment. The punishment, then, was not the work of anger but a dispensation

full of wisdom. So that the human race would hate sin as the cause of death, the all-wise God passed the sentence of death after the commandment was broken. On the one hand he was creating a hatred of sin, and on the other he was preparing in advance the remedy of salvation for the race, the incarnation of the Only-begotten, through which resurrection from the dead and immortality have been won for us. And what is harsh about the sentence, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return"? "I changed you from earth into a far better nature," he says, "but since you would not keep my commandment, you shall return to your former nature." And why does the sin seem small? God gave him authority over everything and kept him from only one thing. Yet Adam left everything else and plucked this fruit first and alone. This is what the Master reproached him for: "Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat this alone?" The devil also showed that they had not eaten from any other tree, by what he said to Eve: "Why is it that God said, You shall not eat from every tree in paradise?" If he had known that they had eaten, he would not have thought they had received a commandment about all the trees. So the transgression was not small, for the first thing they tasted was the one thing they had been told not to touch.

QUESTION 255. Whom did Moses call sons of God? Those who take them to be angels are out of their minds. He called sons of God those descended from Seth. After Scripture said that Enosh was born to Seth, it added: "He hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God." Aquila has: "Then he began to call in the name of the Lord." This hints that because of his piety he was the first to receive the divine title and was called "god" by his kin. So those born from him were styled sons of God. For this reason the Lord also says through the prophet David, "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High," and, "God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges gods." In this way he names rulers, for he goes on, "How long will you judge unjustly and show favour to sinners?" and so on. In many places of Scripture you will find that those who stand above [?] the mass of men are called gods. [?] So Seth's descendants, whether because they sprang from Enosh, who was the first to be called [god], or simply because they differed in piety from those born of Cain, were called sons of God. They did not mix with Cain's descendants because of the curse the God of all had laid on him. But later they saw that the daughters of Cain's line were beautiful, and they were charmed, as is likely, by the musical instruments those people had invented

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople] (for Jubal, who sprang from them, invented the psaltery and the lyre). They mingled with these women and corrupted their own noble lineage, and they received a punishment sent by God, reaping utter destruction as the fruit of their lawlessness. But we should note that the divine word does not accuse them simply of sin, but of lawlessness pursued with care and zeal. This is shown by the words, "Everyone devises evil diligently in his heart all his days." Those who are vexed at the enormity of sin, but are overcome through slackness of mind rather than wickedness, and afterwards grieve and groan, have some modest excuse in some measure. But those who have turned wholly to licentiousness and wickedness, so far as even to invent new kinds of evil, what pardon do they deserve? Since the law commanding us to honour father and mother had not yet been given, how is Ham condemned as one who wronged his father? God has planted the necessary laws in nature. That is how he condemned Cain, since nature taught him that murder is unlawful. Indeed, Cain used deceit as his accomplice and led his brother far away from their parents before killing him. And when God asked, "Where is Abel your brother?" he denied it, clearly because he knew that what he had dared to do was evil. When the just Judge convicted him, he confessed that he had sinned beyond pardon: "My sin is too great to be forgiven." Adam too, when he became aware of the divine presence, tried to hide, because he knew that stealing is evil. In the same way Ham was charged with wronging his father, as one who had broken the law of nature. That nature also taught people to honour their parents is attested by Ham's brothers, who covered their father with great reverence.

When the flood ended, all of them alike received the divine blessing. So Noah thought it presumptuous to lay a curse on someone who had received the divine blessing, and for this reason he placed it on Ham's son. The punishment is just: since Ham sinned against his father as a son, he is punished through the curse on his son. Besides this, consider also that if Ham himself had received the curse, the punishment would have passed to his whole line. From him sprang the Ethiopians and Egyptians, all Libya, Phoenicia and Palestine. So that he would not involve the whole

line in the punishment, he diverted it to the youngest son. We should also understand that the righteous man's words are a prediction, not a curse. Israel, tracing its descent from Shem, was going to become master of Palestine, which Canaan's descendants had long inhabited. So Noah cast the prediction in the form of a curse, both foretelling what would happen and frightening later generations into not offending against their parents. The blessing of Shem teaches us this clearly: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; Canaan shall be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem." He foretold the many descendants of Japheth and the piety of Shem, for he foretold that God would dwell in the tents of Shem. And God did dwell among the patriarchs descended from Shem and among the prophets who sprang from them, first in the tabernacle and later in Jerusalem. But the prophecy received its exact fulfilment in the mystery of the dispensation, when God the Word himself became man and called the flesh he took from the seed of David and Abraham his temple, for these too were descended from Shem. And Canaan's servitude was fulfilled in the Gibeonites.

QUESTION 258. How can Abraham be called faithful when he said to God, "By what shall I know that I shall inherit it?" The words "By what shall I know?" are not those of a man who disbelieves, but of one who longs to learn how the inheritance would come about. He saw countless multitudes living in Palestine, and he wanted to learn how he would take possession of that land. Would it be by the law of war, or without war? Would its people live, or be killed, or be driven out? That is why the God of all, appearing after the sacrifice, says, "Know for certain that your seed shall be sojourners," and so on, as far as "For the sins of the Amorites are not yet complete." So from the divine answer we can understand the nature of the question. Since he said, "By what shall I know that I shall inherit it?", he was taught how long they would sojourn, how they would suffer, and how much providential care they would receive: those who made war on them would be punished, and they would enjoy the goods of others. He was also taught that he himself would experience none of this but would end his life in peace. God also told him the reason for the delay. So that no one would suppose the Lord God was unable to give him that land because of the great number of its inhabitants, he says, "For the Amorites have not yet done deeds deserving utter destruction." Punishment must not be brought on the basis of foreknowledge before the sin is committed. That there were pious people there at that time is clear both from Abimelech and from those living in
Hebron, who can be heard saying to the patriarch: "You are a king from God among us; bury your dead in our choicest tombs."

QUESTION 259. Why does the angel wrestle with Jacob? He puts courage into a man who was afraid of his brother. That is why he even let him win, as if to say: "You have conquered me, and you are afraid of a man?" But so that Jacob would not grow proud, thinking he had conquered God, he showed by touching his thigh that the defeat was voluntary, for with that touch he made the thigh go numb. Recognising the power of the one who had appeared, Jacob asks for a blessing. The other grants the request and changes his name. Even after Jacob woke, the thigh stayed numb and he limped, so that he would not take the vision for an illusion. And when he asked what his name was, he not only failed to obtain his request but was rebuked for overstepping the limits of nature: "Why do you ask my name?" he says, "And this is wonderful." We should note here too that he called the same being both man and God: "For you have prevailed with God," he said, "and you shall be powerful with men." And Jacob called the name of that place "Form of God": "For I have seen God face to face, and my life was preserved." And again: "The sun rose upon him as the Form of God passed by." From all this we learn that here too it was the only-begotten Son who appeared to Jacob.

QUESTION 260. How is Jacob said to have blessed his sons when he cursed some of them? 1. The patriarch's last words are neither curses nor blessings but predictions: "Gather together," he says, "that I may tell you what will befall you in the last days." He also recalled what some of them had done. This was not because the children were to pay the penalty for their fathers' sins. He was casting his words in the form of curses and blessings for the common benefit of those who would read them. He reproaches Reuben for his self-will, his rashness and his lawless act against his father's bed, and for this he foretells that his descendants will be few. That is the meaning of "Do not boil over like water," that is, "May you not grow hot into many offspring." He is indignant with Simeon and Levi too, lamenting the unjust slaughter of the Shechemites, and he prays to have no share in their lawlessness. Yet he curses not them but

their wicked passions, their anger and their wrath. He called their anger "desire," for the word for anger (orgē) takes its derivation from this, since an angry man longs (oregetai) to take revenge on his enemy. The punishment itself was also a prediction: "I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel." But the tribe of Levi was scattered because of its very high honour. So that Levites and priests would be present in every tribe and their services enjoyed, they received no lot of their own; instead certain cities were assigned to them in each tribe, along with a fixed number of cubits of surrounding land. The tribe of Simeon also had no separate lot; in accordance with the patriarch's prediction, it was scattered among the other tribes. 2. Judah he praises at length: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be on the back of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up." None of these things fits Judah himself, but they fit the tribe that sprang from him. It was the royal tribe: David reigned first, then his descendants. It was also the most powerful of all the tribes. When King David ordered the people to be counted, he found four hundred thousand in Judah and nine hundred thousand in the other tribes. And when they were counted in the wilderness, they proved more numerous than the other tribes. But the prediction was fulfilled exactly in Christ the Lord, who rose from the shoot of Judah, as the patriarch Jacob says, and as the prophet Isaiah says: "A rod came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower went up from the root." The words "He lay down and slept like a lion and like a lion's whelp" also fit him. Just as a lion is fearsome even when asleep, so the Lord's death proved fearsome both to death and to the devil. He called him a lion and a lion's whelp as King and Son of the King, as God and Son of God. He is so in his humanity too, for he sprang from David; and as God he was begotten of the Father before the ages. The words "Who shall rouse him?" show his unspeakable power, for he raised himself, as he himself predicted: "Destroy this temple," and so on. 3. He also foretells the time of his coming: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah," and so on. This is the clearest sign of the Lord's coming. Among the Jews there failed not only kings but also high priests and prophets. When our Saviour was about to be born, foreign kings ruled over them, so that the eternal King, the expectation of the nations, might be revealed. For God promised Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that in their seed he would bless all the nations of the earth. Jacob indicates this here too when he says, "A ruler shall not fail," and so on, as far as "And he is the expectation of the nations"; and of the Jews [?]

[?] "Binding his donkey to a vine," he says, "and the colt of his donkey to the tendril of the vine." All the prophets teach that Israel was called a vine. David says, "You brought a vine out of Egypt," and the Lord says in the Gospels, "A certain man planted a vineyard." By the colt he means the people from the nations, since it was untamed and had had no [?]. The Lord also hinted at this when he told the apostles to go into the village opposite and untie the donkey that was tied there and its colt, "on which," he says, "no one has ever sat."
