For no patriarch, lawgiver or prophet (58) had cared for the salvation of the nations. But the divine apostles, commanded to make disciples of the nations, untied the donkey, that is, human nature bound with the cords of sin. They also untied the colt, the people that had sprung from it. They put their own garments on it, that is, the grace they had received (for all who have been baptised into Christ have put on Christ). So they made the untamed colt obedient to the rein, set the Master on it, and bound it to the vine, that is, to themselves, for the apostles came from the Jews. And believers were joined not only to the apostles but also to the apostles' disciples. Foreseeing this, the patriarch said, "Binding his donkey to a vine, and the colt of his donkey to the tendril of the vine."

[?] Then he foretells the passion as well: "He will wash his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape; his eyes are gladdened with wine, and his teeth are white." He calls his body a robe and his blood wine, since the Master also called the mystical wine blood (59). We hear the evangelist teaching that when the soldier pierced his side with the spear, blood and water came out, and these streams ran down over his body. That is why he says, "He will wash his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape." Then, to show the joy that would come from the passion, he says, "His eyes are gladdened with wine," for the saving passion is the joy of the world. That he called the passion wine is attested by the Lord himself, who says, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." So too he said to the sons of Zebedee, "Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?" The gladness of the eyes, then, signifies the joy that followed the passion. After the passion and the resurrection the disciples were sent out into the whole world, bringing salvation to those who believed. And the [?] of his [?] [footnote: Gen. 49:12]

teaching he compared to very white teeth because of its [?] and its clarity: "For his teeth," he says, "are whiter than milk." This much the patriarch foretold in blessing Judah. 5. For Zebulun he foretold a home by the sea; for Issachar, farming. For Dan, according to some, he foretold the deeds of Samson, who was from this tribe and is counted among the Judges. That, they say, is why he said, "Dan shall judge his own people as one tribe in Israel." Others say he foretold what happened at Laish, now called Paneas. Some men from this tribe set out, fell suddenly on that city, took it by force and settled it, and gave it their own name, calling it Dan. But I think that the divine Spirit, just as it spoke through the patriarch about our Saviour, so in this prediction it also points to the Antichrist: "Dan," he says, "shall judge his own people as one tribe in Israel." For just as the Saviour, sprung from the tribe of Judah, saves the world, so from the tribe of Dan a deadly serpent will come forth. This is what it says: "And let Dan be a serpent sitting by the road, on the path, biting the horse's heel, and the rider shall fall, waiting for the salvation of the Lord." Since he uses every kind of deceit to try to hunt those he has duped into destruction, he likens him to a serpent lurking by a path and harming those who pass by. By the horse I think he means the body, and by the rider the soul. Falling backward, that is, lying on one's back, signifies death, for that is the posture of the dead. By the heel he hints at deceit, since some he deceives, while on others he inflicts very cruel punishments. By the horse he hints at the body, and when it is bitten and destroyed, death follows. [?] But for those who hold such a hope there is salvation [?]. 6. He foretells for Gad the attacks he would suffer from raiders, for this is what he means by "A raiding band shall raid him." He also foretells his coming victory: "And he himself," he says, "shall raid them at their heels." In the same way he foretells Asher's grain-bearing land and Naphtali's growth in numbers, for that is what he said: "A stem let loose, yielding beauty in its offspring." Then he describes the envy directed against Joseph and the plots of every kind laid against him, and he praises the divine care by which Joseph overcame those who made war on him: "For their bows were broken with might, and the sinews of their arms were loosened by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there came he who strengthened you, Israel, from the God of your father. My God helped you and blessed you with the blessing of heaven above and the blessing of the earth that holds all things," and so on. By these words

…of all, he praised his own God, who had made him stronger than the brother who had made war on him, and had shown his son to be invincible, though so many brothers plotted against him. “You have received this care,” he says, “as a reward for your service to your parents.” This is what he means by “Because of the blessing of breasts and womb, the blessing of your father and your mother.” For Joseph had been a devoted nurse to his father in his old age. Jacob says that what was done for him belonged jointly to himself and to Joseph's mother, since she too would have enjoyed this care if she had not departed this life too soon. Then he prays that Joseph will be renowned and become famous among all. “May you prevail,” he says, “beyond the blessing of the enduring mountains and the desire of the everlasting heaps; they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the brothers whom he led.” Aquila rendered “heaps” as “hills.” Since hills and mountains can both be seen from far away, he prays that Joseph, like them, may become well known and the most conspicuous of all.

7. He called Benjamin a ravenous wolf because of the disaster that befell his tribe. That is why he added, “In the morning he will eat, and in the evening he will distribute food.” For after winning the first and second battles, they were later utterly destroyed, except for a few who could easily be counted. The victors took pity on them. Because of their oath they were wary of giving them wives, but they found another way to arrange marriages for them. It should be noted that some have applied this prophecy to the divine Paul. Like a wolf he ravaged the Church, going from house to house, but later he gave out spiritual food to the whole world. When Jacob had said these things and announced his own death, the writer said, “And he lifted his feet up onto the bed and breathed his last, and was gathered to his people.” The God of all also said this to Abraham: “But you shall go to your fathers in peace, having been nourished in a good old age.” From this the Lord also refuted the unbelief of the Sadducees, saying, “Have you not read that the dead are raised? I am the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob. God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” To him be glory forever. Amen.

It proclaims the power and love for humanity of God: the unquenchable fire did not consume the bush, though it was only brushwood. I think it also indicates that Israel would not be destroyed, though the Egyptians plotted against it. It further indicates that the Only-begotten, when he became man and dwelt in a virgin's womb, would keep her virginity intact. Some say that God appeared in a bush
and not in any other plant because no one could carve a god out of a bush. It is likely that the Jews would have dared to do even this if he had appeared in some other plant.

QUESTION 262. What does the leprosy of the hand signify?

The family of Jacob was raised in piety when it entered Egypt. But there it learned the impiety of the Egyptians instead, and when it was set free from their slavery it learned the God of all anew. Through the change in the hand, then, he showed their leprosy and their cleansing. Besides this, God was also arranging something else. He was going to lay down the law concerning lepers and call them unclean, so with this further purpose in view he made leprous the hand of the lawgiver, a hand trained in perfect things. In this way he taught that in truth none of these things is unclean, for how can something involuntary be unclean? That is why the right hand that worked those miracles first became leprous and then served the divine signs. This also taught the lawgiver not to think too highly of himself, but to know his own nature by remembering the right hand that had become leprous.

QUESTION 263. Why did the angel want to kill Moses?

His wife guessed it was because one of the children was uncircumcised, and so she circumcised him at once. Some say, however, that it was because he had been sent to free his kinsmen and yet brought his wife along as a companion on the journey. These people should have realized that he was forced to bring her because he wanted to persuade his father-in-law that he would not neglect his wife or prefer another woman to her. He was not carrying out the divine command carelessly. In fact, as soon as the angel gave him the occasion, he ordered her to go back to her own people. The history shows that this is true: after the exodus from Egypt, when they had crossed the Red Sea and arrived at Mount Sinai, his father-in-law came to him with his wife and two sons. So the angel was arranging something else when he showed his drawn sword. The great Moses was afraid of Pharaoh, and he showed this fear in many places. At one point he said, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, king of Egypt?” At another he said, “Appoint someone else who is able, whom you will send.” And again he said, “I am weak of voice and slow of tongue.” So the angel threatens him with punishment, driving out fear with fear, the lesser with the greater, as if saying through the drawn

He wanted the memory of their salvation to be preserved forever. Therefore, when he gave the law, he said, “If your son asks you, ‘What is the Passover?’ you shall say, ‘On this day the Lord God brought our fathers out of Egypt,’” and so on. For this reason he commands those celebrating this feast to dress like travelers: “Let your loins be girded,” and so on. Philo translated “Pascha” as “crossing-festival,” Josephus as “festival of passing over,” and Symmachus as “passings-over.” Theodotion wrote “phasek,” keeping the Hebrew word itself. The name signifies the salvation of the Hebrew firstborn. He commanded them to take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood of the slaughtered lamb, and smear the doorposts and the lintel. Then, when the destroyer came to strike the firstborn of the Egyptians, he would see the blood and pass over the houses of the Hebrews. This was not because a bodiless nature needed such signs. The symbol was meant to teach them God's care, and to teach us, who sacrifice the spotless Lamb, to recognize the type that prefigured him. He commands them to take not only lambs from the sheep but also kids from the goats. They were not to sacrifice both together. Whoever had a sheep was to sacrifice the lamb, and whoever did not was to sacrifice the kid. He instructs them to take the animal on the tenth day of the first month, so as to have it ready before the feast. It was to be sacrificed on the fourteenth toward evening, because the Lord too was handed over to the Jews in the evening. It was to be eaten with bitter herbs, in memory of their bitter life in Egypt. The unleavened bread signified not only the haste of the journey and the makeshift food, but also that they should carry with them no trace of the Egyptian way of life. This is how the Lord interpreted it when he said, “Beware of the leaven of the scribes and Pharisees.” He also ordered those who could not afford to sacrifice a sheep to join with their neighbors and sacrifice the Passover together. In this way he trained them in brotherly love and in mercy toward the poor. For the same reason he commands that any leftover meat be burned, thereby compelling them to invite the needy to share in the feast. All these things are figures of our mysteries. We too anoint with the blood of our Lamb not only the lintel but also the two doorposts. In the visible sense, this is the tongue

and the lips, which we cleanse and sanctify. In the spiritual sense, the reasoning part takes the place of the lintel, and the spirited and appetitive parts take the place of the two doorposts. It also suits us to eat the meat neither raw nor boiled, but roasted with fire. We do not look with the eye alone, but search out the meaning. Nor do we bring human reasonings into the divine words; Isaiah condemned some people for doing this, as men who mix their wine with water. Instead we use only the divine fire, the grace of the all-holy Spirit. We understand the command not to leave any meat until the next day in this way: the life to come does not need symbols, for there we see the realities themselves. Those who misunderstand the divine oracles and try to twist them to suit their own impiety are the ones who break the lamb's bones. Taking not only from the sheep but also from the kids again proclaims God's love for humanity. Christ endured his saving passion not only for the righteous but also for sinners, and the law commanded a kid to be offered for a sinner. So among those who partake of the divine mysteries, some partake as of a sheep, since they have acquired perfect virtue. Others partake as of a kid, washing away the stains of their sins through repentance. In the same way our Lord fed the crowds who had gathered not only with wheat loaves but also with barley loaves. He also commanded us to keep our loins girded, our feet shod, and our lamps burning, like servants waiting for their master. The Hebrews dressed this way because they were being freed from the Egyptians and brought into the land of the Canaanites. We dress this way because we are passing from this life to another. That is why the divine Paul also exhorts us, crying out, “Clean out the old leaven.” Further on he says, “So let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” From the beginning God foretold the salvation of the nations, for he commanded that proselytes should share in the Passover. He called the proselyte “giora” and gave him equal rights: “For he shall be like a native of the land,” he says. The faithful keep the command “It shall be eaten in one house” by partaking of the divine mysteries in the Church alone and shunning the assemblies of heretics. He also made a law that the firstborn of sheep and cattle should be offered, to remind them of the salvation of the firstborn. He himself did not need the sacrifices; he was working for their benefit. The law itself makes this clear: “If your son asks you, ‘What is this?’” and so on, down to “That is why I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb, and every firstborn of my sons I redeem. It shall be a sign on your hand and fixed before your eyes, for with a
mighty hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt.” So each of these things was done not because God needed it, but for the benefit of the people.
QUESTION 265. How should we understand what the Apostle said, “All were baptized into Moses,” and so on, down to “and the rock was Christ”?

With God, the threats are greater than the punishments. For he says, “Every uncircumcised male who is not circumcised on the eighth day shall be utterly destroyed.” Yet we can see that the circumcised died in the desert in various ways, while the uncircumcised received the promise made to their forefathers instead of punishment, for Joshua circumcised them at Gilgal. Again, he threatened total destruction to houses that kept leaven, but he did not carry it out. So here too he frightens them with threats, as one who loves his children, and says, “Visiting the sins of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me.” God himself makes clear that it is impious to cling to the bare letter, through the passages in which he teaches the opposite. “Children shall not die for their fathers,” he says, “nor fathers for their children, but each shall die in his own sin.” And through Ezekiel he says, “What do you mean by this proverb of yours, ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be used. Rather, the teeth of those who ate the sour grape will be set on edge, for all souls are mine.” What follows has the same meaning. But I think instead that the threat displays God's love for humanity. For the text says “of those who hate me,” which means: I am patient

with the fathers who have sinned, and I am patient with the children too. But if their descendants and their descendants' offspring imitate the wickedness of their forebears, then I will bring punishment. “For I show mercy,” he says, “to thousands and tens of thousands of those who love me.” The history also agrees with this. The sons of Israel went up out of Egypt in the fifth generation. Their fathers and forefathers had served the gods of the Egyptians in Egypt and paid no penalty. But the sons themselves were punished because they imitated that impiety: after so great a kindness and countless miracles, they still did not spit out their impiety. Their children, however, loved God the Savior and enjoyed the promise made to their forefathers. We also see that the promise made to the fathers did not fail, for the nations have received the blessing through the seed of Abraham. Since, then, they were going to worship the calf, he threatens punishment in advance.

QUESTION 267. What is “a fully formed infant”?

They say that once the body has been shaped in the womb, the embryo receives its soul. God likewise first shaped Adam's body and then breathed the soul into it. So the lawgiver lays down a rule for when a pregnant woman miscarries because of a fight. If the infant comes out fully formed, that is, shaped, it is to be called murder, and the one who did it is liable to the penalty for murder. If not, he is acquitted of murder, since what was lost had no soul, but he must pay a fine.

QUESTION 268. Why did he command the tabernacle to be made?

God himself revealed the reason: “You shall make me a sanctuary,” he says, “and I will be seen among you. You shall make it in accordance with all that I show you on the mountain, the pattern of the tabernacle and the pattern of its furnishings.” He had given the law on Mount Sinai, and some would probably suppose that the Divine was confined to that place. So he ordered a tabernacle to be made, and by manifesting himself from there he trained the people in piety. Later, once they had received the promised land, he commanded a temple to be built and the divine services to be performed in it. In this way they would not perform the services anywhere they pleased and fall into the error of the demons. In the same way, while they were crossing the desert, he ordered a tabernacle to be made that could move with them. When they set out, he ordered it to go ahead of them, so that they would not again look for gods to go before

them. When they camped, it was to stand still. The tabernacle bore the image of creation. When God created heaven and earth, he set the firmament in the middle and used it to divide what is above from what is below. In the same way, having ordered a single tabernacle to be made, he commands the curtain to be placed in the middle as a type of the firmament, and by it the ark was set apart. He called the part by the door “Holy,” and the part inside the curtain “Holy of Holies.” As David says, “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the sons of men.” In the same way, the area outside the curtain was open to the priests, but the area inside could not be touched or entered, for the law allowed only the high priest to go in, once a year. Inside were the images of the cherubim, representing the bodiless powers. Between them stood the ark, which held the tablets of the law, the jar of manna, and Aaron's rod that had budded. On top of the ark lay the mercy seat, overshadowed by the wings of the cherubim, and there the God of all made himself manifest. The divine nature has no form or shape, and it is completely impossible to make images of such a being. So he ordered symbols of his greatest gifts to be placed inside. The tablets signified the giving of the law, the rod the priesthood, and the manna the food in the desert. The mercy seat was a symbol of prophecy, for the oracles came from there. So the things inside the curtain bore the type of heavenly things, and that is why it was called the Holy of Holies. The blessed Paul testifies to this when he says, “For Christ did not enter a holy place made with hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself.” The things in the outer part bore the image of earthly things. On the south side stood a seven-branched lampstand with the same number of lamps on it, and these signified the number of the days of the week. On the north side stood a golden table, on which he ordered twelve loaves to be set, along with golden bowls full of frankincense and salt. Between the lampstand and the table stood the golden altar. These represented [?] the fruits that the earth gives to human beings. In front of the tabernacle, outside, stood the bronze altar, which received the sacrifices that were offered. This shows that the sacrifices were superfluous and did not please God. For this reason he allowed them to be performed because of the weakness of the Jews, but outside the tabernacle, since they were not necessary to what was inside. We, however, perform the worship assigned to what was inside: we offer God incense, lamplight, and the mystical sacred rite of the table. The tabernacle was thirty cubits long and ten wide, and this is easy to work out. The south side had twenty boards, and the north side the same number. The other translators called the boards “pillars.” Since each

board was a cubit and a half wide, the twenty boards made up thirty cubits. The side facing west had six boards of the same measure and two corners. These came to twelve cubits: ten formed the inside, and the other two received the joints of the two long sides. He ordered the door to be on the east side so that the rising sun would offer a kind of homage to the entrance, sending its rays straight into it. In this way those who worship God alone would have the sun behind them as they turned toward the tabernacle, and would worship not the sun but its Maker. The tabernacle looked like an enclosure, with boards on every side fitted together. The boards had silver bases and silver capitals, and they were overlaid with gold inside and out. Its roof was made of embroidered fabrics in various colors. One was purple, another rose-colored or scarlet, another like hyacinth, and the fine linen was white. These too were figures of the four elements. Hyacinth resembles the air, and the rose-colored or scarlet resembles fire. The purple points to the sea, which nourishes the shellfish that produces this color. The fine linen points to the earth, since flax grows from it. Over the tabernacle lay coverings of hair, and also dyed skins to keep out the rain. He also gave the priests all kinds of adornment. The variety of the vestments struck the people with awe, and it taught the priests themselves how they ought to beautify and adorn the soul. He calls the inner tunic the “undergarment” and the outer tunic the “overgarment,” and he ordered the outer tunic to be made of hyacinth. He called it “ankle-length” because it reached down to the feet. From its hem he hung golden bells and pomegranates. When the priest entered the innermost shrine of the tabernacle and heard the sound they made, he would be reminded of the one who gave the command and would perform the service with fear. For the same reason the ankle-length robe had the color of the air. It was hyacinth so that by looking at it he might be lifted up. On his head he wore a turban that imitated heaven. A band, which the Seventy called a “mitre,” covered his forehead. In its middle was a golden plate engraved with the unutterable name of God, which the Hebrews call the Tetragrammaton. He indicated this by a riddle, to train the people in reverence: “You shall inscribe on it,” he says, “Holiness of the Lord.” He also ordered a shoulder-cape to be made for the priest, which the Seventy called an “epomis.” In the books of Kingdoms we find it called by its Hebrew name, “ephod.” It had two precious stones, one on each shoulder, engraved with the names of the tribes. On the chest it had the so-called “oracle,” [which ?] the rational

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. [?] the heart. It also had twelve stones of different colours fitted into it. Through it, when war broke out, either victory or defeat was revealed. The history of the Kingdoms also teaches this: when the enemy marched against Israel, Saul did not dare to draw up for battle until he had seen the signs of victory. For this reason the God of all, having said, "And you shall put the oracle of judgement on the breast of Aaron, and join it to the ephod," added, "And you shall put on it the Manifestation and the Truth." He called the signs given from it "Manifestation", and the infallibility of those signs "Truth". It should be understood, however, that the people of that time were rather dull and unable to reach intelligible things, so our all-wise Master worked for their benefit through bodily symbols. For we understand the oracle as the contemplation of intelligible things and the ephod as the practice of virtue. We take the fitting together and joining of the oracle and the ephod as the harmony of faith and good action. That the ephod is put on first, and only then is the oracle joined to it, means that good action is the foundation of the virtues. Question [?].

QUESTION 269. Why did he break the tablets? Because he judged the people unworthy of the legislation. The tablets had the form of a dowry contract, and the bride had turned aside to adultery before the bridal chamber. So he very reasonably tore up the dowry contract. It should be noted that God accepted the supplication at that time and set the punishment aside. But he added, "Yet on the day when I visit, I will bring upon them all their sin." This resembles what the Apostle said: "Not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance; but according to your hardness," and so on. Then the lawgiver heard that the God of all would no longer be with them but would set an angel over them. He asked to know who would be set over them, and he begged God not to give them a fellow servant as their leader but to lead them himself. When he had obtained this request too, he was drunk with a praiseworthy love and longed for things beyond human reach, and he desired to see the invisible nature. But he learned that this is impossible. The things of God's economy and operation, however, can be seen, for this is how one must understand the "back parts" of God. They can be seen by those like Moses. Yet even they do not see them without condition: they must be set on the rock by God himself, which signifies the firmness and steadfastness of faith. And they must look through the cleft of the rock, which signifies the eye of faith, which beholds things that the eyes of the senses cannot reach or see.

QUESTION 270. How did leprosy appear in garments? God brought many such chastisements upon them. For instance, he spoke thus about leprous houses: "When you come into the land of the Canaanites, which I am giving you, I will put an infection of leprosy in the houses of the land you possess," and so on. Through this he teaches that the plagues were sent by God, falling sometimes on garments and sometimes on houses. These plagues showed God's inexpressible love for humankind. When people sinned, he brought the plagues on their garments and houses, and through them he offered healing to those who owned them. The house of Israel resembles the leprous house. The offenders were often removed from it like leprous stones, sometimes by the Assyrians, sometimes by the Babylonians [?], and at other times by the Macedonians. But since the leprosy had become fixed, the lawgiver ordered the house to be completely demolished.

QUESTION 271. What do the two little birds offered for the person being cleansed signify? They contain a type of the saving passion. One of the birds is sacrificed, and the other is dipped in the blood of the sacrificed bird and set free. In the same way Christ the Master was crucified for leprous humanity: his flesh received death, while his divinity made the suffering of his humanity its own. The leper being cleansed is sprinkled with the blood of the slaughtered bird mixed with pure water, using cedar wood, hyssop and spun scarlet, and is shown to be bright and clean. In the same way, whoever believes in Christ the Saviour and is cleansed by the water of the all-holy Spirit casts off the stains of sin. The cedar wood is a symbol of the impassible divinity, for the wood does not rot. The spun scarlet symbolizes the humanity made of soul and body, and the hyssop the warmth and fragrance of the all-holy Spirit. Through these the baptized are freed from the leprosy of the soul. The cotyle of oil signifies the spiritual chrism. The oil smeared on the right ear, the right hand and the right foot shows that the hearing is to be set apart for right words, and the hand and the foot for right actions. When it is also poured on the head, it shows the consecration of the rational faculty. The one who remained a leper, however, [?] outside the Church [?].

QUESTION 272. Why does he forbid animals that are eaten to be slaughtered far from the tabernacle? He knew that some were impious and would offer sacrifices to demons. So he commanded that anyone who wished to slaughter a calf, a sheep or a goat should bring it to the door of the tabernacle, pour out the blood there, and carry the meat home. He ordered that anyone who did not do this should be charged as guilty of murder: "For blood," he says, "shall be reckoned to that man; he has shed blood," and so on. What follows teaches that this is the purpose of the law: "For the priest," he says, "shall offer up the fat as a fragrant odour to the Lord, and they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the vain things after which they go whoring." This law is in force among the Jews, for the priest slaughters the animals that are eaten. He also forbade eating blood and taught the reason: "For the life of all flesh is its blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls; for its blood shall make atonement in place of its life. Therefore I have said to the sons of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood." In effect he says: just as you have an immortal soul, so the irrational animal has the body [?] in place of a soul. For this reason he orders it to be offered in place of yours. If you eat it, you are eating a soul, for it fills the place of a rational soul. That is why he called eating it murder. For the same reason he also forbids eating animals that have died, since their blood has not been drained.

QUESTION 273. From the Ladder, from the chapter on stillness and patience: "Pursuing the middle, I came to be in the midst," and "it gave drink to me in my thirst," up to "I am wholly unable to say." 1. A holy and diligent elder has made a request. It puts forward the contemplation of a divinely inspired and contemplative elder and seeks to have it made clear. And yet, for those who are wise in practical matters, speech is not usually what becomes the teacher; practice and imitation reveal the lesson directly. So it belongs to our elder to solve the riddles of the old elder, which come from practice. He has these realities in his own experience, and where speech cannot resolve a difficulty, practice guides him to understand it. Here, however, he has added the perfection of humility to his other virtues: among those who have no practice, the practitioner asks that the hidden meanings of practical contemplations be put into words. So we, trusting not in ourselves but in his

virtue and his request, will proceed to resolve the difficulties. 2. In the present words that good old elder teaches three stages of advance, or ranks, or degrees, or whatever else those who wish may like to call them. The first is freedom from care about the affairs of life and about the things that perish along with life. The second is unflagging prayer, and the third is the inviolable working of the heart. It is clear, then, that prayer lies in the middle between the two extremes. Whoever has not acquired freedom from care cannot pursue the two that follow. But what follows from this? By pursuing the middle, that is, prayer, he came to be in the midst of good things, even if he had not yet climbed to the summit of goods. 3. Nevertheless, though it was far off, the fullness, delight and sight of the light-bearing vision gave him drink in his thirst. Then I did not enjoy the vision continually; afterwards I was again among the things I had been among before. What there was in the things seen, before the visible form, not even the things seen could teach, though sight usually teaches us most of what we see. For it was not one of the natural and customary sights. Grace granted the seeing of some things and made other things higher than what sight can grasp. Indeed, the architect of this ineffable delight and contemplation did not permit or allow us to receive the knowledge unmixed. Yet I, out of longing and love to learn, still asked how the author of our salvation and of those beautiful visions now exists. The answer was that the vision lay in what was his own, but not in what he arranged in his economy. The latter belonged to his love for humankind and his condescension. The former, because he does not depart from his own nature, indicated what is eternal and unchangeable. Then, since he was leading me up to a nature that surpasses all sight and apprehension, I inquired further, raising another difficulty: if this is so, what are the standing at the right hand, the sitting, and the names of material relations and dispositions? Where can such things properly be spoken of, in a realm where even most of what is seen is not sight but an impression of the imagination? But the one who heard my difficulties rebuked what was, it seems, a meddlesome objection and did not let me indulge in the inquiry. He said that the question was beyond hearing and had its own proper time for revelation. I, still contending, begged him to bring me to that time and not to deprive me of my good desire. But he led me away, as far as possible, from what grieved and distressed me, and said that the time had not yet come, for the fire that kindles incorruption is not yet set ablaze among us. 4. Having reported this vision, that good, God-loving old elder does not boast, nor does he grow proud at having seen such things. Instead he even admits his own ignorance, saying: "I do not know whether I saw these things with the dust, or whether the soul by itself
Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople. soared up towards what is higher and left the body for a short time, the body being separated from its bond with the soul and from its mingling with it."

QUESTION 274. Why did God command the people to be numbered? To show the truth of his own promise. When he made a promise to Abraham, he said: "I will surely multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the shore of the sea." He showed that the promise was true. From the seventy-five who went down into Egypt, six hundred and three thousand six hundred and fifty men able to fight were counted. This number excluded those too old and too young, as well as the women and the tribe of Levi. Teaching this power of his, God also said through Isaiah: "Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you in labour, for he was one, and I called him and multiplied him."

QUESTION 275. Why is barley meal offered for the woman under suspicion? The Master himself explained it: "For it is," he said, "a sacrifice of jealousy, a sacrifice of remembrance, a sacrifice that recalls sin." That is why he ordered that it should have neither oil nor frankincense, for it lacks both fragrance and the light of righteousness. He made this law because he knew their murderous disposition. To keep them from killing their wives on mere suspicion, he ordered the suspected woman to be brought to him, who knows all things clearly, even what is hidden. "For the priest," he says, "shall bring the woman and set her before the Lord, and the priest shall take pure living water before the Lord," and so on. He ordered all this to be done to frighten the suspected woman, so that if she had sinned she would confess and receive forgiveness through repentance. For this reason he also orders her to be brought to God with her head uncovered, teaching that all things are naked and laid bare before him. What follows confirms that he ordered these things in order to frighten her: "And the priest shall make her swear and shall say to the woman: If no one has lain with you, if you have not gone astray to be defiled while under your husband's authority, be free of [?] this conviction that brings the curse. But if you have gone astray while under a husband," and so on, up to: "May the Lord make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the Lord makes your thigh fall away and your belly swell."

He also ordered the woman to consent to the curse and to say, "So be it, so be it." And he ordered the curse to be written down and washed off with water, and the woman to drink that water. But first the sacrifice was to be offered, that is, the barley meal. Then he teaches that if she is innocent she will be kept healthy. But if she is guilty and hiding it, she will learn the power of the curse by experience, as her belly bursts and her thigh falls away. For the punishment comes through the same members through which the sin came. The "oath" should be understood this way: when someone suffers terrible and incurable things, some people are accustomed to say when they swear, "May I not suffer what so-and-so has suffered."

The law was in its beginnings. So the rest had to be brought to their senses by the punishment of transgressors, for fear is fitting for beginners. Yet love for humankind was joined to the punishment, for those who repented enjoyed his kindness. For instance, when fire sent by God had consumed part of the camp and everyone had then gathered to pray, the lawgiver asked for forgiveness, and God in his love for humankind granted it. What follows shows that the punishments were brought on them out of necessity. As soon as the punishment stopped, they revived the memory of Egypt and of the things they had in Egypt. So the writer very fittingly set the divine generosity beside their ingratitude by telling about the manna and showing that it supplied not only the need for bread but also the need for meat. For they ground it in the mill, pounded it in the mortar, boiled it in the pot and made cakes from it. When they lamented, the Lord God was angry, and the prophet was distressed and cried out: "Why have you afflicted your servant, and why have I not found favour before you, that you lay the onrush of this people upon me? Did I conceive this people in the womb?" and so on. In these words he revealed their immaturity and childishness, for he compared them to a nursing infant who can do nothing else and wants only to suck milk. His words were those of a man who was deeply distressed, and the words that follow have the same sense. So he is taught by the Lord God that he governs the people not by human power but by divine grace. For God said: "Gather for me seventy men," and a little later: "And I will take some of the spirit that is upon you and put it upon them, and I will help you bear the onrush of this people, and you will not bear them alone." Through these words the lawgiver learned that he had received grace sufficient for his task of governing. That is why God said, "I will take some of the spirit that is upon you." It was not because he lacked some other power,

but to teach Moses that he had received power sufficient for the need, that he said this. The facts show that in giving to the seventy he did not diminish Moses' grace, for Moses went on governing and working wonders just as before. We see this happening now as well. Many are baptized by one priest, and others are ordained by a high priest and receive the divine gift. Yet they do not diminish the grace of the one who imparted it, and they themselves receive it in full. The Master, however, also confirmed his servant's judgement, for he said to him: "Choose those whom you know."

QUESTION 277. Why did God command the censers of the rebels to be made into a covering for the altar? As a reproof to those who acted insolently against the priesthood and a confirmation of those appointed to serve as priests. For he added: "A memorial for the sons of Israel," and so on. For this reason he also ordered Aaron's rod, which had blossomed, to be placed in the ark. And again he made a law that the priests should perform the sacred rites and the Levites should assist them, approaching neither the altar nor the sacred vessels. Then he teaches what the priests ought to receive. He ordered them to eat the first fruits of grain, wine, oil and bread offered to him. They were also to have the dedicated offerings and the firstborn. For the firstborn of unclean animals he fixed a ransom of five shekels each, according to the holy shekel, which is twenty obols. For the firstborn of clean animals, the blood was to be poured out at the base of the altar and the fat offered, and the priests were to take the meat, just as they receive the breast and the shoulder from the other sacrifices. He called this sharing a "covenant of salt", since, as the divine Apostle says, "those who serve at the altar share in the altar." Some, however, say it is because he commanded salt to be added to the sacrifices. Then he teaches that the priests and the Levites are to receive the tithes of what grows from the earth, of the profits from flocks and herds, and of what comes from trade and any other occupation. The Levites are to offer the tithes of these tithes to the priests. He orders them to partake of these in any place, but what is set apart for them from the sacrifices they are to eat inside the temple. He also calls the tithes "wages for the benefit of the people". In effect he says: while you build or trade or stay at home, these men attend to my service on behalf of all of you. For this is what he said: "For this is your wage in return for your services in the tent of witness."

QUESTION 278. Why was God angry with Moses and Aaron when he brought water out of the rock? They were grieving over their sister's death, and the people were pressing them because there was no water. Annoyed at the people's great lack of self-control, they spoke ambiguous words when they brought out the water. For he said: "Hear me, you disobedient ones: shall I not bring water out of this rock for you?" Therefore God said: "Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the sons of Israel, you shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them." David also says this: "And Moses suffered because of them," and so on. For in his anger with them he spoke ambiguously, and the ambiguity lay not in his mind but in his tongue. For this is what David said: "And he spoke rashly with his lips." It should be understood, however, that God issued this sentence because he was arranging something else.

QUESTION 279. Why was he commanded to call heaven and earth to witness? Not because they are living and rational, but because they contain all created things. The prophet Isaiah did this too: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth," and so on. So did Jeremiah: "Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered greatly, says the Lord." The lawgiver called them as witnesses to the threat, so after the laws were broken they are fittingly said to shudder and be astonished. In the same way Jacob and Laban named the heap [?] "the mound of witness". And Abraham the patriarch and Abimelech, king of Gerar, named the well "the well of the oath", since they made their agreement there with an oath.

QUESTION 280. How should we understand "Rejoice, O nations, with his people, and let all the angels of God strengthen him"? Many tens of thousands of Jews also believed in Christ the Master, as did the greater part of the nations throughout the world. But it was the Jews who had believed who brought the teaching to the nations, for the divine apostles came from the Jews. Foretelling these things, then, the prophet said: "Rejoice, O nations, with his people," that is, with those from the nations who have believed. "And let all the angels of God strengthen them" refers to those who have believed in him. For indeed

…when our Saviour was born, a choir of angels sings of God's love for humanity, crying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men." The archangel Gabriel had foretold that birth, which came without seed and without the pains of childbirth. When he contended with the devil, hosts of angels were present: "For angels came," it says, "and ministered to him." After the resurrection angels keep watch at the tomb and announce the resurrection to the women, and they bring good news to the apostles after the Master's ascent into heaven. An angel told Cornelius about the great Peter, and an angel led Peter himself out of prison. The divine Paul said to those sailing with him: "An angel of the God to whom I belong appeared to me." There are many more examples of this kind. Having said these things about the believers, the prophet also foretells the punishments of the unbelievers and the reasons they will suffer them. He said: "For the blood of his sons is avenged, and he will avenge it, and he will repay vengeance to his enemies, and repay those who hate him, and the Lord will cleanse the land of his people." He calls God's "sons" the saints whom the murderers killed. I pass over the slaughter of the prophets and the Master's saving passion. They stoned Stephen, glorious in his victory, killed the great James with a club, and did countless other things. They also plundered the houses of those who believed in the Lord, as the divine Paul testifies in many places. Writing to the Thessalonians, he says: "For you became imitators of the saints in Jerusalem; for you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord and their own prophets, and drove us out, and do not please God, and are hostile to all people." The Lord too accused them of these things in the parable of the vineyard, where they beat one servant, killed another and stoned another. For this reason he scattered them over the whole world.

QUESTION 282 [?]. Why was Moses, for a small [?], prevented [?] from entering the land? Through these things God teaches us that he demands the highest virtue from those who are perfect in virtue. He is patient with other people even when they commit great transgressions, but he does not grant the saints this same pardon. A certain wise man says this too: "The least may be pardoned out of mercy, but the mighty will be mightily tested." And the Lord says in the holy Gospels: "From one to whom little is given, little will be required." Yet one must also know that the Master arranges some things by means of others. So it was with this great pro-

phet: God did not allow him to lead the people into the promised land, so that the Israelites would not revere him as a god. For the same reason God, who wisely governs our affairs, also kept the place of his tomb unknown. It is also worth knowing that Moses is a type of the law, and so the law too is called "Moses." "They have," it says, "Moses and the prophets," calling the law Moses, and you will find this in many places. We use the names Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel not only for the men but also for their books, and one can see much the same with everyone who has left behind divine writings. In the same way one can see that the name Moses refers not only to the man but also to the law. Moses, then, is a type of the law, and Joshua son of Nun is a type of the Saviour. Moses led the people out of Egypt, but Joshua brought them into the promised land. In the same way the law frees those who obey it from ungodliness, but the grace of the Gospels brings them into the kingdom of heaven.

That is: in few words, in a brief speech, with little teaching, without much labour or lengthy discussion. That is why Paul gives him a fitting answer: "I would pray to God," and so on. He means: "I am eager for everyone to become a Christian, and this is my prayer to God. I am ready to preach faith in Christ with many words or with few, with toil and labour or on the spot. I do not count the toil and labour of teaching and preaching at all. It makes no difference to me whether I labour or not, or whether I spend a long time preaching or a short one, so long as I see some people turning to Christ." He said this to show his own eagerness and zeal, and also to draw Agrippa on. If Agrippa wanted to hear more and receive more complete teaching, Paul would not hold back in the least. He was so ready and willing that he made it a matter of prayer, if only he could reach his goal: "For I would pray that, whether in a short time or a long one, not only you," and so on.

QUESTION 283. What is meant by "designated Son of God in power"? It means the one who came to be known, who was recognized by us and revealed as the Son of God. How was he made known? Through the prophets, through the signs and mighty works he displayed, through his sanctifying Spirit, which he gave to those who believe in him, and through his own

most wondrous rising from the dead. He was foretold by the prophets, made known by the display of his power, revealed through the sanctifying Spirit that he gave to those who believe in him, and shown by his resurrection. Of this one I am a servant. I may be a servant, but I am the servant of this one, whom so many great testimonies have assured us is the Son of God. "Through whom," he says, "we too have received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith." He means: We have the other testimonies we mentioned, but our own case also testifies that he is truly the Son of God. How so? We run and hurry to nations we did not know, and they obey and accept the word of faith. This is truly a testimony that God has appeared. A man leaves his homeland and his family and runs to a foreign land, not for any bodily benefit or gain. Why do I speak of gain and benefit? He toils, goes hungry, is beaten, flogged and despised, and yet he still accomplishes his work and proclaims the faith. He went hungry? Yet he fed others. They despised him? Yet afterwards they admired him. They beat him? Yet they believed. They persecuted him? Yet they sought him out. They flogged him? Yet through his handkerchiefs and aprons they were freed from the scourges of the body. Is this a small testimony, then, or does it fall short of the ones mentioned before, as a way for everyone to recognize that Christ is the Son of God?

QUESTION 284. What is meant by "And I have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit"? It seems to me that this is said with the word order inverted, and that the sense runs on like this: "I have often intended to come to you, so that I might have some fruit." For his presence would certainly have made them bear the fruit of godliness. As for the "fruit," he says: I know that faith has been sown in you, but I also want to have fruit from you, "so that I might have fruit." I count what is yours as mine. So if I see fruit in you, I will rejoice as if I had the fruit myself and could take pride in it. That is the meaning if one takes the passage as inverted, for then what follows will be "And I have been prevented until now." If it is not inverted, it could be understood like this: I have been prevented until now, while I waited to see the fruit of faith in you. Then would we bear fruit anyway? What need is there for your presence? A great deal. He does not say he was waiting for all the fruit, but for "some fruit," so that I myself might make you eager to bear what fruit is still lacking. It is pointless to teach someone who already bears fruit perfectly. In the same way, it is laborious and exhausting to work and plough with the plough of teaching someone who is not at all fit to bear good fruit
For even though they are called, they still need their own will and effort. "For many are called, but few"

QUESTION 285. What is meant by "For the righteousness of God is revealed in it"? "For the righteousness of God": that is, the righteousness of God is revealed and made manifest in his Gospel. How, and in what way? Its manifestation and revelation begin from the faith of the one who comes to it. It then leads the believer on to faith and perfects him in it. This faith is pure and sincere. Human skill does not build it; the light from above gives it freely, in proportion to the person's will. For this is the righteousness of God revealed through the Gospel: finding a seed of faith, it caused the fruit of faith to grow. The meaning of the passage can also be taken another way: the righteousness of God is seen and known in the believer himself. God received a little faith from the believer's own free choice, and he gave him in return the full faith that comes from revelation and divine knowledge. He led him by the hand from imperfect faith and made him ready for the great perfection of faith. Then: "As it is written, The righteous shall live by faith." Do not think, he says, that this is new or recent. It was proclaimed long ago by the prophetic voice of Habakkuk. What voice? "The righteous shall live by faith." That is, the life of the righteous and earnest man. Here he calls righteous the one who has achieved every virtue. This man's life is bounded and enclosed by faith. It begins with the faith of free choice, and it ends and is completed in the faith that comes by divine revelation. So the righteous man always lives by faith. It says "shall live" not because he has not lived and will then cease, but because he will go on living, as he lived before. This amounts to "he always lives by faith." "Shall live" also means that he will remain in it at all times and be made firm in it, so that he would not choose even to live or breathe without it. QUESTION 286. What is meant by the Apostle's saying "Hand him over to Satan"? The divine Paul said "to hand him over to Satan" about the Corinthian who had sinned, and this means, he says, to drive him out of the Church. For those who are driven out of the churches are outside God's care, and they fall under Satan's will and power. He rightly added "for the destruction of the flesh," to show that he does not do even this out of harshness or hatred. He does it so that, learning the difference by experience, they may turn to repentance. And so of the

QUESTION 287. What is meant by "To the end, for her who inherits"? The title raises three questions for us: who is she who inherits, what is the inheritance, and when does the inheriting take place? She who inherits is the Church and all its fullness. The inheritance is what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered the heart of man. He himself made the "when" clear by saying "to the end," which means the age to come, not the present one. Why does he enrol us as heirs? Because he has adopted us as sons. Whom? The worthy. And who are the worthy? Those who keep the commandments. Paul too spoke of her who inherits: "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." And John says: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom." But a bridegroom here on earth lets the intensity of his love cool after the first days. Our bridegroom goes on loving us without end and his longing only grows stronger. John shows this by calling him bridegroom, because his longing is at its height. That is not the only reason he is the bridegroom. He also wants everyone to be one body and one soul through virtue and love. And just as the bride does everything to please her husband, so we too must be, all our lives, like the bride on that day, sitting in the bridal chamber with only one care: how to please the bridegroom. David too mentions this bride when he says: "The queen stood at your right hand," and so on. You have seen her clothing. Do you want to know her sandals too? Paul, the bridegroom's friend, teaches you: "Having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace." Do you want to see her belt as well, and how it is made of truth? "Having girded our loins with truth," he says. Do you want to see her feet too? Listen to the prophet: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, of those

and mother and be joined to his wife. This mystery is great, but I am speaking about Christ and the Church." So he came to her lodging and found her filthy, unkempt, naked and stained with blood. He washed her, anointed her, fed her and clothed her in a garment like no other, becoming her covering himself. Taking her in this state, he leads her up to heaven. The prophet speaks on her behalf. He foretold and proclaimed in advance many things about the bridegroom, about the bridal procession, and about the good things that were waiting for her. That is why here too he speaks for her. And what does she who inherits ask? Let us hear what he says: "Give ear to my words, O Lord."

QUESTION 288. "O Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger." When you hear of wrath and anger in God, do not imagine anything human. These words are a condescension to us. For God is free of all passions, but he speaks this way to reach the understanding of the slower-witted. When we talk with foreigners, we use their language too. When we speak to a child, we lisp along with it, even if we are wise ten thousand times over. Besides, wrath and anger do not necessarily show a passion in the one who directs them. The passion they produce lies in two people: in the one who launches them, and in the one they strike and cause pain. The one who feels wrath or anger is affected by it in some way, and the one who receives the wrath and anger also suffers and is affected. In both, then, passion is seen. But sometimes only the one who directs the wrath and anger can be seen suffering, while the one they are aimed at remains untouched and unchanged. Perhaps he has strengthened his soul through philosophy and risen above the anger of the wrathful and angry. The passion is seen in only one of the two, yet wrath is still called wrath, and anger anger. In the same way, the one who receives the wrath and anger may be the only one affected by passion, while the one who directs them is not changed at all or affected by any passion. By the same reasoning, these would still rightly be called wrath and anger, because they have caused passion and pain in the one who received them. Physicians too, when they cut and cauterize, do not do it out of wrath but in order to heal. They are not angry with the sick; they pity them and free them from their diseases. So when he says, "Do not rebuke me in your wrath," he means: Do not exact from me the penalty for my sins, and do not take action against my offences.
QUESTION 289. "For my bones are troubled." By "bones" here he means all his strength, and by "trouble" he means the blow, the chastisement and the punishment.

Some say that by "trouble" here he means the [fear] that comes from sin. This tends to happen especially with lustful desires, and also with anger and misfortune. All of these trouble the soul and the bones. The pupils of the eyes are distorted, and the eyes do not see properly. When a charioteer is thrown into confusion, the horses run wild. In the same way, when reason is thrown into turmoil, everything is confused and everything is distorted. And how does this trouble arise? This too must be explained. It does not happen in the soul as it does at sea, through the onset of winds or some unexpected circumstance. It happens through our own carelessness. When desire is kindled, it is up to us whether an occasion for sin arises or not. If you do not kindle [?] the flame, the furnace does not blaze up. If you do not feed it with fuel, linger over beautiful faces, go to the theatre of lawlessness, fatten your flesh with luxury, or drown your reason in wine, the flame does not rise. The beast does not grow fiercer, and the purity of the mind is not torn apart as if by savage winds. "Are these things enough, then," someone asks, "to escape the flame of sin?" They are not enough. Other things must be added: constant prayer, the company of holy people, moderate fasting, a simple diet and necessary work. Above all else, there must be the fear of God, the judgement to come and the promises of good things. Through all of these you can bridle raging desire and calm the stormy sea. "O Lord, I have cried to you; hear me." Nearly everyone knows the words of this psalm and keeps singing it at every stage of life, yet people do not know the meaning of some of its sayings. This is no small reason for reproach: to sing it every day and never once try to learn the meaning of what is sung. It shows sluggishness and utter laxity to go on singing the psalm constantly, from earliest youth to extreme old age, knowing only the words and none of their meaning. It is like sitting beside a hidden treasure, or carrying around a sealed purse. No one has been stirred even by curiosity to learn what on earth is being said. Nor can one say that the psalm is so clear that it lulled everyone to sleep and left them nothing to search for. It is obscure, and it can rouse anyone who is not deeply asleep, or rather even someone who is. QUESTION 291. "With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord." Here we learn two virtues: intense eagerness and a focused mind. Besides these we learn a third thing: that the voice is his own.

For not everyone cries out with the voice, or to God, or with his own voice, but all of these must come together. Someone who cries out against his enemies will utter the voice not of a human being but of a beast or a serpent. Someone who is careless and does not listen to what he is saying is not crying to God; he is speaking idly and to no purpose. Someone who does not rouse his mind is again not crying out, however loudly he shouts. For by "voice," as I have often said before, he does not mean the force of the breath but the focused mind. But that is not the case here. Here he brings these three things together: he cries out, he cries to God, and he cries with his own voice. That is why he says twice: "With my voice … with my voice." QUESTION 296 [?]. What is meant by "Michal blessed David"? "Michal blessed David" becomes clear partly from the explanation given earlier, for it is said in place of "she despised him." The woman thought it beneath a king's dignity and majesty to spend his time dancing and leaping. Saul's daughter was not unreasonable in thinking that a king should not let himself be carried away into dancing… But the divine longing he displayed, being so captured by love for the one he longed for, was beyond a woman's understanding, and it exposed her ignorance of the goads that drove David's longing. Holy Scripture notes that she never became the mother of a child, and in this way it announces the penalty for her mockery of David. Michal is allowed to fall into mocking David so that, owing a penalty, she would be made to pay it with childlessness. She is made to pay with childlessness so that no one from the seed of Saul, which [God] was rejecting [?], would succeed to the royal office. It also prevented strife and bloodshed between a son born of her and the sons born later to David's other wives. Why did David put on the ephod? Scripture mentions an ephod in David's case, even though, as a man living piously, he had no right to put on a priest's vestment. Some have explained it this way. Samuel had departed this life, and his sons stood accused. A priest had to go before the ark of God, and there was no one judged worthy of this service. So the king took up this ministry out of necessity, since he himself had brought the ark back from the foreigners. That is also why the ephod gave an oracle promising Israel victory, and David credits the victory to God. Nor was he dishonouring the priestly vestment by doing this. He revered it and considered it worthy of the highest honour. By taking refuge in it, he showed how much honour was owed to those who are truly priests, since their vestment brings a king glory, victory and so much favour. That is what some say. Others, however, think that King David would never have dared

…to put on the priestly robe; rather, they say, there was a garment reserved for kings which also bore the name of the priestly robe, and it was this that the king was wearing at that time. What was Adam doing in paradise? Adam, once placed in paradise, did not live an idle or inactive life. He cultivated virtue and busied himself with the works that belong to it. That is why, when he gave up guarding virtue and what had been entrusted to him, he was condemned to exile from paradise. The tree was in the middle of paradise because it was the tree of life, and it bears a certain analogy to the heart. Just as the heart is set in the middle of a living creature's body, so that tree, being the tree of life, was planted in the middle of paradise. And if you also like the anagogical sense, the most general virtue, they say, as it is seen in the rational creature, spreads over every action as if from a central summit. Life flows out from a central place and so gives life to all the parts of a living creature and holds them together. In the same way this virtue goes out as if from a central spring, and it waters and nourishes the other virtues ranked beneath it. It would also be close to the mark to think that the tree of life is said to have been planted in the middle of paradise because Christ, our life, also accepted the cross for us in the middle of the earth. For they say that the life-bearing tree, the cross, was fixed at the very centre of the earth. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is mentioned, but no place is assigned to it. Why? Because evil has no place of its own. It only exists as something parasitic alongside virtue. But it is better to discuss this later. QUESTION [?]. Why was the lamb sacrificed toward evening? The lamb was sacrificed toward evening because it foreshadowed the true lamb and shepherd, Christ our God. For at the evening of the ages the Creator too underwent a voluntary death for us. The sacrifice was offered when the moon was full because the Saviour of our race was called not only man but also God. The light stands as a type of the Godhead, and the body of the moon as a type of the flesh he assumed. Moreover, at the creation of the world the moon was brought forth shining with full light, and the Saviour's death for our race brought about the renewal and restoration of the whole universe. So it was fitting that he who orders all things wisely should appoint the moon to give undiminished light at that time. QUESTION [?]. What does 'I will set my bow in the cloud' mean? The children of the Greeks consider the bow in the cloud a natural phenomenon, which takes its form from the same things that produce clouds and [the sun?]. But to the divinely

inspired Moses, at least as far as the plain meaning of the words goes, this did not seem so. Rather, the bow seemed to come into being at the same time as the covenant was given. 'For behold,' he says, 'I set my bow in the cloud,' as though it were being set there only then and serving as the sign of the covenant. Still, there is nothing absurd in thinking both that the bow is the beginning [?] of a natural phenomenon and that the Deity took it up to confirm his covenant with Noah. It is as if he said: as long as this happens and nature produces its proper work, there will be no flood. In the same way one might say, 'Until the moon is taken away,' and 'As long as the sun runs across the heavenly pole and gives light to the things on earth.' That is: as long as nature keeps its proper order and is not turned toward dissolution, the human race will not be punished by a flood. The king of Syria sent to Elisha to find out about his own life, even though he worshipped idols rather than God. He did so because rumour everywhere proclaimed Elisha a prophet, and the illness that had come upon the king forced him to ask how it would end. QUESTION [?]. If Noah was righteous, why was he overcome by drunkenness without paying any penalty? Noah was righteous, yet he was overcome by drunkenness and paid no penalty. This is because he did not become drunk through self-indulgence, and he had no law forbidding him to drink wine to excess. Besides, he fell into drunkenness out of ignorance of how wine should be used, not from drinking a great deal. Mixed wine does not fill the brain so much with clouding vapours or darken the mind's governing faculty. Taken unmixed, however, it sends these vapours up hotter and sharper, and it produces this effect even from a small drink, especially in people who are not used to it. Moreover, the divine Paul has already made the case for him before us when he says, 'Sin is not counted where there is no law.' So you will find that under that old way of life those admirable men did many things out of inexperience for which no penalty followed. But now that we have laws and the knowledge of what we must do is perfectly clear, it is right that those who transgress meet the punishment for breaking the law. QUESTION [?]. Where can one learn from Scripture that Adam was deceived by the devil? You asked where one can learn from Scripture that Adam was deceived by the devil. All the pious believe this, but Scripture presents Eve as deceived only through the serpent, and Adam through her,

so the answer to the question is quite clear. For the Lord himself taught us in the Gospels, saying, 'He was a murderer from the beginning.' He is not pointing to Cain here, as some have thought. He lays the charge on Satan himself. The serpent, which served as the devil's instrument, presents no difficulty, but it could not possibly be regarded as the real agent and first cause of the deception. The evil one brought the deception to Eve through this creature rather than another because the woman was fond of it, owing to its general cleverness, and because it was able to imitate. Besides, the devil saw that this creature had a certain innate shrewdness, and so he thought it suitable to serve him as the instrument of his deception, since [?]… And the words 'Lord, my heart was not lifted up, nor were my eyes raised high, nor did I walk among great things, nor among things too wonderful for me' might perhaps be taken of David himself. David was invested with kingship and often set up trophies over his enemies. Before that he had gone from being a shepherd to living in palaces and had been granted more than he had ever hoped for. Later he showed anger against Nabal, and he charged his son to exact the death penalty from Joab and Shimei, along with other things of this kind. All this makes David even more admirable if, tested in so many such ways, the steadiness of his soul was not shaken. Though granted more than he had hoped for, he did not exalt himself or lift up his heart, imagining his own position to be greater than was fitting. Instead he referred everything to the almighty Providence that rules over all things,

bringing and laying everything before it, never forgetting [?] the words 'But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people.' If anyone wishes to take the saying as referring also to someone else who has achieved the virtue of humility, as a monument and portrait, so to speak, of a man whose mind is humbled and contrite, he too would not be far from what is reasonable. In any case, as can be gathered from many passages, the great David too was adorned with humility. Some have thought that the saying also fits the whole of human nature. Because of the weakness of the flesh, they say, and the passions that spring up and dwell in the body, human nature can never stretch upward and rise above itself. It is dragged down as if by a weight, burdened now by this and now by that. It is never free of what troubles and constrains it, and it cannot even think the greatest thoughts about itself. But it does well to consider itself earth and ashes, unworthy of rising beyond what is human. Otherwise, by eating from the tree out of a desire for divinity, it would be brought down even from the rank that properly belongs to it. From this it lifts up the soul and nourishes it with sweet food, those thoughts on which it cannot be nourished together with the body [?]. For indeed: 'As a weaned child upon its mother…' Some carry the interpretation over to our Lord Jesus Christ and hold that it is a prophecy describing his life and victory. Their view too would not rank second among those who have studied the saying. Take 'They pierced my hands and my feet': [David] speaks it, but it was fulfilled in Christ. The same is true of the saying 'They laid me in the lowest pit' and 'They divided my garments,' and of countless others. Paul saw this too, and he urges us to take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ. For Christ our God, though he is above all height and all eminence, was not lifted up and was not raised high. It is fitting [?] to quote the apostle: 'He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself even to death.' And he himself says at the time of his passion, 'I could appeal to my Father, and he would provide me with more than twelve legions of angels.' But in my opinion [?], no greatness or wonder beyond him either existed or was imagined, and he never turned to be carried beyond it. For what could be more wonderful or greater than the nature established above all greatness and dignity [?]? Yet not even as a man did he compete or keep company with those clothed in great glory and pomp in earthly, fleshly matters. Quite the opposite: he ordered his whole self with humility and moderation. That is why the prophet says, 'Rejoice, daughter of Zion,' and then gives the reason for the joy: 'For meek and

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople.] [?] your king comes to you.' The word 'weaned' would also fit what has been said, because he brought the soul he had assumed back to its ancient, original dignity. This would be the meaning of 'As a weaned child upon its mother.' Someone might also understand it to mean that, after completing his life among men in a way befitting both God and man, he returned to the bosom of the Father, which he had never left. He too would be saying something reasonable. For when he went back up there and received judgement over all, he justified all in himself. This is also what the words 'So you will repay upon my soul' would indicate.

QUESTION 300 [?]. Why does God appear to Moses in a bush and not in some other plant? For many reasons. But before giving the reasons why he appeared in this way, it is better to say that the symbol signifies three things. First, the bush was enveloped in fire but not consumed. In the same way Israel was handed over to trials and punishments and to the flame of misery that their captors kindled for them, but they were kept from perishing and being reduced to ashes by the right hand of God alone. Second, God the Word, the Father's light and the immaterial fire of the Godhead, flashed within the earthy, material womb of the Virgin, and he would keep the one who received him unburned and unharmed. Or, if you prefer, the same fire of the Godhead, united with human nature, would make it glow and deify it, but would not burn it up or destroy it. The mystery of the bush prefigures such things [?]. And it is the bush that is set under the fire, and not some other plant, perhaps because the desert bore no other plant besides this one. It is also so that we may learn something about the fire of the Godhead. When it enveloped human nature, which had put forth sins like thorns, it set that nature ablaze but did not consume it. The thorns around it, however, it burned up and destroyed. Or, if you prefer, it is also because of the multitudes of the nations. They were swept along by groveling notions about God and steeped, as it were, in godlessness. They put forth the shoots of sin, and their worship was rotten in its very structure. These nations were about to be burned and purged of their thorny, weed-choked error by the coming and illumination of the Holy Spirit, and to receive the rays of the divine fire. For 'He,' it says, 'will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.' So that what is being depicted might be portrayed more vividly and clearly, the bush is used, serving the fire without being burned by it. For it creeps low, is thorny and weak in substance, and spreads out along the [surface] of the earth. In these respects the nations correspond to it. Further, there is hardly anything

lowlier than such a plant. It grows to some extent, but it never rises off the ground and always creeps along it. Fire, on the other hand, is light, and of all the things perceived by the senses it is the most buoyant and rises highest. It was to be shown that the nature of the Godhead, which dwells beyond all beings and is higher than them (for Scripture often calls God fire), did not disdain to come down to the lowlier nature of human beings, kneaded together with clay and earth. So it was fitting that a plant suited to this illustration was chosen. You might also observe that the Hebrew nation was somehow inclined to desert to polytheism, since it had been mixed up with the customs of the Egyptians for many years. So that no opening toward polytheism might arise for them, the miracle was shown in such an ugly, lowly plant, one useless for carving idols. Otherwise, struck with amazement at what they saw, they might have recorded [?] the very form [?] of God as a god and worshipped it. Or they might have carved images and likenesses out of it and worshipped the works of their hands as their gods. These were people who at such cost made a calf and worshipped the image of an ox's head as God, though they had seen no divine sign in it whatever. What would they not have dared if fire had appeared to them, burning without consuming, on one of the beautiful plants that are useful for people's needs? This is especially true since they had heard the lawgiver say, 'God spoke to Moses out of the bush.'

QUESTION 301 [?]. God broke up and divided the people of the Hebrews, settling one part in Samaria and leaving the other in Judea. For it is written that the Lord said to Solomon, 'I will surely tear the kingdom [from you].' Since it was he who tore it apart, why does he subject to reproaches and accusations those who underwent a division that came from God?
