If God is the one tearing apart, who would condemn [?] the schism and division? Who will deliver [?]…

Such, then, if I remember correctly, was your difficulty. One must understand, not only in the present difficulty but in all others of a similar kind, that God's sentences of punishment which come before the event are not themselves the cause of the event. Even among us human beings, let alone with the Deity, someone who foresees and foretells a future event cannot justly be held to be its cause. Such things are said in divine Scripture so that we may not be led to attribute the punishments brought upon us for our sins to some other power or principle. The divine word heads off this suspicion by foretelling what will befall us because of our sins. This is one reason why the cause of such things is referred to the Divine. The second is that, although he is able to check our inclination toward the worse, he does not use force or drag us toward the opposite. Of this kind also is the saying 'He who makes peace and creates

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople.] [evil?]' and 'I know that Pharaoh will not listen to you; for this reason I will harden his heart.' 'I will harden' does not mean that he himself will reshape Pharaoh's heart into hardness. It means that, since Pharaoh was inclining and bent toward hardness, God does not rein him in, so as not to take away the free will of human nature. Since the Egyptian had set out of his own free will, God will not change him or force him into acting against his will. That is what 'I will harden' means. The phrase may also carry another implied meaning. 'I will harden' can stand for 'Upon him who is hard and unyielding in mind I will bring hard things, worthy of the cruelty of his character.' So it is here too, as we said. The Divine foresaw that, of their own impulse and will, they would revolt from Rehoboam and follow Jeroboam, a servant and a rebel, and that the nation would be split into two parts. God, who knew this beforehand as he knows everything else, foretells what will happen and says, 'I will tear the kingdom,' for the two reasons given above. Even though the Divine speaks this way everywhere and refers everything to himself, they did not stop running off to other gods. They served Astarte, who among the Greeks is Artemis, and Chemosh, and the flies, and credited them with the providence and preservation of their own lives. What would they not have dared if they had found some pretext in the meaning of the sacred Scriptures for thinking that someone else determined their punishments, and that their slide into worse things came from another source? You can also see in the trial of righteous Job that God permits the temptations and sets certain limits for the tempter, such as: 'This you are allowed to test, but that you must not touch.' Everything depends on the almighty right hand. In some things it helps and works along with us, and in others it permits and does not prevent. Something similar seems to be the case with 'The anger of the Lord was again kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Number Israel."' He incites David to number Israel because the righteous Judge's anger and punishment were owed to Israel for their sins. It is no one else who stirs David up but he who was angry with Israel and was about to bring the penalty upon them. We know that they are responsible for the sin, and the divine oracles testify to it. But the divine sentence is the maker of the harmful things that come upon us for our sins, for it belongs to a righteous judge to fit the punishment to the gravity of the deeds. Those who sinned are responsible for the anger, and the anger brought punishment upon them, using David as an intermediary. They had offended against David, and he too had sinned against God, for he did number the people. Yet he quickly condemned himself before the others, for it says, 'David's heart struck him because he had numbered the people.' But for what transgression did the people at that time deserve to suffer punishment, if not, clearly, for the rebellion against

…of their king David? This was when they broke away from law and just rule and joined in the rising and revolt of the man who raised tyrannical hands against his father and king, and who neither revered nature nor felt shame before the dignity of kingship. From then on bloodshed flowed freely as they turned on one another, and every law of nature was trampled underfoot: children often bore swords against their fathers, and the dearest son lay dead, the work of a father's hand. Such are the evils of civil strife. Israel, then, deserved to suffer punishment for this slaughter of one another. And since Israel had to be punished, the inciting of David to number the…

The numbering of the people by the king was not in itself one of the gravest offences, even if it is now presented as the cause of the punishment. This is shown by the later numbering carried out by the same David. Nothing evil came of that one; it was neither charged with wickedness nor did it bring down any penalty. It took place toward the end of the king's reign, when the number of the Levites was also counted. Scripture hints at this as well, for it places "The anger of the Lord was again kindled against Israel" before "he incited David." In this way it leads and rouses the hearer to see that God's anger was kindled not because the people were numbered, but because of the rebellion, tyranny and bloodshed that had already taken place among them. Placing the anger before the numbering shows that the anger was not brought on by the numbering. And it is David himself who is incited, and no one else, because Absalom's rebellion came about through his own sin. "For because," it says, "you have murdered and committed adultery, you will be subjected to others; and more than that, your wives will be handed over to others before your very eyes" — which is exactly what Absalom did. So the sinner himself is incited, so that he may become aware of his own fault and cry out, "I have sinned, and I have done wrong; but these people, what have they done?" Then through his confession and repentance the slaughter would abate, and when it ceased, salvation would come to the nation. Or rather, to tell it from the beginning: the people owed the penalty. Therefore the anger of God was again kindled against Israel. The anger incites David to the numbering. Once the people had been numbered, the plague fell on them. While the plague was raging, David came to awareness of his transgression, and awareness led him to repentance. Repentance moves forgiveness and mercy from above, and these stop the slaughter. So the calamity fell upon the people as if from a head, from the one who had sinned, and in turn the suffering was halted through his repentance.

QUESTION 302. Why is the divine David permitted to fall into sin, and so great a sin at that? Perhaps for other, secret reasons as well. But at any rate, it may be so that he would stand as an example of repentance for human life.

…attested to have lived according to God's heart. He fell, yet he quickly rose again and strove through repentance and tears to wash away his slip. How then must not we, who fall not once but continually, try to wipe out our sins with warm tears and a contrite heart? And further, it may be so that none of those who shine in good deeds like human stars should, if they slip into some transgression, give themselves over to despair and [?]. Instead, having before them that blessed David, who committed so great a transgression yet found so swift a cure, they too may rise up to the same zeal, recover from their fall, give themselves wholly to repentance, and hold fast to their former good deeds. Perhaps God also permits David to fall into sin so that the Jewish nation, hearing the testimonies of Holy Scripture about him, should not raise him up to be a god. For the same reason the body of Moses was removed, and to this day it remains unknown to the children of Israel. The divine Paul also hints at something like this about himself when he says, "so that no one may think more of me than what he sees and hears." Indeed, when some of the pagans saw him and Barnabas working wonders, they rushed to offer sacrifices to them as gods.

QUESTION 303. Why did God call Israel his firstborn? God calls Israel firstborn when he was sending Moses to Pharaoh. In this way he showed how much love and affection he had for Israel. It is as if he were saying to Moses: "Tell Pharaoh: the affection you have and keep for your firstborn son is the same affection that God, you must understand, has for the race of Israel." That is also why, when Pharaoh refused to grant Israel freedom and departure, the plague was let loose on the firstborn of Pharaoh and of the Egyptians. Further, God is the maker and creator of all nations, and so he also provides for them all. In later times he was going to turn all the nations to the knowledge of himself, to call them, and to make them his sons and heirs of grace. But before that he chose the nation of Israel, so that through it he might gather the others as well. The apostles show this: they sprang from Israel, but became teachers and gatherers of all the nations. For this reason the name "firstborn" was granted to the Israelites. Yet this firstborn does not receive the more perfect things of true religion, because he proved hard and disobedient, not only in Egypt but also in the desert after the exodus from Egypt. Therefore he is not deemed worthy of the more perfect mysteries, but for the time being is schooled by the law that holds second rank. For there was the law written by the finger of God and engraved on tablets not made by hands, which prefigured our own law, the law of Christ. The Jewish nation was not deemed worthy to receive it because of

their impiety and lawlessness over the calf. Instead it receives the second law, which Moses wrote on tablets he had hewn himself. If they had received the very tablets written by God, hewn in a way no human hand could achieve, they might perhaps have regarded them as gods and kindled God's wrath against themselves all the more. For the reason we have given, then, the more perfect mysteries are not handed down to them. But in the last days the Word of God became man and adopted the nations as sons. To them he gives no longer the worship in type and shadow, which has grown old, but the pure beauty of true religion, young and flourishing in truth and in reality. Since, then, all the nations were adopted as sons, it was fitting that the people of Israel, who were called to adoption before them, should be called firstborn. Consider another point here as well. The Word of God, in his humanity, plainly came from the stock of Israel, and through him every Egyptian firstborn, that is, every ungodly and godless offspring, is handed over to death and corruption. Since, then, the destroyer of the Egyptian firstborn sprang from Israel, he calls Israel too firstborn. This, then, is also what the Evangelist records: "Out of Egypt I called my Son." These matters should therefore be examined more closely.

QUESTION 304. How do the heavens declare the glory of God? The heavens have no mouth, yet they declare the glory of God. For the Creator is seen in the greatness and beauty of his creatures, and for those who have any sense, the wonder they feel at creatures is carried back and passes over to their Maker. So the heavens proclaim the Creator's power not with words but with deeds, and they summon those who look at them rightly to give glory. If you wish to take it in the sense of spiritual contemplation, you will find that the heavens are the apostles. They declared the Gospel of Christ to the whole world, and they showed and taught people to glorify God, who took on what is ours for our sake. Or, if you like, the heavens declared the glory of Christ our God when, without leaving his Father's bosom, he deigned to take flesh from a Virgin, and Bethlehem and the cave held him. For at that time the beings counted as belonging to the heavens, both the visible and those beyond the visible, served and ministered to the wonder. The visible heaven appointed the star as a kind of public herald and sent it ahead; it proclaims the glory of the Master and escorts the hidden King with a single bodyguard. The other sent forth a multitude of the heavenly host, praising the Creator and telling in song the wonder that was taking place. It would not be unreasonable to call the angels heavens, since they came down from above to the things of earth. And if you wish to see the sun too, darkening its face at the Lord's passion and, by putting off its beautiful light,
proclaiming the divinity and power of the one who suffered, you would come close to the contemplative interpretation as well.

"You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished." They say this means that when the nations were rebuked, turned away from their own error and became part of Christ's flock, the devil who had called them out to impiety perished. For both the one who is ungodly himself and the one who drags others into ungodliness may be called ungodly. But it would be closer to the meaning to take it this way. When the Saviour had come to earth, he called everyone alike, Jews, Greeks and barbarians, to the knowledge of himself, and through baptism he brought a rebuke that, as it were, purified and perfected them from their former impieties. All who received the rebuke obediently and sincerely became part of the company of the saved. But anyone who balked at the rebuke, accepting neither the cleansing of baptism nor the illumination of faith that comes through it, will perish as ungodly and deserving of destruction. I know also that the word epitimia, especially among the wise men outside the Church, means honour, distinction and glory. If one takes the word in this sense, then the passage would say this: Christ honoured and glorified the nations, for he made those who obey him sons and heirs of his kingdom, while those who are unworthy of the inheritance and the adoption will perish, because they are ungodly.

QUESTION 306. Why were the magi from the East, and not from any other land [?], the first to come to the place where the Lord was born? For many reasons, I think. First, they were fulfilling a prophecy that says, "Kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring gifts." For at that time the Persians held power over those regions. Their land also produces fine gold, myrrh and frankincense. Besides, the kingdom of the Egyptians had passed to the Assyrians, and that of the Assyrians had passed to the Persians, so that the Persians then held precedence among the kings on earth. It was therefore fitting that those who held first place at that time should come to the first and only King of the ages, Christ our God, who had appeared on earth, to worship him and bring him gifts. By this act they confessed that the newborn King was also the

Master, Lord and King of them too, though they ruled almost the whole earth and held precedence over all, and that he was worshipped and escorted by them. Abraham the patriarch also came from that region; he was the first to set out from the land of the Chaldeans and proclaim the knowledge of God. If someone says that this is why these men too were moved to come from there before all others to worship the Saviour, it would not be far from right understanding either. Such a dispensation clearly trumpets that the same God was at work then and now, then in types, now in the realities themselves and in truth. Consider this as well. The kings of the Assyrians often sacked Jerusalem and plundered the treasures in the divine temple, and at times they even gave the temple itself to the flames, along with all the other things that history relates about these events. But the rule of the Assyrians passed to the Persians, and with it all their wealth passed to them, both what they had taken as spoil and what they received as tribute from their subjects. So God leads the Persians to worship the King of Israel, who is Christ our God, to whom the temple in Jerusalem had been dedicated and the sacrifices offered. And they run swiftly and make their offering. In place of the dishonour their fathers had done to God's holy things, they offer honour. In place of blasphemies they offer praise of God, and worship in place of their other drunken outrages, and gifts in place of what had been plundered. In this way they make a kind of apology for their ancestors' audacity and seek pardon for them through their own act. They offer gold in place of the gold and sacred treasures they had plundered; frankincense in place of the sacrifices they had stopped; and myrrh for those they had once slain long ago during the siege, whom they would have raised up and restored if they could [?]. They bring myrrh as a kind of honour to the dead, and perhaps they also show their intention: that, as far as it lay with them, they would have chosen to rebuild the ruined temple and the city of Jerusalem. For myrrh usually binds together what has been separated and torn apart. It is true that under Ezra and Zerubbabel some of the plundered sacred objects were brought back. But this was done incompletely, since our Redeemer and Saviour had not yet come, and the plunderers did not return the plundered things in person, but through others. The arrival of the Persians first would also be a sign announcing in advance that those from the nations will recognize their own Master before Israel does. And if one wishes to take the gifts that were

brought this way, that the gold was offered to him as King of all, as a kind of tribute and sign of obedience, the frankincense as to God, and the myrrh as to one who would die for our sake, this too would fit well enough with what has been set out.

QUESTION 307. Why does Herod order the magi who had come to worship our Saviour Christ, "Search carefully for the child, and when you find him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him"? As far as the literal sense goes, the reason is this. He was king of Judea, and when he heard of the birth of a king he was troubled and sought to kill the one he expected to remove him from his throne. Since it was not easy to find the child, he resorted to a trick and a deception. That is why he says, "so that I too may come and worship him." But that is the literal understanding. Perhaps, however, he is unwittingly prophesying the future: that not only will the nations worship Christ through the Persians, but after their worship all Judea too will worship him. If you like, the typological reading can be drawn from this very point. For Herod would represent the two peoples. He was from the nations, yet he reigned over Jews. So, unwillingly and without knowing what he was saying, he would nevertheless be prophesying, and confessing, as if on behalf of the whole human race, nations and Jews alike, the worship due to God who came to dwell among men. Nothing prevents him from prophesying. Caiaphas too did not know what he was saying. His heart was stirred to a murderous frenzy, yet his lips uttered a prophecy when he said, "It is better that one man die than that the whole nation perish." And indeed, if Christ our God had not died, the human race would not have been saved. Each of them was unworthy of the prophetic gift. Even so, the dignity of the priesthood and that of kingship still enjoyed some measure of grace, since they had not yet dared to commit the murder of the Master. In the same way you might see

…worshipping the resurrection. They know him as true God who became man for the salvation of the human race, and they serve and adore him sincerely. And indeed the Romans attacked them in war, overthrew the city, laid waste the temple, and put the nation to the sword. In the Old Scriptures you will also find a donkey that learned the future in advance and taught it beforehand. From all this you will see that nothing prevents Herod too from having said what he said to the magi as a prophetic type.

QUESTION 308. Why does the Forerunner rebuke Herod? John the Forerunner and Baptist rightly rebukes Herod for turning aside into lawlessness. Herod came from a foreign stock, being a descendant of the elder Herod. Even so, he reigned over Jews and lived by the laws and customs of the Jews, and under those laws he was not permitted to take Herodias as his wife, since she had a child by his brother. When a brother dies childless, the law allows union with his wife, "so that," it says, "he may raise up offspring for his brother." But when offspring and children had been left, relations with a brother's wife were an abomination. The Forerunner makes his rebuke not so much out of concern for Herod as out of care to set the people right. When the offences of rulers and kings go unrebuked, the people are readily encouraged to imitate them; but when such conduct is checked, the subjects too are compelled to be more careful about breaking the law. I also now recall reading in a [?] history that Herod's passion for his brother's wife was not restrained even while his brother was still alive. For both these reasons, the Forerunner would bring his rebuke against Herod all the more firmly and boldly.

QUESTION 309. How should we understand the saying "Among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen"? I have spoken elsewhere too about how no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen among those born of women, and how the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. But nothing prevents me, since you have asked, from discussing this point: that the meaning of the saying is that there has not arisen under the law

…presents no prophet greater than he. For he was the nearest in time to Christ, and he is recorded as "the voice of one crying out," trumpeting, "Prepare the way of the Lord." The text, then, says that no one else greater than he has arisen, but it does not force us to understand that he rose to a rank higher than everyone. That none of the others is greater than the Forerunner in no way prevents many from reaching equality with him. As for "the one who is least is greater than he," some have taken it to refer to Christ, since at that time the Master was reckoned the lesser in age, in bodily growth and in the opinion of most people. But I have given this view the treatment it deserves elsewhere too. Besides, the phrase "among those born of women" contains something that conflicts with this explanation. For Christ was not born simply of a woman, but of a Virgin, and the Virgin could not properly be called a woman, unless one wishes to use the word loosely, as the divine Paul does somewhere when he says, "born of a woman." Christ, then, having come forth from a Virgin and not, properly speaking, from a woman, would place himself outside the comparison with John. Others say that "the least in the kingdom of heaven" here means the one who has been deemed worthy of grace, so that the sense would be this: of those who were born under the law, no one would be greater than John; but of those who appeared after grace, in so far as they were deemed worthy of what he did not live to obtain, in this respect the lesser would have the advantage over him. For whoever is ranked first in greatness and glory among the types and foreshadowings will find no grounds for equality with someone who seems to hold even the lowest rank among those ordered and revealed in the truth and in the realities themselves. John did become an eyewitness of Christ. He ministered to the mystery of baptism, and he stood as a resounding witness to the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. Yet he departed this life while the law and the shadow were still preserved in their remnants, and grace had not yet shone out purely and fully. For only after he had been held in prison and had suffered an unjust death for rebuking the breach of the laws of Moses did our Lord Jesus Christ begin to preach the kingdom of God. For this reason, of all who have been born again through water and the Spirit and have been deemed worthy of the coming and the gifts of the Paraclete, none would rank second to John. Indeed, even the one who has received the lowest rank [holds] the advantage over him…

…would bring out something greater. And unless one takes the phrase “before grace” to mean that the Lord's verdict, that no one is greater than John, was pronounced about the time before grace, you would have to rank him even above our most glorious Lady the Theotokos and above the chief apostles, which no reasoning would allow. But the discussion of this point, having long been subject to the way of life that suits me, finds the present demand for precision a burden.

QUESTION 310. Why was our Lord Jesus Christ pierced with a lance during his saving passion? During his saving passion Christ our God is pierced in the side with a lance. By this he both renews and prefigures for us two baptisms, one by water and the other by blood. For these did not flow from the saving side by the ordinary course and sequence of nature: the wound was made after death, and after the wound the side poured out streams. And he receives the wound in the side, and not in another part, because the woman was formed from Adam's side, and through her sin was brought about for Adam. So Christ our God, the new Adam, is struck in the side, as if by that wound he were destroying sin and freeing Adam from the fall that came upon him through his side. In this way the saying is fulfilled here too: “Where sin abounded” (that is, in Eve, who came from Adam's side), “there grace overflowed,” that is, in the side of Christ. For sin abounds in that first side, because evil sprang from there. And grace overflows in turn in the Lord's side, not only because sin was struck and destroyed in it, but also because the fountain of salvation and cleansing gushed out from it and remains, never running dry. So in the end a side becomes the healing of a side: the one struck by a lance heals the one struck by sin.

QUESTION 311. What does “Lord, do not let this sin stand against them” mean, and did the prayer reach its fulfilment? The words “Lord, do not let this sin stand against them” and what follows did not, as one might naively suppose, come to fulfil- (7) [?] “before the”: Colbertine manuscript, “of the first.” (8) So the same manuscript, for “one might say.”

PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE. -ment, nor did the prayer reach its end in that sense. Our Master, who loves humankind and is the Saviour of our race, does pray that the sin should not stand against those who crucified him. In this way he sketches for us patterns of love for humankind and of goodwill toward one another, so that we may not be carried away into rage, anger and curses even against those who seem bent on killing us. But he also prays that the sin should not stand against them if they themselves stop short of evil and are not carried further toward the same cliff of wantonness and lawlessness. And upon all who did stop short of evil, no punishment for their sins came. For many of the Jews not only received pardon but also learned the truth instead, ran to true religion, and were shown to be sons and heirs of the kingdom of heaven. But those who did not halt their headlong rush into evil, and instead heaped murder upon murder and ran aground on the extreme of madness, paid the penalty justly. Even so, the Saviour's prayer remained and did not miss its aim. I know that some propose another interpretation of the saying. They say that those who crucified Christ and were present at the passion were not Jews, but rather Romans and people from other nations. The Jews had declared, “According to our law he ought to die, but it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” Then, once they had handed Christ over to Pilate, it was the Roman soldiers and people of the other nations who carried out everything done against Christ. Even at the betrayal of the Master, since the Jews were subject to the Romans and were not permitted to do as they wished, they did not dare to be present at the arrest on their own, but brought the cohort and the tribune along with them. So our Lord Jesus Christ, who loves the human race and cares for his own creation, shaped his will and his love for humankind into the form of a prayer and said, “Do not let this sin stand against them,” and then, “For they do not know what they are doing.” And in truth the throng of Romans and the people from the nations did not know what they were doing, for they had not been initiated into what the law and the prophets had proclaimed about him beforehand. So, they say, he prays for the Romans and the nations, and the fruit of the prayer appears at once. At the very moment of the passion you can see the centurion crying out that the crucified one was the Son of God. A little later you can see that wonderful man Longinus, who not only confessed and believed in Christ but also ran the race of martyrdom for him and showed in his blood how pure and unwavering his faith was. And many
others of those present at the time you will find were counted worthy of adoption as sons of God and did not fall away from eternal [?]…

QUESTION 312. How many men named Asterius were there, and what was the belief of each [?]? Two men named Asterius flourished at the same time: one a shield-bearer of the Arian madness, the other a nursling of the true doctrines. The second studied under the great Julian and was trained in the monastic contests while still a youth. Later he led an ascetic monastery, and among his disciples, along with many other distinguished men, was the renowned Acacius of Beroea. The lover of the Arian heresy, on the other hand, practised the art of the sophists from his youth and was raised in the error of the pagans. Late in life he pretended to be a Christian and went over to the Arian party. The latter paid the penalty at Antioch for his unbridled tongue, the work of the prayer of the wonderful Julian; it was that tongue that roused the holy man to bring just punishment upon him. So the one was a nursling of orthodoxy and the other a herald of error. Nor does the man who composed the description of the martyr Euphemia have anything in common with the champion of impiety. First, the impious man paid the penalty quickly, whereas the author of the description of that painting reached a ripe old age, as he mentions in some of his discourses. Second, the one was filled with the Arian madness, while this man teaches the orthodox doctrines in his own discourses. He does not blaspheme the Son and Word of God as coming from nothing, as the raving Asterius did, but speaks of him as God who always exists and is always with the Father. Third, the heretic Asterius received the episcopate, not of Amasea but of some other city near Antioch, from his fellow heretics as a wage for his impiety. Later his like-minded friends summoned him to Antioch to support their impious doctrine, and there, through the prayers of the wonderful Julian, as was said above, he ended his life miserably. Besides all this, the one teaches his flock, works hard at the virtues, and is shown to be a dwelling place of every way of life pleasing to God, while the other is known to have nothing of the kind.

QUESTION 313. On Jacob and Leah. Scripture makes it clear that after seven years Jacob received Leah as his wife instead of Rachel. It also teaches clearly that he married Rachel in return for further service, which likewise lasted seven years. But it does not state clearly whether he took her at once upon promising the service, or married her only after completing the whole of it. As far as the words go, it leaves the matter in doubt: did he receive Rachel as his wage immediately upon promising the service, or only after the labour had been performed and the promise fulfilled, and then

took her in marriage? From the wording, the sense could go either way. But certain considerations incline the mind rather to the view that he took the woman as his wife immediately after the promise. If he had married her only after completing the seven years, Jacob would plainly have spent not merely twenty years in Laban's house, as he himself says, but more. For if he married Rachel after fourteen years, further time must certainly have passed: time in which her barrenness was proven, time in which she gave Jacob her maidservants to bear children, time in which they conceived and bore the children, and after that still more time, in which Rachel was freed from the reproach of barrenness and gave birth to Joseph. Then, after Joseph's birth, Scripture indicates another six years in which Jacob served Laban for a wage of sheep. So the total would not come to only twenty years; once the intervening periods are added, in which Rachel was barren and the maidservants bore children, the total grows larger. And what wage is assigned to Jacob for serving Laban in the time between the fourteen years and the six? For in none of the periods does Jacob appear to have toiled at his service without pay. For the first seven years Leah was his wage in place of Rachel; for the second, Rachel; and for the last six years, the wage paid to him in sheep. So for the time between the fourteen years and the last six, what other wage is recognized? If Jacob married Rachel only after completing the fourteen years, and the maidservant and Rachel then spent further time, first in barrenness and then in childbearing, the wage for that time too ought to have been made known. But nowhere in Scripture does such a wage appear, nor is any period besides the fourteen and the six years counted in as an addition.

QUESTION 314. Now the passage in Second Kingdoms reads, “He incited David,” while in First Chronicles it is given as, “Satan stood up against Israel and incited David to number the people.” These are not contrary to each other, even if they seem to be. The wrath of God incited David, that is, moved and stirred him to the numbering, because of the people's apostasy. And “Satan” generally

is used in the divine Scripture to mean “buffeting” and “temptation.” So if God had not been angry, David would not have been incited, that is, he would not have turned to the idea of numbering the people. And if he had not been incited, the temptation, that is, “Satan,” would not have fallen upon Israel either. The numbering itself is called the cause of the temptation, although it was rather the apostasy that gave birth to the cause. For Moses also numbered the people, and David did so again after the plague, and neither blame nor plague fell upon any of those numberings. That “Satan” is taken to mean temptation and buffeting is also clear from other passages. For it says, “He raised up a satan against Israel, Ader the Jew [?].” And the apostle Paul says, “A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, to buffet me,” that is, a messenger and agent of temptation and buffeting, the one through whom buffetings and temptations come upon me. The saying might allude either to Alexander the coppersmith, who did Paul much harm, or to the tyrants and teachers of false doctrine of that time who rose up against him and became the causes and agents of many temptations for him.

QUESTION 315. The saying “I have found David, a man after my heart” would not be found [?] in these exact words in the Old Testament. It is true that the Psalms sing, “I have found David my servant; with holy oil I anointed him,” but that differs in wording from the saying quoted. Closer would be what the prophet Samuel said to Saul. Reproaching him for transgressing the commandments of the law and foretelling that he would lose the kingdom, he said to him: “Since you are not willing to walk in the ways of the Lord and his commandments, God will choose for himself a man after his own heart, who will do everything that is pleasing before him.” This is fuller than the psalm verse, yet even it does not match word for word the saying, “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart.” Still, the divine Paul knew it and gave it that form when he addressed the people in Acts. David is said to have been found a man after God's heart for this reason: of the many commandments by which the character of virtue is marked, none sets a person so close to God, or raises him so far toward likeness to God as human nature allows, as repaying enemies with good. For the Lord's word in the Gospels says, “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful; for he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil.” And again: “Do good to those who hate you, so that you may become like my Father in heaven.” So David, having achieved this virtue, even though in other matters, being human,

he fell, was fittingly found after God's heart [?]. David excelled in piety and the rest of virtue not only in comparison with Saul but in comparison with nearly all who came after him. For it says, “No one was like David in doing what was right before the Lord.” This is why the prophet, foreseeing David's virtue, says, “God will choose for himself a man after his own heart, and he will do everything that is pleasing before him.” But nothing prevents us from moving from the letter to the deeper sense and saying that the oracle was fulfilled not only in that David but much more in Christ, who descends from the seed of David and Jesse, and of whose kingdom there will be no end. For the sacred Scripture says of him elsewhere: “He will call upon me as Father, and I will make him firstborn, high above all the kings.” So God, revealing through the prophet this one, who is of the seed of David according to his humanity but God the Word from God, Christ our Saviour, says that he has found him after his heart. It is as though he were joined to one and the same will, even though he was known in the compound of human nature, and in him the counsel and working of the Father's will was undivided. For it says, “What the Father wills, the Son also wills,” and there are countless other such sayings. And strictly speaking, he is the one who has fulfilled everything that is pleasing [?]. David, on the other hand, might give some people a handle [?] in what he did: most obviously in the matter of Uriah, and in the numbering of the people, and perhaps also in his headlong rush and anger against Nabal, and [?] in that, by not keeping everything in the law, he fell under a kind of curse. For he does not appear to have eaten the Passover, and he transgressed not a few things in the law, even if not the vital ones. There is also the command he gave his son against Joab and Shimei, and the words, “You shall not build me a house, for you are a man of blood.” Even if these have explanations that lead to David's acquittal, at first sight they stand in the way, for many readers, of his having done everything after God's heart. As for the fact that in the wilderness the manna was sent down to Israel in the morning and the quail in the evening, it may be understood along these lines. The manna came down in the morning because it was a type of the heavenly bread, Christ our God, who as the Sun of Righteousness and the dawn came to us who sat in darkness. Since the visible manna is likened to the Sun of Righteousness and to the dawn, it fittingly comes down in the morning, keeping the correspondence with what it resembles. The quail comes down in the evening and supplies the Israelites with animal sacrifice, because it pointed to the worship under the law, which was performed in shadows and in the fainter traces of the truth. Moreover, the smoke and the gloomy

fumes from the sacrifices darkened the air. So it was fitting that what foreshadowed the sacrifice of the law was brought down to the Israelites toward evening. Likewise, if anyone wishes to take this as a foreshadowing of faith in Christ, he would not stray from what is reasonable [?]. And if anyone should say that the manna prefigured the body of Christ, which the Saviour took and gave to his disciples, saying, “Eat, all of you,” he would reasonably find a meaning in its being brought to the Israelites in the morning. For the catholic Church of God keeps this practice now: in the morning hour it celebrates the sacred, pure and bloodless sacrifice and receives the grace of the all-holy Spirit.

QUESTION 317. In the words spoken to Abraham, “I will set my covenant between me and you,” “covenant” here means circumcision. And “between me and you” means: this covenant of mine will mediate between the two of us, so that the promises I make to you will be without falsehood. But “between me and you” can also suggest a span of time, if one were to measure it by circumcision. It is as if he said: I who now establish the covenant with you will one day become man, and this covenant of mine, namely circumcision, which takes its beginning from you, will remain in force until me and then cease. For after the circumcision of Christ the Master, circumcision of the foreskin according to the law no longer had any place. Those who were circumcised after that were circumcised as transgressors. The circumcision ordained by God came to an end in Christ himself.

QUESTION 318. Why did Jesus rebuke [?] Peter when he was distressed at the thought of his death? Because, even though Peter seemed to have spoken those words out of burning affection and fiery love, they still brought pleasure to the devil. For Christ's not suffering would have been the greatest gain to Satan, since he would then not have been driven out of his tyranny over humankind. That is why the rebuke says, “Get behind me, Satan, for you are not thinking the things of God.” What does the [?] threatening against the father signify?
